Option A: Leydig cells, also known as interstitial cells of Leydig, are present in the interstitial connective between seminiferous tubules.

The testis contains numerous seminiferous tubules separated by connective tissue in between. Seminiferous tubules are lined by several spermatogonia cells, which produce spermatozoa, and Sertoli (sustentacular) cells, which have a supportive function. 

The connective tissue in between the tubules is made up of Leydig cells, collagen fibers, fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells, blood vessels, and lymphatics. Leydig cells are large, round, or polyhedral cells with eccentric nuclei. They are lightly stained and often have a foamy appearance. They secrete testosterone upon stimulation by luteinizing hormone from the anterior pituitary.

The image below shows seminiferous tubules and Leydig cells.

Option B: Islets of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part of the pancreas.

Islets are characterized by secretory cells supported by reticulin fibers and contain numerous fenestrated capillaries. There is a delicate capsule around each islet. The islet cells are paler than the surrounding exocrine cells, as they have less rough endoplasmic reticulum.

The islet of Langerhans is mainly composed of three types of cells:

  • α or A cells - located peripherally and secrete glucagon 
  • β or B cells - located centrally and produce insulin 
  • δ or D cells - scattered between beta cells and secrete somatostatin

The image given below shows the islets of Langerhans.

Option C: Hassall's corpuscles are small rounded structures present in the medulla of the thymus. Each corpuscle has a central core of degenerated epithelial cells and macrophages surrounded by concentrically arranged epithelial cells. The degenerated cells ultimately give pink staining hyaline mass. The function of the corpuscles of Hassall is still not known.

text: Injury at which of the following marked sites causes failure of dorsiflexion?
expl:
Correct answer: A. 3

The site marked as '3' in the x-ray given above is the neck of the fibula. Injury at this site causes failure of dorsiflexion (foot drop) due to injury to the common fibular nerve (also know as common peroneal nerve)

The common fibular nerve is derived from the dorsal branches of the 4th and 5th lumbar and 1st and 2nd sacral ventral rami. It runs obliquely along the lateral side of the popliteal fossa to the fibular head. It lies between the biceps femoris and the lateral head of the gastrocnemius. It then curves laterally around the neck of the fibula and gets divided into superficial and deep fibular nerves.

  Superficial fibular nerve Deep fibular nerve
Motor innervation
  • Peroneus longus
  • Peroneus brevis
  • Extensor digitorum longus
  • Extensor hallucis longus
  • Tibialis anterior
  • Peroneus tertius
Sensory innervation
  • Lateral aspect of the lower leg
  • Dorsum of the toes except for the lateral side of the 5th toe and the first interdigital web-space

 
  • The first interdigital space
 

 

Injury to the common peroneal nerve (common fibular nerve) at the level of the neck of the fibula causes foot drop. Ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension, and eversion of the foot are lost, while the inversion and plantar flexion are usually preserved. Sensory innervation to the dorsum of the foot, including the first web space, is lost. The ankle reflex is usually preserved.

text: A defect in which of the following aortic arches causes the defect shown in the image?
expl:
Correct answer: D. 6th left

The image above shows a patent ductus arteriosus due to a defect in the left side of the 6th aortic arch.

Usually, in term infants, the ductus arteriosus closes within 72 hours of birth. Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close results in patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).

PDA usually presents with a hyperdynamic precordium, bounding peripheral pulses, wide pulse pressure, a machine-like continuous or systolic murmur, cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary vascular markings, hepatomegaly, increasing oxygen dependence, carbon dioxide retention, and renal failure.

In a majority of cases, PDA closes spontaneously. If spontaneous closure fails to occur, COX inhibitors like indomethacin or ibuprofen can be used. Surgical ligation is indicated in case of contraindications to medical management or failure of the same.

Other options

Option A: The 4th right aortic arch gives rise to the proximal part of the right subclavian artery. 

Option B: The 4th left aortic arch gives rise to the arch of the aorta. Defects involving the 4th left aortic arch could cause a variety of aortic arch anomalies, such as interruption of the aortic arch, but not PDA.

Option C: The 6th right aortic arch forms the proximal part of the right pulmonary artery.

subject: Anatomy
text: A patient presents with swelling under the left ear lobule and complains of pain. Which of the following structures is the likely cause of the pain?

options.D: Investing layer of deep ce​rvical fascia

expl:
Correct answer: B. Greater auricular nerve

The cause of the pain in this patient complaining of pain in the parotid region is likely to be the greater auricular nerve.

The greater auricular nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin overlying the parotid gland and the ear lobule. Pain associated with swelling and inflammation in the parotid region could be transmitted through the greater auricular nerve. The parotid gland is covered by a parotid capsule that is derived from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia. Any acute inflammation of the gland such as acute sialadenitis results in pain in the pre­auricular region. The pain is mainly due to stretching of the capsule resulting in stimulation of the greater auricular nerve.

Other options:

Option A: The facial nerve is not the primary cause of pain in the parotid region due to swelling. The Hitzelberger sign(numbness in the posterosuperior meatal wall of the external auditory canal), associated with facial nerve involvement, is seen in acoustic neuroma and is not the cause of pain in this scenario. 

Option D: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia is not the correct answer because the investing layer of deep cervical fascia itself does not transmit pain sensation. The investing layer of deep cervical fascia is a layer of connective tissue that envelops the neck and extends to cover the parotid gland, forming the parotid capsule. While inflammation or swelling in the parotid gland can stretch the capsule and cause pain, the actual transmission of pain sensation is mediated by sensory nerves, such as the greater auricular nerve, which innervates the skin over the parotid gland and the ear lobule.

The greater auricular nerve (Option B) is a more appropriate answer in this context, as it is responsible for carrying the pain sensation from the area of swelling and inflammation in the parotid region.

Option C: The auriculotemporal nerve can cause referred pain due to caries tooth, ulcerative lesions of the oral cavity, temporomandibular joint disorders, and sphenopalatine neuralgia. However, it is not the primary cause of pain in the parotid region due to swelling.

text:
Which of the following muscles are supplied by Superior Gluteal Nerve?

  1. Gluteus Medius
  2. Gluteus Minimus
  3. Tensor fascia lata
  4. Piriformis
expl:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3

Gluteus Medius, Gluteus Minimus, and Tensor fascia lata are supplied by Superior Gluteal Nerve. Piriformis is supplied by the nerve to the piriformis. 

The dorsal branches of the L4, L5, and S1 rami give rise to the superior gluteal nerve. It is accompanied by superior gluteal vessels. This nerve leaves the pelvis via the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis and divides into superior and inferior branches. It supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae.

The dorsal divisions of the S1 and S2 rami give rise to the nerve to the piriformis. 

Gluteus medius and gluteus minimus act as the abductors of the hip joint. Stabilizing the pelvis on the femur during walking is done by these muscles. It is demonstrated by asking the subject to stand on one limb. If the ipsilateral abductors are normal, the pelvis remains in a horizontal position. If the ipsilateral abductors are weak, then the pelvis tilts towards the opposite (unsupported) side. This is called positive Trendelenburg’s sign.

text: A 25-year-old male presented with symptoms of inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joint of the 4th and 5th digits. He was also not able to hold a piece of paper between his fingers. What is the likely site of injury?
expl:
Correct answer: C. C

The given clinical situation with a positive card test and an inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joint of the 4th and 5th digits, suggests an ulnar nerve injury. The most likely site of injury would thus be medial epicondyle: site C

Injury at the medial epicondyle damages the ulnar nerve, leading to paralysis of flexor carpi ulnaris (loss of ulnar deviation) and medial half of flexor digitorum profundus (loss of distal interphalangeal joint flexion). It leads to hypothenar paralysis (lead to atrophy) and sensory loss. Also, flexor digitorum superficialis (supplied by median nerve) and extensor digitorum (supplied by the radial nerve) are still functional. Hence complete paralysis of the 3rd and 4th digits is not seen.  The positive card test is due to the weakness of palmar interossei leading to loss of adduction.

Ulnar nerve branches and supply: 

Superficial branch supplies palmaris brevis, skin on the palmar surface of medial 1½ fingers. The deep branch runs within the concavity of deep palmar arch and supplies all intrinsic muscles of the hand (except first 2 lumbricals and thenar muscles).

subject: Anatomy
text:
Which of the following muscles form the pelvic diaphragm?

A. Iliococcygeus
B. Pubococcygeus
C. Obturator internus
D. Deep transverse perinei
expl:
Correct answer: A. A, B

Iliococcygeus and pubococcygeus are parts of the pelvic diaphragm, which is also known as the levator ani.

The levator ani muscle is a complex unit that consists of 3 muscle components:

  • Pubococcygeus
    • Pubovaginalis - elevates the urethra and hence contributes to urinary continence
    • Puboperinealis - draws the perineal body towards the pubic symphysis
    • Puboanalis - elevates the anus and keeps the urogenital hiatus narrowed
  • Puborectalis
  • Iliococcygeus

Levator ani muscles are the most important muscles in the pelvic floor and maintain a constant state of contraction. They provide a stable floor and support the weight of the abdominopelvic contents against intra-abdominal forces. Weakening of levator ani and pelvic fascia from stretching or tearing during childbirth, may decrease support for the vagina, bladder, uterus, or rectum or alter the position of the neck of the bladder and urethra.

Other options: 

The obturator internus forms the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa and is not a part of the levator ani.

The deep transverse perineal muscle is the content of the deep perineal space and contributes to the formation of the perineal body.

subject: Anatomy
text: Given below is the image of a 33-hour chick embryo. Which of the following is derived from the marked structure?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Ribs

The structure marked in the given image is the para-axial mesoderm. The ribs are derived from the para-axial mesoderm.

During the third week of embryological development, the process of gastrulation occurs, which refers to the formation of the three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. This is followed by the formation of the notochord, which is the axial structure, which induces the formation of the neural tube above it. During the formation of the neural tube, some cells at the lateral border dissociate and form the neural crest cells, which is sometimes referred to as the fourth germ layer.

After the formation of the notochord, which is the axial structure, the mesoderm on either side can be seen to be organized into three layers as follows:

1. Para-axial mesoderm - Thickened plate of the mesoderm close to the midline, on either side of the notochord. This forms the somitomeres and somites, which have the following derivatives: 

  • Dermatome: Forms the segmental dermis of the skin
  • Myotome: Forms the skeletal muscle
  • Sclerotome: Forms the vertebral column and ribs

2. Intermediate mesoderm - Longitudinal strip of mesoderm that connects the para-axial with the lateral plate mesoderm. The urinary (Option A) and genital systems are derived from the intermediate mesoderm.

3. Lateral plate mesoderm - A thinner layer of mesoderm that lies laterally. This layer develops a large cavity called the intraembryonic coelom that gives rise to pericardial, pleural (Option C), and peritoneal cavities.

The neural crest cells also contribute to the formation of structures as follows:

In the trunk region, they form melanocytes, sensory ganglia (Option B), sympathetic and enteric neurons, Schwann cells, and adrenal medulla cells.
In the cranial region, they contribute to the craniofacial skeleton, neurons for cranial ganglia, satellite glial cells, and melanocytes.

subject: Anatomy
text: Which of the following is false regarding the anatomy of the adrenal glands?

options.A: The right adrenal gland is‌ semi lunar in shape
options.B: The left adrenal gland is ‌closely related with tail​ of pancreas and spleen
options.C: The adrenals are yellow on‌ gross appearance
options.D: The adrenals are retroperi‌toneal in location

expl:
Correct answer: A. The right adrenal gland is semi lunar in shape

Option A is false as the right adrenal gland is pyramidal in shape while the left adrenal gland is semi-lunar/crescent shaped.

The adrenal glands, also called the supra-renal glands, are endocrine glands which are located at the upper pole of each kidney. They are grossly yellow in appearance and are retroperitoneal in location. Both glands are surrounded by areolar tissue and perirenal fascia. Shape Pyramidal or triangular Semi-lunar or crescenteric
Parts  Apex and base Upper end and lower end

The surface of the cerebrum consists of folds called gyri separated by fissures called sulci. text: Identify the structure marked as A.

Correct answer: B. Terminal bronchiole

The arrow-marked structure in the given image is the terminal bronchiole. It can be identified by the absence of cartilage, which would be present in the bronchus, and the presence of cilia and stratified columnar epithelium, which would not be seen in respiratory bronchioles and alveolar sac.

The following is a summary of the intrapulmonary passages:

Trachea → Main Bronchi → Lobar Bronchi → Segmental Bronchi → Terminal Bronchiole → Respiratory Bronchiole → Alveolar Duct → Alveolar Sac → Alveoli

Bronchi and bronchioles can be distinguished by the presence of cartilage and glands in the bronchi which are not present in the bronchioles.

Terminal bronchioles represent the most distal parts of the conducting passage. Each terminal bronchiole ends by dividing into respiratory bronchioles. Terminal bronchioles contain cilia and stratified columnar epithelium, whereas respiratory bronchioles contain few or no cilia, and simple cuboidal epithelium. Another differentiating point between the two is that terminal bronchioles would not communicate with the alveoli but respiratory bronchioles would have a communication with the alveoli.

Each respiratory bronchiole ends by dividing into a few alveolar ducts. Each alveolar duct ends in a passage, the atrium, which leads into a number of rounded alveolar sacs. Each alveolar sac is studded with a number of air sacs or alveoli. 

A: Terminal Bronchiole, B: Respiratory Bronchiole, C: Alveolar Sac, D: Alveolar Duct

text: A patient's right hip drops when he takes the right foot off the ground. Which of the following would not be involved in the patient?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Sciatic nerve

A patient with dropping of the right hip on lifting the right foot off the ground, has a positive Trendelenburg’s sign. The sciatic nerve would not be involved.

A positive Trendelenburg's sign is seen in the paralysis of the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus muscles, both of which are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve. In the scenario mentioned, since the patient has dropping of the hip on the right side, the structures on the left side would be affected.

Mechanism of actions of gluteus medius and minimus: 

  • When the leg on one side is lifted off the ground,  making it the unsupported side,  gluteus medius and minimus muscles on the opposite side, which is the supported side, exert traction on the hip bone by acting from the femur. This action results in slight raising of the pelvis on the unsupported side, which helps maintain the trunk in the upright position.
  • When the gluteus medius and minimus are paralyzed, the pelvis on the unsupported side sinks when the patient lifts the foot off the ground. This causes the patients to have a characteristic lurching gait.

subject: Anatomy
text: Which of the following statements is incorrect about the anomaly shown below?

options.A: It occurs due to the persi‌stance of prechordal plat​e
options.B: It occurs due to the defec‌tive migration of primord​ial cells to the genital ‌ridge
options.C: It contains skin, cartilag‌e and bone
options.D: It is a benign tumor of co‌ccyx

expl:
Correct answer: A. It occurs due to the persistance of prechordal plate

The image shows a sacrococcygeal teratoma, which occurs due to the persistence of pluripotent cells of the primitive streak in the sacrococcygeal region.

During the third week of embryological development, the process of gastrulation occurs, which refers to the formation of the three germ layers. These germ layers are formed from the primordial germ cells of the epiblast, which are pluripotent. The process begins with the formation of the primitive streak on the epiblast, which develops into the primitive node in the cranial region, and a primitive pit. The cells from the epiblast, migrate towards the primitive streak and invaginate into the primitive pit and organizes itself into cells arranged in three layers, which eventually develop into ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. The prechordal plate simply refers to the cells that have invaginated in the cranial region.

Sacrococcygeal teratomas occur due to remnants of pluripotent cells from the primitive streak due to defective migration of the cells (Option B). As these cells are from the epiblast, teratomas contain tissues from all germ layers which may include skin, hair, cartilage and bone (Option C). These tumors are benign in nature (Option D), but may rarely become malignant. If they occur in the cranial end of the primitive streak, they form oro-pharyngeal teratomas (as shown below), whereas if they occur in the caudal end of the primitive streak in the coccygeal region, they are called sacro-coccygeal teratomas.

text: What is the role of the marked structure in the given image?

Correct answer: A. Motor function

The marked structure is the subthalamic nucleus, which is a part of the basal ganglia and is concerned with motor function.

The basal ganglia refers to the mass of grey matter located within the cerebral white matter and is responsible for a number of coordinated functions including the control of extra-pyramidal pathways for motor coordination. There are two major pathways involved which are, the direct and indirect pathways.

The direct pathway stimulates the cortex to produce movement, whereas the indirect pathway inhibits it. The striatal activity in the direct pathway is mediated by D1 dopamine receptors and in the indirect pathway by D2 dopamine receptors. The subthalamic nucleus is a part of the indirect pathway. A lesion at subthalamic nuclei leads to loss of inhibitory effect of the indirect pathway resulting in dopaminergic overactivity responsible for features of hemiballismus.

subject: Anatomy
text: On neurologic examination, a patient is not able to identify an object but is able to recognize the object from its texture, colour and pattern. Which of the following is likely to have been affected?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Inferior temporal lobe

The clinical scenario suggests that the patient has visual agnosia and the likely site of involvement would be the inferior temporal lobe.

  • Agnosia refers to the inability to visually identify objects and is also called optic aphasia. According to De Jong, visual agnosia is further classified into:
    • Apperceptive visual agnosia - the visual image appears distorted to the patient and hence they are unable to recognise it. This occurs due lesions in the parieto-occipital region
    • Associative visual agnosia - inability to visually identify objects in the absence of visual impairment, with ability to identify the object using other sensory modalities (as suggested in the scenario). This occurs due to lesions of occipito-temporal junction, which is present in the inferior temporal lobe. Prosopagnosia is a type of associatetive visual agnosia which refers to the inability to visually identify faces. 

The occipital lobe acts as the primary visual area and a lesion in this region would result in cortical blindness and achromatopsia, which is the inability to visualise colour. In the given scenario, as the patient is also able to identify colour, it indicates that the occipital lobe (Option A) is unaffected and (hence inferior temporal lobe is the better answer). 

Stereognosis is the ability to identify an object by a perception of the form and nature of an object without looking at it. In the given scenario, the patient is able to recognize the object from its texture and pattern which indicates that stereognosis is intact. Loss of this ability is known as astereognosis which occurs in lesions of the superior parietal lobule (Options B and C) and dorsal column pathways.

subject: Anatomy
text: Apocrine glands are present in which of the following?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Axilla

Apocrine glands are present in the axilla.

Exocrine glands can be classified into three subtypes, based on the manner in which their secretions are poured out of the cells:

  1. Apocrine 
  2. Merocrine
  3. Holocrine

In apocrine glands, the apical parts of the cells are shed off to discharge the secretion. Examples of apocrine glands are :

  • Secretion of milk fat by mammary glands
  • Atypical sweat glands in the axilla, perianal region, periumbilical skin, mons pubis.
  • Ceruminous glands of the external auditory meatus are modified apocrine glands

Apocrine glands are large glands found in the dermis or subcutaneous fat. They are a type of sweat gland. It consists of a basal secretory coil followed by a straight duct that opens into the pilary canal above the duct of the sebaceous gland. In hairless skin, it directly opens onto the skin surface. 

Apocrine activity is minimal before puberty, after which it is androgen-dependent and responsive to emotional stimuli. It is controlled by adrenergic nerves and is sensitive to adrenaline and noradrenaline. The secretion is initially sterile and odorless, but it undergoes bacterial decomposition to generate odorous and musky compounds. Obstruction of apocrine sweat ducts and associated upper hair follicles in the axillae, breast areolae, and pubic region, mainly in women, is thought to cause Fox–Fordyce disease. It is also implicated in the causation of a painful, occasionally debilitating condition called hidradenitis suppurativa.

The given image shows an illustration of apocrine secretion.

subject: Anatomy
text: The spinal sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve has 2nd order neurons to carry which sensation?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Pain

The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) is responsible for sensory input from the face, as well as motor functions such as chewing. Its sensory pathway involves three branches: the ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2), and mandibular (V3) divisions. The first-order neurons for each division originate from different sensory ganglia:

1.Ophthalmic Division (V1):
   First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion (also called the semilunar or Gasserian ganglion).

2. Maxillary Division (V2):
   First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion.

3. Mandibular Division (V3):
   First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion.

These first-order neurons carry sensory information from the face to the brainstem. Upon entering the brainstem, the fibers synapse with second-order neurons in specific nuclei:

1. Principal Sensory Nucleus (Main Sensory Nucleus):
    a.Receives input from all three divisions of the trigeminal nerve.
    b.Located in the pons.
    c.Second-order neurons here carry discriminative touch and proprioceptive information.

2. Spinal Trigeminal Nucleus (Spinal Nucleus of Trigeminal):
   a.Receives input mainly from the maxillary and mandibular divisions.
   b.Located in the medulla.
   c.Second-order neurons here carry pain and temperature sensations.

After synapsing in these nuclei, the sensory information is further relayed to higher brain centers for processing and perception.

text: Which of the following is not seen in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Tail of caudate nucleus

The tail of the caudate nucleus is not seen on the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. It is present on the roof of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle.

The inferior horn is the largest compartment of the lateral ventricle and extends up to 2.5 cm from the temporal pole. The relations are: 

Roof - Tapetum of corpus callosum laterally and tail of caudate nucleus medially.

Floor (lateral to medial) - Collateral eminence produced by collateral fissure, hippocampus.

The floor of the temporal horn consists of the hippocampus medially and the collateral eminence, formed by the infolding of the collateral sulcus, laterally. The inferior part of the choroidal fissure, located between the fimbria of the fornix and the inferolateral aspect of the thalamus, lies in the medial wall. 

The lateral ventricle is divided into the body and 3 horns. The locations of the parts are: 

  • Body - parietal lobe
  • Anterior horn - frontal lobe
  • Posterior horn - occipital lobe
  • Inferior horn - temporal lobe.

The anterior horn extends from the genu of the corpus callosum up to the interventricular foramen. The relations of the anterior horn are: 

  • Anteriorly - Genu and rostrum of the corpus callosum
  • Roof - Anterior part of the body of the corpus callosum
  • Floor and lateral wall - Caudate nucleus
  • Medial wall - Septum pellucidum and anterior column of fornix

The body or central part extends from the interventricular foramen to the splenium of the corpus callosum. The relations of the body are: 

  • Roof - Body of the corpus callosum
  • Medial wall - Septum pellucidum
  • Floor (from lateral to medial) - Caudate nucleus, stria terminalis, thalamostriate vein, thalamus, choroid plexus, and body of the fornix

The posterior horn extends from the splenium to the occipital pole. The relations are: 

  • Roof and lateral wall - Tapetum of corpus callosum
  • Medial wall - Forceps major and calcar avis (calcarine sulcus

Note: There is no lateral wall for the lateral ventricle.

subject: Anatomy
text: Which of the following marked areas in the histopathological specimen shows calcification?
expl:
Correct answer: C. 3

The given specimen is that of an epiphyseal cartilage, where zone 3 corresponds to the zone of calcification.

Epiphyseal cartilage is divided into five zones :

  • The resting zone consists of hyaline cartilage without morphological changes in the cells (option 1)
  • In the proliferative zone, chondrocytes divide rapidly and form columns of stacked cells parallel to the long axis of the bone (option 2)
  • The hypertrophic cartilage zone contains large chondrocytes whose cytoplasm has accumulated glycogen. The resorbed matrix is reduced to thin septa between the chondrocytes.
  • Simultaneous with the death of chondrocytes in the calcified cartilage zone, the thin septa of cartilage matrix become calcified by the deposit of hydroxyapatite.
  • In the ossification zone, endochondral bone tissue appears (option 4). Blood capillaries and osteoprogenitor cells formed by mitosis of cells originating from the periosteum invade the cavities left by the chondrocytes. The osteoprogenitor cells form osteoblasts, which are distributed in a discontinuous layer over the septa of the calcified cartilage matrix. Ultimately, the osteoblasts deposit bone matrix over the three-dimensional calcified cartilage matrix.

The epiphyseal cartilage is responsible for the growth in the length of bone and it disappears in adults, which is why bone growth ceases in adulthood.

subject: Anatomy
text: Which of the following statements is true concerning the anatomy of the breast?

options.A: Inner quadrants contain mo‍st breast tissue
options.B: Ligaments of cooper are fo‍und only in lower quadran​ts
options.C: Tail of Spence extends acr‍oss anterior axillary fol​d

expl:
Correct answer: C. Tail of Spence extends across anterior axillary fold

The tail of Spence extends across the anterior axillary fold and is a small extension of the upper lateral quadrant of the breast.

The breast lies in the superficial fascia of the pectoral region. It is divided into four quadrants, i.e. upper medial, upper lateral, lower medial and lower lateral. 

Vertically, it extends from the second to the sixth ribs. Horizontally, it extends from the lateral border of the sternum to the midaxillary line. A small extension of the upper lateral quadrant, called the axillary tail of Spence, passes through an opening in the deep fascia and lies in the axilla. The opening is called the foramen of Langer. 

The breast lies on the deep pectoral fascia covering the pectoralis major and serratus anterior superiorly, the external abdominal oblique and its aponeurosis inferiorly, and the clavipectoral fascia laterally. Fibrous strands or sheets consisting of condensations of connective tissue extend between the posterior lamina of the superficial fascia and the dermis. These suspensory ligaments (retinacula or Cooper’s ligaments) are often well-developed in the superior parts of the breast and support the breast tissue, helping to minimize drooping.

The breasts normally comprise up to 20 discrete lobes that contain ductal-glandular tissue consisting of branching ducts and terminal secretory lobules in a connective tissue stroma. Each lobe is derived by branching from one central lactiferous duct in the nipple. The terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU or lobule) is the functional milk secretory component of the breast. 

The upper outer quadrant of the breast contains a greater volume of tissue than the other quadrants. This is the reason for the majority of the carcinomas arising in the upper outer quadrant.

text: A professor underwent a left parotidectomy. Post surgery she complains of left lower lip paralysis. Which structure is involved?

Correct answer: B. Facial nerve- Cervical branch

Lower lip paralysis is caused by damage to the cervical branch of the facial nerve.

The cervical branch of the facial nerve is responsible for innervating the platysma muscle, which is one of the muscles involved in the movements of the lower lip. Damage to this nerve can potentially lead to paralysis of the lower lip.

The facial nerve is the motor nerve of the face. Its five terminal branches emerge from the parotid gland and diverge to supply the various facial muscles as follows : 

  • Temporal — frontalis, auricular muscles, orbicularis oculi
  • Zygomatic — orbicularis oculi (lower eyelid part)
  • Buccal — muscles of the cheek and upper lip
  • Marginal mandibular — muscles of the lower lip
  • Cervical — platysma

Correct answer: C. Aberrant right subclavian artery

The CT finding in the image is suggestive of an aberrant right subclavian artery.

An aberrant right subclavian artery occurs when the right fourth aortic arch and right dorsal aorta involute cranial to the seventh intersegmental artery.

This artery arises distal to the left subclavian artery and crosses the midline posterior to the esophagus. Because of the absence of a normal right subclavian-carotid junction to pull down the right recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) during embryologic development, the right RLN follows a straight path from the vagus to the larynx and is called a non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve.

Most patients with this anomaly are asymptomatic, and the aberrant subclavian artery is of no clinical consequence. Dysphagia caused by compression of the esophagus by an abnormal subclavian artery is called dysphagia lusoria.

text: The marked structure serves as a surface landmark for which anatomical structure?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Stem of the lateral sulcus

The marked structure indicates the pterion and it serves as a landmark for the stem of the lateral sulcus.

The frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones meet at the pterion. It is a landmark for the stem of the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure), the most prominent sulcus of the cerebral hemisphere. It separates the frontal lobe from the temporal lobe. Deep to the lateral sulcus lies the insular cortex.

Pterion marks as a surface landmark for the following structures:

  • Middle meningeal artery and vein: fractures in this area can rupture the middle meningeal artery, leading to an epidural hematoma.
  • Broca’s area: Located in the dominant hemisphere (usually left) in the inferior frontal gyrus, it lies in proximity to the pterion
  • The insular cortex and parts of the basal ganglia, such as the putamen, are located deep to the pterion, beneath the lateral sulcus.
  • Stem of the lateral sulcus, also called the Sylvian fissure. It houses the middle cerebral artery and its branches, playing a crucial role in brain vascularization and cortical organization.

During surgeries, the pterion is a common site for trephining (making a hole in the skull).

Other Options:

Option A: The pineal gland is located in the posterior aspect of the cranial fossa in the brain. It is located deep in the brain, near the midline.

Option B: Wenicke's area is in the superior temporal gyrus in the dominant cerebral hemisphere. It is found in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus.

Option D: The internal carotid artery siphon is a part of the internal carotid artery's course. Characterized by its S-shaped curvature as it traverses the cavernous sinus and enters the cranial cavity. This configuration helps dissipate pulsatile energy, reducing stress on cerebral vessels, and allows adaptability to cranial movements while maintaining cerebral perfusion.

text: A 60-year-old male recovering from facial nerve palsy complains of food getting stuck between the cheek and teeth while eating. What is the muscle affected in this case?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Buccinator

This patient, recovering from facial nerve palsy, getting food stuck between the cheek and teeth while eating, is because of the buccinator being affected.

The buccinator is a muscle of facial expression. It is innervated by the facial nerve. It is known as the whistling muscle.

The buccinator muscle is primarily responsible for keeping food between the teeth during mastication by pressing the cheek against the teeth (involved in flattening the cheeks against the gums and teeth).

In facial nerve palsy, paralysis of the buccinator muscle can lead to food accumulating in the cheek pouch, as the muscle is unable to contract properly.

Other options:

Option C : Zygomaticus Major: Responsible for pulling the corner of the mouth upward and outward, contributing to smiling. It does not influence food placement during mastication.

Option D : Orbicularis Oris: Encircles the mouth and helps in closing the lips. While it is involved in mastication and speech, its paralysis would not cause food to accumulate in the cheek.

text: Which of the following is not a derivative of neural crest cells?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Retinal pigment epithelium

Retinal pigment epithelium is not a derivative of neural crest cells.

Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is derived from the neuroectoderm. The RPE develops from the outer layer of the optic cup, a structure that arises from the neural tube (neuroectodermal origin), not from neural crest cells.

Neural crest cells are a group of cells that migrate during embryonic development and give rise to various structures, including parts of the nervous system, face, and heart.

Neural crest cells (NCC) are present adjacent to the neural tube and are sometimes referred to as the fourth germ layer. It contributes to the formation of many organs and tissues:

In the trunk region, they form: 

  • Melanocytes (Option D)
  • Sensory ganglia
  • Sympathetic and enteric neurons
  • Schwann cells 
  • Adrenal medulla cells

In the cranial region, they contribute to the: 

  • Craniofacial skeleton
  • Neurons for cranial ganglia-Ciliary ganglion  (Option C)
  • Ciliary muscles  (Option A)
  • Satellite glial cells
  • Melanocytes

Some of the other neural crest derivatives are:

  • C cells of the thyroid gland
  • Conotruncal septum in the heart
  • Odontoblasts
  • Smooth muscle cells to blood vessels to the face and forebrain.

subject: Anatomy
text: The cranial component of the neural crest cells leads to the formation of?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Conotruncal septum

The cranial component of neural crest cells (NCC) leads to the formation of Conotruncal septum.

The conotruncal septum is also known as the aortopulmonary septum. The formation of the aortopulmonary septum in the truncus arteriosus divides the outflow channel of the heart into the ventral aorta and the pulmonary trunk. Persistent truncus arteriosus results when the conotruncal ridges fail to form. 

The development of the heart begins in the third week of embryogenesis with the formation of the cardiogenic mesoderm. The heart tube forms through fusion of paired endocardial tubes, which then undergo looping and septation to establish the four chambers. By the end of the eighth week, the heart achieves its definitive structure, with separate atria, ventricles, and major vessels.

The heart develops from mesodermal origins, with different parts deriving from specific embryonic structures:

  • First Heart Field (Primary Heart Field): Forms the left ventricle and part of the atria.
  • Second Heart Field: Contributes to the right ventricle, outflow tract (conus arteriosus and truncus arteriosus), and part of the atria.
  • Neural Crest Cells: Contribute to the septation of the outflow tract and the formation of the aorticopulmonary septum.
  • Proepicardium (Epicardial Cells): Forms the epicardium and contributes to coronary vessels.
  • Sinus Venosus: Forms part of the right atrium (sinus venarum) and the coronary sinus.
  • Endocardial Cushions: Form the atrioventricular valves and contribute to septation.

Other options:

Option A: SA node is derived from the primary heart field - sinus venosus.

Option B: AV cushions are derived from adjacent endocardial cells. The endocardial cells along with the epicardium and mesenchyme, form the AV cushions.

Option D: Chordae tendineae are formed from mesenchymal tissue within the heart.

text: A 15-year-old boy underwent splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenic purpura. During the procedure, the surgeon noticed bleeding while separating the spleen from the stomach. Which vessels are most likely implicated in this bleeding?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Short gastric vessels

This patient, undergoing splenectomy, while separating the spleen from the stomach, is likely bleeding from the short gastric vessels.

In an open splenectomy, the gastrosplenic ligament is opened and short gastric vessels are ligated and divided.

The spleen is attached to the stomach through the gastrosplenic ligament. The gastrosplenic ligament attaches the greater curvature of stomach to the upper pole of the spleen.

Contents of the gastrosplenic ligament include:

  • Short gastric vessels
  • Left gastroepiploic vessels

Hence, while separating the spleen from the stomach, there are maximum chances of bleeding if there is injury to the short gastric vessels.

Other Options:

Option A: Left gastric vessels: Left gastric vessels run along the lesser curvature of the stomach. It is unlikely to be the source of bleeding in this case.

Option C: Right gastro-epiploic vessels: The right gastroepiploic vessels run along the pylorus and inferior region of the greater curvature of the stomach. It is not a part of the gastrosplenic ligament.

Option D: Splenic vessels: The splenic artery and vein run along the superior border of the pancreas. They are not directly involved in the separation of the spleen from the stomach.

text: Identify the marked structure
expl:
Correct answer: A. Primitive streak

The marked structure is the primitive streak.

The primitive streak appears in the early stages of gastrulation, a process that reorganizes the epiblast into three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. It appears as a linear thickening on the dorsal surface of the epiblast in the bilaminar embryonic disc. It is found in the caudal (tail-end) region of the developing embryo.

Functions of the primitive streak:

  • Serves as the site where cells migrate inward to form the mesoderm and endoderm.
  • Marks the beginning of gastrulation.
  • Defines the body axis (head-to-tail, left-to-right).

Other Options:

Option B: Notochord: A rod-like structure derived from mesoderm that forms after the primitive streak and is crucial for the development of the neural tube. Located cranially relative to the primitive streak.

Option C: Neural Groove: A depression in the ectoderm that forms during neurulation, leading to the development of the neural tube. It appears after the primitive streak.

Option D: Secondary Neural Plate: Part of the neural plate involved in the later stages of neural tube development. It is not directly related to the primitive streak.

subject: Anatomy
text: Which of the following is the first to be formed by the migration of the epiblast along the primitive streak?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Endoderm

Endoderm is the first to be formed by the migration of the epiblast along the primitive streak.

Gastrulation is when the single-layered blastula reorganizes into a multi-layered structure called the gastrula. This process establishes the three primary germ layers that give rise to all tissues and organs of the body. During gastrulation, epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak to form the three germ layers: endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm.

Cells from the epiblast migrate inward (invagination) through the primitive streak.

The first group of migrating epiblast cells replaces the hypoblast to form the definitive endoderm. The endoderm gives rise to structures like the gastrointestinal tract, liver, and lungs. 

Subsequent migrating cells spread between the epiblast and the newly formed endoderm to create the mesoderm, which forms structures like muscles, bones, and the cardiovascular system.

Remaining epiblast cells that do not migrate through the primitive streak form the ectoderm, which gives rise to the epidermis and the nervous system.

Other Options:

Option B: Cardiac Mesoderm: The mesoderm forms after the endoderm and differentiates later into subtypes, including the cardiac mesoderm.

Option C: Epidermis: The epidermis arises from the ectoderm, which forms after both the endoderm and mesoderm.

Option D: Neural Groove: The neural groove is part of the ectoderm and forms during neurulation, which occurs much later than the formation of the endoderm.

text: During walking, the hip bone on the side of the suspended leg is raised by the action of which muscle present in the supporting leg?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Gluteus Medius

Gluteus Medius of the supporting leg is responsible for raising the hip bone on the side of the suspended leg.

Actions of Gluteus Medius:

  •  Hip abduction
  •  Stabilizes the pelvis during gait.
  •  Assists the internal rotation of the thigh.

Gluteus medius and gluteus minimus act as the abductors of the hip joint. Stabilizing the pelvis on the femur during walking is done by these muscles. It is demonstrated by asking the subject to stand on one limb.

Trendelenburg Sign:
Trendelenburg sign is a clinical sign used to assess the function of the gluteus medius.
It is positive when the pelvis drops on the opposite side of the stance leg, indicating weakness or dysfunction of the gluteus medius on the supporting leg.
In a healthy individual, the gluteus medius contracts to prevent the pelvis from tilting when one leg is lifted. If the gluteus medius is weak or paralyzed, the pelvis tilts toward the side of the suspended leg.

Option B: Gluteus Maximus: Extends and externally rotates the hip; key for climbing stairs and rising from sitting. Weakness causes difficulty in hip extension, affecting activities like standing up or climbing.

Option C: Obturator Internus: Externally rotates and stabilizes the hip joint; abducts the thigh when the hip is flexed. Dysfunction can impair hip rotation, commonly affected in pelvic injuries.

Option D: Quadratus Femoris: Externally rotates and adducts the hip. Injury or entrapment of the nerve to quadratus femoris can cause deep hip pain and weakness in rotation.

subject: Anatomy
text: An absent gag reflex can result from injury to which of the following nerves?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Ⅸ and Ⅹ

An absent gag reflex can result from injury to the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) and the vagus nerve (X).

The afferent nerve for the gag reflex is the glossopharyngeal nerve, while the efferent nerve consists of both the glossopharyngeal (to the stylopharyngeus muscle) and vagus. Both these nerves pass through the jugular foramen and damage to them may be the cause for loss of gag reflex.

Pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and vagus nerve form the pharyngeal plexus of nerves. These plexes mainly supply the pharynx. It also has contributions from the superior cervical ganglion.

Nerve supply by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve are:

  • All the muscles of the soft palate(except tensor veli palatini - supplied by mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve)
  • All the muscles of the pharynx(except the stylopharyngeus - supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve).

The glossopharyngeal nerve is rarely damaged alone. Lesions will result in loss of sensation of the posterior third of the tongue, reduced gag reflex, loss of sensation over the ipsilateral soft palate, etc. Motor fibres to the stylopharyngeus and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland are also supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. Sensory supply includes uvula, posterior one-third of the tongue, tympanic cavity etc.

The main functions of IX and X can be tested together by assessing swallowing, phonation/articulation and sensation from the pharynx/larynx. 

Glossopharyngeal and vagus nerve examinations include:

  • Observing the position and symmetry of the palate and uvula at rest and with phonation (“aah”).
  • By assessing the strength of the cough

subject: Anatomy
text: If a tumor compresses the structures passing through the opening marked in the given image, which of the following sensations would be affected?

options.C: Sensation in the anterior ​scalp and dorsum of the n​ose

expl:
Correct answer: C. Sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose

The marked foramen is the superior orbital fissure. If a tumour compresses the structures passing through this foramen, it would impair sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose, as this would affect the frontal nerve and nasociliary nerve.

The superior orbital fissure is an important anatomical opening in the skull that allows several critical structures to pass through. Among these structures, the frontal nerve and nasociliary nerve are branches of the ophthalmic nerve, the first division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1), which is responsible for sensory innervation to parts of the face.

The frontal nerve provides sensation to the forehead, the anterior scalp, and the dorsum of the nose, while the nasociliary nerve supplies sensation to parts of the nasal cavity. Therefore, if a tumour or lesion compresses the structures passing through the superior orbital fissure, it would likely affect the sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose because these areas are innervated by the branches of the trigeminal nerve that pass through this fissure.

Other options: 

Option A: Sensation of the nasopharynx is innervated by other branches of the trigeminal and glossopharyngeal nerve, not by structures passing through the superior orbital fissure.

Option B: While some sensation from the nasal cavity comes from the trigeminal nerve, the specific branches affected by a lesion in the superior orbital fissure are more focused on the anterior areas of the face.

Option D: Sensation of the chin is primarily innervated by the mandibular branch (CN V3) of the trigeminal nerve, which passes through the foramen ovale, not the superior orbital fissure.

text: A chronic tobacco consumer went to the dental clinic with bleeding lesions on his tongue and was diagnosed with carcinoma of the tongue. Which of the following papillae, which do not have taste buds, is least likely to be involved in such a cancer?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Filiform

Among the different types of papillae on the tongue, the one that does not have taste buds is the filiform papillae.

Filiform papillae are minute cylindrical or conical projections that are mainly present on the dorsal part of the anterior 2/3rd of the tongue. The filiform papillae do not contain taste buds. They are covered by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

Other papillae of the tongue are: 

Circumvallate papillae are 8-12 in number which are large cylindrical structures. They form a V-shaped row just in front of the sulcus terminalis. Usually, the entire papillae are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Taste buds are present in the lateral wall of these papillae which surrounds the papillae circumferentially.

Fungiform papillae are large, rounded, and red and are mainly present on the lingual margins and also on the dorsal surface of the tongue. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. They are supplied by the facial nerve.

Foliate papillae are red, leaf-like mucosal ridges that are present bilaterally in two zones at the sides of the tongue near the sulcus terminalis. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

subject: Anatomy
text: Which artery is used for arteriovenous shunting with the great saphenous vein for hemodialysis, and is located behind the medial malleolus and 2.5 cm in front of the tendocalcaneus?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Posterior tibial artery

The posterior tibial artery, located behind the medial malleolus and 2.5 cm in front of the tendocalcaneus, that is used for arteriovenous (AV) shunting with the great saphenous vein for hemodialysis.

The posterior tibial artery is situated behind the medial malleolus and approximately 2.5 cm in front of the tendocalcaneus, making it a suitable site for creating an AV fistula with the great saphenous vein. This location allows for optimal access and ensures that the shunt can handle the necessary blood flow for effective dialysis with the great saphenous vein. However, they are not commonly used for AV shunting in common practices.

Arteries used for AV shunting include the radial artery and the brachial artery in the upper arm, which are frequently employed for hemodialysis access. In the lower leg, the anterior tibial artery and the peroneal (fibular) artery are less commonly used for this procedure. 

Other options:

Option A: In comparison, the anterior tibial artery is located on the anterior aspect of the leg and runs down the front of the tibia, not behind the medial malleolus.

Option C: The peroneal (fibular) artery is situated on the lateral side of the leg, travelling alongside the fibula, and is also not located behind the medial malleolus. 

Option D: The fibular circumflex artery is a small artery and is not commonly used for hemodialysis access. It is not a standard choice and does not fit the anatomical location described, as it is a branch of the anterior tibial artery.

subject: Anatomy
text: What is the outer covering of the condition shown in the image?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Amnion

The diagnosis based on the given image is omphalocele and is covered by the amnion.

Omphalocele is a midline abdominal wall defect where the bowel and other solid viscera protrude through the umbilicus. In this condition, the herniated organs are covered by both peritoneum and an amnion. The umbilical cord inserts directly into this sac, which helps in identifying the condition. The defect occurs due to the failure of the physiological hernia to return to the body cavity by the 11th week of gestation.

The size of an omphalocele can vary significantly. It may be relatively small, containing only the gut, or it can be classified as a giant omphalocele if it measures 4 cm or more in diameter, encompassing the gut, liver, and other abdominal organs. The condition is often associated with other congenital anomalies such as trisomies 13, 15, 18, or 21, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, exstrophy of the bladder or cloaca, and pentalogy of Cantrell.

Treatment for omphalocele involves covering the exposed organs to prevent fluid loss and protect them from infection. Prophylactic antibiotics may be administered in case of rupture. Surgical correction is usually performed once the baby is stable. In omphalocele, since the umbilicus is covered by a reflection of the amnion, this membrane also covers the omphalocele itself, differentiating it from other types of abdominal wall defects.

Note : Gastroschisis is a condition where the intestinal loops herniate through the defect in the abdominal wall. The defect usually lies on one side of the umbilicus (right side commonly). The loops of the bowel are not covered by amnion. It is associated with elevated alpha-fetoprotein levels.

It also shows the axillary artery traversing inferior to the median pectoral nerve and the thoracoacromial artery. The medial pectoral nerve and the thoracoacromial artery both contribute to the neurovascular supply of the pectoral muscles.

After originating from the medial cord, the medial pectoral nerve passes anterior to the axillary artery. This nerve is specifically known for its anatomical path of piercing the pectoralis minor muscle before branching out to supply both the pectoralis minor and the pectoralis major muscles.

subject: Anatomy
text: A patient presents with sciatica and tenderness in the hamstring muscles. Which nerve supplies the hybrid muscle that is likely to be spared in this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Obturator nerve

The adductor magnus is the hybrid muscle that is likely to be spared in this condition.

In sciatica, the sciatic nerve is typically affected, which branches into the tibial nerve and the common peroneal nerve. The adductor magnus muscle is an example of a hybrid muscle with dual innervation:

  • The adductor part of the adductor magnus is innervated by the obturator nerve.
  • The hamstring part of the adductor magnus is innervated by the tibial nerve.

During sciatica, the tibial nerve is often affected, which would impact the hamstring part of the adductor magnus. However, because the adductor part of the adductor magnus is innervated by the obturator nerve, it remains functional and is likely to be spared.

The obturator nerve arises from the anterior division of the ventral rami of L2-L4. Near the obturator foramen, it divides into anterior and posterior branches.

  • Anterior division supplies pectineus, adductor longus, adductor brevis, and gracilis
  • Posterior division supplies adductor magnus, obturator externus. It also supplies adductor brevis if the muscle is not supplied by the anterior division

The image given below shows the course of the obturator nerve.


Other options:

Option A: The common peroneal nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve and can also be affected in sciatica. It is responsible for innervating muscles in the anterior and lateral compartments of the leg.

Option B: The tibial nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve and is often affected in sciatica. It supplies the hamstring part of the adductor magnus, which would be impacted during sciatica.

Option C: The femoral nerve is not involved in sciatica. It supplies the quadriceps and other muscles in the anterior compartment of the thigh, and does not innervate the adductor magnus.

subject: Anatomy
text: An elderly woman reports difficulty in buttoning her shirt and increased clumsiness during daily activities. On examination, she is unable to make an 'O' shape by opposing her thumb and index finger. Which of the following muscles is most likely involved?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Abductor pollicis brevis

The difficulty in buttoning the shirt and the inability to make the "O" shape with fingers suggest the involvement of the abductor pollicis brevis muscle.

This is a case of anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) syndrome. The AIN is a purely motor branch of the median nerve that affects specific muscles in the forearm, the flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus leading to difficulty in performing tasks requiring fine motor control, such as the "OK" sign. Among the options provided, the abductor pollicis brevis is uniquely and consistently innervated by the recurrent motor branch of the median nerve, making it susceptible to dysfunction in conditions affecting the median nerve.

Other options:

Option A: The opponens pollicis is innervated primarily by the lateral terminal branch of the median nerve, with some contributions from a branch of the deep terminal branch of the ulnar nerve. While it plays a role in thumb opposition, it is not consistently affected in anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) syndrome, which primarily impacts deeper flexor muscles like the flexor pollicis longus. Therefore, it is less likely to be the cause of the patient’s inability to perform the "OK" sign.

Option B: The palmar interossei muscles are innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. Because they do not receive any innervation from the median nerve, they are not implicated in AIN syndrome. Their primary function involves the adduction of the fingers.

Option C: The flexor pollicis brevis has dual innervation: the superficial head is supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve, while the deep head is innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. This dual supply makes it less likely to be solely affected in AIN syndrome.

subject: Physiology
text: Given below is the demonstration of tetanization in the gastrocnemius muscle of a frog. Identify the tetanising frequency.
expl:
Correct answer: B. 30-35 Hz

Tetanizing frequency demonstrated by the muscle is 33Hz. In the above graph, we know,

  • The speed of the paper is 1000mm/sec.
  • The y-axis represents millivolts, the x-axis represents time.
  • The scale on the x-axis is 10mm.
  • The area under the graph represents the muscle contraction.

Contraction period (latent period to maximum force of contraction) includes 3 scales = 30 mm. 

As paper speed is 1000mm/sec,

Contraction period = 30mm = (30/1000) = 30 msec. 

Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period = 1000/30 = 33Hz.

Tetanization

The features of muscle contraction can be demonstrated by eliciting single muscle twitches. The adding together of individual twitch contractions to increase the intensity of overall muscle contraction is Summation. Summation occurs in two ways:

  • by increasing the number of motor units contracting simultaneously, which is multiple ﬁber summations.
  • by increasing the frequency of contraction, which is called frequency summation and can lead to tetanization.

When the frequency of a contraction reaches a critical level, the successive contractions eventually fuse together, and the whole muscle contraction appears to be completely smooth and continuous, this is called tetanization. 

Tetanization occurs in two ways:

  • Complete tetanus occurs when no relaxation occurs between stimuli.
  • Incomplete tetanus when periods of incomplete relaxation take place between the summated stimuli.

text: The oxygen carrying capacity of a 18 year old boy with haemoglobin of 14g/dl is
expl:
Correct answer: D. 18

The oxygen carrying capacity of a boy with haemoglobin 14g/dl is 18.

When blood is saturated with 100% O2, the haemoglobin is also 100% saturated and each gram of normal haemoglobin contains 1.39 mL of O2.

However, blood normally contains some inactive haemoglobin derivatives, and the measured value in vivo is thus slightly lower hence, each gram of haemoglobin in vivo contains 1.31 mL of O2 (Hufner’s constant).

According to the above question, when Hb=14g/dl, O2= 1.31*14= 18.34 

The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve

  • Demonstrates a progressive increase in the percentage of haemoglobin bound with oxygen as blood Po2 increases, which is called the percent saturation of haemoglobin.
  • Blood leaving the lungs and entering the systemic arteries usually has a Po2 of about 95 mm Hg, the usual oxygen saturation of systemic arterial blood averages 97 per cent.
  • Conversely, in normal venous blood returning from the peripheral tissues, the Po2 is about 40 mm Hg, and the saturation of haemoglobin averages 75 per cent.

text: A 30-year-old patient with respiratory volume of 500 mL. The intraplueral pressure measured -4 before inspiration and -8 at the end of inspiration. The pulmonary compliance of the patient is
expl:
Correct answer: A. 125 ml/cm H2O

Pulmonary compliance of this patient is 125 mL/cm of H2O.

Compliance is developed due to the tendency for tissue to resume its original position after an applied force has been removed.

After an expiration during quiet breathing, the lungs have a tendency to collapse and the chest wall has a tendency to expand. The interaction between the recoil of the lungs and recoil of the chest can be measured through a spirometer and a curve of airway pressure plotted against volume is the pressure-volume curve of the total respiratory system (Ptr).

Compliance of the lung and chest wall is measured as the slope of the Ptr curve, or, as a change in lung volume per unit change in airway pressure (ΔV/ΔP).

Compliance = Change in lung volume / Change in pressure

Compliance = 500/4

Compliance = 125 ml/cm H20

text: Reflex responsible for tachycardia during right atrial distension is:
expl:
Correct answer: B. Bainbridge reflex

Reflex responsible for tachycardia during right atrial distension is Bainbridge Reflex.

The stretch receptors of the atria that elicit the Bainbridge reflex transmit their afferent signals through the vagus nerves to the medulla of the brain. Then efferent signals are transmitted back through vagal and sympathetic nerves to increase heart rate and strength of heart contraction. Thus, this reflex helps prevent damming of blood in the veins, atria, and pulmonary circulation.

Other options:

Option A: Bezold–Jarisch Reflex: Activation of chemosensitive vagal C fibers in the cardiopulmonary region causes profound brady­cardia, hypotension and a brief period of apnoea followed by rapid shallow breathing.

Option C: Cushing Reflex: When intracranial pressure is increased, the blood supply to Rostral Ventro-Lateral Medulla (RVLM) neurons is compromised. The local hypoxia and hypercapnia cause an increase in discharge from the neurons, producing hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration.

Option D: J Reflex: The stimulation of the J-receptors (C receptors/juxta-pulmonary capillary receptors) causes apnea followed by rapid breathing, bradycardia, and hypotension.

There is a control system in our body when no stimulus is required but still the system anticipates and makes corrective changes.

text: Cellular junctions present in a cardiac muscle are all except:
expl:
Correct answer: A. Zonula occludens

Zonula occludens is the other name for the tight junction. It is absent in a cardiac muscle.

Cardiac muscle cells are connected by Fascia adherens (a structural analog of zonula adherens), Gap junctions and Macula adherens.                                                                       

Cardiac muscle fibers are made up of many individual cells connected in series and parallel to one another. The areas where the end of one muscle fiber abuts on another are called intercalated disks. At each intercalated disc, the plasma membrane fuses with one another forming gap junction which provides low resistance bridges for the spread of excitation from one fiber to another permitting the cardiac muscle to function as a syncytium.

text: Efferent arteriolar constriction causes all except:

options.C: Decreases oncotic pressure‌ in glomerular capillarie‍s
options.D: Increases hydrostatic pres‌sure in glomerular capill‍aries

expl:
Correct answer: C. Decreases oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries

Efferent arteriolar constriction increases oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries.

Efferent arteriolar constriction has a biphasic response on GFR depending on the severity of resistance.

Moderate efferent arteriolar constriction causes increased glomerular hydrostatic pressure and slightly increased GFR. 

However, in cases of severe efferent arteriolar constriction (more than threefold increase in efferent arteriolar resistance), the renal blood flow is significantly reduced. This results in increased plasma protein concentration, thereby increasing the glomerular colloid oncotic pressure. As the increase in colloid oncotic pressure exceeds the increase in hydrostatic pressure, the net force for filtration decreases, resulting in decreased GFR.

text: Absolute refractory period is due to:

options.C: Closure of active gates of‌ sodium channel
options.D: Closure of inactive gates ‌of sodium channel

expl:
Correct answer: D. Closure of inactive gates of sodium channel

Absolute refractory period is due to closure of inactive gates of sodium channel.

Voltage-gated sodium channels have 3 states that you can find them in. They can either be closed, open, or inactive.

When the stimulus causes activation of the open gates, sodium rushes into the cell causing the membrane potential to become more positive. After 0.5 to 1 millisecond, the inactive gate automatically closes and no stimulus, no matter how strong, can excite the nerve. This is called the absolute refractory period.

text: Slow waves are generated by:
expl:
Correct answer: C. Interstitial cells of Cajal

The interstitial cells of Cajal undergo cyclic changes in membrane potential due to unique ion channels that peri­odically open and produce inward (pacemaker) currents that generate slow-wave activity.

Interstitial cells of Cajal are the pacemaker cells of the GIT that initiate the basic electrical rhythm (BER). These are stellate mesenchymal pacemaker cells with smooth muscle-like features.

In the stomach and the small intestine, these cells are located in the circular smooth muscle layer near the myenteric plexus. In the colon, they are at the submucosal border of the circular muscle layer.

The slow waves usually do not by themselves cause muscle contraction in most parts of the gastrointestinal tract, except perhaps in the stomach. Instead, they mainly excite the appearance of intermittent spike potentials, and the spike potentials in turn actually excite the muscle contraction.

Note: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal.

text: A patient has a ​blood glucose level of 200 mg/dL and GFR of 90 ml/min. What is the amount of glucose excreted if the transport maximum of the patient is as shown below?
expl:
Correct answer: D. 30 mg/min

The amount of glucose excreted in the above scenario is 30 mg/min.

Calculation:

Step 1: Calculate total filtered glucose:

In this question,

  • GFR = 90 ml/min
  • Plasma glucose concentration = 200 mg/dL= 2 mg/ml (1 dL=100 ml).
  • Total filtered glucose = GFR X Plasma glucose concentration.

                               = 90 ml/min X 2 mg/ml
                               = 180 mg/min.

Step 2: Check transport maximum:

In the above question transport maximum is 150 mg/min.

Step 3: Calculate the excretion:

Excretion = Total filtered glucose - Total reabsorbed glucose (Transport Maximum)

  = 180-150 mg/min
  = 30 mg/min

Correct answer: A. Alpha actinin

Alpha actinin is the constituent of the marked area.

The image depicts sarcomere and the arrow points towards Z-line. Alpha actinin binds actin to Z-lines.

The orderly arrangement of actin, myosin, and related proteins that produces this pattern. The area between two Z-lines is called sarcomere.

The thick filaments, which are about twice the diameter of the thin filaments, are made up of myosin, which are lined to form A bands; the thin filaments are made up of actin, tropomyosin, and troponin. The array of thin filaments extends out of the A band and into the less dense staining I bands.

The lighter H bands in the center of the A bands are the regions where, when the muscle is relaxed, the thin filaments do not overlap the thick filaments.  The Z lines allow for anchoring of the thin filaments.

Actinin, titin and desmin are additional structural proteins.Titin connects Z-lines to the M line and provides the scaffolding to the sarcomere.  Desmin adds structure to Z-lines by connecting Z-line to plasma membrane.

subject: Physiology
text: Identify the ions A and B based on conductance graph of a neuron shown below:
expl:
Correct answer: A. Na, K

Channel A: Na+, Channel B: K+

Na+ channels are fast activating and are responsible for depolarization phase of action potential.

K+ channels are slow activating and open for prolonged duration than the sodium channels. They are responsible for repolarization phase of action potential. Also, the postassium channels return slowly to their closed state, which is responsible for after-hyperpolarization.

The sequence of events during the action potential occur in 7 steps as described below.

1. Resting state - Both channels are closed

2. Na+ channels open in response to depolarizing stimulus. Sodium enters into the cell. The membrane reaches threshold potential.

3. The sodium influx causes opening of more sodium channels through positive feedback mechanism. Rapid depolarization occurs.

4. Sodium conductance decreases.

5. Na+ channels close and K+ channels open. Repolarization occurs.

6. Sodium channels are reset, and are ready to respond to another depolarizing stimulus (relative refractory period). During this phase, the potassium channels remain open and slowly return to closed state causing after-hyperpolarization.

7. Both channels are closed. The membrane returns to RMP.

options.C: Central capillary dilatati‌on → wheal with exaggerat‍ed surrounding flare

Brachial plexus trunk injury leads to anesthetized skin over the region. On performing a histamine test on such an individual, one can expect central capillary dilatation → wheal without surrounding flare. The incomplete triple response over the anesthetic skin is characteristic of postganglionic lesions.

Intradermal injection of histamine usually causes a triple response in the surrounding skin i.e, red reaction→ flare → wheal

  • Red reaction is independent of innervation and is due to histamine-mediated relaxation of the precapillary sphincters

  • The triple response persists after total sympathectomy
  • Flare is absent in locally anesthetized skin

CVC - Cardiovagal center

subject: Physiology
text: The mechanism by which glucose is absorbed in the intestine is:
expl:
Correct answer: B. Secondary active transport

Glucose is absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport.

On the basolateral side, there is active transport of sodium ions out of the cell into the interstitial fluid. This depletes sodium inside the cell. Because of this Na+ concentration difference, more Na+ binds to the SGLT on the luminal side. This increases the affinity of SGLT for glucose and glucose binds to it.

Then, both the Na+ and glucose are transported together to the interior of the cell. Thus, glucose is absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport. The energy for glucose transport is provided indirectly, by the active transport of Na+ out of the cell. The glucose moves out of the cell into the blood across the basolateral membrane by facilitated diffusion mediated via GLUT.

text: Pacemaker generating the rhythm for breathing is ________

options.B: Dorsal group of neurons in‌ the medulla

expl:
Correct answer: C. Pre-Bőtzinger complex

Pre-Botzinger complex generates the rhythm for automated breathing.

  • These are also known as pacemaker cells located in the medulla.
  • These are the first set of neurons that initiate inspiration.
  • These neurons discharge rhythmically, and they produce rhythmic discharges in the phrenic motor neurons.

Breathing is under the control of both the following:

  • Voluntary control: Located in the cerebral cortex (via corticospinal tract)
  • Automatic control: Driven by pacemaker cells in the medulla (Pre-Botzinger complex). These activate motor neurons via cervical (Phrenic nerve innervating diaphragm) and thoracic spinal cord (external intercostal muscle).

There is a reciprocal innervation to expiratory and inspiratory muscles in that motor neurons supplying expiratory muscles are inactive when motor neurons supplying inspiratory muscles are active, and vice versa.

 

Inspiration
Initiation Pre-Botzinger complex (Pacemaker cells) in Medulla
Maintenance Apneustic center in lower Pons stimulates Dorsal group of neurons in the medulla
Termination  Apneustic center inhibited by Vagus and Pneumotaxic center

Regulation of expiration: During quiet breathing, expiration is a passive process; there is no firing of neurons. Ventral respiratory group of neurons are involved in forceful expiration like during exercise.

Mnemonic DIVE: Dorsal respiratory group for Inspiration and Ventral respiratory group for Expiration.

expl:
Correct answer: C. Gate control theory

Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) used for pain relief is based on the gate theory of pain. This method uses electrodes to activate Aα and Aβ fibers near the injury to relieve pain.

Gate control theory is based on the inhibition of pain pathway in the spinal cord. Various sensory inputs from a particular dermatome reach the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. The pain is transmitted via A-delta and C fibers, whereas, A-beta fibers carry tactile sensations (touch, pressure) and A-alpha fibers carry proprioception.

When these large-diameter A-beta/A-alpha fibers are stimulated, they inhibit the pain pathway in the spinal cord. This inhibition is thought to result from the local lateral inhibition of interneurons in the spinal cord.

Gate control theory operates at the substantia gelatinosa of the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.

text: Intercellular communication in eukaryotes is by?

Correct answer: C. Exosome

Intercellular communication in eukaryotes is by Exosome.

In the last decade, a class of small, heterogeneous, secreted vesicles, broadly termed as extracellular vesicles have been identified.

These extracellular vesicles have been implicated as a new and important mediator of cell-cell communication that likely contributes importantly to both normal and pathologic physiology.

These vesicles are enclosed by a lipid bilayer.

Dihydropyridine receptors (DHPRs) are voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in the T tubule membrane. 

The ryanodine receptor (RyR) is a ligand-gated Ca2+ channel with Ca2+ as its natural ligand.

subject: Physiology
lesson: Physiology Aiims 2020 (May And Nov Ini Cet)
text: In negative feedback, feedback gain of infinity is seen in which of the following?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Blood volume control by kidney

In negative feedback, feedback gain of infinity could be seen in blood volume control by the kidney.

When the blood volume falls below the equilibrium, the renal–body fluid mechanism causes the blood volume returns back to the equilibrium point resulting in zero error and hence the gain of kidney in its ability to regulate blood volume is infinity (∞).

The degree of effectiveness with which a regulatory system maintains constant conditions is determined by the gain of the negative feedback system. 

Gain= Correction/Error

Example: If an external or internal factor led to a decrease in mean blood pressure from 100 mm Hg to 80 mm Hg. Activation of a negative feedback mechanism i.e. baroreflex leads to a correction of blood pressure to 96 mm Hg. So in this case,

  • Correction = 16 mm Hg
  • Error = 4 mm Hg
  • Gain = Correction/Error = 16/4 = 4

Note: A gain of 0 would imply a total failure of the regulatory system and a gain of infinity (∞) would indicate complete restoration of the regulated variable.

subject: Physiology
lesson: Physiology Aiims 2020 (May And Nov Ini Cet)
text: The image below shows simple muscle twitch along with the time trace, recorded in a frog gastrocnemius muscle. Calculate the minimum tetanizing frequency. (The time tracer was made with a 100Hz tuning fork).
expl:
Correct answer: D. 20 per second

The tetanizing frequency of the muscle, based on the given diagram, is 20 per second.

Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period. It is the frequency at which individual muscle fibres twitch that fuse and cause sustained muscle contraction, where the contraction period is the time taken from latent period to maximum force of contraction.

In this case, the time tracer was taken using a 100Hz tuning fork. Which means the tracer recorded 100 waves per second.
Therefore, the duration of each wave in time tracer = 0.01 seconds.

In the image given in the question, between the point B (end of latent period) to point C (maximum force of contraction), there are about 5 waves.
Hence, the duration of contraction = 5 x 0.01 = 0.05 seconds.

Substituting the value in the formula, we get:
Tetanizing frequency = 1/0.05 sec = 100/5 = 20/sec.

Tetanization:

The features of muscle contraction can be demonstrated by eliciting single muscle twitches. The adding together of individual twitch contractions to increase the intensity of overall muscle contraction is Summation. Summation occurs in two ways:

  • by increasing the number of motor units contracting simultaneously, which is multiple ﬁber summations.
  • by increasing the frequency of contraction, which is called frequency summation and can lead to tetanization.

When the frequency of a contraction reaches a critical level, the successive contractions eventually fuse together, and the whole muscle contraction appears to be completely smooth and continuous, this is called tetanization. Beyond this point, a further increase in the frequency, will not result in increased force of contraction.

Tetanization occurs in two ways:

  • Complete tetanus occurs when no relaxation occurs between stimuli.
  • Incomplete tetanus when periods of incomplete relaxation take place between the summated stimuli.
