Option D: Rimonabant is an inverse agonist at cannabinoid receptor CB1 which decreases neurotransmitter release at GABAergic and glutamatergic synapses; its usage for smoking cessation and treat obesity was stopped after serious side effects notably severe depression and increased risk of suicide. However, it continues to be used off-label for smoking cessation.

subject: Pharmacology
text: A patient who was on warfarin therapy for atrial fibrillation is prescribed a cephalosporin antibiotic for the treatment of a lower respiratory tract infection. He reports back to the hospital after having developed hemarthrosis. Which of the following cephalosporins is likely to have caused this?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Cefoperazone

The cephalosporin antibiotic most likely to have caused hemarthrosis in this patient on warfarin therapy is cefoperazone.

Cephalosporins containing a methylthiotetrazole (NMTT) group can prolong the prothrombin time. This results in clinically significant bleeding in patients already on anticoagulant therapy or having vitamin K deficiency. 

This is because NMTT cephalosporins inhibit the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase in the liver, which is the key enzyme for vitamin K-dependent carboxylation, a posttranslational modification that is essential for the biological functions of coagulation factors. 
NMTT group containing cephalosporins include latamoxef, cefmenoxime, cefoperazone, cefotetan, cefamandole.

Vitamin K epoxide reductase is also the target of anticoagulants like warfarin. Oral administration of vitamin K can prevent this problem.

subject: Pharmacology
text: Which of the following is a novel anti-depressant?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Vilazodone

Vilazodone is the novel antidepressant.

The antidepressant effect of vilazodone is due to its enhancement of serotonergic activity in the CNS through selective inhibition of serotonin reuptake. It binds with high affinity to the serotonin reuptake site but not to the norepinephrine or dopamine reuptake site. As a result, vilazodone potently and selectively inhibits the reuptake of serotonin.

Vilazodone is also a partial agonist at serotonergic 5-HT1A receptors; the result of this activity on serotonergic transmission also plays a role in its antidepressant effect.

Thus it offers a novel combination of selective serotonin reuptake inhibition (SSRI) and serotonergic (5-HT1A) receptor partial agonist activity. Because of these characteristics, vilazodone has been termed a serotonin partial agonist–reuptake inhibitor (SPARI).

Vilazodone is never combined with a monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitor or given within 14 days of discontinuing or initiating MAO inhibitor therapy due to the serious risk of serotonin toxicity.

Other options:

Option A: Lurasidone is a second-generation antipsychotic that is a 5-HT2A and D2 receptor antagonist. it is used in the treatment of schizophrenia and bipolar depression (as monotherapy or as an adjunct).

Option C: Asenapine is a second-generation antipsychotic which is also a 5-HT2A and D2 receptor antagonist, used in the management of schizophrenia and acute mania.

Option D: Blonanserin is a second-generation antipsychotic, which acts as an antagonist at D2, D3, and 5-HT2A receptors. Blonanserin has a low affinity for 5-HT2C, adrenergic α1, histamine H1, and muscarinic M1 receptors, but displays a relatively high affinity for 5-HT6 receptors. It is used in the management of schizophrenia.

subject: Pharmacology
text: A 57-year-old man was brought to the hospital with complaints of dizziness and breathlessness. During his physical examination, you notice the following discolouration over his face. He is presently being treated with amiodarone, metoprolol, verapamil, lisinopril, and amlodipine. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Amiodarone

The image shows grey-blue discoloration over this patient's face and the drug responsible for this is amiodarone.

Long-term treatment with amiodarone is responsible for skin pigmentation. Elderly men are at an increased risk of developing this. 

Ultraviolet light reacts with amiodarone and its metabolites to cause local vasodilatation. This increases the diffusion of amiodarone and its metabolites, resulting in their deposition in the tissues, causing pigmentation. Therefore, it is usually seen in sun-exposed areas.

Cessation of amiodarone, avoiding exposure to sunlight using sunscreen cream is recommended.

Amiodarone is an iodine-containing compound that is structurally related to thyroid hormone. It is a class III antiarrhythmic drug, which increases the duration of an action potential by blocking potassium channels. It thereby increases the time taken for repolarization. It also prolongs the refractory period and suppresses abnormal automaticity. It also has weak calcium channel blocking, sodium channel blocking, and adrenergic blocking actions.

It is used to maintain normal sinus rhythm during atrial fibrillation and prevent recurrent ventricular tachycardia. 

Adverse effects of amiodarone:

  • Prolonged usage of amiodarone causes interstitial lung disease.
  • Heart blocks, bradycardia and QT prolongation
  • Hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism
  • Corneal micro-deposits and vortex keratopathy, optic neuropathy

Drug interactions of amiodarone

  • Causes digoxin toxicity by decreasing its renal clearance.
  • Increases concentration of quinidine and procainamide
  • Potentiates the anticoagulant effect of warfarin when given simultaneously

subject: Pharmacology
text: Which of the following is a centrally acting opioid antitussive?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Levopropoxyphene

Levopropoxyphene is a centrally acting opioid antitussive.

Levopropoxyphene is an opioid derivative that is a strong and partial μ receptor agonist that helps to reduce the cough reflex and therefore, is used in the management of acute debilitating cough. The usual antitussive dose is 50–100 mg every 4 hours. It has no analgesic activity. However, it is known to cause some sedation.

Other options:

Option A: Ambroxol is derived from bromhexine. It is a mucoactive agent that helps alter the viscoelastic properties of mucus and increase mucociliary clearance, thereby providing relief in productive cough. It is commonly available as intramuscular or intravenous, lozenges, syrups, or tablets.

Option B: Diphenoxylate is an opioid agonist that is structurally similar to meperidine. It is used in the treatment of acute, chronic, and traveler's diarrhea. Upon administration, it undergoes de-esterification to difenoxin, which is its active metabolite. Its side effects include constipation, toxic megacolon, paralytic ileus and can give rise to CNS depression in children.

Option D: Levorphanol is a synthetic opioid that is also a 5HT/Norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor and an NMDA receptor antagonist which is chiefly used in the management of moderate to severe pain and has a relatively rapid onset of action. Its side effects include delirium and hallucinations.

subject: Pharmacology
text:
The anti-epileptic drugs which can also be used for the treatment of neuropathic pain are

  1. Pregabalin
  2. Carbamazepine
  3. Lamotrigine
  4. Gabapentin
expl:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

The anti-epileptic drugs which can also be used for neuropathic pain are 1, 2, and 4 which are pregabalin, carbamazepine and gabapentin respectively.

Pregabalin is an anti-epileptic drug that acts by binding to α2δ, a protein that is a subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels and causes a decrease in glutamate release at excitatory synapses. It is used in the management of neuropathic pain associated with diabetic peripheral neuropathy, spinal cord injury or postherpetic neuralgia.

Gabapentin is an anti-epileptic drug that, like pregabalin, acts by binding to α2δ protein. It is used in the management of neuropathic pain due to postherpetic neuralgia in adults.

The binding of gabapentin and pregabalin, also called "gabapentinoids" due to their structural similarity to GABA, to calcium channel subunit a2δ protein, is considered to mediate the anti-convulsant effects of gabapentin and pregabalin. They are used in focal onset seizures with or without progression to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures when used in addition to other anti-epileptic drugs.

Carbamazepine is an iminostilbine derivative. It blocks voltage-activated sodium channels, slowing their rate of recovery and limiting the repetitive firing of action potentials. It is used in the treatment of:

  • Generalized, focal-to-bilateral and idiopathic tonic-clonic seizures
  • Focal seizures
  • Neuropathic pain associated with trigeminal and glossopharyngeal neuralgias.

Lamotrigine is an anti-folate agent whose mechanism of action is similar to that of carbamazepine i.e. it delays the recovery from inactivation of recombinant sodium channels. It also inhibits the release of glutamate by acting directly on the sodium channels. Therefore, when used concurrently with carbamazepine, is associated with toxicity in some patients due to increase in 10,11- epoxide of carbamazepine. It is useful in the management of:

  • Focal and secondarily generalized tonic-clonic seizures in adults
  • Lennox-Gastaut syndrome - a childhood disorder characterized by multiple type seizures, mental retardation, and refractoriness to anti-seizure medication.

subject: Pharmacology
text: A breast cancer patient post-chemotherapy developed a low-grade fever with anemia and leukocytopenia (<4000/cm3; DNC: 30). Which of the following antibiotics will not be used in the empirical management of this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Linezolid

Linezolid cannot be used in this patient as bone marrow suppression is a side effect of this drug and hence it can worsen the post-chemotherapy bone marrow suppression in this patient.

Linezolid can cause myelosuppression which can present as anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and pancytopenia. It is commonly associated with thrombocytopenia and is seen 7-10 days following administration. This is usually reversed on discontinuation of the drug. 

Other adverse effects of linezolid:

  • It inhibits mitochondrial protein synthesis and may lead to peripheral neuropathy, optic neuritis, and lactic acidosis in patients receiving the drug for longer durations.
  • It can cause serotonin syndrome when coadministered with adrenergic or serotonergic drugs like SSRIs due to its nonspecific MAO inhibition.

It is a protein synthesis inhibitor of the class oxazolidinones. It mainly acts against gram-positive organisms. It is approved for the treatment of the following conditions:

  • Skin and skin structure infections by staphylococcus(Both MRSA and MSSA) and streptococcus.
  • Community-acquired pneumonia due to streptococcus pneumoniae.
  • Nosocomial pneumonia due to staphylococcus aureus. 

Other options:

Cefepime: It is a fourth-generation antipseudomonal cephalosporin. It is useful in enterobacter and pseudomonas infections that are resistant to other cephalosporins.

Piperacillin-Tazobactam- It is a combination of piperacillin which is a ureidopenicillin and tazobactam which is a beta-lactamase inhibitor. It is useful in various infections including nosocomial infections, intraabdominal infections, pneumonia, and UTI. It is highly effective against E Coli and Klebsiella.

Meropenem: It belongs to the carbapenem group of beta-lactam antibiotics. They are more active against gram-negative organisms. Coadministration of cilastatin is not required with this drug. (Cilastation should be coadministered with imipenem as imipenem is sensitive to renal peptidase degradation)

subject: Pharmacology
text: A female patient on oral contraceptive pills (OCP) was diagnosed to have tuberculosis and started on antitubercular therapy (ATT). She was advised to use an additional barrier method of contraception.  What is the reason for this advice?

options.D: Rifampicin induces OCP met‌abolism and cause failure​

expl:
Correct answer: D. Rifampicin induces OCP metabolism and cause failure

Rifampicin is a potent cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzyme inducer. When given along with oral contraceptive pills(OCP) it would induce the metabolism of OCPs leading to contraceptive failure. This is the reason for the patient being advised to use an additional method of contraception.

Important enzyme inducers are:

  • Barbiturates
  • Phenytoin
  • Carbamazepine
  • Rifampicin
  • Cigarette smoking
  • Chronic alcoholism

Important drugs that inhibit CYP450 isoenzyme are:

  • Macrolide antibiotics
  • Azole antifungals
  • Chloramphenicol
  • Omeprazole
  • Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) 
  • HIV protease inhibitors
  • Cimetidine
  • Ciprofloxacin
  • Metronidazole

subject: Pharmacology
text: A 35-year-old chronic hypertensive woman visits the outpatient department for pre-conceptional counseling. Which of the following anti-hypertensives should she discontinue?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors

Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors should be discontinued in pregnancy as they can cause hypoplasia of organs, growth retardation, and fetal loss.

ACE inhibitors cause reduced perfusion and oligohydramnios leading to fetal growth retardation, calvarium maldevelopment, hypoplasia of lungs and kidneys, and limb contractures.

Antihypertensive drugs to be avoided in pregnancy:

  • ACE inhibitors and Angiotensin receptor blockers(ARB) - Can cause growth retardation and fetal damage.
  • Diuretics - Can decrease uteroplacental perfusion
  • Nonselective beta-blockers
  • Sodium nitroprusside - It is contraindicated in eclampsia.

Antihypertensive drugs that can be used in pregnancy:

  • Labetalol - Combined α + β blocker
  • Nifedipine - Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. It is useful in preeclampsia but should be stopped before labor as they weaken the uterine contractions.
  • Methyldopa
  • Hydralazine

Note:

Thiazide diuretics like hydrochlorothiazide are considered to be safe in pregnancy and are useful in the management of chronic hypertension in pregnant women.

subject: Pharmacology
text: A pregnant woman was prescribed indomethacin. Which of the following effects does the drug have on the fetus?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Premature closure of ductus arteriosus

Indomethacin can cause premature closure of ductus arteriosus if given to a pregnant woman.

Indomethacin is approved for the closure of persistent ductus arteriosus in premature infants. It is given intravenously. One of its limiting factors is the development of renal toxicity in neonates.

Indomethacin is a nonselective COX inhibitor. It has anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic properties. It can be used in the management of conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, gouty arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, etc. But its use is limited due to the high rate of intolerance and availability of safer agents.

Adverse effects: Diarrhea with ulcerative bowel lesions, acute pancreatitis, and hepatitis are seen. Frontal headache is the most frequent CNS effect. Dizziness, light-headedness, vertigo, and mental confusion can occur. Neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and rarely aplastic anemia can also occur.

Note:

Prostaglandin analogs are indicated in the maintenance of patency of the ductus arteriosus.

subject: Pharmacology
text: Which of the following can be prescribed in case of an open angle glaucoma with bronchial asthma?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Latanoprost

Latanoprost can be given in a case of open-angle glaucoma with bronchial asthma.

Latanoprost is a PGF2α analog and it is not associated with systemic side effects like bronchospasm and hence can be given for asthmatic patients. Prostaglandin analogs are the first choice drugs for open-angle glaucoma.

Mechanism of action: It reduces intraocular pressure by altering the ciliary muscle tension and improving the outflow of the aqueous humor.

Advantages of latanoprost:

  • Good efficacy
  • Once-daily application
  • Absence of systemic side effects

Disadvantage: High cost

Adverse effects:

  • Blurring of vision
  • Iris pigmentation
  • Thickening and darkening of eyelashes
  • Macular edema can occur especially in aphakic patients.

Other options:

Option A- Timolol is a non-selective beta-blocker used topically in glaucoma. It is associated with systemic effects by absorption through the nasolacrimal duct and can cause life-threatening bronchospasm in asthmatics and COPD patients. Hence they are not given in in this case.

Option B- Gemeprost is a PGE1 analog used for the termination of early pregnancy.

Option D- Mannitol infusion is given for acute congestive glaucoma and not for open-angle glaucoma. It causes decongestion of the eye by its osmotic action.

text: As a medical practitioner in India, how will you prescribe alprazolam to a patient?

options.A: 1 mg OD before bedtime for‌ 7 days
options.D: 0.5 mg daily before bedtim‌e for 7 days

expl:
Correct answer: D. 0.5 mg daily before bedtime for 7 days

The correct method of prescribing alprazolam is 0.5mg daily before bedtime for 7 days.

The drugs are prescribed in generic names legibly and preferably in capital letters. The prescription should have details to identify the patient and medication that needs to be dispensed and the therapeutic purpose. The use of abbreviations, especially Latin is discouraged. The dosage should be written in metric measure.

Guidelines for drug prescription:

The parts of an ideal prescription are as follows.

  • Date
  • Name and address of the doctor
  • Superscription(Rx symbol)
  • Information about the patient
  • Name and dose of the drug prescribed(Inscription)
  • Dispencing directions to the pharmacist(Subscription)
  • Instructions for the patient
  • Signature of the doctor

subject: Pharmacology
text: A patient started on antihypertensive presented with the following picture. Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Lisinopril

The image shows edema over the lips and face and its occurrence following intake of an antihypertensive is suggestive of drug-induced angioedema. Lisinopril being an ACE inhibitor is most likely to be responsible for this condition.

Angioedema with ACE inhibitors:

In very few patients(0.1%-0.5%), ACE inhibitors cause rapid swelling in the nose, throat, mouth, glottis, larynx, lips, or tongue. Once the drug is stopped symptoms improve drastically over hours. Angioedema of the intestine can occur very rarely. 

ACE inhibitor-associated angioedema is a class effect, and patients who develop this adverse event should not be prescribed any other drugs within the ACE inhibitor class.

Other adverse effects of ACE inhibitors:

Hypotension - A sudden fall in blood pressure can occur following the first dose of ACE inhibitors.

Cough - It can produce a bothersome dry cough due to the accumulation of bradykinin, substance P, or prostaglandins in the lungs. The cough usually disappears within 4 days of the stoppage of the drug.

Hyperkalemia due to K+ retention can occur.

Acute renal failure can occur with ACE inhibitors in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis, stenosis of the artery to a single remaining kidney, heart failure, or volume depletion due to diarrhea or diuretics.

It should be discontinued in pregnant women as it can cause developmental defects.

It can also cause maculopapular skin rash in some cases.

Other options:

Option B: Nifedipine is a calcium channel blocker. Common adverse effects include headache, flushing, and dizziness. Peripheral edema may rarely occur.

Option C: Atenolol is a beta 1 selective antagonist. Bradycardia, fatigue, cold extremities are common adverse effects. CNS side effects like nightmares and depression are less frequent with atenolol than other beta-blockers.

Option D: Clonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist. The main adverse effects of clonidine are dry mouth and sedation. Bradycardia and sexual dysfunction are other effects.

subject: Pharmacology
text: A patient on aspirin presented with occult blood in the stool. This is due to inhibition of____ by aspirin
expl:
Correct answer: B. Thromboxane

Aspirin causes inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1(COX-1) which would inhibit the formation of thromboxane A2. Thromboxane A2 is an inducer of platelet aggregation and is a potent vasoconstrictor. Hence inhibition of its formation is responsible for the bleeding complications of aspirin.

Aspirin is a noncompetitive, irreversible inhibitor of the cyclooxygenase(COX) enzyme. It is a nonselective COX inhibitor and inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2. 

Uses of aspirin:

  • Analgesic and antipyretic uses.
  • Acute rheumatic fever
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Post myocardial infarction and stroke due to its antiplatelet action.
  • Prevention of preeclampsia

Adverse effects:

Nausea, vomiting, epigastric discomfort, and increased occult blood in stools are seen with analgesic doses(0.5-2g/day). Antiinflammatory doses(3-5g/day) can produce salicylism characterized by dizziness, tinnitus, vertigo, hyperventilation, reversible loss of hearing and vision, etc. It can cause elevation of liver enzymes and hepatic damage. Hypersensitivity reactions are also seen.

Reye's syndrome is a rare condition that can occur when salicylates like aspirin are given in children having viral infections like influenza.

subject: Pharmacology
text: A 60-year-old postmenopausal female patient with a previous history of Colle's fracture came with complaints of lower backache. On evaluation, her T score was -2.5. Which of the following statements are false about the management of her condition?

options.A: Teriparatide should be sta‌rted before supplementing​ with bisphosphonates
options.B: Bisphosphonates are not gi‌ven for more than a year
options.C: Calcium requirement is 120‌0 mg per day
options.D: Oral vitamin D3 is given a‌long with oral calcium

expl:
Correct answer: B. Bisphosphonates are not given for more than a year

Bisphosphonates are given for periods of more than one year (Option B is false). In this case, as the patient is having a history of osteoporotic fracture, teriparatide can be given before bisphosphonates.

Pharmacologic management of osteoporosis:

Bisphosphonates: These are pyrophosphate analogs that act by directly inhibiting bone resorption. The antiresorptive action is mainly due to its direct inhibitory effect on osteoclasts. It causes osteoclast apoptosis as well as the prevention of hydroxyapatite dissolution. Long-term bisphosphonates therapy is given for durations of 3-5 years, depending on the fracture risk of the patient. Since they are associated with osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femur fractures, a drug holiday may be advised after long-term management.

Teriparatide is a recombinant PTH analog that has an anabolic effect on bone homeostasis by increasing osteoblastic activity. It increases bone mineral density and decreases the risk of fractures in postmenopausal women. Indications of teriparatide therapy include the history of osteoporotic fracture, multiple risk factors for fracture, intolerance, or failure of previous osteoporosis therapy. It is only approved for 2 years of use. Clinical trials that used teriparatide prior to bisphosphonate have been proven effective.

Denosumab is a human monoclonal antibody with a mechanism of action similar to that of osteoprotegerin (OPG). It binds to RANK Ligand (RANKL), thereby inhibiting its binding to the RANK receptor of the surface of osteoclasts. This prevents RANK receptor activation and subsequent bone resorption.

Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) - Estrogen has a protective effect that prevents accelerated bone loss. This is carried out by reducing the bone resorption effects of parathyroid hormone (PTH). Keeping in line with these effects, osteoporosis prevention in postmenopausal women has been attributed to the use of SERMs such as raloxifene. It acts as an estrogen agonist on the bone and liver.

Calcium and Vitamin D supplementation: Calcium supplementation in the elderly suppresses bone turnover and improves bone mineral density. 1200mg of calcium is daily required in adults of more than 50 years of age. Vitamin D supplementation with 400-800IU/day improves intestinal calcium absorption, suppresses bone remodeling, and improves bone mineral density.

subject: Pharmacology
text: A patient presented with a history of multiple episodes of vomiting. He was given an intravenous drug, and later, he developed abnormal movements. Which of the following can be used to treat him?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Benzhexol

Benzhexol should be used in the management of this patient. The development of abnormal movements following an anti-emetic injection suggests that the antiemetic used in this case is probably metoclopramide.

Metoclopramide is a dopamine receptor antagonist used as a prokinetic and anti-emetic agent. It can produce extrapyramidal side effects and dystonia is seen acutely following intravenous injections. Anticholinergics like benzhexol (trihexyphenidyl) are used in the management of these side effects. Benzhexol is a centrally-acting anticholinergic agent. It acts by restoring the cholinergic balance in the striatal interneurons.

Extrapyramidal side effects of metoclopramide are commonly seen in children and young adults with higher doses. Acute dystonia occurs after intravenous administration, while parkinsonian-like symptoms develop weeks after therapy. It is managed with the discontinuation of metoclopramide and with anticholinergics or antihistaminics. Irreversible tardive dyskinesia can occur with chronic treatment.

Other adverse effects:

It can cause galactorrhea by its dopamine antagonism. Methemoglobinemia can occur if used in infants.

Other options:

Option A: Hyoscine (scopolamine): It is a muscarinic receptor antagonist used in the management of motion sickness and vomiting.

Option B: Cyproheptadine is an H1 receptor antagonist used in the management of various allergy-related conditions like allergic rhinitis, anaphylaxis, urticaria, etc.

Option C: Levodopa is the precursor of dopamine and it is given in combination with carbidopa for the management of parkinsonism.

@

subject: Pharmacology
text: What formula is the dosing rate of a drug based on?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Clearance x plasma concentration

The formula for drug dosing rate is clearance x plasma concentration.

The equation for dose rate given here is based on steady-state concentration. When a drug is given repeatedly at short intervals it will accumulate in the body until the elimination of the drug matches its input. So steady-state concentration is the plasma concentration at which the drug elimination and drug input balance each other.

Steady-state concentration(Cpss) = Dose rate / Clearance

From this equation dose rate for a target steady-state plasma concentration is calculated as 

Dose rate = Clearance(CL) x target plasma concentration(Cpss)

subject: Pharmacology
text: A patient on digoxin, potassium chloride, clarithromycin, atenolol, and triamterene developed atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular rate. Serum digoxin levels were raised. Which of his medications is responsible for the same?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Clarithromycin

Elevated serum digoxin levels and the development of atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular rate are suggestive of digoxin toxicity. Clarithromycin when given along with digoxin can cause digoxin toxicity.

P-glycoprotein pumps play a major role in the elimination of digoxin. Drugs that inhibit P-glycoprotein can thereby decrease the elimination of digoxin and lead to digoxin toxicity. Macrolide antibiotics like clarithromycin and erythromycin are inhibitors of the P-glycoprotein. So clarithromycin when given along with digoxin can cause digoxin toxicity.

Other drugs that inhibit P-glycoprotein are - Amiodarone, quinidine, verapamil, diltiazem, cyclosporine, itraconazole, propafenone, and flecainide.

Digoxin is one of the cardiac glycosides which is derived from the digitalis plant and used clinically.

It inhibits Na+/K+ ATPase, a membrane-bound transporter to increase intracellular sodium. As a result, there is less expulsion of calcium from the cell by sodium-calcium exchanger (NCX). Increased calcium inside the myocyte leads to an increase in cardiac contractility.

The most common cardiac manifestations of digitalis toxicity include atrioventricular junctional rhythm, premature ventricular depolarizations, ventricular bigeminy, ventricular tachycardia, and second-degree AV blockade.

Factors that increase the risk of digoxin toxicity are:

  • Hypercalcemia
  • Hypomagnesemia
  • Hypokalemia- It increases the binding of the digoxin to the Na+/K+ ATPase pump. 
  • Drugs causing hypokalemia- loop and thiazide diuretics, amphotericin B, corticosteroids
  • Drugs that decrease digoxin elimination (inhibitors of P-glycoprotein)
  • Renal failure
  • Hypothyroidism

 Triamterene, atenolol, and potassium chloride cause hyperkalemia, and therefore do not cause digoxin toxicity.

@

subject: Pharmacology
text:
What is the mechanism of action of methotrexate in osteosarcoma?

UMP- Uridine monophosphate

DHFR- Dihydrofolate reductase
expl:
Correct answer: B. Competitive inhibitor of DHFR

The anticancer activity of methotrexate is by inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).

Methotrexate belongs to the antimetabolite class of anticancer drugs. The antifolate action of the drug is responsible for its anti-cancer properties.

Mechanism of action:

It is a folic acid analog and binds to the active catalytic site of dihydrofolate reductase(DHFR). This would inhibit the formation of tetrahydrofolate(THF) which is needed for purine nucleotides, thymidylate, and the amino acids serine and methionine. This would interfere with the production of DNA, RNA, and important cellular proteins.

Low doses of methotrexate are used in the management of rheumatic diseases. It is due to the inhibition of amino-imidazole carboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR) transformylase and thymidylate synthetase. This results in increased levels of adenosine that inhibits inflammation.

Adverse effects:

Common side effects are nausea and mucosal ulcers. Others include anemia, leukopenia, stomatitis, GI ulcerations, and alopecia. Dose-related hepatotoxicity is also seen. The GI effects and hepatotoxicity can be reduced by the use of leucovorin or folinic acid. 

@

subject: Pharmacology
text:
What should not be consumed by patients with bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis on metronidazole?

MAOI-Monoamine oxidase inhibitor

SSRI- Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
expl:
Correct answer: B. Alcohol

Alcohol should not be consumed by a patient on metronidazole. Metronidazole produces a disulfiram-like reaction. If the patient consumes alcohol during or within 3 days of therapy, they may experience abdominal distress, vomiting, headache, and flushing. 

Disulfiram and disulfiram-like reactions:

Disulfiram inhibits the aldehyde dehydrogenase(ALDH) activity and thereby increases the concentration of acetaldehyde in the blood. When a person treated with disulfiram consumes alcohol he or she would develop symptoms of acetaldehyde poisoning. The symptoms are:

  • Flushing
  • Pulsating headache
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Sweating
  • Tachycardia
  • Hypotension
  • Orthostatic syncope
  • Vertigo
  • Blurred vision

Certain drugs can also produce disulfiram-like reactions if alcohol is consumed along with these drugs. Patients should be warned not to use alcohol along with these drugs. The drugs include:

  • Metronidazole
  • Tinidazole
  • Cefoperazone
  • Sulfonylureas

subject: Pharmacology
text: A patient with chronic kidney disease underwent a nephrectomy. Which of the following can be administered as a postoperative analgesic in this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Acetaminophen

Acetaminophen can be given as an analgesic for the patient as it is the least nephrotoxic among the given options.

Analgesia in CKD patients:

Acetaminophen is considered a safer non-narcotic analgesic in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. For more severe pains opioid analgesics like tramadol or fentanyl are used. 

Even though acetaminophen is considered safe, with chronic high dosage it can also become nephrotoxic.

NSAIDs like naproxen, indomethacin, diclofenac, etc are not used in CKD patients because of their direct nephrotoxic effects. In healthy normal individuals, NSAIDs have little effect on renal function and blood pressure. But in conditions where the regulatory systems are impaired as hypovolemia, congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, chronic kidney disease, or other conditions where the renin-angiotensin system is activated, renal function by the formation of prostaglandins are very important.

NSAIDs cause impairment of prostaglandin-induced inhibition of chlorine reabsorption and antidiuretic hormone action. This will cause salt and water retention. It also inhibits COX-2 derived prostaglandins which regulate the renal medullary blood flow and would lead to a rise in blood pressure, increased cardiovascular thrombotic events, and cardiac failure. It can also cause electrolyte abnormalities like hyponatremia and hyperkalemia.

 

@

subject: Pharmacology
text: A patient with renal insufficiency presented with very low urine output, pedal edema, headache and BP 160/90. Which anti-hypertensive can be administered?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Chlorthalidone

The antihypertensive that can be given in this case is chlorthalidone. The patient in this case is having renal insufficiency but there is no proteinuria mentioned in the question stem. So among the given options, the thiazide diuretic chlorthalidone can be administered as antihypertensive in this patient. 

Management of hypertension in chronic kidney disease(CKD):

ACE inhibitors or ARBs are considered the first-line drugs in patients with proteinuria. These agents effectively reduce blood pressure, proteinuria and prevent kidney decline. Calcium channel blockers can be added if necessary.

For patients who do not have proteinuria, there is no established first-line therapy. One or two of the following drugs can be used:

  • Thiazides/thiazide-like diuretics
  • ACE inhibitors or ARBs
  • Calcium channel blockers

In patients presenting with fluid retention or fluid overload, thiazide diuretics such as chlorthalidone and hydrochlorothiazide are recommended for management. In CKD stages 1 to 3 (GFR >=30ml/min), thiazides are recommended, while loop diuretics such as bumetanide, furosemide are used in stages 4-5 (GFR < 30ml/min).

Other options:

Option A: Aliskiren is a direct renin inhibitor. It effectively lowers blood pressure, reduces albuminuria, and limits left ventricular hypertrophy.

Option C: Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker. A common side effect of amlodipine is the production of peripheral edema.

Option D: Prazosin is a selective α1 antagonist. It is generally not used as an initial agent to treat hypertension, except in symptomatic prostatism or nightmares linked to posttraumatic stress disorder. Headache is one of the side effects of prazosin.

@

subject: Pharmacology
text: Which of the following interleukin (IL) is inhibited by tocilizumab?
expl:
Correct answer: A. IL-6

Tocilizumab inhibits IL-6.

Tocilizumab is a newer humanized antibody. It binds to the soluble, membrane-bound IL-6 receptors and inhibits IL-6 mediated signaling. IL-6 can cause T-cell activation, acute-phase protein synthesis, and stimulation of inflammatory processes in diseases like rheumatoid arthritis.

Uses:

  • Rheumatoid arthritis - It is a biological DMARD and is indicated in adult patients having moderate to severe disease with inadequate response to one or more DMARDs.
  • Juvenile idiopathic arthritis - It can be given for active systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis(SJIA) or polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis(PJIA) in patients of 2 years of age or more.

Adverse effects:

Common adverse effects include upper respiratory infections, hypertension, headache, and elevation of hepatic enzymes. It is also associated with serious infections including TB and opportunistic infections. Neutropenia and reduction in platelet count can also occur.

Other options:

Option B- IL-2 receptor inhibitors are daclizumab, basiliximab. They are used as immunosuppressive agents following renal and heart transplants.

Option C- IL-4 receptor inhibitor is dupilumab. They have been shown to reduce exacerbations in asthma. 

Option D- IL-5 inhibitors are mepolizumab, reslizumab, benralizumab. They have been shown to reduce exacerbations in asthma. 

@

subject: Pharmacology
text: The extent of drug absorption is represented by:
expl:
Correct answer: B. Area under the curve

The extent of drug absorption is represented by the area under the curve.

The rate and extent of absorption of a drug from dosage form administered by any route refer to the bioavailability of a drug. Bioavailability is determined by the concentration-time curve in blood or by its excretion in urine. The area under the blood concentration-time curve (AUC) is proportional to the dose and the extent of bioavailability of a drug.

Bioavailability is defined as the fraction of unchanged drug that reaches systemic circulation. It can be represented by the formula:

Bioavailability(F) = Quantity of drug reaching systemic circulation/ Quantity of drug administered.

Bioavailability depends on two factors:

  • Absorption
  • 1st pass metabolism

The area under the plot of plasma concentration of a drug versus time after dosage is called the area under the curve or AUC. It can be used as a measure of the bioavailability of a drug and to calculate its clearance rate from the body. 

The image given below shows the AUC (bioavailability) in a plasma concentration-time curve:

 

Bioavailability of drug injected intravenously is 100%, but it is lower after oral ingestion because of incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism in the intestinal wall/liver.

The image below shows the difference between the bioavailability of drugs injected intravenously(iv) and orally(PO). Note the area under the respective curves is shaded in red and blue colours which represent the absorption of the drug.

subject: Pharmacology
text: Which of the following statement is correct regarding the given graph?

options.A: Drug 1 represents agonist ​and drug 2 represents inv​erse agonist
options.B: Drug 3 represents agonist ​and drug 4 represents inv​erse agonist
options.C: Drug 1 represents agonist ​and drug 4 represents inv​erse agonist
options.D: Drug 2 represents partial ​agonist and drug 3 repres​ents inverse agonist

expl:
Correct answer: C. Drug 1 represents agonist and drug 4 represents inverse agonist

The correct statement is Drug 1 represents agonist and drug 4 represents inverse agonist.

Graph 1 represents the agonist: An agonist is an agent which initiates the normal physiological response when combined with a receptor.

Example: Salbutamol is a beta-2 receptor agonist.

Graph 2 represents a partial agonist: An agent which produces a submaximal or partial effect when combined with a receptor.

Example: Buprenorphine and butorphanol are partial agonists at opioid receptors.

Graph 3 represents the antagonist: An agent which blocks or reduces the action of an agonist on a receptor, but does not have any effect of its own.

Example: Naltrexone and naloxone are antagonists at opioid receptors

Graph 4 represents an inverse agonist: An agent which activates a receptor to produce an effect in the opposite direction to that of the agonist.

Example: β-Carboline is an inverse agonist at benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptor.

subject: Pharmacology
text: Which among the following drugs is the new FDA approved immune check point inhibitor for carcinoma endometrium?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Pembrolizumab

The new FDA-approved immune checkpoint inhibitor for carcinoma endometrium is pembrolizumab.

Pembrolizumab acts by inhibiting programmed death receptor - 1 (PD-1) and was used for the treatment of advanced melanoma. Now, the FDA has approved the use of pembrolizumab for any cancer with mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency or high microsatellite instability (MSI-H).

On March 21, 2022, the food and drug administration approved pembrolizumab, as a single agent, for patients with advanced endometrial carcinoma that is microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) or mismatch repair deficient (dMMR), as determined by an FDA-approved test.

Other options:

Option A: Nivolumab is an immune checkpoint inhibitor that acts by inhibiting programmed death receptor - 1 (PD-1) and is used for the treatment of advanced melanoma and relapsed/refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma.

Option C:  Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits the HER2 receptor. It is used in the treatment of HER2-positive breast cancer.

Option D: Ipilimumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds to cytotoxic T lymphocyte–associated Protein 4 (CTLA-4) and is approved for the treatment of late-stage melanoma.

subject: Pharmacology
text: Which of the following is not an immune checkpoint inhibitor?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Cetuximab

Cetuximab is not an immune checkpoint inhibitor. Cetuximab is a monoclonal antibody against epidermal growth factor receptor(EGFR). It is used for the treatment of colon cancer and head and neck squamous cell cancer.

Other options.

Option A: Nivolumab is an immune checkpoint inhibitor. It acts by inhibiting programmed death receptor - 1 (PD-1) and is used for the treatment of advanced melanoma and classical Hodgkin lymphoma. 

Option B: Pembrolizumab is an immune checkpoint inhibitor. It acts by inhibiting programmed death receptor - 1 (PD-1) and is used for the treatment of advanced melanoma. In 2021, approval was granted for the treatment of patients with endometrial carcinoma that progressed after systemic treatment, in combination with lenvatinib.

Option C: Atezolimumab is an immune checkpoint inhibitor. It acts by inhibiting programmed death-ligand - 1 (PDL-1) and is used for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer. 

Important note:

The FDA on May 2021 approved the use of nivolumab in patients having completely resected esophageal or gastroesophageal junction cancers with residual pathologic disease who have received neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy.

subject: Pharmacology
text: NAPQI is the metabolite of which of the following drug toxicity?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Paracetamol

N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) is a metabolite of paracetamol drug toxicity. 

Paracetamol is an analgesic and antipyretic with weak anti-inflammatory action. It is mainly metabolized in the liver by conjugation with glucuronic acid and sulfate and is excreted in the urine.

At toxic doses, the glucuronide and sulfate conjugation pathway becomes saturated. The metabolites of paracetamol get converted into NAPQI. NAPQI is highly reactive and causes enzymatic dysfunction in the liver. Normally, minor amounts of NAPQI produced in our body are rapidly eliminated by conjugation with reduced glutathione(GSH) and then excreted into the urine.

Therefore, paracetamol toxicity is treated with N-acetyl cysteine(NAC), which replenishes GSH. NAC thereby helps in the excretion of NAPQI from the body. N-acetyl cysteine is an anti-oxidant and functions by detoxifying NAPQI.

Paracetamol poisoning is the most common cause of liver failure necessitating transplantation.

The maximum dose of acetaminophen that can be given is 4 g/day.

subject: Pharmacology
text: Identify the correct match, regarding the drug and its adverse effect.
expl:
Correct answer: D. Verapamil - constipation

The correct match is verapamil causes constipation.

Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker used for the treatment of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, and atrial flutter. Bradycardia and constipation are the important side effects of verapamil.

Other options:

Option A: Hydralazine is a vasodilator used in the treatment of heart failure, and hypertensive emergencies, especially preeclampsia. The drug is used as a combination pill containing isosorbide dinitrate (BiDil) in the treatment of heart failure. The important side effect of hydralazine is drug-induced lupus.

Option B: Atenolol is a cardioselective beta-1 blocker used in the treatment of angina and hypertension. Atenolol doesn't cause hemolytic anemia.

Option C: Aliskiren is a direct renin inhibitor used as an alternative antihypertensive drug for those who do not respond or do not tolerate 1st line drugs. The side effect of aliskiren is hyperkalemia and not hypokalemia.

subject: Pharmacology
text: A lady who had undergone mastectomy for breast cancer is being treated with tamoxifen. How long should it be stopped for before she can conceive?

options.D: Can be stopped and conceiv​ed soon after stopping

expl:
Correct answer: B. 3 months

In a post-mastectomy patient undergoing therapy with tamoxifen, it should be stopped for 3 months before she can conceive.

Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) and is used as a chemotherapeutic agent in receptor positive breast cancer patients to prevent recurrence after surgery. It is the drug of choice in pre-menopausal women. It has an agonistic action on the endometrium, leading to an increased risk of endometrial cancers (2 fold risk). Hence, it is not used in post-menopausal women.

It is contraindicated in pregnancy due to teratogenic effects such as craniofacial abnormalities and reproductive tract abnormalities. For the same reason, it has to be stopped for 3 months (due to long half-life) prior to conceiving. It is also stopped during lactation as it is secreted in breast milk. Other complications of tamoxifen include deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and hot flashes.

Other breast cancer risk reduction techniques:

  1. Lifestyle modification: Low-calorie diet, daily exercise, no smoking, no drinking, etc.
  2. More frequent screening with mammogram +/- MRI
  3. Chemoprevention: Preferred in women >35 years of age in patients who are ER/PR positive. Given for 5-10 years.
    • SERMS (selective estrogen receptor modulators) - Tamoxifen and raloxifene. These have adverse effects. 
    • Aromatase Inhibitors (AIs): They are used only in post-menopausal women.
  4. Risk-reduction surgeries: preferred in patients with BRCA1/2 mutations or patients with first-degree relatives with breast cancers. Provides >90% risk-reduction. preferred in patients who have completed their family.
    • Bilateral mastectomy
    • Salpingo-oophorectomy: Best results when done < 40 years of age.

subject: Pharmacology
text: A young boy with a history of multiple blood transfusions presents with bone pain for the past 6 months.  A peripheral smear showed sickle-shaped RBCs. Which of the following drugs are not used in the treatment of his condition?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Bebtelovimab

Bebtelovimab is not used in the treatment of sickle cell disease. The clinical features of multiple blood transfusions, bone pain, and sickle cells on peripheral smear are suggestive of sickle cell disease.

Bebtelovimab is the new monoclonal antibody used for the treatment of COVID-19. It works by binding to the spike protein of the COVID-19 virus. It has been found useful in reducing the risk of hospitalization or death. Bebtelovimab retains the activity against the omicron variant.

Other options:

Option B: Voxelotor is an inhibitor of hemoglobin S polymerase and stabilizer of sickle cell hemoglobin (HbS) that is used in the therapy of sickle cell disease.

Option C: Hydroxyurea improves fetal haemoglobin (HbF) and is the primary drug for controlling HbS in sickle cell disease. Thus improving the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood. Hydroxyurea also inhibits the enzyme ribonucleotide reductase (RNR), which is a rate-limiting step in the biosynthesis of DNA. This property of hydroxyurea is used in the treatment of various cancers, and myeloproliferative disorders like chronic myelogenous leukemia, and polycythemia.

Option D: L-glutamine is a naturally occurring amino acid with antioxidant properties. It increases the availability of reduced glutathione which may lessen oxidative damage in sickle red blood cells.

subject: Pharmacology
text: The half-life of letrozole is:
expl:
Correct answer: A. 45 hours

The half-life of letrozole is 45 hours.

Letrozole is a reversible aromatase inhibitor. It is a non-steroidal compound that inhibits the aromatization of estrogen thereby causing estrogen depletion. Letrozole is rapidly absorbed with 99.9% oral bioavailability and has a t½ of around 41 hours.

Letrozole is used as the first-line drug for estrogen-positive breast cancer following mastectomy in post-menopausal women.

Adverse effects of letrozole are due to the depletion of estrogen. The commonly seen adverse effects are hot flashes, vaginal dryness, nausea, diarrhea, dyspepsia, accelerated bone loss, and thinning of hair.

subject: Pharmacology
text: Identify the false statement about eicosanoids.
expl:
Correct answer: A. Synthesized from arginine

A false statement about eicosanoids is they are synthesized from arginine. Eicosanoids are synthesized from arachidonic acid (Option B)

Eicosanoids are the most universally distributed autocoids in the body. Prostaglandins, thromboxanes, and leukotrienes comprise eicosanoids. Every cell is capable of synthesizing one or more eicosanoids. Platelets primarily synthesize thromboxanes (Option D).

Eicosanoids are synthesized from arachidonic acid. Arachidonic acid is derived from membrane phospholipids. The release of arachidonic acid (AA) from the membrane phospholipids is mainly mediated by phospholipase A.

AA is metabolized by cyclooxygenases to produce prostaglandins and lipoxygenases to produce leukotrienes and lipoxins.

Inhibitors of metabolism of arachidonic acid:

  • Corticosteroids cause inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis by inhibiting phospholipase A2.
  • Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory (NSAIDs) drugs inhibit the synthesis of prostaglandins by inhibiting the enzyme cyclooxygenase.
  • Zileuton inhibits the enzyme lipoxygenase thereby decreasing the synthesis of leukotrienes.

Chemically, all prostaglandins are considered to be derivatives of prostanoic acid, having a five-carbon ring (Option C).

subject: Pharmacology
text: The given diagram shows the steps in bacterial cell wall formation. Identify the site of action of beta-lactam antibiotics.
expl:
Correct answer: D. 4

Beta lactams act on step 4 in the given image.

Mechanism of action of beta-lactams: They are the cell wall synthesis inhibitor. The β-lactam antibiotics inhibit this last step in peptidoglycan synthesis. They inhibit the enzyme transpeptidase which is required for cross-linking of the peptidoglycan chain. Transpeptidases cleave the terminal D-alanine of the peptide chains and form cross-linkages between them. This cross-linking provides rigidity and stability to the cell wall.   

Transpeptidases and other related proteins constitute penicillin-binding proteins(PBP) and, are located in the bacterial cell membrane. β-lactam antibiotics are bactericidal. This is because bacterias swell and burst due to deficient cell walls when they divide in the presence of β-lactam antibiotics. Penicillins, cephalosporins, monobactams, and carbapenems are examples of β-lactam antibiotics.

Gram-positive bacteria are more susceptible to β-lactam antibiotics than gram-negative because their cell wall is almost entirely made of peptidoglycan.

Resistance to β-lactam antibiotics develops due to the production of the beta-lactamase enzyme and the development of altered penicillin-binding proteins like in methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). β-lactamases inactivate β-lactam antibiotics by opening the β-lactam ring. This could be overcome by using drugs that inhibit this enzyme. Examples of β-lactamase inhibitors are clavulanic acid, sulbactam, and tazobactam.

Other options:

Option A: Fosfomycin inhibits step 1 in the image. It inhibits the cytoplasmic enzyme enol pyruvate transferase that catalyses the initial step in the bacterial cell wall and hence cell wall synthesis. It is used for the treatment of urinary tract infections.

Option B: Bacitracin inhibits step 2 in the image. It is a cell wall synthesis inhibitor that interferes with dephosphorylation in the cycling of the lipid carrier which transfers peptidoglycan subunits to the growing cell wall. It is only given for topical application because of its severe nephrotoxicity when given systemically.

Option C: Vancomycin inhibits step 3 in the image. It binds to the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of the newly formed peptidoglycan pentapeptide. This prevents further elongation of the peptidoglycan and its cross-linking. It is used against MRSA and Clostridium difficile infection. Redman syndrome due to histamine release following infusion is an important side effect.

Note: The FDA has approved the use of cefepime-enmetazobactam, a combination of a fourth-generation cephalosporin and beta-lactamase inhibitor for use in complicated UTIs (including pyelonephritis).

subject: Pharmacology
text: Phospholipase C acts via which of the following G protein-coupled receptors?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Gq

Phospholipase C acts via the Gq type of G protein-coupled receptors.

G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are cell membrane receptors that span across the membrane 7 times. They also serve as receptors for various peptide hormones, neurotransmitters, amino acids, etc.

Subtypes of GPCRs are distinguished by their alpha subunits. The important subtypes of GPCRs are Gs, Gp, Gq, and Go.

GPCRs act via various second messengers. The important ones with their action on the effector are:

  • Gs causes activation of adenylyl cyclase and results in Ca2+ channel opening.
  • Gi causes inhibition of adenylyl cyclase and results in K+ channel opening.
  • Go causes Ca2+ channel inhibition.
  • Gq causes activation of phospholipase C which generates the second messengers inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG). The water-soluble IP3 diffuses to the cytosol and mobilizes Ca2+ from endoplasmic reticular depots.
