subject: Pathology
text:
Match the following cell types with their associated malignancy.

1. Popcorn cell a. Acute promyelocytic leukemia
2. Faggot cell b. Lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma
3. Cerebriform nuclei c. Burkitt lymphoma
4. Starry sky d. Sezary syndrome
expl:
Correct answer: A. 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c

The correct matches are as follows:

1. Popcorn cell b. Lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma
2. Faggot cell a. Acute promyelocytic leukemia
3. Cerebriform nuclei d. Sezary syndrome
4. Starry sky c. Burkitt lymphoma

 

Popcorn cell is a lymphohistiocytic (L&H) variant of Reed Steenberg (RS) cells that are characteristic of lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma. It has a delicate multilobed, puffy nucleus resembling popped corn. The image below shows a popcorn cell seen in lymphocytic predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma.

Multiple Auer rods clustered together within a single cell resembling a bundle of sticks are known as faggot cells and are highly suggestive of acute promyelocytic leukemia. Histopathology from bone marrow aspirate reveals numerous Auer rods (needle-like azurophilic granules) in the cytoplasm of the promyelocytes. Faggot cells are shown below.

Sézary-Lutzner cells - cells with cerebriform nuclei (infolded/hyper-convoluted nuclear membrane).

The histological hallmark of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides type) is the presence of Sezary-Lutzner cells, which form band-like aggregates within the superficial dermis and invade the epidermis as single cells and small clusters called Pautrier microabscess (marked by arrow). These cells have markedly infolded nuclear membranes giving them a cerebriform contour as seen below.

Microscopy in Burkitt lymphoma shows a characteristic starry sky pattern. The neoplastic cells are homogeneous, medium-sized B cells with frequent mitotic figures and reactive macrophages scattered through the tumor, with their pale cytoplasm in a background of blue-staining tumor cells giving the tumor a so-called "starry sky" appearance.

The image given below shows a starry sky pattern seen in Burkitt lymphoma.

subject: Pathology
text: Hereditary angioedema is due to a defect in which of the proteins mentioned below?
expl:
Correct answer: A. C1 inhibitor

Hereditary angioedema is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by a deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitors. C1 esterase inhibitors usually target proteases like C1r and C1s, factor XII and the kallikrein system. Therefore, their deficiency leads to unregulated activation of kallikrein, leading to increased bradykinin.

Clinical features include swelling of the skin and mucosal surfaces, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, which may be aggravated after minor trauma or emotional stress. The condition can be treated by giving C1 inhibitor concentrates from human plasma. 

The main inflammatory mediator responsible for these symptoms is bradykinin. Bradykinin is an inflammatory mediator formed by the cleavage of kininogen, in the presence of the enzyme kallikrein. Bradykinin has the following effects:

  • Increases the vascular permeability
  • Causes contraction of smooth muscle
  • Dilates the blood vessel 
  • Mediates pain

Other options:

Options B and C: Decay-accelerating factor (DAF) and CD59 are two proteins that are linked by a glycophosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor to the plasma membrane. DAF prevents the formation of C3 convertases and CD59 inhibits the formation of the MAC. An acquired deficiency of the enzyme that creates GPI anchors leads to a deficiency of these regulators and excessive complement activation and lysis of red cells resulting in Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria(PNH).

During inflammation, C5a (Option D), C3a, and C4a, which are all cleavage products of their corresponding complement components, stimulate mast cells to release histamine. They have effects similar to those of mast cell mediators involved in anaphylactic reactions and therefore, are called anaphylatoxins. C5a is also chemotactic for neutrophils, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils. Additionally, it activates the lipooxygenase pathway of arachidonic acid metabolism in neutrophils and monocytes, resulting in the further release of inflammatory mediators.

subject: Pathology
text:
A 35-year-old woman presents with fatigue. Investigations revealed the following: Hb, 5 gm %; MCH, 24; low MCV; leukocytes, 11,000/uL, and platelets, 5 lakhs. The peripheral smear is shown below. What is the diagnosis?

Normal values:

  • Mean cell volume (MCV): 90 ± 8 fL
  • Mean cell Hb (MCH): 30 ± 3 pg
expl:
Correct answer: B. Iron-deficiency anemia

The given scenario of a 35 year old woman, her iron profile and peripheral smear showing microcytic hypochromic anemia are suggestive of iron-deficiency anemia (IDA).

IDA is an example of microcytic hypochromic anemia. The causes of IDA can be inadequate diet, impaired reabsorption, increased requirement and increased blood loss.

The manifestations of IDA depend upon the underlying cause. In general, IDA presents with koilonychia, alopecia, atrophic changes in the tongue, gastric mucosa, malabsorbtion and pica (craving for consumption of non-edible materials)

Peripheral smears show small and pale red cells typically described as microcytic (reduced MCV) and hypochromic (enlarged zone of central pallor). Poikilocytosis can be seen in the form of elongated red cells, known as pencil cells. Target cells can be found in cases of severe IDA.

Diagnosis is mainly by laboratory studies. The typical findings are:

  • Low hemoglobin and hematocrit
  • Low serum iron and ferretin
  • Increased Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC)
  • Hepcidin is low (decreased stores of iron inhibit hepcidin synthesis)

IDA is treated by giving oral and parenteral preparations if iron or packed cell transfusion depending upon the severity of the anemia.

Option A: Megaloblastic anemia is defined by a high MCV

Option C: Thalassemia presents much earlier in infancy, with reduced MCV and a normal/increased RBC count

Option D: Essential thrombocytosis is characterized by isolated rise in platelet count (>450,000) along with normal hemoglobin, hematocrit and iron stores.

text:
Which of the following statements is true about interleukin-12?

1. Increases production of interferon-γ
2. Inhibits T cells
3. Inhibits B cells
4. Produced by macrophages
expl:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 4

The true statements are that interleukin-12 (IL-12) is produced by macrophages and increases the production of interferon-γ (IFN-γ).

IL-12 is produced by dendritic cells and macrophages. Its principle actions are to promote the production of IFN-γ, which drives TH1-type responses and further stimulates macrophage activation. It also promotes the differentiation of CD4+ T-cells to Th1 cells.

subject: Pathology
text:
A chronic smoker presents to the clinic with shortness of breath. A mass is noted at the lower lobe periphery of the lung. A diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma is made. The biopsy will be positive for:

1. Thyroid transcription factor-1 
2. p40
3. Napsin A
4. Chromogranin
expl:
Correct answer: A. 1, 3

The biopsy of adenocarcinoma of the lung will be positive for thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1) and napsin A.

Adenocarcinoma is an invasive malignant epithelial tumor with glandular differentiation or mucin production by the tumor cells. It is associated with tobacco smoking, but less so than other histologic subtypes. It is the most common subtype in non-smokers and is associated with the loss of function of EGFR, ALK, ROS1, MET or RET genes.

The majority express TTF-1, which is a protein required for normal lung development. Napsin A is a new marker and is more sensitive and specific than TTF-1 in the diagnosis of adenocarcinoma.

Adenocarcinomas grow in various patterns: acinar, lepidic, papillary, micropapillary, and solid. The lesions are small and are usually located in the periphery.  At the periphery of the tumor there is often a lepidic pattern of spread, in which the tumor cells “crawl” along normal-appearing alveolar septa. 

Clinical features usually have an insidious onset. The incidence is usually at age 50 or more. The major presenting complaints are cough, weight loss, chest pain, and dyspnea.    

Other options:

Option B: p40, along with p63 is a marker for squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.

Option D: Chromogranin is a marker for small cell carcinoma of the lung.

subject: Pathology
text: The following image shows an instrument used to estimate hemoglobin levels. What does it measure?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Acid hematin

The instrument in the image is Sahli's hemoglobinometer and is used to measure acid hematin levels of a given blood sample. 

In Sahli's method, oxyhemoglobin is converted to acid hematin with the action of dilute hydrochloric acid (N/10 HCl). The brown color of the acid hematin is matched to its intensity with a standard brown glass comparator in a visual colorimeter called Sahli’s colorimeter.

Sahli's method is a simple bedside test and is cost-effective. However, it has some disadvantages which include visual errors, inability to measure other forms of hemoglobin, fading of the comparator over time, and the color of acid hematin fading quickly.

Perl's Prussian blue stain is used in histopathological studies to detect the presence of iron in the specimen. Iron is stained blue with this stain.

It is used in hereditary hemochromatosis to stain liver tissue, which shows hepatocellular iron. It also stains the iron-laden mitochondria of ring sideroblasts seen in lead toxicity and myelodysplastic syndrome

subject: Pathology
text: A woman presents with lesions on the inner thighs and peri-anal region. They are nodular,  4-6 mm in size, and appear pale. The histopathological image shows multiple intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies consistent with Henderson-Patterson bodies. The diagnosis is:
expl:
Correct answer: C. Molluscum contagiosum

The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the histological image is molluscum contagiosum, which shows intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies, called Henderson–Patterson bodies or molluscum bodies.

Infection is usually spread by direct contact, particularly among children and young adults. Multiple lesions occur on the skin and mucous membranes, with a predilection for the trunk and anogenital areas. Individual lesions are firm, pruritic, pink to skin-colored umbilicated papules. A curd-like material can be expressed from the central umbilication.

Smearing this material onto a glass slide followed by Giemsa staining shows diagnostic molluscum bodies, which are ellipsoid, homogeneous, cytoplasmic inclusion bodies that are found in the cells of the stratum granulosum and the stratum corneum and are up to 35 μm in size.

The image below shows umbilicated papules of molluscum contagiosum. 

 

Other options: 

Option A: Trichodysplasia spinulosa is a condition characterized by painless erythematous papules on the face with folliculocentric keratin spines. It is caused by trichodysplasia spinulosa-associated polyomavirus. Histologic features are keratin plugging, abundant dystrophic and cornfield inner root sheath epithelium, and numerous, large eosinophilic trichohyalin granules.

Option B: Koilocytes are characteristically seen in HPV infections, such as condylomata acuminata. Koilocytes are lining cells which have perinuclear cytoplasmic vacuolization.

Option D: Donovan bodies are seen in donovanosis, caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. Donovan bodies are minute, encapsulated coccobacilli in macrophages, which can be demonstrated in Giemsa-stained smears of the exudate.

subject: Pathology
text: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is caused by all of the following cytokines except:
expl:
Correct answer: D. INF- γ

INF-γ is not involved in Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (JHR).

JHR is a condition that occurs in patients infected by spirochetes who undergo antibiotic treatment. The reaction occurs within 24 hours of antibiotic treatment. Clinical features are fever, chills, nausea and vomiting, tachycardia, hypotension, flushing, myalgia, and exacerbation of skin lesions.

Syphilis is the leading spirochetal infection associated with JHR. Other infections are Lyme disease, louse-borne relapsing fever, leptospirosis, and tick-borne relapsing fever. Antibiotics that have been most associated are penicillins, tetracyclines, and erythromycin.

Mild reactions are self-limiting and often resolve spontaneously within 24 hours. Prevention of the JHR is by giving TNF-alpha antibodies and in some cases steroids.

subject: Pathology
text: Choose the correct statement regarding the telomerase theory of aging.

options.A: Telomere stability is asso‍ciated with aging
options.B: Abnormal telomerase activa‍tion is associated with a​ging
options.C: Decreased telomere length ‍is associated with aging
options.D: Increased telomere length ‍is associated with aging

expl:
Correct answer: C. Decreased telomere length is associated with aging

A decreased telomere length is associated with aging.

Telomeres are short TG-rich repeated sequences of DNA present at the ends of linear eukaryotic chromosomes. Telomeres do not code for any proteins. They are important for ensuring the complete replication of chromosome ends and for protecting the ends from fusion and degradation.

Normally, with every cell division, there is some shortening of telomeres at the ends of chromosomes. Once the telomeres are shortened beyond a certain point, it may cause cell-cycle arrest or apoptosis. This is called replicative senescence.

Telomerase is the enzyme that prevents the shortening of telomeres. It is a specialized RNA-protein complex that uses its own RNA as a template for adding nucleotides to the ends of chromosomes.

This enzyme is usually present in germ cells but is absent in most somatic cells. Therefore most of the somatic cells age, their telomeres become shorter and they exit the cell cycle, resulting in an inability to generate new cells to replace damaged cells. Abnormal telomerase reactivation in somatic cells leads to evasion of senescence and apoptosis. It enables the cells to divide several times than usual.

In stem cells and cancer cells, telomerase is usually reactivated and telomere length is stabilized, allowing the cells to proliferate indefinitely.

subject: Pathology
text: A child presents with recurrent chest infections and abdominal pain. There is a history of 1 blood transfusion in the past. On examination, he had icterus and mild splenomegaly. Electrophoresis shows increased HbA2, HbF, and S spike. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Sickle cell disease

The given scenario with electrophoresis showing increased HbA2, HbF, and S spike is suggestive of sickle cell disease. 

Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to the point mutation in the β-globin gene which results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. This causes the production of sickle-shaped red blood cells due to the polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbS).

Factors that predispose to sickling are infection, dehydration, and acidosis.

The clinical features of sickle cell disease are due to the tendency of HbS molecules to stack into polymers when deoxygenated. The features are:

  • Moderately severe hemolytic anemia with jaundice.
  • Painful bone crisis- hand-foot syndrome or dactylitis of the bones of hands and feet.
  • Acute chest syndrome typically presents with fever, cough, chest pain, and pulmonary infiltrates.
  • Hyposthenuria- inability to concentrate urine.
  • Aplastic crisis stems from the infection of red cell progenitors by parvovirus B19, which causes a transient cessation of erythropoiesis and a sudden worsening of the anemia.
  • Spleen
    • In children- splenic sequestration crises occur which results in splenomegaly due to red pulp congestion.
    • Adolescence or early adulthood- autosplenectomy occurs due to splenic infarction, fibrosis, and progressive shrinkage.
    • Increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms like pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenza septicemia, but can be reduced by vaccination and prophylactic antibiotics.
  • Other clinical features- priapism, leg ulcers, stroke, retinopathy, pigment gallstones, and growth retardation.

The diagnosis is suggested by the clinical findings, the presence of irreversibly sickled red cells on peripheral smear, and hemoglobin electrophoresis showing increased levels of HbA2, HbF, and S spike. The changes in the skull resemble a crewcut in radiographic studies as a result of compensatory erythroid hyperplasia.

The image given below shows the sickling of RBCs in sickle cell disease.

The image given below shows Howell-Jolly bodies seen in asplenia.

Note: The sickle cell trait protects against falciparum malaria in certain African populations.

Other options:

Option A: Beta-thalassemia is an autosomal codominant disorder, caused by mutations in alpha or beta globin that reduce hemoglobin synthesis. Peripheral smear shows microcytic, hypochromic cells with anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, target cells, and basophilic stippling. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows increased HbF and HbA2.

Option B: HbC disease is caused by mutation in the beta-globin chain in which glutamate is replaced by lysine in the sixth position of the beta-globin chain. Patients usually present with very mild anemia and microcytosis. Peripheral smear shows hexagonal HbC crystals. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows increased HbC levels.

Option D: Acute coronary syndrome is very rare in children and may be associated with Kawasaki disease. Children with Kawasaki disease present with fever, conjunctival ingestion, strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, and hand and foot changes. They are treated with intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin.

subject: Pathology
text: Why do neoplastic cells utilize Warburg metabolism?

options.A: It decreases glucose utili‍sation by neoplastic cell​s
options.B: It forms metabolic interme‍diates which are needed f​or cell growth and multip​lication
options.C: It provides more energy in‍ the form of increased AT​P production
options.D: It prevents apoptosis and ‍makes the cancer cells im​mortal

expl:
Correct answer: B. It forms metabolic intermediates which are needed for cell growth and multiplication

Neoplastic cells utilize Warburg metabolism for the generation of metabolic intermediates, which are needed for cell growth and multiplication.

The Warburg Effect is a phenomenon in which there is an increase in the rate of glucose uptake and conversion into lactate(fermentation), even in the presence of oxygen. Cancer cells derive energy mainly from glycolysis. 

Cancer cells utilize glycolysis (2 ATP) over mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (36 ATP) for glucose metabolism, even though the latter produces more ATP. It is because pure oxidative phosphorylation produces abundant ATP, but also burns glucose to CO2 and H2O, leaving no carbon moieties suitable for use as building blocks for lipids or proteins.

For this reason, rapidly growing cells, by undergoing glycolysis, produce carbon moieties that are needed for growth and cellular maintenance.

The image given below shows the comparison of glucose metabolism in normal cells versus cancer cells.

As a result of decreased ATP production, the main metabolic function of mitochondria in growing cells is not to generate ATP, but to carry
out reactions that generate cellular building blocks. For example, lipid biosynthesis.

Warburg effect is produced by growth factor receptors downstream signalling pathways. These include receptor tyrosine kinase/PI3K/AKT and MYC.

Clinically, cancer cells exhibiting the Warburg effect show a property of glucose hunger. This is used to visualize them via positron emission tomography (PET) scanning.

subject: Pathology
text: An elderly patient presents with anemia and hemoglobinuria. Investigations reveal increased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). The peripheral smear image is given below. Which of the following physical examination findings can support the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Mechanical second heart sound

The above scenario with anemia, increased LDH, and hemoglobinuria along with peripheral smear showing schistocytes are suggestive of macroangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA). The presence of a mechanical second heart sound can support the diagnosis. 

Macroangiopathic hemolytic anemia is a type of hemolytic anemia that results from trauma to red cells by artificial mechanical cardiac valves that produce turbulent blood flow and pressure gradients that cause hemolysis from shear forces. This traumatic damage leads to intravascular hemolysis and the appearance of red cell fragments (schistocytes), burr cells, helmet cells, and triangle cells in blood smears.

The given below peripheral smear shows schistocytes and helmet cells.

Laboratory findings in hemolytic anemia resulting from trauma to red cells:

  • Hemoglobin- decreased
  • Reticulocytes- increased
  • Platelets- normal
  • Unconjugated bilirubin- increased
  • Lactate dehydrogenase- increased
  • Haptoglobin- decreased
  • Hemoglobinuria due to intravascular hemolysis

Treatment is conservative. But, if more than mild anemia develops, reintervention to correct regurgitation may be required.

Option A: Splenomegaly is seen in various disorders of white and red cells. But splenomegaly in intravascular hemolysis is less likely.

Option B: Frontal bossing is seen in thalassemia due to expansion of hematopoietically active marrow. An X-ray of the skull shows a 'crewcut' appearance. Peripheral smear in thalassemia shows microcytic hypochromic cells with anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, and target cells.

Option D: Goiter is usually associated with iron deficiency anemia. A peripheral smear shows microcytic hypochromic cells.

subject: Pathology
text: All of the following statements are true regarding neutrophil extracellular trapping (NET) except that

options.A: It is detected in blood du‍ring sepsis.
options.B: It is produced in response‍ to bacterial infection.
options.D: It is chromatin with antib‍acterial enzymes.

expl:
Correct answer: C. Mitochondrial DNA is seen.

Mitochondrial DNA is not seen in neutrophil extracellular traps (NET).

Neutrophilic extracellular traps are networks of extracellular fibers that provide a high concentration of antimicrobial substances at the site of infection and prevent the spread of the microbes by trapping them in the fibrils.

Neutrophilic extracellular traps (NET) are the meshwork of nuclear chromatin of neutrophils. The loss of nuclei leads to the death of the neutrophils. They concentrate antimicrobial peptides and enzymes to fight against bacteria and fungus (not viruses). They are detected in the blood during sepsis. They are produced by neutrophils in response to:

  • Infectious pathogens: mainly bacteria and fungi
  • Inflammatory mediators: chemokines, cytokines (mainly interferons), complement proteins, and reactive oxygen species (ROS)

Note: The nuclear chromatin in the NETs, which includes histones and associated DNA, has been postulated to be a source of nuclear antigens in systemic autoimmune diseases, particularly systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

subject: Pathology
text: A patient underwent cystoscopy, which showed multiple yellow-white plaques in the trigone of the bladder. The histopathology image is given below. What is the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Malakoplakia

The cystoscopy findings of multiple yellow-white plaques in the trigone of the bladder and histopathology image showing Michaelis–Gutmann bodies are consistent with the diagnosis of malakoplakia.

Malakoplakia is a rare inflammatory reaction seen in chronic cystitis. It is caused due to acquired defects in phagocyte function, chronic bacterial infection by Escherichia coli or Proteus species, and immunosuppression (renal transplant patients).

The term malakoplakia means soft plaques. Grossly, malakoplakia appears as soft, yellow, slightly raised mucosal plaques. 

Microscopically, they are composed of large, foamy macrophages mixed with occasional multinucleate giant cells and lymphocytes. The macrophages in malakoplakia have abundant granular cytoplasm due to phagosomes stuffed with undigested bacterial products and intracellular deposition of calcium and iron within enlarged lysosomes form laminated basophilic concretions. These are known as Michaelis–Gutmann bodies, pathognomonic of malakoplakia (shown below).

 

The image given below shows the Von Kossa stain demonstrating calcium and iron-containing Michaelis-Gutman bodies (MG bodies) in malakoplakia.

 

Note: Xanthogranulomatous cystitis is morphologically and probably pathogenetically similar to malakoplakia, but it lacks Michaelis–Gutmann bodies.

Other options:

Option A: Interstitial cystitis, also known as chronic pelvic pain syndrome, is a disorder of the urinary bladder that presents with urinary tract symptoms of more than six weeks duration of unknown etiology. Grossly, it is associated with chronic mucosal ulcers called Hunner's ulcers. Microscopically, there is a non-specific increase in mast cells in the submucosa. Biopsy should be done in all cases to rule out carcinoma in situ.

The cystoscopy image shows Hunner's ulcer, seen in interstitial cystitis.

 

Option C: Polypoid cystitis is an inflammatory lesion resulting from irritation of the bladder mucosa, most commonly due to indwelling catheters. The urothelium is thrown into broad bulbous polypoid projections due to marked submucosal edema. They must be differentiated from papillary urothelial carcinoma.

The given image below shows polypoid cystitis showing broad polypoid growth, prominent blood vessels, and metaplastic urothelium in H&E stain.

 

Option D: Acute cystitis is characterized by an inflammation of the urinary bladder following infection, most commonly by Escherichia coli, Proteus, Klebsiella, and Enterobacter. It is more commonly seen in women due to the short urethra. Microscopically, there is hyperemia and neutrophilic infiltration of the mucosa.

subject: Pathology
text: Which of the following measures are associated with an increased life span?

options.A: Moderate or regular exerci‍se for 30 min
options.D: Pharmacological interventi‍on with proton pump inhib​itors

expl:
Correct answer: C. Decreasing calorie intake by 30 percent

Decreasing calorie intake by 30 percent will increase lifespan.

Caloric restriction reduces both the degree of oxidative damage and the associated decline in function. It decreases the steady-state concentrations of products of oxidative damage to proteins, DNA, and lipids. This is due to decreased production of mitochondrial superoxide anion and hydrogen peroxide and increased antioxidant production. Overall, caloric restriction depresses the rate of energy metabolism.

Caloric restriction increases longevity both by reducing the signaling intensity of the insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) pathway and by increasing sirtuins (NAD-dependent protein deacetylases).

The attenuation of IGF-1 signaling leads to lower rates of cell growth and metabolism that reduces cellular damage. A similar effect is produced by rapamycin. An increase in sirtuins (particularly sirtuin-6) promotes the expression of several genes whose products increase longevity by activating DNA repair enzymes through deacylation.

Caloric restriction delays the onset of age-associated diseases such as cancer (including lymphomas and breast and prostate cancers), nephropathy, and cataracts. The onset of diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and the development of autoimmune diseases is also decreased by caloric restriction.

subject: Pathology
text: A 56-year-old man was diagnosed with COVID-19 and was put on mechanical ventilation. He passed away after a week. What is the likely post-mortem change seen in the lungs?

options.A: Thick layer of fibrin lini‍ng the alveoli
options.D: Pulmonary artery hypertrop‍hy with increased resista​nce

expl:
Correct answer: A. Thick layer of fibrin lining the alveoli

The clinical scenario of a patient with COVID-19 pneumonia on mechanical ventilation is suggestive of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). A thick layer of fibrin or waxy hyaline membranes lining the alveolar walls are characteristic of ARDS.

COVID-19 is a respiratory disease caused by SARS-CoV-2. These are enveloped positive-sense RNA viruses. The spread of SARS-CoV-2 is believed to be primarily via respiratory droplets, direct contact, airborne, and fomites.

The major complication in patients with severe COVID-19 is ARDS requiring oxygen therapy and mechanical ventilation. ARDS is a clinical syndrome characterized by acute onset, severe dyspnea, tachypnea, hypoxemia, and pulmonary infiltrates leading to respiratory failure.

Etiological factors can be divided into direct and indirect causes of lung injury as follows:

Direct lung injury Indirect lung injury
Pneumonia Sepsis
Aspiration of gastric contents Transfusions
Near drowning Drug overdose
Toxic inhalational injury Multiple transfusions
Pulmonary contusion Pancreatitis
COVID-19 Severe trauma like burns, flail chest, head trauma, multiple bone fractures

Damage to the endothelial and alveolar epithelial cells, with inflammation, is the key initiating event and the basis of lung damage. Neutrophils play a significant role in tissue injury in this condition.

There are three stages in the development of ARDS:

  1. Exudative phase- occurs for the first 7 days of the illness. This is associated with damage to alveolar-capillary endothelial cells and type I pneumocytes. This results in a breach in the tight alveolar barrier. The release of proinflammatory cytokines leads to the recruitment of neutrophils and the development of a hyaline membrane in the alveoli.
  2. Proliferative phase- occurs from day 7-21. Recovery from mechanical ventilation is seen in most patients.
  3. Fibrotic phase- is associated with increased mortality. Extensive alveolar duct and interstitial fibrosis are seen.

The image given below shows hyaline membrane formation in the alveolar walls seen in ARDS.

The chest X-ray features in ARDS usually develop 12-24 hours after initial lung insult as a result of proteinaceous interstitial edema. Within one week, a hyaline membrane occurs due to type 1 pneumocyte damage. There are diffuse bilateral coalescent opacities consistent with pulmonary edema. 

The image given below shows chest x-ray findings seen in ARDS.

Berlin's definition of ARDS predicts increased mortality. It considers the following parameters:

  1. Chest X-ray showing bilateral opacities
  2. Respiratory failure within 1 week of alveolar insult
  3. Decreased PaO2/FiO2 ratio to less than 300
  4. Symptoms of respiratory failure are not due to heart failure/fluid overload

Diagnosis of COVID-19 is done by nucleic acid amplification testing of respiratory tract secretions by nasopharyngeal swab. It is associated with elevated inflammatory markers, such as interleukin 6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor, ferritin, C-reactive protein, lactate dehydrogenase, and D-dimer.

Chest CT may be more sensitive than radiographs, but CT should be used principally for medical management of respiratory disease, not as a primary diagnostic tool for COVID-19.

The image given below shows the management of COVID-19 infection.

subject: Pathology
text: A female patient presented with fatigue. Routine complete blood count analysis showed hemoglobin of 9 g/dL, MCV 60fL, and RBC count of 5.2 million. A peripheral smear showed microcytic hypochromic anemia. Which of the following is the next best investigation for this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: B. HbA2 levels

The next best investigation for this patient would be determining the HbA2 levels, as the history of reduced hemoglobin, reduced MCV (microcytic anemia) and normal to high RBC count is suggestive of thalassemia.

The MCV count divided by the RBC count is called the Mentzer index, which is lower than 13 in thalassemia due to the normal to high RBC count in the denominator. In iron deficiency anemia, it is higher than 13 as the MCV and the RBC count both are reduced.

Alpha- and beta-thalassemia are inherited disorders in which there is reduced production of alpha-globin or beta-globin chains, respectively. This leads to precipitation of the excess (unpaired) chains, interfering with red blood cell (RBC) production and survival.

Clinical features in thalassemia include anemia, jaundice, skeletal deformities including facial deformities, changes in body habitus, growth impairment, and hepatosplenomegaly. Due to frequent blood transfusions, iron overload is also seen. 

Peripheral smear is likely to show microcytic hypochromic anemia with target cells, teardrop cells, and some coarse basophilic stippling in certain cases.

The image given below shows peripheral smear findings in thalassemia.

An X-ray of the skull shows a crewcut appearance due to expansion of hematopoetically active marrow.

Thalassemia is usually managed by blood transfusions every 2-4 weeks and chelation therapy with deferoxamine, deferasirox, and deferiprone for iron chelation. Splenectomy is indicated when the transfusion requirement to maintain ideal hemoglobin increases. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is the only known curative treatment for thalassemia.

Other options:

Option A: Serum ferritin level is used to diagnose iron-deficiency anemia (IDA). They are usually low in IDA.

Option C: Serum folate level is used to diagnose macrocytic anemia due to a deficiency of folic acid.

Option D: Serum homocysteine levels are increased in vitamin B12–deficient macrocytic anemia.

@

subject: Pathology
text: A 56-year-old man presents with dragging pain in the abdomen. On examination, there is massive splenomegaly. Peripheral smear shows leukocytosis with increased myelocytes, metamyelocytes and basophils. Which of the following translocation is seen in this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: A. t(9;22)

The clinical scenario of massive splenomegaly and peripheral smear shows leukocytosis with increased myelocytes, metamyelocytes and basophils are suggestive of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). A translocation between t(9;22) is seen in this condition. 

CML is a myeloproliferative neoplasm. It is caused due to BCR (on chromosome 22) - ABL (on chromosome 9) fusion gene translocation mutation. It results in the formation of the Philadelphia chromosome which is of CML.

The image given below shows Philadelphia chromosome showing reciprocal (9;22)(q34;q11) translocation seen in CML.

The resulting BCR-ABL translocation results in the activation of tyrosine kinase that signals pro-growth and pro-survival pathways like RAS and JAK/STAT pathways resulting in the proliferation of hematopoietic stem cells.

Patients typically present with a dragging sensation abdomen due to splenomegaly or splenic infarct, fatigue, malaise, and weight loss.

On peripheral smear there is leukocytosis with leukocyte count, often exceeding 100,000 cells/mm3 (neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils, and basophils), blasts are usually less than 10% of the circulating cells, the platelet count is usually increased.

The image below shows peripheral smear findings of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) with neutrophils, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and band cells.

Bone marrow is hypercellular due to increased numbers of maturing granulocytic precursors with sea-blue histiocytes (macrophages with wrinkled, green-blue cytoplasm).

Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) or polymerase chain reaction(PCR) to detect the BCR-ABL gene. Leucocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score is decreased in cases of CML.

Sokal scoring is used in assessing the prognosis of this patient. The prognosis of CML can be assessed based on:

  • Age
  • Spleen size
  • Platelet count
  • Percentage of blast cells in the blood

FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors for the treatment of CML are imatinib, nilotinib, dasatinib, bosutinib, and ponatinib.

 Complications, if left untreated:

  • Accelerated phase- increased anemia, thrombocytopenia, and basophilia
  • A blast crisis- may transform into acute leukemia (AML/ALL)

Other options:

Options B and D: t(8;14) and t(8;22) are seen in Burkitt lymphoma. It is associated with increased MYC levels. All endemic cases of Burkitt lymphoma are caused by the Ebstein-Barr virus. Microscopy shows a characteristic starry sky pattern.

The image given below shows a starry sky pattern seen in Burkitt lymphoma.

Option C: t(15;17) is seen in acute promyelocytic leukemia. It is characterized by promyelocytes with Auer rods on bone marrow aspirate. All-trans-retinoic acid is used for the treatment.

The image given below shows bone marrow findings in acute promyelocytic leukemia.

@

subject: Pathology
text: Which of the following is true regarding Mendelian mode of inheritance?

options.A: Every 10th patient has a Y‌-linked disorder
options.B: 1/3rd of Mendelian disorde‌rs is autosomal recessive​
options.C: Every 5th patient has an X‌-linked recessive disorde​r
options.D: 2/3rds of Mendelian disord‌ers are autosomal dominan​t

expl:
Correct answer: D. 2/3rds of Mendelian disorders are autosomal dominant

2/3rds of Mendelian disorders, which corresponds to approximately 66% disorders, are autosomal dominant is the true statement about the Mendelian mode of inheritance. Autosomal dominant patterns of inheritance comprise 65% of all Mendelian disorders (monogenic human diseases). 

Mendelian disorders (classic inheritance)

  • Autosomal dominant
  • Autosomal recessive
  • X-linked dominant
  • X-linked recessive

Of all the Mendelian disorders, also known as monogenic human disease, about 65% are autosomal dominant, 25% are autosomal recessive, and 5% are X-linked.

Other options:

Option A: Every 10th patient has a Y-linked disorder - This statement is incorrect. Y-linked disorders are extremely rare, and their prevalence is much lower than 1/10 (10%).

Option B: 1/3rd of Mendelian disorders is autosomal recessive - This statement is incorrect. Approximately 25% of Mendelian disorders are autosomal recessive, not 1/3rd (33.33%).

Option C: Every 5th patient has an X-linked recessive disorder - This statement is incorrect. Approximately 5% of Mendelian disorders are X-linked, not 1/5 (20%).

subject: Pathology
text: An elderly male who is a known smoker presented with chronic cough, significant weight loss, and fatigue. Serum calcium level is raised. A lung biopsy was done, and it showed large atypical cells with hyperchromasia. What is the probable diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Squamous cell carcinoma

The most probable diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario is squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.
 
Squamous cell carcinoma is most commonly found in men and is strongly associated with smoking. It predominantly arises in the central or hilar region. Histologically, it is characterized by the presence of keratin pearls and intercellular bridges.
 
Hypercalcemia is one of the most common paraneoplastic syndromes associated with squamous cell cancer (SCC) of the lung. Increased levels of parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTH-rP) are the most likely mechanism of his hypercalcemia. The symptoms could include anorexia, nausea, vomiting, constipation, lethargy, polyuria, polydipsia, and dehydration.
 
The image given below shows keratin pearls seen in squamous cell carcinomas.

Other options:

Option A: Large cell neuroendocrine tumor - These tumors are a subtype of large cell carcinoma and show neuroendocrine features on immunohistochemistry. They are aggressive and can be associated with paraneoplastic syndromes, but they do not commonly cause hypercalcemia.

Option B: Small cell carcinoma - This is a highly aggressive neuroendocrine tumor strongly associated with smoking. It frequently presents with paraneoplastic syndromes, including SIADH and ectopic ACTH production, but hypercalcemia is less common. Histologically, it is characterized by small cells with scant cytoplasm, ill-defined cell borders, and finely granular nuclear chromatin.

Option C: Adenocarcinoma - This is the most common type of lung cancer and is more common in non-smokers and women. It usually arises in the peripheral lung tissue and is associated with glandular differentiation or mucin production. Histologically, adenocarcinoma is characterized by glandular or acinar structures and/or intracytoplasmic mucin.

subject: Pathology
text: A young patient presents with a large retroperitoneal hemorrhage. He also gives a frequent history of intermittent swelling of knees on strenuous exercise. There is no history of any mucosal bleed. Which among the following clotting factors is responsible for the above-mentioned condition?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Factors VIII and IX

The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario hemophilia A. The clotting factors responsible for the above-mentioned condition are factors VIII and IX.

Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder. It occurs due to a deficiency of clotting factor VIII, which causes inadequate thrombin generation and results in the inability to form a tight fibrin clot to support the platelet plug.

Symptoms include easy bruising, intramuscular hematomas, hemarthroses, hematuria, and bleeding from minor traumatic lacerations of the mouth can persist for hours or days. Retroperitoneal hemorrhages can accumulate large volumes of blood and may cause a hypovolemic shock.

Laboratory findings in hemophilia A:

  • Factor VIII - reduced
  • Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) - prolonged
  • Platelet count - normal
  • Bleeding time - normal
  • Prothrombin time - normal

Mild cases of hemophilia are treated by the administration of desmopressin acetate. Moderate to severe cases need the replacement of deficient clotting factors (factor VIII in hemophilia A). Monoclonal antibody emicizumab can restore activated factor VIII activity in patients with hemophilia.

Other options:

Option B: Factors XI and XII - Deficiencies of these factors are not associated with the clinical presentation described in the question. Factor XI deficiency (hemophilia C) can cause mild bleeding disorders, but it is generally not associated with severe hemorrhages or joint swelling. Factor XII deficiency is typically asymptomatic and not associated with bleeding disorders.

Option C: Von Willebrand factor - A deficiency in von Willebrand factor results in von Willebrand disease, which can cause excessive bleeding similar to hemophilia. However, von Willebrand disease usually presents with mucosal bleeding (e.g., epistaxis, menorrhagia, and gum bleeding), which is not described in this case.

Option D: Lupus anticoagulant - This is an acquired condition seen in antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APS), which can cause thrombotic events rather than bleeding. It is not associated with retroperitoneal hemorrhage or joint swelling upon strenuous exercise.

subject: Pathology
text: An elderly male went for a medical examination. Laboratory investigations showed a marked elevation of lymphocytes with marked leukocytosis. The peripheral smear of the patient is given below. What is the appropriate next step for this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Flow cytometry

The likely diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the peripheral smear showing smudge cells is chronic lymphocytic leukemia. The next step in his management should be flow cytometry.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a peripheral B-cell neoplasm usually affecting adults, more commonly men. Patients are often asymptomatic at diagnosis. When symptomatic, it presents non-specifically with easy fatigability, weight loss, and anorexia. Generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are present in most symptomatic patients. 

The chromosomal defects in CLL include

  • Deletion of 13q (commonest and has a good prognosis)
  • Deletion of 11q
  • Trisomy 12q
  • Deletion of 17p (poor prognosis)

The peripheral blood smear in cases of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) contains small round lymphocytes having condensed chromatin and scant cytoplasm. Some of these cells may get disrupted while preparing the smears, producing smudge cells. An absolute lymphocyte count of >5000/mm3 is required for diagnosis. Hypogammaglobulinemia is commonly seen, making the patient susceptible to infections. A few patients may develop hemolytic anemia or thrombocytopenia due to autoantibodies made by non-neoplastic B cells.

Immunophenotyping using flow cytometry is the investigation done to arrive at the diagnosis. The classical immunophenotypic feature of CLL is CD19+, CD20+, CD 23+, and CD5+.

On lymph node biopsy: Lymph nodes are composed of small lymphocytes admixed with larger activated lymphocytes. The large lymphocytes contain mitotically active cells and gather in loose aggregates, which are referred to as proliferation centers. These proliferation centers are pathognomic to CLL when present.

Expectant management is the treatment of choice for asymptomatic patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia. The gold standard for therapy is a combination of fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab.

Richter’s syndrome is a complication of CLL in which there is a transformation to an aggressive lymphoma, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL).

 Other options:

Option A: Stem cell transplantation - This is not the first step in the management of CLL. It may be considered in certain high-risk patients or those with refractory disease, but only after confirming the diagnosis and assessing the disease stage.

Option B: Bone marrow biopsy - While it can provide valuable information about the extent of infiltration, it is not the initial test for diagnosing CLL. Flow cytometry is the preferred diagnostic method.

Option D: Start high-dose chemotherapy - This is not the first step in managing CLL. Treatment decisions should be based on clinical stage, prognostic factors, and the patient's overall health. Moreover, asymptomatic patients with CLL are often managed with a watchful waiting approach.

subject: Pathology
text: A 25-year-old male presented with low hemoglobin, platelet count of 25,000/mL, gum bleeding, and raised PT & aPTT. The image of his peripheral smear is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. AML with t(15;17)

The peripheral blood smear shows numerous Auer rods in the cytoplasm of progranulocytes, which are characteristic of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The presentation of the patient with gum bleeding points to the diagnosis of AML with t(15;17).

Auer rods (needle-like azurophilic granules) are predominantly seen in acute promyelocytic leukemia, which is a subtype of acute myeloid leukemia. It is associated with t(15;17), which results in the formation of the fusion gene called PML-RARA. The condition is associated with a high incidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Treatment includes the administration of all-trans retinoic acid.

subject: Pathology
text: A chronic smoker who worked in a cement factory for the past 20 years developed mesothelioma. The association is likely to be due to ______.
expl:
Correct answer: B. Asbestosis

The association in this case is between occupational exposure to cement for 20 years and the occurrence of mesothelioma, which is mediated by the development of asbestosis as a result of prolonged inhalation of asbestos.

Asbestosis occurs due to the inhalation of crystalline hydrated silicates (asbestos). It occurs in two distinct geometric forms, serpentine and amphibole. It is characterized by diffuse parenchymal interstitial fibrosis. It usually begins in the lower lobes of the lungs and may present with dyspnea and cough, usually after 20-30 years of exposure. Other asbestos-related diseases include pleural plaques, recurrent pleural effusions, lung carcinoma, and mesothelioma.

Asbestos bodies are a hallmark finding. They appear as golden brown, fusiform, or beaded rods. These are formed when the asbestos fibers are phagocytosed by the macrophages and are coated by iron-containing proteinaceous material derived from phagocyte ferritin.

The image below shows asbestos bodies.

Other options:

Option A: Silicosis is due to the inhalation of crystalline silicon dioxide (silica) as seen in individuals employed in sandblasting or rock mining. Macrophages phagocytose inhaled silica particles, thereby activating and releasing inflammatory mediators, like IL-1 and IL-8.

Histopathology reveals coalescent nodules of whorled collagen fibers surrounded by a peripheral zone of dust-laden macrophages. Radiologically, egg-shell calcification of the lymph nodes is seen.

Shown below is an image of a silicotic nodule with collagen whorls as seen in this condition.

Option C: Anthracosis/coal workers' pneumoconiosis is a pulmonary condition seen in coal miners. The inhaled carbon pigment is engulfed by alveolar or interstitial macrophages, which accumulate in the connective tissue. On prolonged exposure, lung tissue undergoes progressive massive fibrosis, which is called complicated coal workers' pneumoconiosis. The upper lobes of the lungs are commonly involved.

Microscopic features consist of coal-laden macrophages, black pigment, and dense collagenous interstitial fibrosis. 

The image below shows anthracosis—black pigment engulfed within macrophages as well as in the form of deposits.

Option D: Bagassosis is an occupational lung disease caused by the inhalation of bagasse or sugarcane dust. A thermophilic actinomycete, Thermoactinomyces sacchari, is the causative organism. The symptoms are breathlessness, cough, hemoptysis, and fever. Initially, it can result in acute diffuse bronchiolitis. If left untreated, it can progress to diffuse fibrosis, emphysema, and bronchiectasis.

subject: Pathology
text: A child presents with intermittent jaundice and splenomegaly. There is a history of similar complaints in the elder brother. Peripheral smear shows the following finding. How will you investigate this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Osmotic fragility test - Hereditary spherocytosis

The most likely diagnosis based on the given clinical condition and the peripheral smear showing spherocytes is hereditary spherocytosis. The investigation that can be done in this condition is the osmotic fragility test.

Hereditary spherocytosis is a type of hereditary hemolytic anemia that is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. The mutations commonly affect ankyrin, band 3, spectrin, or band 4.2.

This disorder can present at a young age with severe jaundice, anemia, and splenomegaly. The unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia predisposes the patient to develop gallstones in early adulthood. Pigment stones are found in 40-50% of the affected adults.

Laboratory findings include normocytic anemia with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The peripheral smear will show large spherical red blood cells without central pallor. 

Laboratory investigations that are done to confirm the diagnosis:

  • Osmotic fragility test
  • Acid glycerol lysis test
  • Eosin-5’-maleimide (EMA)–binding test
  • SDS-gel electrophoresis test                                                      

There is no specific treatment available besides splenectomy.  

Other Options:
 
Option B: Coombs test - AIHA (Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia) - This test is performed to determine if the patient's red blood cells are coated with immunoglobulins or complement, leading to their destruction. AIHA typically does not present with a family history.
 
Option C: G6PD deficiency - This condition is characterized by hemolytic anemia triggered by oxidative stress, such as infections or exposure to certain drugs. G6PD deficiency is diagnosed by measuring G6PD enzyme activity or genetic testing.
 
Option D: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria - This rare acquired hemolytic anemia is characterized by episodes of hemolysis and hemoglobinuria, particularly during sleep. The diagnosis is made by testing for the presence of GPI-anchored proteins using flow cytometry.

subject: Pathology
text: An African child is found to have a mass in the jaw. A biopsy of the mass was done, and it appears as shown in the image below. The child also had a translocation of t(8;14). What is the probable diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Burkitt lymphoma

The most probable diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the histopathology showing a “starry sky” pattern is Burkitt lymphoma.

Burkitt lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. It is characterized by the translocation of the c-Myc gene on chromosome 8. This leads to increased MYC protein levels. The translocation most commonly seen in Burkitt's lymphoma is t(8;14).

It can occur in 3 forms that have distinct clinical characteristics:

  • African (endemic) Burkitt lymphoma presents as a mass involving the mandible. It may also involve the abdominal viscera, particularly the kidneys, ovaries, and adrenal glands.
  • Sporadic (non-endemic) is often seen as a mass involving the ileocecum and peritoneum.
  • Aggressive lymphoma or acute leukemia is seen in immunocompromised individuals

Histopathology shows tumor cells with round or oval nuclei, coarse chromatin, small nucleoli, minimal cytoplasm, and a high mitotic index. The phagocytes have abundant clear cytoplasm, creating a characteristic “starry sky” pattern. Bone marrow aspiration shows tumor cells with royal blue cytoplasm containing clear cytoplasmic vacuoles.

The tumor cells express surface IgM, CD19, CD20, CD10, and BCL6, a phenotype consistent with a germinal center B-cell origin.

Other options:

Option A: Acute myeloid leukemia is most commonly seen in elderly people. Histopathology from bone marrow aspirate reveals Auer rods (needle-like azurophilic granules) in the cytoplasm of the progranulocytes. Myeloblasts have two to four nucleoli and multiple coarse azurophilic granules. 

The criterion for making a diagnosis of AML according to WHO requires one of the following:

  • Blast cell count of ≥20% either in the peripheral blood or bone marrow
  • Blast cell count of <20% in the presence of any one of the following three cytogenetic abnormalities t(15;17), t(8;21), and inversion 16 or t(16;16)

The peripheral blood smear shows numerous Auer rods in the cytoplasm of progranulocytes, characteristic of acute myeloid leukemia.

 

 

Option B: Follicular lymphoma presents in middle age with no sex predilection. The most common presenting symptom is painless generalized lymphadenopathy. Most follicular lymphomas have characteristic (14:18) translocation, leading to overexpression of BCL2. Lymph nodes exhibit a nodular or nodular and diffuse growth pattern.

Two cell types are predominantly present in varying proportions: 

  • Centrocytes - Small cells with a cleaved nucleus and scant cytoplasm
  • Centroblasts - Large cells with open nuclear chromatin, several nucleoli, and modest amounts of cytoplasm

The following image shows a lymph node biopsy in follicular lymphoma:

Option C: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm. It is associated with lytic bone lesions, hypercalcemia, renal failure, and acquired immune abnormalities.

Histopathological findings include

  • Flame cells with fiery red cytoplasm
  • Mott cells with multiple grapelike cytoplasmic droplets
  • Inclusions bodies: Russell bodies (if cytoplasmic) or Dutcher bodies (if nuclear)

subject: Pathology
text: A child presented to the hospital with cola-colored urine, hypertension, and puffiness of eyes. Laboratory investigations were done and creatinine was 2.5 mg/dL. Treatment was started, and despite treatment, the patient did not improve for the next 3 weeks. The creatinine value increased to 4.5 mg/dL. Which among the following electron microscopic findings will be seen in this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Subepithelial deposits

The diagnosis based on the above clinical scenario is post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). Subepithelial deposits will be seen on electron microscopy.

The rapid decline in renal function and raise in creatinine value to 4.5 mg/dL within 3 weeks, is suggestive of PSGN progressing to RPGN (Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis). If the histopathology finding of the patient was asked then the answer would be crescent formation, which is characteristic of RPGN. Since the electron microscopy finding in the given patient is asked, the answer is subepithelial deposits, which is the characteristic finding of underlying pathology i.e. PSGN.

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is caused by Group A β-hemolytic streptococcal infections. It is uncommon before the age of 3 years and most prevalent in kids between the ages of 5 and 12 years. 

The patient typically develops an acute nephritic syndrome

  • 1 to 2 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis or
  • 3 to 6 weeks after streptococcal pyoderma

From asymptomatic microscopic hematuria with normal renal function to gross hematuria with acute renal failure, the severity of kidney involvement varies. Patients may experience different levels of edema, hypertension, and oliguria depending on the extent of the renal involvement.

Laboratory findings: More than 90% of patients see a considerable reduction in serum C3 levels during the acute phase, which lasts 6 to 8 weeks before returning to normal. 
In order to confirm the diagnosis, evidence of preceding streptococcal infection is required. The antistreptolysin O titer frequently rises following pharyngeal infections. The anti-deoxyribonuclease B level is the most effective single antibody titer to demonstrate cutaneous streptococcal infection.

Microscopic Findings in PSGN:
  • Light microscopy: Enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with diffuse mesangial and endothelial proliferation and leukocyte infiltration.
  • Immunofluorescence: Granular deposits of IgG and complement C3 along the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) and in the mesangium 
  • Electron microscopy: Primarily subepithelial humps are seen. Subendothelial deposits can be seen in early disease stages.

Below is the image showing light microscopy findings of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Other options:

Option A: Subendothelial deposits - These are characteristic of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) type I. MPGN typically presents with nephrotic or nephritic features but does not necessarily follow a streptococcal infection. 

Option C: Crescentic glomerulonephritis, also known as rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN)is a type of nephritic syndrome associated with severe glomerular injury with necrosis and formation of crescents. The disease progresses rapidly and leads to renal failure in weeks to months when not treated. 

Option D: Mesangial deposits - These are characteristic of IgA nephropathy, which typically presents with recurrent episodes of gross hematuria following upper respiratory infections, rather than acute nephritic syndrome following streptococcal infection.

subject: Pathology
text: A patient was transfused 4 units of blood 2 hours ago, and now she complains of chest discomfort. X-ray shows bilateral fissural thickening. Which of the following is the most probable cause?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Fluid overload

The given clinical condition is most likely due to fluid overload.

Fluid overload also called transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) is the main cause of death from transfusion. Risk factors include older age, renal failure, preexisting fluid overload, cardiac dysfunction, administration of a large volume of RBCs, and an excessive rate of transfusion in relation to the patient’s hemodynamic tolerance.

TACO results in dyspnea, hypoxia, bilateral and predominantly alveolar infiltrates on chest x-ray, frequent systolic hypertension, and elevated brain natriuretic peptide. Fever may also present.

Prevention involves identifying at-risk patients, close monitoring, a slow transfusion rate, and the use of diuretics in hemodynamically stable patients with a history of TACO. Treatment requires stopping the transfusion and administrating oxygen and diuretics.

Other options:

Option A: ABO incompatibility reactions may present with hypotension, tachypnea, tachycardia, fever, chills, chest, and back pain, hemoglobinuria, and hemoglobinemia. In the most severe cases, DIC, acute renal failure, shock, and death may occur.

Option C: Hypocalcemia can be caused by citrate, which is used as an anticoagulant. It manifests as circumoral paresthesia, and changes in cardiac function may result from multiple rapid transfusions.

Option D: Graft-versus-host disease typically presents 5–10 days after transfusion, and it manifests as cytopenia, fever, a characteristic skin rash, diarrhea, and abnormal liver function.

@

subject: Pathology
text: A 48-year-old man presents with complaints of facial puffiness, frothy urine, and hypertension. He gives a history of infection with hepatitis B. Urine examination reveals microscopic hematuria. The histopathological image of the kidney biopsy shows a spike and dome pattern. What is the diagnosis of this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Membranous nephropathy

The diagnosis of the patient based on the given clinical scenario and the histopathology showing spike and dome pattern is membranous nephropathy.

Membranous nephropathy is one of the most common causes of nephrotic syndrome in adults. It occurs commonly in men aged between 30-50 years. The majority of cases are idiopathic/primary that occur due to the autoantibodies against the renal antigen phospholipase A2 receptor. These autoantibodies are absent in secondary membranous nephropathy.

The various conditions leading to secondary membranous nephropathy are

  • Drugs: Captopril, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs NSAIDs, penicillamine, etc.
  • Infections: Hepatitis B and C, syphilis, malaria
  • Malignancy of lung, colon, and melanoma
  • Autoimmune diseases like SLE, Sjorgen syndrome, sarcoidosis, primary biliary cirrhosis, etc.

As in this case, there is a history of hepatitis B infection, the likely etiology is secondary membranous nephropathy. Hence, PLA2R autoantibodies are absent. 

Patients present with symptoms of nephrotic syndrome, nonselective proteinuria, and microscopic hematuria.

Diagnosis:

  • Light microscopy shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall without cellular proliferation. Irregular spikes and dome pattern on silver staining.
  • Immunofluorescence microscopy shows granular deposits containing IgG and complement proteins along the glomerular basement membrane. IgG4 is the principal immunoglobulin deposited in most cases of primary membranous nephropathy.
  • Electron micrograph: electron-dense subepithelial deposits (epimembranous spikes) and effacement of foot processes of podocytes
Management is primarily by the administration of immunosuppressive drugs such as steroids, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, and mycophenolate mofetil.
 
Image: The silver stain of the glomerulus highlights the proteinaceous basement membranes in black. There are characteristic "spikes" of the basement membrane between the immune deposits of membranous nephropathy. As the disease progresses, these spikes thicken to form dome-like protrusions. The black basement membrane material shown here appears as projections in the capillary loops. 

Other options:

Option A: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (peaks between 2–6 years).

Biopsy findings in this condition are as follows:

  • Light microscopy - glomeruli appear normal (hence called 'minimal change')
  • Immunofluorescence studies - no Ig or complement deposits
  • Electron microscopy - diffuse effacement of foot processes of visceral epithelial cells (podocytopathy)

Option C: FSGS is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults. It is a podocytopathy, with characteristic degeneration and focal disruption of visceral epithelial cells as well as effacement of foot processes. The electrophoretic pattern is more likely to yield a less prominent band in A, a more prominent band in C as there is a fall in the level of albumin with rising in the level of α2.

The histology of FSGS reveals focal and segmental hyalinosis and sclerosis of the capillary wall. Lipid droplets and foam cells are present in the sclerosed area.

Option D: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is characterized by the sudden onset of gross hematuria, edema, hypertension, and renal insufficiency. It usually occurs following a throat infection by nephritogenic strains of group A β-hemolytic streptococci. 

Microscopic findings in PSGN:
  • Light microscopy: Enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with diffuse mesangial and endothelial proliferation and leukocyte infiltration.
  • Immunofluorescence: Granular deposits of IgG and complement C3 along the glomerular basement membrane(GBM)and in the mesangium. 
  • Electron microscopy: Electron-dense deposits, or humps, are observed on the epithelial side of the GBM.
