subject: Obstetrics & Gynecology
text: A female patient has a history of three miscarriages. Identify the investigation that was done from the image shown below.
expl:
Correct answer: C. Hysterosalpingography

The investigation shown in the given image is hysterosalpingography. The given hysterosalpingogram shows a unicornuate uterus.

Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is an imaging modality in which radiopaque contrast is injected through the cervical canal to assess the endometrial cavity, the fallopian tubes, and the endocervical canal.

HSG should be done between days 5 and 10 of the menstrual cycle, in the preovulatory phase, as an outpatient procedure. Leech Wilkinson cannula, Rubin's cannula, or Foley's catheter no.14 is introduced into the endometrial cavity through the cervical os, and the contrast is injected. The uterine cavity and fallopian tubes are then visualized and X-rays are obtained.

HSG can be used for the following:

  • To assess tubal patency in infertility 
  • To detect uterine anomalies, synechiae, and polyps
  • To detect incompetence of the cervical os

Contraindications to HSG:

  • Acute pelvic infection 
  • Active uterine bleeding
  • Pregnancy/ suspected pregnancy
  • Contrast allergy
  • Premenstrual phase

HSG is a safe procedure, however, complications such as ascending spread of infection, chemical peritonitis, allergic reaction to the dye, or pelvic endometriosis may occur. 

Other options:

Option A: Hysteroscopy is an operative procedure in which the uterine cavity can be visualized by passing a fiberoptic telescope via the cervix. It can be diagnostic or therapeutic. A hysteroscopic image of a uterus with carcinoma is shown below.

Option B: Saline infusion sonography is a procedure where normal saline is injected into the uterine cavity and the uterus is imaged with transvaginal sonography. It is shown in the image below.

Option D: Transvaginal ultrasonography is a noninvasive imaging technique using the transvaginal approach. It provides a more detailed evaluation of the pelvic organs as compared to the transabdominal approach.

subject: Obstetrics & Gynecology
text: A 56-year-old multipara woman presented with grade II/III uterine prolapse with cystocele. She complains of passing urine on coughing and sneezing. What is the type of urinary incontinence seen in this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Stress incontinence

The type of urinary incontinence present in a patient with prolapse and cystocele experiencing urination on coughing and sneezing is stress incontinence.

Stress incontinence refers to the involuntary leakage of urine when there is increased intra-abdominal pressure (eg, coughing, sneezing, laughing, Valsalva maneuver). Absence of detrusor muscle contraction is seen in urodynamic studies.

Causes:

  • Age and menopause - due to estrogen deficiency
  • Multiparity - due to loss of pelvic muscle tone
  • Obesity
  • Smoking
  • Constipation, chronic cough
  • Pelvic organ prolapse
  • Pregnancy - due to the effect of progesterone and pressure of the gravid uterus on the bladder neck.
  • Puerperium - due to descent of the bladder neck, loss of urethro-vesical angle, and reduced pelvic muscle tone 
  • Surgical repair of vesicovaginal fistula

Grading of genuine stress incontinence (GSI) :

  • Grade I: Incontinence with only severe stress, such as coughing, sneezing, and jogging.
  • Grade II: Incontinence with moderate stress, such as fast walk, going up and down the stairs.
  • Grade III: Incontinence with mild stress such as standing.

Investigations are only done prior to surgery to confirm the diagnosis. They include:

  • Stress test
  • Cotton swab or Q-tip test
  • Marshall and Bonney’s test
  • Urethroscopy
  • Urodynamic studies.

These are not required prior to conservative management.

Conservative management includes Kegel's pelvic exercises, electric nerve stimulation, devices like pessaries, vaginal cones, and artificial sphincters. Medical treatment with estrogen creams, alpha agonists, venlafaxine, and imipramine may be useful.

Other options:

Option A: Overflow incontinence is an old term that refers to the inability to empty the bladder, with involuntary, continuous urinary dribbling. Currently, it refers to another presentation of urge incontinence. 

Option B: Urge incontinence is the involuntary escape of urine when there is an imminent need to urinate. It occurs due to detrusor muscle overactivity or detrusor instability. It is seen more commonly in old women with decreased bladder capacity, decreased sensation, and CNS inhibition. 

Option D: Neurogenic bladder occurs in patients with neurogenic dysfunction leading to detrusor hyperreflexia. Conditions such as multiple sclerosis, stroke, Parkinson's disease, and spinal injury give rise to this. They present with urgency or urge incontinence.

subject: Obstetrics & Gynecology
text: A 32-year-old married woman who came for the evaluation of infertility was found to have a septum in her uterine cavity. What would be the appropriate management of this case?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Hysteroscopy and septoplasty

The appropriate management for a 32-year-old woman with a septate uterus is hysteroscopy and septoplasty.

Hysteroscopic septoplasty refers to the resection of the uterine septum under hysteroscopic guidance. The septum can be resected either with a resectoscope or a laser. It does not scar the uterus and avoids the necessity of cesarean sections for future pregnancies. There is a reduced risk of pelvic adhesions, compared with transabdominal approaches.

A septate uterus is characterized by a septum in the endometrial cavity. It is caused by the failure of the medial segments of the Müllerian ducts to regress. This creates a permanent septum within the uterine cavity. 

The septum can project partially from the fundus or extend completely to the cervical os. It is the most common congenital uterine malformation in women with infertility.

Other options:

Option A: Hysterectomy is not advisable since the patient has come for infertility evaluation and desires pregnancy.

Options B & D: Laparoscopy/laparotomy and metroplasty are not preferred for the treatment of a septate uterus due to the following:

  • Requirement of cesarean section for subsequent pregnancies to prevent uterine rupture.
  • Postoperative pelvic adhesions leading to infertility.
Note: Jone's and Tompkin's metroplasties are surgeries for the septate uterus that involve a transabdominal approach. They cause uterine scarring and are hence not preferred.

subject: Obstetrics & Gynecology
text: A 30-year-old G4A3 woman had a history of miscarriage at 8 weeks, the second miscarriage at 11 weeks with no cardiac activity, and the third pregnancy loss at 24 weeks with preterm delivery due to early-onset preeclampsia. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome

The given clinical scenario of a G4A3 woman with miscarriages at 8 and 11 weeks, and preterm delivery due to preeclampsia at 24 weeks is suggestive of antiphospholipid antibody (APLA) syndrome. 

APLA is an autoimmune disorder commonly associated with fetal death, preterm delivery, early-onset preeclampsia, and fetal growth restriction due to placental insufficiency and thromboses. Pregnancy loss usually occurs before 10 weeks.

Diagnosis of APLA requires at least 1 clinical criterion and 1 laboratory criterion.

  • Obstetric criteria
    • One or more unexplained deaths of a morphologically normal fetus at or beyond 10 weeks or
    • Severe preeclampsia or placental insufficiency requiring delivery before 34 weeks, or
    • Three or more unexplained consecutive spontaneous abortions before 10 weeks
  • Laboratory criteria
    • Presence of lupus anticoagulant, or
    • Anticardiolipin antibodies, or
    • Anti-β2 glycoprotein antibody

Recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL), also referred to as a recurrent miscarriage or habitual abortion, is historically defined as 3 consecutive pregnancy losses prior to 20 weeks from the last menstrual period. 

Common causes include:

  • Parental chromosomal abnormalities
  • Untreated hypothyroidism
  • Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus
  • Uterine anatomic abnormalities,
  • Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome 

Other options:

Option A: There is no history of STD or skin lesions suggestive of syphilis and according to Kassawitz rule, in women with untreated syphilis having a series of pregnancies, the likelihood of fetal infection in later pregnancies becomes less; usually, only the first pregnancy is an abortion, the following pregnancy losses will be stillbirths in the next trimester rather than recurrent pregnancy loss.

Option C: TORCH infections may play a role in sporadic spontaneous pregnancy loss, rather than recurrent pregnancy losses.

Option D: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) refers to the onset or first recognition of diabetes during pregnancy, usually at the 24-28 weeks screening test. Women with uncontrolled overt or pregestational diabetes with elevated HbA1c or prepran­dial glucose in the first trimester have an increased risk for early miscarriage, but there is a history or lab findings suggestive of gestational diabetes mellitus.

subject: Obstetrics & Gynecology
text: A 26-year-old female patient came with a history of fatiguability and constipation for the past 1 year. She has a history of multiple blood transfusions after delivery 4 years ago. She has had a lactational failure and never regained her periods after the delivery. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Sheehan syndrome

The most likely diagnosis in a woman with lactational failure and postpartum amenorrhea, now presenting with fatiguability and constipation is Sheehan syndrome. A history of multiple blood transfusions after delivery indicates major obstetric blood loss, which resulted in pituitary ischemia leading to this condition.

Sheehan syndrome is panhypopituitarism due to pituitary ischemia and necrosis following massive obstetrical hemorrhage.

The most severe form presents with shock due to pituitary apoplexy. It is characterized by a sudden onset headache, nausea, visual deficits, and hormonal dysfunction due to acute pituitary hemorrhage or infarction. Less severe forms present with anovulation and amenorrhea.

Damage to specific pituitary cell types leads to lactational failure, loss of axillary and pubic hair, and symptoms of hypothyroidism or adrenal insufficiency. Prolactin deficiency is most commonly encountered, but adrenal insufficiency is the most life-threatening complication. Hence, the adrenal function should be immediately assessed if there is any suspicion of Sheehan syndrome.

Option B: Hypothyroidism can present with vague symptoms such as fatigue, constipation, and amenorrhea. However, postpartum hypothyroidism usually presents 4-8 months after delivery after a thyrotoxic phase with palpitations and thyroid enlargement.

Option C: Premature ovarian failure presents with menopausal symptoms. It is due to primary ovarian dysfunction. It is diagnosed when serum FSH levels are >30-40 mIU/mL on two occasions, at least one month apart.

Option D: Delayed transfusion reaction presents days to weeks after the transfusion. It may be asymptomatic or with low-grade fever. Coombs test may be positive, unconjugated bilirubin increased, and the rise in hemoglobin levels following the transfusion will be less than expected.

subject: Obstetrics & Gynecology
text: The ultrasound of a young woman with infertility is suggestive of a uterine anomaly. Which of the following is used to confirm the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Hysteroscopy + laparoscopy

Among the given options, hysteroscopy with laparoscopy is used to confirm the diagnosis. 

For infertility evaluation, hysteroscopy and laparoscopy can detect müllerian anomalies, screen for co-existent endometriosis, and exclude other tubal or uterine cavity pathology.

This approach can differentiate between a septate and a bicornuate uterus. On laparoscopy, the presence of a uterine fundus indicates that the uterus is septate, while its absence indicates it is bicornuate. The capacity of each horn in a bicornuate uterus and the depth and thickness of the uterine septum prior to surgical resection can also be assessed. 

MRI is the gold standard investigation for the diagnosis of Mullerian anomalies. It clearly delineates both the internal and external uterine anatomy. Complex anomalies and common associations like renal or skeletal anomalies can also be evaluated. It is also less invasive than hysteroscopy and laparoscopy in diagnosing Mullerian anomalies.

Other options:

Option A: Hysterosalpingography (HSG) provides information about the interior contour of the uterine cavity but cannot accurately visualize the external contour of the uterus. 

Option C: Laparoscopy alone as a diagnostic procedure cannot visualize the interior contour of a hollow viscus like the uterus. This can be done only with the help of hysteroscopy or imaging such as sonography, HSG, or MRI.

Option D: Transvaginal sonography is used for the initial detection of uterine anomalies causing infertility or spontaneous abortions. Complete evaluation of these anomalies is done by MRI.

Note: 

  • Hysteroscopy is the gold standard investigation to visualize the uterine cavity and tubal ostia. It also has therapeutic benefits in cases of endometrial polyps, submucous resection of myoma, hysteroscopic adhesiolysis, and resection of uterine septum. 
  • Laparoscopy is the gold standard investigation to evaluate tubal factors of infertility.

subject: Obstetrics & Gynecology
text: A 26-year-old pregnant woman, on examination was found to have infra-umbilical flattening. The fetal heart sounds were heard over the lateral side. What could be the fetal presentation/position?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Occipitoposterior

The presence of infra-umbilical flattening and fetal heart sounds on the lateral side indicates that the fetus is in the occipito-posterior position.

Occipito-posterior (OP) position of the fetus is when the occiput is situated posteriorly over the sacroiliac joint, or directly over the sacrum. The fetus is in vertex presentation.

Examination findings of OP position:

  • On inspection, the abdomen appears flattened below the umbilicus (infra-umbilical flattening).
  • Pelvic grips:
    • The head is not engaged.
    • The sinciput (cephalic prominence) is not prominently felt.
  • Auscultation: Fetal heart sounds are heard maximally over the flanks. However, in the direct OP position, they are heard in the midline.

There are three variants of OP position:

  • Left OP position (fourth position of the vertex) - When the occiput points towards the left sacroiliac joint. 
  • Right OP position (third position of the vertex) - When the occiput points towards the right sacroiliac joint. It is more common than the left OP position.
  • Direct OP position - When the occiput points directly towards the sacrum.

All three positions may be primary (present before the onset of labor) or secondary (develops after the onset of labor). 

Other options:

Option A: Brow presentation is a rare type of cephalic presentation where the position of the head is in between full flexion and full extension. The part of the head between the orbital ridge and the anterior fontanel presents at the pelvic inlet.

Option B: Knee presentation is a type of breech presentation. Here, the thighs are extended but the knees are flexed, presenting at the pelvic inlet. The head will be palpable as a hard globular mass at the fundus.

Option D: Right dorso-anterior position is when the fetal back is directed anteriorly. This occurs in a transverse lie. On examination, the abdomen appears wide, and a hard plane of resistance is felt. The fundus extends just above the umbilicus. The head is felt in one iliac fossa and the breech is felt in the other.

subject: Obstetrics & Gynecology
text: A primi at term presented with labor pain and multiple painful vesicular lesions on her vulva. No rashes were found on other parts of the body. What will be the management of this case?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Acyclovir and elective Cesarean section

The given clinical scenario of a primi in labor pain with multiple, painful vesicular lesions on her vulva is suggestive of an active herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection. Management involves the administration of acyclovir and elective cesarean section.

HSV infection in pregnancy can be caused by either HSV-1 or HSV-2 and transmitted by sexual contact. The infection can be primary, nonprimary, first episode, and recurrent.  

HSV infection (both HSV 1 and 2) during pregnancy has a risk of vertical transmission of the infection to the fetus. The risk is higher in the primary than in the recurrent infection. The maximum risk of fetal infection is during labor, although it can occur in utero and post-natally from direct contact. 

Suspicious lesions should be sent for PCR testing or culture. Antiviral treatment with acyclovir should be given if found positive. Women with no active genital lesions, asymptomatic, or those with active lesions in non-genital areas can undergo normal labor and delivery. 

Management of HSV infection during pregnancy:

  • Oral acyclovir or valacyclovir for primary or recurrent infections during pregnancy.
  • IV acyclovir followed by oral acyclovir for severe or disseminated infection
  • Oral analgesics or topical anesthetics for pain relief
  • Catheterization for urinary retention

Cesarean delivery reduces the risk of vertical transmission during labor and is indicated in:

  • Cases of active genital lesions - both primary and recurrent
  • Prodromal symptoms like vulval itching or burning

Other options:

Option B: The presene of active lesions is a contraindication for induction of labor.

Option C: Spontaneous delivery is contraindicated in the presence of active lesions.

Option D: Even after treatment with acyclovir, normal delivery is not indicated owing to the risk of dormant viral transmission to the fetus.

subject: Obstetrics & Gynecology
text: A 30-year-old married woman came for an infertility evaluation. On performing further investigations, intramural fibroids of sizes 7x5cm and 5x3cm were seen at the right and left cornual ends of the uterus. Her husband's semen analysis was found to be normal. What is the appropriate management of this case?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Myomectomy

The most appropriate management for a woman with infertility due to intramural fibroids at both the cornual ends of the uterus is myomectomy. The infertility, in this case, is due to the fibroids blocking the right and left cornua of the uterus.

Myomectomy refers to the removal of fibroids and preserving the uterus. It is indicated in women presenting with infertility, those who desire pregnancy, or those who wish to retain the uterus.

Intracavitary fibroids can be resected via the hysteroscopic approach, while subserosal or intramural fibroids require laparotomy or laparoscopic myomectomy.

Other options:

Option A: Uterine artery embolization is not done in this case, as it may decrease fertility, as a result of pelvic adhesions. It is a technique in which polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), gel foam particles, or metal coils are injected into the uterine arteries. This embolization reduces vascularity and the size of the fibroid. It is best suited to control menorrhagia in multiparous women.

Option C: Artificial reproductive techniques are not indicated in this case as infertility is seen to be due to the fibroids blocking the cornual ends of the uterus. However, it may be considered at a later stage.

Option D: GnRH analogs when used for 6 months, can reduce the tumor size by targeting the growth effects of estrogen and progesterone. It can be used in women with infertility caused by cornual fibroids. They are often used preoperatively to reduce the size of the fibroid and facilitate a hysteroscopic approach to surgery. However, it is expensive and can cause menopausal symptoms if used for >6 months. Fibroids are known to regrow 3-4 months after stopping the therapy.

subject: Obstetrics & Gynecology
text: A 28-year-old married woman who is anxious to conceive presents with copious vaginal discharge, without any itching. Her last menstrual period was 13 days ago. What is the cause of her vaginal discharge?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Physiological

The given clinical scenario of a young woman with copious, non-pruritic (without itching) vaginal discharge occurring 13 days after menstrual period (period of ovulation) is most likely to be leucorrhoea (physiological).

The term leucorrhoea can be used in conditions where normal vaginal secretion is increased in amount. An increase in this normal vaginal secretion develops physiologically:

  • At puberty
  • At ovulation
  • During pregnancy
  • During the premenstrual phase, occasionally

It may be cervical or vaginal in origin. A speculum examination of the vagina can distinguish between the two. If the discharge is cervical in origin, an excessive mucoid discharge will be visible at the external os.

Normal discharge appears clear or white, without any odor or itching, and will have a pH of 3.8-4.2.

Other options:

Option A: Candidiasis is caused by infection with Candida albicans and presents with pruritus, burning, and dysuria with vulvar erythema, edema, and excoriations. A curdy white discharge will be present. 

Option B: Bacterial vaginosis is caused by an alteration in the normal vaginal flora and presents without itching and a malodorous grey-white discharge. It is diagnosed using Amsel's criteria, where at least three of the four following criteria should be present to confirm the diagnosis:

  • Homogenous vaginal discharge
  • Vaginal pH > 4.5
  • Amine-like odor on adding KOH (Whiff test positive)
  • Clue cells (>20% of cells)

Option C: Trichomoniasis is caused by Trichomonas vaginalis and presents with a copious, frothy, offensive yellow-green discharge with vaginal soreness or irritation and urinary frequency. On examination, the vagina looks red and inflamed. The inflamed cervix looks like a strawberry with punctate hemorrhagic spots.

subject: Obstetrics & Gynecology
text: A patient developed atonic postpartum hemorrhage after a normal vaginal delivery. She was shifted to the OT and the obstetrician planned ligation of vessels to arrest the bleeding. What is the order of ligation of the blood vessels supplying the uterus?

options.A: Uterine artery - Ovarian a​rtery - Internal iliac ar​tery
options.B: Uterine artery - Ovarian a​rtery- External iliac art​ery
options.C: Uterine artery - Ovarian a​rtery - Vaginal artery

expl:
Correct answer: A. Uterine artery - Ovarian artery - Internal iliac artery

The order of ligation of vessels to arrest bleeding in atonic postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is the uterine artery - ovarian artery - internal iliac artery.

The ascending branch of the uterine artery is ligated between the upper and lower segments of the uterus, at the lateral border. If the bleeding continues, the ovarian and uterine artery anastomosis is ligated just below the ovarian ligament. If the bleeding still persists, the anterior division of the internal iliac artery is ligated 5 cm distal to the common iliac bifurcation.  

Unilateral or bilateral ligation of the internal iliac artery ligation causes a reduction in the pulse pres­sure in the arteries distal to the ligation. This increases the chances of hemostasis via pressure and clot formation.

Surgical methods to control PPH are outlined as stepwise uterine devascularization procedures:

  • Compression sutures: B-Lynch suture
  • Ligation of uterine arteries
  • Ligation of ovarian and uterine anastomosis
  • Ligation of internal iliac artery
  • Angiographic embolization of the bleeding vessel

Pelvic packing (usually done prior to embolization) and hysterectomy are other surgical methods employed to control PPH.

subject: Obstetrics & Gynecology
text: A teenage patient presented with a history of dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain. On ultrasonography, a transverse vaginal septum was seen. What is the most common complication that can be seen in this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Endometriosis

The most common complication that can be seen in this patient is endometriosis.

Transverse vaginal septum leads to obstructed flow of menstrual blood. This may lead to retrograde menstruation, which increases the likelihood of the development of endometriosis, according to Sampson's theory of endometriosis.

Transverse vaginal septum occurs as a result of the failure of Müllerian duct fusion or failure of vaginal plate canalization. It may be obstructive or non-obstructive. The commonest site of a transverse septum is the junction between the upper and middle third of the vagina.

Patients with an obstructive or imperforate vaginal septum present with symptoms similar to the imperforate hymen. Symptoms include amenorrhoea, cyclical abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, and a palpable pelvic mass. The vagina may appear shortened and the cervix may not be identifiable. Secondary sexual characteristics appear normal. The diagnosis can be confirmed with ultrasound or MRI.

There is an increased risk of endometriosis. Other complications such as pyomucocolpos, pyometra, and pyosalpinges can also develop in infants with obstructive vaginal septums. 

Treatment is by manual dilatation of the perforation or surgical excision of the septum. 

Other options:

Option B: Tubo-ovarian abscess develops in pelvic inflammatory disease.

Option C: Dermoid cysts are cystic ovarian tumors that are often associated with mucinous cystadenomas.

Option D: Theca lutein cysts are found in association with hydatidiform moles, choriocarcinoma, and gonadotropin or clomiphene citrate therapy. They regress with the management of the mole and choriocarcinoma and discontinuation of gonadotropin therapy.

subject: Obstetrics & Gynecology
text: A 28-year old pregnant woman came for a routine antenatal check-up in her second trimester. Four years back, she delivered 2 healthy full-term twins. What would her obstetric score be?
expl:
Correct answer: C. G2P1

The obstetric score of a pregnant woman who previously delivered twins would be G2P1 (gravida 2 para 1).

The term gravida refers to the number of times the woman has been pregnant, irrespective of whether it crossed the period of viability. The current pregnancy is included in this count. Since she has been pregnant once before with twins and is currently pregnant now, gravida will be 2.

The term para refers to the number of previous pregnancies reaching a period of viability (gestation of 28 weeks). It does not increase to a higher number if multiples (twins/triplets) are delivered in a given pregnancy and still count as one birth. A current pregnancy, if any, is not included in this count. Therefore, para here will be 1 since she had one birth of twins and the present pregnancy is not counted.

Both gravidity and parity refer to the pregnancies and not the fetuses.

Note: The period of viability is when the fetus is capable of independent existence. The WHO defines it to be 24 weeks while the Indian definition is 28 weeks.

subject: Obstetrics & Gynecology
text: A 27-year-old woman who is on oral contraceptive pills for contraception has forgotten to take her pills on 4 different days in the last 2 weeks. She presents to the primary health center, asking for advice. What would you suggest to her?

options.A: Take 4 pills now, continue​ the schedule, use barrie​r method of contraception‍
options.B: Take 1 pill now, continue ​the schedule, and use bar​rier method of contracept‍ion
options.C: Take 1 pill now, use barri​er method, and consider e​mergency contraception in‍ case of recent intercour‌se
options.D: Discard the pack, start a ​new pack with alternate m​ethod of contraception

expl:
Correct answer: D. Discard the pack, start a new pack with alternate method of contraception

A woman who has missed 4 oral contraceptive pills in the last two weeks should take one hormonal pill as soon as possible and finish all hormonal pills in the pack as scheduled, throw away the 7 non-hormonal pills in a 28-pill pack and start a new pack the next day. 

Missed pills Management

Missed 1 or 2 pills/ started new pack 1 or 2 days late?

 

You have two options: take one hormonal pill right away, or take two pills at your usual scheduled time. 

The risk of pregnancy is minimal to none.

 

Missed 3 or more pills in the first or second week/started new pack 3 or more days late?

Take one hormonal pill immediately and then continue taking your pills as scheduled. 

Make sure to use a backup method of contraception for the next seven days.

Additionally, if you've had sexual intercourse within the last 72 hours, consider taking emergency contraceptive pills.

 
Missed 3 or more pills in the third week?

Take one hormonal pill as soon as you can and complete the entire pack of hormonal pills according to the schedule. 

Discard the seven non-hormonal pills in a 28-pill pack. 

Begin a new pack the following day.

 
Missed any nonhormonal pills? (last 7 pills in 28-pill pack)

Dispose of any missed non-hormonal pills. 

Continue taking your combination oral contraceptives (COCs), one pill each day. 

Begin the new pack as you normally would.

 

If any non-hormonal pills were missed, she can discard the remaining pills. Start the new pack of oral contraceptives and continue taking as usual.

If she vomits within 2 hours of taking a pill, another pill from the pack should be taken as soon as possible. After that, continue taking the pills as scheduled. If the vomiting or diarrhea persists for >2 days, follow the instructions for 1 or 2 missed pills as mentioned above.

The contraceptive method should be discontinued and changed in the following situations:

  • Unexplained or prolonged heavy vaginal bleeding that suggests an underlying condition not related to the method
  • Starting anticonvulsant medication or treatment with rifampicin
  • Migraines
  • Non-ambulatory conditions lasting for >1 week like major surgery, leg in a cast, etc. Combined oral contraceptives can be restarted 2 weeks after ambulation.
  • Suspected heart or liver disease, hypertension, deep vein thrombosis, stroke, breast cancer, diabetes, or gall bladder disease

subject: Obstetrics & Gynecology
text:
A 30-year-old female patient, on treatment for infertility, came with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and mild vaginal bleeding. Her beta hCG level was 2800 mIU/mL. On ultrasound, a 3cm mass was seen in the left adnexa. It contained a gestational sac with no fetal cardiac activity. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?

hCG- Human chorionic gonadotropin
expl:
Correct answer: B. Single dose methotrexate

A patient on infertility treatment, with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding with beta hCG levels of 2800 mIU/mL, and a gestational sac in the left adnexa points to the diagnosis of unruptured ectopic pregnancy and the most appropriate management is single-dose methotrexate.

A pregnancy is considered ectopic if implantation occurs at a site outside the uterine cavity. The majority of ectopic pregnancies occur in the fallopian tube, the ampulla being the most common site.

Management of ectopic pregnancy: 

Expectant management: Ectopic pregnancies measuring <3 cm and with declining beta hCG levels initially <1500 mIU/mL may resolve without inter­vention and can be managed expectantly. 

Medical management with single or multiple-dose methotrexate is preferred if:

  • Hemodynamic stability
  • Serum beta-hCG ≥1500 mIU/ml and ≤5000 mIU/mL
  • Mean sac diameter <3.5cm with no fetal cardiac activity detected on transvaginal ultrasound.
  • Patients are willing and able to comply with post-treatment follow-up and have access to emergency medical services within a reasonable time frame in case of a deterioration in the clinical status.

Methotrexate(MTX) can be given as a single IM dose of 50 mg/m2 or as a multiple-dose regimen of 1mg/kg on days 1, 3, 5, and 7.

Surgical management with salpingectomy or salpingostomy is done when:

  • Criteria for expectant and medical management are not met
  • Gestational sac >3.5 cm
  • Fetal cardiac activity present
  • Beta hCG > 5000 mIU/mL
  • Significant pain and hemoperitoneum 
  • Failure of expectant or medical management
  • Clinical status of patient warrants urgent intervention
  • Doubtful compliance with medical management 

Milking of the tube through the fimbriae carries a high risk of bleeding, damage to the tube, the persistence of trophoblastic tissue, and recurrence of ectopic pregnancy.

subject: Obstetrics & Gynecology
text:
A 30-year-old woman on oral contraceptives for the past 6 months presents with 6 weeks of amenorrhea. What would be the best method of assessing the gestational age of this patient?

LMP- Last menstrual period

USG- Ultrasonography
expl:
Correct answer: A. Crown rump length by USG

The best method of assessing the gestational age of a patient on oral contraceptives with 6 weeks of amenorrhea is by measuring the crown-rump length (CRL) using ultrasonography.

Gestational age refers to the duration of pregnancy calculated from the first day of the LMP. It is usually expressed in weeks. Following the use of oral contraceptives, ovulation may have been later than 2 weeks after the LMP. Therefore, gestational age calculated with the help of LMP will be inaccurate.

First-trimester ultrasound measurement of CRL is the best method to assess gestational age. It is measured from the vertex to the coccyx.

  • CRL (in mm) + 6.5 = gestational age in weeks (or)
  • CRL (in mm) + 42 days = gestational age in days.

CRL measurement is shown in the image below:

Ultrasonographic parameters for estimation of the gestational age according to the trimester are as follows:

Trimester

Parameter

1st 

Crown-rump length (CRL)

2nd and 3rd 
  • Biparietal diameter (BPD)
  • Abdominal Circumference (AC)
  • Head Circumference (HC)
  • Femur Length. (FL) 
Other options:
 
Option B: Adding 280 days to the LMP will provide the expected delivery date (EDD). Adding 9 months + 7 days to the LMP or 280 days to the LMP is Naegele’s formula for calculating the EDD.
 
Option C: Measurement of fundal height in cm (with a variation of 1-2cm) is roughly equal to the gestational age in weeks, after 24 weeks of pregnancy. This is measured from the superior border of the symphysis pubis to the top of the uterine fundus when the bladder is empty.

subject: Anaesthesia
text: 1. A smoker who was given an interscalene block for an arthroscopic acromioclavicular joint reconstruction 2 days ago was followed up by a Chest x-ray which showed as below. He is asymptomatic at present and is comfortably resting on the bed. What is the next step in management?

options.A: Insert chest drain as soon as possible
options.D: Wait and watch and give supplementary oxygen if needed

expl:
Correct answer: D. Wait and watch and give supplementary oxygen if needed

The next step of management is to wait and watch and give oxygen if needed. This is a case of postoperative asymptomatic pneumothorax. As the patient is asymptomatic with no symptoms of dyspnoea or respiratory distress the best way to manage is to wait and watch.  Postoperative pneumothorax is seen mostly in patients with pre existing lung conditions like asthma or in chronic smokers. The pre-existing blebs or bullae in the individuals rupture due to pressure gradients created by the positive pressure from ventilation or the arthroscopic pump and shaver system used during surgery. The pressure gradient from the positive pressure of anesthesia and the ipsilateral lung is highest in the lateral decubitus position. The other complications that can occur are subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum.

subject: Anaesthesia
text: 2. Which of the following is contraindicated in patients with acute intermittent porphyria?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Thiopentone

Thiopentone cannot be administered in a patient with acute intermittent porphyria. Thiopentone is a barbiturate induces aminolevulinic acid synthetase, which increases the formation of porphyrins. This will precipitate porphyria attacks, especially acute intermittent porphyria or variegate porphyria in susceptible individuals. Other effects: Thiopentone * is cerebroprotective as it reduces CSF volume by facilitating its absorption.  * also decreases cerebral blood flow, cerebral blood volume and helps in lowering intracranial pressure. * should be avoided in hypovolemic or shock patients because of the significant reduction in cardiac output (69%) and arterial blood pressure due to vasodilation and venous pooling. * produces dose-related central respiratory depression, producing a characteristic ventilatory pattern called 'double apnea'.

subject: Anaesthesia
text: 3. Identify the given instrument?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Laryngeal mask airway

text: 3. What is the mechanism of action of local anesthetics?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Block sodium channels

Local anesthetics primarily act by blocking the sodium channels bound to the membrane.  Sodium channels have one larger α subunit and one or two smaller β subunits. These voltage-gated sodium channels exist in 3 states : * Resting (non conducting) * Open (conducting) and  * Inactivated (non conducting) The local anesthetics bind to the α subunit of sodium channels, thereby preventing their activation and inhibiting the influx of sodium.  Local anesthetics have a higher affinity for the sodium channels in open and inactivated state than in the resting state. Local anesthetic inhibition is both voltage and frequency-dependent and is higher when nerve fibers are firing rapidly than with slow, infrequent depolarizations. Note: Local anesthetics may also bind and inhibit calcium, potassium, transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) and many other channels and receptors. But blocking of sodium channels is the best answer, of all the given options. Pearl PF0745: Classification of local anesthetics based on chemical structure

text: 4. Which of the following induction agents is most appropriate for a patient with cardiac disease?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Etomidate

Etomidate is considered to be the most appropriate induction agent for cardiac patients.  Etomidate has minimal effect on cardiovascular function due to its lack of effect on the sympathetic nervous system and on the function of the baroreceptors. They act on alpha 2 adrenoreceptors and increase blood pressure which helps to maintain cardiovascular stability after the induction.  Etomidate is the induction agent of choice in patients with cardiovascular disease, reactive airway disease, and intracranial hypertension, Due to its unique hemodynamic stability, it is used as a short-term sedative in hemodynamically unstable patients like patients requiring cardioversion or in patients with unstable angina for minor operative procedures. Long-term use of etomidate in trauma or terminally ill patients will cause a reversible inhibition on 11 beta-hydroxylase which decreases cortisol production and increase 11 deoxycorticosterone. This results in adrenocortical suppression. Other options: Option A- Ketamine has a stimulatory effect on the sympathetic nervous system and results in increased blood pressure, heart rate, and cardiac output. This leads to an increase in myocardial oxygen consumption and so it is contraindicated in ischemic heart disease. Option C- Propofol is a myocardial depressant agent. It reduces sympathetic activity, leading to vasodilatation that results in a reduction of blood pressure and a decrease in cardiac output. Option D- Thiopentone is also a myocardial depressant agent. It causes peripheral vasodilatation, reduction in the ventricular filling, negative inotropic effect, and reduction in a sympathetic outflow from CNS. this results in a reduction in blood pressure and a decrease in cardiac output.

subject: Anaesthesia
text: 3. BIPAP cannot be considered in patients with which of the following findings?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Unconscious patients

Patients being unconscious in considered a contraindication for BiPAP. BiPAP (Bilevel Positive Airway Pressure) therapy is a non-invasive ventilation technique that requires patient cooperation and the ability to breathe spontaneously. It relies on the patient's ability to initiate and maintain breathing efforts while receiving pressure support from the device. An unconscious patient, by definition, lacks the ability to consciously control their breathing and cannot actively participate in the breathing process. Therefore, BiPAP therapy is contraindicated in unconscious patients as they cannot tolerate the interface and settings required for this type of ventilation. In such cases, invasive mechanical ventilation, which provides full ventilatory support, is typically necessary to maintain adequate gas exchange and support respiratory function. Positive-pressure ventilation helps with stiff lungs and high airway resistance. Here, gas flow and pressure can be adjusted to improve inflation. Disadvantages include poor ventilation-perfusion matching, lower cardiac output, and lung injury. Increased chest pressure reduces blood return to the heart. Barotrauma results from high pressures, and volutrauma occurs from repeated alveolar collapse and reopening. Air flows to the upper lung areas, while blood flows to the lower regions, increasing the dead space. Other Options: Option (a) Low pO2 levels: BiPAP therapy is often utilized to improve oxygenation in patients with hypoxemia (low blood oxygen levels). By delivering positive airway pressure, BiPAP helps to recruit collapsed alveoli, improve lung ventilation-perfusion matching, and enhance oxygen diffusion into the bloodstream. Therefore, low pO2 levels are not a contraindication for BiPAP therapy; instead, they may indicate the need for BiPAP to support oxygenation. Option (c) High CO2 levels: BiPAP therapy can also be beneficial for patients with hypercapnia (elevated blood carbon dioxide levels), such as those with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation or obesity hypoventilation syndrome. By providing inspiratory pressure support and positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), BiPAP assists ventilation, enhances alveolar ventilation, and helps to eliminate excess carbon dioxide from the body. Therefore, high CO2 levels alone do not contraindicate the use of BiPAP therapy; rather, BiPAP may be indicated to improve ventilation and reduce CO2 levels. Option (d) Obstructive sleep apnea: BiPAP therapy is commonly employed as a non-invasive treatment for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), a sleep disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of upper airway collapse during sleep. By delivering two levels of pressure – higher pressure during inspiration (IPAP) and lower pressure during expiration (EPAP) – BiPAP helps to keep the upper airway open, prevent apnea events, and improve sleep quality. Therefore, obstructive sleep apnea is not a contraindication for BiPAP therapy; rather, BiPAP is a recommended treatment modality for managing this condition.

Blood-gas partition co-efficient determines the solubility of the anesthetic agent in the blood. The higher the blood-gas partition coefficient, the higher will be the solubility of the anesthetic agent. This leads to its greater uptake by pulmonary circulation. The higher the uptake of the anesthetic agent, the higher the difference between the inspired and alveolar concentrations, which leads to a slower rate of induction and recovery. Desflurane has a very low blood:gas partition coefficient (0.42). Thus, the alveolar and blood concentrations rapidly rise to the level of inspired concentration, providing rapid induction of anesthesia and rapid recovery. text: 5. A young male patient was given regional block with 0.25% bupivacaine for a minor surgical procedure. Shortly after the injection, the patient suddenly became unresponsive and the pulse was not recordable. Which of the following would be the best course of management for this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: A. CPR with 20% intralipid

The clinical picture of an unresponsive patient with an absent pulse following bupivacaine administration is most likely due to bupivacaine-induced cardiotoxicity resulting from accidental intravascular injection of local anesthetic. The best course of management in this scenario would be administering CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation), along with a 20% intralipid injection. Bupivacaine is a long-acting local anesthetic that is the most cardiotoxic among the local anesthetics. It depresses the rapid phase of depolarization in Purkinje fibers and ventricular muscle due to a decreased availability of fast sodium channels in cardiac membranes. This reduced rate of depolarization depresses myocardial contractility. Hence, bupivacaine is a potent cardio depressant. Cardio-vascular effects of bupivacaine-induced toxicity are as follows: * Left ventricular depression * Atrioventricular heart block * Ventricular arrhythmias and ventricular fibrillation * Sinus bradycardia can lead to cardiac arrest Initial management includes immediate initiation of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and defibrillation as per the advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) algorithm. Following CPR, intralipid therapy is initiated. Its mechanism is explained by the lipid sink theory which states lipophilic drugs (bupivacaine) are absorbed into the lipid emulsion of the plasma, hence, removed from tissues affected by toxicity. Intralipid therapy is administered as : * 20% IV dose as a rapid bolus (1.5 mL/kg) * Infusion of 0.25 mL/kg/min for 10 min after the patient is hemodynamically stable Local anesthesia systemic toxicity (LAST) can also affect the central nervous system (CNS), which is more susceptible to local anesthetic action as compared to the cardiovascular system. Dizziness, tinnitus, and disorientation are the initial symptoms. Shivering, muscular twitching, and tremors follow. Tonic-clonic seizures occur. Finally, respiratory depression can lead to respiratory arrest. text: 1. A patient undergoing surgery receives succinylcholine for muscle relaxation and later develops hyperthermia, rigidity, tremors, and tachycardia. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Dantrolene

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of malignant hyperthermia. The drug of choice for the condition is dantrolene. Dantrolene is a direct-acting skeletal muscle relaxant that acts on the RyR1 (ryanodine receptor) calcium channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscles and inhibits calcium-induced calcium release. This results in the uncoupling of membrane depolarisation and muscle contraction, thus inhibiting muscle contraction. Malignant hyperthermia is a genetic condition in which mutated RyR1 receptors are present in the skeletal muscles. In the presence of certain triggers, this mutated RyR1 causes severe dysfunction in the RyR1 channels. This leads to the accumulation of calcium ions in the skeletal muscle, resulting in sustained muscle contraction, rigidity, increased heat production, acidosis, hyperkalaemia, and increased end-tidal CO₂. Drugs triggering malignant hyperthermia: * Succinylcholine * Halothane * Isoflurane * Sevoflurane Susceptible patients: * Patients with a positive family history. It can be inherited as an autosomal dominant trait. * Patients with congenital myopathies. Treatment: Dantrolene sodium is the drug of choice for malignant hyperthermia. Once the diagnosis is made, the causative inhalational agent should be stopped immediately. Supportive treatment with rapid cooling, inhalation of 100% oxygen, control of acidosis, and treatment of hyperkalaemia should be given.

In the given clinical scenario, where a patient is scheduled for elective hip surgery in 5 days and is taking aspirin, a multivitamin, enalapril, and metoprolol, the recommended perioperative management includes discontinuing enalapril, as it is an ACE inhibitor. ACE inhibitors are discontinued 24 hours before surgery due to the risk of hemodynamic instability. ACE inhibitors block the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), leading to vasodilation and reduced blood pressure. During anaesthesia, there is already vasodilation and decreased sympathetic tone → combining this with ACE inhibitors can cause severe hypotension that is resistant to fluids.  Aspirin can be maintained unless the patient is scheduled for neurosurgery or retinal surgery, provided the dosage remains unchanged. Metoprolol, being a beta-blocker, should always be continued. 5. What is the newly added sixth link in the chain of survival according to the latest AHA update?

AHA-American Health Association
expl:
Correct answer: B. Recovery and Rehabilitation

The newly added sixth link in the chain of survival according to the latest AHA update is Recovery and Rehabilitation. The AHA (American Heart Association) Chain of Survival is a critical concept in improving survival rates for individuals experiencing cardiac arrest. It consists of a series of actions that, when performed promptly and effectively, increase the chances of survival. Traditionally, the chain includes five key links: early recognition and activation of emergency response, early CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation), rapid defibrillation, advanced life support, and post-cardiac arrest care. Each of these steps plays a vital role in ensuring timely intervention, restoring circulation, and providing critical care to improve patient outcomes. In recent updates, the AHA has introduced a sixth link to the Chain of Survival: Recovery. This emphasizes the importance of long-term rehabilitation, psychological support, and follow-up care for cardiac arrest survivors. Recovery includes interventions such as physical therapy, lifestyle modifications, and emotional support to help survivors regain quality of life and reduce the risk of future cardiac events. This addition highlights the growing recognition that survival is not just about resuscitation but also about ensuring a patient's overall well-being beyond the immediate crisis.

text: 1. Which of the following anaesthetic agents act on NMDA receptors?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Ketamine

Ketamine is a phencyclidine derivative that inhibits NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptors resulting in a decrease in excitatory stimulation by glutamate in the brain. It is a strong analgesic and amnestic agent.  On the cardiovascular system, it directly has a cardio-depressive effect and indirectly stimulates it by activating the sympathetic system and inhibiting the vagus nerve. It predominantly shows a stimulatory effect hence causing tachycardia, increased cardiac output, and increased systemic and pulmonary hypertension. On the respiratory system, it has a bronchodilator effect on bronchial smooth muscles. It increases salivary secretion and bronchial secretion. It also acts on other systems and increases the intracranial and intraocular pressures. Uses: * Ketamine is the intravenous agent of choice for patients with shock, low cardiac output states, and reactive airway diseases. * It is also used in patients with congenital heart diseases, especially with right-to-left shunts * Perioperative analgesia Ketamine should be avoided in patients with a history of seizures, psychiatric illness, or vascular aneurysms. It is also contraindicated in open-eye injuries and eye surgeries. Adverse effects: * Hallucination is the most common side effect of ketamine. * Emergence reaction (vivid dreaming, illusion, etc) * Increases brain oxygen consumption and metabolic rate leading to increased intracranial tension. Other options: Option A: Propofol facilitates the inhibitory neurotransmission by action on GABA-A receptors. It has a rapid onset of action (within 15 sec). Induction dose is usually 1-2 mg/ kg and the maintenance dose is 100-200 µg/ kg/ min. Propofol is formulated as a lipid emulsion and appears as a milky white liquid. It has antiemetic properties which help reduce post-operative nausea and vomiting. Option C: Midazolam is a benzodiazepine that facilitates GABA-A receptors' action by increasing the frequency of opening of GABA-mediated chloride channels. It is used in treating seizures and is used in daycare surgeries as an induction agent due to its short half-life.  Option D: Thiopentone sodium belongs to the barbiturate group which acts on the GABA-A receptors. This site is separate from the GABA-A site to which benzodiazepines bind. They potentiate the action of GABA in increasing the duration of openings of chloride-specific ion channels.

text: 6. A patient undergoing elbow surgery was given a local anaesthetic during the procedure. Local anaesthetics acts by ___________________.
expl:
Correct answer: A. Blocking voltage gated sodium channels

Local anaesthetics primarily act by blocking the voltage-gated sodium channels bound to the membrane.  Sodium channels have one larger α subunit and one or two smaller β subunits. These voltage-gated sodium channels exist in 3 states : * Resting (non-conducting) * Open (conducting) * Inactivated (non-conducting) The local anaesthetics bind to the α subunit of sodium channels, thereby preventing their activation and inhibiting the influx of sodium. They have a higher affinity for the sodium channels in the open and inactivated state than in the resting state. Local anaesthetic inhibition is both voltage and frequency-dependent and is higher when nerve fibres are firing rapidly than with slow, infrequent depolarizations. Note: Local anaesthetics may also bind and inhibit calcium, potassium, transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) and many other channels and receptors, but blocking sodium channels is its primary action. text: 1. Which of the physiological parameters does the waveform in the image represent?
expl:
Correct answer: D. End-tidal carbon dioxide

A capnograph is a device that displays and records end-tidal carbon dioxide, usually as a function of time. The normal waveform has four different phases: Phase I: Inspiratory baseline, represents the CO2-free gas from the airways (anatomical and apparatus dead space). Phase II: Expiratory upstroke, mixing of dead space gas with alveolar gas. Phase III: Alveolar plateau, represents CO2-rich gas from the alveoli. The last of the alveolar gas is sampled to measure ETCO2. Phase 0: Inspiratory downstroke and the beginning of inspiration. Alpha angle: The transition from phase II to III. The alpha angle can be used to assess the ventilation/perfusion of the lung. V/Q mismatches will have an alpha angle greater than 90 degrees. Beta angle: The transition from phase III to 0. The beta angle can be used to assess rebreathing. If rebreathing occurs, the angle is greater than 90 degrees.

text: 5. A patient with severe Maxillofacial trauma after a road traffic accident presented with SpO2 80% at room air. In a situation where the patient cannot be intubated and cannot be ventilated (CICV), what is the next most appropriate immediate step in management?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Perform cricothyroidotomy

In the above clinical scenario of an RTA patient with severe maxillofacial trauma, where endotracheal intubation (Cannot Intubate, Cannot Ventilate) has failed to secure the airway, an alternate airway in the form of a surgical airway is indicated. Thus, performing a needle cricothyroidotomy is the next best step in the management of this patient.  This should be followed by percutaneous transtracheal oxygenation to provide temporary ventilation. In conditions that obstruct the airway, like edema of the glottis, laryngeal fracture, or severe oropharyngeal hemorrhage, a surgical airway is indicated.  Needle cricothyroidotomy involves inserting a needle through the cricothyroid membrane to provide short-term ventilation till a definitive airway can be achieved. A Y-connector is attached, and oxygenation is provided at 15 L/min. Surgical cricothyroidotomy involves inserting an endotracheal or tracheostomy tube after making a transverse incision over the cricothyroid membrane. An emergency surgical airway is preferred over tracheostomy as it is easier to perform, is associated with less bleeding, and can be done quickly. Other options: Option A: Nasopharyngeal intubation is contraindicated in cases of severe maxillofacial trauma because of risk of basilar skull fracture (risk of injury to brain by putting the tube) and distorted anatomy making it unsafe or impossible to perform. Option B: Supraglottic airway devices are used in difficult airway management but in case of severe macillofacial trauma, it is not preferred as it cannot bypass the distorted anatomy or complete obstruction of upper airway. Option D: Administer Succinylcholine and Retry Intubation in a case of a patient that cannot be intubated and cannot be ventilated (CICV) is very dangerous and ineffective as repeating might do more harm by increasing airway trauma, edema and worsened oxygenation.

text: 1. A patient was given halothane for a surgical procedure. After few minutes, the anaesthetist noticed that he developed rigidity and hyperthermia. Which of the following ions is the reason for the above symptoms?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Calcium

The given clinical scenario of rigidity and hyperthermia with halothane suggests the diagnosis of malignant hyperthermia. The ion responsible for it is calcium. Malignant hyperthermia is a rare genetic hypermetabolic muscle disease, the characteristic signs, and symptoms of which most commonly appear with exposure to inhaled anesthetics or succinylcholine.  The pathophysiology behind the development of malignant hyperthermia is that there is an uncontrolled increase in intracellular calcium in skeletal muscle. The sudden release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum removes the inhibition of troponin, resulting in sustained muscle contraction. Markedly increased ATPase activity results in an uncontrolled hypermetabolic state with significantly increased oxygen consumption & CO2 production, producing severe lactic acidosis and hyperthermia. Pearl PF1601: Malignant hyperthermia key features Pathophysiology: * Prolonged opening of functionally altered ryanodine receptors, leading to uncontrolled release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum resulting in sustained muscle contraction. Drugs known to trigger malignant hyperthermia: * Inhaled anesthetics: Halothane, Isoflurane, Sevoflurane, Desflurane, Ether, Methoxyflurane * Depolarising muscle relaxant: Succinylcholine Clinical signs: * Increased metabolism: Increased EtCO2, decreased SpO2, metabolic acidosis * Increased sympathetic activity: Tachycardia, hypertension, arrythmia * Muscle damage: Masseter spasm, generalised rigidity, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis, myoglobinuria * Hyperthermia: Fever, sweating  Treatment:  * Discontinuation of all anesthetic agents * Hyperventilation with 100% O2 * Dantrolene: 2.5 mg/kg intravenously every 5 min until the episode is terminated (upper limit - 10 mg/kg). * Correction of acid-base, electrolyte abnormality  * Cooling the patient

text: 6. An 18-year-old boy is rushed to the ER after having choked on a bone while eating. He is responsive but unable to speak. What is to be done next?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Perform Heimlich maneuver

In a choking child (more than 1 year old) or an adult, the first step to be done is to perform Heimlich maneuver which involves delivering abdominal thrusts. The rescuer should stand or kneel behind the patient and wrap his arms around the patient’s waist. A fist is made with one hand and using the other hand, the fist is driven into the patient’s abdomen with a rapid, forceful upward thrust so as to dislodge the foreign body. This is continued until the foreign body is expelled or if the patient becomes unresponsive. If the patient becomes unresponsive, immediately start CPR. The Heimlich maneuver is performed as follows: * Stand behind the person and slightly to one side. * Place your arms around the person's waist. * Make a fist with one hand and place the thumb side against the person's upper abdomen, above the navel and below the ribcage. * Grasp your fist with your other hand and give quick, inward and upward thrusts to the abdomen, using enough force to dislodge the object. * Repeat thrusts until the object is expelled or the person becomes unconscious. In a choking infant who is responsive, 5 back slaps between the shoulder blades and 5 downward thrusts on the chest are given in order to dislodge the foreign body. If the patient becomes unresponsive, immediately start CPR. Other options: A) Bag and mask ventilation involves providing breaths of air using a bag and mask to a person who is not breathing adequately. While it may be necessary if the person becomes unconscious, it is not the immediate next step for a conscious individual who is unable to speak due to choking. B) Endoscopic removal involves using a flexible tube with a camera to visualize the airway and remove the obstructing object. This may be considered if the initial Heimlich maneuver is unsuccessful in dislodging the object. C) Deliver 5 backslaps and 5 chest compressions: This technique, known as back blows and chest thrusts, is recommended for infants under one year of age in cases of choking. In this scenario with an 18-year-old boy, the Heimlich maneuver is the more appropriate action to attempt to clear the airway obstruction.

text: 7. You are a junior resident in the ICU. A senior doctor asks you to manage a mechanically ventilated patient whose arterial blood gases showed features of hypoventilation with respiratory acidosis. Which of the following parameters can you modulate to improve the condition of the patient?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Increase Respiratory Rate

Since this patient has features of hypoventilation and respiratory acidosis this is a case of type 2 respiratory failure and needs correction of hypoxia and hypercapnia. Thus, the respiratory rate should be increased, which increases ventilation and decreases the CO2 content, leading to improvement in the condition of this patient.  The most common ventilator mode to use in a newly intubated patient is ACMV(Assist Control Mode Ventilation). The common terms used in association with a ventilator: * Ventilation/minute ventilation is calculated as respiratory rate (RR) times tidal volume (Vt). In a mechanically ventilated patient, the CO2 content of the blood can be modified by changing the tidal volume or the respiratory rate. * Tidal volume is the volume of air moved in and outside the lungs in each respiratory cycle. * Oxygenation of the lungs can be changed by altering the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2%) or the positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP). * FiO2 is the percentage of oxygen in the air mixture that is delivered to the patient. * PEEP: The positive pressure that will remain in the airways at the end of the respiratory cycle. * Peak pressure is a measure of airway resistance as well as compliance and includes the tubing and bronchial tree. * Plateau pressures are a reflection of alveolar pressure and thus of lung compliance. Initial ventilatory settings are as given below: * Tidal volume - 4-6 ml/kg of IBW (Ideal Body Weight) * Respiratory rate - 12 Breaths/ min * FiO2 - 100% to begin with and titrated to lesser values to prevent oxygen toxicity * PEEP - Begin with 5 cm H2O, titrate to 10 cm H2O (Carefully increased as high PEEP may impair ventricular filling in a patient with blunt chest trauma) An ABG should be obtained 30 minutes after intubation and changes to the ventilator settings should be made in accordance with ABG findings. Peak and plateau pressures should be checked on the vent to assure there are no problems with airway resistance or alveolar pressure in order to prevent ventilator-induced lung injury. Based on the ABG, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and hyperventilation can be corrected by altering some ventilator settings. * To increase the oxygenation either FiO2% or PEEP has to be increased. Raising the PEEP has a risk of barotrauma and hypotension while increased FiO2 can cause oxidative damage in the alveoli. A target of 92-94% should be maintained. A sudden drop of saturation can be caused by tube misplacement, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, atelectasis, or the development of mucus plugs. * Hypercapnia can be managed by modifying alveolar ventilation which is dependent on tidal volume or the respiratory rate. Raising the rate or the tidal volume, will increase ventilation and decrease CO2. While increasing the rate, it will also increase the amount of dead space and can lead to the development of auto-PEEP. Dynamic hyperinflation or auto-PEEP is a process in which some of the inhaled air is not fully exhaled at the end of the respiratory cycle. The accumulation of trapped air will increase pulmonary pressures and cause barotrauma and hypotension. To prevent and resolve auto-PEEP, enough time should be given for the air to leave the lungs during exhalation.  Note: Causes of elevated peak pressure and normal plateau pressure: Kinked ET tube, Mucus plug, Bronchospasm. Causes of elevated peak and elevated plateau pressure: Mainstem intubation, Pneumothorax, Atelectasis, Pulmonary edema, ARDS.

expl:
Correct answer: C. Train of four

Train of four protocol is the best method to clinically assess neuromuscular blockade. Train of four protocol is one of the methods used in the clinical assessment of neuromuscular blockade. text: 6. Which of the following arises from 6th pharyngeal arch?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Ductus arteriosus

Ductus arteriosus arises from the 6th pharngeal arch. Pharyngeal arches appear in the 4th or 5th week of development and contribute to the formation of the head and neck region. text: 9. Which of the following develops from the dorsal mesogastrium?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Spleen

The spleen develops from the mesoderm in the dorsal mesogastrium. The mesenchymal cells in the dorsal mesogastrium form small lobular masses of splenic tissue called spleniculi. A patient with leprosy presented with the deformity as shown below. Which nerve injury causes the given condition ?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Ulnar nerve

The given image shows extension at the metacarpophalangeal joint and flexion at interphalangeal joints of the ring and little finger, caused by ulnar nerve injury. It produces a claw hand (main en griffe). Leprosy can affect peripheral nerves and lead to their associated conditions. In ulnar nerve palsy, only the medial two fingers develop clawing, while in a combined median and ulnar nerve palsy, all four fingers develop clawing.  The ulnar nerve supplies the medial two lumbricals in the hand. The lumbricals have a combined action on metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint flexion and interphalangeal (IP) joint extension (glass holding posture). In ulnar nerve injury, since the medial lumbricals are not functional, the forearm muscles are unopposed. Hence, there is hyperextension at MCP joints and flexion at IP joints. This causes claw hand deformity. There is also numbness of the ulnar one and a half fingers.  Elbow fractures or dislocations lead to high lesions of the ulnar nerve. Here, the hand is not markedly deformed because the ulnar half of the flexor digitorum profundus is paralyzed and the fingers, therefore, appear less clawed. This is called the high ulnar paradox. The following tests are done to test the integrity of the ulnar nerve: * Egawa's test - In a positive test, due to the weakness of the dorsal interossei, side-to-side movements of the middle finger is weak. * Book test or Froment's sign - The patient is asked to hold a book forcefully while the doctor tries to pull it. In a positive test, due to weakness of adductor pollicis muscle, adduction of thumb is lost. The patient tries to hold the book by using flexor pollicis longus muscle. This produces flexion at the inter-phalangeal joint while holding the book. * Card test - In the case of weak palmar interossei, it is easy for the examiner to pull out the card when held between the fingers. This is due to the loss of adduction by palmar interossei muscles. Other options Option B - In radial nerve palsy, the patient presents with 'wrist drop' in case of paralyzed wrist extensors, and 'finger drop' when extensor digitorum is paralyzed. When there is compression in the axilla, radial nerve palsy is called Saturday night palsy. There is paralysis of the triceps, and weakness of the wrist and hand. In high lesions, there is sensory loss on the dorsum of the hand over the anatomical stuff box.  Option C - In median nerve injury, paralysis of opponens pollicis muscle leads to 'ape thumb' deformity. In forearm or elbow injuries, there is paralysis of long flexors of the thumb, index, and middle fingers, radial wrist flexors, and forearm pronators. This leads to the characteristic 'pointing index finger'. There is sensory loss over three and a half digits on the radial side.  Option D -Posterior interosseous nerve injury, is seen in posterior interosseous syndrome. text: 3. What is the embryological basis of the developmental defect shown in the image below?

options.A: Failure in closure of anterior neuropore of neural tube
options.B: Failure in closure of posterior neuropore of neural tube
options.C: Failure in closure of complete neural tube
options.D: Failure in closure of caudal neuropore of neural tube

expl:
Correct answer: A. Failure in closure of anterior neuropore of neural tube

The image shows anencephaly. Failure of the anterior end (cranial end) of the neural tube to close is known as exencephaly. As a result of this, the skull vault does not form. This leaves the malformed brain exposed. The exposed brain tissue degenerates, leaving a mass of necrotic tissue. This defect with the absence of a major portion of the brain, skull, and scalp is known as anencephaly. The brain stem remains intact. In some cases, the closure defect of the neural tube extends caudally, and the spinal cord is affected. This condition is known as craniorachischisis, where there is anencephaly plus a large defect involving the spine.  Neurulation refers to the formation of the neural tube from the neural plate. The neural tube gives rise to the central nervous system.  Steps of neurulation * The notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken and form the neural plate. * The neural plate lengthens and the lateral edges elevate to form the neural folds, and the mid-region gets depressed to form the neural groove. * The neural folds approach each and fuse in the midline in a craniocaudal direction to form a tube-like structure called the neural tube. * The anterior opening of the neural tube (cranial neuropore) closes by day 25 and the posterior opening (caudal neuropore) closes by day 28. * The neural tube becomes the central nervous system.

text: 4. A newborn presented to the NICU with respiratory distress and meconium discharge from the umbilicus. The condition occurs due to the patency of the which structure?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Vitellointestinal duct

The presence of meconium discharge at the umbilicus is suggestive of vitelline fistula, which occurs due to patent vitelline duct, which connects the primitive gut to the yolk sac. The primitive gut is connected to the definitive yolk sac through a narrow stalk-like communication known as the vitellointestinal duct. It is also known as vitelline duct or yolk stalk or omphalomesenteric duct.  Due to the folding of the embryo in the cephalocaudal and lateral directions, the embryo gets enclosed all around by ectoderm, except in the region through which the vitellointestinal duct passes. In this region, there is a circular aperture, which is now called the umbilical opening. The vitellointestinal duct completely obliterates by the 7th week of development. Vitelline duct abnormalities: * Meckel's diverticulum: In about 2% of the individuals, a portion of the vitelline duct persists an outpouching of the ileum called, Meckel diverticulum. The diverticulum is usually asymptomatic unless it contains heterotopic pancreatic or gastric mucosa, which may lead to bleeding, ulceration, or perforation. * Vitelline cyst: In some individuals, both the ends of the vitelline duct transform into fibrous cords. However, the middle portion of the duct forms a large cyst called, enterocystoma, or vitelline cyst. As the fibrous cords run across the peritoneal cavity, it may lead to intestinal obstruction, strangulation, or volvulus. * Vitelline fistula: When the vitelline duct remains patent over its entire length, it forms a direct communication between the primitive gut and the umbilicus, a condition called an umbilical fistula or vitelline fistula. The newborn characteristically presents with meconium discharge from the umbilicus.

text: 6. Identify the structure marked in the diagram showing the development of ovarian follicles.
expl:
Correct answer: B. Antral follicle

The structure marked in the image is of a secondary follicle, also called an antral follicle. Development of ovarian follicles:  At birth, the ovarian cortex contains numerous primordial follicles which contain primary oocytes surrounded by a single layer of flat follicular cells. Most of these follicles degenerate in the prepubertal life and are called atretic follicles. At puberty, around 20 primordial follicles get activated in each menstrual cycle. Out of these 20 primordial follicles, only one follicle is dominant which reaches maturity and releases the oocyte during ovulation.  The different stages of development of the primordial follicle are:  a) Primary follicle: * Follicle cells change from flattened cells to cuboidal and the stromal cells surrounding the follicle differentiate into spindle-shaped cells called 'theca externa'. * The oocyte increases in size and secretes a proteoglycan material around it which forms the layer called 'Zona Pellucida' which is seen between the plasma membrane of the oocyte and the granulosa cells.  b)Secondary follicle(Antral follicle): * The primary follicles continue to increase in size and the granulosa cells multiply. * Numerous cavities coalesce to form a single fluid space called antrum. * The granulosa cells envelop the oocyte to form a structure called Cumulus oophorus. c) Tertiary follicle (Graffian follicle): * Numerous secondary follicles are formed but only one tertiary follicle develops while others regress and become atretic follicles. * As the antrum draws the fhe follicle increase in size and expands to a diameter of 2 cm to become Graffian follicle. * The oocyte and the surrounding granulosa cells called corona radiata break away from the follicular wall and float in the follicular fluid. * The primary oocyte completes its first meiotic division to form the secondary oocyte and a polar body. * The secondary oocyte is arrested in the metaphase of the second meiotic division until fertilization takes place. * The follicle ruptures to release the oocyte which is captured by for the fimbriae. d) Corpus Luteum: * The remainder of the follicle after ovulation is called the Corpus luteum. It synthesizes a carotenoid pigment called lutein which gives it a yellowish colour. * If the oocyte is not fertilized then corpus luteum degenerates 12-14 days after ovulation to become corpus albicans. * If fertilization occurs then the hCG produced by the trophoblast maintains the corpus luteum. It releases progesterone, estrogen, and relaxin, and regresses at around 8 weeks when the placenta takes over.

text: 12. At what level does the spinal cord end in infants?
expl:
Correct answer: C. L3

In infants, the spinal cord ends at the L3 level. As the child grows, the spinal cord moves up with age. Thus in adults, the distal termination of the spinal cord is at the lower border of L1. text: 13. Identify the given histology slide:
expl:
Correct answer: D. Pancreas

The above image shows pancreatic islet cells. Islet of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part of the pancreas. Islets are characterized by secretory cells supported by reticulin fibers, and containing numerous fenestrated capillaries. There is a delicate capsule around each islet. They are paler than the surrounding exocrine cells, as they have less rough endoplasmic reticulum. The image given below shows the histology of the pancreas: The islets of Langerhans contain four major and two minor cell types: Four main types are β, α, δ, and PP (pancreatic polypeptide) cells: * α or A cells- located peripherally and secrete glucagon  * β or B cells- located centrally and produce insulin  * δ or D cells- scattered between beta cells and secrete somatostatin * PP cells- are present in islets and also in the exocrine pancreas. They secrete a pancreatic polypeptide, which exerts several gastrointestinal effects, such as stimulation of secretion of gastric and intestinal enzymes and inhibition of intestinal motility.  Minor cell types: * D1 cells secrete vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), a hormone that induces glycogenolysis and hyperglycemia. It also stimulates gastrointestinal fluid secretion and causes secretory diarrhea. * Enterochromaffin cells synthesize serotonin and are the source of pancreatic tumors that cause carcinoid syndrome. Other options: Option A: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs. The structure of lymph nodes consists of an outer cortex and inner medulla. The cortex contains an aggregation of B-lymphocytes (primary follicles) and quiescent secondary follicles with a pale central germinal center. The inner medulla consists of medullary cords (lymphocytes and plasma cells) and medullary sinuses. Between the cortex and medulla, there is an ill-defined zone called the paracortex, which contains T lymphocytes. The image given below shows the histology of the lymph node: Option B: Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries. The glomerular capillary wall is the filtering membrane and consists of fenestrated endothelial cells, basement membrane, and visceral epithelial cells called podocytes, which contain foot processes. The white pulp is made up of aggregations of lymphocytes that surround a small artery or arterioles. The red pulp is a modified lymphoid tissue infiltrated with all the cells of circulating blood. It is like a sponge permeated by spaces (splenic sinusoids) lined by reticular cells. The zone of red pulp immediately surrounding white pulp is the marginal zone.
