text: 4. A lady with her 9-month-old baby presented to the doctor asking for another BCG vaccine dose for her child, as there is no visible BCG vaccination scar. The doctor checked the vaccination card and confirmed that the birth dose was given. The Mantoux test was done and came back negative. What is the next step?

options.C: BCG vaccination at 12 months of age
options.D: Do Mantoux test and wait for the result

expl:
Correct answer: A. Reassurance to mother

After BCG vaccination, the presence of a scar is not a reliable indicator of protection. Some children may not develop a visible scar despite receiving the vaccine. Therefore, the mother should simply be reassured. Since the vaccination card confirms that the birth dose of BCG was given, and the Mantoux test is negative, no repeat BCG dose is required.  BCG (bacillus of Calmette and Guerin) is the only live bacterial vaccine. The WHO has recommended the Danish 1331 strain for the production of the BCG vaccine. It protects against severe forms of childhood tuberculosis and tuberculous meningitis. It also reduces morbidity and mortality from primary tuberculosis. There are two types of BCG vaccine: the liquid (fresh) vaccine and the freeze-dried vaccine. The freeze-dried vaccine is a more stable preparation (option B) than the liquid vaccine. Currently, the vaccine is distributed in the freeze-dried form because of better storage qualities. Normal saline is recommended for reconstituting the vaccine, as distilled water may cause irritation. The reconstituted vaccine may be used up within 3 hours. The usual strength for vaccination is 0.1 mg in 0.1 ml volume. The dose given at birth (option A) and for newborns < 4 weeks of age is 0.05 ml. It is injected intradermally (option C) just above the insertion of the left deltoid muscle using a tuberculin syringe.   Other options: Option B and C: BCG revaccination is not included in the official immunisation schedule in India under the expanded programme on immunization. Option D: Mantoux test is already done and is negative, so no further action is needed.

text: 5. A Community Health Centre (CHC) receives a supply of 30 vaccine vials. Out of these, 3 vials (2 vials of Measles-Rubella (MR) vaccine and 1 vial of Pentavalent vaccine) are already opened and maintained under proper cold chain conditions. The Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM) prepares to administer these vaccines. What will she do according to the open vial policy?

options.A: Use MR vaccine and discard Pentavalent vaccine
options.B: Use Pentavalent vaccine and discard MR vaccine

expl:
Correct answer: B. Use Pentavalent vaccine and discard MR vaccine

According to the open vial policy, the ANM can use the pentavalent vaccine and discard the MR vaccine. Open vial policy allows for the reuse of partially used multidose vials of applicable vaccines under the Universal Immunization Programme in subsequent sessions for up to 4 weeks, subject to certain conditions and thereby reducing vaccine wastage. It is applicable only for DPT, TT, hepatitis B vaccine, OPV and liquid pentavalent vaccine. It is not applicable for BCG, measles, rotavirus vaccines and JE vaccines. Vaccine vials opened in session-site can be use in more than one session up to four weeks if expiry date has not passed, if storage and transport was appropriate, no contamination has occurred in vial septum, asepsis in withdrawing was practiced and if vaccine vial monitor has not reached the discard point. * Open vials should not be submerged in water. * Ensure all opened vials have the recorded date and time of opening. * At the end of a session, all vaccines should be returned to the cold chain point and segregated as reusable and non-reusable. * All open vials of BCG, measles and JE must be destroyed after 48 hours or before the next session, whichever is earlier. * In case of any adverse events following immunization, all open vials should not be discarded until investigation is complete. * All vials must be transported in zipper bags in the vaccine carrier and recorded in the stock register. * Ice packs used should be well-sealed. Pearl PF0969: Vaccine Vial Monitors * Vaccine vial monitors are used to monitor heat exposure of vaccines. * It is a chemical indicator that records the cumulative heat exposure through a gradual change in color. * If the color of the inner square is the same color or darker than the outer circle, it indicates that the vaccine has been exposed to too much heat and it must be discarded. * Currently, there are four types of VVMs (VVM2, VVM7, VVM14, and VVM30). They are chosen to match the heat sensitivity of the vaccine. * The VVM can be located on the label of the vaccine or on the neck or cap of the ampule/vial. * VVMs also help in reduction of vaccine wastage by indicating which batch of vaccines can be used first.

text: 6. Measles vaccine is classified under which type of vaccine?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Live vaccine

Measles vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine prepared from live or wild organisms grown in culture and attenuated to retain immunogenicity. It is available as a freeze-dried product and recommended only in the live attenuated form for safe and effective immunization. The vaccine is supplied as a freeze-dried product, reconstituted with sterile diluent, and one dose of 0.5 ml contains ≥1000 viral infective units of the vaccine strain. The reconstituted vaccine is generally injected subcutaneously, but it is also effective when administered intramuscularly.  It should be stored at 2–8°C after reconstitution and used within 4 hours, since it loses about 50% potency after 1 hour at 20°C. When administered, measles vaccine induces seroconversion in 95–98% of recipients after a single dose, ensuring strong immunity. The first dose (MCV1) is given at 9 completed months, with a second dose (MCV2) at 15–18 months to ensure full coverage.Reaching all children with 2 doses of measles containing vaccine (MCV) should be the standard for all national immunization programmes. In countries with high measles risk, MCV is also given as part of outbreak control or supplementary doses up to 5 years of age. It is often used in combination vaccines like MR (measles-rubella), MMR (measles-mumps-rubella), and MMRV (measles-mumps-rubella-varicella).   Adverse Reactions :  * After vaccination, a mild “measles-like illness” (fever and rash) may occur in 5–10 days, lasting for 1–2 days. * Other reactions include minor upper respiratory infections, mild diarrhea, or fever that resolves in 1–3 days. * Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS) can occur if the vaccine vial is contaminated or used beyond 4 hours after reconstitution, leading to severe symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhea, high fever, and even death within 48 hours. Contraindications: * immunosuppression (e.g., HIV-infected persons with evidence of severe immunosuppression). * Pregnancy – should be avoided for at least 4 weeks following MMR vaccination. Persons with moderate or severe acute illness should postpone vaccination until recovery. Pearl PF0040: National Immunization Schedule (India)

text: 7. Which of the following is classified as Medical Eligibility Criteria 1( MEC-1) for the use of oral contraceptive pills(OCPs)?
expl:
Correct answer: C. HIV

According to the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (MEC), HIV falls under category 1, meaning OCPs can be used in any circumstance. Combined oral contraceptives contain estrogen (ethinylestradiol/mestranol) and progestins (levonorgestrel, norethisterone, desogestrel). Their primary mode of action is inhibition of ovulation: estrogen suppresses FSH to prevent follicular growth, while progestins suppress LH to block ovulation. This negative feedback on the hypothalamo-pituitary axis prevents the mid-cycle gonadotropin surge. Additionally, they act by producing a non-receptive endometrium, thickening cervical mucus to block sperm penetration, and possibly altering tubal motility to prevent fertilization. Progestins also counteract estrogen’s proliferative effect on the endometrium, reducing the risk of hyperplasia and controlling withdrawal bleeding. WHO category 1- Indication of OCPs * Age: Menarche to 40 years * Postabortion * Anemia (iron deficiency, malaria) * HIV or AIDS (additional to condom use) * GTN following normal hCG level * History of ectopic pregnancy * Endometriosis, uterine fibroid, ovarian or endometrial cancer * Dysmenorrhea, DUB * Pelvic inflammatory disease * Epilepsy * Thyroid disease * Varicose veins * Tuberculosis * Benign breast disease Contraindications of OCPs :

text: 8. On January 1, 2024, a community with a population of 10,000 had 100 existing cases of tuberculosis (TB). During the year, 30 patients were cured and 10 patients died. Additionally, 20 new TB cases were reported, of which 5 were cured before December 31, 2024. What is the incidence of TB at the end of the year and the prevalence of TB for the year?
expl:
Correct answer: A. 2/1000,12/1000

Incidence is the number of new cases occurring in a defined population during a period of time. Here, 20 new TB cases occurred in 2024 in a population of 10,000, so: * Incidence = (Number of cases of a disease in a specified period of time/Population at risk during that time) x 1000 * incidence = (20/10,000) × 1000 = 2/1000 Prevalence is the proportion of all cases, old and new, present during a specified period. At the end of 2024, the community had 100 old cases plus 20 new cases, giving a total of 120 cases. So: * Prevalence = (Number of all cases of a specified disease at a given point in time/Estimated population at the same point in time) * prevalence = (120/10,000) × 1000 = 12 per 1000 Pearl PF0953: Incidence and Prevalence Incidence in Epidemiology: * Incidence is the number of new cases occurring in a defined population during a period of time. * Incidence = (Number of cases of a disease in a specified period of time/Population at risk during that time) x 1000 * Incidence rate is expressed in person-time units, usually per 1000 per year. * It provides insight into the effectives of health services and programs. * Incidence rate of spells of sickness =  (Number of spells of sickness starting in the specified period/Mean number of people exposed to that risk in the specified time) x 1000 * It is generally used for acute illnesses. * Special types of incidence rates: * Attack rate: It is used when there is a risk for a limited period of time. * Secondary attack rate: It is the number of exposed persons developing the disease within the range of incubation period following exposure to a primary case. * Incidence can be determined from cohort studies and longitudinal studies. Prevalence in Epidemiology: * Prevalence is the proportion of all cases, old and new, of a particular disease at a given point in time or over a period of time in a given population. * It is a proportion, not a rate or ratio. * It can be determined from cross-sectional studies. * Types: * Point prevalence is the prevalence at a point in time. Usually, prevalence is point prevalence unless otherwise specified. * Period prevalence is the prevalence over a period of time. * Prevalence is always expressed in percentage. * Prevalence = (Number of all cases of a specified disease at a given point in time/Estimated population at the same point in time) x 100 * It is useful to determine the magnitude of health problems. Relationship between Incidence and Prevalence: * Prevalence depends upon incidence and duration. * Prevalence = Incidence x Mean Duration * Longer the duration of the disease, greater the prevalence. * In acute diseases,because of rapid recovery/death prevalence will be relatively lower than incidence.This is because in some diseases (eg. food poisoning), the disease is so short lived, there are no "old cases". * In chronic diseases like TB, prevalence will be higher than incidence. * If a new treatment for a disease is effective, incidence does not change but prevalence decreases as duration of disease decreases. * If treatment only prevents death but doesn’t cure the disease, it may cause a paradoxical increase in prevalence.

text: 9. A study was conducted on workers in an aniline dye factory. One group consisted of workers exposed to the dye, and the other group included clerical staff with no exposure. All relevant information was collected from factory records spanning the past 20 years. What type of study does this represent?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Retrospective study

Factory workers exposed to aniline dye were compared with clerical staff using records from the past 20 years. Since both the exposure and outcomes had already occurred, and the study moved forward from those past records to analyze disease occurrence, it points towards a retrospective cohort study. A cohort study progresses from cause (exposure) to effect (disease). * Types of cohort study: * Prospective (concurrent) cohort studies * Retrospective (historical) cohort studies * Combination cohort studies * Steps of cohort study: * Selection of study subjects * Obtaining data on exposure * Selection of comparison groups * Follow-up * Analysis in terms of incidence rates and estimation of risk * Advantages of cohort study: * Incidence can be calculated * Several possible outcomes related to exposure can be studied at the same time * Provides direct estimate of relative risk * Calculation of dose-response ratio * Minimization of certain biases * Disadvantages of cohort study: * Cannot use for uncommon diseases * Expensive, requires a large population and longer time * Many common administrative and ethical problems * High attrition and selection of subjects is difficult * Dynamism of diagnostics is difficult to incorporate * Tends to alter the behaviour of subjects known as Hawthorne effect. Other options: Option A: In a case-control study, the study begins with the outcome and goes retrospectively to find out the exposure among the cases and controls.For example, to find the exposure to smoking associated with already diagnosed lung cancer patients. Option B: An ecological study is any kind of study in which data is collected about a population and is analyzed at that level. Unlike the case with cohort studies, in these studies, no data is available or analyzed about individuals. Option D: A cross-sectional study Is an observational study used to calculate a disease's distribution and prevalence.

text: 10. In a study to see the effect of a new antihypertensive drug, two groups were made, one group was given the new drug, and the other group was given a different drug. Their mean BP was compared later. Which kind of statistical study is this?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Unpaired T test

The test of choice to measure the difference in means between two groups in a study, with one group being a control is Unpaired T test. In this scenario, two groups are being compared hence, Student's t test/ Unpaired t test will be used. If 2 groups are being tested, then T tests are used. In that, if the same group is tested before and after, paired T test is used. Otherwise, unpaired T test is used. Other options: Option A: The chi-square test is used to compare qualitative data between 2 groups with independent measures. Option B: The analysis of variance test (ANOVA) is used to test the difference between two or usually more than two groups (means) and here the inferences are made by analyzing the variances. Option D: Paired t-test compares paired data or pre-intervention and post-intervention data of the same group. This doesn't apply here as the groups are not paired. Pearl PF0591: Tests of Significance How to choose which test to use? * See the variable. Are the variables quantitative or qualitative? * If the variables are qualitative (nominal), then Chi square test is used. * If the variables are quantitative, then see whether 2 groups are being tested, or more than 2 groups. * If 2 groups are being tested, then T tests are used. In that, if the same group is tested before and after, paired T test is used. Otherwise, unpaired T test is used. * If more than 2 groups are being tested, then use ANOVA. The tests: 1. T Tests * Unpaired t tests * Also known as the student’s t test, independent t test, two-samples t test. * It's the most commonly used t test and it tests the difference between two groups (the means of 2 groups) independent of each other and indicates how significant the differences are. * Paired t tests * "Pairs before marriage are not the same after!" * So remember paired test is mainly used in comparison of a before and after scenario  * Also known as correlated t test, dependent samples t test. * It is mainly used on dependent samples For example, the cholesterol level of a person before and after using a specific drug. * It can also be used when you put the same condition under test using different items or things. For example, same crash safety tests for different cars. * T scores  * The t score is referred to as the ratio of the difference between two groups and the difference within the groups. * The smaller the t score, the more similarity there is between two groups and vice versa.   2. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) * The analysis of variance test (ANOVA) is used to test the difference between two or usually more than two groups (means) and here the inferences are made by analyzing the variances.   3. Chi-Square Test * The Chi-Square test (χ2) is a non-parametric(non-numeric) test and it is used to test hypotheses in relation to nominal scale data or categorical data. * It is a test of proportions and associations. * A Chi-square distribution is usually positively skewed but it approaches a normal distribution as its degrees of freedom increases. * If the frequency of any of the cells of the categorical table is <5, then Fisher’s exact test is used.

text: 18. A man working as a mason in a Kota stone factory presents with dyspnea and has following chest X-ray findings. Which occupational exposure is most likely responsible for his condition?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Silicosis

A patient with dyspnea and eggshell calcifications on chest X-ray, combined with a history of occupational exposure to silica dust, is strongly suggestive of silicosis. Silicosis is an occupational disease and is caused by exposure to silica. It is seen in people who work in mining, stone cutting, sandblasting, and quarrying.It is the most common pneumoconiosis in the world. In silicosis, macrophages phagocytose inhaled silica particles, thereby activating and releasing inflammatory mediators (IL-1, IL-8) that cause fibroblast recruitment. In simple silicosis, the chest X-ray shows small rounded opacities in the upper lobes. When there is progressive nodular fibrosis, irregular masses >1 cm are seen, referred to as complicated silicosis. When these masses enlarge further, it is called progressive massive fibrosis (PMF). Calcification of hilar lymph nodes leads to the appearance of eggshell calcification. Silicosis increases the risk of lung cancer. It also increases susceptibility to tuberculosis as pulmonary macrophages are inhibited from killing the phagocytosed mycobacteria by crystalline silica. Other options: Option B: Asbestosis occurs due to the inhalation of crystalline hydrated silicates (asbestos). It is characterized by diffuse parenchymal interstitial fibrosis.  Option C:Anthracosis/coal workers' pneumoconiosis is a pulmonary condition seen in coal miners. With continued exposure, lung tissue undergoes progressive massive fibrosis Option D: Tuberculosis is a specific infectious disease caused by M. tuberculosis. The disease primarily affects lungs and causes pulmonary tuberculosis. It can also affect intestine, meninges, bones and joints, lymph glands, skin and other tissues of the body.

text: 26. Long-term use of combined oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) provides protection against which of the following cancers except?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Cervical

Long-term use of combined oral contraceptives increases the risk of cervical cancer, especially in women with persistent HPV infection, while offering protection against ovarian, endometrial, and colorectal cancers. Mode of Action of Combined Oral Pills: The primary mechanism of action of combined oral pills is to prevent the release of the ovum from the ovary by blocking pituitary secretion of gonadotropin required for ovulation. In addition, the progestogen component makes the cervical mucus thick and scanty, thereby inhibiting sperm penetration. Progestogens also reduce tubal motility and delay the transport of sperm and ovum to the uterine cavity. Benefits of Combined Pills: * Highly effective in preventing pregnancy when taken as prescribed (almost 100% effective). * Protection against other diseases such as benign breast disorders, including fibrocystic disease and fibroadenoma, ovarian cysts, iron-deficiency anaemia, pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy. * Can be safely used in large family planning programmes, making them important for population control efforts. Adverse Effects of Combined Pills: * Cardiovascular effects: Increased risk of myocardial infarction, cerebral thrombosis, and venous thrombosis, especially with advancing age and smoking. * Metabolic effects: Elevation of blood pressure, changes in serum lipids (increase in LDL, decrease in HDL), altered carbohydrate metabolism with elevated blood glucose and insulin. * Liver disorders: Risk of hepatocellular adenoma and gallbladder disease; cholestatic jaundice can occur in some users. * Effects on lactation and fertility: Reduced breast milk quantity and premature cessation of lactation; slight delay in return of fertility after discontinuation. * Other risks: Possible ectopic pregnancies with progestogen-only use, and potential concerns regarding foetal development if taken inadvertently during pregnancy.

27. In a group, the mean blood glucose level is 105 mg/dL with a standard deviation of 10 mg/dL. Assuming a normal distribution, what is the expected range of blood glucose values for approximately 95% of the population?

SD-Standard deviation
expl:
Correct answer: D. 85–125 mg/dL

The expected range of blood glucose values for approximately 95% of the population will be 85–125 mg/dL.  For a normal distribution, ~95% of observations lie within ±2 SD of the mean. To determine the range within two standard deviations in a normal distribution, we use the formula: Range Mean ±2 × Standard Deviation (SD) Given data: Mean = 105, Standard Deviation = 10 So, Range  = Mean +/- 2 SD. Calculation: Lower limit=105−(2×10)=105−20= 85  Upper limit=105+(2×10)=105+20=125 Hence, the range of blood pressure of 95% of the population will be 85–125 mg/dL. text: 28. A patient with leprosy received treatment for 4 months but then discontinued it for 1 year. Now, the patient presents again with a skin lesion. What should be the next step in management?

options.A: Start treatment with the new pack and new schedule
options.B: Continue the old treatment and give the remaining doses
options.C: Increase the dosage for the time being and then continue the old regimen

expl:
Correct answer: A. Start treatment with the new pack and new schedule

When a patient discontinues leprosy treatment for such a long duration (1 year), the case is treated as a treatment default. In such situations, WHO/NLEP guidelines recommend restarting the entire full course of  the multidrug therapy(MDT). A defaulter who returns to the health centre for treatment should be given a new course of MDT when he or she shows signs such as reddish and/or raised skin lesions, appearance of new skin lesions since the previous examination, new nerve involvement, lepromatous nodules, or signs of reversal reaction. Leprosy is managed based on the bacterial load. According to revised diagnostic and treatment criteria, WHO defines paucibacillary (PB) disease as the presence of no bacilli on smears or biopsy and less than or equal to 5 skin lesions with no peripheral nerve involved. Multibacillary (MB) leprosy is characterised by bacilli on smears or biopsies of more than 5 skin lesions and more than or equal to 1 peripheral nerve involvement. WHO currently recommends treating PB leprosy with a combination of 3 drugs—rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine—for 6 months. Meanwhile, MB leprosy is treated using the same 3 drugs for 12 months. While the NLEP guidelines earlier mentioned a 2-drug MDT for PB leprosy, the National Strategic Plan and Roadmap for Leprosy (2023-2027) now recommends a uniform MDT of 3 drugs for both PB and MB leprosy. Chemoprophylaxis for leprosy should be given in: * Contacts who are more than 2 years * Those with close contact with the patient for more than 20 hours per week for more than 3 months        A single dose of rifampicin is recommended for the close contact of a patient with leprosy provided they do not develop any signs or symptoms pertaining to leprosy. Pearl PF0982: Lepra Reactions Lepra Reactions:

text: 29. Which of the following is a facility offered by Ayushman AROGYA mandirs?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Essential drugs

Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (formerly Health & Wellness Centres) are mandated to provide free and essential medicines as part of comprehensive primary healthcare services. Ayushman Arogya Mandirs are envisaged to deliver an expanded range of services that go beyond Maternal and child health care services to include care for non-communicable diseases, palliative and rehabilitative care, Oral, Eye and ENT care, mental health and first-level care for emergencies and trauma, including free essential drugs and diagnostic services. Ayushman Arogya Mandir represents a shift from a selective model of healthcare to one that offers a comprehensive package of services, including preventive, promotive, curative, rehabilitative, and palliative care. The scheme has two complementary components. The first aims to establish 1,50,000 Ayushman Arogya Mandirs to provide universal, free, and comprehensive primary health care, with an emphasis on wellness and expanded services delivered closer to communities. The second component is the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY), which offers health insurance coverage of ₹5 lakhs per year to more than poor and vulnerable families for secondary and tertiary level treatments.

text: 31. A patient is diagnosed with cancer and is undergoing chemotherapy. What type of prevention is this?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Tertiary prevention

The clinical scenario of a patient diagnosed with cancer and undergoing chemotherapy points towards tertiary prevention, as it is already diagnosed and treatment aimed at reducing the number and impact of complications. The tertiary level of prevention signifies intervention in the late pathogenesis phase. Tertiary prevention can be defined as "all measures available to reduce or limit impairments and disabilities, minimize suffering caused by existing departures from good health, and promote the patient's adjustment to irremediable conditions". Examples include occupational and physical therapy in burns patients and cardiac rehabilitation in post-myocardial infarction patients. Other options: Option A: Secondary prevention includes early disease detection and targets healthy-looking individuals with subclinical forms of the disease. Secondary prevention is defined by an intervention that halts the progress of the disease at its incipient stage and prevents complications. A Papanicolaou (Pap) smear is an example of secondary prevention aimed at diagnosing cervical cancer in its subclinical state before progression. Option C: Primordial prevention prevents the emergence or development of risk factors in population groups or countries where they have not appeared yet through individual and mass education. For example lifestyle modifications such as eating patterns and physical exercise to prevent obesity in later years. Option D: Primary prevention is the action taken before the onset of the disease to prevent the possibility that a disease will ever occur. Here, intervention is initiated in the pre-pathogenesis phase of a disease. It is accomplished by population strategy and high-risk strategy. Examples of primary prevention are immunization and sanitising hands. Pearl PF0215: Levels of Prevention

text: 32. A group of students who were mainly consuming khesari dal and rice water developed weakness in their legs. On examination, their legs moved in a crossed manner while walking, and some were seen walking on their toes. Which of the following vitamin prophylaxis could have prevented this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin C

The clinical scenario of students consuming mainly khesari dal and rice water and later presenting with weakness of legs and scissor-like walking(crossed legs) gait is suggestive of neurolathyrism. Vitamin C in doses of 500-1000mg can be used for the prevention and treatment of lathyrism. Lathyrism is a paralyzing disease of humans and animals. It is due to the consumption of Khesari dal/Lathyrus sativus or its variants such as sweet pea(Lathyrus odoratus). It is mostly consumed by agricultural labourers of poor economic status because it is relatively cheap. It can present as skeletal, vascular, or neural manifestations. It usually affects young males aged 15-45 years and it is manifested in stages:  * Latent stage: The individual is apparently healthy, but when subjected to a physical ungainly gait. if the pulse is withdrawn from the diet, it will result in complete remission of the disease. * No-stick stage: the patient walks with short, jerky steps without the aid of a stick. * One-stick stage: The patient walks with a crossed gait and a tendency to walk on toes. stick is used for balance due to muscular stiffness. * Two-stick stage: Due to excessive bending of knees and crossed legs, the patient needs two crutches for support. The gait is slow and clumsy and the patient gets tired easily after walking a short distance.  * Crawler stage: Finally, the erect posture becomes impossible as the knee joints cannot support the weight of the body. The patient is reduced to crawling by throwing his weight on his hands. The patient is initially able to walk with short jerky steps without any aids, but the progressive spastic paralysis causes a crossed gait, and the patient has to use sticks to maintain his balance. Eventually, the knee joints are unable to support the weight of the body and the patient cannot stand erect at all. Long-term consumption of khesari dal leads to neurolathyrism. It is characterized by gradual spastic paralysis of the lower limbs. The interventions that can be used to prevent lathyrism include: * Vitamin C prophylaxis. * Limiting the proportion of the dal to less than a quarter of the total cereals and pulses consumed in a day. * Removal of the toxin by parboiling and steeping method.

text: 1. Which of the following is caused by exposure to cotton dust?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Byssinosis

Byssinosis is caused by exposure to cotton dust. Byssinosis is an occupational disease due to chronic exposure to cotton dust as in textile and rope-making industries. Chest X-ray shows hyperlucency, diaphragmatic flattening, and emphysema. A chest CT demonstrates ground glass opacities largely distributed in the basal regions with centrilobular nodules. Other options :  Option A: Anthracosis/coal workers' pneumoconiosis is a pulmonary condition seen in coal miners. The inhaled carbon pigment is engulfed by alveolar or interstitial macrophages, which accumulate in the connective tissue. Initially, it causes simple coal workers pneumoconiosis with little or no pulmonary dysfunction. With continued exposure, lung tissue undergoes progressive massive fibrosis which is called complicated coal workers' pneumoconiosis. The upper lobes of the lungs are commonly involved. Option B: Silicosis is a form of pneumoconiosis which is a cause of permanent disability and mortality. It occurs in people working in sandblasting, pottery, and ceramics industry, mining, and construction work. It occurs due to the inhalation of silica dust. The patient presents with a cough, exertional dyspnea, and chest pain.  Option D: Bagassosis is an occupational lung disease caused by the inhalation of bagasse or sugarcane dust. A thermophilic actinomycete, Thermoactinomyces sacchari is the causative organism. The symptoms are breathlessness, cough, hemoptysis, and fever. Initially, it can result in acute diffuse bronchiolitis, If left untreated it can progress to diffuse fibrosis, emphysema, and bronchiectasis. Pearl PF1017: Pneumoconiosis & Causative agents

text: 6. Orthotolidine test is used to determine ________

options.C: Free and combined chlorine in water

expl:
Correct answer: C. Free and combined chlorine in water

Orthotolidine (OT) test is used to determine free and combined chlorine in water. Pearl PF0273: Chlorination of Water * Chlorination is widely used for large scale purification of water and for drinking water. * It is bactericidal and moderately virucidal but not sporicidal, except in high doses. * Alongside its anti-pathogenic attributes, it oxidizes iron, manganese and hydrogen sulphide. It also destroys some taste and odor producing components. It controls algae and slime organisms and aids in coagulation. * Action of chlorine: * Hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid are formed when chlorine is added to water. Hypochlorous acid ionizes to form hydrogen and hypochlorite ions. * H2O + Cl2 → HCl + HOCl HOCl → H + OCl * The disinfecting action of chlorine is predominantly due to hypochlorous acid. Hypochlorous acid is the most effective form of chlorine and it is almost 70 – 80 times more effective than hypochlorite ions. * Chlorine acts best in water that has a pH of around 7. * Principles of chlorination: * The water to be disinfected must be clear of turbidity as turbidity impedes efficient chlorination. * The chlorine demand of water is the difference between the amount of chlorine added to the water and the amount of residual chlorine remaining at the end of a specific period of contact (usually 60 minutes) at a given temperature and pH of the water. This has to be estimated before chlorination is done. * The point at which the chlorine demand of water is met is called the breakpoint. It is beyond this that residual free chlorine begins to appear. * Contact period of free chlorine for at least one hour is required to kill bacteria and viruses. * Minimum recommended concentration of free chlorine is 0.5 mg/litre for one hour. Free residual chlorine provides a margin of safety against microbial contamination that occurs in storage or transport. * The sum of the chlorine demand of the specific water plus free residual chlorine of 0.5 mg/litre constitutes the correct dose of chlorine to be applied. * Methods of chlorination * Chlorine gas: It is the first choice as it is cheap, quick and efficient in action and easy to apply. Special chlorinating equipments like Paterson’s chloronome are used for application of chlorine gas. * Chloramines: These loose compounds of chlorine and ammonia give more persistent forms of residual chlorine. text: 18. A 45-year-old man living in Nellore, Andhra Pradesh presents with the following lesions on his teeth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Fluorosis

The above image along with the endemic area of Andhra Pradesh is diagnostic of Dental fluorosis. Dental fluorosis (also termed mottled enamel) is an extremely common disorder, characterized by hypomineralization of tooth enamel caused by ingestion of excessive fluoride during enamel formation. Fluorosis occurs when drinking water contains excess amounts of fluorine, in the range of 3-5mg/L. It is endemic in parts of India- Andhra Pradesh (Nellore, Nalgonda, Prakasam), Punjab, Haryana, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu.  Mechanism: * In the extra-cellular environment of maturing enamel, an excess of fluoride ions alters the rate at which enamel matrix proteins (amelogenin) are enzymatically broken down and the rate at which the subsequent breakdown products are removed. * Fluoride may also indirectly alter the action of protease via a decrease in the availability of free calcium ions in the mineralization environment. * This results in the formation of enamel with less mineralization. * This hypomineralized enamel has altered optical properties and appears opaque and lustreless relative to normal enamel. Classification: The two main classification systems which are used in the grading of severity of dental fluorosis are Dean’s system and TF system. Symptoms correspond to levels of fluoride intake: * Dental fluorosis: (1.5mg/L) Occurs if excess fluoride is ingested during the period of tooth calcification, i.e. in the first 7 years of life. Best seen on the upper incisors and almost exclusively affects only permanent teeth. It causes mottling on dental enamel, the appearance of chalky-white patches on the teeth, and loss of shine in the early stages. The white spots progressively turn yellow and can even become brown-black. The loss of enamel gives a corroded appearance.  * Skeletal fluorosis: (3-6mg/L) Occurs due to the heavy deposition of fluoride in the skeleton. Fluorosis stimulates osteoblastic activity, fluorapatite crystals are laid down in bone and these are usually resistant to secondary osteoclastic resorption. This leads to calcium retention, osteosclerosis, and osteophytosis. Ossification of ligaments and fascial attachments is characteristic. * Crippling fluorosis: (>10mg/L) Can lead to permanent disability.  Genu valgum and osteoporosis of the lower limb are seen in a newer form of fluorosis in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh. It is seen in people consuming jawar (sorghum), as it promotes greater retention of ingested fluoride. Interventions for Fluorosis  * Change the drinking water source with a lower fluoride content (0.5 to 0.8 mg/L). Running surface water contains lower quantities of fluorides than groundwater sources. * Chemical treatment in a water treatment plant can be moderately expensive. The National Environmental Engineering Research Institute, Nagpur developed a technique for removing fluoride by a chemical treatment called the Nalgonda technique.  * Fluoride supplements should not be prescribed for children who drink fluoridated water. * The use of fluoride toothpaste in areas of endemic fluorosis is not recommended for children up to 6 years of age

A pregnant lady presented to the casualty after she was scratched by a street dog while she was walking on the streets an hour ago. She has only some minor abrasions with no bleeding. What treatment should be offered to her?

options.A: No treatment as she is pregnant now
options.C: Local wound cleaning and rabies vaccine
options.D: Local wound cleaning, Rabies vaccine and Immunoglobulins

expl:
Correct answer: C. Local wound cleaning and rabies vaccine

This case is classified under WHO category II since there was no bleeding present at the site of the dog bite and she has to be given Rabies vaccine along with local wound cleaning.  Since Rabies is a lethal disease, there is no contraindication for post-exposure prophylaxis following high-risk exposures, even in pregnancy, infancy, immunocompromised patients, and even in children with AIDS/HIV.  Note: Patients taking chloroquine have to be given the vaccine intramuscularly as there is a reduced response to the intradermal route.  For pre-exposure prophylaxis, previous allergic reaction to any components of the vaccine is a contraindication. Pearl PF1934: Rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins schedules According to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India: WHO category II or III exposures should receive post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) immediately. One intradermal (ID) dose is 0.1 mL of vaccine and one intramuscular (IM) dose is an entire vial of vaccine, irrespective of the vial size. Should a vaccine dose be delayed for any reason, the PEP schedule should be resumed (not restarted). Rabies Immunoglobulin(RIG):  * Passive immunization * Single-dose; after initiation of PEP and not beyond 7 days after the first dose of vaccine * Max dose: hRIG - 20IU/kg , eRIG - 40IU/kg body weight * Vaccines should never be withheld regardless of the availability of RIG. * Alternatives for RIG- WHO recommends monoclonal antibodies (mAb) as a 'cocktail' containing at least two antibodies against the rabies virus. Administration of RIG: * RIG should be administered into or around the wound site or sites. * The remaining RIG, if any, should be injected IM at a site distant from the site of vaccine administration. * RIG may be diluted to a volume sufficient for all wounds to be effectively and safely infiltrated. Prioritization of RIG allocation (numbered according to priority order): * Multiple bites * Deep wounds * Bites to head, neck, and hands * Patients with severe immunodeficiency * Confirmed/probable rabies in biting animal * Bites, scratches, and exposure of mucous membranes caused by a bat Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) PrEP is considered in the following conditions: * High-risk groups- laboratory staff, wildlife wardens, veterinarians, animal handlers, and travelers to endemic regions. * Remote, rabies-endemic areas where access to PEP is difficult * Areas where dog bite incidence is >5% per year * Areas where vampire bat rabies is known to be present. Pre-exposure rabies vaccination consists of two intramuscular (IM) or two intradermal (ID) doses. These are given on days 0 and 3. * Adults - the vaccine should always be administered in the deltoid area of the arm * Young children (under 1 year of age)- Administration into the anterolateral area of the thigh is recommended. * Rabies vaccine should never be administered in the gluteal area. Administration in this manner will result in lower neutralizing antibody titers. For exposed or re-exposed patients who can document previous completion of PEP the following guidelines would be applicable: * Proper wound management should be done. * There is no need for the administration of RIG. * One site ID or IM vaccine administration on days 0 and 3. Only adequate wound washing would be required in case of re-exposure where the animal bite victim has documented proof of complete PEP within the last three months. The following cases are treated as fresh cases and given full PEP: * Those who have previously received full post-exposure treatment with neural tissue vaccines (NTV) or vaccines of unproven potency * Those who cannot document complete PEP or PrEP treatment

text: 31. Which test uses the graph given below to assess the viral load in a test sample ?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Real time RTPCR

The image shows the Ct value(Cycle threshold) of Real-time RTPCR which can be used to assess the viral genetic load.   The image shows a graph with cycle number on the X-axis and relative fluorescence on the Y-axis. At 25.6 there is an exponential rise in the fluorescence which is the Ct value for the sample. The cycle threshold (Ct) can be defined as the thermal cycle number at which the fluorescent signal exceeds that of the background and thus passes the threshold for positivity. The first step for a real-time RTPCR is by extracting the viral RNA from the sample followed by purifying and concentrating it. They are then added to a mixture of primers, nucleotide bases, enzymes for the reaction, and fluorescently labeled probes (short stretches of nucleic acid which stick to the target ). The primers initially attach to the viral nucleic acid which is RNA and a complementary DNA strand is made using the nucleotides in the mixture. It is then subjected to repeated thermal cycles so that the copies of the viral targets are increased. The labeled probes stick to the viral genome and emit a fluorescent signal. An exponential rise occurs early when the viral load in the sample is high when compared to a less viral load. A typical RT-PCR assay will have a maximum of 40 thermal cycles. The lower the Ct value the higher the quantity of viral genetic material in the sample. A 3-point increase in Ct value is roughly equivalent to a 10-fold decrease in the quantity of viral genetic material. Low Ct values more likely indicate acute disease and high infectivity whereas high Ct values can be attributed to reduced viral load but might need clinical interpretation. Note: Ct values cannot be used to compare different types of assays nor does it provide information on the course of the illness. However, it can be used for clinical management in a hospital setting.

text: 8. If a wide range of values are present in a community, what is the best measure of central tendency?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Median

The best measure of central tendency if there are a wide range of values is median. If we take an example of a dataset of (1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 11, 41), we can see that 41 seems to be well away from the mean of 7.45 of the dataset.  If we eliminate this outlier, we can get a new dataset of (1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 11) with a median of 4.5 and a mean of 4.1. We see that the median only changed by 10% (went down to 4.5 from 5), while the mean decreased by 45%. Therefore, the median is less affected by outliers or extreme values.  The median is not sensitive to extreme values or outliers and thus it is the preferred measure of central tendency in a distribution with a wide range of values. * The median is the central element in a distribution when all the elements are arranged in order. * In a distribution that has an odd number of elements, the median is the middle value. * In a distribution that has an even number of elements, the median is the average of the middle values, i.e., the arithmetic mean of the two middle values. * The drawback of the median is that it doesn’t respond to the actual values of the elements but only to the number of values above or below it. * The median is the same as the 50th centile. * It is sometimes symbolized by Mdn. * The median can be arrived at in ordinal, interval and ratio data scales.

text: 14. Which of the following is the most common cause of macrocytic anemia?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Alcohol

Alcohol is the most common cause of macrocytic anaemia.  Macrocytic anemia can be megaloblastic anemia and non-megaloblastic anemia. Alcohol causes non megaloblastic macrocytic anemia.  Other causes of macrocytic anaemia:  * Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency * Bone marrow disorders  * Liver disease  * Drug-induced  * HIV  * Multiple myeloma  * Complication of bariatric surgery  Megaloblastic anemia is a type of macrocytic anemia with impaired nucleic acid metabolism. Nuclear maturation lags behind cytoplasmic maturation. The causes include: * Vitamin B12 deficiency * Folate deficiency * Drugs (Methotrexate) Vitamin B12 or cobalamin is a water-soluble vitamin that is derived from animal products such as red meat, dairy, and eggs. Other causes of B12 deficiency includes * Malabsorption (Pernicious anemia) * Total or partial gastrectomy * Ileal resection * Tropical sprue Clinical features of cyanocobalamin and folate deficiency (megaloblastic anemia) include: * Anorexia, weight loss, diarrhea, or constipation * Oral manifestations: glossitis, angular cheilosis * Mild fever in more severely anemic patients * Jaundice (unconjugated) * Reversible melanin skin hyperpigmentation * Bruising (thrombocytopenia) and infections (low leucocyte count) * Complications in pregnancy: recurrent fetal loss and neural tube defects * Cardiovascular disease: cerebrovascular, peripheral vascular, and coronary heart disease with deep vein thrombosis * Neurologic manifestations: Bilateral peripheral neuropathy or degeneration of the posterior and pyramidal tracts of the spinal cord (SACDSC). Seen in only B12 deficiency. * Psychiatric disturbances

Interest and Information Stage: The individual becomes interested in innovation and tries to collect more information. He tries to know about qualities, features, functions, risk, producers, brand, colour, shape, price, incentives, availability, services, and other relevant aspects. 3. Evaluation Stage: The consumer considers accumulated information and use it to evaluate the innovation and judge the worth of innovation. He compares different aspects of innovation like qualities, features, performance, price, after-sales services, etc., with the existing products to arrive at the decision whether the innovation should be tried out. 4. Adoption Stage: If trial produces satisfactory results, finally the consumer decides to adopt/buy the innovation. subject: Community Medicine
text: 19. The number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births is called ___.
expl:
Correct answer: B. Maternal mortality ratio

Maternal mortality ratio is defined as the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births during a given time period. Other options: Infant mortality rate (IMR) is defined as the ratio of infant deaths registered in a given year to the total number of live births in the same year. Maternal mortality rate is the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 women of reproductive age in a given time period. Pearl PF0987: Maternal Mortality Ratio Maternal death is defined as the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, irrespective of the duration and site of pregnancy, from any cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management but not from accidental or incidental causes. * Maternal mortality ratio is the number of maternal deaths in a given period per 100,000 live births during the same period. * MMR = Number of maternal deaths in a period x 100,000 (or 1000)/Number of live births in the same period * Main global causes of maternal deaths are severe bleeding, indirect causes (anemia, malaria, heart diseases), infections, unsafe abortions, eclampsia, obstructed labor and other direct causes like ectopic pregnancy, anesthesia related complications, etc. * In India, the most common causes of maternal deaths are hemorrhage (leading cause), sepsis, obstructed labor, hypertensive disorders, etc. Pearl PF0988: Perinatal Mortality Rate * The term ‘perinatal mortality’ includes both late fetal death (stillbirths) and early neonatal deaths. * Babies chosen for inclusion in perinatal statistics should be above a minimum birth weight (1000g at birth). If the birth weight is not available, a gestation period of at least 28 weeks should be used (as the weight at 28 weeks corresponds to 1000g). If both are not available, then crown to heel length of at least 35cm should be used. * Generally, the PMR = Late fetal deaths and early neonatal deaths weighing over 1000g at birth x 1000/Total births(live+dead) weighing over 1000g at birth. * The PMR is the yard-stick of obstetric and pediatric care before and around the time of birth. * The PMR of India (2016) is 24 per 1000 births. * The main causes of perinatal mortality are intrauterine and birth asphyxia, low birth weight, birth trauma, and intrauterine/neonatal infections. Please note that the actual perinatal period commences from the 22nd week of life, but at that time the fetus weighs only about 500g. Therefore, only for statistical calculations and international comparisons, to calculate the perinatal mortality rate, the period from the 28th week of life is taken, as then the baby weighs about 1000g. As mentioned, babies included in the perinatal statistics must weigh above 1000g.

Pie Charts * Pie charts are also used for nominal or ordinal data. * The categorical data are represented as segments of a circle. 4. Frequency polygons * Frequency polygons are used for mainly ratio and interval scale data. * In a frequency polygon, the mid-points of each class interval are joined together by straight lines. 5. text: 22. Which of the following demographic indicators is used to compare the life expectancy of two different countries?
expl:
Correct answer: B. HDI

The demographic indicator used to compare the life expectancy of two different countries is Human Development Index(HDI). Human Development Index (HDI) is a measure of a country's average achievements in three dimensions of human development. The components include: * A long and healthy life, as measured by life expectancy at birth * Knowledge (literacy), as measured by mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling, and * A decent standard of living, as measured by GNI (gross national income) per capita. HDI values range from 0 to 1, with 1 as the maximum value.  Life expectancy at 1 year, literacy and infant mortality rate are components of the Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI).

Auspitz sign is a characteristic feature seen in psoriasis. The presence of silvery-white scaly lesions on the extensor aspect of the elbows and knee is a characteristic feature seen in psoriasis. It is treated with antibiotics like flucloxacillin, clarithromycin, clindamycin, and benzylpenicillin. Another infection similar to erysipelas is cellulitis. text: 2. Which of the following side effects are seen most commonly with Isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid)?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Embryopathy

Isotretinoin is a vitamin A derivative which is highly teratogenic when orally administered. It is commonly used to treat cystic nodular acne. It inhibits the migration of neural crest cells during embryogenesis and affects the development of multiple organs. These defects are collectively termed retinoic acid embryopathy. Embryopathy or developmental disorder of an embryo comprises a large variety of abnormalities and is more common than any individual defect. Specific anomalies may include ventriculomegaly, maldevelopment of the facial bones or cranium, microtia or anotia, micrognathia, cleft palate, conotruncal heart defects, and thymic aplasia or hypoplasia. Isotretinoin also increases the risk of spontaneous abortions and stillbirths in pregnancies exposed in the first trimester of this medicine. Presenting with pregnancy during treatment with isotretinoin is a failure of prevention strategies. The guidelines for isotretinoin usage are as follows: * Isotretinoin is a teratogenic drug that should not be taken during pregnancy and nursing. * Patients should take 2 pregnancy tests before starting isotretinoin and take a monthly pregnancy test while on the medication, and another test 1 month after stopping the medication. * It is recommended to use two birth control methods concurrently, beginning one month before treatment to one month following the end of isotretinoin treatment. * Isotretinoin should be reserved for the treatment of severe, nodulocystic acne and should not be used for milder forms of acne. Other options: Option B: Lithium is used in the treatment of bipolar disorder. It is a teratogen associated with Ebstein's anomaly which is a rare cardiac condition characterized by severe tricuspid regurgitation and right atrial enlargement. Option C: Valproic acid is the anti-epileptic which confers the greatest risk to the developing fetus while used in pregnancy. It is associated with an increased risk of neural tube defects in the fetus. Option D: Tetracyclines are associated with yellowish-brown discoloration of deciduous teeth when used after 25 weeks of gestation.

Erythema and scaling occur in the scalp face and seborrheic area. The itching will be absent often. It is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune disease against the basal keratinocytes. It is a chronic disease with a number of relapses and remissions. The most common presentation of lichen planus is a well-defined area of purple-colored, itchy, flat-topped papules. This description is known as the characteristic "6 P"s of lichen planus: planar (flat-topped), purple, polygonal, pruritic, papules, and plaques. Clinically, oral lichen planus can present as Wickham striae (image below), white papules, white plaque, erythema, erosion, or blisters. They may be symmetrical and bilateral. Buccal mucosa, dorsum of the tongue, and gingivae are commonly affected. Early diagnosis and management play an important role in the prevention of progression to malignancy. Complications of lichen planus include: * Hair: Patches of cicatricial scarring alopecia * Nails: Various nail changes are seen associated with lichen planus.  * Dorsal Nail Pterygium: The most specific nail change in lichen planus where the fusion of dorsal nail fold and nail bed leads to pterygium formation. * Thinning of the nail plate: The most common nail change is the exaggeration of longitudinal lines and linear depressions. * Pup-tent sign: Elevation of the nail in the shape of a tent * Trachonychia: All 20 nails of hands and feet undergo dystrophy * Subungual hyperkeratosis and onycholysis * Longitudinal melanonychia in lichen planus of the nail bed * Permanent destruction of several toenails with ulceration of soles (rare variant) * Mucous membranes: Squamous cell carcinoma may occur on the lip, buccal mucosa, or gum margin. Patients present with pruritic, purple, polygonal, papules. The lesions have thin white lines on their surface known as Wickham’s striae. They are commonly seen on the volar aspect of the wrists, the lumbar region, and around the ankles. The mucosal involvement is also seen. The commonest mucosal sites are buccal mucosa and tongue, rarely it can also be found on the anus and genitalia. Nail involvement can be seen as thinning of nail plate leading to an exaggeration of longitudinal lines, and linear depressions. The nails can also be destroyed leading to anonychia. They might have a circle of clear zone around it which is known as the Woronoff ring. This finding is seen in psoriasis. Option D- Michaelis–Gutmann bodies are large, foamy macrophages mixed with occasional multinucleate giant cells and lymphocytes. text: 1. A patient presents with a hypopigmented lesion on his back. On examination, there is a complete loss of fine touch and temperature sensation over the lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Hansen's disease

The clinical scenario points to a case of leprosy/ Hansen's disease.  Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, cutaneous and peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. The most commonly affected peripheral nerves are the posterior tibial nerve, followed by the ulnar, median, and lateral popliteal nerves. The most commonly involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve.  Leprosy has a long incubation period, usually ranging from 2 to 12 years. It commonly presents as an area of numbness on the skin or a visible skin lesion, which could be a hypopigmented or erythematous macule. Ridley-Jopling classification of leprosy: * * Tuberculoid (TT) * Borderline tubercular (BT) * Borderline (BB) * Borderline lepromatous (BL) * Lepromatous (LL)
Indeterminate (IL)

One or a few hypopigmented or faintly erythematous, ill-defined to well-defined macular lesions with mild to moderate impairment of touch and/or thermal sensations. No thickening of peripheral nerves.
Borderline tuberculoid (BT)

Macular or plaque-type lesions numbering three to nine or more and asymmetrically located on any part of the body, with variable sizes and contours. Satellite lesions may be present. Loss of sensation is less intense than it is in TT lesions.

Several peripheral nerves are likely to be enlarged in an asymmetrical pattern, with sensory and motor deficits. Increased susceptibility to develop Type 1 leprosy reaction.
Tuberculoid (TT) Well-defined, hypopigmented macule or as a raised, erythematous/brown/copper-colored plaque with a well-defined edge up to three in number. 

Complete loss of fine touch and temperature sensations over the lesion.

Larger corresponding cutaneous nerves are thickened in a limited number of case
Mid-borderline (BB)

An unstable form of leprosy. Multiple plaque lesions and macular lesions; lesions are of various shapes and sizes, are bilateral, and usually occur in a more or less symmetrical. Minimal loss of sensation over the lesions.

Many nerves may be thickened, and this effect may be asymmetrical.
Borderline lepromatous (BL)

Numerous bilateral, round or oval, macular, diffusely infiltrated, erythematous, or hypopigmented lesions with moderately defined borders. Some loss of sensation may be detected, particularly over older lesions.

Widespread but asymmetrical thickening of peripheral nerves
Lepromatous (LL)

Innumerable bilateral, symmetrically distributed, diffusely indurated, erythematous, copper-colored, or skin-colored patches or plaques. There is no loss of sensation over these lesions.

Bilateral earlobe thickening and eyebrow loss occur. Coarse induration on the face gives rise to leonine facies.

Involvement of peripheral nerves occurs late and is bilateral and symmetrical, with sensory loss in a “glove-and-stocking” distribution.
Cardinal signs for the diagnosis of leprosy: * Characteristic skin lesions- hypopigmented or erythematous lesions with definite impairment of sensation. * Peripheral nerve involvement- thickening of the nerve with sensory impairment. Nerve tenderness can also be seen. * Detection of acid-fast bacilli in slit-skin smear, skin biopsy, or positive biopsy PCR. The presence of two of the three signs can establish the diagnosis of leprosy. Other tests done for diagnosis of leprosy include nerve biopsy in pure neural leprosy and PGL-1 antibody in cases with low bacterial load.

For a better cosmetic outcome for elective procedures, a 5 cm transverse incision two fingers' breadth above the sternal notch can be used. * Dissection: Dissect tissues in the midline. Displace or ligate any dilated veins encountered to control bleeding. * Muscle separation: Separate and retract the strap muscles of the neck laterally to expose underlying structures. * Thyroid isthmus management: Displace the thyroid isthmus upwards or divide and ligate it with sutures. * Local anaesthesia: Inject a few drops of 4% lignocaine into the trachea to suppress coughing. * Tracheal incision: Fix the trachea with a hook and make a vertical incision between the third and fourth tracheal rings(Option D), converting it into a circular opening. text: 2. A patient was diagnosed with ear wax and was subjected to syringing to remove the wax. She developed a syncopal episode while doing the procedure when the tip of the syringe touched the ear canal. Which of the nerves is responsible for this episode of syncope?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Arnold's nerve

The posterior wall of the external auditory canal is supplied by the auricular branch of the Vagus (Arnold's nerve). When this nerve is stimulated, a vasovagal response is initiated which results in the syncopal episode.  When the vagus nerve is stimulated, a parasympathetic response occurs leading to braycardia and decreased blood flow into the brain which causes syncope. Nerve supply of External auditory canal: * Anterior wall and roof- the auriculotemporal branch of mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (CN V3) (Option A). * Posterior wall and floor - the auricular branch of Vagus (Arnold's nerve). text: 3. A worried mother brought her 6-year-old unimmunized child to the ER with complaints of fever, cough, and shortness of breath. Examination reveals a bull-neck appearance and a pseudomembrane over the tonsils that bleeds when removed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Diphtheria

The given clinical scenario of a 6-year-old suffering from fever, cough, and shortness of breath with a pseudomembrane and bull neck appearance on examination is suggestive of diphtheria. Diphtheria is caused by the bacteria Corynebacterium diphtheriae which spreads via droplets through the respiratory tract (most important), cutaneous lesions, and fomites. Respiratory tract diphtheria is characterized by a thick, adherent pseudomembrane (grey or white) on one/both tonsils and adjacent pharynx. Underlying soft tissue oedema and enlarged lymph nodes can cause a bull-neck appearance.  Patients with laryngeal diphtheria are at risk for suffocation because of local soft-tissue oedema and airway obstruction by the diphtheritic membrane. Management includes antitoxin therapy as a single empirical dose of 20,000-100,000 units and antibiotics. Penicillin G/ Benzylpenicillin is the drug of choice for diphtheria. However, in case of an allergy to the same, Erythromycin is used. Other antibiotics used are clindamycin, rifampin, and tetracycline. A greyish-white membrane forms over the tonsils in the oropharynx and spreads to the soft palate and posterior pharyngeal wall. The membrane in diphtheria extends beyond the tonsils onto the soft palate and is dirty grey. It is adherent, and its removal leaves a bleeding surface. In the larynx, the diphtheritic membrane may cause airway obstruction. Cervical lymph nodes, particularly the jugulodigastric, become enlarged and tender, sometimes presenting a bull-neck appearance. The patient is ill and toxaemic, but fever seldom rises above 38°C. D/D for membrane over tonsil: * Streptococcus & other pyogenic organisms * Diphtheria * Infectious mononucleosis * Vincent’s angina * Leukaemia * Candida * Agranulocytosis * Malignancy * Aphthous ulcer * Traumatic ulcer Other options : Option A: Infectious mononucleosis most commonly presents in adolescents with initial symptoms of fever, sore throat, fatigue, myalgia, and malaise. Pharyngitis is often the most prominent sign, with the enlargement of the tonsils and an exudate resembling that of streptococcal pharyngitis. It can be associated with tender, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy.  Option B: In acute membranous tonsillitis, exudates from the crypts coalesce to form a membrane on the surface of the tonsil that is easily wiped away without any bleeding. Option D: Oral candidiasis/Oral thrush associated with candida albicans presents as white plaque-like lesions with cheesy exudate on an erythematous mucosa. They are typically painful and can be easily brushed off.

text: 4. A 6-year-old boy fell from the bed and developed swelling in the nose and difficulty in breathing. Examination revealed smooth rounded swellings on either side of the septum, through both the nares. On palpation, it was soft and fluctuant. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Incision and drainage

This clinical vignette is strongly suggestive of a septal hematoma. The most appropriate next step in management would be incision and drainage of the hematoma.  Septal hematoma is caused due to collection of blood in between the perichondrium or periosteum and the cartilage of the nasal septum. It may be caused due to trauma, septal surgery, or spontaneously as in bleeding disorders. Clinically, patients may present with bilateral nasal obstruction, pain, pressure over the nasal bridge, or a frontal headache. On examination, bilateral hematomas will be seen as purplish or reddish smooth swelling on either side of the septum. Palpation will reveal a soft, fluctuant swelling. All septal hematomas must be drained to prevent the formation of septal abscess or organization of the hematoma by fibrosis leading to a permanently thickened septum. Drainage of the hematoma should be done either through aspiration with a wide gauge needle or through an incision made over the mucosa at the point of greatest fluctuation. It must be followed by nasal packing. Patients should thereafter be started on systemic antibiotics. Given below are a clinical image and a illustrated image of septal hematoma. Pearl PF1620: Septal Haematoma * Septal hematoma is a collection of blood under the perichondrium or periosteum of the nasal septum * Causes: Trauma, septal surgery and bleeding disorders * Clinical features: Bilateral nasal obstruction (most common presenting feature), frontal headache * Treatment: * Aspiration of small hematomas * Incision and drainage of large hematomas followed by nasal packing * Systemic antibiotics to prevent abscess formation * Complications: Septal abscess, depression of dorsum, permanently thickened septum

Correct answer: D. Glomus tumour

They are paragangliomas of the glomus bodies found in the mastoid. Glomus tumor is the most common benign neoplasm of the middle ear. It is of 2 types: * Glomus jugulare: Origin is from the dome of the jugular bulb causing neurological signs of IXth to XIIth cranial nerve involvement. * Glomus tympanicum: Promontory in the  middle eari s the source of Glomus tympanicum. It comprises of * 10% familial * 10% multicentric * 10% functional It is 5 times more common in women. Common presenting features include: * Progressive conductive hearing loss * Tinnitus in glomus tumors is pulsatile, of swishing character, synchronous with a pulse, and can be temporarily stopped by carotid pressure. * Audible bruit heard over the mastoid with a stethoscope in all stages Investigations would include: * Phelp's sign-on CECT scan helps to distinguish glomus tympanicum from the glomus jugulare tumor by identification of caroticojugular spine which is eroded in the latter. * MRI gives the soft tissue extent of the tumor. * Four vessel angiography is necessary when the CT head shows the involvement of a jugular bulb, carotid artery, or intradural extension. * A biopsy is never done since it’s a highly vascular tumor.  The below-given image shows a triangular red-colored glomus tumor behind the tympanic membrane in the middle ear. text: 4. Which of the following is least likely to cause mucormycosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Broad spectrum antibiotics

Among the given options, the condition least likely to cause mucormycosis is the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Mucormycosis is an opportunistic mycosis. It is typically seen in patients with diabetes mellitus and immunocompromised patients. Mucormycosis recently emerged as an important superinfection in COVID-19 patients, especially in India. The surge in cases is most likely due to diabetes mellitus and steroid use. Risk factors for the infection include the following: * Uncontrolled diabetes * Acidosis (especially diabetic ketoacidosis) * Steroid treatment * Lymphomas and leukemias * Immunodeficiencies * Severe burns  The rhino-orbital-cerebral is the most common form of mucormycosis. The blackish discoloration is due to direct fungal invasion causing arterial and venous thrombosis leading to gangrene. Diagnosis is made by biopsy with histopathologic examination. The biopsy shows characteristic wide, ribbon-like aseptate hyphal elements that branch at right angles. The below image shows biopsy findings seen in mucormycosis. Treatment includes intravenous administration of amphotericin B and wide excision of necrotic tissues. Along with the reversal of underlying conditions and risk factors.

text: 6. A 35-year-old woman takes aspirin for a headache, later she presented with wheezing and breathlessness. These symptoms are likely to be associated with which of the following conditions?

Correct answer: B. Nasal polyp

This clinical vignette is suggestive of aspirin intolerance. Samter triad is a non-IgE mediated hypersensitivity reaction associated with the intake of aspirin or other cyclooxygenase inhibitors. Samter's triad is also known as aspirin-induced asthma or aspirin-sensitive asthma. It consists of: * Nasal polyposis * Bronchial asthma * Aspirin intolerance Patients with Samter's triad will have persistent nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, anosmia, nasal polyps, and recurrent chronic rhinosinusitis. Asthma and aspirin intolerance develop later. 4. A patient with CSOM presented to the OPD with seizures, headache, vomiting and photophobia. On eye examination, homonymous hemianopia was noted. CT brain showed the following findings. Identify the condition.

Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM)
expl:
Correct answer: A. Temporal lobe abscess

The clinical vignette depicting features of seizures, headache, vomiting, and photophobia in a patient with a chronic ear infection and the CT image showing a ring-enhancing lesion point to a diagnosis of a temporal lobe abscess. Temporal lobe abscess is an intracranial complication that can arise from chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM). Brain abscess typically progresses through 4 stages. * The first stage is the stage of invasion (initial encephalitis), which often goes unnoticed. Symptoms such as headache, malaise, low-grade fever, and drowsiness may be present. * The second stage is the stage of localization (latent abscess), during which a capsule forms around the abscess, effectively localizing the pus. * The third stage is the stage of enlargement (manifest abscess). The abscess enlarges, leading to increased intracranial pressure (ICP) and the development of edema surrounding the abscess. As a result, symptoms worsen. * The final stage is the stage of termination (rupture of abscess). At this point, the abscess expands and eventually ruptures into the ventricle or subarachnoid space, which can result in potentially fatal meningitis. Characteristic findings associated with temporal lobe abscess include nominal aphasia, homonymous hemianopia, seizures, contralateral motor paralysis, pupillary changes, and oculomotor palsy. Signs of raised ICP like headache, nausea, vomiting, lethargy, drowsiness, confusion, papilledema, and coma may also be seen. The preferred diagnostic imaging modality for temporal lobe abscess is a CT scan of the brain. This imaging study reveals a ring-enhancing lesion indicative of a brain abscess. Medical treatment involves initiating intravenous antibiotics, typically metronidazole. Raised ICP can be addressed using dexamethasone or mannitol. Surgical intervention is the definitive management and involves drainage of the abscess followed by radical mastoidectomy to address the underlying CSOM. Other options: Option B: Cerebellar abscess is a form of brain abscess and is usually associated with an otogenic source of infection. text: 12. A 2-year-old child was eating peanuts when he suddenly developed respiratory distress, cough, and was unable to speak. What is the initial treatment for this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Perform Heimlich maneuver

In a choking child (more than 1 year old) or an adult, the first step to be done is to perform Heimlich maneuver, which involves delivering abdominal thrusts. The rescuer should stand or kneel behind the patient and wrap his arms around the patient’s waist. A fist is made with one hand and using the other hand, the fist is driven into the patient’s abdomen with a rapid, forceful upward thrust so as to dislodge the foreign body. This is continued until the foreign body is expelled or if the patient becomes unresponsive. If the patient becomes unresponsive, immediately start CPR. In a choking infant who is responsive, 5 back slaps between the shoulder blades and 5 downward thrusts on the chest are given in order to dislodge the foreign body. If the patient becomes unresponsive, immediately start CPR. Other Options: Option A: The blind finger sweep should be avoided in infants to avoid pushing the object further inside the airway. However, it can be done for unresponsive adults with complete FBAO. With the patient's face up, the mouth is opened by grasping both the tongue and lower jaw and lifting the mandible. The index finger is inserted along the inside of the cheek and using a hooking action, the foreign body is dislodged and removed. Option B: Endoscopic removal is wrong as an initial treatment because it's not an immediate life-saving measure and requires time to set up and organize. It can be attempted once the airway is stabilized.  Option C: Immediate X-ray is wrong as initial treatment because it delays essential life-saving intervention. Not all foreign bodies are radio-opaque (especially peanuts) and the patient needs immediate intervention for respiratory distress.

text: 1. Which of the following vitamin deficiencies can cause laryngismus stridulus?

Laryngismus stridulus is primarily associated with a deficiency in vitamin D. Laryngismus stridulus can be defined as laryngeal spasm caused by the sudden contraction of laryngeal muscles due to a reduced level of calcium. It is likely to be caused by vitamin D deficiency. Vitamin D, also known as cholecalciferol, plays a significant role in calcium and phosphate levels homeostasis. Its active form, calcitriol or  1,25 dihydroxycholecalciferol is produced by sequential hydroxylation in the liver and kidneys. It primarily increases the serum calcium and phosphate levels. Deficiency of vitamin D leads to rickets. Causes of vitamin D deficiency  : * Inadequate sunlight exposure. * Poor dietary intake. * Malabsorption disorders such as celiac disease. * Liver or kidney disorders affecting vitamin D metabolism. * Calcium Deficiency: Even with sufficient vitamin D, a diet low in calcium can lead to rickets. * Phosphate Deficiency: Rarely, genetic disorders like hypophosphatemic rickets, which affect phosphate metabolism, can cause rickets. There is increased risk of . Radiological features show cupping at metaphyses, fraying, and widening of the growth plate. Daily treatment with oral Vitamin D preparations is recommended, as daily supplementation is more physiological. The duration of treatment is at least 12 weeks. Vitamin D dosage is 2000 I.U in infants and 3000 I.U in children over one year of age. Stoss therapy was earlier used for treating Vitamin D deficiency. Here, 300,000-600,000 IU of vitamin D was administered orally or intramuscularly in 2 or 4 doses over 1 day. text: 3. Which of the following is responsible for balance and equilibrium?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Semicircular canal

The semicircular canals that are a part of the bony labyrinth are responsible for balance and equilibrium. The semicircular canals are three loop-shaped structures filled with endolymph fluid and lined with hair cells that detect angular acceleration in three planes (horizontal, vertical, and oblique). When the head moves, the fluid inside these canals shifts, causing the hair cells to bend. This bending generates nerve impulses that are transmitted to the brain via the vestibular nerve, informing the brain about the direction and speed of head movement. This mechanism is essential for maintaining posture, coordinating eye movements, and ensuring balance. Other options: Option A: The vestibule, which includes the utricle and saccule, also contributes to balance by detecting linear acceleration and the position of the head relative to gravity. However, the semicircular canals are primarily responsible for detecting rotational movements, making them key to the sensation of balance and equilibrium. Option C: The organ of Corti is the sense organ of hearing and is situated on the basilar membrane of the cochlear duct. It detects sound vibrations and converts them into electrical signals for the auditory nerve. It is involved in hearing, not balance or equilibrium. Option D: The cochlea is a spiral-shaped organ responsible for converting sound waves into electrical signals. It contains hair cells that detect sound vibrations and transmit them as nerve impulses to the auditory nerve, allowing us to perceive sound.
