text: 4. On the day of delivery, a newborn baby is undergoing a screening test for hearing. Which of the following tests is likely to be performed?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Otoacoustic emissions (OAE)

A newborn baby on the same day of delivery will undergo the Otoacoustic emissions (OAE) test as a screening test for hearing. Universal Newborn Hearing Screening (UNHS) has become a standard practice in most developed countries. The identification of all newborns with hearing loss before 6 months has become an attainable and realistic goal. The goal is to screen newborn babies before 1 month of age, diagnose hearing loss before 3 months of age and start intervention as early as possible, or latest by 6 months of age. In India, a two-stage screening protocol is followed according to which infants are screened first with otoacoustic emissions (OAE). Infants who fail the OAE are screened with auditory brainstem response (ABR) or Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA), which is also the definitive test. All babies kept in NICU must be screened by BERA test as per the protocol. The first screening is usually conducted at birth or before discharge. Conducting the first screening before discharge is preferred to ensure better coverage and reduce loss to follow-up. A second screening is scheduled anytime between 1–3 weeks or during the next scheduled visit at 6 weeks.  All babies with abnormal BERA should undergo detailed ENT evaluation and hearing-aid fitting (cochlear implants) and auditory rehabilitation must be done before 6 months of age. Pearl PF1979: OAEs - Otoacoustic emissions It is an objective test that records the low-intensity sounds produced by the outer hair cells of a normal cochlea. It is of two types: * Spontaneous type- it is generated spontaneously and is present in 50% of normal individuals. * Evoked types- also called Kemp echoes or cochlear echoes, are generated in response to sound stimulus and found in all individuals with normal hearing. The two subtypes are transient evoked and distortion product. The applications are as follows: * Best audiometric test for screening in neonates, infants, and small children for deafness due to inner ear causes. * Helps to differentiate cochlear and retrocochlear hearing loss- normal OAE indicates normal cochlea and hence retrocochlear pathology in a patient with sensorineural deafness. * Early detection of noise-induced hearing loss- since it is generated by outer hair cells that are prone to damage by noise trauma. Pearl PF1553: BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) or ABR (Auditory Brainstem Response) It is an objective test that records electrical activity occurring in the auditory pathway. Normally, 7 waves are produced in the first 10ms.  * Wave I – distal part of the cochlear nerve * Wave II –proximal part of the cochlear nerve * Wave III – cochlear nucleus * Wave IV – superior olivary complex * Wave V – lateral lemniscus * Wave VI – inferior colliculus * Wave VII - medial geniculate body Findings: * Conductive or cochlear pathology- delayed wave-I but inter-peak latency of I-V is normal * Retrocochlear pathology- wave-I present, rest of the waves absent * Acoustic neuroma or vestibular schwannoma- increased inter-peak latency of wave I-V and increased inter-aural latency of wave V > 0.2ms. Uses: * To objectively find hearing threshold- wave-V appears 10dB above the hearing level obtained through PTA * Best audiometric test for: * Confirming hearing loss in infants * Diagnosing acoustic neuroma * * Differentiating cochlear and retro-cochlear hearing loss * Diagnosing non-organic hearing loss. Pearl PF1978: Pure tone audiometry (PTA) A pure tone is the sound of a single frequency. An audiometer is a device that generates pure tones and its frequency can be increased or decreased by 5Hz. The threshold for air conduction (AC) of sound frequencies from 125-8000 Hz and the threshold for bone conduction (BC) of sound frequencies from 250-4000 Hz is measured and the result is plotted on an audiogram. Normal thresholds: * For AC: 15 dB * For BC: 25 dB Symbols used in pure tone audiometry:  
Disease Findings in PTA audiogram
Conductive hearing loss AC abnormal, BC normal, air-bone gap present
Sensorineural hearing loss Both AC and BC are abnormal and no air-Bone gap
Mixed hearing loss Both AC and BC abnormal and air-bone gap present
Presbycusis, ototoxicity, noise-induced hearing loss (higher frequencies affected first) Downsloping or descending audiogram 
Early stages of Meniere's disease (lower frequencies affected first) Upsloping or ascending audiogram
Congenital hearing loss and cochlear otosclerosis (mid-frequency hearing loss) U-shaped or trough-shaped or cookie bite shaped audiogram
Early cases of noise-induced hearing loss

Acoustic dip - characteristic dip in both AC and BC at 4000 Hz
Otosclerosis  Carhart's notch- dip at 2000 Hz in BC curve

text: 5. A 14-year-old male presented with recurrent epistaxis. There is no history of trauma. He also complained of nasal obstruction and rhinorrhea. On examination, there is a firm purplish mass on the posterior nasopharynx. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

A young male with recurrent epistaxis and complaints of nasal obstruction with a mass on the nasopharynx suggests a diagnosis of Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA) is a highly vascular and locally aggressive tumour seen almost exclusively in adolescent males, associated with significant morbidity and occasional mortality. JNA accounts for only 0.05% of all head and neck tumours. Patients usually present with a triad of progressive nasal obstruction, recurrent epistaxis and a mass in the nasal cavity and nasopharynx.\ It has the potential to cause proptosis, affecting both the orbit and intracranial extension, eventually leading to cranial nerve palsies and loss of vision.  Angiofibroma can be diagnosed using CT, MRI, and magnetic resonance angiography. Anterior bowing of the maxillary wall due to the presence of a mass in the pterygomaxillary space on CT known as the Holman-Miller sign is a characteristic finding of JNA. Recurrence has been reported up to 35%. Management: Surgical excision is the treatment of choice. Recurrent angiofibroma is treated with revision surgery, Radiotherapy is considered where the recurrence tumour is inaccessible. Other options: Option A: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma presents in elderly patients of East-Asian ethnicity and smoking history. They present with hearing loss and involvement of cranial nerves. Option B: The foreign body in the nose presents at an earlier age and doesn't have recurrent epistaxis or a mass on examination.  Option C: Antrochoanal polyp is a type of non-neoplastic nasal polypoidal masses of edematous nasal or sinus mucosa which arises from the mucosa of the maxillary antrum near its accessory ostium. The clinical features include unilateral nasal obstruction, mucoid nasal discharge, and a hyponasal voice.

text: 6. A 5-year-old child was brought to OPD with a history of URTI. He also has features of mouth breathing, sleep apnoea and nasal obstruction. The mother has noticed that the child increases the volume while watching TV. What is the appropriate management?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion

The given clinical scenario of a child with mouth breathing, sleep apnoea, nasal obstruction, and decreased hearing points towards the diagnosis of serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy. Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion would be the most appropriate management. Adenoid hypertrophy causes typical facies characterized by an elongated face with a dull expression, an open mouth, a hitched-up upper lip, prominent upper teeth causing crowding (malocclusion of teeth), a high arched hard palate (due to loss of tongue's molding action on the palate), and a pinched-in nose due to disuse atrophy of the alae nasi. Enlarged adenoids in children can present as nasal obstruction, recurrent acute otitis media, and serous otitis media. Chronic nasal obstruction resulting in mouth breathing leads to this characteristic facial appearance in children. Patients can also present with a speech disorder, most probably, rhinolalia clausa (hypo-nasality) due to adenoid hypertrophy. Serous otitis media also known as secretory otitis media, mucoid otitis media, or glue ear is characterized by the accumulation of nonpurulent, serous effusion in the middle ear cleft. Glue ear can occur either due to eustachian tube dysfunction (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis or tonsillitis or rhinitis, cleft palate, tumours of nasopharynx) or due to increased secretory activity of the middle ear mucosa (allergy, unresolved otitis media, viral infections). Glue ear is commonly seen in children aged 5-8 years and is associated with insidious onset of hearing loss (not exceeding 40 dB), mild ear aches, and a history of upper respiratory tract infections. Delayed or defective speech may also result from hearing loss. Otoscopy shows:  * Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex * Thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus  * Fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen when the tympanic membrane is transparent.  The otoscopy image of serous otitis media is shown below: Enlarged adenoids in children can present as nasal obstruction, rhinolalia clausa, recurrent acute otitis media, and serous otitis media. Adenoid facies, characterized by an elongated face, open mouth, teeth crowding, high arched hard palate, and pinched-in nose, may also be present. The tuning fork test reveals a conductive type of hearing loss and audiometry reveals hearing loss in the range of 20–40 dB. The fluid accumulation in glue ear causes decreased mobility (compliance) of the tympanic membrane leading to a flat or dome-shaped curve or type B curve on a tympanogram. Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.  * Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, and antibiotics. * Surgical management is done if the condition cannot be controlled with medications. It includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid with grommet insertion. Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy may be required and are usually done at the time of myringotomy. Other options: Option A: Grommet insertion alone will help resolve otitis media but the primary pathology of adenoid hypertrophy will not be addressed.  Option C: Myringotomy with grommet insertion- Myringotomy will relieve the glue ear but will not address adenoids and lead to the recurrence of symptoms. Option D: Myringotomy involves creating a small incision in the eardrum that will relieve the otitis media but symptoms will recur due to persistent adenoid hypertrophy.

text: 8. In the case of anterior ethmoidal neuralgia, where is the anterior ethmoidal nerve most commonly compressed?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Middle meatus

The middle meatus is the most common site of compression of the anterior ethmoidal nerve, causing neuralgia. Anterior ethmoidal neuralgia, also known as Sluder's neuralgia is caused when the anterior ethmoidal nerve, a branch of the nasociliary nerve (which is itself a branch of the ophthalmic nerve, CN V1), is compressed. The most common site of compression is at the middle meatus, where the nerve may be impinged by anatomical variations, inflammation, or other pathologies affecting the paranasal sinuses. The anterior ethmoidal nerve enters the nasal cavity by descending through the cribriform plate near the crista galli. Once in the nasal cavity, the nerve descends along the lateral wall of the nasal cavity. It runs above the superior border of the middle meatus and provides sensory innervation to the mucosa of the anterior part of the lateral wall of the nasal cavity The patient typically presents with severe, sharp, and stabbing pain localized to the forehead and the root of the nose, often radiating to the periocular region. The pain is usually unilateral but can occasionally be bilateral. Associated symptoms may include tenderness over the affected area and occasionally nasal congestion or discharge if there is concurrent sinusitis. Computed Tomography (CT) or Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of the paranasal sinuses can be employed to identify anatomical variations, mucosal thickening, or other potential sources of nerve compression. Management involves analgesics (such as NSAIDs or acetaminophen), and in more severe cases, neuropathic pain medications like gabapentin or pregabalin can be used to alleviate pain. Nasal corticosteroids or saline nasal irrigation may be prescribed to reduce inflammation and relieve associated nasal symptoms. Surgical intervention is considered in cases where conservative treatments are ineffective and anatomical abnormalities are identified.

text: 9. A 33-year-old male met with a road traffic accident. There is persistent watery discharge mixed with blood from his nose for 3 days which cannot be sniffed back. Which of the following should not be done in this condition?

options.B: Plan surgical treatment with functional endoscopic sinus surgery
options.C: Bed rest and avoiding strenuous activity

expl:
Correct answer: B. Plan surgical treatment with functional endoscopic sinus surgery

In the given scenario of a male presenting with watery nasal discharge mixed with blood that cannot be sniffed back following a road traffic accident is suggestive of CSF rhinorrhea. Surgical treatment with functional endoscopic sinus surgery should not be done in this patient. CSF rhinorrhea refers to the leakage of cerebrospinal fluid into the nose. It can occur as clear fluid or be mixed with blood, particularly in cases of acute head injuries. Fracture of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid is the most common cause of this. Other causes include accidental or surgical trauma, infection and inflammation of the sinuses, neoplasms, and congenital lesions associated with skull base defects or may occur spontaneously. When CSF rhinorrhea occurs after head trauma, it often contains a mixture of blood, leading to a characteristic appearance known as the double-target sign when collected on a piece of filter paper. This sign presents as a central red spot (indicating blood) surrounded by a lighter peripheral halo. CSF fluid gushes down on straining and bending forward. It cannot be sniffed back. CSF doesn’t stiffen a handkerchief, but nasal secretions do because of their mucus content. High-resolution computerized tomography (HRCT) is the investigation of choice for localizing the site of the leak.(Option A) Beta-2 transferrin protein detection by electrophoresis is a sensitive and specific test for detecting CSF rhinorrhea. Beta trace protein is another protein that is secreted by meninges and choroid plexus and is specific to CSF. Treatment of CSF rhinorrhea: * Bed rest with head elevation. * Avoid blowing the nose, sneezing, and straining. (Option C) * Prophylactic antibiotics can be administered to prevent meningitis. (Option D) * Early cases of post-traumatic CSF rhinorrhea are managed conservatively by placing the patient in a semi-sitting position. * Persistent cases may be treated surgically by intracranial or nasal endoscopic approach.(option B)

History

Thin, watery, and clear

More than 30 mg/dl

Always present. It is specific to CSF

It shows a central red spot (blood) and a peripheral lighter halo. text: 10. A 20-year-old pregnant female presents with conductive hearing loss of 54db, not associated with tinnitus. Pure tone audiometry shows a notch at 2000 Hz. Which of the following is correct regarding the pathophysiology of the disease?

options.A: Ossicular fixation with intact tympanic membrane
options.B: Ossicular fixation with perforated tympanic membrane
options.D: Erosion of stapes footplate with perforated tympanic membrane

expl:
Correct answer: A. Ossicular fixation with intact tympanic membrane

The given clinical scenario of a young pregnant female with bilateral conducting hearing loss and notch at 2000Hz (Carhart's notch) is suggestive of otosclerosis where there is an ossicular fixation with the intact tympanic membrane. Otosclerosis is the disease of the bony labyrinth in which a normally dense endochondral layer of the bony otic capsule is replaced by irregularly laid spongy bone. It has a positive family history with an autosomal dominant trait. It is more commonly seen in females between 20-30 years of age and the hearing loss is aggravated during pregnancy and menopause. It may be associated with osteogenesis imperfecta and a viral infection like measles.  Stapedial otosclerosis is the most common type of otosclerosis. Here the lesion starts just in front of the oval window in an area called fissula ante fenestram. There is fixation of stapes footplate. Patients present with a bilateral conductive type of hearing loss, tinnitus (commonly in cochlear type and active stage), paracusis willisii (better hearing in noisy surroundings than in a quiet place), vertigo, and a monotonous, well-modulated soft speech. The tympanic membrane is quite normal and mobile. Eustachian tube function is also normal. Pure tone audiometry shows a dip at 2000 Hz in the bone conduction curve known as the Carhart's notch. Tympanometry shows an As type of tympanogram in which there is reduced compliance at or near the ambient air pressure. On examination, Schwartz sign/flamingo flush showing a red blush of the tympanic membrane due to vascularity can be seen. Treatment includes medical, surgical management, and hearing aids. Medical management with sodium fluoride is used in the active stage to speed up the maturity of the active focus and halt further cochlear loss. The treatment of choice is surgical management which includes stapedotomy/stapedectomy with the placement of a prosthesis. Hearing aids are used in patients who refuse or are unfit for the surgery.

text: 11. A 6-week-old boy was brought by his parents with complaints of noisy breathing, present since a few days after birth. Inspiratory stridor is heard. It subsides with prone positioning and increases with crying. What is the likely diagnosis?

It is characterized by excessive flaccidity of the supraglottic larynx which is sucked in during inspiration producing stridor and sometimes cyanosis. The presentation is just after birth and subsides by 2 years. Stridor improves(decreases) in the prone position, and worsens during feeding. The cry is normal. Treatment of Laryngomalacia: Mostly, it self-corrects by 2 years of age. A tracheostomy may be required for some cases of severe respiratory obstruction. Supraglottoplasty is required in cases of severe laryngomalacia. Stridor is noisy respiration produced by turbulent airflow through narrowed air passages. Stridor may be heard during inspiration, expiration or both. Inspiratory stridor is seen in supraglottic lesions. It is often produced in obstructive lesions of the supraglottis or pharynx, e.g. laryngomalacia or retropharyngeal abscess. Expiratory stridor is produced in lesions of the thoracic trachea, primary and secondary bronchi, e.g. bronchial foreign body, and tracheal stenosis. text: 1. An elderly diabetic male patient presented with a black, foul-smelling discharge from the nose. On examination, a blackish necrotic mass filling the nasal cavity and eroding the septum and hard palate. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is an opportunistic infection caused principally by species of Rhizopus, Mucor, and Lichtheimia. The most prevalent species is Rhizopus oryzae. It commonly occurs in patients with diabetes mellitus and immunocompromised individuals. Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is the most common form of mucormycosis. It commonly occurs in patients with diabetes mellitus. The presenting features are facial pain, numbness, loosening of teeth, conjunctival swelling, congestion, and blurry vision. When the disease spreads to the orbit, proptosis can be present. It can later spread to the brain's frontal lobe and cavernous sinus.  The local tissue destruction with blackish nasal discharge is typically seen in invasive mucormycosis. The blackish discolouration is due to direct fungal invasion causing arterial and venous thrombosis leading to gangrene.  A definitive diagnosis is done with a biopsy and histopathologic examination. It is the most sensitive and specific method. It reveals aseptate fungi with thick-walled, ribbon-like hyphae branching at right angles. Culture isolation is performed on Sabouraud agar without cycloheximide, resulting in grey-white colonies with a thick, cottony, and fluffy surface. Among the imaging techniques used for diagnosis, MRI is more sensitive to detecting orbital and nervous involvement than CT. Contrast-enhanced MRI is the imaging technique of choice. The 1,3 beta D-glucan assay, which is helpful for the identification of most fungi, cannot be used for the diagnosis of mucormycosis. Management: The underlying cause and risk factors should be addressed. * Aggressive surgical debridement of involved tissues should be considered as soon as the diagnosis of any form of mucormycosis is suspected.  * Initial therapy with amphotericin B as the drug of choice. * Posaconazole and isavuconazole are broad-spectrum azoles that can be used as step-down therapy after response to amphotericin B. The benefit of hyperbaric oxygen has not been proven yet and is not considered a standard treatment. Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is characterized by complications such as cavernous sinus thrombosis when advanced cases are encountered. Clinical features suggestive of cavernous sinus thrombosis are bilateral proptosis, chemosis, vision loss, and impairment of extraocular muscle function (ophthalmoplegia).  Other options: Option A: Bacterial rhinosinusitis typically presents with purulent nasal discharge, pain, and fever, and the CT scan would show mucosal thickening without the characteristic hyperattenuation. Option C: Allergic fungal sinusitis is an allergic reaction to the causative fungus. It is prevalent in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised hosts. There is no invasion of the sinus mucosa with fungus. It presents with sinonasal polyposis and mucin, which consists of eosinophils, Charcot-Leyden crystals, and fungal hyphae. A CT scan shows mucosal thickening with centrally hyperdense areas. (Double density sign) There is an expansion of the sinus or bone erosion due to pressure, but no fungal invasion. Option D: Invasive aspergillosis tends to affect immunocompromised individuals and cause more aggressive symptoms like facial swelling, necrosis, and a more destructive pattern on CT.

text: 2. A middle-aged lady choked while eating fish and has associated symptoms of choking, hoarseness of voice, and foreign body sensation in the throat. On examination, the fishbone was lodged in the pyriform fossa. During its endoscopic removal, which of the following nerves is most susceptible to injury?

options.C: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
options.D: External branch of Superior laryngeal nerve

expl:

The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is most susceptible to injury. The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs submucosally in the lateral wall of the pyriform sinus. The pyriform fossa lies on either side of the larynx and extends from the pharyngoepiglottic fold to the upper end of the esophagus and forms the lateral channel for food. It is bound medially by the aryepiglottic fold and the posterolateral surfaces of the arytenoid and cricoid cartilages. It is bound laterally by the thyrohyoid membrane and the thyroid cartilage. The internal laryngeal nerve supplies the larynx above the vocal cords. The thyrohyoid membrane connects the thyroid cartilage and hyoid bone. Option D: Thyroid surgery, tumours, neuritis, or diphtheria can also affect the external laryngeal nerve, resulting in paralysis of the cricothyroid.

text: 3. Which of the following head and neck cancers is most commonly associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Oropharyngeal carcinoma

HPV infection is most commonly associated with oropharyngeal carcinoma. HPV 16 and 18 are considered high-risk subtypes and are associated with cervical cancer and precancerous cervical lesions. There is also evidence linking HPV 16 and 18 with cancers of the anus, vulva, vagina, penis, and oropharynx. The E6 protein of high-risk types binds to the p53 gene, while the E7 protein inactivates the pRb gene. p53 and pRb are tumour suppressor genes that, when inactivated, result in uncontrolled cell proliferation. The presence of koilocytes is a histopathological marker of the virus. These cells have a perinuclear halo in the cytoplasm, and these cells disappear when dysplasia advances. Laryngeal papillomas are benign tumours of the larynx caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV types 6 and 11), which is most likely acquired at birth from mothers who had vaginal HPV disease. Juvenile papillomatosis, or respiratory papillomatosis, is the most common benign laryngeal neoplasm in children. Important agents associated with malignant conditions: * HHV-8 (mainly), cytomegalovirus - Kaposi’s sarcoma * Epstein-Barr virus – Burkitt’s lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma * HPV 16 and 18 – Cancer cervix * HBV and HCV – Hepatocellular carcinoma * Schistosoma – Bladder carcinoma The head and neck cancers include cancers of the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, paranasal sinuses, nasal cavity, and salivary glands. Squamous cell cancer is the most common head and neck malignancy, often linked to tobacco and alcohol use. Non-squamous malignancies include thyroid cancer, salivary gland cancer, and sarcomas. The risk factors for head and neck malignancies are listed below: * Oral cavity cancer:  * Tobacco, smokeless tobacco like Bidi, Chutta, Paan (oral tobacco mixed with betel leaf, areca nut, and salted lime), Khaini, and marijuana * Alcohol, poor oral hygiene, and intake of red meat and salted meat * Infections with human papillomavirus and HIV  * Genetic conditions like Li-Fraumeni, ataxia telangiectasia, Bloom syndrome, and Fanconi's anaemia * Oropharyngeal cancer:  * Smoking and alcohol * HPV 16 and 18 * Cancer of the larynx and hypopharynx (Option D):  * Tobacco and alcohol * Nickel, mustard gas, and asbestos exposure * Long-term exposure to sulphuric acid and hydrochloric acid in battery plant workers. * Postcricoid carcinoma is associated with previous radiation and sideropenic dysphagia * HPV infection and immunosuppression * Nasopharyngeal cancer: (Option A)  * Chinese population * Epstein-Barr virus infection * Nitrosamines in salted fish and meat * Vitamin C deficiency * Cancers of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinus:  * Tobacco * Occupational exposure to dust from wood, textiles, and leather. Nickel and chromium dust and mustard gas exposure.  * HPV 16 and 18 Option B: Plummer-Vinson syndrome is a known risk factor for post-cricoid hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.

text: 4. A patient presents to the emergency room after an RTA with a history of diplopia, epistaxis, and restricted eye movements. The radiological examination is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Orbital floor fracture

The given clinical scenario plus the supportive CT image showing the "hanging drop sign" is suggestive of a blowout fracture of the orbital wall. Blowout fractures are isolated comminuted fractures caused by direct trauma to the orbit that result in a backward displacement of the eyeball and an increase in the intraorbital pressure. This causes a fracture at the weakest point of the orbital wall, which is usually the posteromedial portion of the maxillary bone in the orbital floor. The second most common site for orbital blowout fractures is the medial wall of the orbit. An isolated fracture of the orbital floor when a large blunt object strikes the globe is called a blowout fracture. The orbital contents herniate through the antrum into the maxillary sinus, which may lead to enophthalmos and entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle. The floor is made of zygomatic, maxillary, and palatine bones. The patient with a blowout fracture usually presents with immediate periorbital edema and blood extravasation in and around the orbit. Proptosis of the eyeball secondary to orbital edema or hemorrhage with paraesthesia along the infraorbital nerve is also very common. Clinical signs: periocular swelling (early stage), enophthalmos, ecchymosis, and subconjunctival haemorrhage. Infraorbital hypoesthesia may be present because of entrapment of the infraorbital nerve. Imaging by a plain x-ray in water's view or by CT demonstrates depression of bony fragments and orbital contents herniating through the orbital floor into the maxillary antrum. This is called the "hanging drop sign" or "teardrop sign". Definitive treatment is by surgical repair 10-14 days after injury with initial supportive management with analgesics and antibiotics. Le Fort fracture is the term used to describe different types of maxillary fractures. Investigations: * X-ray (Water's view) shows a teardrop opacity in the maxillary sinus. * A CT scan is used to confirm the site and size of the fracture and entrapment of muscle. * Initial treatment consists of observation, oral antibiotics, ice packs, and nasal decongestants. Indications of surgery: * Enophthalmos greater than 2 mm * Persistent and progressive diplopia in the primary position * Entrapment of orbital contents * Large fracture involving at least half of the orbital floor If any of these conditions are present, surgical correction is required within 2 weeks. text: 5. A child was extubated after a surgical procedure that required prolonged ventilation. Shortly after the endotracheal tube is removed, the child exhibits stridor on auscultation. What part of the airway is most likely affected?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Subglottic narrowing

This child presenting with stridor after prolonged intubation most likely has subglottic stenosis post-intubation. The subglottis is the narrowest part of the paediatric airway, making it particularly prone to injury and stenosis following prolonged mechanical ventilation. The most common cause of subglottic stenosis in children is prolonged endotracheal intubation. Prolonged endotracheal intubation leads to ischemia and pressure necrosis of the subglottic mucosa. This results in a fibroinflammatory response, which progresses to wound contracture and airway narrowing. This explains the gradual onset of dyspnoea and stridor with preserved phonation. Pulmonary function tests reveal a fixed upper airway obstruction pattern. Diagnosis is by laryngoscopy or bronchoscopy, which allows direct visualisation of the subglottic area to assess the degree of stenosis. CT or MRI may be used to evaluate the extent of narrowing and identify any underlying structural damage. Treatment can be via endoscopic balloon or mechanical dilation; laser therapy or surgical resection may be needed to remove the stenosis in severe cases. In severe cases, a tracheostomy may be required to bypass the obstructed segment and allow for breathing. This condition is staged by the Cotton-Meyer grading. Subglottic stenosis and laryngomalacia are the causes of stridor in neonates. Stridor is a noisy form of respiration produced by turbulent airflow through narrowed air passages. It may be heard during inspiration, expiration, or both. * Inspiratory stridor is often produced in obstructive lesions of the supraglottis or pharynx, e.g., laryngomalacia or retropharyngeal abscess. * Biphasic stridor is seen in lesions of the glottis, subglottis, and cervical trachea, e.g., laryngeal papillomas, vocal cord paralysis, and subglottic stenosis. * Expiratory stridor is produced in lesions of the thoracic trachea and primary and secondary bronchi, e.g., bronchial foreign body and tracheal stenosis. text: 6. A female singer presents with difficulty producing high-pitched sounds following thyroid surgery. There is no hoarseness in her voice, but she is unable to elevate her pitch. Which nerve is most likely injured?

options.A: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (IBSLN)
options.D: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN)

expl:
Correct answer: D. External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN)

The nerve most likely injured in the given case is the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN). The affected muscle is likely the cricothyroid muscle, one of the paired intrinsic muscles of the larynx, which is responsible for elongating and tensing the vocal cords to produce higher pitches. This muscle's function is directly influenced by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, which supplies it and facilitates the adjustment of pitch. The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve descends along the larynx, situated beneath the sternothyroid muscle, to innervate the cricothyroid muscle. By activating this muscle, the external branch enables the tension of the vocal cords to be increased, thereby contributing to the production of higher-pitched sounds. This intricate nerve-muscle interaction highlights the specialised role of the cricothyroid muscle in pitch modulation and vocal quality. Other options: Option A: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies the mucous membrane of the larynx up to the level of the vocal folds and no motor supply. Option B: Injury to the right recurrent laryngeal nerve results in hoarseness and dysphonia due to paralysis of the right vocal cord, whereas paralysis of both vocal cords results in aphonia and inspiratory stridor. It supplies all intrinsic muscles of the larynx, except the cricothyroid. Option C: Lesions of the glossopharyngeal nerve result in the loss of the gag reflex and other sensory loss like taste sensation and loss of pain on tongue, tonsil, pharynx and soft palate. It is motor to the stylopharyngeus, secretomotor to parotid glands, and gustatory to the posterior one-third of the tongue. Pearl PF1091: Nerves of Larynx

text: 8. A 60-year-old man reports gradual hearing loss over several years. He reports difficulty hearing conversations, particularly in noisy environments, and has difficulty perceiving high-pitched sounds. There is no vertigo, tinnitus, or ear fullness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Presbycusis

This clinical vignette points towards a diagnosis of presbycusis. It is a type of sensorineural hearing loss associated with the physiological ageing process in the ear. The pathogenesis of presbycusis includes: * Degeneration of the organ of Corti * Degeneration of the spiral ganglion * Degeneration of the stria vascularis * Stiffening of the basilar membrane. Clinically, it usually manifests in elderly adults over 65 years of age. It is gradually progressive and tends to affect the higher frequencies first. Characteristically, patients with presbycusis have significant difficulty hearing in the presence of background noise. Additionally, patients with presbycusis may also have a paradoxical hypersensitivity to loud sounds. This is due to the recruitment phenomenon. They may also have tinnitus. It significantly affects the quality of life, and patients tend to present with progressive social withdrawal.  On examination, tuning fork tests will show a picture of symmetrical sensorineural hearing loss with * Positive Rinne's test in both ears, meaning the air conduction is better than bone conduction (AC>BC) in both ears * Weber's test will show no lateralisation, meaning the sound is heard equally on both sides.  Diagnosis can be confirmed with audiometry. Treatment of presbycusis mainly includes using a hearing aid.  Other options: Option A: Acoustic neuromas are noncancerous, usually slow-growing tumours that form along the vestibulocochlear nerve. They arise from Schwann cells. Schwannomas can occur on any cranial or peripheral nerve in the body, but in the brain, acoustic neuromas are the most common schwannomas. Option B: Meniere's disease is usually unilateral. It is characterised by episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and a sense of ear fullness. Pure tone audiometry reveals a sensorineural type of hearing loss with lower frequencies affected first. Option D: Otosclerosis is a disease of the otic capsule that usually presents with bilateral progressive conductive hearing loss. Patients with otosclerosis characteristically hear better in noisy than in quiet surroundings (Paracusis Willisii). Tuning fork tests show negative Rinne's test, i.e., BC > AC. Weber's may be central, as this is typically symmetrical. Pearl PF1978: Pure tone audiometry (PTA) A pure tone is the sound of a single frequency. An audiometer is a device that generates pure tones and its frequency can be increased or decreased by 5Hz. The threshold for air conduction (AC) of sound frequencies from 125-8000 Hz and the threshold for bone conduction (BC) of sound frequencies from 250-4000 Hz is measured and the result is plotted on an audiogram. text: 9. A middle-aged male presents to the emergency room after a road traffic accident. Upon examination, the external auditory meatus has blood clots. What is the investigation of choice?
expl:
Correct answer: D. CT Temporal bone

The clinical history of a road traffic accident causing bleeding through the ears is highly suggestive of a basilar skull fracture or ring fracture. Hence, the investigation of choice in the given clinical vignette is a CT scan of the temporal bone Signs of basilar skull fractures: * Haemotympanum: Pooling of blood behind the tympanic membrane, associated with fracture of the temporal bone. It is one of the earliest signs of a basilar fracture. * Periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes): Pooling of blood surrounding the eyes, associated with fractures of the anterior cranial fossa. * Mastoid ecchymosis (Battle’s sign) refers to the collection of blood in the posterior aspect of the ear (mastoid region), indicating a middle cranial fossa fracture. * CSF rhinorrhea or otorrhea: Double target sign, a double-ring pattern described with CSF-containing bloody fluid from the ear or nose, when dripped onto paper or linen. Following a head injury, the battle’s sign and raccoon eyes are usually delayed findings, developing between 6 hours to 3 days post-trauma. The onset of CSF leaks following trauma may be delayed by several hours to days. Suspected fluid is confirmed as CSF by testing for β2-transferrin. Most CSF leaks are conservatively managed. Persistent leaks >7 days have a heightened risk of meningitis and are often surgically repaired. Nasopharyngeal airways and nasogastric tube insertion are relatively contraindicated in basilar skull fractures due to the risk of intracranial placement. NIPPV is avoided due to the risk of pneumocephalus.  The image below shows raccoon eyes and a battle sign. Pearl PF0368: Types of skull vault fracture Diastatic fracture - Separation of sutures due to blow with blunt weapon or from cerebral edema. It is also called sutural fracture. Fissured fracture/Linear fracture: * Linear skull fractures are breaks in the bone that traverse the full thickness of the skull from the outer to inner table. * They are usually fairly straight with no bone displacement. * The common cause of injury is blunt force trauma where the impact energy transferred over a wide area of the skull. Pond fracture - Occurs in children due to elasticity of bones. It is also known as indented fracture. Depressed fracture - Caused by a heavy weapon with a small striking surface. Its shape indicates the type of weapon which is produced. So it is also called 'signature fracture'. Comminuted fracture - It is also called spider web fracture and has a stellate appearance where there is no displacement of fracture. text: 10. Which of the following structures usually has the tip of the uncinate process attached to it?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Middle turbinate

The tip of the uncinate process is attached to the middle turbinate. The upper attachment of the uncinate process varies significantly and may connect to the lateral nasal wall, extend upward into the base of the skull, or medially attach to the middle turbinate. These variations influence the drainage patterns of the frontal sinus. The anteroinferior border of the uncinate process is connected to the lateral wall. The posteroinferior end of the uncinate process attaches to the inferior turbinate, dividing the membranous section of the lower middle meatus into an anterior and a posterior fontanelle. The structures seen in the middle meatus are the uncinate process, a bony projection inferiorly stemming from the inferior turbinate and superiorly varying in attachment, and having an anterosuperior to posteroinferior curve mirroring the bulla ethmoidalis located above and lateral to it. The bulla ethmoidalis is a large ethmoidal air cell that projects into the middle meatus. The semilunar space between the bulla and uncinate is called hiatus semilunaris. The area limited medially by the uncinate process and laterally by the lamina papyracea is the infundibulum, in the inferior aspect of which the maxillary sinus ostium drains. The frontal sinus opening is usually near the anterosuperior attachment of the uncinate process (which is variable), while the middle ethmoidal air cells open at the bulla ethmoidalis. The osteomeatal complex is the name given to the area containing the openings of these various sinuses in the middle meatus. Hypertrophy, pneumatization of the middle turbinate (concha bullosa), cancerous masses on the middle turbinate, etc., can cause the osteomeatal complex area to narrow considerably and result in sinusitis of the frontal, ethmoidal, and maxillary sinuses. The image below shows the computed tomography (CT) scan of the ostiomeatal complex Important steps in FESS: * Uncinectomy or Infundibulotomy * Identification and enlargement of the maxillary ostium * Bullectomy * Penetration of basal lamella and posterior ethmoidal cells * Clearance of frontal recess and frontal sinusotomy * Sphenoidotomy * Nasal packing Indications of FESS: * Chronic bacterial sinusitis refractory to medical treatment. * Recurrent acute bacterial sinusitis. * Polypoid rhinosinusitis. * Fungal sinusitis with fungal ball. * Antrochoanal polyp. * Mucocele of frontoethmoid or sphenoid sinus. * Endoscopic septoplasty. * Epistaxis control by endoscopic cautery. * Foreign body removal from the nose or sinus. Other options: Option B: The inferior turbinate is an independent bone, and the nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus located below it. Option C: The superior turbinate, located posteriorly and superiorly to the middle turbinate can become pneumatized. The superior meatus is located below it, and the posterior ethmoid cells open into it.

text: 11. A 5-year-old child is brought to the outpatient department by his mother with irritability, poor school performance, and a history of recurrent ear infections. Otoscopic examination shows a dull, retracted tympanic membrane with fluid behind it. There is no blood clot present in the ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Otitis media with effusion

In the given clinical scenario, the patient's history of recurrent ear infections and dull, retracted tympanic membrane with fluid and absent blood clots points to the diagnosis of otitis media with effusion (OME). Serous otitis media, also known as secretory otitis media, otitis media with effusion (OME), mucoid otitis media, or glue ear, is characterised by the accumulation of nonpurulent, serous effusion in the middle ear cleft.  Glue ear can occur either due to eustachian tube dysfunction (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis, tonsillitis or rhinitis, cleft palate, tumors of nasopharynx) or due to increased secretory activity of the middle ear mucosa (allergy, unresolved otitis media, or viral infections). Glue ear is commonly seen in children aged 5-8 years and is associated with insidious onset of hearing loss (not exceeding 40 dB), mild ear aches, and a history of upper respiratory tract infections. Delayed or defective speech may also result from hearing loss. Otoscopy shows:  * Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex * Thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus  * Fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen when the tympanic membrane is transparent.  The otoscopy image of serous otitis media is shown below: Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.  * Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, and antibiotics. * Surgical management is done if the condition cannot be controlled with medications. It includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid with grommet insertion. Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy may be required and are usually done at the time of myringotomy. Hearing tests suggestive of conductive hearing loss as seen in serous otitis media: * Rinne negative (BC>AC). * Weber—lateralized towards the worse ear * Audiogram—AC abnormal, BC normal, air-bone gap present * Impedance audiometry—flat curve (reduced compliance, shift to the negative side) A B-type tympanogram is expected in a case of serous otitis media. Here, compliance decreases. The fluid accumulation causes decreased mobility of the tympanic membrane, leading to a flat or dome-shaped curve. This results in a B-type tympanogram, as shown below: Note: The tympanograph is Flat when there is Fluid in the middle ear. Other options: Option B: Cartwheel appearance is seen in acute otitis media. It is an acute infection of the middle ear by pyogenic organisms. It presents with marked earache, and hearing loss is seen in later stages. Option C: Cholesteatoma is an abnormal collection of keratinising squamous epithelium in the middle ear or mastoid that leads to bone destruction. It can be congenital or acquired, with acquired cases arising from tympanic membrane retraction or epithelial migration through a perforation. The expanding mass erodes nearby structures, potentially causing serious complications. Option D: Tympanosclerosis involves calcification and fibrosis of the tympanic membrane, usually following chronic otitis media. It does not cause bone erosion or a retraction pocket.

It is more commonly seen in trumpet players, glass-blowers, or weight lifters due to a raised transglottic air pressure in these people. It can be classified into internal, external, or combined types of laryngocele. * Internal laryngocele is limited within the larynx and appears as a distension of the false cord and aryepiglottic fold. * External laryngocele has a distended saccule that herniates through the thyrohyoid membrane and appears as a swelling in the neck. * Combined or mixed laryngocele has both internal and external laryngoceles as its components where the air-filled sac extends both within the larynx and externally through the thyrohyoid membrane into the neck, and potentially into the mediastinum. External laryngocele presents as a reducible swelling in the neck that increases in size on coughing or performing the Valsalva maneuver. text: 4. A 35 year old male presented to the clinic with complaints of episodic vertigo, sense of ear pressure and fullness, decreased hearing, and a low-tone roaring tinnitus. What is the possible clinical diagnosis?

The possible clinical diagnosis for a 35-year-old male presenting with episodic vertigo, ear pressure and fullness, decreased hearing, and low-tone roaring tinnitus is Meniere's disease. It is also called endolymphatic hydrops. The primary pathology in Ménière’s disease is the distension of the endolymphatic system due to an increased endolymph volume. This can result either from increased production of endolymph or its faulty absorption or both. Normally, endolymph secreted by stria vascularis fills the membranous labyrinth and is absorbed through the endolymphatic sac. Meniere's disease is a chronic condition of the inner ear that affects balance and hearing. It is characterized by recurrent episodes of vertigo, which are brief and intense episodes of spinning dizziness. Patients may also experience a sense of pressure or fullness in the affected ear, along with fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus (ringing or buzzing in the ear). The tinnitus associated with Meniere's disease is typically low-tone roaring in nature. Other options: * Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is another common cause of vertigo, marked by brief episodes of dizziness or vertigo that are brought on by particular head movements. Common triggers include actions such as rolling over in bed or looking upwards. BPPV does not typically cause ear pressure, hearing loss, or low-tone roaring tinnitus. * Labyrinthitis is an inflammation of the inner ear, usually caused by a viral or bacterial infection. It can cause vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus, but it is usually accompanied by other symptoms such as ear pain, fever, and a general feeling of illness. * Syncope refers to a temporary loss of consciousness and muscle tone, often caused by a decrease in blood flow to the brain. It is not associated with the symptoms described in the scenario, such as vertigo, ear pressure, hearing loss, or tinnitus.

text: 7. During autopsy, the doctor tied the bronchus and immersed the lung in water to check whether it floats or sinks. This test is identified as ______ .
expl:
Correct answer: C. Hydrostatic test

Hydrostatic test is done to determine whether the newborn has respired or not. It is also known as Floatation test/ Breslau’s first life test/ Raygat’s test. It is based on the principle that the specific gravity of the unrespired lungs varies from 1.04 to 1.05 and that of  the respired lungs is 0.94, because of the increase in volume due to inhalation of air. Procedure: * Put each lung separately into a jar of water, see whether it sinks or floats. * Cut each into 10 to 12 pieces observe the blood exuding.Test each of them for buoyancy. * Pick up the floating pieces, and press firmly under water. Observe the nature of bubbles streaming up. Note whether they continue to float or not. Interpretation: * If the lung pieces float in water, it means that respiration has taken place, indicating a live birth. * If the pieces sink, respiration has not taken place, which means it is a stillborn. A respired lung (live birth) may sink in water in the following conditions : * Lung edema * Lung collapse * Pneumonia * Congenital syphilis An unrespired lung (still birth) may float due to gases of decomposition, as seen in putrefaction, or due to artificial inhalation. Hydrostatic test is not necessary when: * The fetus is born before 180 days of gestation. * The fetus is a monster and thereby incapable of leading a separate existence. * The fetus shows signs of intra-uterine macerations. * The umbilical cord has separated and the umbilicus has cicatrised. * The stomach contains milk showing active digestive system. Other options: Gettler's test is done for drowning. It estimates the chloride content of blood from both sides of the heart. * Normally, chloride content is equal in the right and left chambers of the heart (approx. 600 mg/100 ml). * In freshwater drowning, due to hemodilution, the chloride content is decreased on the left side of the heart by 50%. * In saltwater drowning due to hemoconcentration, the chloride content is increased in the left side of the heart by 30-40%. Ploucquet’s test: Weight of lungs Before respiration: 1/70 of body weight, after respiration: 1/35 of body weight  Diatom's test: Diatoms are a class of microscopic unicellular algae found suspended in most natural waters. The presence of diatoms in the brain or bone marrow indicates antemortem inhalation of water/ antemortem drowning. Diatoms are not found in the brain or bone marrow in case of dry drowning and when a dead body is thrown into the water. At the present time, the diatom test should be used only as an indicative aid and not as legal proof of drowning. Pearl PF1099: Hydrostatic Test/Floatation Test/Raygat's Test It is based on the lung changes in a foetus after respiration. Principle : Respired air remains in the lungs as residual air which cannot be removed after death. Hence lung floats in water. False negative test in: * Atelectasis * Pulmonary edema * Pneumonia * Congenital syphilis * Air absorbed from air passages if circulation continued for long time after cessation of respiration * More air exhaled from the lungs compared to air entering during inspiration * Obstruction by alveolar duct membrane False positive test in: * Putrefied foetus * Artificial inflation Hydrostatic test is not required when * Fetus is monstrous * Foetus is macerated or mummified. * Foetus is born before 180 days of gestation. * Stomach contains milk. * Umbilical cord has separated and scar has been formed.

expl:
Correct answer: B. 5 months

The Crown heel length of a 5-month-old fetus would be 25 cm. There is no stage of primary relaxation. * It is seen in cases of deaths coupled with emotional disturbances like in case of excitement, fear, severe pain, exhaustion at the time of death, cerebral hemorrhage, injury to the nervous system, drowning, strychnine poisoning. * It is an ante mortem phenomenon and it indicates the manner of death and not the time since death. Other options: Option B: Cutis anserina (goose-skin or goose-flesh), in which the skin has a granular and puckered appearance can be seen on the anterior surfaces of the body, especially on the thighs.  It is produced by the spasm of the erector pilae muscles, attached to each hair follicle, and can occur in the living when the skin comes in contact with cold water. It can occur on submersion of the body in cold water immediately after death, while the muscles were still warm and irritable. It can also be produced by rigor mortis of the erector muscles. Option C: Rigor mortis is a postmortem phenomenon indicative of molecular death. It is useful in estimating the time since death. The mechanism of rigor mortis is due to muscle ATP breakdown below the critical level.  It appears 2-3 hours after death and is usually preceded by postmortem flaccidity. It involves both the voluntary and involuntary muscles of the body and persists for about 12-24 hours.  Option D: Washerwoman’s hands is a specific change that is seen in the skin of the palm and sole, which comprises of wrinkled, swollen, whitish sodden appearance of hands or feet. It can also be considered as water maceration of skin of the hand, due to absorption of water into the outer layers of skin. Though the washerwomen’s hand and feet changes are usually seen in dead bodies recovered from water, this cannot be considered as a sign of antemortem drowning. Dehydration or drying and shrivelling of the cadaver occurs from water's evaporation, but the body's natural appearance and general facial features are preserved.. The mummified body is odourless. It is a late sign of death. It begins in the exposed parts of the body like the face, hands, and feet. Then it extends to the entire body including the internal organs which may later disappear due to putrefaction and maggot activity. During the process of mummification, the whole body loses weight up to 60 to 70% and all the internal organs become a single mass.  Factors necessary for the production of mummification are the absence of moisture in the air and the continuous action of dry or warm air. It occurs in bodies buried in shallow graves in dry sandy soils, where evaporation of body fluids is very rapid due to the hot dry winds in summer. Chronic arsenic or antimony poisoning favours the process. Differential decomposition is a condition in which some parts of the body show mummification and other parts show adipocere formation.

text: 7. Identify the postmortem finding in a patient with a stab wound on the left side of the chest.
expl:
Correct answer: A. Cardiac tamponade

The postmortem finding shows blood in the pericardium and it is a case of cardiac tamponade. Cardiac tamponade is the accumulation of fluid in the pericardial space significant enough to cause an obstruction to the inflow of blood to the ventricles. This reduces cardiac output and arterial pressure causing hypotension.  They can be caused due to a variety of injuries like: * Crush injuries, like traffic accidents in which the wheels pass over the heart, cause rapid displacement of blood from the vessels into the chambers which increase the intracardiac pressure. The increased intracardiac pressure causes the heart to burst open and then the blood escapes into the pericardium. * Stab injuries, where the left or right ventricle is pierced which allow blood to escape through the myocardium into the pericardium. The blood in the pericardium causes external compression of the heart thereby reducing myocardial contractility, which is fatal. If the left ventricle is pierced then the thickness of the wall may restrict the bleeding allowing time for surgical management. However, a stab of the right ventricle is rapidly fatal as the rate of flow of blood into the pericardium is higher than its removal from the pericardial sac. Around 200 to 300 ml of blood can interfere with myocardial contractility and cause death. * Fractures of ribs or sternum, can cause minor injuries in which the victim may live for some hours or days.However, death may occur from shock, hemorrhage, hemothorax, or cardiac tamponade if it is prolonged or a major injury.  It is characterized by: * Hypotension. * Pulsus paradoxus. * Increased pulse rate. * Prominent X descent. * Muffled heart sound. * Ewart’s sign (bronchial breathing at left angle of scapula). * Beck’s triad: Falling BP, Raised JVP, Small quiet heart. Investigation: * X-ray chest - Big globular heart. * ECG - Low voltage, Electrical alternans. * ECHO - Echo free zone around the heart. * Cath - Diastolic collapse of right atrium and right ventricle. Treatment: Drainage of fluid.

text: 11. What is the upper limit of Medical Termination of Pregnancy , according to the MTP Act of 2021?
expl:
Correct answer: C. 24 weeks

The upper limit of MTP is 24 weeks.  The opinion of one doctor is sufficient for abortions up to 20 weeks. For abortions from 20-24 weeks, the opinions of 2 doctors are required. Medical termination of pregnancy is legal in India for therapeutic, eugenic, humanitarian, and eugenic reasons. It should be conducted only by registered medical practitioners in government hospitals, or other private hospitals that are recognized by the government. The registered medical practitioner should have assisted in conducting 25 cases of medical termination of pregnancy in a recognized hospital. If a person or hospital goes against this rule, they are liable to be punished rigorously for a period of 2 years, which may extend to 7 years. Pearl PF1107: Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act - MTP Act 1971 MTP Act 1971 Indications : * Therapeutic : When continuation of pregnancy endangers the life of the woman, or may injure her physical or mental health.  * Eugenic : The risk of child being born with serious mental or physical abnormality. This includes first trimester viral infections, maternal drug intake (thalidomide, cortisone, antimitotics), xray or radioisotope treatment of the mother, insanity of parents and viral hepatitis. * Humanitarian : Pregnancy resulted from rape. * Social : Pregnancy resulted from failure of contraceptives.  Rules : * Only a registered medical practitioner who is qualified (one who has assisted in performance of 25 cases of MTP in a recognized hospital) can terminate a pregnancy. * MTP should be carried out in a government or government recognised hospital. * Private hospitals may take up MTP if they obtain a license from the chief medical officer of the district. * The consent of the woman is required for conducting an abortion. The written consent of the guardian is required if the woman is a minor or mentally ill. Consent of the husband is not necessary. * If the woman is not willing, abortion can not be performed on the request of the husband alone. * The woman need not produce proof of her age. The statement of the woman that she is over 18 years of age is accepted. * It is enough for the woman to say that she was raped, and it is not necessary that a complaint was lodged with the police. * Professional secrecy has to be maintained. * If the period of pregnancy is below 20 weeks, it can be terminated on the opinion of a single doctor. * If the period of pregnancy is between 20-24 weeks, two doctors must opine that there is an indication. Once there is an indication, the termination can be done by any one doctor. * In an emergency, the termination can be done by a single doctor, even without the required training, even after 20 weeks, without consulting a second doctor, in a private hospital which is not recognised.  * The termination of pregnancy by a person, who is not a registered medical practitioner (the person concerned), or in an unrecognised hospital (administrative head) shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than 2 years, but which may extend to 7 years. Confidentiality : The head of the hospital must maintain a register for recording the details of MTP. This register is a secret document which should be kept under safe custody for five years, and each patient is given a reference number. The name of the patient should not be entered anywhere, any case sheet or operation theatre register or any other record.

text: 1. Which of the following tests cannot be used to detect blood stains?

Faint yellowish-red to brownish crystals of hemin or hematin chloride in clusters are seen if the suspected material is stained with blood. text: 4. According to the law, nothing is an offence if a person is of an unsound mind and is not able to understand that the nature and consequences of his/her act are wrong. Which rule of insanity applies in this case?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Mc Naughten's rule

Mc Naughten’s rule is the correct answer. Mc Naughten’s rule states “Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who at the time of doing it by reason of unsoundness of mind is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law”. * The rules are: * McNaughten's rule states that every man is to be presumed to be sane, and possesses a sufficient degree of reason to be responsible for his crimes until the contrary is proved. * To establish an insanity defense, it must be clearly proved that, at the time of the committing of the act, the accused was laboring under ‘such a defect of reason, from a disease of the mind, as not to know the nature and quality of the act he was doing; or if he did know it, that he did not know he was doing what was wrong’. Other options: Options A and C: Durham's rule and Curren's rule are the other tests for insanity. Durhams's rule states that an accused person is not criminally responsible if his unlawful act is the product of mental disease or mental defect. Curren’s rule states that an accused person is not criminally responsible if, at the time of committing the act, he did not have the capacity to regulate his conduct to the requirements of the law as a result of mental disease or defect. Option D: Irresistible impulse test- This rule is similar to Curren's rule. Pearl PF1095: BNS Section 22, McNaughten's rule McNaughten's rule, Section 22 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023:  Criminal responsibility of the insane. It states that an accused is not criminally responsible if he was suffering from: * Defect of reason and unsoundness of mind: the law recognizes only those diseases which impair the thinking abilities of the mind. So, not all medically insane people are legally insane, as emotional disturbances that affect the mind are not considered if they do not directly affect cognition. * That he did not know the nature and the quality of the act he is doing:  the law needs the unsoundness of mind to exist at the time of the act to such a degree that the person is not aware of what he is doing and whether it is right or wrong to do. Absence of a motive or forethought is also considered as a criteria for determining unsoundness of mind.

Correct answer: C. Cadaveric spasm

It is seen in cases of death associated with emotional disturbances like cases of excitement, fear, severe pain, and exhaustion at the time of death. text: 9. All of the following changes occur in chronic starvation except?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Hyperthermia

All of the following changes occur in chronic starvation except hyperthermia. Hypothermia is seen in chronic starvation. The changes that occur in chronic starvation are as follows: loss of well-being, hunger, rapid weight loss, easy fatigue, lethargy, cachexia, anemia, hypotension, hypothermia, and polyuria. Edema of the lower limbs is seen due to hypoproteinemia. There is increased susceptibility to infections. Blood sugar, cholesterol, protein, and chloride levels are decreased. Non-protein nitrogen and urea plasma free acids and ketone bodies are raised. Death occurs due to exhaustion, brown atrophy of heart and intercurrent infection. Hypothermia and dehydartion may also play a role in  causing death. Postmortem examination of internal organs reveals:  Atrophied and darker muscles, brown atrophy of the heart, atrophy of the stomach and intestines, shrunken spleen, atrophied kidneys and decreased blood volume suggestive of anemia.  The gall bladder may be distended with bile. Pearl PF1956: Internal Findings of Starvation * General – Fat is absent from subcutaneous tissues and muscles. * Brain – is pale and soft with congested meningeal vessels (at times). * Heart – is smaller due to brown atrophy. Heart chambers are usually empty, pale and collapsed, and show hypostatic congestion. * Gastro intestinal tract: Stomach is small, contracted, and empty. Mucous membrane of stomach and upper part of intestine is stained with bile. Large intestine has hard fecal matter. * Gall bladder - is unusually distended. It contains dark and filled with dry and inspissated bile. * Liver - shows necrosis * Spleen, kidneys and pancreas are small and shrunken * Urinary bladder - is empty

text: 10. A public witness of the incident is asked to attend the court and record his evidence. Which type of evidence is provided by the witness to the court?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Oral evidence

The evidence provided by a public witness of the incident to the court is oral evidence. Oral evidence is given by a person who has personal knowledge of the facts associated with a particular incident. It is the evidence given by an eyewitness. The oral evidence should be direct whenever possible according to Section 60 of the Indian Evidence Act(IEA). It includes all the statements made by the witness in relation to the inquiry which is permitted by the court.  Other options:  Option B: Hearsay evidence is a type of evidence given by a person who has no personal knowledge of the facts in relation to the incident but only repeats what he heard others saying.  Option C: Subpoena is also known as summons. It is an authoritative call to appear in court. It is a document compelling the attendance of a witness in a Court of law under penalty, on a particular day, time, and place, for the purpose of giving evidence. It is issued by the Court. Section 61 to 69 of CrPc deals with the summons.  Option D: Circumstantial evidence is also known as indirect evidence. It is not the direct testimony of an eye witness but has a bearing upon the fact of the other and subsidiary facts which are relied upon as consistent. This type of evidence needs the Court of Law to make reasonable inferences based on the information presented.

text: 11. Which of the following is not a feature of the stage of excitement in acute cocaine poisoning?

options.C: Tingling and numbness in hands and feet
options.D: Dilated pupils , rapid pulse and sweating.

expl:
Correct answer: B. Cocaine bugs

Cocaine bugs are not a feature of the stage of excitement in acute cocaine poisoning. Cocaine is obtained from the leaves of Erythroxylum coca. Cocaine can be administered by snorting, intravenous route, or smoking. The manifestations of cocaine intoxication occur in two stages- the stage of excitement and the stage of depression. In the stage of excitement, the features seen are dry mouth, dysphagia, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypertension, dilated pupils, and increased temperature. There may be a feeling of well-being, and the patient may be excited, restless, and talkative. This progresses into a calm, dull state. Neurological manifestations include exaggerated reflexes, tremors or convulsions, hallucinations, tingling, and numbness in the hands and feet. The stage of depression is characterized by feeble respiration, excessive sweating, collapse, convulsions, and death.  Chronic cocaine users may have the feeling of insects crawling on their skin or the presence of grains of sand under the skin giving rise to an itching sensation. This is known as cocaine bugs or Magnan's symptom. Ulceration of the nasal septum may be seen in chronic abusers who sniff cocaine.  Treatment includes gastric lavage with warm water containing potassium permanganate, charcoal, or tannic acid if taken orally. When it is through the nose or throat, a wash with water is done. In case of intravenous intoxication, a ligature is applied above the site of the injection. The antidote for cocaine intoxication is inhalational amyl nitrite. Other measures include control of convulsions, airway, and circulatory stabilization, administration of IV thiamine, and naloxone. text: 12. A 50-year-old factory worker was brought to the emergency room with complaints of headache, vomiting, and blurring of vision after he consumed local spirit. Which of the following is used for the treatment of his condition?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Fomepizole

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of methanol toxicity. Ethanol and fomepizole is used for the treatment of this condition. Methanol poisoning is caused due to ingestion of illicit liquor which contains ethanol adulterated with methanol. Methanol is metabolized to formaldehyde and formic acid by alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases, respectively. The metabolites of ethanol are responsible for the toxic effects. Clinically, patients present with headache, vomiting, abdomen pain, uneasiness, confusion, delirium, and coma. Formic acid specifically damages the retina and optic nerve and results in blurring of vision and blindness. Elevated levels of formic acid and other organic acids result in metabolic acidosis in arterial blood gas analysis(ABG). Treatment of methanol poisoning includes gastric lavage with sodium bicarbonate if the patient is brought within 2 hours of ingesting methanol to combat acidosis. Ethanol infusion since ethanol is preferentially metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase over methanol and helps by reducing the rate of generation of formaldehyde and formic acid. Fomepizole is a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase and the drug of choice for methanol poisoning. Folate therapy with calcium leucovorin reduces blood formate levels by enhancing its oxidation. Hemodialysis is used in severe cases of methanol toxicity. Other options:  Option B: Flumazenil is the inverse agonist of benzodiazepine receptors and is used for the treatment of benzodiazepine overdose. Option C: N-acetyl cysteine is used as an antidote for the treatment of paracetamol poisoning. Option D: Naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist used for the treatment of opioid overdose. text: 4. A farmer is brought to the hospital following a snake bite on the right foot. Two fang marks were observed on the dorsum of the foot along with minimal pain, swelling and bleeding at the site. The vitals were stable. Which of the following is the immediate step of management?

options.B: Use sling or splint for right lower limb (pressure) immobilization
options.C: Look for dead snake brought by relatives

expl:
Correct answer: B. Use sling or splint for right lower limb (pressure) immobilization

The immediate management of snakebite will include immobilization using a sling or splint. Immobilization is done to minimize the spread of the venom. Hospitalization, followed by ASV administration is the definitive management of snake bites. Measures that can be done in the case of snakebite: * Apply firm pressure over the bitten area, which delays the absorption of venom * Pressure immobilization is recommended for elapid and sea-snake bites, but not for viper bites as it may cause local necrosis * Clean the wound with soap and water, or iodine and cover it with a sterile dressing  * Immediately apply a broad firm bandage (Sutherland wrap) on the bitten area and around the limb. As much of the limb should be bandaged as possible. It should be tight enough to occlude the superficial venous and lymphatic return, but not the arterial or deep venous flow.  * In bites on the trunk, head, or neck, apply firm pressure over the bitten area * Immobilize the limb, as movement can accelerate the spread of venom * Make the patient lie on one side in the recovery position so that the airway is clear, in case of vomiting or fainting Measures contraindicated in the case of snakebite: * Suction and incision of the wound * Electric shock treatment of wound site * Application of tourniquets because they obstruct arterial flow and cause ischemia * Ice water immersion of the bitten limb

text: 10. What is the most commonly affected organ in an air blast due to shockwave?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Lung

Lungs are considered to be severely damaged organs in the air due to variations in density between the alveolar walls and the contained air. A blast causes the most damage at an interface between tissues in contact with the atmosphere, which is why the lung usually suffers the most severe damage. Blast injury is a complex type of physical trauma resulting from direct or indirect exposure to an explosion. Primary blast injuries result from the rapid overpressure or shock waves produced by an explosion. These injuries result from the dramatic changes in barometric pressure projecting outwards from the point of detonation. They predominantly cause damage to air-filled hollow organs of the body from rapid pressure change (barotrauma). This includes the middle ear, lungs, and GIT. The most sensitive and most frequently injured hollow organs are the tympanic membranes > lungs. Blast damage to the lungs is the most common cause of life-threatening injury following an explosion. Solid organs are the most resistant to blast injuries as the parenchymal disruption requires very high levels of overpressure. The liver is the least vulnerable to blast wave (primary blast) injury.

4. A body brought for autopsy was cold and had developed rigor mortis in all 4 limbs and livor mortis at
the back, there is no sign of putrefaction. What is the estimated time since death?
expl:
Correct answer: A. 6-12 hrs

In the given clinical scenario of a body brought for autopsy, which was cold and showed rigor mortis in all four limbs along with livor mortis on the back, but no signs of putrefaction, the estimated time of death would be approximately 6-12 hours, since putrefaction has not yet occurred. Rigor mortis is a postmortem phenomenon indicative of molecular death. It is useful in estimating the time since death. The mechanism of rigor mortis is due to muscle ATP breakdown below the critical level.  It appears 2-3 hours after death and is usually preceded by postmortem flaccidity. It involves both the voluntary and involuntary muscles of the body and persists for about 12-24 hours.  Postmortem hypostasis/Postmortem staining/Postmortem lividity/Livor mortis/Suggilation refers to bluish-purple or reddish-purple discolouration of the superficial layers of the skin due to the collection of blood in toneless capillaries.  It is an early postmortem change that occurs due to engorged vessels showing through the skin seen on the dependent parts due to the pooling of blood under the effect of gravity. This staining starts as mottled patches 1-3 hours following death and develops to a uniform area of staining in 3-6 hours. Full development and fixation of hypostasis occur within 6-12 hours. This finding usually develops within 4 hours and persists until putrefaction.  Decomposition or putrefaction refers to the disintegration of the body tissues after death. Multiplication of the bacteria begins within 4 hours after death and by 18 to 36 hours gases collect in the body causing bloating and distortion. The body then undergoes putrefaction and liquefaction of the tissues 5 to 10 days after death. text: 5. A boy is severely beaten by 4 to 5 people and arrives at the hospital with serious injuries. A dying declaration is recorded. Which of the following statements about dying declarations in India is false?

options.B: It must always be recorded by a magistrate
options.D: An oath is not administered before recording a dying declaration.

The statement that is not applicable to the dying declaration is it must be always recorded by a magistrate. While it is ideal for a Magistrate to record a dying declaration, there is no legal provision that states that it must always be recorded by a magistrate. The statement can be recorded by a magistrate, the doctor, the village headman, a police officer, or any member of the public.  A dying deposition, on the other hand, must always be recorded by a Magistrate.  A dying declaration (Sec. 32 IEA) is a form of a written or oral statement made by a person whose imminent death is a result of an unlawful act. The statement made relates to the facts of the cause of death and the circumstances surrounding it. Procedure: * As soon the severely injured person is brought to the hospital, the medical officer should inform the magistrate to have a dying declaration recorded. The fitness of the declarant to make the statement should be examined first. * The doctor can record it himself or herself if he thinks that the person will not survive till the arrival of the magistrate. In such a case, the police or the doctor concerned must note down the reason as to why waiting for the magistrate for recording this statement was not feasible. * Treatment should not be delayed while recording dying declaration. * An oath is not administered in these circumstances because of the belief that the dying person tells the truth. (Option C) * No outsider is allowed to be present * After completing writting, it has to be read back to the patient who has to approve it by signing/thumb impression. The signature of two witnesses is also mandatory. A dying deposition is a form of oral evidence that is recorded in the presence of the accused or their lawyer, with the provision of cross-examination. There is no legal provision for a dying deposition in the Indian Evidence Act (it is not followed in India).
