text: 6. A person was stabbed in the thigh with a knife, resulting in a wound measuring 1 cm in length and 3 cm in depth. How would you classify this wound?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Penetrating wound

In the given clinical scenario, a person is stabbed in the thigh with a knife, resulting in a wound measuring 1 cm in length and 3 cm in depth is suggestive of a penetrating wound. A penetrating wound is an injury that occurs when an object, such as a knife, bullet, or any sharp instrument, breaks through the skin and enters deeper tissues of the body. These types of wounds can damage organs, blood vessels, and nerves, depending on the depth and location of the penetration. Penetrating wounds may lead to significant blood loss, infection, or trauma to vital structures, requiring prompt medical attention. Treatment typically involves controlling bleeding, preventing infection, and repairing any internal damage, often requiring surgical intervention. The severity of a penetrating wound depends on the force of impact, the object involved, and the area affected. Other options: Option B: A perforating wound occurs when an object penetrates the body and exits, creating both an entry and an exit wound. These wounds can cause significant internal damage, including injury to organs, blood vessels, and tissues. Option C: A crush injury occurs when a part of the body is subjected to intense pressure or force, typically from a heavy object. This can lead to tissue damage, fractures, nerve injury, and in severe cases, organ damage or compartment syndrome. Option D: An incised wound is clean-cut, regular, well-defined caused by sharp lightweight weapons like a knife, razor, scalpel, etc. Incised wounds will have a characteristic head of wound and tailing of a wound. The edges are well-defined and usually everted, free from contusions and abrasions. It is usually spindle-shaped. The depth is more at the commencement and progressively becomes shallower, known as tailing. Tailing determines the direction of the force applied when creating the wound. text: 10. Two construction workers were working together when a hammer slipped from one worker's hand and struck the other on the head. An X-ray revealed a fracture. What type of fracture could this be?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Depressed skull fracture

The clinical history and the X-ray image are suggestive of a depressed skull fracture of the frontal bone. A depressed skull fracture happens when a section of the skull bone is driven inward following a traumatic impact. This injury creates a noticeable indentation or depression in the skull and typically results from a direct blow to the head. The management of depressed skull fractures: * The first step is to order a CT scan to know the degree of depression and to exclude the presence of an intracranial hematoma or contusion. * The depressed fracture is elevated and managed as an open fracture (surgery) if: * The degree of depression is greater than the thickness of the adjacent skull. * The wound is open and grossly contaminated. * There are focal neurological deficits. * Less severe depressed fractures are managed by the closure of the overlying scalp laceration, if present. Other options: Option A: A Linear fracture is a type of skull fracture where the bone breaks in a thin, straight line without displacement. It is often caused by blunt force trauma and typically does not involve significant damage to surrounding tissues. Option B: A Hinge fracture is a type of skull base fracture where the skull splits along the base, resembling an open hinge. It is usually caused by severe trauma and can be associated with brain injury and damage to vital structures. Option C: A Ring fracture is a circular fracture around the base of the skull, typically occurring in the posterior fossa around the foramen magnum. It is often caused by severe trauma, such as a fall from a height or forceful impact on the head. These occur If the kinetic energy of the fall is not absorbed by fractures of the legs, pelvis, or spine, the impact is transmitted up the cervical spine. This force may be rammed into the skull, carrying a circle of occipital bone with it. Pearl PF0368: Types of skull vault fracture Diastatic fracture - Separation of sutures due to blow with blunt weapon or from cerebral edema. It is also called sutural fracture. Fissured fracture/Linear fracture: * Linear skull fractures are breaks in the bone that traverse the full thickness of the skull from the outer to inner table. * They are usually fairly straight with no bone displacement. * The common cause of injury is blunt force trauma where the impact energy transferred over a wide area of the skull. Pond fracture - Occurs in children due to elasticity of bones. It is also known as indented fracture. Depressed fracture - Caused by a heavy weapon with a small striking surface. Its shape indicates the type of weapon which is produced. So it is also called 'signature fracture'. Comminuted fracture - It is also called spider web fracture and has a stellate appearance where there is no displacement of fracture.

Which of the following techniques can be used to figure out a person's identity using the beheaded skull bone and photograph of the person?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Superimposition

The technique used to figure out a person's identity using the beheaded skull bone and photograph of the person is superimposition. The superimposition technique is applied to the skull to determine whether it belongs to the person in the photograph. The following points can be used for comparisons such as the eyes, nasion, prosthion, zygomas, lower border of the nose, supraorbital ridges, lower border of the zygomas, angle of the jaw, external auditory meatus, teeth and the lower border of the upper jaw. Other options: Option B: Anthropometry is based on the principle that the skeletal dimensions do not change after the age of 21 years and the variation in the size of the different parts to one another. Descriptive data such as the color of the hair, eyes, complexion, and body marks are recorded. Body measurements are estimated such as height, anteroposterior diameter of head and trunk, the span of outstretched arms, the length of the left middle finger, left little finger, left forearm, left foot, length, and breadth of right ear, and color of left iris from the photographs.  Option C: DNA fingerprinting for forensic analysis is done to detect DNA from small amounts of samples from the crime scene. DNA fingerprinting uses restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLPs) or Polymerase chain reaction(PCR) to identify a person's unique pattern of DNA.  Option D: Cheiloscopy is also known as lip printing. Here, the fissures and grooves on the lip characteristic of a person are examined.

text: 7. In a suspected murder case, the court summoned a doctor to provide his opinion and testify as a witness. This form of evidence is commonly referred to as ____?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Expert witness

The doctor in this scenario is referred to as an expert witness. As per Section 39 (1) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) (earlier Section 45 of the Indian Evidence Act), an expert witness is a person who is skilled in technical or scientific matters and capable of drawing opinions and conclusions from the facts observed by him or by others.  Examples: Doctor, firearm expert, fingerprinting expert, handwriting expert.  Witness: A witness is a person who gives evidence regarding facts. Sections 124 to 139 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) (earlier Sections 118 to 134 of the Indian Evidence Act) deal with various aspects of witnesses. Other types of witnesses: * A common witness is a person who gives evidence about the facts observed by them. The first-hand knowledge rule refers to the concept that the witness must show that he was capable of perceiving the fact by one of his own senses and that he actually observed this fact. It applies to all common witnesses who give evidence about the facts observed or perceived by him/her. A doctor can be both a common and an expert witness. Common witness - When he describes the wounds on the body. Expert witness - When he says that the wounds were antemortem or post-mortem, or they were suicidal, homicidal, or accidental, or gives an opinion regarding the cause of death. * A hostile witness is one who has some interest or motive for concealing part of the truth or for giving completely false evidence (Sec 227 of BNS/Sec 191 IPC). There must be some evidence to prove that the witness has retracted from his earlier statement or is not desirous of disclosing the truth, or has exhibited an element of hostility. If a witness is declared as hostile, he can be cross-examined by the same side's lawyer.

text: 9. A body was brought in for post-mortem examination, and the following can be seen. What type of wounds are these?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Defense wounds

The given image shows irregular and ragged cut wounds over the palmar surface of the hands and fingers, which is suggestive of defense wounds. Defense wounds are the wounds that occur as a result of the victim's attempt to save himself from an injury. It can be active or passive. Active defense wounds occur when the victim tries to grasp the weapon, while passive wounds result when the victim raises the hands, arms, or legs in an attempt to protect the eyes, head, or neck. The morphology of the wound depends upon the type of weapon and the attack. In a sharp injury due to a single-edged weapon, a single cut may be seen on the palm or the bends of fingers. In the case of a double-edged sharp weapon, cuts are seen on both palm and fingers. The cuts are irregular in-depth and are ragged. The defense wounds signify homicide, and in females, they often indicate sexual assault.  Other options: Options B and C: Antemortem and postmortem wounds are of medicolegal importance while evaluating trauma. text: 11. A child presents to the emergency department with complaints of severe abdominal pain and vomiting. The parents give a history of the child ingesting 10-20 ferrous sulfate tablets. Which of the following can be used in the management of this condition?

Initial symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, and gastrointestinal bleeding. In severe cases, cyanosis and hyperventilation due to metabolic acidosis can develop. This can sometimes be followed by an asymptomatic phase. Later, hypoglycemia and hepatic and renal failure can develop. Pyloric stenosis and gastric scarring can develop due to its corrosive nature. text: 1. A man who was arrested died while he was in police custody. Who will conduct the inquest in this case?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Judicial Magistrate

A magistrate inquest will be carried out for death under police custody. BNSS 196/Section 176 Cr. P.C. deals with magistrate inquest in which the cause of death is not under natural circumstances. Magistrate inquest may be conducted by the District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Tahsildar, or any other Executive Magistrate empowered by the State Government. While conducting this inquiry, the Magistrate has all the powers that they would normally have when investigating an offence. This ensures an independent and impartial inquiry into the circumstances of death, disappearance, or rape occurring while a person or woman is in police or judicial custody.  A death is considered custodial when it occurs in any form of detention, including while the person is being arrested, detained, escaping, or attempting to escape from custody.  The Judicial Magistrate or Metropolitan Magistrate conducting the inquiry must, within 24 hours of the death, forward the body to the nearest civil surgeon or other qualified medical professional appointed by the government for postmortem examination. Indications for Magistrate Inquest: * Death under police custody * Death due to police firing * Death in prison, reformatories, borstal schools * Dowry death * Death in a psychiatric hospital * Exhumation * Death or disappearance of any person, or rape of a woman who is under the custody of police or any other person authorized by the court. Other options: Option A: 194 BNSS or Section 174 CrPC deals with the police inquest. It is done in suicide, homicide, killing by any animal or machinery or accident, and death under circumstances that raise suspicion of another person committing the offence. In all cases where the police normally conduct inquests, the magistrate can hold an additional inquest, or in place of the police inquest. Option B: Coroner's Inquest is not practised in India. It is done in the U.K. and the U.S.A. The coroner, who is usually a first-class magistrate or attorney, conducts an inquest in all unnatural and suspicious deaths. The doctor is summoned to his Court to give evidence at the inquest.   Option C: The medical examiner's system is not followed in India. It is followed in certain states of the USA and Japan. A medical practitioner known as a 'Medical Examiner' is appointed to perform the functions of a Coroner. He gets first-hand information on the investigation and crime scene, which, when correlated with autopsy findings, carves out a better picture. Though he is not entitled to any judicial powers, the inquest conducted in the presence of a doctor makes it superior to any other method.

text: 3. A family was found dead in a closed room without windows, and smoke coming from a woodfire was present. Which of the following features is likely to be seen on their bodies?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Cherry red hypostasis

In the case of a family found dead in a closed room with smoke from a wood fire, there is likely to be cherry red discoloration on their bodies. This discoloration is due to carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning, which can occur from smoke in an enclosed space. The colour of postmortem staining in CO poisoning is cherry red. Carbon monoxide is a byproduct of incomplete combustion of organic materials, such as wood. When inhaled, CO binds to hemoglobin in the blood with an affinity approximately 240 times greater than that of oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin (COHb). This reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, leading to tissue hypoxia. The cherry red discolouration is a hallmark of CO poisoning. This occurs because COHb imparts a bright red colour, distinct from the darker hue associated with deoxygenated hemoglobin.  Postmortem hypostasis/Postmortem staining/Postmortem lividity/Livor mortis/Suggilation refers to bluish-purple or reddish-purple discolouration of the superficial layers of the skin due to the collection of blood in toneless capillaries.  It is an early postmortem change that occurs due to engorged vessels showing through the skin seen on the dependent parts due to the pooling of blood under the effect of gravity.  This staining starts as mottled patches 1-3 hours following death and develops to a uniform area of staining in 3-6 hours. Full development and fixation of hypostasis occur within 6–12 hours. This finding usually develops within 4 hours and persists until putrefaction. Fixation of hypostasis occurs earlier in the summer. It is delayed in asphyxial deaths and in intracranial lesions. Pearl PF1096: Color of Postmortem Hypostasis in Various Conditions

text: 5. A patient was brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. During an autopsy, apparent bleeding was seen on the surface of his brain. Which type of hemorrhage would not be washed away under direct running water?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

Subarachnoid haemorrhage will persist when washed under running water during an autopsy. Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is bleeding in the space between the brain and the arachnoid membrane which is the subarachnoid space. During an autopsy, the blood from a subarachnoid haemorrhage is not easily washed away by running water. This is because it is located in this deep layer, which can trap the blood within the brain's sulci and gyri. While doing the autopsy, there is typically some fresh blood present. However, it cannot be washed off because the blood is situated beneath the very thin and transparent arachnoid layer. This makes the blood from a SAH less likely to be displaced compared to haemorrhages located in other regions, such as epidural or subdural spaces. Thus, despite running water during an autopsy, the blood from a subarachnoid haemorrhage often remains in place, making it detectable even after washing.

text: 6. A vegetable vendor was found dead in his apartment, and his body had undergone advanced stages of decomposition. Which of the following methods can be used to identify him a week later?
expl:
Correct answer: D. DNA profiling

DNA profiling is the most reliable method for identifying a deceased person whose body has undergone advanced decomposition.  DNA profiling can also aid in identifying skeletonized or severely decomposed human remains. This process typically involves comparing the genetic profile from the remains with reference samples from relatives, often the victim's parents. DNA profiling, also known as genetic fingerprinting, is a forensic method used to identify individuals based on their unique genetic makeup, is precise and has high specificity. While decomposition can damage biological tissues, DNA can often be recovered from highly decomposed bodies. DNA can be extracted from bones, teeth, or preserved tissue samples. In contrast, other methods like visual identification (face recognition), fingerprint analysis, or dental records may be compromised or unfeasible when a body is in an advanced state of decomposition, making DNA profiling the preferred and most reliable choice for identification in such scenarios.

text: 8. In a case of alcohol abuse, which of the following preservatives is used to preserve blood during an autopsy?
expl:
Correct answer: A. NaF+ K oxalate

Sodium fluoride (NaF) (10 mg/ml) and potassium oxalate (anti-coagulant) can be used to preserve blood during an autopsy. Sodium Fluoride (NaF) inhibits glycolysis by preventing the breakdown of glucose, which could alter the blood alcohol content. It also has antimicrobial properties to prevent the growth of bacteria and fungi and potassium oxalate acts as an anticoagulant to prevent blood clotting and helps analyse the sample. A preservative is not necessary if: * The viscera can be analysed in 24 hours * If the sample can be stored in a refrigerator or icebox * Bone, hair, nail specimens * Lung for inhaled poisons * The viscera should not be preserved in formaldehyde because extraction of non-volatile poisons becomes difficult. Other options: * NaCl (Sodium Chloride): While useful in various laboratory settings, sodium chloride does not prevent glycolysis or microbial growth in blood samples, making it unsuitable for preserving blood for alcohol content analysis. * Rectified Spirit: It is a highly concentrated form of ethanol. Adding rectified spirit to a blood sample intended for alcohol analysis would contaminate the sample and invalidate the results. * Formalin: Primarily used for preserving tissues by fixing them, formalin is not suitable for preserving blood samples for alcohol analysis, as it can interfere with the chemical assays used to measure ethanol levels.

text: 10. A 15-year-old boy presents to the ER with complaints of muscle twitching and tremors. He gives a history of consuming crushed seeds from a plant. Shortly after, he begins to experience refractory seizures and assumes a characteristic posture with arching of the back and rigid extension of the limbs. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Strychnine poisoning

The given clinical vignette suggests the diagnosis of strychnine poisoning. Strychnine poisoning occurs if a person ingests crushed seeds of Strychnos nux vomica. If swallowed uncrushed, the seeds of nux vomica have no poisonous action. The fatal dose is 15–30 mg of strychnine or one crushed seed.  Strychnine is a competitive antagonist of glycine at the postganglionic receptors in the motor neurons of the anterior horn of the spinal cord. This leads to increased activity in the motor neurons.  Patients typically present with * Convulsions are clonic initially but eventually become tonic. * Risus sardonicus results from the contraction of the jaws and facial muscles, in which the corners of the mouth are drawn back. * The convulsions are most marked in anti-gravity muscles so that the body typically arches in hyperextension, the posture known as opisthotonus. * If the spasm involves the abdominal muscles, the body bends forward (emprosthotonos), or to the side (pleurosthotonus). * If death is preceded by a severe convulsion, as in strychnine poisoning, it causes an increase in the body temperature known as postmortem caloricity. The first step in the management of strychnine poisoning is to control convulsions with benzodiazepines or barbiturates to control seizures, and the patients should be placed in a dark room to avoid triggering further convulsions. Activated charcoal can be used to adsorb unabsorbed poison after a thorough stomach wash. Acidification of urine can be done to increase the excretion of strychnine. Other options : Option A: Tetanus - Tetanus toxin initially binds to receptors on the presynaptic membranes of motor neurons and migrates to the spinal cord and brainstem. The toxin diﬀuses to inhibitory neurons (γ-aminobutyric acid) from the brainstem and inhibits its function. Option B: Clostridium - Clostridium tetani secrete 2 types of toxins, namely, tetanolysin and tetanospasmin.  The toxin peptide degrades synaptobrevin, a protein required for the attachment of neurotransmitter vesicles on the presynaptic membrane, before its release. The motor neurons are not inhibited as the release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters glycine and GABA is blocked. This causes hyperreflexia, muscle spasms, and spastic paralysis result. Option C: Botulism - Botulinum toxin targets the presynaptic terminals of motor neurons and inhibits the release of acetylcholine. As a result, muscle paralysis occurs, leading to the temporary weakening or cessation of muscle activity in the affected area. Pearl PF0407: Signs and Symptoms of Strychnine Poisoning * Mnemonic to remember signs and symptoms. * We know that CRAMPing of muscles leads to the exhaustive death of the person in strychnine poisoning. Therefore: * Convulsions * Reflex increased * Awful taste * Mind is conscious * Pupils dilated * Clonic-tonic convulsions * Opisthotonos: arching back * Emprosthotonos: arching forward * Pleurothotonus: bending sideward * Risus Sardonicus: fixed contraction of the facial muscles resulting in a peculiar distorted grin. Medico-legal implications:. * Although a poison, in relatively low doses can be used as a medical stimulant for respiration. Strychnine poisoning case may resemble tetanus. text: 11. Following the death of a person, his family who lived abroad was unable to reach him, and hence his body needed to be preserved. Which of the following substances can typically be detected in his body, even if the person did not consume the substance shortly before death?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Alcohol

Alcohol can normally be detected in visceral organs, even if the person did not consume the substance shortly before death. After death, the body undergoes various biological processes, including putrefaction. During putrefaction, bacteria present in the gastrointestinal tract and other tissues can ferment carbohydrates, leading to the production of alcohol.  Therefore, the presence of alcohol in visceral organs during an autopsy can sometimes be attributed to postmortem production rather than recent ingestion. Other options : Aconite, arsenic, and morphine are not naturally produced by the body or formed after death. These substances must be ingested or administered. Finding these substances in the body indicates pre-death exposure, unlike alcohol, which can sometimes be produced after death.

text: 1. A female body was brought in for autopsy. The body was discovered in a closed room with a heat stove running during the dead body recovery, with cherry red discolouration on the skin and mucosal regions. What is the most probable cause of her death?
expl:
Correct answer: A. CO poisoning

In the given case of a female found dead in a closed room with smoke from a heat stove, with cherry red discolouration on the skin and mucosal regions, the most probable cause of her death is carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning, which can occur from smoke in an enclosed space. The colour of postmortem staining in CO poisoning is cherry red. Carbon monoxide is a byproduct of incomplete combustion of organic materials, such as wood. When inhaled, CO binds to haemoglobin in the blood with an affinity approximately 240 times greater than that of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb). This reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, leading to tissue hypoxia. The cherry red discolouration is a hallmark of CO poisoning. This occurs because COHb imparts a bright red colour, distinct from the darker hue associated with deoxygenated haemoglobin.  Postmortem hypostasis/postmortem staining/postmortem lividity/livor mortis/suggilation refers to bluish-purple or reddish-purple discolouration of the superficial layers of the skin due to the collection of blood in toneless capillaries.  It is an early postmortem change that occurs due to engorged vessels showing through the skin seen on the dependent parts due to the pooling of blood under the effect of gravity.  This staining starts as mottled patches 1-3 hours following death and develops to a uniform area of staining in 3-6 hours. Full development and fixation of hypostasis occur within 6–12 hours. This finding usually develops within 4 hours and persists until putrefaction. Fixation of hypostasis occurs earlier in the summer. It is delayed in asphyxial deaths and in intracranial lesions. Pearl PF1096: Color of Postmortem Hypostasis in Various Conditions

text: 2. In a bomb blast explosion, a person suffered a crush injury as a building fell on top of him. Which type of bomb blast injury is most commonly observed?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Quaternary

A building crushing a person classifies as a quarternary blast injury.   Blast injuries are classified as: * Primary injuries – effect of transmitted blast waves on gas-containing structures. External injuries are absent and are characterised by internal injuries. The middle ear, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract are the most susceptible to this. * Secondary injuries – injuries caused by shrapnel and other airborne debris propelled by the explosion. These injuries may affect any part of the body and sometimes result in penetrating trauma. Most casualties are caused by secondary injuries. * Tertiary injuries – caused by blast wind that can throw victims against solid objects. * Quaternary injuries – all other injuries caused by explosions are not included in the above three categories. e.g., flash burns, crush injuries, respiratory effects due to toxic dust, gas, etc. Pearl PF2146: Types of Blast Injuries

text: 4. A dead person was discovered in a swimming pool. On autopsy, his stomach and lungs were full of water, and there was mucoid froth in his nose and mouth. What is the most likely cause of death?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Wet drowning

The above case scenario with frothing is suggestive of wet drowning.  Given below are the features of antemortem drowning: * Froth – The presence of copious amounts of fine, shaving-lather-like froth at the mouth and the nostrils is the most characteristic finding of antemortem drowning. It is caused by the vigorous agitation of the tracheal and bronchial mucous secretions, edema fluid, and alveolar surfactant during respiratory efforts.  * Cutis anserina – The contraction of the erector pilorum muscles causes puckering and a grainy appearance of the skin. This resembles goose skin; hence, it is called cutis anserina. * Emphysema aquosum – overinflation of the lungs Paltauf’s spots – subpleural hemorrhages that reflect hemolysis within intra-alveolar hemorrhages * Washerwoman’s hand – Maceration of the skin on the palms and soles gives a wrinkled, sodden, and bleached appearance due to submersion. * Cadaveric spasm – Gravel, weed, soil, grass, etc. are firmly held in the clenched hands due to cadaveric spasm. This is a vital sign of antemortem drowning. The material also indicates the place of submersion. * Rigour mortis – This appears early in cases of a violent antemortem struggle. * Face – It is bloated and discoloured, with cyanosis. * Eyes – Conjunctiva are suffused and pupils dilated. * Tongue – It may be swollen and protruded. * Antemortem injuries – These may be sustained by striking objects, such as rocks, during the fall into the water body. Examination for such injuries must be performed only after the body is dry. Internal findings: * Lungs – They appear voluminous and distended, showing ballooning. The cut section will exude copious amounts of frothy, bloodstained fluid. * Larynx, trachea, and bronchioles – The presence of sand, silt, and aquatic vegetation in the trachea and lower respiratory tract are characteristic findings of antemortem drowning. * Heart and blood vessels – A Gettler test can be done to estimate the chloride content in the right and left sides of the heart to differentiate between freshwater and saltwater drowning.  * Diatom test – Diatoms are microscopic algae. Their presence in the organs, particularly in the bone marrow, is suggestive of antemortem drowning. * Stomach and small intestines – These organs may contain water in some cases. Water present in the small intestine is positive evidence of death by drowning. * Middle ear – The presence of water in the middle ear is highly suggestive of antemortem drowning. * Brain – It is congested and oedematous, with loss of the grey-white junction. Other options: Option A: Water would not be found in the lungs or stomach in the case of dry drowning. Option C: A near drowning occurs when a person survives a drowning incident, even if complications cause their death later. This term does not apply in this scenario because the person has already died. Option D: In this instance, cardiac arrest is a consequence rather than the main cause. Due to oxygen deprivation, the drowning incident caused the cardiac arrest. The initial cause of drowning is directly indicated by the presence of water in the stomach and lungs. Pearl PF0229: Differentiating features between Antemortem amd Postmortem drowning
       Antemortem drowning       Postmortem drowning
Foam/froth at nostrils or mouth Not present
Cadaveric spasm Not present
Lungs usually are voluminous, bulky, water-logged and over-inflated ,called as emphysema aquosum. Passive collection of water  in the lungs without any formation of columns of froth,has been called as oedema aquosum.
Presence of foam, fluid, debris, weeds, vegetation, etc. in the bronchi and bronchioles. Foreign matter may passively find access only to the upper respiratory passage.
Demonstration of diatoms in the lungs, liver, brain, bone marrow, etc. Diatoms may reach the lungs but not to the distant organs because of absence of circulation.
Stomach may contain water and foreign material like sand, weed, dirt etc which may be swallowed while struggling for life. Water could enter the stomach. However, quantity of foreign matter may become the decisive issue.

text: 5. A woman underwent surgery, but the surgeon discovered a cyst and removed her ovaries. She is of reproductive age with an incomplete family. What consent was violated?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Informed consent

This kind of consent is informed consent since the patient has been made aware of the benefits and complications and has agreed to the procedure. Informed consent is one given by the patient after understanding the nature of the condition, proposed treatment, outcomes of the recommended treatment, alternative options to treatment, and the risks and benefits involved. The patient can accept or reject the procedure. This is also called the rule of full disclosure.  "Consent" refers to a voluntary agreement, compliance, or permission. It can be expressed or implied. Expressed consent can be oral or written and refers to consent in which the terms are clearly stated in distinct and explicit language. "Opt out" refers to a patient's refusal of the procedure, test, or treatment. It is the physician's duty to disclose the risks or consequences of refusal adequately and appropriately to the patient.  Option B: Implied consent is that which is not written or expressly stated. It is implied that the patient is giving consent to examination in a general sense. For example, when a patient visits the hospital with an illness, it implies that he has given consent to a physical examination to find out the nature of his illness. Another example of implied consent is when a patient exposes his arm for injection. It is legally effective. Option C: The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur (the thing or the act speaks for itself) is a situation whereby an obvious gross act of negligence leads to damage to the patient. For example, prescribing high doses of NSAIDs to a patient with a history of perforated peptic ulcer. The negligent act is so obvious that the patient need not prove the negligence. Option D: According to BNS Section 30 (IPC 92), a doctor is permitted to perform life-saving procedures on a patient with life-threatening injuries. For example, in a case where conservative measures have failed to control intractable postpartum haemorrhage, an emergency hysterectomy can be performed without obtaining consent in order to save the patient's life. The guiding principle is whether the delay in treatment in order to obtain consent would result in harm to the patient. This is the doctrine of anticipation. Under some circumstances, like emergencies, informed consent may be neither possible nor necessary.

text: 6. On the same day, a doctor received two summonses: one to appear in court as an expert witness in a rape and murder case, and another for medical negligence after amputating the wrong leg of a patient. What should the physician do in this situation?

options.A: Attend the summons for the murder case
options.B: Attend the summons for the medical negligence case
options.C: Attend the court for the summons received first and inform the other court accordingly
options.D: Inform both the courts and wait

expl:
Correct answer: A. Attend the summons for the murder case

If a witness is summoned by both a criminal and a civil court on the same day, priority should be given to attending the summons for the criminal case first, which is the murder and rape case in this scenario. He should also notify the civil court of his inability to attend, providing valid reasons. A summons is a document compelling the attendance of a witness in a court of law under penalty, on a particular day and time, to give evidence. In this situation, the physician has a legal and ethical obligation to appear in court as an expert witness for the rape and murder case. This is a criminal case, and a summons to testify in a criminal proceeding is given priority. The medical negligence case is a civil case, and it is of a lower priority. The principle here is that the state's interest in a criminal prosecution, particularly a serious one involving a felony like murder, outweighs the private interests in a civil lawsuit. text: 7. A patient is brought in a comatose state with low blood pressure, respiratory depression, and pinpoint pupils. What is the appropriate antidote in this situation?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Naloxone

The given clinical vignette suggests opioid poisoning, which is treated with naloxone. Naloxone is a competitive pure opioid antagonist that reverses all effects of an opioid overdose except sedation. It is a pan-antagonist with an affinity for all known opioid receptors. It stimulates the release of prolactin in women. Opioid-induced respiratory depression is mediated by the action of µ receptors (µ2) in the brainstem respiratory centres. Naloxone is an opioid antagonist that can reverse the respiratory depression induced by opioids. Opioid Overdose: Symptoms: * Triad of coma, respiratory depression, and pinpoint pupils (miosis) * Hypotension * Bradycardia * Shallow breathing * Hypothermia Characteristics of opioid toxicity: * Opioid intoxication toxidrome—respiratory and mental status depression, analgesia, miosis, orthostatic hypotension, nausea and vomiting, histamine release resulting in localized urticaria and bronchospasm, ileus secondary to decreased GI motility, and urinary retention secondary to increased vesical sphincter tone. * Miosis is not universally present from intoxication with every opioid; normal or even enlarged pupils have been documented secondary to diphenoxylate, meperidine, morphine, pentazocine, and propoxyphene toxicity. * Opioid-induced acute lung injury, previously known as non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, is an uncommon complication associated with heroin overdose. Airway protection and ventilatory maintenance are the most important treatment steps for opioid intoxications because respiratory depression is the major morbidity and the cause of essentially all the mortality. * After adequate ventilation is ensured, administer naloxone. * A single dose of activated charcoal can be administered in case opioid ingestion occurred within one hour.  Opioid withdrawal symptoms (mnemonic—O MY WITHDRAWALS): * Mydriasis * Yawning * Weakness * Insomnia, irritability * Tremors, tachycardia * Hyperthermia, hypertension * Diarrhoea * Rhinorrhea * Apneic attacks * Weight loss * Anxiety * Lacrimation * Sweating Other options: Option B: Naltrexone is a long-acting, pure opioid antagonist used for maintenance therapy in opioid and alcohol dependence, but it is not suitable for acute overdose because it is oral and slow-acting. Option C: Flumazenil acts as an antagonist to benzodiazepines and is employed to counteract their sedative effects or to manage benzodiazepine overdose in emergency situations. Option D: Atropine is used in the treatment of cholinergic toxicity due to organophosphates (DDT, parathion, malathion). Symptoms of cholinergic toxicity include bradycardia, respiratory depression, and autonomic symptoms of salivation, lacrimation, urination, and defecation. Pearl PF0755: Pure opioid antagonists Naloxone: A short-acting opioid antagonist with a duration of action of 1-2 hours. Used in opioid overdose and respiratory depression in newborn due to perinatal opioid use. Naltrexone: A Long-acting opioid antagonist with a with effects lasting till 48 hours. Used for prevention of relapse in opioid addiction treatment. It is associated with hepatotoxicity. It does not suppress craving in opioid addiction but suppresses craving in chronic alcoholics. Nalmefene: A Long-acting opioid antagonist with a half-life of 8-10 hours administered intravenously. Used in opioid overdose like naloxone.

text: 8. The railway police has brought a person with suspected poisoning. On examination, he was confused with slurred speech, hot skin, dry mouth, and dilated pupils. What is the probable poisoning?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Datura

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Datura poisoning. Datura has two main types: Datura alba with white flowers and Datura nigra with purple flowers. The fruit is spiny and contains many small, yellowish-brown seeds. All parts of the plant are toxic, especially the seeds and fruits. Datura contains alkaloids like atropine, hyoscyamine, and scopolamine, which are potent anticholinergic agents. They block muscarinic receptors both peripherally and centrally, resulting in the classical anticholinergic toxidrome. This typical presentation is seen in children who accidentally ingest datura seeds, especially from roadside or railway plants, where datura often grows wild—hence known as "railway poison". Signs of poisoning include 8 D's:  * Dryness of mouth * Dysphagia * Dilated pupils * Drunken gait * Delirium * Dry-hot skin * Drowsiness   * Death due to respiratory failure. Gastric emptying is often delayed, and the small, plentiful seeds can become trapped among the gastrointestinal folds after ingestion. Thus gastric decontamination can be an important therapy. Physostigmine, a reversible acetylcholine esterase antagonist, is an effective treatment for severe anticholinergic poisoning. text: 9. Following exposure to a blast, a patient presents with lung injury and tympanic membrane rupture. Which level of blast wave effect is responsible for these injuries?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Primary

The primary level of blast wave effect is responsible for these injuries. A blast causes the most damage at an interface between tissues in contact with the atmosphere, which is why the lung usually suffers the most severe damage. Lungs are considered to be severely damaged organs in the air due to variations in density between the alveolar walls and the contained air. Blast injury is a complex type of physical trauma resulting from direct or indirect exposure to an explosion. Primary blast injuries result from the rapid overpressure or shock waves produced by an explosion. These injuries result from the dramatic changes in barometric pressure projecting outwards from the point of detonation. They predominantly cause damage to air-filled hollow organs of the body from rapid pressure change (barotrauma). This includes the middle ear, lungs, and GIT. Blast injuries are classified as: * Primary injuries – effect of transmitted blast waves on gas-containing structures. External injuries are absent and are characterised by internal injuries. The middle ear, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract are the most susceptible to this. * Secondary injuries – injuries caused by shrapnel and other airborne debris propelled by the explosion. These injuries may affect any part of the body and sometimes result in penetrating trauma. Most casualties are caused by secondary injuries. * Tertiary injuries – caused by blast wind that can throw victims against solid objects. * Quaternary injuries – all other injuries caused by explosions are not included in the above three categories. e.g., flash burns, crush injuries, respiratory effects due to toxic dust, gas, etc.  The most sensitive and most frequently injured hollow organs are the tympanic membranes and lungs. Blast damage to the lungs is the most common cause of life-threatening injury following an explosion. Solid organs are the most resistant to blast injuries, as the parenchymal disruption requires very high levels of overpressure. The liver is the least vulnerable to blast wave (primary blast) injury. text: 10. A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic man presents with altered consciousness, disorientation and severe agitation. He reports his last alcohol intake was 48 hours ago. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Delirium tremens

The clinical scenario of a 45-year-old chronic alcoholic man with altered consciousness, disorientation and severe agitation and his last alcohol consumption 48 hours ago points to delirium tremens. Delirium tremens is a medical emergency that occurs during alcohol withdrawal. It is an acute condition and usually develops within 72 hours after the last drink. It has symptoms of both delirium and alcohol withdrawal. The clinical features of delirium tremens are: * Altered sensorium with disorientation * Perceptual distortions, most frequently tactile or visual hallucinations * Autonomic hyperactivity with tachycardia, fever, anxiety, insomnia, and hypertension. And sweating * Fluctuating levels of psychomotor activity, ranging from agitation to lethargy Altered sleep-wake cycle  Wernicke’s encephalopathy (alcoholic encephalopathy) is associated with thiamine deficiency. Alcohol abuse may lead to thiamine deficiency because of poor nutritional habits or malabsorption. It is an acute neurological disorder characterised by: * Global confusion * Ocular abnormalities like horizontal nystagmus, gaze palsy, anisocoria, and sluggish pupillary reflex * Ataxia—mainly affecting the gait * Vestibular dysfunction It may resolve with thiamine therapy or progress to Korsakoff's syndrome. Other options: Option B: Alcohol-induced psychosis is a severe mental condition triggered by excessive alcohol use, leading to hallucinations, delusions, and confusion. It typically occurs during withdrawal or chronic alcohol abuse and requires immediate medical intervention. Option C: Opioid withdrawal can cause symptoms like drug craving, feelings of temperature change, musculoskeletal pain, and GI distress. Signs of opioid withdrawal include confusion, drowsiness, vomiting, and diarrhoea. It is not typically life-threatening, especially compared to alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, which can lead to seizures or delirium tremens. Hence, opioid withdrawal is rarely fatal.  Option D: Alcohol-induced hallucinations occur due to excessive alcohol use or withdrawal, causing false visual, auditory, or tactile perceptions. They are distinct from delirium tremens and can persist even with clear consciousness. Pearl PF1275: Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome

text: 10. In which type of hanging does weight of the head, arms and chest act as a constricting force?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Partial

The weight of the head, arms, and chest acts as a constricting force in partial hanging. Types of hanging: * Complete hanging: Here the weight of the entire body acts as a constricting force. * Partial hanging: The bodies are partially suspended, the weight of the head (5-6 kgs), arms, and chest act as a constricting force. * Typical hanging: In this, the ligature runs from the midline above the thyroid cartilage symmetrically upward on both sides of the neck to the occipital region. A knot of the ligature is on the backside of the neck. * Atypical hanging: The knot of the ligature is anywhere other than on the backside of the neck. Usually, the knot is near the mastoid process or angle of mandible. Occasionally, it may be under the chin. In India, the knot is tied under the angle of the right jaw. On drawing the bolt, the person drops to the length of the rope. The sudden stoppage of the moving body associated with the position of the knot causes the head to be jerked violently. Judicial hanging: * The face of the person is covered with a dark mask, stand on a platform above trapdoors,which open downwards when the blot is drawn. * Rope is looped around the neck and the person is allowed to drop for 5-7 meters according to weight, age and build. * Sudden stop causes fracture dislocation at the level C-2, C-3 or C-3/C-4 vertebra and rupture between pons and medulla (hangman fracture). * Death is instantaneous, but the heartbeat may continue for 15-20 minutes and spasmodic muscle jerking may occur for a considerable time. * Asphyxial signs are not seen in correctly performed judicial hangings. text: 2. A farmer is brought to the hospital 8 hours later, following a snake bite. He complained of headache, blurred vision, tingling sensation around the mouth, dizziness, vertigo, and multiple episodes of vomiting since the bite. He has signs of respiratory depression and a pulse 50. The local wound showed mild swelling and blistering. There are no apparent bleeding manifestations. He was administered 10 vials of antivenom. Which of the following is the next step of management?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Neostigmine with atropine

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of a neurotoxic snake bite. Since this patient has already passed 8 hours without any bleeding manifestations, the bite of a hemotoxic snake is unlikely and the better management would be to address his neurotoxic symptoms with the administration of neostigmine with atropine. The neurotoxic symptoms are reversible with the use of antivenoms or anticholinesterase drugs, such as neostigmine. Atropine is administered to counter the muscarinic side effects of neostigmine.  Neurotoxic symptoms include:  * Headache * Blurred vision * Perioral paraesthesia (tingling sensation around the mouth) * Vomiting * Dizziness * Vertigo * Hyperacusis * Gooseflesh * Hypersalivation Respiratory failure is precipitated either by airway obstruction or paralysis of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, at this stage or later. If it progresses to paralysis, it initially presents with ptosis and external ophthalmoplegia, which may appear between a few minutes after the bite or after some hours. ASV(Anti Snake Venom) is the mainstay of snakebite treatment. Neurotoxicity effects may wear off spontaneously in about a week and are completely reversible in response to antivenom or anticholinesterase. Atropine can be used in the management of venom that acts postsynaptically. Ventilatory support is provided in cases complicated with severe respiratory depression, in the event of failure of other measures of management.  ASV used in India is effective against: * Cobra * Common krait * Russel viper * Saw scaled viper Measures that can be done in the case of snakebite: * Apply firm pressure over the bitten area, which delays the absorption of venom * Pressure immobilization is recommended for elapid and sea-snake bites, but not for viper bites as it may cause local necrosis * Clean the wound with soap and water, or iodine and cover it with a sterile dressing  * Immediately apply a broad firm bandage (Sutherland wrap) on the bitten area and around the limb. As much of the limb should be bandaged as possible. It should be tight enough to occlude the superficial venous and lymphatic return, but not the arterial or deep venous flow.  * In bites on the trunk, head, or neck, apply firm pressure over the bitten area * Immobilize the limb, as movement can accelerate the spread of venom * Make the patient lie on one side in the recovery position so that the airway is clear, in case of vomiting or fainting Measures contraindicated in the case of snakebite: * Suction and incision of the wound * Electric shock treatment of wound site * Application of tourniquets because they obstruct arterial flow and cause ischemia * Ice water immersion of the bitten limb

These include: * Survivor of sexual assault, rape or incest. * Minors * Mentally ill women including mental retardation * Change of marital status during the ongoing pregnancy (widowhood and divorce) * Women with physical disabilities (Major disability criteria - Rights of persons with disabilities act - 2016) * Women with pregnancy in humanitarian settings or disaster or emergency situations as declared by the government. * Fetal malformations that have a substantial risk of being incompatible with life or if the child is born, may suffer from serious physical or mental * abnormalities to be seriously handicapped. It can only be revealed to a person in force authorised by law. The ground for failure of contraception is extended to women and their partners. Pearl PF1638: Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act - MTP Act 1971 MTP Act with 2021 amendments  Indications: * Therapeutic - to save the life of the mother * Eugenic - to prevent the risk of the child being born with serious mental or physical abnormality i.e. first-trimester viral infections, teratogenic drug intake, radiation exposure * Humanitarian - pregnancy resulted from rape or incest * Social - pregnancy resulted from failure of contraceptives  Rules: * Only a registered medical practitioner who is qualified (one who has assisted in the performance of 25 cases of MTP in a recognized hospital) can terminate a pregnancy. * MTP should be carried out in a government or government-recognized hospital. Private hospitals may take up MTP if they obtain a license from the chief medical officer of the district. * The termination of pregnancy by a person, who is not a registered medical practitioner (the person concerned), or in an unrecognised hospital (administrative head) shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than 2 years, but which may extend to 7 years.  Consent: The consent of the woman is required for conducting an abortion. The written consent of the guardian is required if the woman is minor or mentally ill. Consent of the husband or partner is not necessary.  If the woman is not willing, abortion cannot be performed at the request of the husband alone. The woman need not produce proof of her age. It is enough for the woman to say that she was raped, and it is not necessary that a complaint was lodged with the police. text: 5. You are working as an internal medicine consultant at a private clinic. A patient with chronic renal disease requiring hemodialysis is admitted under you. You advise diet and fluid control and keep him under observation. However, the patient progresses to take ayurvedic supplements and sometimes skips your instructions without disclosing it. His conditions worsen and he develops difficulty in breathing. His attendant files a complaint in court alleging the negligence of the doctor. Which of the following acts as a defence for the doctor in court?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Contributory negligence

In the given case, since the patient did not adhere to the proper instructions of the doctor, it was partly or wholly his fault. This is termed contributory negligence. Proper documentation as to how ordinary care was not exercised on part of the patient can be useful in a court of law. Contributory negligence occurs when a patient or his personal attendant shows unreasonable conduct or absence of ordinary care, which when combined with the negligence of the doctor, has contributed to the injury. In this case, the patient’s or attendant’s negligence should be the direct, proximate cause and without which the injury would not have occurred Other options: Option A: Vicarious liability is not a defence against professional negligence. Vicarious liability (liability for the actions of another): An employer is responsible not only for his own negligence but also for the negligence of his employees. Option B: Res ipsa loquitur means 'the thing speaks for itself'. It is used as supportive evidence of negligence on part of the doctor eg: leaving behind a scalpel or scissor whilst operating leading to sepsis/peritonitis speaks for itself. Option C: Therapeutic misadventure may serve as a defence against negligence. It basically refers to an adverse outcome that could not have been anticipated despite reasonable care. eg: a rare side effect of a drug or blood loss due to an anomalous artery despite exercising caution. Pearl PF1453: Contributory negligence Contributory negligence occurs when a patient or his personal attendant shows unreasonable conduct or absence of ordinary care, which when combined with the negligence of the doctor, has contributed to the injury. In this case, the patient’s or attendant’s negligence should be the direct, proximate cause and without which the injury would not have occurred. So, contributory negligence occurs when both the doctor and patient are negligent. The direct or proximate cause of the injury should be the patient’s negligence, which means that if the patient was not negligent, the injury could have been prevented. Contributory negligence usually occurs when the doctor is negligent and the patient: * Fails to give an accurate medical history, and as a result, the doctor may misdiagnose or mistreat the patient. * Fails to follow the doctor’s instructions * Refuses to take the treatment * Leaves the hospital against doctor’s advice * Does not inform the doctor or seek further medical assistance if the symptoms persist or worsens. Contributory negligence is a defence for doctor’s negligence in civil cases. However, from case to case, the liability of a doctor may vary from complete non-liability to substantial liability for the damages. Under the doctrine of comparative negligence, the court has the right to hold both parties liable for their negligent actions. Limitations / Exceptions to contributory negligence: A. The doctor will be held guilty in the following conditions: 1. The doctor failed to provide proper instructions to the patient * Ex: Doctor applies a tight plaster cast (doctor is negligent) to the patient’s leg and did not tell the patient to inform if he develops any numbness (no proper instruction). The patient develops numbness and has not informed the doctor (patient is negligent). After few days patient developed a permanent injury.  2. Last clear chance doctrine: It is applicable when the doctor fails to take necessary action to prevent damage due to a negligent act of the patient, even after getting a clear chance to take such action. * Ex: Doctor applies a tight plaster cast (doctor is negligent) to the patient’s leg and told the patient to inform if he develops any numbness (gave proper instruction). The patient developed numbness and has not informed the doctor (patient is negligent). Next day patient informed the doctor, but the doctor did not remove the cast and said he was busy (There was a clear last chance, but the doctor neglected again). After few days patient developed a permanent injury. B. The doctor/person will not be held guilty in the following conditions: 1. Avoidable consequences rule: It occurs when an injury is caused due to doctor’s negligence, and the patient has done a negligent act, which further aggravated the injury caused by the doctor, and the patient could have avoided the consequence by not doing such act. In such cases, the doctor need not pay anything, and the patient will be held guilty. * Ex: A patient had a lacerated wound. The doctor examined the patient and had not done any dressing or provided any antibiotics (the doctor is negligent). However, the doctor instructed the patient to avoid contamination and asked him to visit the clinic next week. When the patient went home, he applied cow dung on his wound every day thinking that the wound would heal faster and didn't visit the doctor after one week. The wound got infected and developed pus and aggravated the injury. * Here, despite the doctor being negligent in the first instance, the patient is responsible for his injury as he performed an unnecessary, avoidable act, which aggravated the injury. The doctor need not pay anything. 2. Good Samaritan doctrine: A person who assists another person who is in serious danger cannot be charged with contributory negligence. unless such assistance is reckless or rash. * Ex: A person was travelling on a road and saw a car accident, where the victim was unconscious and was stuck inside the car. He called the ambulance. The paramedical staff instructed him not to mobilize the victim until they arrived. Meanwhile, the car was caught in fire (serious danger), and the person tried to remove the victim carefully out of the car (assisted the victim and was not reckless). However, the victim already had a cervical bone fracture due to the accident, which got mobilized while he was being removed out of the car and as a result, suffered an injury to the spine that led to paralysis (victim’s injury was aggravated). In such a case, the good samaritan doctrine would apply and the person who tried to help, will not be charged under contributory negligence.

text: 7. Which of the following statements does not apply during cross-examination in a court of law?

options.A: Witness is examined by the defense lawyer
options.C: Objective of cross-examination is to weaken case of opponent
options.D: There is no time limit to cross examination

expl:
Correct answer: B. Leading questions are not allowed

Leading questions are allowed in a cross-examination according to Section 146 (4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA). However, they are not allowed during the direct examination conducted by the summoning counsel. If the judge is satisfied that the witness is hostile, leading questions may be allowed during direct examination. Leading questions (Section 146(1) of BSA) are defined as questions that suggest an answer that is favorable for the case of the summoning counsel or in alignment with their claim. Other options: Options 1, 3, 4 - In cross-examination, the witness is examined by the defense lawyer or adverse party with an objective to elicit favorable facts to their case, to test the accuracy of the witness statements, to unearth new or old facts, and also to discredit the witness. While leading questions are allowed in cross-examination, the Judge can disallow indecent questions (Section 154 of BSA) or questions asked with an intention to insult or offend the witness in any form (Section 155 of BSA). There is no time limit to the duration of cross-examination. The sequence of examination in the recording of evidence is as follows -
Sequence of examination Objective
• Examination-in-Chief/Direct examination by the party that summoned the witness To elicit the facts of the case from the witness. Leading questions are not allowed.
• Cross-examination by the defense lawyer To elicit facts favorable to their case and test the reliability of the witness. Leading questions are allowed.
• Re-examination by the party that summoned the witness To resolve doubts that formed during cross-examination and re-emphasize the party's perspective

text: 1. A young male patient presents with a history of high-grade fever for the last 5 days. When his hands were examined, the following lesions were seen which were painless and a new regurgitant murmur is heard. Echocardiogram shows the presence of a mass on the mitral valve. Correct answer: B. Splenomegaly

In the above clinical scenario of a patient presenting with high-grade fever, new-onset murmur, and faint, red, painless macules on palms and soles (called as Janeway lesions), the most probable diagnosis for this patient would be infective endocarditis (IE). The most common abdominal finding is splenomegaly.. Infective endocarditis is characterized by the presence of large, friable, irregular vegetations on heart valves. Patients with infective endocarditis can have cardiac or non-cardiac manifestations. Cardiac manifestations of IE: * Presence of new regurgitant murmurs * Congestive heart failure due to valve dysfunction * Perivalvular abscesses and intracardiac fistulae- This is caused due to the extension of infection beyond the valves and into the adjacent myocardial tissue * Conduction system defects- due to the damage of the interventricular septum by the abscess. * Embolization of coronary arteries Noncardiac manifestations of IE are: * Arterial emboli- causing pain of ischemia of the organs * Roth's spots- retinal hemorrhages with a pale center * Janeway lesions- In contrast to Osler's nodes, these are faint, red, painless macules on palms and soles. They occur as a result of septic embolization and are commonly associated with staphylococcal IE. * Glomerulonephritis * Positivity for rheumatoid factor * Petechiae on the oral and conjunctival mucosa * Splinter subungual hemorrhages-painless, dark red lines in the nailbed. * Mycotic aneurysms * Splenomegaly * Osler’s nodes (shown in the image below) are tender, red nodules that typically appear on the pads of the fingers and toes. Occurs due to immune complex deposition and vasculitis. Image given below shows Roth spots. Pearl PF0379: Modified Duke's criteria for diagnosis of infective endocarditis Diagnosis of Infective endocarditis is by Duke's Criteria, which requires either: * Clinical criteria * Pathologic criteria If clinical criteria are used, definitive endocarditis is defined by the presence of 2 major or 1 major + 3 minor or 5 minor criteria. Presence of single pathological criteria is definitive of infective endocarditis.

Clinical Criteria

Major Criteria

1. Positive blood culture

Typical microorganism for IE from 2 separate blood cultures.

(or)

Persistently positive blood culture of an organism consistent with IE from:

  • Blood cultures drawn >12 h apart.
  • All of 3 or a majority of ≥4 separate blood cultures, with first and last drawn at least 1 h apart.

(or)

Single positive blood culture for Coxiella burnetti or phase I IgG antibody titer of >1:800.

 

2. Evidence of endocardial involvement

Echocardiographic identification of oscillating intracardiac mass on valve or implant or in the path of regurgitant jets

(or)

New Valvular regurgitation

Minor Criteria

1. Predisposing heart lesion or intravenous drug use

2. Fever ≥38.0°C (≥100.4°F)

3. Vascular lesions: Major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage, conjunctival hemorrhages, Janeway lesions.

4. Immunological evidence: Glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, rheumatoid factor.

5. Microbiologic evidence: Positive blood culture but not meeting the major criterion, or serologic evidence of active infection with an organism consistent with infective endocarditis.
 
Pathological Criteria

1. Microorganisms demonstrated by culture or histologic examination, in vegetation, embolus from vegetation, or intracardiac abscess

(or)

2. Histologic confirmation of active endocarditis in vegetation or intracardiac abscess
Note: The diagnosis of endocarditis is rejected if an alternative diagnosis is established, if symptoms resolve and do not recur with ≤4 days of antibiotic therapy, or if surgery or autopsy after ≤4 days of antimicrobial therapy yields no histologic evidence of endocarditis. text: 6. A 52-year-old woman presented with deformity of the hand as shown below. There is decreased motion in the small joints and loss of wrinkle lines on the facial skin. Her chest radiograph showed prominent bilateral lower lobe infiltrates. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by progressive fibrosis caused by excessive deposition of extracellular matrix in various tissues and organs. The key features of SSc include vascular injury, inflammation, and the presence of disease-specific autoantibodies. SSc is classified into two types based on the extent of skin involvement. * Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis / CREST syndrome * Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis In limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc) or CREST syndrome, fibrosis affects the acral areas of the body - mainly the face and the skin distal to the elbows and knees. The progression of skin fibrosis is slow, but microvascular changes, such as Raynaud’s phenomenon, often appear years before skin involvement. LcSSc generally has a favorable prognosis, with a 10-year survival rate exceeding 90%. CREST syndrome consists of the following: * Calcinosis cutis * Raynaud’s phenomenon * Esophageal dysmotility * Sclerodactyly * Telangiectasia The images shows features of Raynaud's phenomenon and calcinosis cutis: The antibodies tested in systemic sclerosis include: * Antinuclear antibody (ANA) - positive in most cases of systemic sclerosis. The absence of this antibody suggests considering an alternate diagnosis. * Antitopoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) antibody - usually positive with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis. * Anti-RNA polymerase I and III antibodies - usually positive with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis. * Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) - usually positive in limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. The common pulmonary manifestations of scleroderma include interstitial lung disease(ILD), and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) leading to cor pulmonale. Management is based on disease-modifying and organ-specific drugs. For  * Raynaud’s phenomenon and digital ulcers: Warm socks and gloves are recommended. Calcium channel blockers, sildenafil, fluoxetine and losartan can be added if symptoms persist. Prostacyclin and bosentan can be used for healing of digital ulcers.  * GI complications: Esophageal dysmotility can be treated with domperidone or metoclopramide. text: 9. A 65-year-old male patient presented with chest pain, exertional dyspnea and syncope. He was diagnosed as a case of Aortic stenosis and his Chest Xray was taken which is shown below.What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Post stenotic dilatation of aorta

The most likely diagnosis is post stenotic dilatation of aorta.  Post-stenotic dilatation is seen in patients with AS and/or aortic regurgitation, patients with a haemodynamically normal bicuspid aortic valve and following aortic valve replacement.  The aetiology is unknown  and it may involve an abnormality in the process of extracellular matrix remodelling in the aortic wall including inadequate synthesis, degradation and transport of extracellular matrix proteins.It can be attributed to haemodynamic factors caused by a stenotic valve( aortic stenosis commonly),involving high velocity and turbulent flow downstream of the stenosis, or due to intrinsic pathology of the aortic wall. Aortic stenosis is narrowing of the aortic valve. It may be caused due to the calcification of normal aortic valve, calcification of congenital bicuspid valve and rheumatic heart disease. Three cardinal clinical features of aortic stenosis are: * Exertional dyspnea: This occurs due to the left ventricular(LV) diastolic dysfunction. Frostbite typically involves the extremities or the exposed regions of the face. Rewarming by exercise, rubbing, or friction is not advised.  * Analgesics such as ibuprofen are often required during rewarming. * Antithrombotics, thrombolytics, and vasodilators such as prostacyclin can be given to improve circulation after rewarming. * Frost bites are associated with an increased risk of infections and tetanus. Therefore, the injured area should be cleaned with soap or antiseptic, and sterile dressings should be applied. Tetanus prophylaxis must be given, but, empirical antibiotics are not recommended. * The patient must be monitored for the development of compartment syndrome. * Elective late amputation after imaging may be required in severe cases.

AKI (acute kidney injury) is defined as a decline in kidney function within 7 days, resulting in the accumulation of nitrogenous waste and other toxic metabolites usually excreted in the urine. It includes a variety of conditions that share some common features such as elevated creatinine levels and reduced urine output. It is broadly divided into three categories: Intrinsic causes can further be divided into acute tubular necrosis, acute glomerulonephritis, and acute interstitial nephritis. Ischemia and nephrotoxins are the main causes of acute tubular necrosis. Nephrotoxins can be exogenous, such as vancomycin, cisplatin, and iodinated contrast agents used for CT imaging. Endogenous toxins include myoglobin, uric acid, and haemoglobin. Crush injuries, heat stroke, and myopathies can result in rhabdomyolysis, releasing large amounts of myoglobin. Common causes include hypovolemia, liver failure, and congestive heart failure. The urine/plasma creatinine ratio is ≥ 40, and urinary sodium is usually < 20mEq/L/L. text: 32. A patient presented with symptoms of fatigue and a blood smear showed macrocytic anemia. Her methyl malonate levels were normal , however, homocystinuria was seen. Serum B12 values are normal. What is the appropriate management?

Correct answer: D. Folate therapy

Administering folate for patients with peripheral neuropathy and macrocytic anemia can improve the blood picture but aggravate the neurological symptoms due to unmasking of vitamin B12 deficiency. text: 1. A 45-year-old female patient presents to you with complaints of dryness in the mouth and eyes. Serum testing reveals positive anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies. The test shown in the image below was positive with a score of 5 mm in 5 minutes without anesthesia. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Sjogren syndrome

The test shown above is Schirmer's test and the likely diagnosis is Sjögren's syndrome.  Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune disorder that involves lymphocytic infiltration of the exocrine glands. This manifests as xerostomia (dry mouth) and keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes). It is associated with autoantibodies anti-Ro/SS-A and anti-La/SS-B. Keratoconjunctivitis sicca can be diagnosed by Schirmer's test. This test measures the quantity of tears produced. Two marked strips of paper are placed between the globe and the lower eyelid and the patient is instructed to close their eyes for 5 minutes. The tears produced spread along the paper by capillary action. The distance is measured. A score of more than 10 mm is considered to be normal while that of less than 5 mm is considered deficient.  A number of other systems can be involved as well. For example, atrophic gastritis, esophageal mucosal atrophy, and vaginal dryness. Extraglandular or systemic manifestations can also be present. These manifest as fatigue, arthritis, Raynaud's phenomenon, and myalgia.  Diagnosis of primary Sjögren's syndrome requires the following:  * Eye and/or mouth dryness * Eye tests disclose keratoconjunctivitis sicca * Mouth evaluation reveals dry oral mucosa and/or * Presence of anti-Ro or anti-La autoantibodies A labial (lip) biopsy is a must to confirm the diagnosis and determine the prognosis.  Treatment of Sjögren's syndrome is directed at treating the symptoms and complications. Artificial tears can be used for dry eyes and propionic acid gel for vaginal dryness. Pilocarpine can help increase oral secretions and hydroxychloroquine can be used to treat arthritis. On examination, the skin over her hands is shiny, taut, and thickened with non-pitting edema.There is associated interstitial lung disease and presence of ANA antibodies, topoisomerase I antibodies and Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis here ?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis

The clinical scenario with ANA antibodies,topoisomerase I antibodies and Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies is diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Systemic sclerosis is an autoimmune disorder of connective tissue resulting in fibrosis of the skin, internal organs, and vasculature. It is characterized by Raynaud’s phenomenon, ischemia of the digits, sclerodactyly, and cardiac, lung, gut, and renal disease. The peak age of onset is between the fourth and fifth decades of life. It is divided into: * Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (30% of cases) - poor prognosis * Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (70% of cases) The antibodies tested in systemic sclerosis include: * Antinuclear antibody (ANA) - positive in most cases of systemic sclerosis. The absence of this antibody suggests considering an alternate diagnosis. * Antitopoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) antibody - usually positive with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis. * Anti-RNA polymerase I and III antibodies - usually positive with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis. * Anti centromere antibody (ACA) - usually positive in limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. text: 3. A 30-year-old female with a history of recurrent headaches presented for further evaluation. On further workup, hemoglobin and total WBC count were normal while an elevated platelet count was seen. Bone marrow aspiration showed increased megakaryocytes and a JAK2 mutation. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Essential thrombocytosis

The likely diagnosis in this patient is essential thrombocytosis also known as essential thrombocythemia. Essential thrombocytosis is a clonal stem cell disorder characterized by elevated platelet count with no evidence of prolonged platelet survival. It is estimated that a significant number of patients with essential thrombocytosis are diagnosed incidentally when the patient obtains a complete blood count for an unrelated reason. Symptoms such as headaches, dizziness, and, visual changes can be seen in the minority of symptomatic patients. Complications such as thrombosis, bleeding (likely due to qualitative and quantitative alterations in the platelets), and first-trimester pregnancy loss are seen in patients with significant thrombocytosis. Thrombocytosis also leads to certain microvascular manifestations such as : * Headaches * Lightheadedness or syncope * Atypical chest pain * Acral paresthesia * Livedo reticularis * Erythromelalgia (transient burning sensation of hands and feet) * Transient visual disturbances such as amaurosis fugax, scintillating scotomata, etc  Bone marrow biopsy reveals prominent large to giant megakaryocytes with abundant cytoplasm and lobulated nucleoli. A vast majority of patients demonstrate JAK2, CALR, or the MPL mutation. Other options: Option A: Patients with polycythemia vera present with elevated hemoglobin levels. Option C: Although primary myelofibrosis is associated with JAK 2 mutation, bone marrow aspiration yields a dry tap due to fibrosed bone marrow. Option D: Chronic myeloid leukemia is characterized by the presence of a Philadelphia chromosome resulting from reciprocal translocation t(9;22) forming the BCR-ABL fusion gene. They have hypercellular marrow due to a massively increased number of maturing granulocytic precursors
