text: 5. A veterinary surgeon presents with complaints of fever, muscle pain, joint pain, fatigue, and weight loss for the past few weeks. On further inquiry, he says that his fever persists for weeks before it resolves only to be followed by a relapse. You obtain his blood sample and inoculate it on the medium given below to isolate the suspected organism. Which of the following is the most likely organism?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Brucella

This clinical vignette is suggestive of Brucellosis caused by organisms belonging to the Brucella species. The culture medium depicted in the given image is the Castenada biphasic medium.  Brucella are small, non-motile, aerobic, capnophilic coccobacilli. The most important species that are pathologic to humans are B.melitensis, B. suis, and B.abortus. Brucellosis is a zoonosis. It is transmitted to humans from contact with or consumption of contaminated products from goats, sheep, cattle, buffaloes, pigs, and other animals. Once the infection is transmitted, these bacteria resist intracellular digestion and proliferate within the reticuloendothelial system for a long time. This is the reason why brucellosis often becomes chronic and is resistant to simple antimicrobial therapy. The host immune response is mainly cell-mediated involving activated macrophages, helper T-cells, and mediators such as TNF alpha, TNF gamma, IL-1, and IL-12.  Clinically, patients may present with an acute infection comprised of undulant fever, as in this patient, characterized by a rising and falling fever. They may also have arthralgia, muscular pain, sweating, loss of weight, and appetite. CNS symptoms such as fatigue, irritability, and depression might also occur. Chronic infection tends to be episodic with non-specific symptoms.  Laboratory diagnosis of brucellosis is important and includes several methods such as-  * Polymerase chain reaction is a sensitive and reliable method of detection.  * Culture of Brucella species can be done from specimen including blood, bone marrow aspirate, lymph node aspirate, CSF, and urine. Preferred method and medium of culture includes the Castaneda method. It is a biphasic medium. The solid component is the agar slant and the liquid is the broth. The medium is inoculated with the specimen and incubated for four days in an upright position. Serial subcultures can be obtained by slanting the broth over the agar periodically to inoculate new colonies.  * Serological methods include standard agglutination test (SAT), complement fixation test, Coomb’s antiglobulin test, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Cut-offs for significant titers are variable depending on the endemicity. Endemic areas or history of laboratory exposure require agglutinin titers of 1:320–1:640 or higher and in nonendemic areas, a titer of more than or equal to 1:160 is considered diagnostic. * Tests for animals and animal products include tests such as the milk ring tests and Rose Bengal card tests. * Milk ring test- A sample of milk is mixed well with hematoxylin stained brucella antigen and incubated. If the sample contains antibodies to brucella antigens, agglutination occurs with the agglutinate rising to the top as a blue ring. If the sample does not contain antibodies to brucella antigens, the whole of the sample is uniformly stained blue.  Treatment includes antimicrobial therapy with at least two agents for six weeks duration. The preferred combination is IM streptomycin 0.75-1g per day for two to three weeks along with doxycycline 100mg BD for six weeks.  Prevention of Brucellosis is important by screening and abiding by safety standards in farms and dairy industries, and also by pasteurization of milk and milk products.

text: 7. A 72-year-old retired pilot presents to a neurologist, accompanied by his wife, with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus ,ataxia, and visual disturbances. FLAIR MRI scans is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Variant CJD

The clinical scenario of rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, ataxia and visual disturbances along with the FLAIR MRI which shows hockey stick sign, is diagnostic of variant CJD. The hockey stick sign refers to the hyper-intense signal involving the pulvinar and dorsomedial thalamic nuclei bilaterally on FLAIR or DWI. This sign is commonly indicative of variant (infectious acquired) CJD. Whereas MRI in sporadic CJD reveals abnormalities in the cortical grey matter called cortical ribboning. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is a spongiform encephalopathy that is characterized by rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, akinetic mutism, cerebellar/visual disturbances. It is fatal and death usually within a year or less from the onset. The proteins that make up the prions (PrP) are present even normally in the cells. This normal form, PrPc, is in a predominantly α-helical configuration and is sensitive to proteases. However, the prions (infectious form) are in an abnormal β-pleated configuration and are called PrPSc. This pathological form is not degradable by proteases and converts the normal form- PrPc to the abnormal form- PrPSc. This abnormal protein gets deposited as plaques and degeneration of surrounding neuronal and glial tissue occurs characterized by intracellular vacuoles, leading to a characteristic spongiform encephalopathy. There is no associated inflammatory response to these agents.  Four types of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease have been described: * Sporadic (sCJD): Most common; * Variant (vCJD): Bovine spongiform encephalopathy (mad cow disease), Kuru; * Familial (fCJD): These individuals carry a PrPc mutation and include Gerstmann-Sträussler- Scheinker syndrome and fatal familial insomnia; * Iatrogenic (iCJD): Maybe seen occurring after corneal transplantation, liver transplantation, use of contaminated neurosurgical instruments, use of cadaver-derived hormones, or stereotactic depth electrodes.  Clinically, CJD presents with predominantly CNS manifestations with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus (startle myoclonus is common), ataxia, akinetic mutism, visual disturbances, and pyramidal/extrapyramidal dysfunction. Insomnia, apathy, and other behavioral abnormalities may be seen.  CSF is predominantly normal but may show a positive assay for 14-3-3 protein. MRI on FLAIR sequencing and diffusion-weighted imaging will show increased intensity in the basal ganglia region and a characteristic 'cortical ribboning', in sporadic CJD. Diagnosis of CJD can be established on brain biopsy either by measuring PrPSc or by demonstrating the characteristic neuropathological features of spongiform encephalopathy. EEG may show periodic triphasic or multiphasic sharp-wave complexes seen as spikes or spike-wave pattern. Management is mainly supportive as the disease is usually fatal within a year of onset of symptoms.

text: 10. Identify the tachycardia depicted in the given ECG.
expl:
Correct answer: B. Atrial flutter

The given ECG is suggestive of atrial flutter. The given ECG shows narrow QRS complexes, hence it is supraventricular tachycardia. The RR intervals are regular and the normal P waves are replaced by sawtooth-shaped waves (red arrows), known as flutter waves. Hence, it is most likely to be atrial flutter. In atrial flutter, the ventricular rate is determined by the AV conduction ratio. The commonest AV ratio is 2:1. As the atrial rate is around 300 bpm, AV conduction ratio of 2:1 results in a ventricular rate of ~150 bpm.

The given image shows digital clubbing. text: 15. Which disease is being represented in the image below?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Cushing's syndrome

The given picture describes Cushing's. Cushing's syndrome is characterized by clinical features that result from chronic exposure to excess glucocorticoids that can be due to * Prolonged exogenous administration of glucocorticoids (Iatrogenic: Most common cause of Cushing's syndrome)  * Excess endogenous cortisol secretion * Ectopic ACTH production Important clinical features: * Moon facies * Purple skin striae * Abnormal masculinization (acne, bruising, enlargement of the clitoris in girls) * Pubertal developmental delay and amenorrhea in girls * Proximal muscle weakness * Osteoporosis * Hypertension * Hyperpigmentation * Hypokalemic alkalosis * Hyperglycemia * Sepsis The high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is done only after a diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome is established in a patient. The high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is used in patients with confirmed Cushing syndrome. It helps to differentiate between Cushing's disease (i.e a pituitary cause) and ectopic ACTH production. The basis for this test is that in subjects with Cushing's disease, a higher dose of dexamethasone (usually 8 mg) is required to suppress ACTH secretion and drop cortisol levels in serum, urine, and saliva. Standard 2-day (high dose) dexamethasone suppression test: * Serum cortisol level and/or 24-hour urinary free cortisol is measured as a baseline, and then dexamethasone 2 mg orally is taken every 6 hours for 48 hours; urine for free cortisol is collected during the test and serum cortisol is checked 6 hours after the last dose. The suppression of cortisol secretion to >50 % of the baseline is considered positive and indicative of Cushing's disease The following four investigations are used to establish an initial diagnosis of endogenous Cushing's syndrome as per the clinical guidelines of the endocrine society. * 24-hour urinary free cortisol (increased 3x above normal) * Midnight salivary cortisol ( >5nmol/L) * Overnight dexamethasone suppression (plasma cortisol >50 nmol/L at 8-9 AM after 1 mg dexamethasone at 11 PM) * Standard 2-day (low dose) dexamethasone suppression test (plasma cortisol > 50 nmol/L after 0.5 mg dexamethasone 6th hourly for 48 hours). Pearl PF0309: Causes of Cushing's Syndrome Iatrogenic (Most common cause) * Exogenous administration of glucocorticoids Endogenous Causes * ACTH Dependent – (90 % of endogenous causes) * Cushing’s disease – ACTH-producing pituitary adenoma * Ectopic ACTH syndrome – Due to ACTH secretion by * Bronchial or pancreatic carcinoid tumors * Small-cell lung cancer * Medullary thyroid carcinoma * Pheochromocytoma * ACTH Independent – (10% ) * Adrenocortical adenoma * Adrenocortical carcinoma Rare causes * Macronodular adrenal hyperplasia * Primary pigmented nodular adrenal disease * McCune – Albright syndrome

text: 16. A 10-year-old child was brought to the OPD following a sting on his toe. On examination, he had tachycardia, hypertension, tongue fasciculations, hypersalivation, and dilated pupils. Local examination of the wound showed mild erythema. He remembers the animal having a curved tail upwards. Which of the following has most likely bitten him?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Scorpion

The clinical stem with the description of the animal is suggestive of a scorpion bite. Most scorpion stings cause pain at the site of the bite. Systemic toxicity occurs in <10% of stings but is more commonly seen in infants and children. The venom is a clear, colorless toxalbumen and is generally classified as either hemolytic or neurotoxic.  The venom is a potent autonomic stimulator resulting in the release of massive amounts of catecholamines from the adrenals. It also has a direct effect on the myocardium. It can present as neurotoxicity with restlessness or seizure-like activity, abnormal oculomotor function, loss of pharyngeal muscle control leading to respiratory compromise. Tongue fasciculations and hypersalivation are also common. Cardiovascular toxicity from systemic envenomation includes tachycardia, hypertension, pulmonary edema, and cardiogenic shock. If the scorpion has hemolytic venom, the reaction is mainly local, with edema, pain, and reddening. This usually lasts for one to two hours.  Treatment: * Pain- Paracetamol, NSAIDs, or opioids  * Sedation for agitation, oculomotor abnormalities, uncoordinated neuromuscular activity, muscle spasms- Benzodiazepines  * Hypertension and pulmonary edema -Prazosin counteract the adrenergic surge that can lead to these effects * Cardiogenic shock- Antivenom, prazosin, nitroglycerin, dobutamine * Cholinergic effects- Atropine * Supportive care wound care Note: Massive amounts of catecholamines are also released by a species of spider called the Black Widow spider which is fatal if bitten.

Which of the following agents is most likely responsible for her condition?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Cytomegalovirus

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is an important cause of morbidity and mortality after allogeneic transplant. Interstitial pneumonia (IP) is the most common manifestation of CMV, in transplant recipients. The predominant pathogen to infect the renal transplant recipients in the period around 1 to 4 months following the transplantation is cytomegalovirus (CMV).The most common CMV presentation in kidney transplant patients is fever (most common), leukopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, myalgia, and arthralgia.  CMV infection in immunocompromised hosts: The infection is contained by host immune response where virus remains latent in leukocytes. Then reactivates when host becomes immunocompromised, and may cause: * Retinitis (especially in AIDS patients) * Pneumonia (especially in transplant patients) * Esophagitis Diagnosis: * Giant cells with “owl’s eye” intranuclear inclusionbodies found in tissues/urine * Serology (negative monospot test as compared to EBV mononucleosis) * Detection in buffy coat culture (CMV infects WBCs) Other options: * Option a: Adenovirus is associated with conjunctivitis and acute respiratory disease in military recruits, among other diseases. * Option c: Although influenza can cause pneumonia, there is no mention of season, and CMV is still the most common cause in transplant patients. * Option d: Respiratory syncytial virus is usually seen in children (especially premature infants). text: 19. A 30-year-old female present with unsteady gait, forgetfulness, and labile moods. One physical exam, the neurologist notices that her iris appear multicolored with concentric rings around the periphery as below.The most likely diagnosis is______
expl:
Correct answer: B. Wilson's disease

The image above shows fine, pigmented and granular deposits in the cornea. This finding along with the clinical scenario is characteristically seen in Wilson’s disease. Wilson's disease: * Autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutation of the ATP7B gene, resulting in impaired copper excretion into bile and a failure to incorporate copper into ceruloplasmin. * Located on chromosome 13 * This disorder is marked by the accumulation of toxic levels of copper in principally the liver, brain, and eye. * In the liver, copper binds to a α2-globulin (apoceruloplasmin) to form ceruloplasmin. Circulating ceruloplasmin is eventually degraded within lysosomes, after which the released copper is excreted into bile. This degradation/excretion pathway is the primary route for copper elimination. * Deficiency in the ATP7B protein causes a decrease in copper transport into bile, impairs its incorporation into ceruloplasmin, and inhibits ceruloplasmin secretion into the blood. These changes cause copper accumulation in the liver and a decrease in circulating ceruloplasmin. The accumulated copper causes toxic liver injury. * Toxic injury to the brain primarily affects the basal ganglia, particularly the putamen, which shows atrophy and even cavitation. * Kayser-Fleischer rings, are dark rings that appear to encircle the iris of the eye. They are due to copper deposition in part of the cornea (Descemet's membrane). Diagnosis of Wilson disease is based on: * decrease in serum ceruloplasmin * an increase in hepatic copper content (the most sensitive and accurate test). * increased urinary excretion of copper (the most specific screening test). * neurologic involvement presents as movement disorders (tremor, poor coordination, chorea or choreoathetosis) or rigid dystonia (spastic dystonia, mask-like facies, rigidity and gait disturbances. * psychiatric symptoms such as depression, phobias, compulsive behavior, and labile mood. * hemolytic anemia may occur due to the toxicity of copper to red cell membranes. * Histology * Excess copper deposition can often be demonstrated by special stains (rhodamine stain for copper, orcein stain for copper-associated protein). * Fatty change (steatosis) * Hepatocyte ballooning with prominent Mallory-Denk bodies. Note:Sunflower cataracts are another ocular manifestation of Wilson disease and occur when copper deposits accumulate in the lens.

text: 20. Which is the best confirmatory method to ensure that the central line is in the jugular vein?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Chest Xray

A chest X-ray is the best method to confirm the position of the central line in the jugular vein. The position of the catheter is confirmed by radiological confirmation with an X-ray. Comparison of the blood’s color or PaO2 with an arterial sample can also be done, however, they can be misleading or inconclusive, and more than one confirmation method should be used. In cases where transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is used, the guidewire can be seen in the right atrium, confirming venous entry. Central line catheterization: Indications: * monitoring central venous pressure (CVP) * administration of fluid to treat hypovolemia and shock * infusion of caustic drugs and total parenteral nutrition * gaining venous access in patients with poor peripheral veins. Contraindications: * tumors or clots * tricuspid valve vegetations that could be dislodged or embolized during cannulation * site-related complications-subclavian vein cannulation is relatively contraindicated in patients who are receiving anticoagulants(due to the inability to provide direct compression in the event of an accidental arterial puncture), avoid central venous cannulation on the side of a previous carotid endarterectomy due to the possibility of unintentional carotid artery puncture. Sites: * the subclavian vein is associated with a greater risk of pneumothorax, but a reduced risk of other complications during prolonged cannulations  * right internal jugular vein provides a combination of accessibility and safety * left-sided internal jugular vein catheterization has an increased risk of pleural effusion and chylothorax * the external jugular veins can also be used as entry sites, but due to the acute angle at which they join the great veins of the chest, are associated with a slightly increased likelihood of failure to gain access. * femoral veins can also be cannulated, but are associated with an increased risk of line-related sepsis. Risks: * site infection, bloodstream infection, air or thrombus embolism * arrhythmias (indicating that the catheter tip is in the right atrium or ventricle), hematoma, pneumothorax, hemothorax, hydrothorax, chylothorax * cardiac perforation, cardiac tamponade, trauma to nearby nerves and arteries

21. A 56-year-old female with a history of myocardial infarction 2 years back now came with complaints of a cough and breathlessness on walking for a short distance. On examination, there was dullness to percussion and reduced breath sounds on the right side. Chest X-ray showed moderate pleural effusion. Thoracocentesis was performed under ultrasound guidance and the lab investigations are given below. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis in this patient?

 Pleural fluid findings: 

* Appearance: turbid

* pH: 7.1

* Protein: 3.2 g/dL

* Lactate dehydrogenase: 80 U/L (normal serum LDH - 50-150 U/L)

* Pleural fluid protein/serum protein ratio : 0.34

* Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH : 0.3

* Glucose: 54 mg/dL

* WBC count: 4000 cells/μL with > 50% lymphocytes

* Adenosine deaminase: 30 U/L

* AFB smear microscopy: negative

* Gram staining and microscopy: no organisms, no pus cells
expl:
Correct answer: C. Congestive heart failure

This patient's clinical presentation and laboratory findings are suggestive of congestive heart failure in which the effusion is transudative in nature. In this patient,  * Pleural fluid protein/serum protein ratio : 0.34 (<0.5) * Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH : 0.3 (<0.6) * Pleural fluid LDH is < 2/3rd the upper limit of normal serum LDH (normal serum LDH - 50-150 U/L) In this patient, according to Light's criteria, the pleural effusion is transudative. Examples of transudative pleural effusions are effusions due to congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, and nephrosis. Exudative pleural effusions are caused by malignancies, bacterial infections, rheumatoid pleuritis, and pulmonary embolism Other options: Option A: In parapneumonic pleural effusion too, the effusion is exudative with pH < 7.2 and glucose < 60 mg/dL. However, the WBC count is usually >10,000 cells/μL with a predominance of neutrophils. Appearance is generally cloudy. Option B: Pleural effusion associated with malignant pleural effusion is exudative in nature. Option D: Although tubercular pleural effusion is also exudative with a predominance of lymphocytes, adenosine deaminase levels < 40 U/L as in this patient rules out tubercular effusion. text: 22. A patient presents with frequent urination, nocturia, and enuresis. 24-hour urine volume was measured and recorded to be 7 liters. The urine osmolarity was 260 mOsm/L. ADH assay was performed and the recorded values were reported as 0.8 pg/ml. An MRI of the brain was performed and T1 weighted indicated the absence of the bright spot. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Pituitary DI

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of pituitary diabetes insipidus. Approach to the question: * A 24-hour urine volume greater than 3 liters is suggestive of polyuria. * Urine osmolarity < 300 mOsm/ L is suggestive of DI or primary polydipsia. * ADH assay < 1pg/mL = Primary polydipsia or central DI. * Finally, the absence of a pituitary bright spot in the MRI brain is suggestive of central diabetes insipidus. In nephrogenic DI, the ADH levels will be greater than 1pg/mL. In the case of primary polydipsia, a pituitary bright spot will be observed. In solute loss (mannitol or hypertonic saline infusion), urine osmolality is greater than 300 mOsm/L.

text: 23. A 65-year-old man presented with chronic pain in his hand, knees, and hips,aggravated on climbing stairs, while pain in his hands increases when he writes or types. He also complains of stiffness in his joints in the morning, which lasts for around half an hour. On examination of the hands, Herbeden's and Bouchard's nodes are visible. X-ray of the knee showed narrowed joint space with osteophytes. Which among the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Osteoarthritis

The clinical vignette points to a diagnosis of osteoarthritis (OA).  Osteoarthritis is the most common cause of chronic knee pain in persons aged over 45 years. The early phases typically present with episodic joint pain following overactive use of the diseased joint. As the disease progresses, the pain becomes continuous and may be associated with stiffness of the affected joint. Morning stiffness if present, is usually brief for around 30 minutes. Clinical signs include:  * Tenderness of the joint * Bony swelling * Decreased and painful range of movement  * Crepitus when the joint is moved * Weakness and wasting of muscles acting on the joint * Signs of inflammation  * Deformity and instability in severe cases  The joints involved in osteoarthritis are: * Distal and proximal interphalangeal joints (DIP, PIP) * First carpometacarpal joint (base of the thumb) * Hip * Knee * First metatarsal phalangeal joint (MTP) * Cervical and lumbosacral spine The wrist, elbow, and ankle joints are usually spared.Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes are nodules in osteoarthritis that are palpable in the distal interphalangeal joint and proximal interphalangeal joints respectively. The characteristic features of OA seen on plain radiographs are: * Marginal osteophyte formation * Localized joint space narrowing * Sclerosis of the underlying bone * Subchondral bone cysts * Loose bodies and chondrocalcinosis The image below is an X-ray of osteorthritis showing the presence of osteophytes, narrowing of the joint space (arrow), and subchondral bone sclerosis.

text: 25. A 30-year-old woman presents with headache, vomiting, amenorrhea, galactorrhea, loss of libido, acromegaly, and infertility. On examination, she has bitemporal hemianopia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Mammosomatotrope adenoma

The symptoms of headache, vomiting, galactorrhea, infertility, decreased libido, acromegaly is suggestive of excess prolactin and growth hormone along with features of raised intra-cranial tension. The most likely diagnosis is a mammosomatotrope adenoma of the pituitary.  Prolactinomas are the most frequent type of hyperfunctioning pituitary adenomas. They are usually found in adults. They may be functioning or non-functioning. Based on the size, they can be called microadenomas if <1 cm in diameter and macroadenomas if ≥1 cm in diameter.  The symptoms include * Headache and vomiting * Bitemporal hemianopia suggestive of a local mass effect * Increased intracranial pressure due to a pituitary tumour * In females- amenorrhea, galactorrhea, loss of libido, and infertility * In males- impotence, loss of libido, and gynecomastia The diagnosis of prolactinoma is most likely to be associated with a prolactin level >200 μg/L. Treatment is only required in symptomatic cases as microadenomas rarely progress to macroadenomas. Dopamine and dopamine agonists are used and they act as inhibitory signals to prolactin secretion in the pituitary. Cabergoline is a long-acting dopamine receptor agonist with high D2 receptor affinity and is the preferred drug for the treatment of hyperprolactinemia Excessive GH secreted before puberty results in gigantism. Acromegaly occurs when excessive GH is secreted after puberty (after fusion of long bone epiphysis). Increased secretion of growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor- 1 (IGF-1) results in acral bone overgrowth. Patients present with frontal bossing, increased hand and foot size, mandibular enlargement with prognathism, and widened space between the lower incisor teeth. Soft tissue swelling results in increased heel pad thickness, increased shoe size, ring tightening, characteristic coarse facial features, and a large fleshy nose. Other manifestations seen in GH excess are cardiomyopathy, left ventricular hypertrophy, obstructive sleep apnea, diabetes mellitus, etc. Serum IGF-1 levels and GH suppression test with oral glucose are useful in the diagnosis. The levels of GH do not reduce in response to the oral glucose load. GH-secreting adenomas are managed with surgery. Transsphenoidal resection is the preferred surgery. Other options: Option A: Corticotroph adenoma secrete ACTH. They present with features of Cushing's disease.  Option B: Gonadotroph adenoma secrete FSH and LH. They can present with  polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), infertility, menstrual irregularities, ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) in women, and testicular hypertrophy and sexual dysfunction in men. Option D: Gliomas are neoplasms that originates from glial cells. They present with headaches, nausea, vomiting, seizures, and in more advanced cases weakness or altered mental status. text: 27. A patient was asked to copy the face of a clock and his drawing is shown below. What is the correct term to be used here?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Hemispatial neglect

Hemispatial neglect is the inability to report, respond, or orient to stimuli in one-half of the space despite having no motor or sensory deficits.  A patient with neglect is asked to draw a clock, their drawing might show only the numbers 12 to 6, or all 12 numbers might be on one half of the clock face with the other half distorted or blank, like the image shown in the image below. Neglect patients may also ignore the contralesional side of their body; for instance, they might only shave, or apply makeup to, the non-neglected side. These patients may frequently collide with objects or structures such as door frames on the side being neglected. Other options: Option A: Confabulation is a phenomenon in which the patient fills in memory gaps with inaccurate information. Further investigating the statement made by the patients may reflect past experiences or bizarre, fantastic stories.  This fabrication of false information is not done on purpose. Option C: Apraxia: Inability to perform a movement or task when asked despite having the desire and physical capability to carry it out. Types of apraxia: * Kinetic: Inability to execute the fine acquired motor movement, the lesion is in the precentral cortex. * Ideomotor: Fails to perform on command. The lesion is in the parietal lobe. * Constructional: liability to reproduce simple geometric figures by drawing. The lesion is in the pathway between the occipital or parietal area. * Ideational: Loss of ability to formulate an ideational plan for the execution of the complex act. The lesion is in the dominant parietal lobe. Option D: Astrexis/Flapping tremor is a type of negative myoclonus characterized by irregular lapses of the posture of various body parts. Mostly associated with hepatic encephalopathy.

text: 28. A 55-year-old male patient presented to the hospital with palpitations. On examination, a diastolic murmur is heard in the left third intercostal space and pistol shot sound is heard over the femoral arteries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Aortic regurgitation

The presence of a diastolic murmur along with the pistol shot sound over the femoral is most likely to be due to aortic regurgitation. Due to aortic regurgitation, there is a backflow of the blood from the aorta to the ventricle, during the diastole. This increases the end-diastolic (EDV) volume in the left ventricle and at the same time decreases the diastolic blood pressure (DBP). Increased EDV leads to an increase in stroke volume and systolic blood pressure (SBP). The patient develops wide pulse pressure due to increased SBP and decreased DBP. The clinical manifestations in AR is mainly due to the wide pulse pressure. As the regurgitation worsens, the ventricle undergo dilatation and eccentric hypertrophy to eject the additional amount of regurgitant blood. Eventually, these adaptive measures fail and left ventricular failure develops. Pearl PF1019: Different signs in Aortic Regurgitation

text:
1. An elderly woman presented with symptoms of confusion, thirst, and abdominal pain. On examination, she had pallor and thoracic spine tenderness. Her lab investigations showed the following findings. An X-ray of her skull is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

* Hb - 6.9g/dL

* WBC 4000/cm3 with normal differential count

* Serum calcium 13mg/dL

* Creatinine 2.3mg/dL

* Total protein 9g/dL

* Albumin 2.4g/dL

* Urinalysis: positive for Bence-Jones proteins
expl:
Correct answer: B. Multiple myeloma

The given clinical features along with hypercalcemia, elevated creatinine suggestive of renal failure, anemia, osteolytic bone lesions (CRAB features), hypoalbuminemia with elevated total proteins and Bence Jones proteinuria make multiple myeloma the most likely diagnosis. Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia with the proliferation of plasma cells derived from a single clone. It is associated with an increased osteoclast activity with suppression of osteoblast activity, causing punched-out lytic lesions in the bone and hypercalcemia. Signs and symptoms * Bone pain is the most common symptom * Pathologic fractures * Recurrent bacterial infections * Renal failure * Normocytic normochromic anemia, elevated ESR, Hypercalcemia, normal ALP (ALP is a marker of bone growth and hence is not increased in multiple myeloma) * Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray * Electrophoresis: Monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin * Urinalysis: Free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins) * Bone marrow biopsy: 10 to 20% plasma cells (normal is < 5%) * Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation (High level of M proteins in myeloma causes red cells in the peripheral blood smears to stick to one another in linear arrays, a finding referred to as rouleaux formation) Revised International Myeloma Working Group criteria for the diagnosis of multiple myeloma: Presence of ≥10% clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow or confirmation of a plasmacytoma in bone or extramedullary tissue by biopsy Plus Any one or more of the following myeloma-defining events: *  Evidence of end-organ damage specific to plasma cell proliferative disorder (CRAB features) * HyperCalcemia: Serum calcium level >1 mg/dL higher than the upper limit of normal or >11 mg/dL * Renal insufficiency: Creatinine clearance <40 mL/min or serum creatinine >2 mg/dL * Anemia: Haemoglobin level of >20 g/L (2gm/dl) below the lowest limit of normal, or Hb <10 g/dL * Bone lesions: At least one osteolytic lesion identified on X-ray, CT or PET-CT. * Any one or more of the following biomarkers of malignancy: * Clonal bone marrow plasma cells ≥60% * Serum involved/uninvolved free light-chain ratio of 100 or greater * >1 focal lesion on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) that is at least 5 mm or greater in size. Note: * The presence of at least one of these markers is considered sufficient for a diagnosis of multiple myeloma, regardless of the presence or absence of symptoms or CRAB features. * Each of these markers has been shown to be associated with an approximately 80% or higher risk of developing myeloma-related organ damage within two years. Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) is usually due to a solitary parathyroid adenoma and is not associated with anemia and hypoalbuminemia. It is characterized by hypercalcemia and low serum phosphorus in presence of elevated PTH levels. 24-hour urine calcium should be checked which will be normal or elevated in PHPT but will be decreased in familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia. Prior neck irradiation is the only known risk factor. The clinical features are known as the "bones, stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans" which include: * Renal: renal stones (most common clinical manifestation), nephrocalcinosis, UTI, renal insufficiency * Musculoskeletal: Osteitis fibrosa cystica, osteopenia causing osteoporosis, proximal myopathy * Gastrointestinal: constipation due to hypercalcemia, peptic ulcer disease, and rarely pancreatitis * Neuropsychiatric: decreased concentration, fatigue, and depression First-line treatment includes bisphosphonates and calcitonin is usually used as a bridge until sustained action of bisphosphonates is seen. Surgery is the definitive management for PHPT and Sestamibi scan is the most accurate and reliable investigation for imaging parathyroid glands prior to surgery. Elevated ALP  levels are seen in concomitant bone diseases, and such patients may develop postoperative hypocalcemia due to hungry bone syndrome. Milk alkali syndrome occurs on ingestion of large amounts of calcium and vitamin D supplements. It results in hypercalcemia, alkalosis, and renal impairment leading to nephrocalcinosis and nephrolithiasis. Pearl PF0580: WHO Classification of Plasma Cell Neoplasms

Plasma cell neoplasms and variants

Plasma cell myeloma
  • Non secretory: No secretion of Ig, No M component.
  • Smoldering: M protein in serum ≥ 30 g/L and/or ≥10% clonal plasma cells in bone marrow, and no related organ or tissue impairment.
  • Plasma-cell leukemia: >20% plasma cells in the peripheral blood or Absolute plasma cell count of >2 X 109/L.

Plasmacytoma
  • Solitary plasmacytoma: Localized tumour of monoclonal plasma cells with no clinical features of plasma cell myeloma.
  • Extramedullary(extraosseous) plasmacytoma: Localized plasma cell neoplasms that arise in tissues other than bone.

Monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition diseases
  • Primary amyloidosis: Tumor secreting light chains that are deposited as beta-pleated sheet structure (amyloid light chain).
  • Systemic light and heavy chain diseases: Secrete abnormal light or heavy chain or both, which do not form beta pleated sheet, stain Congo Red or contain amyloid P component.

Laboratory investigations in a patient with hypothyroidism would show low levels of total and free T3, T4, and rT3, with high TSH levels and normal combined protein levels. Normally, the thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) is released by the hypothalamus. It stimulates the pituitary gland to release the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which in turn stimulates the thyroid gland to produce T3 and T4 hormones. Elevated TSH with a low level of free T4 is suggestive of primary hypothyroidism. In the case of secondary hypothyroidism, TSH levels may be low, normal, or even slightly increased. The latter is due to the secretion of immunoactive but bio-inactive forms of TSH. The diagnosis is confirmed by the detection of a low unbound T4 level.  Patients with hypothyroidism often present with tiredness, weakness, dry skin, hair loss, difficulty concentrating, poor memory, constipation, cold intolerance, and weight gain with poor appetite. On examination, they may have cool peripheral extremities, puffy faces, hyporeflexia, bradycardia, and peripheral edema. The best outcomes occur when levothyroxine therapy is started immediately after diagnosis. The clinical effects of levothyroxine replacement are slow to appear.  If there is no residual function, the daily replacement dose of levothyroxine is usually 1.6 μg/kg body weight (typically 100–150 μg), ideally taken at least 30 minutes before breakfast. TSH responses are gradual and should be determined 2 months following the initiation of treatment or change in dose. Once the full replacement is achieved and TSH levels are stable, TSH measurement is recommended at annual intervals. In patients who have developed hypothyroidism following treatment of Graves' disease, lower doses are needed for replacement. text: 15. A 30-year-old man presented with excessive fatiguability towards the end of the day that improved with rest. He also gives history of ptosis, difficult in speech and swallowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Myasthenia gravis

In the above clinical scenario of a patient with fatiguability that worsen with repetitive movements but resolve after rest, ptosis, dysarthria, and dysphagia. is very characteristic of myasthenia gravis. Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles. Females are more commonly affected than males and the disease tends to occur in middle age. It is due to the autoantibody-mediated destruction of the acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the post-synaptic membrane. This consequentially leads to a decreased transmission at the neuromuscular junction. Failure of transmission results in muscle weakness. Clinical features of myasthenia gravis: * Muscle weakness and fatiguability increase with repeated use or during late in the day and may improve following rest or sleep. Limb weakness is proximal and asymmetrical * Cranial muscles particularly the lids and extraocular muscles are involved early in the course - diplopia, ptosis * Facial weakness - snarling expression on smiling * Weakness in chewing * Speech with nasal timbre due to the weakness of palate and tongue * Difficulty in swallowing * Deep tendon reflexes are intact * Myasthenic crisis - acute exacerbation of muscle weakness especially intercostal and diaphragmatic muscles resulting in ventilatory failure. It is most commonly due to infection and anticholinesterase medication overuse. Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymoma and other autoimmune diseases such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Grave's disease, neuromyelitis optics, systemic lupus erythematosus, etc. Diagnosis: * Ice-pack test - application of ice pack over the eyes improves ptosis (decreases activity of acetylcholinesterase, this increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and increase transmission) * Antibodies associated with myasthenia gravis: Anti-AChR antibodies, Anti-MuSK antibodies, Anti-LRP4 antibodies * Repetitive nerve stimulation test shows a decremental response. * Edrophonium chloride or Tensilon test - improvement of symptoms occurs on injecting edrophonium. Edrophonium is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. This increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and improves transmission. Treatment: * Anticholinesterase drugs - Pyridostigmine. * Thymectomy. * Immunosuppression therapy with glucocorticoids, azathioprine, tacrolimus, rituximab, etc. * Plasmapheresis and intravenous immunoglobulin. Other options: Option B: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is an autoimmune disorder affecting the presynaptic membrane at the neuromuscular junction. It is due to the autoantibodies against the P/Q-type calcium channels at the motor nerve terminal which results in the impaired release of Ach from the presynaptic nerve terminal. Patients present with proximal muscle weakness of the lower limbs, ptosis, and diplopia. However, symptoms might improve after brief exercise. Deep tendon reflexes are absent or reduced. They also experience autonomic dysfunction and present with dry mouth and impotence. It is most commonly associated with small cell lung cancer.  Repetitive nerve stimulation test shows an incremental response at higher rates. Treatment involves plasmapheresis, immunotherapy, and drugs such as 3,4-Diaminopyridine (3,4-DAP) and pyridostigmine. Option C: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is X-linked muscular dystrophy due to mutations in the dystrophin gene. It most commonly affects boys in their childhood.  Patients initially present with proximal muscle weakness predominantly of the lower limbs. Calf muscle hypertrophy is a cardinal feature. Other features include mental retardation, cardiac failure, and myoglobinuria. Elevated serum creatinine kinase levels and genetic testing are diagnostic of DMD. Option D: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease that most commonly presents with arthralgia with early morning stiffness. It predominantly occurs in middle-aged women. Other important features of SLE include malar rash, discoid rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, pleuritis, pericarditis, and  lupus nephritis. Anti nuclear antibodies, Anti-dsDNA antibodies, anti-smith antibodies are positive in SLE. Heatstroke/ thermic fever/ heat hyperpyrexia is due to the failure of the heat regulation center of the hypothalamus. It is caused by failure of cutaneous circulation and sweating. The predisposing factors include high temperature, increased humidity, minor infections, old age, lack of acclimatization, alcoholism. Heatstroke can be: * Exertion-induced heat stroke is seen in people with prolonged exposure to or physical exertion in high temperatures, usually without adequate training. * Sedentary heatstroke is a disease of elderly or infirm people whose cardiovascular systems are unable to adapt to the stress of a hot environment and release sufficient heat such that body temperature rises. All the signs of shock are present. Patients usually present with a sudden collapse accompanied by loss of consciousness. Typical vital sign abnormalities include tachypnea, tachycardias, hypotension, and a widened pulse pressure. Other specific signs include rapid Kussmaul type of breathing, the absence of sweating with dry, hot skin, delirium, coma, convulsions, rhabdomyolysis, multiorgan failure. Although there is no single specific diagnostic test, clinical features of exposure to heat stress, CNS dysfunction, and core temperature >104.9-degree Fahrenheit (> 40.5 degrees Celsius) help establish the preliminary diagnosis. The body temperature must be measured rectally. Treatment includes rapidly cooling the body with ice water till the rectal temperature falls below 1020F. Autopsy findings include the presence of edema and reduction of Purkinje's cells in the cerebellum. There is no role of antipyretics in the control of environmentally induced hyperthermia. The patient can also develop hydrocephalus. The CSF sample shows pellicle or cobweb-like clots. Acid-fast bacilli can be best isolated from these. There is usually lymphocytic leukocytosis, low glucose concentration, and elevated proteins. CSF culture remains the gold standard for diagnosis.  The clinical triad of fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity is common to all types of meningitis. Nuchal rigidity is the resistance of the neck to passive flexion and is pathognomonic of meningeal irritation. Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are other features of meningeal irritation. Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) is a complication that presents as papilledema, disorientation, or dilated poorly reactive pupils. text: 5. A young patient presents with a severe headache. He has never experienced a headache of this severity before. He has hypertension and nuchal rigidity on examination. Which of the following could be the diagnosis?

Correct answer: B. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

The clinical manifestations of neck stiffness and severe headache (like never before) suggests a diagnosis of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is the bleeding into the subarachnoid space, which is the area between the arachnoid membrane and the pia mater surrounding the brain. The diagnosis is suspected when a hyperattenuating material is seen filling the subarachnoid space. Most commonly this is apparent around the circle of Willis, on account of the majority of berry aneurysms occurring in this region, or in the Sylvian fissure. Young males with a history of spontaneous sudden onset severe headaches with seizures should raise suspicion for subarachnoid hemorrhage (aneurysmal). The most common cause of SAH is head trauma and the second common cause is the rupture of a saccular aneurysm. Symptoms include: * Severe headache (thunderclap headache) * Rapid onset vomiting * Confusion or a lowered level of consciousness * Seizures * Neck stiffness or neck pain Other options: Cluster headache is a rare form of primary headache. It is characterized by deep excruciating pain that is usually retroorbital, and unilateral. It usually lasts for short duration of 8-10 weeks a year followed by a pain-free interval. It is associated with lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, and ptosis. In acute cases, oxygen therapy is useful. Subcutaneous and nasal sumatriptan can be used. The classic clinical triad of fever, headache, and neck rigidity is suggestive of meningitis. Other common complaints are nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. Nuchal rigidity (“stiff neck”) is the pathognomonic sign of meningitis. Hip and knee flexion on passive flexion of the neck is called Brudzinsky's sign. Encephalitis presents similar to meningitis with fever, altered mental status, and focal or diffuse neurological symptoms. Pearl PF1866: Intracranial haemorrhage

The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario is Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS). GBS is an acute, fulminant polyradiculoneuropathy that is autoimmune in nature. GBS is caused when immune response/antibodies against external antigens like infections, vaccines, etc target similar proteins present in the person's nervous tissue. Clinical features are rapidly evolving areflexic motor paralysis with or without sensory disturbance. Respiration is compromised when it involves respiratory muscles. In such cases, ventilatory support is needed. High-dose intravenous immune globulin (IVIg) or plasmapheresis are equally effective for typical GBS. IVIg is the initial therapy chosen because of its ease of administration and good safety record. Other options: Option B: Myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular disorder due to autoimmune damage to the acetylcholine receptors. It is characterized by weakness and muscle fatiguability. Proximal limb weakness is also present.  Option C: Polymyositis is one of the inflammatory myopathies characterized by symmetric and proximal muscle weakness. This weakness usually worsens over several weeks to months. It is more common in women. Most patients improve with immunotherapies, but they require lifelong treatment. Option D: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease characterized by multiple episodes of neurological deficits due to patchy white matter lesions that involve various sites of the brain. It is caused by an autoimmune response directed against components of the myelin sheath. The demyelinated plaques are the hallmark of MS Pearl PF1047: Mechanism of Immunopathogenesis of Guillain-Barre Syndrome The following sequence of events, takes into consideration, the development of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) associated with Campylobacter jejuni infection. * B cells recognize glycoconjugates on jejuni (Cj) that cross-react with ganglioside present on Schwann cell surface and subjacent peripheral nerve myelin. * Most of the B cells are activated via a partially T cell–dependent route and secrete primarily IgG autoantibodies. 10. Elective splenectomy is preferred in which of the following conditions?

G6PD deficiency- Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
expl:
Correct answer: C. Hereditary spherocytosis

Elective splenectomy is done in case of hereditary spherocytosis. Hereditary spherocytosis is a type of hereditary hemolytic anemia that is passed down in an autosomal dominant pattern. Mutations of the red blood cell surface proteins spectrin and ankyrin can result in unstable cell membranes, leading to hemolysis. This disorder can present at a young age with severe jaundice and fatigue. The unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia predisposes the patient to develop gallstones. Laboratory findings include normocytic anemia with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The peripheral smear will show large spherical red blood cells without central pallor. The diagnosis can be confirmed by the acid glycerol lysis test and the eosin-5′-maleimide (EMA)–binding test.  There is no specific treatment available besides splenectomy. However, due to the possible adverse effects, it is only indicated in severe cases and after the child attains puberty in moderate cases. It should be followed up with the appropriate antibiotic and vaccine prophylaxis. Other options: Option (A): Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is a type of inherited hemolytic anemia. It is associated with exacerbations after consuming anti-malarial drugs and in periods of oxidative stress. The peripheral smear shows characteristic "bite cells". In G6PD deficiency, uncontrolled oxidative stress causes hemoglobin to denature and form Heinz bodies. G6PD deficiency is largely preventable by avoiding exposure to triggering factors. Option (B): Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is a hemolytic disorder that also presents with pancytopenia and a tendency to form venous thrombi. It occurs due to defective GPI anchors on the red blood cell surface which are normally used to anchor CD 59 (cell-protective proteins) to the surface. These patients can present with episodes of dark brown urine in the morning, anemia, pancytopenia, and recurrent abdominal pain due to thrombosis of abdominal veins.  Bone marrow transplantation is done for the treatment. Recently humanized monoclonal antibody eculizumab is used. Option (D): Hairy cell leukemia is a distinctive B cell neoplasm, that predominantly affects middle-aged males. Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase is the cytochemical stain characteristically shown by leukemic hairy cells. Patients commonly present with massive splenomegaly due to infiltration of the leukemic cells. Pancytopenia due to marrow involvement can also be seen. These tumors respond well to chemotherapy and BRAF (B-type Raf proto-oncogene) inhibitors, and they have an excellent prognosis. text: 11. A patient presents with complaints of sudden onset headache, palpitation, and profuse sweating. The patient has had multiple similar episodes in the past. During these episodes, the patient's blood pressure is elevated. A 24-hour urinary metanephrine is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Pheochromocytoma

The most likely diagnosis in this patient is pheochromocytoma. Pheochromocytoma is a rare tumor of the sympathetic system arising from the adrenal medulla. Patients commonly present with a classical triad of palpitation, headache, and profuse sweating. Patients also present with hypertension and cardiac arrhythmias. These symptoms are due to an excess of catecholamines secreted by the tumor. Other options: Option A: Addison's disease is a primary adrenal insufficiency in which the adrenal is unable to secrete adequate amounts of cortisol (glucocorticoid), and aldosterone (mineralocorticoid). The features are fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, low blood pressure, postural hypotension, hypoglycemia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, salt craving, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Option B: Renal artery stenosis is a relatively common finding in older patients with chronic essential hypertension. However, it is clinically significant (i.e. renovascular hypertension) only if the stenosis is greater than 75% in both renal arteries or 50% stenosis with post-stenotic dilatation. Main causes include atherosclerosis (most common), usually seen in patients > 45 years and fibromuscular dysplasia, seen in women < 50 years. Option D: Hyperthyroidism presents with clinical features that include heat intolerance and sweating, tachycardia, and palpitations, weight loss with increased appetite, diarrhea, and oligomenorrhea. Clinical findings include exophthalmos, tremors, and myopathy. Factors indicating more chances of malignancy: * An increased PASS (phaeochromocytoma of the adrenal gland scale score) * High number of Ki-67-positive cells * Vascular invasion or a breached capsule Diagnosis: * Urinary catecholamine and VMA level assay are most sensitive screening test. * MRI is the IOC. * Biopsy and CT Contrast scan are contraindicated in order to avoid Hypertensive crisis. text: 12. A 70-year-old patient with a history of smoking presents with high-grade fever, cough, confusion, and diarrhea. Chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates in bilateral lower lung fields. On sputum gram stain, no organisms were detected. Laboratory results reveal Na: 126mEq/L, AST:62, ALT:56, RBS:112 mg/dl, serum bilirubin of 0.8mg%, and a positive HIV test. Correct answer: B. Legionella

The given clinical scenario of the patient in the setting of an HIV infection, hyponatremia, and negative sputum gram stain is suggestive of legionnaire's disease. Legionnaire’s disease is caused by Legionella pneumophila. They are found in lakes, streams, and other water bodies. Infection is mostly spread by inhalation of the bacteria from aerosols produced by contaminated air conditioners, humidifiers, nebulizers, etc. It is mostly asymptomatic under the age of 40 years. Some risk factors for increasing the severity of the infection are smoking, older age and immunosuppression (as seen in this patient). It may present as a severe, rapidly progressive disease with high fever, chills, hypoxia, diarrhea, and delirium. On chest x-ray, patchy, often multilobar consolidation is seen. Pleural effusion may also occur. Initial lab findings include leukocytosis or leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia, elevated liver enzymes, and renal dysfunction. A milder form of a clinical syndrome known as Pontiac fever, which is usually self-limiting and only has mild symptoms of fever, myalgia, and headache. Microscopy of the sputum samples shows numerous leucocytes without any organism. Gram staining of the sterile sites like pleural fluid and lung tissues show faint gram-negative bacilli. They require a counterstain of basic fuschin as safranin stains the bacteria very poorly. They are a group of fastidious, aerobic gram-negative bacteria. They can be grown on a buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar. Diagnosis is established with the help of direct fluorescent antibody tests and BCYE culture specimens. Urine antigen tests and molecular assays may also be used. The below image shows the Direct Fluorescent Antibody Test. As L. pneumophila is an intracellular pathogen, antibiotics that reach high intracellular concentrations must be used. Macrolides and quinolones are the antibiotics of choice and are effective as monotherapy. Alternatively, agents like doxycycline may also be used. B-lactams, monobactams, and aminoglycosides are not considered to be effective. The total duration of therapy is 10-14 days for immunocompetent hosts and up to 3 weeks for immunosuppressed patients.  Other options: The clinical scenario in the setting of hyponatremia and elevated liver enzymes, in the absence of sputum gram stain points more towards legionella as the underlying pathogen rather than Streptococcus, Pneumocystis, or Klebsiella.

text: 15. Which of the following is the most common cause of mortality in diabetic ketoacidosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Cerebral edema

Cerebral edema is the leading cause of mortality in diabetic ketoacidosis. text: 16. Which of the following is not included in the Gaisböck syndrome?

Patients with Gaisböck syndrome do not have hypotension, but rather present with hypertension. text: 17. A patient presents with dyspnea and distended neck veins that increase on inspiration. There is no murmur. What is the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Constrictive pericarditis

The patient presenting with dyspnea and Kussmauls signs as evidenced by the distended neck veins that increase on inspiration, likely has underlying constrictive pericarditis. Constrictive pericarditis: It is a condition where a thickened, fibrotic, and often calcified pericardium restricts the diastolic filling of the heart. In developing countries, infectious etiologies like tuberculosis or viral infections are the most common cause of this condition. Cardiac surgery and radiation therapy are also common causes. Other causes include connective tissue disease, uremia, neoplasm, or idiopathic. Clinically the patients may present with dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, ascites. On examination neck veins may be distended and will show a positive Kussmauls sign. On auscultation, heart sound smay be distant and a pericardial knock at the cardiac apex may be heard. This occurs due to the abrubt cessation of ventricular filling. JVP findings - There is a rapid 'x' and 'y' descent. The rapid 'y' descent is more prominent and reflects rapid early ventricular diastolic filling. This occurs due to the constricting pericardium, increasing the atrial pressures. Diagnosis: Diagnosis is difficult and is confirmed by multiple investigations * Hallmark findings of pericardial constriction are pericardial thickening, calcification, and abnormal ventricular diastolic function. * The X-ray can be normal or there may be non-specific cardiac enlargement, calcification, and roughened cardiac outline. * CT and MRI are more sensitive investigations. Constrictive pericarditis will have prominent y descent, prominent x descent, and Kussmaul's sign. Normally, the venous pressure should fall by at least 3 mmHg with inspiration. Kussmaul’s sign is defined by either a rise or a lack of fall of the JVP with inspiration. Other options: Option B: Aortic regurgitation would present with a diastolic murmur. Option C: Tricuspid stenosis may also present similarly with congestive hepatomegaly, and venous distention, however, in this patient the absence of a murmur makes the diagnosis unlikely. Tricuspid stenosis will have prolonged y wave on JVP. Option D: Pulmonary arterial hypertension would present with a prominent jugular "a" wave, palpable left parasternal lift, and loud S2 which are not seen in this patient.

text: 18. A 5-year-old child presented with recurrent respiratory infections with thickened sputum. Chest X-ray showed bronchial wall thickening. He has been suffering from steatorrhea since birth. Which of the following is the first differential diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Cystic fibrosis

The given clinical history suggests a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis. The gross image shows pus-filled bronchial air spaces and dilated bronchi extending into the periphery, typical of bronchiectasis. Therefore, the genetic defect and the associated complication are defective ATP-gated chloride channels and bronchiectasis respectively. Cystic fibrosis (CF)/mucoviscidosis is an autosomal recessive disorder with a mutation in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator (CFTR) gene on chromosome 7q.  Following is the diagrammatic representation of the 6 categories of mutations seen in CFTR protein. Systemic manifestations of CF: Respiratory system: 1. Recurrent sino-pulmonary infections with pathogens including Staphylococcus aureus, Hemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas aeroginosa, and Burkholderia cepacia. 2. Chronic cough with thick foul smelling/ sometimes bloody sputum 3. Lung manifestations like bronchiectasis, atelectasis, infiltrates, and hyperinflation. 4. Nasal polyps. 5. Clubbing. Gastrointestinal system: 1. Intestinal abnormalities including meconium ileus, steatorrhea, and rectal prolapse. 2. Pancreatic insufficiency and pancreatitis. 3. Liver cirrhosis and prolonged neonatal jaundice. 4. Failure to thrive due to severe malnutrition. Others: 1. Salt-loss syndromes. 2. Congenital absence of vas deferens leading to obstructive azoospermia. Diagnostic tests: 1. Immunoreactive trypsinogen for newborn screening of cystic fibrosis. 2. Sweat chloride test: Increased chloride concentration >60 mEq/L is diagnostic. 3. Genetic testing for CFTR gene mutations is the gold standard and should be done for all cases. 4. Nasal transepithelial potential difference can be estimated in equivocal cases. Diagnostic criteria: Presence of * Clinical symptoms affecting at least one organ system (respiratory, gastrointestinal, or genitourinary) or * Positive newborn screening or * A sibling with cystic fibrosis. Evidence of dysfunction of the CFTR gene by * Two positive sweat chloride test results obtained on separate days or * Identification of two CFTR mutations by genetic testing or * An abnormal measurement of nasal potential difference. text: 22. A young male patient presents with ptosis and muscle weakness which reportedly worsens in the evening and improves in the morning. This is relieved by neostigmine. What is the likely diagnosis?

It is due to the autoantibody-mediated destruction of the acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the post-synaptic membrane. This consequentially leads to a decreased transmission at the neuromuscular junction. Failure of transmission results in muscle weakness. Females are more commonly affected than males and the disease tends to occur in middle age. Clinical features of myasthenia gravis: * Muscle weakness and fatiguability increase with repeated use or late in the day and may improve following rest or sleep. Limb weakness is proximal and asymmetrical * Cranial muscles particularly the lids and extraocular muscles are involved early in the course - diplopia, ptosis * Facial weakness - snarling expression on smiling * Weakness in chewing * Speech with nasal timbre due to the weakness of the palate and tongue * Difficulty in swallowing * Deep tendon reflexes are intact * Myasthenic crisis - acute exacerbation of muscle weakness especially intercostal and diaphragmatic muscles resulting in ventilatory failure. It is most commonly due to infection and anticholinesterase medication overuse. Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymoma and other autoimmune diseases such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Grave's disease, neuromyelitis optics, systemic lupus erythematosus, etc. Diagnosis: * Ice-pack test - application of ice pack over the eyes improves ptosis (decreases activity of acetylcholinesterase, this increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and increases transmission) * Antibodies associated with myasthenia gravis: Anti-AChR antibodies, Anti-MuSK antibodies, Anti-LRP4 antibodies * Repetitive nerve stimulation test shows a decremental response. * Edrophonium chloride or Tensilon test - improvement of symptoms occurs on injecting edrophonium. Edrophonium is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. This increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and improves transmission. Treatment: * Anticholinesterase drugs - Pyridostigmine. * Thymectomy. * Immunosuppression therapy with glucocorticoids, azathioprine, tacrolimus, rituximab, etc. * Plasmapheresis and intravenous immunoglobulin. It has an adult-onset and is associated with the degeneration of striatal neurons. Features such as chorea and dementia are commonly seen in these patients. The characteristic features of HD include involuntary movements, dementia, and behavioral changes. Option C: ALS is the most common progressive motor neuron disease. The pathologic hallmark of ALS includes the involvement of lower motor neurons of the ventral/ anterior horn of the spinal cord, cranial nerves innervating the bulbar muscles, and the afferent corticospinal upper motor neurons in layer five of the motor cortex. Progressive upper motor neuron (UMN) palsy (exaggerated reflexes, extensor plantar), lower motor neuron (LMN) palsy (muscle weakness, atrophy, fasciculations), and pseudobulbar palsy (dysarthria, tongue spasticity), with normal bladder, bowel and sensory function are suggestive of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). ECG changes in acute PE are characterized by the classic S1Q3T3 changes, due to right ventricular strain and ischemia: * A prominent S wave in lead I  * Q wave in lead III  * An inverted T wave in lead III It is an insensitive sign but specific. text: 28. A chronic smoker presented with bilateral pitting pedal edema, and abdominal distension. On examination, he had ascites and auscultation revealed an S3. Which of the following defects can be seen in this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Tricuspid regurgitation

The clinical features of bilateral pedal edema, abdominal distention, S3 heart sound are suggestive of right ventricular (RV) failure. The history of chronic smoking suggests that the patient is suffering from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)which results in cor pulmonale. Tricuspid regurgitation may be the underlying valvular defect in this patient. The main pathophysiology behind cor pulmonale is pulmonary hypertension and increased right ventricular (RV) afterload which is sufficient to cause RV dilation with or without hypertrophy. This alters both the structure and function of the RV. In parenchymal lung diseases, primary pulmonary vascular disorders, or chronic hypoxia, the pulmonary vessels undergo vascular remodeling, vasoconstriction, and destruction leading to increased pulmonary artery pressures and increased RV afterload. Anatomically, the right ventricle is thin-walled, compliant, and can handle volume overload better than pressure overload. Sustained pressure overload eventually leads to RV dysfunction and failure. Dyspnea is the most common symptom. Other symptoms include pedal edema, abdominal distension due to ascites, the murmur of tricuspid regurgitation, an S3 gallop, and a palpable RV heave along the left sternal border. The jugular venous pressures (JVP) are elevated with prominent v waves indicative of tricuspid regurgitation. Other features include hepatomegaly, pulsatile liver, tenderness in the right upper quadrant, and pitting pedal edema. The ECG in severe pulmonary hypertension shows P-pulmonale, right axis deviation, and RV hypertrophy. Spirometry and lung volumes show obstructive and/or restrictive defects seen in parenchymal lung diseases. Echo can be used to measure RV wall thickness and chamber dimensions, while doppler ECHO can be used to assess pulmonary artery pressures. Cardiac catheterization confirms the diagnosis of pulmonary hypertension and can exclude elevated left-sided pressures as a cause of heart failure.

text: 9. The finger-nose test is done to check the integrity of which of the following structures?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Cerebellum

The finger-nose test is done to assess cerebellar function. Coordination in the upper limb is tested by finger-nose test. The patient is asked to touch his nose with the index finger of one hand. Then he is asked to touch the examiner's index finger. He is asked to do this multiple times, while the examiner keeps moving his index finger from place to place. It is important to ensure that the patient has to stretch his upper limb to reach the examiner's finger, so that the coordination can be assessed over the full range of motion of the upper limb. Lower limb coordination is tested by heel-shin test. The test is done with the patient lying down on a bed. They are asked to put the heel of one leg onto the shin of the other leg, just below the knee. They are then asked to run the heel down the front of the shin till the dorsum of the foot. Patients with cerebellar lesions will have a tremor when trying to place the heel on the shin, and will be unable to accurately run the heel down the entire length of the shin. The functioning of the posterior column tracts (option B) is assessed by Romberg's test. While performing Romberg's test, the patient is asked to stand with his feet close together, initially with his eyes open. If the patient is able to maintain their balance with the eyes open, they are asked to close their eyes. If they lose their balance and sway or fall with their eyes closed, the test is said to be positive. The examiner needs to be prepared to support the patient in case they are about to fall.  Patients with disorders of the posterior column tracts will have impaired proprioception, and will have a positive Romberg's test. If the patient has dizziness or a tendency to fall even with the eyes open, then the lesion is likely to be in the vestibular system or cerebellum, and other relevant tests should be performed.

text: 15. Which of the following is the best method to detect HbA1c?

text: 23. A 40-year-old patient with a history of tuberculosis presents with dyspnea on exertion. On examination, it is noted that the JVP rises during inspiration. A chest radiograph of the patient is given below. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Constrictive pericarditis

The given clinical scenario of a patient with a history of tuberculosis now presenting with positive Kussmaul's sign, and pericardial calcification seen on chest radiograph suggest a diagnosis of constrictive pericarditis.  Constrictive pericarditis is a chronic type of pericarditis that results when there is healing of acute fibrinous pericarditis or absorption of chronic pericardial effusion. While the most common cause in developing countries is tuberculosis, in developed countries, it occurs following viral pericarditis, cardiac surgery, mediastinal irradiation, or as a manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis and SLE. The main abnormality which occurs in constrictive pericarditis is the inability of the ventricles to fill because of the rigid and thickened pericardium. Unlike tamponade, this restriction is not uniform through the diastole. Ventricular filling is normal early in the diastole but stops suddenly when the elastic limit of the pericardium is reached. Y-descent on the JVP curve is prominent in constrictive pericarditis because it represents the rapid early filling of the ventricles. A sudden stop in ventricular filling and subsequent rising pressure is seen as a square root sign in the JVP curve. The patient presents with exertional dyspnea and orthopnea. There may be a paradoxical rise in venous pressure during inspiration (Kussmaul's sign). Apart from constrictive pericarditis, Kussmaul's sign can be positive in tricuspid stenosis, restrictive cardiomyopathy, right heart failure, and pulmonary embolism. The ECG often shows low-voltage QRS complexes and diffuse flattening of T-waves. A chest radiograph may show pericardial calcification, especially in tuberculous pericarditis.

The only cause of metabolic alkalosis from the given options is vomiting. The compensatory response is respiratory, where the body retains CO₂ (hypoventilation) to counteract the alkalosis. This explains the elevated pCO₂ 48 mmHg [normal limits (35 - 45 mmHg)]. However, compensation is incomplete, as the pH remains alkalotic. expl:
Correct answer: C. Supranuclear facial palsy on the right side

The given clinical scenario of a young male presenting with weakness of the lower half of the left side of his face and presence of wrinkling on the forehead and normal eyelid closure indicates an upper motor neuron lesion (UMN). The most appropriate diagnosis is supranuclear facial palsy on the right side. In facial palsy, the angle of the mouth deviates towards the normal side. In this patient, since the mouth deviates towards the right, the left facial nerve is affected.  In an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion, wrinkling on the forehead and eyelid closure remains intact. In this lesion, the contralateral side of the face is affected. The first-order neurons from the right cerebral hemisphere cross over (right to left) at the cortical level and relay in the left facial nerve nucleus in the pons. From here the second-order neurons (left facial nerve) descend and supply the left side of the face.  Hence, right UMN lesion causes paralysis of the lower half of the face on the left side and can cause drooping on the left side.

text: 4. What is correct about first-degree heart block?

options.A: Normal PR and prolonged RR interval
options.B: Prolonged PR and normal RR interval
options.D: Short PR and normal RR interval

expl:
Correct answer: B. Prolonged PR and normal RR interval

The correct statement about the first-degree heart block is the ECG shows prolonged PR and normal RR interval. First-degree heart block is characterized by a fixed, prolonged PR interval without any dropped beats. It indicates a delay in conduction through the AV node, but all atrial impulses still reach the ventricles. It is most often asymptomatic. Canon waves are observed in JVP. It carries a very good prognosis and no treatment is needed. A heart block is caused by an interruption of impulse conduction within the conducting system of the heart. It may be sinoatrial, atrioventricular, or intraventricular. Atrioventricular blocks are further divided into type I, type II and type III blocks. The type II blocks are subdivided into Mobitz type I and Mobitz type II blocks.  First Degree Heart Block: It occurs due to slowing of conduction through the AV junction. It is characterized by prolonged PR > 0.2s and equal RR intervals. Second Degree Heart Block: It occurs due to the intermittent failure of electrical impulse conduction from the atrium to the ventricle. It is characterized by a missed QRS. It is of two types: * Mobitz type 1/ Wenckebach occurs due to the decremental conduction of electrical impulses in the AV node. It is characterized by a progressive PR elongation leading to an eventual drop in the QRS complex. This may be seen in young athletes. * Mobitz type 2 occurs in the distal or infra-His conduction system and is often associated with intraventricular conduction delays.  It is characterized by an intermittent failure of conduction of the p wave without any change in the preceding impulses. On ECG there is a fixed PR interval and missed QRS. Third Degree Heart Block/Complete Heart Block It occurs when none of the impulses from the atria are conducted to the ventricles. It is characterized by * Escape rhythm * RR equal, PP equal * P waves > QRS waves * No relationship between P & QRS. Pearl PF1792: Types of Heart block Pearl PF1793: Normal ECG waves and intervals

text: 6. A young lady presents with recent-onset palpitations and dizziness. Her ECG shows absent P waves and an irregularly irregular RR interval. Her pulse rate is 140 bpm and BP is 80/60 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Synchronized cardioversion

In the given clinical scenario, the patient presenting with recent-onset palpitations and dizziness with ECG showing irregularly irregular rhythm with absent p waves, is suggestive of atrial fibrillation. Since the patient is hemodynamically compromised (hypotension), synchronized cardioversion is the most appropriate management. Urgent electrical cardioversion is indicated if a patient with AF has shock or severe hypotension, pulmonary edema or ongoing myocardial infarction. Although there is a risk of potential thromboembolism if the patient has not been put on anticoagulation before, the need for rate control outweighs this risk. In these patients, heart rate control is achieved using IV β-blockers or calcium channel blockers like verapamil (Option B) or diltiazem. Additionally, they are also given subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin as soon as possible. In hemodynamically stable patients with AF of >48 hours duration or unknown duration, there is a high risk of formation of a thrombus in the left atrium. If the patients are cardioverted at this stage, this thrombus can embolize into the systemic circulation, leading to end organ damage, such as stroke. Therefore, for these patients, any of the following two management strategies can be followed: * Give anticoagulation for 3 weeks → cardioversion (pharmacological or electrical) → continue anticoagulation for 4 more weeks * Start anticoagulation and do transesophageal echocardiography → if thrombus is absent, do cardioversion (pharmacological or electrical) → continue anticoagulation for 4 more weeks. If a thrombus is present, then cardioversion is delayed by 3 weeks. Direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are preferred over warfarin for anticoagulation. However, warfarin is the preferred drug if the patient has a mechanical prosthetic valve, advanced CKD or moderate-severe mitral stenosis. Apart from anticoagulation, the most important aspect of the treatment of chronic AF is rate control. The drugs used for this are β blockers (such as metoprolol) and calcium channel blockers (such as diltiazem and verapamil). Reversion to sinus rhythm can be done electrically or using medications. Pharmacological cardioversion can be done using ibutilide, dofetilide and amiodarone (class III antiarryhthmics- Option A) or flecainide and propafenone (class Ic drugs). Atrial fibrillation rhythm is irregularly irregular. P waves are absent, these irregular waves are known as fibrillation waves, characteristic of atrial fibrillation. Other options: Option C: Adenosine is the first-line drug for Supraventricular tachycardia. It blocks conduction across the AV node and terminates the SVT. It is given as a 6-18 mg bolus
