text: 9. A patient presents with progressive increase in shortness of breath. On examination, left parasternal heave is noted. On auscultation, a systolic murmur is heard. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Pulmonary stenosis

The patient presents with worsening shortness of breath, and examination reveals a left parasternal heave and a systolic murmur on auscultation, pointing to the diagnosis of pulmonary stenosis. Pulmonary stenosis is a congenital heart defect where there is a narrowing of the pulmonary valve or the area just below the valve, obstructing blood flow from the right ventricle to the lungs. This leads to increased pressure in the right ventricle, causing it to work harder to pump blood. The condition may range from mild to severe and can result in symptoms like shortness of breath, fatigue, and cyanosis in severe cases. On physical examination, a left parasternal heave is often noted due to right ventricular hypertrophy, and auscultation typically reveals a systolic ejection murmur heard best at the upper left sternal border. If left untreated, severe pulmonary stenosis can lead to right heart failure and other complications. Treatment may involve balloon valvuloplasty or surgery, depending on the severity of the obstruction. Other options: Option A: Pulmonary regurgitation is the backward flow of blood into the right ventricle due to insufficient closure of the pulmonary valve. It often presents with a diastolic murmur heard at the left upper sternal border and can lead to right heart enlargement if severe.  Option C: Pulmonary artery hypertension is a condition characterized by elevated blood pressure in the pulmonary arteries, leading to strain on the right side of the heart. Symptoms may include shortness of breath, fatigue, and chest pain, and it can result from various causes like lung diseases or heart conditions. Option D: Pulmonary embolism is a blockage in one of the pulmonary arteries, usually caused by a blood clot that travels to the lungs from the legs (deep vein thrombosis). It can lead to symptoms like sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, and potentially life-threatening complications if untreated.

The given clinical scenario of a patient with a history of infection two weeks ago who develops progressively ascending, bilaterally symmetric flaccid weakness in the lower limbs, later affecting the upper limbs and on examination absent spinal cord reflexes are seen. These findings suggest a likely diagnosis of Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (AIDP). AIDP is the most common type of Guillain-Barre syndrome(GBS). GBS is usually associated with a history of upper respiratory infection (URI) or acute gastroenteritis (AGE) 1-3 weeks prior. The causative organisms may be Campylobacter jejuni, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. It presents with ascending motor paralysis, primarily affecting the lower limbs before progressing to the upper limbs. Sensory deficits may or may not be present, while deep tendon reflexes are absent. In severe cases, transient bladder dysfunction can occur. Autonomic manifestations include loss of vasomotor control, postural hypotension, and cardiac dysrhythmias. Histological examination shows inflammation of peripheral nerves, manifested as perivenular and endoneurial infiltration by lymphocytes, macrophages, and a few plasma cells. On electron microscopy, an early effect on myelin sheaths is seen. There is segmental demyelination induced by the actions of activated macrophages. There are several types of Guillain–Barre syndrome: * Demyelinating: * Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) - most common. * Axonal: * Acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN). * Acute motor-sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN). * Regional GBS syndromes: Miller–Fisher syndrome (MFS). Diagnosis is made upon clinical presentation. CSF findings of elevated protein without pleocytosis help to rule out other similar conditions. Treatment includes initiating intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIg) or plasmapheresis. IVIg is the initial therapy preferred, as it has a better safety record. In severe cases, patients may require ventilatory support.   Other options:  Option B: Multiple sclerosis is characterized by chronic inflammation and demyelination that causes multiple neurological symptoms such as optic neuritis, muscle spasticity, and facial weakness. The presence of oligoclonal bands on protein electrophoresis is diagnostic.  Option C: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) differs from Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) as it involves both upper and lower motor neuron degeneration, whereas GBS is a purely lower motor neuron disorder. Additionally, ALS progresses gradually without sensory loss, while GBS has an acute onset and may involve sensory symptoms. Option D: Transverse myelitis differs from Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) as it involves spinal cord inflammation, leading to a sensory level, bowel/bladder dysfunction, and often spasticity, whereas GBS primarily affects the peripheral nerves with ascending flaccid paralysis. Additionally, MRI shows spinal cord lesions in transverse myelitis, while GBS is diagnosed through nerve conduction studies and CSF analysis. Some B cells, activated via a T cell–independent mechanism, secrete primarily IgM * The activated B cells escape from Peyer’s patches into regional lymph nodes. * Activated T cells also function to assist in the opening of the blood-nerve barrier, facilitating penetration of pathogenic autoantibodies. * The earliest changes in myelin consist of edema between myelin lamellae and vesicular disruption of the outermost myelin layers. * These effects are associated with activation of the C5b-C9 membrane attack complex and mediated by calcium entry; it is possible that the macrophage cytokine tumor necrosis factor (TNF) also participates in myelin damage. text: 12. Chvostek's sign is seen in?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Hypocalcemia

The Chvostek's sign is seen in hypocalcemia. Chvostek's sign is a clinical indicator of hypocalcemia, seen in conditions like hypoparathyroidism and vitamin D deficiency. It is elicited by gently tapping the facial nerve just anterior to the ear, which triggers involuntary twitching of the facial muscles, particularly around the mouth and eye. While a positive Chvostek's sign suggests neuromuscular excitability due to low calcium levels, it is not always specific, as mild twitching can also occur in healthy individuals. This sign is often assessed alongside Trousseau's sign to confirm hypocalcemia. Trousseau’s sign indicates hypocalcemia and is demonstrated by inflating a blood pressure cuff above the systolic level for 180 seconds. This causes an involuntary carpal spasm, resulting in contraction of the hand and fingers. It signifies increased neuromuscular excitability due to low calcium levels. Symptoms and signs of hypocalcemia include: * laryngeal spasms   * mild digital circumoral numbness * cardiac arrhythmias * paresthesia * Chvostek's sign and Trousseau's sign, as shown in the images below.

text: 15. A patient with a history of pneumonia develops pleural effusion. What is the expected finding in the pleural fluid analysis for parapneumonic effusion?

options.A: Pleural protein ratio less than 0.5 of serum protein
options.B: Pleural LDH less than 2/3rd of serum LDH
options.D: Pleural LDH less than 0.6 of serum LDH

expl:
Correct answer: C. Pleural pH less than 7.2

In the above clinical scenario of a patient with a history of pneumonia who develops a pleural effusion, the expected finding in the pleural fluid analysis for parapneumonic effusion is pleural pH less than 7.2. Pleural effusion refers to the pathological accumulation of fluid in the pleural space due to: * excess fluid formation from the interstitial spaces of the lung, parietal pleura or peritoneal cavity * decreased fluid removal by the lymphatics Pleural effusion may present with: * dyspnea * pleuritic pain * dry cough * associated symptoms like fever, weight loss, oedema, and ascites depending on the aetiology. On examination, there may be: * tachypnea, in a large effusion * dullness to percussion * decreased/absent breath sounds at the base(s) * other signs present vary with the underlying aetiology. The aetiology of pleural effusion can be: * Exudative: Due to a disruption in pleural fluid formation and drainage because of local factors. * Transudative: Due to a disruption in pleural fluid formation and drainage due to systemic factors. Light’s criteria can be used to differentiate between transudative and exudative pleural effusions. Exudative effusions will meet at least one of the following criteria: * Pleural fluid protein/serum protein >0.5. * Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH >0.6. * Pleural fluid LDH is more than two-thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum and pleural pH less than 7.2. Recommended tests for all diagnostic thoracocentesis include: * Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and protein * Microscopy and culture * Cytology and differential count * Glucose, pH, triglycerides, amylase, hematocrit, AFB culture, and PCR can be done if a particular aetiology is suspected. If the difference between the protein levels in the serum and the pleural fluid is > 3.1 g/dL, it is likely to be transudative pleural effusion. If the glucose levels are less than 60mg/dL, then the effusion is likely due to exudative causes like malignancy, bacterial infections (parapneumonic effusion), and rheumatoid pleuritis. If the pleural fluid cytology, culture, glucose, and staining do not yield any result, perform spiral CT to rule out pulmonary embolism and assess the markers of tuberculosis. 17. A 50-year-old patient presents with respiratory difficulty and a history of chronic smoking for the last 30 years. Pulmonary function testing shows a decrease in FEV1% and FEV1/FVC ratio. What is the most probable diagnosis?

COPD-Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
expl:
Correct answer: A. COPD

The given clinical scenario including symptoms of respiratory difficulty and history of chronic smoking along with pulmonary function testing revealing a reduced FEV1% and FEV1/FVC ratio is indicative of an obstructive disorder - Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD). These values are measured as a part of the pulmonary function test known as spirometry. At a given lung volume, when a person inhales to the total lung capacity and exhales as hard and completely as possible, the volume of expired air is recorded as forced vital capacity (FVC), and the volume of air expired in the first second is called the forced expiratory volume (FEV1). In obstructive disorders, a large amount of air gets trapped in the lungs. Due to airway obstruction, it is more difficult to exhale than inhale. As a result, residual volume increases greatly. Difficulty in exhalation leads to a decreased FVC. FEV1 decreases much more than the decrease in FVC. Hence the FEV1% also falls. Obstructive disorders include-  * Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) - emphysema, chronic bronchitis * Bronchiectasis * Asthma The severity of COPD is assessed by using the Global Initiative for Lung Disease (GOLD) criteria. In pulmonary function testing, a postbronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio of <0.70 is considered diagnostic for COPD.  The Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) system categorizes COPD into the following stages,

text: 18. A 6-month-old child is noted to have muscle weakness. Vitals Pulse: 80/min, BP 70/50 mm Hg. The workup shows metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia and hypomagnesemia. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Gitelman syndrome

The given clinical scenario of a 6-month-old child presenting with muscle weakness with a pulse of 80/min and BP 70/50 mm Hg (hypotension) with metabolic alkalosis, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesemia is suggestive of Gitelman syndrome. Gitelman syndrome occurs due to a mutation of Na+/Cl- cotransporter in the distal collecting tubule (DCT). The resulting impairment of the tubular transport leads to the following features: * Mild natriuresis with normal-low BP. * Increased renin and aldosterone. * Hypokalemia. * Metabolic alkalosis. * Hypercalcemia and hypocalciuria. * Hypomagnesemia. The clinical features of this condition are similar to the effects of thiazide diuretics. These drugs also act on the Na+/Cl- cotransporter. Hence, the response to thiazide diuretics may be blunted. Treatment is with potassium-sparing diuretics like spironolactone and amiloride. Option A: Bartter syndrome affects the Na+/K+/Cl- channels. It causes hypocalcemia and hypercalciuria. Option C: Conn syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) is caused by excessive aldosterone production, leading to hypertension and low potassium, while Gitelman syndrome is a genetic kidney disorder causing low potassium, low magnesium, and low blood pressure. Unlike Conn syndrome, Gitelman syndrome does not cause hypertension but leads to chronic electrolyte imbalances. Option D: Dent's disease is a rare X-linked renal disorder characterized by proximal tubulopathy, leading toband progressive kidney dysfunction. It is caused by mutations in the CLCN5 or OCRL genes, affecting renal tubular function.

text: 19. A patient presents with a unilateral throbbing headache in the temporal region and light sensitivity associated with photophobia, nausea and vomiting. She reports that each episode lasts for a maximum of 24 hours, which was relieved by giving triptans. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Migraine

The clinical picture of throbbing unilateral headache, light sensitivity associated with photophobia, nausea and vomiting and responsiveness to triptans indicates a diagnosis of migraine. Migraine is the second most common cause of headaches, after tension headaches. It is characterized by unilateral and throbbing headaches of moderate to severe intensity. Other features of migraine include deep-seated pain and sensitivity to environmental and sensory stimuli. The headache can be triggered by glares, bright lights, sounds, hunger, stress, physical exertion, hormonal fluctuations during menses, lack of or excess sleep, or alcohol. Management of migraine includes nonpharmacologic management and pharmacologic measures. Triggers unique to the patient should be avoided. Lifestyle modifications to avoid excessive caffeine and alcohol, and to maintain a healthy sleep cycle are necessary. Pharmacological treatment can be divided into abortive treatment of acute attacks and prophylaxis to prevent acute attacks. Acute attacks can be treated with acetaminophen, aspirin NSAIDs, antiemetics and triptans. Triptans (Sumatriptan, Zolmitriptan) are used in moderate to severe migraine or when simple analgesics have not been effective. Prophylaxis with beta-blockers like propranolol, valproate, and topiramate. Migraine is associated with the release of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) within the trigeminal nucleus. Hence, newer therapies using CGRP antagonists and monoclonal antibodies to CGRP and its receptor are effective in treating and preventing migraine. They are considered to be as effective as triptans and are better tolerated.  Other options: Option A: Anxiety primarily involves psychological symptoms like excessive worry, restlessness, and rapid heartbeat, while migraines are neurological and present with severe headaches, nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound. Anxiety can sometimes trigger migraines, but they are distinct conditions with different underlying causes. Option B: Hypertension is a chronic condition characterized by persistently high blood pressure, often without immediate symptoms, while migraines are episodic and involve severe headaches with nausea and sensory sensitivity. Unlike migraines, hypertension can lead to long-term complications like heart disease and stroke. Option D: Tension headache is a common type of headache characterized by a dull, bilateral, pressing or tightening pain, often described as a "band around the head." It is typically triggered by stress, poor posture, or muscle tension and does not involve nausea or sensitivity to light and sound. Pearl PF1050: Simplified diagnostic criteria for migraine Repeated attacks of headache lasting 4-72 h in patients with a normal physical examination, no other reasonable cause for the headache, and At Least 2 of the following features * Unilateral pain * Throbbing pain * Aggravation by movement * Moderate or severe intensity Plus at Least 1 of the following features * Nausea/vomiting * Photophobia and phonophobia

text: 20. A 47-year-old hypertensive woman came to your clinic complaining of bone pain. She has a history of recurrent renal stones. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Thiazide diuretics

Given the clinical picture of a 47-year-old hypertensive woman with bone pain and recurrent renal stones, the most likely diagnosis is hyperparathyroidism (often primary hyperparathyroidism) and the most appropriate management for the given condition is thiazide diuretics. Thiazides reduce calcium excretion in the urine, which can help prevent the formation of kidney stones in hyperparathyroidism and help manage the hypercalcemia associated with it. Hyperparathyroidism is a condition characterized by the overproduction of parathyroid hormone (PTH) by the parathyroid glands, leading to elevated levels of calcium in the blood (hypercalcemia). There are two main types: primary hyperparathyroidism, where an abnormality within the parathyroid glands (often an adenoma) causes excessive PTH production, and secondary hyperparathyroidism, typically caused by chronic kidney disease, which leads to low calcium levels and compensatory increased PTH secretion.
Primary hyperparathyroidism Secondary hyperparathyroidism Tertiary hyperparathyroidism

Primary hyperparathyroidism is one of the most common endocrine disorders, and it is an important cause of hypercalcemia. Tumours of the parathyroid glands usually come to attention because of excessive secretion of PTH rather than mass effects. It can also be associated with MEN1 and MEN 2A syndromes.  The clinical manifestations of hyperparathyroidism can be summarized as “painful bones, renal stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans.” Skeletal manifestations of hyperparathyroidism include bone resorption, osteitis fibrosa cystica, and brown tumours. Renal changes include nephrolithiasis (stones) and nephrocalcinosis. Localisation of parathyroid is difficult. Nuclear medicine scanning with radiolabeled Sestamibi is a widely used technique. Sestamibi accumulates in parathyroid adenomas. This radionuclide is concentrated in the thyroid and parathyroid tissue but usually washes out of normal thyroid tissue in under an hour. It persists in abnormal parathyroid tissue. It is now regarded as the most accurate and reliable method for imaging the parathyroid glands. Option C: Calcitriol is not appropriate in this case, as it is a form of active vitamin D that increases calcium absorption, which could exacerbate hypercalcemia. Option D: Calcium gluconate is not appropriate here, as calcium gluconate is used to treat hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia. Pearl PF0938: Causes of Hypercalcemia

21. A boy comes with the history of passing of black urine during the night time, and on further investigation, CD55 and CD59 markers were negative . Which condition is the boy most likely suffering from?

The boy is most likely suffering from Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH). This condition is characterized by hemolysis and dark-coloured urine (due to hemoglobinuria), and the negative CD55 and CD59 markers indicate a deficiency of protective proteins in red blood cells, which is a hallmark of PNH. PNH is an acquired chronic hemolytic anaemia with persistent intravascular hemolysis. It is due to an acquired mutation in the X-linked phosphatidylinositol class A PIG-A gene causing deficiency of GPI. GPI  Anchors CD55 & CD59 to cell membrane. The deficiency of CD55 and CD59 makes the RBC sensitive to complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis. PNH is characterized by hemolytic anaemia, pancytopenia, and venous thrombosis involving cerebral, hepatic, renal, portal, and abdominal veins. Laboratory findings show- * Decreased haemoglobin concentration * Decreased haptoglobin levels  * Increased unconjugated haemoglobin * Elevated LDH  * Increased reticulocyte count  * Negative Coombs test. PNH is diagnosed using flow cytometry. Note- The tendency of red cells to lyse at night is explained by a slight decrease in blood pH during sleep. This increases the activity of complement. Option B: In Acquired Immune Hemolytic Anemia(AIHA) , autoantibodies against RBC antigens are produced which coat the RBC membrane. The Fc portion of the antibody is recognized by the Fc receptor on macrophages causing phagocytosis. 22. A child with short stature and developmental delay comes to your clinic. On investigation, low calcium, high phosphate and very high PTH are found. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? 

PTH-Parathyroid hormone
expl:
Correct answer: C. Pseudohypoparathyroidism

Based on the given clinical scenario of a child with short stature and developmental delay with low Calcium, high Phosphate and very high PTH, the most likely diagnosis is Pseudohypoparathyroidism (PHP) Pseudohypoparathyroidism (PHP) is a condition where the body is resistant to parathyroid hormone (PTH) despite its excessive production. This leads to low calcium, high phosphate, and very high PTH, as the kidneys and bones do not respond to PTH signals. The associated short stature and developmental delay are characteristic of Albright’s hereditary osteodystrophy (AHO), a subtype of PHP. In hypoparathyroidism, there is low PTH, leading to low calcium and high phosphate. However, in this case, the child has very high PTH, which suggests that the parathyroid glands are producing enough hormone, but the body's tissues are not responding to it properly. Pseudohypoparathyroidism is an inherited disorder that is characterized by hypocalcemia and characteristic skeletal features, known as Albright's hereditary osteodystrophy (AHO). It is due to the loss of function mutation in genes encoding the alpha subunit of the stimulatory G-protein Gsα. This blocks the action of PTH, leading to reduced serum calcium and increased serum phosphate. The correct statement regarding intrinsic acute kidney injury is BUN: Creatinine < 20:1 AKI (acute kidney injury) is defined as a decline in kidney function within 7 days, resulting in the accumulation of nitrogenous waste and other toxic metabolites usually excreted in the urine. It includes a variety of conditions that share some common features such as elevated creatinine levels and reduced urine output. It is broadly divided into three categories: * Prerenal azotemia  * Intrinsic parenchymal disease * Postrenal obstruction Intrinsic causes can further be divided into acute tubular necrosis, acute glomerulonephritis, and acute interstitial nephritis. Ischemia and nephrotoxins are the main causes of acute tubular necrosis. Nephrotoxins can be exogeneous such as vancomycin, cisplatin, and iodinated contrast agents used for CT imaging. Endogenous toxins include myoglobin, uric acid, and haemoglobin. Crush injuries, heat stroke, and myopathies can result in rhabdomyolysis releasing large amounts of myoglobin. The urine/plasma creatinine ratio is usually ≤ 40. In acute tubular necrosis, urinary sodium is >20 mEq/L.  Prerenal azotemia arises due to a reduced renal plasma flow. Common causes include hypovolemia, liver failure, and congestive heart failure. The urine/plasma creatinine ratio is ≥ 40 and urinary sodium is usually <20mEq/L. Bladder outlet obstruction, urethral obstruction, and benign prostatic hyperplasia lead to postrenal azotemia. Urinary sodium can be variable. text: 24. A patient has visual disturbance and pain abdomen after drinking from a local shop. Which metabolite is responsible for that?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Formic acid

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of methanol toxicity, and the metabolite responsible is formic acid. Methanol poisoning is caused by to ingestion of illicit liquor which contains ethanol adulterated with methanol. Methanol is metabolized to formaldehyde and formic acid by alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases, respectively. The metabolites of methanol are responsible for the toxic effects. Clinically, patients present with headache, vomiting, abdomen pain, uneasiness, confusion, delirium, and coma. Formic acid specifically damages the retina and optic nerve and results in blurring of vision and blindness. Elevated levels of formic acid and other organic acids result in metabolic acidosis in arterial blood gas analysis(ABG). Treatment of methanol poisoning includes gastric lavage with sodium bicarbonate if the patient is brought within 2 hours of ingesting methanol to combat acidosis. Ethanol infusion since ethanol is preferentially metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase over methanol and helps by reducing the rate of generation of formaldehyde and formic acid. Fomepizole is a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase and the drug of choice for methanol poisoning. Folate therapy with calcium leucovorin reduces blood formate levels by enhancing its oxidation. Hemodialysis is used in severe cases of methanol toxicity. text: 26. The INR ratio recommended for the administration of warfarin in patients with mechanical heart valves is ______________
expl:
Correct answer: C. 2.5 – 3.5

The INR ratio recommended for the administration of warfarin in patients with mechanical heart valves is around 2.5-3.5. Prothrombin time is sensitive to the reduction in levels of prothrombin, factor VII, and factor X. The test is performed by adding thromboplastin, which is a reagent containing tissue factor, phospholipid and calcium to citrated plasma and determining the time to clot formation. Due to the variable sensitivity of thromboplastin, the International normalized ratio (INR) was developed to standardize the reporting of prothrombin time. In INR, the patient’s prothrombin time is divided by mean normal prothrombin time and this ratio is multiplied by the International Sensitivity Index (ISI) of the particular thromboplastin reagent. Warfarin therapy should be monitored with INR every 3–4 weeks. The target INR is 2.0–3.0. In patients with mechanical heart valves, the target INR is 2.5–3.5. Other options: Option A: The INR range of 1.0-1.5 means the state of body is in hypercoaguable state and itis too low for beneficial effects, hence it is not recommended. Option B: In most of the patients on regular warfarin therapy,  the  target INR is around 2.0-3.0, but it is not recommended in patients with mechanical heart valve. Option D: INR >3.5 (3.5- 4.5)can result in increased adverse effects like bleeding and is not recommended for any condition.

Acute kidney injury (AKI) is defined as an increase in serum creatinine by 1.5 times of baseline value over 7 days. Acute kidney injury is defined as an abrupt (within hours) decrease in kidney function, which encompasses both injury (structural damage) and impairment (loss of function). It is characterized by abrupt deterioration in kidney function, manifested by an increase in serum creatinine level with or without reduced urine output. AKI is defined as any of the following: * Increase in serum creatinine to ≥1.5 times baseline (50% higher), which is known or presumed to have occurred within the prior 7 days. * Increase in serum creatinine by ≥0.3 mg/dL from baseline within 48 hours. * Urine volume of <0.5 ml/kg/h for 6 hours.

text: 30. A patient presents with fatigue and chronic diarrhea for 4 months. Endoscopy reveals several ulcers in the gastric antrum and the descending duodenum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of gastrinoma Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.  Zollinger Ellison Syndrome (ZES)/Gastrinoma is a neuroendocrinal tumour characterized by hypersecretion of gastrin resulting in gastrointestinal tract ulcers. It occurs more commonly in a sporadic pattern but can be associated with MEN-1 (multiple endocrine neoplasia-1) syndromes in the familial pattern. Gastrinoma is most commonly located in the gastrinoma triangle (Passaro's triangle) bounded by the lines connecting the: * cystic duct * the junction between the second and third parts of the duodenum * the junction between the neck and body of the pancreas The most common presentations of gastrinoma are epigastric pain, diarrhoea, and peptic ulcers. The ulcers occur at typical locations (proximal duodenum) and atypical locations (distal duodenum, jejunum). Duodenal ulcers are the most common. Gastrinoma if associated with marked gastric acid production and recurrent peptic ulcer is called Zollinger Ellison syndrome. Diagnosis:  The gastric pH <2, basal acid output >15 mEq/hr and serum gastrin concentration more than 1000 pg/ml (normal is <100 pg/ml) confirm the diagnosis of gastrinoma. When the diagnosis is in doubt (like gastrin levels 100-1000 pg/ml), then a secretin test is performed. A secretin test is considered positive when serum gastrin levels are more than 200 pg/ml on secretin administration and confirms the diagnosis of gastrinoma. For localization of the tumour for surgical management, CT or MRI scans should be done first. If the tumour is not localized on these scans, then somatostatin receptor scintigraphy or endoscopic ultrasound is done for better localization. Treatment of ZES : High-dose Proton Pump Inhibitor followed by surgery. Surgeries that can be done are: * Distal Pancreatectomy– if lesion in body or tail of the pancreas * Enucleation– if lesion in the head of the pancreas * Full-thickness excision– if lesion in duodenum * MEN associated– surgery done only if size>2.5cm Other options: Option A: VIPoma is characterized by watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome). It is caused by the release of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) from the tumor. Option C: Glucagonomas, α-cell tumors are associated with increased serum levels of glucagon. The patient presents with mild diabetes mellitus, a characteristic skin rash (necrolytic migratory erythema), and anemia. They occur most frequently in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women and are characterized by extremely high plasma glucagon levels. Option D: Insulinomas, β-cell tumors are the most common pancreatic endocrine neoplasms. These are usually benign and often cause symptomatic hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemic symptoms appear when blood glucose levels fall below 50 mg/dL. The symptoms usually develop after fasting or exertion and improve after glucose intake. Pearl PF2047: Clinical features of gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome) Most common symptom: Abdominal pain. Gastrin hypersecretion stimulates gastric acid secretion, leading to peptic ulcers that occur at atypical sites like the duodenum and jejunum and are refractory and multiple. Diarrhea is due to * Acid-induced injury to the small intestine mucosa * Inability of the intestinal tract to absorb large volumes of fluids secreted by the stomach * Inactivation of pancreatic lipase by low pH * Precipitation of bile salts. The unique characteristic of acid-induced diarrhea is that it is controlled by nasogastric aspiration of gastric secretions. text: 31. A 52-year-old woman complains of fatigue, dry skin and cold intolerance since 2 weeks. She was started on amiodarone 1 month ago for persistent atrial fibrillation. Tests show high TSH (15 mU/l) and low free T4 levels. How would you manage this patient?

Thyroxine supplementation is indicated for amiodarone induced hypothyroidism which is characterized by symptoms of hypothyroidism (fatigue, dry skin, cold intolerance) and lab findings (elevated TSH, reduced free T4) following amiodarone use. Amiodarone-induced hypothyroidism (AIH) can occur shortly after (as early as 2 weeks) amiodarone use due to iodine induced thyroid suppression (Wolff Chaikoff effect). It is characterized by clinical features of hypothyroidism and lab findings of elevated TSH and reduced free T4. It occurs more frequently in women and those with positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies. It is managed by thyroxine supplementation, without the need to discontinue amiodarone (Option A). Amiodarone is an iodine-containing compound that is structurally related to thyroid hormone. It is a class III antiarrhythmic drug, which increases the duration of an action potential by blocking potassium channels, thereby increasing the time taken for repolarization. It is used to maintain normal sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillation. Amiodarone can cause hypothyroidism due to the Wolff-Chaikoff effect, where excessive iodine leads to transient inhibition of organification and synthesis of thyroid hormones. Patients with underlying autoimmune thyroid disease are at increased risk of amiodarone-induced hypothyroidism. Other adverse effects of amiodarone include hypotension, bradycardia, myocardial depression, photosensitization, corneal microdeposits (corneal verticillata), pulmonary fibrosis, and peripheral neuropathy. Other options:  Option C: Corticosteroids would be indicated in amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis and not amiodarone induced hypothyroidism. Option D: Patients who are asymptomatic, with subclinical hypothyroidism following amiodarone use can be managed by observation and regular monitoring with thyroid function tests. Subclinical hypothyroidism is characterized by TSH level > 4.5 and ≤ 10 mU/l, normal FT4 and absence of clinical features of hypothyroidism.

text: 16. A 10-year-old child presents with brown-colored urine, flank pain, and fatigue for the last 3 days. He has 2+ proteinuria with 20 red cells/HPF and dysmorphic red blood cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

A child presenting with acute onset (3 days) flank pain, cola-colored urine, and mild to moderate proteinuria is suggestive of a nephritic syndrome picture. The only disease which causes this out of the given options is post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). PSGN is primarily caused by group A β-hemolytic streptococcal infections in children aged 5 to 12 years. It is caused by immune complexes containing streptococcal antigens (M protein of cell wall) and specific antibodies. PSGN typically manifests as an acute nephritic syndrome, appearing either 1 to 2 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis or 3 to 6 weeks after streptococcal pyoderma. The severity of kidney involvement can vary, ranging from asymptomatic microscopic hematuria with normal renal function to gross hematuria with acute renal failure. Edema, hypertension, and oliguria may be present depending on the extent of renal involvement. Laboratory findings commonly include a significant decrease in serum C3 levels during the acute phase, with values returning to normal within 6 to 8 weeks. To confirm the diagnosis, evidence of a preceding streptococcal infection is necessary. The antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer often increases following pharyngitis, while the anti-deoxyribonuclease B level is a reliable indicator of cutaneous streptococcal infection. Light microscopic examination reveals enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with diffuse mesangial and endothelial proliferation, as well as leukocyte infiltration. Immunofluorescence analysis demonstrates granular deposits of IgG and complement C3 along the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) and in the mesangium. Electron microscopy primarily shows subepithelial humps, with subendothelial deposits observed in early stages of the disease. Managing the acute effects of renal insufficiency (sodium restriction and diuretics) and hypertension is the mainstay. Antibiotic therapy with a 10-day course of penicillin is recommended to limit the spread of nephritogenic pathogens. But antibiotics do not alter the natural course of PSGN. Complete resolution of the hematuria and proteinuria in the majority of children occurs within 3–6 weeks of the onset of nephritis but 3–10% of children may have persistent microscopic hematuria, non-nephrotic proteinuria, or hypertension. text: 22. A female weighing 40 kg has a serum sodium level of 120 mEq/L. Calculate the sodium deficit for a desired sodium concentration of 140 mEq/L.
expl:
Correct answer: A. 400 mEq

The sodium deficit in this case is 400 mEq. It is calculated by Sodium deficit (mEq) = Total body water (TBW) x (Desired sodium concentration - Current sodium concentration) Where, TBW = 0.6 x body weight in kilograms, for males, and         = 0.5 x body weight in kilograms, for females Hence, in this case: Sodium deficit = 0.5 x 40 x (140 - 120)                           = 0.5. x 40 x 20                            = 400 mEq Rapid sodium correction of 4–6 mEq/L should be achieved in the first 6 hours of therapy for patients with acute hyponatremia. In chronic hyponatremia, sodium correction must be slow and gradual, less than 6–8 mEq/L in the first 24 hours and/ or under 18 mEq /L in the first 48 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome.

text: 26. A male patient was brought to the emergency room with complaints of headache, vomiting, and blurring of vision after he consumed some locally produced spirit. Which of the following is used for the treatment of his condition?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Fomepizole

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of methanol toxicity. Ethanol and fomepizole is used for the treatment of this condition. Methanol poisoning is caused due to ingestion of illicit liquor which contains ethanol adulterated with methanol. Methanol is metabolized to formaldehyde and formic acid by alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases, respectively. The metabolites of methanol are responsible for the toxic effects. Clinically, patients present with headache, vomiting, abdomen pain, uneasiness, confusion, delirium, and coma. Formic acid specifically damages the retina and optic nerve and results in blurring of vision and blindness. Elevated levels of formic acid and other organic acids result in metabolic acidosis in arterial blood gas analysis(ABG). Treatment of methanol poisoning includes gastric lavage with sodium bicarbonate if the patient is brought within 2 hours of ingesting methanol to combat acidosis. Ethanol infusion since ethanol is preferentially metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase over methanol and helps by reducing the rate of generation of formaldehyde and formic acid. Fomepizole is a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase and the drug of choice for methanol poisoning. Folate therapy with calcium leucovorin reduces blood formate levels by enhancing its oxidation. Hemodialysis is used in severe cases of methanol toxicity. It can also affect other organs like lymph nodes, spleen, and liver. The classic radiographic appearance is likely normal or could consist of faint bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Perihilar infiltrates are less common in patients with AIDS. CT will show diffuse ground-glass opacities. Histopathology of the tissue will show foamy alveolar infiltrate and mononuclear interstitial infiltrates, which is pathognomonic of PCP. Specific stains like methenamine silver, toluidine blue O, or Giemsa can show the cysts. Other tests that are used for the diagnosis of PCP are polymerase chain reaction, (1→3)-β-d-glucan, etc. The treatment of PCP is with cotrimoxazole (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole). For patients with a PaO2 <70 mmHg or with an arterial-alveolar (a–A) gradient >35 mmHg, adjunct glucocorticoid therapy should be used in addition to cotrimoxazole. IDA is an example of microcytic hypochromic anemia. The causes of IDA can be inadequate diet, impaired reabsorption, increased requirement, and increased blood loss. The manifestations of IDA depend upon the underlying cause. Hence, the initial treatment in a patient with high alcohol intake with new-onset ataxia should be an emergent IV thiamine infusion to prevent the progression of Wernicke encephalopathy. text:
9. An 8-year-old girl presented with frequent episodes of staring spells in school. On further evaluation, she was diagnosed with absence seizures and started on ethosuximide. What is the mechanism of action of this drug? 

GABA: gamma-Aminobutyric acid

options.D: Inhibition of the T-type calcium channels

expl:
Correct answer: D. Inhibition of the T-type calcium channels

Ethosuximide, commonly used in children suffering from absence seizures acts by inhibiting T-type calcium channels. Absence seizures originate in the thalamus and produce the pathognomonic 3 Hz spike and wave pattern on EEG. This pattern is produced due to the intrinsic properties of the low threshold T-type calcium channels of the thalamus. These channels are activated at a much lower threshold and produce larger currents as compared to most other calcium channels in the brain. Hence, inhibition of these T-type calcium currents in the neurons of the thalamus by ethosuximide is effective for the management of absence seizures. The condition is most often initially treated with ethosuximide, which is as effective as, but less toxic than, valproate. EEG is helpful in monitoring the response to therapy and often normalizes when complete seizure control is achieved. Childhood absence epilepsy is associated with a good prognosis, and most patients outgrow it before adulthood. Other options: Option A: Valproate acts by blockage of both sodium and calcium channels. It is effective in the treatment of absence, myoclonic, focal, and tonic-clonic seizures. Option B: Vigabatrin inhibits GABA metabolism and thus increases GABA concentration in the brain. It is the drug of choice for infantile spasms seen in tuberous sclerosis. Option C: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA-mediated synaptic inhibition resulting in GABA potentiation. Benzodiazepines act at GABAA receptors and increase the frequency, but not duration, of openings at GABA-activated Cl− channels. text: 10. At what CD4 count is Kaposi sarcoma likely to occur?
expl:
Correct answer: B. <500/ μL

The likelihood of developing Kaposi sarcoma increases when absolute CD4 lymphocyte count is <500/ μL. Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8) and is very common in patients suffering from acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). KS is considered to be an AIDS-defining disease.  AIDS-associated KS is an AIDS-defining illness and is the most common malignancy associated with HIV infection. Involvement of the oral cavity is most common in AIDS-related KS, but it can be seen in other variants also. Oral KS (OKS) most often involves the hard and soft palate, gingiva, and dorsal tongue with plaques or tumors. The color of the lesions may range from non-pigmented to brownish-red or violaceous. Other forms of KS include * Classic Kaposi sarcoma: It has the following three clinical stages patches, plaques, and nodules. * Endemic African KS * Transplant-associated KS is more common after solid organ transplant patients receive immunosuppression as compared to marrow or stem-cell transplant patients. The given images show coalescent red-purple macules and plaques of the skin. There is no definitive cure but KS is highly radiosensitive and achieves complete response in most cases. In AIDS‐associated KS, instituting highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) often (but not always) results in regression of KS. In localized cutaneous KS, excision and cryotherapy can be used. Intra-lesional administration of vinblastine, interferon‐α2b, and imiquimod is also effective. text: 11. A pregnant woman, after undergoing a cesarean section under spinal anesthesia, had a headache that aggravated in sitting position. Which of the following is not advised for this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Restricted water intake

The given scenario is suggestive of post-dural puncture headache which worsens with restricted water intake. Post-dural puncture headache is believed to result from a puncture of the dura (unintentional or intentional) in the setting of neuraxial anesthesia. This causes leakage of CSF from a dural defect leading to intracranial hypotension. The characteristic feature of a post-dural puncture headache is the frontal or occipital headache. It is associated with nausea, neck stiffness, and lower back pain. Most of the headaches resolve spontaneously within 7 days.  An epidural blood patch is the definitive management. It is ideally performed 24 hours after dural puncture and the development of classic symptoms (Option A). Supine position, IV fluids, caffeine, stool softeners, and analgesia are other factors that help in relieving the symptoms (options B & D). 12. A young man presented with severe muscle weakness and ptosis. Chest X-ray revealed an anterior mediastinal mass. Further investigation reveals the presence of AchR antibodies. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?

AchR -Acetylcholine receptor
expl:
Correct answer: A. Myasthenia gravis

The given clinical scenario of weakness, ptosis, anterior mediastinal mass( thymoma), and the presence of AchR antibodies are suggestive of myasthenia gravis. Myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular junction (NMJ) disorder due to autoimmune damage to the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at the NMJ. It is characterized by weakness and muscle fatigue. Weakness increases with usage and muscle movement is difficult at the end of the day. It affects proximal muscles leading to weakness of the limbs. Ocular features like ptosis and diplopia can also be seen. Myasthenia gravis is often related to thymomas. Symptoms of myasthenia gravis improve after excision of the thymus gland even in the absence of a thymoma.  Treatment includes Anticholinesterase drugs like Pyridostigmine, immunosuppression, and even Thymectomy if the condition is associated with a Thymoma. Recently Rozanolixizumab has been approved for treating cases of generalized Myasthenia gravis. Other options: Option B: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is an autoimmune disorder affecting the presynaptic membrane at the NMJ. Patients present with proximal muscle weakness of the lower limbs, ptosis, and diplopia.  Treatment involves plasmapheresis, immunotherapy, and drugs such as 3,4-diaminopyridine (3,4-DAP) and pyridostigmine. Option C: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked muscular dystrophy due to mutations in the dystrophin gene. It most commonly affects boys in their childhood. Patients initially present with proximal muscle weakness predominantly in the lower limbs. Calf muscle hypertrophy is a cardinal feature. Other features include mental retardation, cardiac failure, and myoglobinuria. Treatment includes corticosteroids, Eteplirsen, and Casimersen.  Option D: Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant disorder affecting multiple systems. It is associated with skeletal muscle weakness, cataracts, endocrinopathy, and cardiomyopathy. The treatment is mainly symptomatic however, mexiletine is indicated for reducing myotonia.

text: 13. A 40-year-old woman comes with complaints of fatigue which worsens towards the end of the day. She also complains of double vision while watching television. The physician suspects a case of myasthenia gravis. Which of the following tests has the highest sensitivity in diagnosing this condition?

options.B: Acetylcholine receptor and muscle-specific receptor tyrosine kinase antibodies

expl:
Correct answer: A. Single-fiber electromyography

Single-fiber electromyography (SFEMG) has the highest sensitivity in the clinical diagnosis of myasthenia gravis. During single-fibre electromyography, action potentials of two muscle fibres innervated by one motor axon are recorded, and the variability in the interval between them, called jitter, is increased in myasthenia gravis. It is the most sensitive test used for the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis. Myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular junction (NMJ) disorder associated with a decrease in postsynaptic depolarization due to the blocking of acetylcholine receptors by autoantibodies. It is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles. Ocular features like ptosis and diplopia can also be seen. When it becomes generalized, the proximal muscles of the limbs are affected first. Despite the muscle weakness, the deep tendon reflexes remain normal. The snarling expression on smiling (facial weakness), nasal timbre of speech (weakness of palate and tongue), and difficulty swallowing may be seen. Bulbar weakness and respiratory depression are seen more frequently in MuSK antibody–positive myasthenia gravis. Treatment includes anticholinesterase drugs like pyridostigmine and immunosuppression. Other options: Option B: The acetylcholine receptor antibody (AChR-Ab) test should be done in all patients (most specific). If negative, test for MuSK antibodies. Option C: Repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) is considered abnormal if there is a decremental response of >10%.  Option D: CT scan of the chest is likely to show thymic hyperplasia and thymoma which are frequently associated in patients with myasthenia gravis.

text: 15. A 45-year-old male patient with past history of tuberculosis was brought to the emergency department with complaints of breathing difficulty. text: 17. A chronic alcoholic patient consuming alcohol for the last 20 years had his last drink 3 days back. He presents with altered sensorium, disorientation, tremors, and a feeling of insects crawling over his body. Which of the following should be given to this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Lorazepam + thiamine

The given clinical scenario of alcohol withdrawal with altered sensorium, and a feeling of insects crawling over his body points towards the diagnosis of delirium tremens. Lorazepam + thiamine should be given to this patient. Delirium tremens is treated using benzodiazepines like lorazepam starting with a higher dosage which is gradually tapered as withdrawal symptoms disappear. In cases of chronic alcohol use, vitamin deficiency (especially thiamine) may be co-existing and hence bolus doses of thiamine are given to prevent/treat Wernicke encephalopathy. Delirium tremens occurs after 2-4 days of abstinence in a heavy or chronic drinker. It is characterized by autonomic hyperactivity, tremors, delusions, and hallucinations. It usually resolves spontaneously in 7 days but may cause the death of the patient due to cardiovascular collapse, infections or self-injury. Haloperidol is generally not the first-line drug in case of alcoholic withdrawal. It might be used as an add-on in agitated patients. text: 18. A 10-month-old boy who is a known case of cerebral palsy, was brought to the OPD for a routine check-up. The child had a past history of weakness in both upper and lower limbs which improved with time. Correct answer: A. Spastic diplegia

The given clinical scenario of a child with cerebral palsy, who has residual weakness in his lower limbs as compared to his upper limbs is highly suggestive of spastic diplegia. Spastic diplegia is more commonly seen in premature infants with a history of birth asphyxia due to damage to immature white matter. It is 2nd most common type of cerebral palsy in India after spastic quadriplegia. Both the lower limbs are involved. During development, characteristic commando crawling is seen. Brain MRI shows scarring and shrinkage in the periventricular white matter with compensatory enlargement of the cerebral ventricles. It is the most common cause of motor disability in childhood.  The subtypes of cerebral palsy and the pathology involved are given below:

text: 20. A 60-year-old male patient is being treated for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and comes for follow-up. He is tachypneic with a resting oxygen saturation of 86%. Which of the following will increase the survival in this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Long term oxygen therapy

Long-term oxygen therapy will increase survival in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).  Supplemental oxygen is indicated in patients with resting O2 saturation of ≤88% or ≤89% with signs of pulmonary arterial hypertension or right heart failure. It has been proven to prolong survival and the benefits are directly proportional to the duration of oxygen administration (hours per day). Studies did not show significant benefits in patients with moderate hypoxemia.  Patients with dependent edema, P-pulmonale on ECG, or hematocrit value >56% with PaO2 value between 56-59 mm Hg or SaO2 of 89% are also eligible for oxygen therapy. COPD is a disease state characterized by chronic airflow obstruction.  It includes emphysema, chronic bronchitis, and small airway disease. Patients present with cough, sputum production, and dyspnea on exertion. Diagnosis is based on pulmonary function tests and the severity is graded according to the global initiative for chronic obstructive lung disease (GOLD) criteria.  Pharmacotherapy of COPD includes: * Muscarinic antagonists: ipratropium, tiotropium * Beta-agonists: salbutamol, salmeterol * Theophylline * Inhaled corticosteroids Acute exacerbations are managed with inhaled beta-agonists, muscarinic antagonists, oxygen, mechanical ventilation in the form of noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation, and antibiotics. Smoking cessation and lung volume reduction surgery in some emphysematous patients are the other interventions associated with reduced mortality. Other options: Option B: Long-term oral glucocorticoids are not recommended to treat COPD due to the significant adverse effects such as osteoporosis, weight gain, and cataracts. Option C: Inhaled corticosteroids are mainly used to reduce exacerbations. Patients with two or more exacerbations per year or hospitalized patients with one exacerbation can be considered.  Option D: Phosphodiesterase 4 inhibitors (PDE4) inhibitor roflumilast can be used to reduce the frequency of exacerbations in severe COPD and chronic bronchitis.

text: 1. A patient with renal disease undergoes a biopsy. On Congo red staining, the deposits show apple-green birefringence under polarized light. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Amyloidosis

The given clinical case of renal biopsy showing apple-green birefringence under polarized light on congo red staining is suggestive of amyloidosis Amyloidosis refers to extracellular deposits of fibrillar proteins. Abnormal fibrils are produced by the aggregation of misfolded proteins. The fibrillar deposits bind a wide variety of proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans, including heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate, and plasma proteins, notably serum amyloid P component (SAP). Amyloid appears as an amorphous, eosinophilic, hyaline, extracellular substance. It could be classified as systemic, localized, and hereditary amyloidosis. Microscopically, all types of amyloid deposits are made up of continuous, nonbranching fibrils. A characteristic cross-β-pleated sheet conformation is visualized on X-ray crystallography and infrared spectroscopy. The stain used for amyloid deposits is congo red staining, which imparts pink to red color to the amyloid under ordinary light and apple-green birefringence under polarised microscopy. The image shows a congo-red stained biopsy specimen with the following: (A) Focal positive staining (orange-red) of amorphous extracellular material (B) Apple-green birefringence under polarized light  The next best step is to determine the type of precursor protein by immunohistochemistry, immunoelectron microscopy, or extraction and biochemical analysis using mass spectrometry. Other options: Option A: In Minimal change disease, Biopsy findings include the following:  * Light microscopy- glomeruli appear normal (hence called "minimal change") * Immunofluorescence studies- no Ig or complement deposits * Electron microscopy- diffuse effacement of foot processes of visceral epithelial cells/podocytes Option B: Diabetic nephropathy shows no Congo red positivity. text: 2. A 28-year-old female was brought to the emergency department by her husband after a suspected suicide attempt by drug overdose. She is experiencing seizures and difficulty breathing. On examination, she has a fever, a heart rate of 186 beats per minute, and a blood pressure of 70/50 mmHg. Additionally, she has a dry mouth and dilated pupils. Her arterial blood gas (ABG) shows a pH of 7.1, bicarbonate at 14 mmol/L, and pCO2 at 30 mm Hg. The ECG findings are also provided. What is the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Tricyclic antidepressant overdose

The given clinical scenario of a patient having seizures, metabolic acidosis, tachycardia, hypotension, and pupillary dilatation and an ECG finding showing a wide QRS complex and prolonged QT interval, is suggestive of tricyclic antidepressant toxicity. ECG of a patient with tricyclic antidepressant overdose shows three major findings: sinus tachycardia (from anticholinergic and adrenergic effects), prolongation of the QRS complex (from slowed ventricular conduction), and prolongation of the QT interval (from delayed repolarization). Tricyclic antidepressant overdose: Clinical features: Seizures, respiratory depression, drowsiness, delirium, Sinus tachycardia, hypotension, prolonged PR/QRS/QT interval, arrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia, fibrillation). Anticholinergic symmptoms like dilated pupils, dry mouth, urinary retention, hyperthermia Treatment: Oxygen supplementation and IV fluids. Activated charcoal if the patient is brought within two hours of ingestion (unless ileus present), IV sodium bicarbonate (attenuates the TCA-induced cardiotoxicity and metabolic acidosis) Note: Dialysis is not very helpful in the management of TCA overdose. ECG of a patient with tricyclic antidepressant overdose shows three major findings, sinus tachycardia (from anticholinergic and adrenergic effects), prolongation of the QRS complex (from slowed ventricular conduction), and prolongation of the QT interval (from delayed repolarization) as given below, Other options: Option B: Atropine is an anticholinergic drug. It acts through reversible, competitive inhibition of the postsynaptic muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. It is indicated in the treatment of organophosphate/muscarinic poisoning, in bradycardia, and to reduce salivary secretions. The adverse effects of atropine are due to the antimuscarinic effects, including xerostomia, blurring of vision, photophobia, tachycardia, flushing, warm, dry skin, constipation, urinary retention, anhidrosis, delirium, and coma. Intoxication with atropine results in all the above symptoms along with convulsions, and circulatory collapse due to respiratory failure. Death may occur secondary to respiratory paralysis. Option C: Lithium Toxicity is associated with symptoms like nausea, vomiting, ataxia, coarse tremors, dysarthria, seizure, and hyperreflexia. There is no specific antidote, and treatment is mainly supportive. In severe toxicity, dialysis is the most effective treatment. It is associated with Ebstein anomaly. Option D: The most common cardiac manifestations of digitalis toxicity include atrioventricular junctional rhythm, premature ventricular depolarizations, ventricular bigeminy, ventricular tachycardia, and second-degree AV blockade. After cardiovascular system, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea i.e., GIT effects are more pronounced. Altered color perception can also be seen in case of digoxin toxicity.

text: 3. A patient with a history of road traffic accident (RTA) presents with massive blood loss and has been transfused with 4 units of packed red blood cells within a few hours. Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities is most likely to occur?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Hypocalcemia

The given clinical vignette of an RTA patient transfused with 4 units of packed red blood cells within a few hours is highly suggestive of Massive (transfusion of 50% of the patient’s total blood volume over 3h) Transfusion-Associated citrate toxicity, which will lead to hypocalcemia. Massive transfusion is defined as the transfusion of at least 10 units of red cells in 24 hours or 4 units in 1 hour. Large amounts of citrate are given with massive blood transfusion since blood is anticoagulated with sodium citrate and citric acid. This citrate chelates calcium from the blood and causes hypocalcemia. The complications of citrate infusion are: Electrolyte abnormalities: * Hyperkalemia: RBC leakage during storage * Hypocalcemia: citrate chelates calcium  * Hypomagnesemia: Citrate binds magnesium * Metabolic alkalosis: each mmol of citrate generates 3 mEq of bicarbonate. As a result, metabolic alkalosis occurs. Pearl PF0120: Complications of massive transfusion: The concept behind It Massive transfusion (MT) is defined as transfusion of 10 units of pRBCs in 24 hours or more than 4 units of pRBCs in one hour. Complications from massive transfusion include: * Hypothermia * Alkalosis/Acidosis * Coagulopathy * Hypocalcemia * Hypomagnesemia * Hyperkalemia Understanding the concept: * Hypothermia: Blood products are normally stored between 1°C and 6°C, and rapid transfusion of large quantities will lead to hypothermia. * Coagulopathy: MT with PRBCs alone causes a dilutional coagulopathy, whereas massive hemorrhage causes a consumptive coagulopathy. However, the incidence of coagulopathy can be minimized by the infusion of fresh frozen plasma, platelets, and RBCs in a 1:1:1 ratio.  * Alkalosis: As citrate is metabolized to bicarbonate, patients who require MT frequently develop a metabolic alkalosis.  * Acidosis: Due to tissue hypoperfusion * Hyperkalemia & late Hypokalemia: Initially, the patient develops hyperkalemia on massive transfusion. Later, red blood cells begin active metabolism and intracellular potassium uptake. This increased uptake along with metabolic alkalosis (resulting from citrate administration), lowers the serum potassium. * Hypocalcemia: Binding of calcium to citrate (which is used in the anticoagulation of the stored blood). * Hypomagnesemia: Binding of magnesium to citrate

4. A 35-year-old man presents with persistent hypercalcemia for the past 1.5 years. His parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels are within the normal range. What is the most likely underlying cause?

PTH - parathormone
expl:
Correct answer: B. Sarcoidosis

The given clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of sarcoidosis. In sarcoidosis, granulomas increase vitamin D activation, causing chronic hypercalcemia while PTH remains normal. Hypercalcemia may be seen, due to increased synthesis of calcitriol – 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D, by alveolar macrophages. More commonly, there may be hypercalciuria, which can lead to nephrocalcinosis. Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease that most commonly presents as cough, dyspnea, dry eyes, and usually has bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Lesions of the eyes and skin are also very common in these patients. It is seen more in middle-aged women than in men. Sarcoidosis results from an increase in CD4+ T-cells (increased CD4+:CD8+ ratio). As a result, cytokines like IL-2, TNF, IL-8, and IFN-gamma will increase.  It presents with granulomas in multiple organs. They are classically described as non-caseating granulomas composed of epithelioid macrophages with giant cells. There is no central necrosis as there would be in tubercular granulomas. Naked granulomas are non-caseating granulomas minimally surrounded by lymphocytes. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) levels are elevated in this condition as sarcoid granulomas secrete it. Star-shaped inclusions called asteroid bodies and laminated calcium and protein-containing bodies called Schaumann bodies are also found in the giant cells of most of these granulomas. These are not pathognomonic to sarcoidosis and can also be found in other granulomatous diseases like tuberculosis. Other options: Option A: Malignancy usually causes acute, severe hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH, not chronic hypercalcemia with normal PTH. Option C: Parathyroid hyperplasia is a cause of primary hyperparathyroidism, so PTH would be elevated, not normal. It typically involves all four parathyroid glands.  Option D: CKD typically causes hypocalcemia due to phosphate retention and impaired vitamin D activation, not hypercalcemia. text: 5. A patient presents with progressive shortness of breath for the last 6 months, accompanied by dry cough. Auscultation reveals bilateral basal end-inspiratory crepitations. There is no history of fever, joint pain, or occupational exposure. What is the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

Progressive dyspnea with dry cough, basal end-inspiratory crepitations, and absence of systemic or occupational features is classic for IPF (idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis). Interstitial lung diseases are characterized by inflammation and fibrosis involving the lung parenchyma. Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive, and ultimately fatal lung disease characterized by fibrosis and scarring of lung tissue, leading to declining lung function and respiratory failure. Clinical features include progressive dyspnoea more common with exertion, dry cough, and basal end-inspiratory crackles or rales on auscultation. Digital clubbing is seen. Pulmonary function tests will show a restrictive deficit and reduction of TLC, FEV1, and FVC. There is also a reduction in DLCO and may be the first finding seen in PFT. IPF is the most common interstitial lung disease occurring due to an unknown cause. HRCT shows predominant subpleural and basal involvement, in the form of reticulation, honeycombing, and traction bronchiectasis. This is known as the usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern. Note that ground glass opacities are absent in this pattern. Pirfenidone and Nintedanib slow disease progression by reducing fibrosis. Management is oxygen therapy, pulmonary rehabilitation, and symptom management (e.g., antitussives for cough). Other options: Option A: Cor-pulmonale is a complication of chronic lung disease that presents with signs of right heart failure (edema, JVP, hepatomegaly), not with progressive dry cough and basal crepitations. Option B: Sarcoidosis usually presents with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, systemic features (like uveitis, skin lesions, arthritis), and not with basal crepitations as in IPF. Option D: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is linked to a clear history of occupational or environmental antigen exposure (like birds, molds, farming), which is absent in this case. Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis is a lung disease caused by inhaling various antigens, leading to inflammation in the alveoli and small airways. It presents in acute, subacute, and chronic forms, with the acute form characterized by fever, chills, malaise, dyspnea, and cough. Diagnosis requires a thorough patient history, including occupational exposure assessment. 6. A 30-year-old patient presents with hypertension and hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. CT scan shows a mass of 1.5 cm over the kidney with elevated ARR. What is the next best step for the management of this patient?

ARR - aldosterone renin ratio.
expl:
Correct answer: B. Adrenalectomy

The patient has hypertension, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, elevated ARR, unilateral adrenal mass (1.5 cm) strongly points to aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma, which is managed surgically with an adrenalectomy. Primary hyperaldosteronism is characterized by hypersecretion of aldosterone with suppressed plasma renin levels (due to the negative feedback). The most frequent causes are unilateral adrenal adenoma and bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. Clinical features include * Hypertension (most common) * Hypokalemia * Metabolic alkalosis * Polyuria (due to ANP) * Polydipsia (due to polyuria) * Muscle weakness CT or MRI is used to detect the tumour. In a patient with bilateral micronodular hyperplasia, there could be a unilateral non-functioning tumour. Selective adrenal vein sampling can be done to differentiate between unilateral and bilateral disease. Conservative management with 3-6 months of MRI surveillance is done in non-functional adrenal tumours of < 4cm. Medical management is done in patients with bilateral disease, the commonly implemented therapeutic approach is treatment with spironolactone and antihypertensive medication. Surgical management is done in unilateral and asymmetrical bilateral disease by unilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy. A subtotal resection can be considered in the case of a typical single Conn’s adenoma. However, it is not superior to unilateral adrenalectomy. Other options: Option A: Spironolactone on a lifelong basis is indicated in bilateral adrenal hyperplasia or in unilateral adrenal adenoma if surgery is contraindicated. Spironolactone is a competitive inhibitor of the mineralocorticoid receptor in the late distal tubule and collecting duct of the kidneys. It causes a decrease in sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in the distal tubule. As a result, spironolactone promotes sodium diuresis but maintains body potassium levels. Option C: ACTH stimulation test is used to diagnose adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease), not primary hyperaldosteronism. ACTH stimulation test or cosyntropin test involves the administration of an exogenous, synthetic peptide that has an activity similar to ACTH on the adrenal glands. Serum cortisol levels are measured prior to, and after the administration of the synthetic peptide. Cortisol levels lower than the cut-off value indicate a failure of the adrenal glands to increase the production of cortisol in response to synthetic ACTH, thus confirming the diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency. Option D: Dexamethasone suppression test used for Cushing’s syndrome. The high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is used in patients with confirmed Cushing syndrome. It helps to differentiate between Cushing's disease (i.e. a pituitary cause) and ectopic ACTH production.

text: 7. A pregnant female presents with amenorrhea and galactorrhea. Serum prolactin is elevated. MRI shows pituitary adenoma. What is the best management of this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Bromocriptine

The clinical vignette points to a diagnosis of prolactinoma in a pregnant female, and the best drug for managing this condition is bromocriptine. Pituitary adenomas are benign tumors that arise from hormone-producing cells in the pituitary gland, with lactotrope cell tumors (prolactinomas) being the most common. These tumors can sometimes secrete multiple hormones, such as prolactin, growth hormone, or ACTH. Tumors <1 cm in diameter and no regional invasion are known as microadenomas. It is more commonly seen in women. Tumors > 1 cm in size are known as macroadenomas. It can be locally invasive. Prolactin levels >200 μg/L are suggestive of prolactinomas.  Women present with features such as amenorrhea, infertility, and galactorrhea. Visual field defects can also be seen. Symptoms in males include impotence, infertility, and loss of libido. An MRI is recommended in all patients who present with hyperprolactinemia. Microadenomas can be managed with regular monitoring of prolactin levels and MRI scans, if fertility is not a requisite. Oral dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine and cabergoline are used for medical management. Management of Pituitary Adenoma: * Asymptomatic microadenoma: The approach is "wait and watch." Repeat an MRI after 6 months. Treatment is initiated if the size increases > 1 cm to become a macroadenoma. * Symptomatic microadenoma or macroadenoma: The first line of treatment is medical management with dopamine agonists. The drug of choice is cabergoline, administered in weekly doses. An MRI should be repeated after 6 months to assess tumor size. If there is no reduction, the dose can be increased to a maximum of 2 mg/week. Bromocriptine is preferred for pregnant patients. * Surgical intervention is indicated if there is resistance to medical management (dopamine agonists), unstable pituitary apoplexy, or in pregnancy when there is no response to short-term medical therapy. In these cases, adenoma debulking surgery is performed. * Radiotherapy: Gamma knife stereotactic radiotherapy is reserved for patients with aggressive prolactinomas that do not respond to the maximum tolerated dose of dopamine agonists and/or surgery. Other options:  Option A: Cabergoline is more potent dopamine agonist and better tolerated than bromocriptine in non-pregnant patients. However, in pregnancy, bromocriptine is preferred because it has the largest and longest safety data for maternal and fetal outcomes. Option C: Transsphenoidal surgery  is reserved only for patients who do not respond to medical therapy or if there is acute visual compromise from tumor compression. It is not the first-line treatment in a stable pregnant patient. Option D: Goserelin is a GnRH agonist used for the treatment of endometriosis, dysfunctional uterine bleeding, and prostate and breast cancer, not in prolactinomas. text: 8. A 17-year-old tall male presents to OPD for a routine checkup. He has long limbs, arachnodactyly, and hypermobile joints. 2D echocardiography revealed mitral valve stenosis, and an eye check-up revealed subluxation of the lens. Workup showed the defects are due to an abnormal FBN1 gene mutation. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Marfan Syndrome

The above clinical scenario of a 17-year-old tall male with long limbs, arachnodactyly, hypermobile joints, and 2D echocardiography revealed mitral valve stenosis and subluxation of the lens with an abnormal Fibrillin 1 gene mutation/ FBN1 gene mutation is highly suggestive of Marfan's syndrome.  It is a clinical diagnosis based on skeletal, cardiovascular, and ocular manifestations. Ghent criteria are used for diagnosing Marfan syndrome.  The main features are tall stature, ectopia lentis, and aortic root dilatation.  Skeletal manifestations:  * Tall stature and long limbs  * Pectus carinatum or pectus excavatum * Long and slender fingers (arachnodactyly), contracture of fingers (camptodactyly) * Scoliosis Cardiovascular manifestations: * Thickened atrioventricular valves, valvular prolapse (mitral regurgitation)  * Aortic valve dysfunction due to an aortic root aneurysm * Aortic dissection and rupture due to cystic medial necrosis of the aorta Ocular manifestations: * Ectopia lentis with upward and outward displacement of the lenses due to weakening of the ciliary zonules * Myopia with blurred vision * Retinal detachments * Early cataracts and glaucoma The images below show two important signs seen in Marfan's syndrome:  * Image A shows a positive wrist sign - the ability to join the thumb and fifth finger around the wrist * Image B shows a positive thumb sign - the thumb tip extends from the palm in a closed fist. Other options: Option A: Homocystinuria caused by a deficiency of the cystathionine β-synthase. The deficiency of this enzyme leads to an accumulation of homocysteine in the blood and a clinical syndrome of intellectual disability, subluxated ocular lenses, long and slender extremities, arachnodactyly, and arterial and venous thrombi with megaloblastic anemia.  The image below shows lens subluxation (infero-nasal quad). Option B: High Myopia usually presents with diplopia, ectopic lens, secondary cataract, or glaucoma with retinal detachment. Pearl PF0846: Ehler–Danlos Syndrome (EDS)

text: 9. A 7 year old child is brought to the clinic with complaints of fatigue and poor concentration. The mother reports that the child has been eating non-food items such as soil and paint chips for the past few months. A peripheral blood smear image shows microcytic, hypochromatic red blood cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Iron deficiency anemia

The above clinical scenario of a child with fatigue, poor concentration, and a history of pica (eating soil and paint chips) presents with a peripheral smear showing small RBC with increased central pallor with no basophilic stippling( helps rule out lead poisoning) demonstrates classical features of Iron deficiency anemia(IDA). The causes of IDA can be inadequate diet, impaired reabsorption, increased requirement, and increased blood loss. The manifestations of IDA depend upon the underlying cause. In general, IDA presents with koilonychia, alopecia, atrophic changes in the tongue, gastric mucosa, malabsorption and pica (craving for consumption of non-edible materials) Peripheral smears show small and pale red cells typically described as microcytic (reduced MCV) and hypochromic (enlarged zone of central pallor). Poikilocytosis can be seen in the form of elongated red cells, known as pencil cells. Target cells can be found in cases of severe IDA. Laboratory findings of IDA are: * Reduced hemoglobin and hematocrit values. hypochromia, microcytosis, and poikilocytosis. * Serum iron and ferritin levels are low. * The total plasma iron-binding capacity, which reflects the elevated transferrin level, is high. * Low serum iron with increased iron-binding capacity results in a reduction of transferrin saturation to below 15%. * RBC protoporphyrin levels are increased. * Bone marrow reveals a mild to moderate increase in erythroid progenitors. The absence of stainable iron in macrophages is a diagnostically significant finding Option A: In Vitamin B12 deficiency, patients usually present with larger than normal RBC, no history of Pica, hypersegmented neutrophils (image below) and Macrocytes on PBS. Option B: Thalassemia Major generally presents in infancy, with Microcytic hypochromic anemia as well, requiring multiple blood transfusions, it is a hereditary hemoglobinopathy resulting from deficient synthesis of one or more globin chains. Differentiating IDA and Thalassemia: Both conditions present with microcytosis and anisocytosis, with the Mentzer index being less than 13 (MCV/RBC). Option C: Lead poisoning causes dry throat, burning abdominal pain, peripheral circulatory collapse, insomnia, paraesthesias, depression, coma, and death. Cerebellar ataxia is common in children with acute lead poisoning. A screening test for lead poisoning is the presence of porphyrinuria, mainly due to coproporphyrin III. Peripheral smear shows basophilic stippling. A Burtonian line may be visible on the gums. Pearl PF1623: Differential Diagnosis of Microcytic Anaemia
