text: 10. An 8-year-old boy was brought for evaluation of bony deformities. Physical examination revealed wrist widening, cupping. He is asymptomatic otherwise. Laboratory investigation revealed low plasma Vitamin D and serum ALP levels of 1500. What will be the most appropriate immediate management for this boy?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin D supplementation

The above clinical scenario of an asymptomatic 8-year-old boy with wrist widening and cupping, with low plasma vitamin D on laboratory investigation, is consistent with Rickets. Treatment of nutritional Rickets includes Vitamin D Supplementation. Radiograph of wrist showing cupping and fraying is given below Rickets occurs due to a nutritional deficiency in vitamin D. A Decrease in vitamin D levels leads to decreased calcium and phosphate due to reduced absorption. The decreased calcium stimulates increased parathyroid hormone(PTH) production. ALP level is increased as it is involved in bone mineralization. Clinical features of rickets include: * General features include malnourishment, abdominal distension, proximal muscle weakness, etc. * Head: Softening of the skull bones, called craniotabes, and delayed closure of fontanelles. * Chest: Rachitic rosary, i.e., widening of the costochondral junctions that give the feeling of rosary beads on palpation. Harrison's groove, a horizontal groove in the lower chest, may appear from the inward pull of the softened ribs by the diaphragm during respiration. * Vertebral column abnormalities like scoliosis, kyphosis, and lordosis * In the distal extremities, widening of the wrists and ankles, varus/ valgus deformities, windswept deformity (valgus on the side and varus on the contralateral side), and anterior tibial bowing. Metabolic bone disorders due to nutritional deficiencies include: * Vitamin D deficiency leads to Rickets in children * Osteomalacia- in adults Treatment: Vitamin D–dependent rickets is treated long-term with active vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D or calcitriol). The typical starting dose ranges from 0.25 to 2 µg/day, which is gradually reduced after clinical and radiological healing of rickets. During early treatment, ensuring adequate calcium intake is essential to support proper bone mineralization and prevent hypocalcemia. Option D: Vitamin C supplementation is recommended for children to prevent Scurvy. Pearl PF2091: Important Clinical Features of Rickets Pearl PF1660: Radiological features of rickets Radiological features of rickets: * Loss of provisional zone of calcification: earliest radiological finding of rickets.  * Delayed appearance of the epiphysis * Widening of growth plate: normal width of growth is 2-4mm. It is increased in cases of rickets due to excessive accumulation of uncalcified osteoid at the growth plate. * Cupping of metaphysis: normally metaphysis meets epiphysis as a smooth line of sclerosis. But in rickets the line is absent and the metaphyseal ends appear irregular and the cartilage accumulating in the growth plate creates a depression in the metaphysis causing cupping. * Fraying: indistinct margins of the metaphysis * Bowing of diaphysis, with thinning of cortices * In healing rickets, zone of calcification becomes denser.  The above features are prominent at the growth plates where growth is greatest: * Knee: distal femur, proximal tibia * Wrist: especially the ulna * Anterior rib ends: rachitic rosary The below image shows bowing of legs in rickets. Pearl PF2079: Radiological Features of Scurvy Radiological features of scurvy: * Generalised osteopenia * Pencil-point cortex: Cortical thinning * Periosteal reaction due to subperiosteal hemorrhage * Scorbutic rosary: Expansion of the costochondral junctions * Hemarthrosis * Wimberger ring: Circular, opaque radiological shadow surrounding epiphyseal centers of ossification, which may result from bleeding * Frenkel line: Dense zone of provisional calcification  * Trummerfeld zone: Lucent metaphyseal band underlying Frankel line * Pelken spur: Metaphyseal spurs which result in cupping of the metaphysis

text: 11. A patient presents with palpitations, headache, and sweating. His BP is 180/100 mmHg. 24-hour urinary metanephrine values are elevated. What is the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Pheochromocytoma

The above clinical scenario of palpitations, headache, and sweating, with BP is 180/100 mmHg, 24-hour urinary metanephrine values are elevated, is consistent with the diagnosis of Pheochromocytoma.  It is a catecholamine-secreting tumor derived from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.It can be sporadic or hereditary. Hereditary pheochromocytoma occurs in association with syndromes such as MEN 2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2), familial paraganglioma syndrome, Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome, and neurofibromatosis (NF) type 1. Clinical features: It most commonly presents as a classic triad of intermittent headache, palpitation, and profuse sweating along with hypertension. The patient can also present with anxiety, panic attacks, nausea, abdominal pain, weight loss, and weakness. Symptoms may be precipitated by surgery, pregnancy, position changes, exercise, and medications such as metoclopramide and tricyclic antidepressants. Investigations: * Biochemical screening test—measurement of urinary and plasma levels of catecholamines and metanephrines.  * MRI is the investigation of choice for localizing the tumor. It is preferred over a CT scan, as the contrast used in CT scans can precipitate paroxysms. * Other imaging modalities like MIBG scintigraphy and DOPA- or FDG-PET scans are used in identifying the primary tumor as well as the extra-adrenal tumors and metastases. Surgical resection of the tumor is the definitive treatment for pheochromocytoma. Preoperatively, hypertension is managed initially with alpha-blockers followed by beta-blockers. Other options: Option B: Carcinoid Tumor usually presents with flushing, diarrhea, wheezing, and elevated 5-HIAA (not metanephrines). Option C: Neuroblastoma usually occurs in children, presents with abdominal mass with hypotonia, ataxia, behavioral symptoms and elevated urinary VMA/HVA, not metanephrines. Option D: Adrenocortical Tumor secretes cortisol/aldosterone/androgens, not catecholamines. Pearl PF1539: Pheochromocytoma Features: * When pheochromocytoma is associated with the MEN syndrome it is rarely malignant. * Phaeochromocytomas are greyish-pink on the cut surface and are usually highly vascularised. * Zellbalen cells and nuclei with salt and pepper chromatin are seen. Factors indicating more chances of malignancy: * An increased PASS (phaeochromocytoma of the adrenal gland scale score) * High number of Ki-67-positive cells * Vascular invasion or a breached capsule Diagnosis: * Urinary catecholamine and VMA level assay are most sensitive screening test. * MRI is the IOC. * Biopsy and CT Contrast scan are contraindicated in order to avoid Hypertensive crisis. Treatment: * Adrenalectomy is preferred TOC. * Size<5 cm -  Laparoscopic adrenalectomy * Preop Alpha blockers should be given * Mitotane should be started as adjuvant or palliative treatment

text: 12. 58-year-old male with a history of multiple sexual partners, presented with Anorexia and Jaundice. Biopsy shows ground-glass hepatocytes. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Hepatitis B

The above given clinical scenario of 58 year 58-year-old Male with a history of multiple sexual partners, presented with Anorexia and Jaundice, and Biopsy shows ground glass hepatocytes are very characteristic of Chronic Hepatitis B infection. These ground-glass hepatocytes are liver parenchymal cells that have an eosinophilic, granular, and glassy appearance on light microscopy. This appearance is due to the accumulation of HBsAg (hepatitis B surface antigen) in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum. After a person is infected with the hepatitis B virus (HBV), the first serologic marker to increase in level is HBsAg. It becomes detectable in the serum between 1-12 weeks. It becomes undetectable 1–2 months after the onset of jaundice and rarely persists beyond 6 months. Once the HBsAg becomes undetectable, the anti-HBs antibody starts rising in serum and remains detectable indefinitely thereafter. The gap between the disappearance of HBsAg and the appearance of anti-HBs antibodies is called the window period. However, if HBsAg persists beyond 6 months, it is likely to be chronic hepatitis B Treatment of chronic hepatitis B is focused on suppressing the level of virus replication. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) is an acyclic nucleotide analog that is used as first-line therapy for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B and lamivudine-resistant chronic hepatitis B. It is potent in suppressing HBV DNA. It is given as an oral once-daily dose of 300 mg for 48 weeks. Tenofovir therapy provided histologic improvement, reduction in fibrosis score, and regression of cirrhosis in patients. Side effects are acute renal failure and low blood phosphate levels. Hepatitis A Hepatocyte swelling, monocyte infiltration, Councilman bodies
Hepatitis B  Ground glass appearance 
Hepatitis C  Lymphoid aggregates with a focal area of macrovesicular steatosis 
Hepatitis D Similar to HBV 
Hepatitis E Patchy necrosis
Other options: Option B: Hepatitis A also presents with anorexia and jaundice, but mainly in children, it is mainly transmitted via the feco-oral route, and does not lead to ground glass hepatocytes. It is a self-limiting condition. Option C: Hepatitis C causes chronic hepatitis and is mostly transmitted via blood transfusions, IV drug use (sexual spread is less common). Histology shows lymphoid aggregates in portal tracts, and macrovesicular steatosis, and councilman bodies are seen. Option D: Hepatitis D only presents as a superinfection or co-infection with Hepatitis B; it does not alone cause much infection. It is the most common cause of fulminant hepatitis. text: 13. A 30-year-old female with a complaint of fatigue and dysphagia presents to the hospital with the peripheral blood smear given in the image. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Plummer Vinson Syndrome

The above clinical scenario of a 30-year-old female with dysphagia and fatigue, and microcytic hypochromic anemia on PBS is consistent with the diagnosis of Plummer-Vinson Syndrome. Plummer-Vinson syndrome is also known as Paterson-Brown-Kelly syndrome, and it predisposes to hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma and consists of four features with a higher incidence in women: * Dysphagia  * Iron-deficiency anaemia    * Weight loss     * Esophageal webs. Treatment includes correcting iron-deficiency anemia, which may improve dysphagia and pain. Oesophageal bougies can be used during upper endoscopy to dilate the post-cricoid webs and allow normal swallowing and passage of food. The image below shows the endoscopic appearance of the post-cricoid esophageal web. Other options: Option A: B12 deficiency presents as megaloblastic anemia with neurological features, not as microcytic RBC with dysphagia. It is more common in pure vegetarian patients. Option B: Hemolytic Anemia typically presents with jaundice, raised LDH, reduced haptoglobin with schistocytes in PBS. Option D: Iron deficiency anemia presents with microcytic hypochromic RBC, but it does not present with dysphagia.

14. A 55-year-old alcoholic patient with hypertension presents with dizziness, palpitations, and syncopal attacks. ECG shows irregularly irregular rhythm with no visible P waves, and JVP was measured. Which of the following changes is seen on the JVP waveform?

JVP- Jugular Venous Pressure
expl:
Correct answer: A. Absent A wave

The above clinical scenario of a 55-year-old male alcoholic patient with hypertension develops dizziness and palpitations, syncopal attacks, with an ECG showing irregular rhythm with no visible P waves where seen is consistent with the diagnosis of atrial fibrillation, which on the JVP waveform presents as an absent A wave, which corresponds to atrial contraction. Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained arrhythmia. There is rapid and irregular atrial activation, which is transmitted through the atrioventricular node. The conducted ventricular rate is usually rapid and irregularly irregular. It can vary from 110-160 beats/minute. A pulse deficit is an important clinical finding associated with the condition. This arises due to preload reduction.  Symptoms include palpitations, fatigue, presyncope, and dyspnea. An ECG shows the absence of P waves.  In acute atrial fibrillation with hemodynamic instability, electrical or chemical cardioversion is the first step. The latter is done by intravenous administration of class III antiarrhythmic - ibutilide. In a stable patient, ventricular rate control is the primary aim. This is done by intravenous or oral administration of beta-blockers. Calcium channel blockers such as verapamil and diltiazem can also be used. Another option is to evaluate the presence of a thrombus in the left atrial appendage. This can be done either by transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) or high-resolution CT. text: 15. A 19-year-old female with a previous history of rheumatic fever presented with shortness of breath, palpitations, and orthopnea. On auscultation loud S1 and mid-diastolic murmur were heard. Which of the following valvular heart diseases best explains the additional heart sound?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Mitral Stenosis (MS)

The above clinical scenario of a 19-year-old female with a history of rheumatic fever, presenting with a loud S1 and mid-diastolic murmur, is consistent with Mitral stenosis. MS is a valvular heart disease, most commonly caused by rheumatic fever. Other causes include: * Mitral annular calcification with leaflet involvement * Systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis * Left atrial myxoma * Infective endocarditis with large vegetation The murmur of MS corresponds to the P wave of the ECG. MS leads to increased pressure in the left atrium. Left atrial abnormality may cause broad, notched P waves in the limb leads and a biphasic P wave in lead V1 with a prominent negative component representing delayed depolarisation of the left atria. P wave may become tall and peaked in the lead II and upright in lead V1 due to severe pulmonary hypertension or when tricuspid stenosis complicates mitral stenosis, leading to right atrial enlargement. The QRS complex is usually normal. In severe pulmonary hypertension, right axis deviation and RV hypertrophy can be seen.   Auscultatory findings in mitral stenosis are: * A mid-diastolic murmur * The first heart sound (S1) is accentuated * The opening snap (OS) is after the A2 sound. It is best heard during the expiration and at the apex of the heart * The OS is followed by a low-pitched, rumbling, mid-diastolic murmur, which is heard best at the apex with the patient in the left lateral recumbent position. This murmur correlates with the severity of the stenosis. Chronic inflammation causes the thickening of the valve leaflets and the shortening and fusion of chordae tendineae, leading to the formation of a funnel-shaped or fish-mouth valve. Calcification immobilizes the leaflets and narrows the valve further.  Other options: Option A: Tricuspid stenosis presents as a mid-diastolic murmur, but is not commonly associated with Rheumatic fever.  Option B: Mitral regurgitation presents as a holosystolic murmur. Option D: Aortic regurgitation presents as an early diastolic murmur. Pearl PF1770: Different signs in Aortic Regurgitation

text: 17. A patient after myocardial infarction, develops a broad QRS complex tachycardia. His BP is 120/70 mm Hg. ECG is given below. What is the best management?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Amiodarone IV

The patient here complaining of chest pain, and palpitations and has ECG changes showing wide QRS complex tachycardia with absent p waves is likely to have acute ventricular tachycardia. Since the patient is stable and has an underlying coronary artery disease the drug of choice is intravenous amiodarone. Intravenous amiodarone is recommended by the AHA/ACC 2015 guidelines for the treatment of hemodynamically stable ventricular tachycardia. Ventricular tachycardias can be defined as three or more pre-ventricular contractions at a rate >100/minute. ECG changes include wide QRS complexes, absence of P waves, and ventriculoatrial dissociation. It can be broadly classified as sustained VT or non-sustained VT. Nonsustained VT has QRS complexes lasting <30 seconds while sustained VT lasts for >30 seconds. In monomorphic VT, all QRS complexes look the same. Polymorphic VT has QRS complexes varying in shape or direction in the same lead.  Most monomorphic VT have an underlying cardiac disease. Symptoms of ventricular tachycardia include palpitations, syncope, and shortness of breath.  In a hemodynamically stable patient, amiodarone, procainamide, and lidocaine can be used to treat the condition. In the presence of heart disease, intravenous amiodarone is the drug of choice. In hemodynamically unstable patients, electrical cardioversion is done. Further management depends on the underlying heart condition and frequency of VT. Frequent episodes warrant the use of antiarrhythmics or catheter ablation.  Torsades de Pointes is a type of polymorphic VT occurring with QT prolongation. It can progress to ventricular fibrillation which is treated with defibrillation. Recurrent episodes can be managed with intravenous magnesium sulfate. text: 19. A 10-year-old boy, during a health checkup organized by the school, was found to have severe limb pain and generalized fatigue since childhood. He was hospitalized multiple times for similar painful episodes. On examination, he is pale and mildly icteric. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows a marked predominance of HbS. What is the most appropriate treatment to reduce the frequency of these painful episodes?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Hydroxyurea

The clinical scenario of a 10-year-old boy with recurrent severe limb pain, chronic fatigue, multiple hospitalizations for similar painful episodes, and examination findings of pallor and icterus, along with hemoglobin electrophoresis demonstrating predominantly HbS, is consistent with the diagnosis of sickle cell crisis. Hydroxyurea is the drug of choice for the prevention of painful crises in sickle cell anemia. Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to a missense mutation (a type of point mutation) in the β-globin gene of hemoglobin, which results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. Clinical features of sickle cell anemia :  - Moderately severe hemolytic anemia with jaundice. - Painful bone crisis: hand-foot syndrome or dactylitis of the bones of hands and feet. - Acute chest syndrome typically presents with fever, cough, chest pain, and pulmonary infiltrates. - Aplastic crisis stems from the infection of red cell progenitors by parvovirus B19, which causes a transient cessation of erythropoiesis and a sudden worsening of the anemia. - Spleen: In children, splenic sequestration crises occur which resulting in splenomegaly due to red pulp congestion. In adolescence or early adulthood, autosplenectomy occurs due to splenic infarction, fibrosis, and progressive shrinkage. - Increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms - Other clinical features include priapism, leg ulcers, stroke, retinopathy, pigment gallstones, and growth retardation. Acute splenic sequestration is a life-threatening complication that presents as abrupt pallor, abdominal pain, distention, and an acute Hb decline of 2g/dl, often falling below 3g/dL. Recurrent painful finger swelling likely indicates dactylitis secondary to sickle cell disease. Treatment includes early intervention and hemodynamic stabilisation using isotonic fluids or blood transfusion.  Hydroxyurea is beneficial in reducing the painful vasoocclusive crisis of sickle cell anemia.  It is a myelosuppressive agent that is effective in reducing the frequency of painful episodes like dactylitis and acute chest syndrome, decreasing the rate of hospitalization, and the requirement for blood transfusion. It is safe and well-tolerated in children and infants. Hydroxyurea is approved for long-term maintenance of sickle cell disease, and is recommended for patients of all ages regardless of symptoms.  Hydroxyurea increases fetal hemoglobin levels by an unknown mechanism and interferes with the polymerization of abnormal HbS. text: 23. A patient in the ICU underwent a failed attempt at subclavian catheterization. Following the procedure, the patient developed respiratory distress and unilateral chest retraction. On examination, BP was low and pulse rate was elevated, with decreased breath sounds. What is the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Pneumothorax

The above clinical scenario of an ICU patient following a failed attempt of subclavian catheterization, developed respiratory distress and retraction, with low blood pressure, elevated pulse, and decreased breath sounds, is characteristic of one of the complications of the procedure, pneumothorax. A tension pneumothorax develops when a ‘one-way valve’ air leak occurs either from the lung or through the chest wall. Air is sucked into the thoracic cavity without any means of escape, completely collapsing and then compressing the afected lung. Common causes of tension pneumothorax are penetrating chest trauma, blunt chest trauma with a parenchymal lung injury and air leak that did not spontaneously close, iatrogenic lung injury (e.g. due to central venepuncture) and mechanical positive-pressure ventilation.  Complications of central vein catheterization are: * Pneumothorax is more common in subclavian vein catheterization as a result of injury to the underlying pleura. * Arterial puncture is the most common mechanical complication. * Cardiac tamponade is the most important life-threatening complication. It occurs as a result of the puncture of the intrapericardial superior vena cava, right atrium, or right ventricle. * Chylothorax can occur particularly in left subclavian vein catheterization. But it is not the most common. * Injury to the associated nerves, like brachial plexus, stellate ganglion, phrenic nerve, or vocal cords. * Thromboembolism- can lead to venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. It is more common with femoral veins. * Infections- the most common late complication. A central venous catheter (CVC) is an indwelling device inserted into a large, central vein and advanced until the terminal lumen resides within the inferior vena cava, superior vena cava, or right atrium. It is indicated for the administration of vasopressors, medications, and total parenteral nutrition. It is also useful in procedures like dialysis, plasmapheresis, and interventions such as transvenous pacemaker placement. Cannulation can be done at various sites, namely the internal jugular, common femoral, and subclavian veins. text: 29. A patient with aplastic anemia undergoes bone marrow transplantation. Within 2 weeks, he presents with complaints of bloody diarrhea. Upon further examination, he was found to have jaundice and blistering rashes on the skin. What is the possible mechanism behind the patient's current clinical picture?

options.D: Preformed antibodies of the host attacking transplanted tissue

expl:
Correct answer: A. Transplanted cells attacking host tissues

The given scenario is suggestive of graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). The possible mechanism behind the patient's current clinical picture is transplanted cells attacking host tissues. Transfusion of irradiated RBCs prevents the incidence of GVHD associated with the transfusion. GVHD occurs when immunologically competent cells or their precursors are transplanted into immunologically compromised recipients. The transferred cells recognize the alloantigens in the host and attack host tissues. It is seen most commonly during hematopoietic stem cell transplantation but may also occur following the transplantation of solid organs.  GVHD may be of two types: acute and chronic. Acute GVHD occurs within days to weeks after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. It mainly involves the immune system and the epithelia of the skin (in the form of generalized rash), liver (in the form of jaundice), and intestines (in the form of bloody diarrhea). But the affected tissues are not heavily infiltrated by lymphocytes. Chronic GVHD may follow acute GVHD or may occur insidiously. These patients have extensive skin damage, with the destruction of skin appendages and fibrosis of the dermis, resembling systemic sclerosis. Cholestatic jaundice and esophageal strictures are also common. There will be involution of the thymus and depletion of lymphocytes in the lymph nodes. There will also be recurrent bouts of life-threatening infections. Some may even develop autoimmunity, owing to the grafted CD4+ helper T cells reacting with host B cells and stimulating them, which may result in autoantibody production. Depletion of donor T cells by irradiation before transfusion can eliminate the occurrence of GVHD. But irradiation also has its adverse effects such as tumor recurrence in leukemic patients, increased incidence of graft failures, and EBV-related B-cell lymphoma. Patients with IE and small vegetations without heart failure, systemic embolization, or persistent bacteremia should be managed initially with intravenous antibiotics as the first-line therapy. Infective endocarditis is an infection of the endothelium of the heart, which can be caused by bacteria, fungi, and other microorganisms.  Acute IE rapidly damages the cardiac structures and spreads to extracardiac sites, frequently involving a highly virulent organism (e.g., S. aureus) attacking a previously normal valve. Patients with infective endocarditis can have cardiac or non-cardiac manifestations. Cardiac manifestations of IE: * Presence of new regurgitant murmurs * Congestive heart failure due to valve dysfunction * Perivalvular abscesses and intracardiac fistulae- This is caused due to the extension of infection beyond the valves and into the adjacent myocardial tissue * Conduction system defects- due to the damage of the interventricular septum by the abscess. * Embolization of coronary arteries Noncardiac manifestations of IE are: * Arterial emboli- causing pain of ischemia of the organs * Osler's nodes -are painful, red, nodular lesions usually located in the pads of the fingers and toes * Roth's spots- retinal hemorrhages with a pale center * Janeway lesions- In contrast to Osler's nodes, these are faint, red, painless macules on palms and soles. They occur as a result of septic embolization and are commonly associated with staphylococcal IE. * Splenic abscess * Cerebral abscess * Immune-complex mediated glomerulonephritis * Positivity for rheumatoid factor * Petechiae on oral and conjunctival mucosa * Splinter subungual hemorrhages-painless, dark red lines in the nailbed. * Mycotic aneurysms * Splenomegaly Treatment for infective endocarditis involves antibiotic therapy initiated immediately upon a definitive diagnosis. The duration of antibiotics is usually a total of 4 to 6 weeks. High serum bactericidal levels are necessary to eradicate organisms in inaccessible avascular vegetations.  Early surgical treatment is usually reserved for cases with paravalvular extension, abscess, severe valve dysfunction, or persistent bacteremia despite optimal antimicrobial therapy. For cases with severe complications, like intractable heart failure, large vegetations, valvular destruction or persistent infection, surgical intervention is required. Other options: Option A and D: Immediate surgical intervention or tricuspid valve replacement is not recommended unless there are complications such as large vegetations, valve dysfunction, abscess formation, or persistent infection despite appropriate antibiotic therapy. The presence of single pathological criteria is definitive of infective endocarditis. Note: The diagnosis of endocarditis is rejected if an alternative diagnosis is established either when: * Symptoms resolve and do not recur with <4 days of antibiotic therapy OR * If surgery or autopsy yields no pathologic or macroscopic evidence of endocarditis in <4 days of antimicrobial therapy. pH<7.35 is acidosis

pH>7.45 is alkalosis

A primary change in HCO3- is termed metabolic

If the change in HCO3- is in keeping with the pH (i.e. if there is acidosis and HCO3- is decreased) the problem is metabolic.

If the change in HCO3- is in the opposite direction of that of the pH (i.e. if there is acidosis and HCO3- is increased or normal) the problem is compensatory metabolic.

A primary change in CO2 is termed as respiratory

If the change in CO2 keeping in line with the pH (if in acidosis CO2 is raised) the problem is termed respiratory

text: 13. A 65-year-old female patient presents to the OPD with complaints of shortness of breath and tiredness. On examination, there were engorged neck veins and JVP showed rapid x and y descent. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Constrictive pericarditis

The clinical features and the JVP findings of rapid X and Y descent  are suggestive of constrictive pericarditis. Constrictive pericarditis: * It is the condition where a thickened, fibrotic, and often calcified pericardium restricts the diastolic filling of the heart. * In developing countries, infectious etiologies like tuberculosis or viral infections are the most common cause of this condition. * Cardiac surgery and radiation therapy are also common causes. * Other causes include connective tissue disease, uremia, neoplasm, or idiopathic. * Clinically the patients present with dyspnea, orthopnea, and fatigue. * JVP findings - There is a rapid 'x' and 'y' descent. The rapid 'y' descent is more prominent and reflects rapid early ventricular diastolic filling. This occurs due to the constricting pericardium, increasing the atrial pressures. Diagnosis: * Diagnosis is difficult and is confirmed by multiple investigations * Hallmark findings of pericardial constriction are pericardial thickening, calcification, and abnormal ventricular diastolic function. * The X-ray can be normal or there may be non-specific cardiac enlargement, calcification, and roughened cardiac outline. * Echo can assess the hemodynamic function but it is accurate in identifying pericardial thickening. * CT and MRI are more sensitive investigations. * CT has an edge over MRI as it can detect calcification associated with this condition. * Pericardial thickness of > 4mm along with clinical features of constriction is highly suggestive of this diagnosis. * Cardiac MR may show diastolic septal bounce. * Hepatomegaly and ascites can be seen associated with this condition. Constrictive pericarditis will have prominent y descent, prominent x descent, and Kussmaul's sign. Normally, the venous pressure should fall by at least 3 mmHg with inspiration. Kussmaul’s sign is defined by either a rise or a lack of fall of the JVP with inspiration. Other important conditions and their JVP tracings are * In Cardiac tamponade, the jugular venous pressure (JVP) tracing of the patient will have a prominent x descent but an absent y descent. * Atrioventricular block will have cannon a waves * Atrial fibrillation will have absent a wave * Tricuspid regurgitation will have accentuated v wave with rapid y descent * Tricuspid stenosis will have prolonged y wave Pearl PF0262: JVP waveform and the abnormalities 1) The a-wave corresponds to atrial contraction.

text: 14. An elderly patient is brought to the emergency in a comatose state. Examination reveals serum glucose levels of 500 mg/dL, arterial pH of 7.33, elevated plasma ketones, and normal serum potassium levels. What should be added to the saline in the management of this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Insulin

In the above clinical scenario, the patient has diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). The patient needs to be started on IV fluids and insulin at a dose of 0.1 unit per kg.  Diabetic ketoacidosis is an acute complication of type 1 diabetes mellitus. The symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and severe abdominal pain. Signs: * Kussmaul breathing * Fruity odor on the patient’s breath * Tachycardia * Dehydration * Hypotension Blood parameters: * Hyperglycemia – 250 – 600 mg% * Pseudohyponatremia- There is 1.6-mmol/L reduction in serum sodium level for each 5.6-mmol/L rise in the serum glucose level. * Overall total-body K+ deficit, however, the serum K+ at presentation may be mildly elevated, secondary to the acidosis * Osmolality– 300–320 mOsm/kg * Plasma ketones– Positive * Metabolic acidosis– Increased anion gap * Serum bicarbonate <15 meq/L– Best initial investigation * Hypertriglyceridemia * Hyperamylasemia Management of DKA * Admit to hospital assess for serum electrolytes and acid-base status * Replace fluids- 2-3 liters (10-20 mL/kg/hr) of normal saline should be administered over 1-3 hours. Subsequently 0.45% saline at 250-500 mL/hr. It can be changed to 5% glucose and 0.45% saline at 150–250 mL/h when plasma glucose reaches 250 mg/dL. * Administer IV short-acting insulin regular insulin. 0.1 units/kg of insulin should be administered immediately as a bolus dose. This is followed by an intravenous infusion of 0.1 units/kg. Serum potassium levels should be checked before initiating insulin. If the levels are high, then it has to be corrected and then insulin should be started. * The above measures should be continued until the serum glucose levels reach 150–200 mg/dL, and acidosis is resolved. Insulin infusion may be decreased to 0.02–0.1 units/kg per hour. * Long-acting insulin can be started when the patient starts eating. The chart shows the management algorithm for DKA. text: 20. A patient with a history of fever for the past 4 days and new onset of breathlessness was admitted to ICU as he was deteriorating. He was unresponsive to the incremental flow rate of oxygen and his oxygen saturation was progressively decreasing. expl:
Correct answer: D. ARDS

The history of fever for less than 1 week, refractory hypoxia, chest x-ray showing bilateral infiltrates, and PaO2/FiO2 <300 mmHg is diagnostic of ARDS. Acute respiratory distress syndrome is characterized by rapid onset dyspnea, hypoxemia, and diffuse lung infiltrates resulting in respiratory failure. ARDS is caused by diffuse lung injury due to varied causes like inhalation injury, pneumonia, gastric aspiration, pulmonary contusion, burns, pancreatitis, and sepsis. In patients with ARDS, there is an inflammatory response in the lungs leading to high levels of neutrophils and their secretory products in the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. This is characteristic of non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema. An early chest x-ray typically reveals diffuse opacities due to consolidation. Later these opacities progress to more extensive and asymmetrical consolidation. The CT scan of the lungs shows heterogeneous involvement and predominantly affects gravity-dependent areas. The affected airspaces are filled with fluid and cannot contribute to ventilation, leading to hypoxemia (due to increased pulmonary shunt) and hypercapnia (due to inadequate ventilation in some areas of the lung); resulting in, ventilation-perfusion mismatch. The hypoxemia in ARDS is refractory to the increasing concentration of inhaled oxygen that occurs due to increased intrapulmonary shunting of blood. The most common cause of death is sepsis in ARDS. Due to improvement in ventilator support systems, respiratory failure causes mortality in less than 20% of cases. Diagnostic criteria in ARDS—Berlin definition: The Berlin definition requires each of the following criteria be present to diagnose ARDS: * Onset- Acute: Respiratory symptoms must have begun within one week of a known clinical insult * Bilateral alveolar or interstitial infiltrates: must be present on a chest X-ray image or CT scan * Respiratory failure must not be fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload. Objective assessment e.g Echo should be done in cases of no known cause. * Impairment of oxygenation must be present: The severity of hypoxemia defines the severity of ARDS

Its activity is greatly reduced in vitamin B12 deficiency, leading to an accumulation of methylmalonic acid. Whereas in folate deficiency, methylmalonic acid levels are normal. This cab be used to differentiate between megaloblastic anaemia due to folate and vitamin B12 deficiency.  There are two vitamin B12-dependent enzymes: * Methionine synthase (Homocysteine methyltransferase): Catalyzes the conversion of homocysteine to methionine * Methylmalonyl CoA mutase: Methylmalonyl CoA, formed as an intermediate in the catabolism of valine, isoleucine and propionyl CoA is converted to succinyl CoA The folate cycle acts as the link between the functions of folate and vitamin B12, and a deficiency of vitamin B12 can cause a functional deficiency of folate. Vitamin B12 acts as a cofactor of methionine synthase, an enzyme involved in the regeneration of tetrahydrofolate from methyl-tetrahydrofolate. The decreased activity of methionine synthase in vitamin B12 deficiency results in the accumulation of methyltetrahydrofolate, which cannot be used, resulting in a folate trap. The expected metabolic abnormality to be seen in this patient is Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hyponatremia. The persistent vomiting results in these abnormalities along with paradoxial aciduria.  * Persistent vomiting results in loss of hydrochloric acid leading to the development of metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-). * Kidneys try to compensate for alkalosis by secreting Na+ and HCO3- causing hyponatremia.However, loss of sodium stimulates the secretion of aldosterone through the RAAS pathway. * The aldosterone causes active reabsorption of sodium in exchange for K+ and H+ ions. * Loss of potassium ions leads to the development of hypokalemia. * Loss of H+ ions in urine lowers the urinary pH resulting in aciduria. It is called paradoxical aciduria, since the body initially lost H+ ions due to loss of HCl, and instead of compensating for that loss, the body is losing more H+ ions through urine. text: 25. A tall male presents with absent pubic and axillary hair, infantile genitalia, high LH and FSH levels with XXY karyotype. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Klinefelter's syndrome

The above clinical scenario is indicative of Klinefelter's syndrome (KS). The classic form of KS (47,XXY) occurs after meiotic nondisjunction of the sex chromosomes during gametogenesis. Mosaic forms of KS (46,XY/47,XXY) are thought to result from chromosomal mitotic nondisjunction within the zygote and occur in at least 10% of individuals with this condition. Other chromosomal variants of KS (e.g., 48,XXYY, 48,XXXY) have been reported but are less common. KS is characterized by small testes, infertility, gynecomastia, tall stature/increased leg length, and hypogonadism. Testes are small and firm (median length 2.5 cm/4 mL, almost always <3.5 cm/ 12 mL) and typically seem inappropriately small for the degree of androgenization. Plasma concentrations of FSH and luteinizing hormone (LH) are increased in most adults with 47,XXY, and plasma testosterone is decreased (50–75%), reflecting primary gonadal failure. Patients with mosaic forms of KS have less severe clinical features, have larger testes, and sometimes achieve spontaneous fertility. Treatment: * Growth, endocrine function, and bone mineralization should be monitored, especially from adolescence. * Educational and psychological support is important for many individuals with KS. * Androgen supplementation improves virilization, libido, energy, hypofibrinolysis, and bone mineralization in men with low testosterone levels but may occasionally worsen gynecomastia. * Gynecomastia can be treated by surgical reduction if it causes concern. * Fertility has been achieved by using in vitro fertilization in men with oligospermia or with intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) after retrieval of spermatozoa by testicular sperm extraction techniques. * Long-term monitoring of men with KS is important given the increased risk of breast cancer, cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, and autoimmune disorders. text: 30. Which of the following is the preferred initial treatment for an empyema that is uni-loculated?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Chest tube drainage and antibiotics

The preferred initial treatment in the case of uni-loculated empyema is chest tube drainage with antibiotics.  Empyema is a collection of pus in the pleural space that can be uni-loculated or complex (with internal septations). It can occur due to a parapneumonic effusion or due to direct inoculation from trauma. Treatment of empyema includes antibiotics and drainage of the infected pleural fluid. Empiric antibiotics are started initially and later changed based on the type of effusion and local guidelines. Thoracocentesis is only for diagnostic purposes and is insufficient for full drainage. The choice of drainage technique is patient-based and varies on several factors including the state of the patient. However, a general concept is as below. * In small uncomplicated parapneumonic effusions, drainage is not necessary unless it causes severe respiratory dysfunction. * In complicated parapneumonic effusions that are free-flowing or uni-loculated, a  chest tube or catheter drainage is the procedure of choice. * Complicated effusions with loculations need additional drains along with a reassessment of the tube position and antibiotic coverage. A CT scan is used to assess the response to treatment and fluid collection. If drainage is not adequate with chest tubes, then additional techniques like intrapleural tissue plasminogen activator/deoxyribonuclease (tPA/DNase) or Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS) can be tried. The rationale of using tissue plasminogen activator/deoxyribonuclease is that it reduces the internal septations and helps in drainage leading to faster resolution of empyema.  VATS is used to visualize the pleural cavity directly and resolve the empyema. Note: Open thoracotomy and decortication are only done in refractory and chronic cases.

In metabolic acidosis, potassium bicarbonate or citrate may also be used as part of the treatment. Use of intravenous KCl is limited to patients who cannot take it orally, in severe hypokalemia (<2.5 mmol/L, patients with complications or at risk of arrhythmias etc.) However, cardiac monitoring is needed in an intensive care setting when the IV route is preferred. Because dextrose can increase insulin release and exacerbate hypokalaemia by pushing potassium into cells, it should be administered in saline solutions instead. The intravenous route when used should be given via femoral veins preferably as it decreases the risk of local concentration and cardiac arrhythmias which can occur when given via the internal jugular or subclavian central lines. Note: In situations involving excessive sympathetic activity, such as acute head injury or theophylline overdose, high-dose propranolol may be used to correct hypokalemia without causing rebound hyperkalemia.

There is a history of a similar episode of icterus 2 years back when the patient had long hours of basketball practice. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Gilbert syndrome

Gilbert syndrome is the most likely diagnosis in this patient. This patient's mild jaundice seen only during a period of stress along with an increase in unconjugated bilirubin and normal AST, and ALT levels strongly point towards a diagnosis of Gilbert syndrome. Gilbert syndrome is a benign, familial disorder inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern characterized by mild intermittent jaundice usually seen during stress, illnesses, or any other precipitating factors. There is no hemolysis or underlying liver disease. The condition is recognized to arise from a mutation in the promoter region of the UGT1A1 gene, which results in mildly decreased UDP-Glucoronyltransferase production. UDP-Glucoronyltransferase is required for the conjugation of bilirubin. Precipitating factors in Gilbert syndrome: * Dehydration * Fasting * Menstrual periods * Illness * Vigorous exercise. Other options: Option A: Dubin-Johnson syndrome is a benign autosomal recessive disease that is characterized by chronic conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and conspicuous brown-black melanin-like pigment deposition in the liver. The disease is caused due to mutation in multidrug resistance protein 2 (MRP-2) in hepatocytes, which is required for the transport of non-bile salt organic anions at the canalicular membranes. Liver biopsy shows characteristic deposition of black-colored pigment. Option B: Crigler-Najjar syndrome is of two types with type 1 having absent/trace UDP-Glucoronyltransferase production and type 2 having <10% of the normal enzyme activity. Hence, type 1 is far more severe and leads to kernicterus and neurological damage in babies. Type 2 may also lead to kernicterus occasionally. Unconjugated bilirubin is elevated. Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in a 25-year-old male is less likely to be due to Criggler Najar type 1 syndrome. text: 9. A young male patient presents with ptosis which reportedly worsens in the evening and improves in the morning. He also complains of excessive fatiguability towards the end of the day which improves with rest. Placing an ice pack over his eyes significantly decreases the ptosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Myasthenia gravis

From the given clinical picture, myasthenia gravis is the most likely diagnosis. This patient has symptoms of ptosis, progressive weakness, and excessive fatiguability which improves with rest.  Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles. It is due to the autoantibody-mediated destruction of the acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the post-synaptic membrane. This consequentially leads to a decreased transmission at the neuromuscular junction. Failure of transmission results in muscle weakness. Females are more commonly affected than males and the disease tends to occur in middle age. Clinical features of myasthenia gravis: * Muscle weakness and fatiguability increase with repeated use or during late in the day and may improve following rest or sleep. Limb weakness is proximal and asymmetrical * Cranial muscles particularly the lids and extraocular muscles are involved early in the course - diplopia, ptosis * Facial weakness - snarling expression on smiling * Weakness in chewing * Speech with nasal timbre due to the weakness of palate and tongue * Difficulty in swallowing * Deep tendon reflexes are intact * Myasthenic crisis - acute exacerbation of muscle weakness especially intercostal and diaphragmatic muscles resulting in ventilatory failure. It is most commonly due to infection and anticholinesterase medication overuse. Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymoma and other autoimmune diseases such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Grave's disease, neuromyelitis optics, systemic lupus erythematosus, etc. Diagnosis: * Ice-pack test - application of ice pack over the eyes improves ptosis (decreases activity of acetylcholinesterase, this increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and increases transmission) * Antibodies associated with myasthenia gravis: Anti-AChR antibodies, Anti-MuSK antibodies, Anti-LRP4 antibodies * Repetitive nerve stimulation test shows a decremental response. * Edrophonium chloride or Tensilon test - improvement of symptoms occurs on injecting edrophonium. Edrophonium is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. This increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and improves transmission. Treatment: * Anticholinesterase drugs - Pyridostigmine. * Thymectomy. * Immunosuppression therapy with glucocorticoids, azathioprine, tacrolimus, rituximab, etc. * Plasmapheresis and intravenous immunoglobulin.

text: 11. A man brings his father who became unconscious while working in a field in the hot sun at 42 degrees Celsius in May. On examination, there were no physical signs of dehydration. Correct answer: C. Sweating

The given clinical scenario of a patient is highly suggestive of heatstroke. The symptom least likely to be seen in this patient is sweating. Heatstroke occurs due to the failure of the heat regulation center of the hypothalamus. The person fails to lose heat by cutaneous circulation and sweating. It is likely to develop when the body temperature rises to a range of 105°F to 108°F. The predisposing factors include high temperature, increased humidity, minor infections, old age, and physical activity Heatstroke can be: * Exertion-induced heat stroke is seen in people with prolonged exposure to or physical exertion in high temperatures, usually without adequate training. * Sedentary heatstroke is a disease of elderly or infirm people whose cardiovascular systems are unable to adapt to the stress of a hot environment and release sufficient heat such that body temperature rises. It is a medical emergency that leads to homeostatic imbalance. The symptoms include dizziness, abdominal distress, vomiting, delirium, and eventually leading to loss of consciousness. On examination, the skin is dry, hot, and flushed, with a complete absence of sweating (anhidrosis).  Other manifestations of heat stroke include: * Seizures and confusion * Dizziness and muscle cramps * Hypotension and cardiac failure * Tachycardia and rapid, deep Kussmaul-type breathing  Heatstroke can cause damage to multiple organ systems, including the brain, kidneys, and liver, which can lead to life-threatening complications. It is essential to initiate rapid cooling and supportive care measures to prevent permanent injury or death. The cooling methods used to treat heatstroke include: Although there is no single specific diagnostic test, the preliminary diagnosis is based on clinical features of heat exposure, CNS impairment, and a core temperature exceeding 104.9°F. Rectal measurement is essential for accurate assessment of body temperature Treatment includes rapidly cooling the body with ice water till the rectal temperature falls below 102oF. text: 13. A young man presents with a sudden onset of severe headache, dizziness, breathlessness, and blurring of vision while trekking on a mountain at an altitude of 5000 meters. He is unable to climb any further. Which of the following indicates the development of high-altitude cerebral edema?

Correct answer: B. Altered mental status

Altered mental status is a clinical finding indicative of the development of high-altitude cerebral edema.  At high altitudes, the partial pressure of oxygen in the atmosphere is low. When people ascend to high altitudes hypoxia causes systemic arteriolar dilatation. Consequently, the capillary pressure rises with increased transudation of fluid into the brain tissue and lungs. This results in cerebral edema and pulmonary edema respectively. Pathophysiology: Vasogenic edema occurs due to the leaking of proteins and water through the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Causes of increased BBB permeability include: * Mechanical factors: loss of autoregulation and increased capillary pressure due to increased sympathetic activity (option D). * Increased chemical mediators of permeability: Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) (option C), nitric oxide, and cytokines (option A). Patients with cerebral edema usually present with: * Headache * Worsening mental status and reduced alertness. * Papilledema leading to a blurring of vision * Breathlessness (due to hypoxia) * Nausea and vomiting. Treatment involves administration of oxygen, descent to a lower altitude, and administration of acetazolamide. Acetazolamide counteracts hypoxia by stimulating respiration and also reduces the formation of cerebrospinal fluid, thereby reducing intracranial tension. Glucocorticoids are administered as well. Portable hyperbaric chambers are increasingly being used in the treatment of high-altitude illnesses when rapid descent is not possible. text: 15. What is the probable diagnosis of the ECG given below?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Hypothermia

The hallmark of this patient's ECG is the Osborn J wave. Hypothermia is defined as core body temperature being less than 95°F. In the initial stages of hypothermia, as a reaction to the general stress, there is sinus tachycardia. As the temperature drops below 90°F, there is sinus bradycardia associated with prolongation of the PR interval, QRS complex, and QT interval progressively. With temperature approaching 86°F, atrial ectopic activity is often noted and can progress to atrial fibrillation. It is at this level of hypothermia that many patients have Osborn waves that consist of an extra deflection at the end of the QRS complex. J waves occur when a heterogeneous distribution of potassium current enhances the activity of a transient outward potassium current in the heart, caused by low temperatures. Osborn waves, also known as J waves, camel-hump waves, or hypothermic waves, are best seen in the inferior and lateral precordial leads. They become more prominent as the body temperature drops, and they regress gradually with rewarming. A progressive widening of the QRS complex occurs when the temperature falls below 86°F, which is associated with an increased risk of ventricular fibrillation and asystole occurs when the temperature drops to about 60°F. Other options: * Hyperkalemia: Tall, tented T waves are seen in hyperkalemia. * Hypokalemia: U waves are seen in hypokalemia. * Hypocalcemia: Prolonged QTc interval, occasional T wave inversion.

A primary change in HCO3- is termed metabolic

text: 20. What is the drug of choice for Legionnaire’s disease?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Azithromycin

The antibiotics of choice in a patient with Legionnaire's disease are macrolides. Legionnaire’s disease is caused by Legionella pneumophila. They are found in lakes, streams, and other water bodies. Infection is mostly spread by inhalation of the bacteria from aerosols produced by contaminated air conditions, humidifiers, nebulizers, etc. It is mostly asymptomatic under the age of 55 years. Infection is usually severe in immunocompromised patients. It may present as a severe, rapidly progressive disease with high fever, chills, hypoxia, diarrhea, and delirium. On chest X-ray, patchy, often multilobar consolidation is seen. Pleural effusion may also occur. This leads to this infection being included in a differential diagnosis of atypical pneumonia. A milder form of a clinical syndrome known as Pontiac fever may also occur which is usually self-limiting and only has mild symptoms of fever, myalgia, and headache. Microscopy of the sputum samples shows numerous leucocytes without any organism. Gram staining of the sterile sites like pleural fluid and lung tissues show faint gram-negative bacilli. They require a counterstain of basic fuschin as safranin stains the bacteria very poorly. They are a group of fastidious, aerobic gram-negative bacteria. They can be grown on a buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar. Diagnosis is established with the help of direct fluorescent antibody tests and BCYE culture specimens. Urine antigen tests and molecular assays may also be used.  Macrolides and quinolones are the drugs of choice for this condition. Macrolides and quinolones are the antibiotics of choice and are effective as monotherapy. Alternatively, agents like doxycycline may also be used. B-lactams, monobactams and aminoglycosides are not considered to be effective. Total duration of therapy is 10-14 days for immunocompetent hosts and up to 3 weeks for immunosuppressed patients. Gram staining of pleural fluid showing the presence of gram-negative bacilli causative organism of Legionnaire’s disease, Legionella pneumophila.

text: 24. A tall male presents with absent pubic and axillary hair, infantile genitalia, high LH and FSH levels with XXY karyotype. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Klinefelter's syndrome

The above clinical scenario is indicative of Klinefelter's syndrome (KS). The classic form of KS (47,XXY) occurs after meiotic nondisjunction of the sex chromosomes during gametogenesis. Mosaic forms of KS (46,XY/47,XXY) are thought to result from chromosomal mitotic nondisjunction within the zygote and occur in at least 10% of individuals with this condition. Other chromosomal variants of KS (e.g., 48,XXYY, 48,XXXY) have been reported but are less common. KS is characterized by small testes, infertility, gynecomastia, tall stature/increased leg length, and hypogonadism. Testes are small and firm (median length 2.5 cm/4 mL, almost always <3.5 cm/ 12 mL) and typically seem inappropriately small for the degree of androgenization. Plasma concentrations of FSH and luteinizing hormone (LH) are increased in most adults with 47,XXY, and plasma testosterone is decreased (50–75%), reflecting primary gonadal failure. Patients with mosaic forms of KS have less severe clinical features, have larger testes, and sometimes achieve spontaneous fertility. Treatment: * Growth, endocrine function, and bone mineralization should be monitored, especially from adolescence. * Educational and psychological support is important for many individuals with KS. * Androgen supplementation improves virilization, libido, energy, hypofibrinolysis, and bone mineralization in men with low testosterone levels but may occasionally worsen gynecomastia. * Gynecomastia can be treated by surgical reduction if it causes concern. * Fertility has been achieved by using in vitro fertilization in men with oligospermia or with intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) after retrieval of spermatozoa by testicular sperm extraction techniques. * Long-term monitoring of men with KS is important given the increased risk of breast cancer, cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, and autoimmune disorders. text: 1. An AIDS-positive patient came with a history of fever, vomiting, and meningismus. Which of the following tests help in the rapid diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Blood assay for cryptococcal antigen

Blood assay for cryptococcal antigen help in the rapid diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis. Latex agglutination tests are mainly used for the detection of carbohydrate antigens of encapsulated microorganisms. In latex agglutination tests, an antigen-specific antibody (either polyclonal or monoclonal) is fixed to latex beads. When the clinical specimen from the patient is added to a suspension of the latex beads, the antibodies bind to the antigens on the microorganism forming a lattice structure, and agglutination of the beads occurs.  Cryptococcal meningitis is the most common cause of meningitis in an immunocompromised HIV patient. It generally occurs in untreated patients, with CD4+ T cell counts <100/μL. It presents with subacute meningoencephalitis with fever, nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, headache, and meningeal signs. The CSF profile shows elevations in WBC with lymphocyte predominance, elevated protein levels, and reduced to normal levels of glucose. The CSF opening pressure is usually elevated Diagnosis is made by demonstration of yeast cells or cryptococcal antigen in CSF. India ink stain is used to demonstrate capsulated budding yeast cells in CSF as they have a distinctive appearance because their capsules exclude ink particles. But its very much subjective and hence is less preferred over other methods for rapid diagnosis. Rapid detection of cryptococcal antigen in CSF and blood can also be done. Colonies develop within a few days on most media at room temperature or 37°C.  Treatment *  Induction – IV or Liposomal Amphotericin B with Flucytosine for at least 2 weeks, continuing with Amphotericin alone ideally until the CSF culture turns negative. *  Maintenance -  Oral Fluconazole until the CD4+ T cell count has increased to >200 cells/μL for 6 months in response to cART. *  Primary Prophylaxis - Oral Fluconazole when CD4+ T cell count is <100/μL.

text: 7. A 4-year-old boy presents with complaints of fever and sore throat. On examination, he has extensive cervical swelling and a well-demarcated white-gray exudative substance adherent to his oropharynx and attempts to remove this pseudomembranous result in bleeding. The parents report that all his childhood vaccines were skipped due to religious beliefs. A throat swab under Albert's staining is as below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Diphtheria

This is a classic clinical description, oral examination with pseudomembrane and the image given above is of a patient with diphtheria.  Corynebacterium diphtheria (also called Klebs- Loeffler bacillus) is a gram-positive bacillus with clubbing at both ends. They possess characteristic polymetaphosphate granules also called metachromatic granules.   The diphtheria toxin is an extremely potent protein toxin that acts by inhibiting protein synthesis by inactivating the elongation factor (EF-2).  Clinically, patients with diphtheria present with fever, sore throat, and pseudomembranous lesions on the tonsillar, pharyngeal, or nasal mucosa. The pseudo-membrane in diphtheria is tightly adherent to the underlying tissues and attempts to remove them result in bleeding. A few patients develop massive edema of the tonsils, submandibular and paratracheal region causing a characteristic bull-neck. It is associated with foul breath, thick speech, and stridor. The systemic manifestations of diphtheria are due to diphtheria toxin and not due to bacteremia. It has a special affinity for myocardium, adrenal glands, and nerve endings and therefore, causes weakness as a result of neurotoxicity, cardiac arrhythmias, or congestive heart failure due to myocarditis. Treatment of diphtheria includes administration of diphtheria anti-toxin. Recommended antibiotics include penicillin G and erythromycin for two weeks. Patients are placed in an isolation room and droplet precautions should be maintained for all cases of respiratory diphtheria. Although patients are not contagious starting 48 hours after antibiotic therapy, droplet precautions are typically maintained until the completion of the antibiotic course and are culture-negative on two cultures taken 24 hours apart. Droplet precautions include the use of masks, gowns, gloves, and protective eye gear when providing direct patient care.  While the development of an effective vaccine has nearly eradicated the disease in many countries, failure to undergo routine vaccination leaves some patients at risk. Vaccination with diphtheria toxoid is recommended for all cases of diphtheria after convalescence, as natural infection may not induce an adequate level of protective immunity. text: 9. A 34-year-old HIV-positive male presented with low-grade fever, cough, night sweats, and weight loss for the past 3 weeks. In view of TB investigations, the Mantoux test was negative, chest X-ray showed non-specific findings and an adequate amount of sputum could not be collected for slide examination. Correct answer: C. Interferon gamma release assay

The test used to diagnose latent TB infection in this patient is the Interferon-gamma release assay(IGRA). TB test done on a whole blood sample is IGRA. In this test, sensitized T lymphocytes (from whole blood) of suspected individuals, are exposed to highly specific M. tuberculosis antigens such as CFP –10 and ESAT 6. This releases the cytokine IFN- gamma into the blood, which is then measured. It has been evaluated for the diagnosis of latent tuberculosis in HIV patients (who frequently have a negative Mantoux test.  IGRAs that have been approved by the US (FDA) are * QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube test (QFT-GIT): It quantitates the amount of interferon-gamma produced by CD4+ T cells in response to the antigens from Mycobacterium tuberculosis. * T-SPOT.TB test (T-Spot): It determines the total number of individual effector T cells expressing Interferon-gamma. * QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT- Plus) IGRAs are more specific than Tuberculin Skin Testing (TST) because of less cross-reactivity to BCG vaccination and sensitization by nontuberculous mycobacteria. There are 3 described methods for tuberculin skin testing (TST): * Mantoux test, also known as the Pirquet test (preferred method) * Heaf test * Tine test The TrueNat TB test is a new molecular test that can diagnose TB and resistance to rifampicin in one hour. This test uses a sputum sample and only about 0.5 ml of the sample is required. Urine lipoarabinomannan (LAM) assay is used for the diagnosis of tuberculosis. Lipoarabinomannan (LAM) antigen is a lipopolysaccharide present in the mycobacterial cell wall, released from metabolically active cells or degenerating cells of patients having tuberculosis. Urine LAM is a useful tool in diagnosing tuberculosis, especially in patients with HIV and a low CD 4 count. QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT- Plus) is an improved version of the QuantiFERON-TB Gold test. QuantiFERON-TB Gold detects only TB-specific CD4+ responses. However, QuantiFeron-TB Gold Plus detects both CD8+ and CD4+ T cell responses to TB specific antigens.

text: 10. While collecting a blood sample for investigations, you accidentally drop and spill a 5 ml tube of blood. Which among the following is the best solution to clean it?
expl:
Correct answer: D. 1:100 Sodium hypochlorite

Sodium hypochlorite solution in 1:100 dilution is used to clean a blood spill of less than 10 ml. Blood spills may occur because a laboratory sample breaks during the procedure or during transport, or because there is excessive bleeding during the procedure. In such cases, clean up the spill and record the incident, using the following steps: * Wear a pair of non-sterile gloves or appropriate PPE. * Use appropriate instruments (like tongs or a pan and brush) to sweep up any broken glass (or container) as possible. Do not pick up pieces with your hands. * Discard the broken glass in a sharps container. If not possible due to the size of the broken glass, wrap it in several layers of paper and discard it carefully in a separate container. It should not be discarded in the regular waste container. * Use disposable paper towels to absorb as much of the body fluids as possible. * Wipe the area with water and detergent until it is visibly clean. * Saturate the area again with 5.25-6.15% sodium hypochlorite, which should be prepared daily. * Spills < 10ml are cleaned with 1:100 dilution sodium hypochlorite * Spills >10ml or involving a culture spill in the laboratory are cleaned with 1:10 dilution sodium hypochlorite. * Follow this decontamination process with terminal disinfection, using a 1:100 dilution of sodium hypochlorite. * Rinse off the tongs, brush, and pan. * Remove and discard the gloves. * Wash hands carefully with soap and water, and dry with a disposable towel. * Record the incident if a specimen was lost, or persons were exposed to blood and body fluids. text: 13. Which of the following is amplified in an RT-PCR test for the COVID-19 virus?

This means that the fever has a periodicity of 48 hours corresponding to one cycle of erythrocytic schizogony. Malignant because it is a more severe and fatal type of malaria. Major manifestations of severe falciparum malaria include unarousable coma/ cerebral malaria (failure to localize or respond appropriately to stimuli or coma persisting for >30 min after generalized convulsion), acidosis, severe normocytic normochromic anemia, renal failure, pulmonary edema, hypoglycemia, shock, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Other manifestations include hemoglobinuria, hyperparasitemia, jaundice, and extreme weakness. Falciparum malaria shows a very high percentage of RBCs containing ring forms. This high-level parasitemia is more often seen in Plasmodium falciparum infection than in infection by other plasmodia. After the ring form in the peripheral blood, the rest of the erythrocytic cycle occurs in the capillaries of the brain and internal organs. The treatment of choice is artesunate given at a dose of 2.4 mg/kg stat IV, followed by 2.4 mg/kg at 12 and 24 hours, and then daily if necessary. text: 9. A 70-year- old woman was diagnosed with right leg cellulitis and was admitted in hospital for 3 days. She was prescribed clindamycin. Two days after her discharge, she developed diarrhoea and abdominal pain. Her temperature was 38.8 degrees. Her blood reports revealed a Hb level of 12g/dl; WBC count of 18,000/mm3; CRP of 160mg/l. What is the most probable etiological agent?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Clostridium difficile

The given clinical vignette of a patient with diarrhoea following antibiotic administration is suggestive of pseudomembranous colitis due to Clostridium difficile.  Clostridium difficile is the most common cause of infectious diarrhoea in nosocomial infections. It is the most common antibiotic-associated diarrhoea. It is commonly seen in individuals who receive a prolonged antibiotic course, which causes a change in the composition of gastrointestinal microbial flora, leading to the colonization of C. difficile. Clinical features: * Lower abdominal pain with loose watery diarrhea. * Fever, leukocytosis * In some patients, the disease may progress to life-threatening pseudomembranous colitis. Investigations: * Nucleic acid amplification tests, including PCR assays, for C. difficile toxin A or B gene in stool  * Stool culture in selective media * Demonstrating toxin by Hep-2 cell cultures * Toxin gene identification by enzyme immunoassay * Colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy reveals a characteristic appearance, with erythema, white plaques, or an adherent pseudomembrane. Nucleic acid amplification tests, including PCR assays, for C. difficile toxin A or B gene in the stool are used as they are both rapid and sensitive while retaining high specificity. Oral vancomycin, metronidazole, and fidaxomicin are used for the treatment of pseudomembranous colitis, depending on its severity.  First choice treatment of C. difficile colitis:
Severity Treatment
Mild to moderate Oral Vancomycin
Severe (WBC >15,000/cu.mm, Creatinine >1.5 times baseline) Oral Vancomycin
Severe, Complicated (Shock, Ileus, Toxic Megacolon) Oral Vancomycin + IV Metronidazole ± Rectal Vancomycin
Recurrent/ multiple episodes Fecal Microbiota Transplantation (FMT)
Fidaxomicin is an alternative in all cases. Metronidazole is now reserved for non-severe infections in settings where access to first-line drugs is limited or cost is an issue.  Recent update: Harrison's 20th edition recommends the use of vancomycin over metronidazole in the treatment of initial episodes which are mild to moderate in severity. Metronidazole is recommended only if vancomycin or fidaxomicin are not accessible. Oral metronidazole is less effective than the other options and may necessitate a longer treatment course for response. Other options: Escherichia coli, Norovirus, Rotavirus are all causes of Traveller's diarrhea. Other causes for Nosocomial diarrhea: * Clostridium perfringens, * Klebsiella oxytoca, * Staphylococcus aureus. text: 10. A patient has complaints of fever with a mild headache associated with some difficulty in swallowing. A throat examination reveals swollen glands and a thick, whitish membrane over his tonsils which bleeds on scraping the lesion. A sample is taken from the exudate and a gram stain is done, which is as shown below. What is the organism associated with the disease?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Corynebacterium diphtheriae

The history of white membrane over the tonsils and gram stain image showing gram-positive bacilli in Chinese letter arrangement points towards the diagnosis of faucial diphtheria caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Corynebacterium diphtheria is a gram-positive bacillus with clubbing at both ends. They possess characteristic polymetaphosphate granules also called metachromatic granules or Babes-Ernst granules. On microscopy, the bacilli are arranged at angles to each other which is seen as the Chinese letter or cuneiform pattern.  Albert’s stain or Neisser’s stain or Loeffler's methylene blue are used to demonstrate the metachromatic granules of Corynebacterium diphtheria. These granules are called as polar bodies as they are situated at the ends of the bacilli. The systemic manifestations of diphtheria are due to diphtheria toxin. It is an exotoxin that consists of two fragments - A and B. It acts by inhibiting protein synthesis. Fragment B helps in binding of the toxin to the cells and fragment A inactivates the elongation factor (EF-2) responsible for protein synthesis. The clinical manifestation of diphtheria depends on the site of infection. Pharyngeal/faucial diphtheria is the most common presentation. The patient has marked adenitis, a bull neck, and severe toxemia. Pseudomembrane over the tonsils are characteristic. Bleeding from the tonsils can occur. It leads to life-threatening complications such as asphyxia, circulatory failure, post-diphtheritic paralysis, and toxemia. Cutaneous diphtheria is due to non-toxigenic strains of diphtheria. It may present as a diphtheritic whitlow or skin ulcer. The image below shows the pseudomembrane over the tonsil typically seen in diphtheria. Image below shows bull neck. Isolation of corynebacterium from patient or close contact confirms the diagnosis. Specimen collection for culture should be done from nose, throat and if possible from below the membrane. It grows readily on Loeffler's serum slope and confirmation can be done by growing on potassium tellurite agar which serves as a selective medium. Image below shows Loeffler's serum slope. Treatment of diphtheria consist of administering diphtheria anti-toxin (20,000 - 100,000 units) and supplementing with antibiotics (penicillin and erythromycin).

text: 11. A patient was diagnosed with Tuberculosis and while testing for resistance he was found to be resistant to Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Amikacin, and Ofloxacin. What is this type of TB called?

text: 12. Which of the following stains is used for the diagnosis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Ziehl-Neelsen stain

Ziehl-Neelsen stain is used for staining M. tuberculosis. Steps involved in Ziehl-Neelsen stain are: * Place sample on slide evenly spread it with rotational movement * Air-dry the slide and fix it by passing it over a flame * Apply carbol fuchsin stain * Wash with water to remove excess stain * Decolourise with alcohol  * Apply methylene blue stain  * Wash with water to remove excess stain * View under microscope Kinyoun modified it so that heat fixing is not required, it is called the cold method. It involves increasing the concentration of phenol acid and the duration of staining. It is then washed with water and decolourised with acid alcohol. Counterstaining with Loeffler's methylene blue or malachite green is done for a minute and viewed under a microscope. The image below shows the steps of Ziehl-Neelsen staining. The best diagnostic procedure for M. tuberculosis is sputum culture. * Sputum microscopy is the most dependable and conventional method for demonstration of AFB(Acid-fast bacteria) by ZN staining method. * The smears are made from the thick purulent parts of the sputum and then are air-dried, fixed by heating, and finally stained by ZN technique. * The stained smear is examined under oil immersion lens (100). Acid-fast bacteria in a stained smear appear bright red against a blue background. * At least 10,000 bacilli should be present per mL of sputum in order to be demonstrable in direct smears. * At least 300 fields should be examined taking about 10 minutes before giving a negative report. * The presence of at least two or more typical bacilli in the smear is reported as positive for AFB (Acid-fast bacteria). The smears are graded depending on the number of tubercle bacilli present in a stained smear on examination by oil immersion lens. text: 14. A truck driver came with complaints of a painless indurated genital ulcer after unsafe intercourse. Which of the following can be used to diagnose the condition in a low-resource setting when an active ulcer is present?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Dark field microscopy

The clinical vignette of a painless, indurated genital ulcer in a truck driver is most likely suggestive of syphilitic chancre / hard chancre caused by Treponema pallidum. The motility of the organism can be demonstrated by dark ground/ field microscopy which can be used in a low economic, low resource setting.  Dark ground microscopy can be used to diagnose syphilis when an active chancre or condyloma lata is present to visualize Treponema pallidum. Dark-field microscopy images have a dark background with a refractile organism. The dark ground microscope has an optical system that enhances the contrast of unstained bodies. It is generally less sensitive. Various types of Spirochetes and their appearances under a dark ground microscope: * Treponemes generally are short, slender with regular and sharp spirals. * Leptospira have a large number of closely wound spirals and characteristic hooked ends. * Borrelia is large with irregular and wide open coils. The image given below shows Treponema pallidum demonstrated by dark ground microscopy and the various appearances of other spirochetes respectively. Other options: Option B: Fluorescent treponema antibody absorption test (FTA-ABS) is an indirect immunofluorescence test used to detect specific treponemal antibodies. It is not available for routine testing as it is done only in suitably equipped labs. Option C: VDRL test is a slide flocculation test in which the serum is inactivated at 56°C for 30 minutes and a measured volume of serum is placed on a special cavity slide. The cardiolipin antigen after preparation is added to the serum sample on a slide and is rotated on a VDRL rotator for a specified period of 4 minutes. In a positive test, the cardiolipin antigen reacts with reagin antibodies present in the infected serum and forms visible clumps. In a negative test, cardiolipin continues to remain as uniform crystals in the serum.
