text: 17. A farmer with a history of flea bite in a godown presents with the features of high fever, painful inguinal lymphadenopathy, vomiting and diarrhea and hypotension. Smears prepared from the discharge of these swellings revealed bacteria with bipolar staining. Which stain will help in the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Wayson’s stain

The given clinical scenario of fever, chills, lymphadenopathy, and a smear showing bipolar staining of bacteria is highly suggestive of bubonic plague caused by Yersinia pestis. The stain used for this organism is the Wayson stain containing methylene blue. Plague is a zoonotic disease caused by Yersinia pestis. It is a gram-negative, non-motile, coccobacillus. The reservoirs of infection are wild rodents like field mice, gerbils, skunks, etc. In India, the gerbil (Tatera indica) is the main reservoir. The important vector of plague is rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis). Humans contract the disease through contact with the infected animal's tissues, flea bites, or droplet infection from pneumonic plague cases.  Human plague mainly presents as: Bubonic plague- Most common form. The patient experiences excruciating lymphadenitis, headache, chills, and an abrupt fever. The lymph nodes in the neck, axilla, or groin enlarge and become known as "buboes". This is followed by the suppuration of the buboes. Bubonic plague cannot spread from person to person as the bacilli are locked up in the buboes and do not find a way or easy exit. Pneumonic plague- It develops as a complication of bubonic-septicemic plague.  Septicemic plague- It occurs when the infection spreads to the blood. Laboratory diagnosis- Microscopy reveals bacteria that show characteristic bipolar staining or safety pin appearance when stained with Wayson's stain. Antibodies to the F1 antigen of the bacteria can also be demonstrated by passive hemagglutination. PCR is used for a rapid presumptive diagnosis. Treatment- Streptomycin, doxycycline, and chloramphenicol can be used. text: 3. Which of the following is an acid-fast organism?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Mycobacterium avium

Mycobacterium avium is an acid-fast organism. Acid-fast staining is based on the principle that tubercle bacilli resist decolourization with acids after staining with aniline dyes. Acid fastness is attributed to the variety of fatty acids, alcohols, and lipids in the tubercle bacilli. Acid-fast organisms usually contain mycolic acid, which is acid-fast in the free state.  The steps to carry out acid-fast staining as modified by Ziehl and Neelsen are: * The slide is stained with carbol fuchsin along with the application of heat. * It is then decolourized with 20% sulphuric acid. Later methylene blue is used for counterstaining. * The acid-fast bacteria retain the fuchsin colour, while other organisms take up the counterstain. Mycobacterium avium complex consists of multiple nontuberculosis mycobacterial species (NTM), which cannot be distinguished in the microbiology laboratory and requires genetic testing. M. avium and Mycobacterium intracellulare are the two original members of the complex. It is a nonmotile, non-spore-forming, gram-positive acid-fast bacillus. MAC infection is an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection, occurring predominantly at CD4+ T cell counts of <50/μL. The most common presentation is disseminated disease with fever, weight loss, and night sweats. Treatment consists of Clarithromycin / Azithromycin with Ethambutol/ Rifabutin. Other options: Option A: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a gram-positive, capsulated, flame-shaped, or lanceolate-shaped diplococcus. Option B: E. coli is a gram-negative, flagellated rod. It is a lactose fermenter and hence, grows on MacConkey medium to produce pink colonies. Option D: Actinomyces are gram-positive, anaerobic, and filamentous bacteria that are non-acid-fast. text: 4. The stain used for identifying Cryptococcus is _____
expl:
Correct answer: C. India ink stain.

The stain used for identifying Cryptococcus is India ink stain. Indian ink is a negative staining method that provides a uniformly coloured background. The unstained organisms stand out in contrast to the background. It is useful in the demonstration of organisms with capsules that do not take simple stains. It is also used to stain slender bacteria like spirochetes. The India ink preparation is employed to detect the presence of Cryptococcus neoformans. It is seen as a globular, encapsulated yeast cell with or without budding, between 5 to 20 μm in diameter in size. Cryptococcus has a polysaccharide capsule which is seen against a black background. Cryptococcus can be cultured from biologic samples like the CSF, sputum, and skin biopsy on routine fungal and bacterial culture media. Colonies are opaque, white-to-cream coloured, and may turn orange-tan or brown after prolonged incubation. They have a mucoid appearance due to the presence of the capsule around the yeast cells. text: 7. Which of the following dimorphic fungi causes subcutaneous mycosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Sporothrix schenckii

The dimorphic fungus that causes subcutaneous mycosis is Sporothrix schenckii. Sporotrichosis is caused by Sporothrix schenckii, a thermally dimorphic fungus that lives on vegetation. The infection occurs following traumatic inoculation. The lesion initially develops as a granulomatous nodule that may progress to form a necrotic or ulcerative lesion. The infection from the lesions in the skin and subcutaneous tissue can spread via the lymphatic channels to the lymph nodes. This condition is known as lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis. It is commonly seen in individuals with advanced AIDS. Clinical features include fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Umbilicated papules that resemble molluscum contagiosum may also be seen.

text: 9. A cattle farmer presented with a lesion on the arm. Gram staining showed gram-positive rods with square ends with a central spore. Identify the organism.
expl:
Correct answer: B. Bacillus anthracis

The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario is cutaneous anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis. Bacillus anthracis is a gram-positive rod with square ends giving it a characteristic box car appearance/bamboo stick appearance. Bacillus anthracis is a large, gram-positive, endospore-forming (non-bulging spores), rod-shaped bacterium. It causes zoonotic infections in humans. It is non-motile and capsulated with a characteristic polypeptide capsule. The image shows the characteristic box car appearance/bamboo stick appearance of bacillus anthracis on Gram staining. Bacillus anthracis is a category A bioterrorism agent which can cause: * Cutaneous anthrax: It is caused by contact with infected animal/ animal products. It is seen in tanners and hide-porters. At the site of entry of organism or spores, a papule develops in about 1–7 days. This develops into a vesicle that later breaks down into an ulcer with a black, central, necrotic eschar surrounded by edematous skin. The lesion is also called a malignant pustule. The majority of the patients recover spontaneously, but a few may succumb to septicemia or meningitis. * Pulmonary anthrax: It is caused by inhaling spores. It is seen in wool sorters. The infection from the lung spreads to the mediastinal lymph nodes and causes hemorrhagic mediastinitis and sepsis.  * Intestinal anthrax: It is caused rarely, by ingesting infected animals.  The image below shows necrotic eschar seen in anthrax: Laboratory diagnosis: * Microscopy of the smears shows bacilli arranged end to end in the form of long chains. This is called bamboo stick appearance. * Under the low-power microscope, the edge of the colony is composed of long, interlacing chains of bacilli, resembling locks of matted hair, called Medusa head appearance. Fluid or pus from cutaneous lesions, pleural fluid, blood, or CSF can be cultured on: * Nutrient agar- frosted glass appearance * Gelatin stab culture- Inverted fir tree appearance * Blood agar- Non-hemolytic colonies * Solid medium with penicillin- String of pearls appearance Other options: Option A: Infection with Bacillus cereus causes food poisoning with a longer incubation period of 8-16 hours. But patients usually have a history of consumption of fried rice. Option C: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative, catalase-positive, oxidase-positive, non-lactose fermenting bacteria that shows swarming motility. Diseases caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa: * Burns infections * Opportunistic and nosocomial infections * Shanghai fever: severe enteric disease and sepsis * Malignant otitis externa in diabetics * Jacuzzi syndrome (Hot tub folliculitis) * Ecthyma gangrenosum * Green-nail syndrome Option D: Brucellosis is a zoonotic infection transmitted to humans from contact with or consumption of contaminated products from goats, sheep, cattle, pigs, and other animals. Clinically, patients may present with an acute infection comprised of undulant fever (Rising and falling fever). They may also have arthralgia, muscular pain, sweating, loss of weight, and appetite. CNS symptoms such as fatigue, irritability, and depression might also occur. Chronic infection tends to be episodic with non-specific symptoms.

subject: Microbiology
text: 11. Which among the following parasites directly invade the skin?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Schistosoma mansoni

The parasite that directly invades the skin is Schistosoma mansoni. Adult worms of S. mansoni live in the inferior mesenteric vein and their infective form is fork-tailed cercaria. Following skin penetration by cercariae, a pruritic rash termed cercarial dermatitis or swimmers itch develops locally which is self-limiting. After 4- 8 weeks of the cercarial invasion, high worm load, and egg antigen stimuli lead to the formation of immune complexes which result in a serum sickness-like illness termed Katayama fever. They present with high-grade fever, rash, arthralgia, and hepatosplenomegaly. When eggs get deposited in the small intestine, patients develop abdominal pain and blood dysentery for a long time called intestinal bilharziasis. The drug of choice is praziquantel 40mg/kg single oral dose. Oxamniquine 15mg/kg single oral dose is also an effective dose. A yellowish-brown egg with a lateral spine near the rounded posterior end is suggestive of Schistosoma mansoni. In Schistosoma hematobium, the egg has a terminal spine. In Schistosoma japonicum, the egg has no spine but shows a lateral small rudimentary knob. The life cycle of schistosomes is represented below: Other options: Option B: Dracunculiasis/Guinea worm disease is a vector-borne parasitic disease caused by Dracunculus medinenesis. Transmission occurs by consumption of water containing cyclops harboring infective stages of the parasite. This disease is totally a water-based disease and has no alternate way of transmission. Option C: Wuchereria bancrofti causes filariasis. The adult worms block the lymphatic vessels leading to inflammation and granuloma formation. This causes hard pitting or brawny edema. It can present as lymphadenitis, lymphedema, hydrocele, and elephantiasis. The disease spreads from person to person through mosquito bites. Option D: Onchocerca volvulus is a tissue nematode. The life cycle of Onchocerca volvulus is completed partly in humans, the definitive host, and partly in female blackflies, the intermediate host. During a blood meal, the female blackfly ingests the microfilariae from the skin and lymphatics of an infected person. Within the vector, the microfilariae develop into the infective stage. When the infected black fly bites another person, it introduces third-stage filarial larvae into the skin of the human host. Pearl PF1690: Eggs in parasitology

text: 12. A 45-year-old man with multiple sexual partners presents with a palmoplantar rash as seen below. On examination, he has epitrochlear lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Secondary syphilis

This clinical scenario of maculopapular rash with flu-like symptoms and epitrochlear lymphadenopathy points to secondary syphilis. Secondary syphilis occurs within 6 weeks to 8 weeks of the onset of the primary chancre. It is characterized by the following: * Onset of systemic manifestations includes symptoms such as malaise, headache, loss of appetite, sore throat * Generalized symmetric, asymptomatic maculopapular rash on the palms and soles. * Generalized adenopathy in 50% of cases * Condyloma lata is the classic finding. They are highly contagious exophytic broad excrescences that ulcer­ate. These are commonly seen on the vulva, perianal area, and upper thighs. The image below shows mucosal and cutaneous lesion of secondary syphilis. Other options: Option A: Psoriasis presents with itching and a papulosquamous rash commonly on the scalp, trunk, and extensor surfaces of the limbs. The lesions are red, scaly, and have well demarcation from the normal skin. They can also be encircled by a clear peripheral zone called the Woronoff ring. Option C: Meningococcemia caused by Neisseria meningitidis presents as acute fever with chills, malaise, and prostration. A petechial rash is seen early in the disease. Metastatic involvement of the joints, ears, eyes, lungs, and adrenals may occur.  Option D: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) are severe mucocutaneous reactions, usually to drugs, characterized by blistering and epithelial sloughing. The two terms describe phenotypes within a severity spectrum, where SJS is the less extensive form and TEN is the more extensive. text: 1. A wildlife photographer presents with a blackish lesion at the site of a mite bite from a few days back. He also gives a history of fever and rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Scrub typhus

In the above clinical scenario, a history of mite bite followed by the development of a characteristic eschar at the bite site along with fever and rash suggests a diagnosis of scrub typhus.  Scrub typhus, also known as chigger-borne typhus, is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. The vector is trombiculid mite. Humans are infected when they are bitten by the mite larvae known as chiggers. The incubation period is 1-3 weeks. Patients develop a characteristic eschar at the site of the mite bite, along with regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash. It can be associated with fever, headache, and conjunctival injection. Meningoencephalitis, myocarditis, and pneumonia can be seen in severe cases. Serologic assays are used for diagnosis. Weil-Felix reaction is a heterophile agglutination reaction used for diagnosis, wherein the sera are tested for agglutinins to the O antigens of certain Proteus strains OX19, OX2, and OXK. OXK is agglutinated only in scrub typhus. Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for both adults and children. In Scrub typhus both the adult and nymphal stages of mites are free living in nature, hence they do not feed on vertebral hosts. The larval stage(chigger) feeds on the vertebrate host and pick up the rickettsiae. Rodents are the mammalian reservoir for scrub typhus. Eschar can be seen in the image below: Other options: Option A: Anthrax- Cutaneous anthrax (Hide Porter’s disease) present as a black eschar at the site of entry. At the site of entry of organism or spores, a papule develops in about 1–7 days. This develops into a vesicle that later breaks down into an ulcer with a black, central, necrotic eschar surrounded by edematous skin. The disease used to be common in dock workers, carrying loads of hides and skins on their bare backs. Renal involvement is unlikely to be seen in this condition. The image below shows its characteristic rash: Option C : Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a rickettsial infection transmitted by ticks (Dermacentor andersoni). It is the most serious type of fever. Symptoms include fever, headache, Rash, muscle pain and lack of appetite. Early treatment with doxycycline is recommended to prevent death and severe illness. The rash is shown in the image below: Option D : Epidemic typhus: Epidemic typhus is caused by Rickettsia prowazekii and the vector is louse. Its incubation period is 10 to 14 days. The disease starts with fever and chills. A characteristic rash appears on the fourth or fifth day, starting on the trunk and spreading over the limbs but sparing the face, palms, and soles. text: 2. A 16-year-old boy presented with fever, headaches, myalgia, and drowsiness. He later developed dizziness and altered consciousness. His mother reports that he had consumed palm fruit on their recent trip to Kerala and has not been feeling well since then. Keeping the patient's history in mind, which of the following viruses should be considered in your differential diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Nipah virus

This patient with fever, headaches, myalgia, drowsiness, dizziness and altered consciousness, with a history of consuming palm fruit is likely to have been infected with the Nipah virus. Nipah virus is a zoonotic virus, which is transmitted by animals to humans.  It is an emerging paramyxovirus that belongs to the genus Henipavirus. It has caused disease in humans who have had contact with infected animals.  It has a wide range of hosts and is associated with high mortality rates. Its natural host is a certain species of fruit bat while pigs may be an intermediate host for transmission to humans. Its transmission can occur by the following methods: * Unprotected exposure to the secretions from the pigs, or unprotected contact with the tissue of a sick animal. * Consumption of fruits or fruit products (such as raw date palm juice) contaminated with urine or saliva from infected fruit bats of the family Pteropodidae. * Human-to-human transmission through close contact with people's secretions and excretions. * The incubation period ranges from 4 to 14 days. Patients present with symptoms of headaches, myalgia, vomiting, and sore throat. This is followed by the onset of encephalitis, which manifests as dizziness, drowsiness, and altered consciousness. Patients may also present with acute respiratory distress. Encephalitis and seizures occur in severe cases, progressing to coma within 24 to 48 hours.  Diagnosis is by means of real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) from bodily fluids and antibody detection via enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) methods. The virus can be isolated by cell culture. There is no treatment or vaccine available for either people or animals. The primary treatment for humans is supportive care.

text: 1. A patient got pricked by a rose thorn and presents with multiple vesicles on hand and multiple eruptions along the lymphatics. What is the most likely causative agent?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Sporothrix Schenckii

Presence of multiple vesicles on hand and multiple eruptions along lymphatics in a patient pricked by a thorn suggests infection with Sporothrix schenckii. Sporothrix schenckii causes sporotrichosis, a chronic granulomatous disease, by traumatic inoculation into the skin. This is usually followed by spread along the draining lymphatics and lymph nodes.  It is a thermally dimorphic fungus. It is in the yeast phase in tissues and in cultures at 37°C, and in the mycelia phase in nature and cultures at 25°C. When it is cultured, the colonies are blackish-brown and fuzzy. The organism produces branching, septate hyphae, and microconidia clustered at the ends of conidiophores. It exists as cigar-shaped yeast cells. Stains used for identifying yeast forms:  * Gomori methenamine silver-cell wall appears black * Periodic acid-Schiff stain - cell wall appears red * Fluorescent antibody staining The image given below shows, (A)- (i) culture at 37°C (ii) culture at 25°C. (B) fungi with clustered microconidia with conidiophore.  (C) Magnified image showing branching and septate hyphae. Clinical features: The initial infection develops as a nodule, which may break down to form a necrotic or ulcerative lesion. Untreated, the disease progresses and new nodules develop along the lymphatics leading to a chain of nodules. Less commonly it may also cause systemic infection following inhalation, which causes local pulmonary disease or may lead to widely disseminated lesions in joints, meninges, and skin. Direct microscopic examination of necrotic material in KOH mount or histopathological examination of tissue sections stained by methenamine silver stain shows the asteroid body. Asteroid body is a rounded or oval, basophilic, yeast-like body 3-5 μmin diameter, with rays of an eosinophilic substance radiating from the yeast cell. Treatment: * Cutaneous infection – Potassium iodide-250mg thrice daily for 2-4 months                     * Lymphocutaneous infection - Itraconazole, fluconazole(400mg/day), terbinafine(250mg/day) and cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen * Disseminated infection - Amphotericin B Other options: Option A: Blastomycosis is an infection caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis. It causes a chronic infection with granulomatous and suppurative lesions, which starts in the lungs but may disseminate to other organs. Symptoms of an acute lower respiratory tract infection with pulmonary infiltrates are the most common clinical presentations. Histopathological staining shows thick-walled yeast, with single broad-based budding (figure 8 appearance). The image given below is that of Blastomyces which is a thick-walled yeast, with single broad-based budding (figure 8 appearance). Option B: Coccidiomycosis is caused by Coccidioides immitis which is a thermally dimorphic fungus. It occurs as a spherule in tissues and culture at 37°C and as the mycelial form in soil and culture at room temperature. They are endemic to the arid desert regions of the southwestern USA and California. Infection is acquired by inhaling dust containing arthrospores of the fungus. Option D: Candida species are yeast-like fungi, which normally inhabit the skin and mucosa. Candida albicans is an ovoid or spherical budding cell, which produces pseudohyphae both in tissues and in culture. Candidiasis is an opportunistic endogenous infection. text: 2. An HIV patient presented with bouts of cough and fever. What is the selective medium used for investigation?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Lowenstein-Jenson medium

A HIV patient with cough and fever is indicative of a tuberculosis infection. Lowenstein-Jenson medium is a selective medium used for Mycobacterium tuberculosis culture.  Lowenstein-Jenson medium is a selective medium used for the culture of Mycobacterium tuberculosis which causes tuberculosis. The presence of malachite green imparts a green colour and makes Lowenstein Jenson medium a selective media by inhibiting other bacteria.   Components of LJ medium: * Egg: Provide fatty acids and protein required for the metabolism. * Malachite green: Prevents growth of contaminants. * Mineral salt solution: Buffer. * Glycerol: Source of carbon, Favours growth of M. tuberculosis, but not M. bovis. * L-asparagine: Source of Nitrogen.  Mycobacterium tuberculosis colonies on LJ medium are dry, rough, raised, and irregular with a wrinkled surface. They are creamy white or buff-colored, tenacious, and difficult to emulsify (rough, tough, buff). Culture media used to cultivate Mycobacterium tuberculosis: * Solid Culture Media: Lowenstein–Jensen: A commonly used, egg-based, selective media. contains malachite green, which prevents growth of other organisms.   * Liquid Culture Media: Middle Brook’s media: Used for preparation of antigens and vaccines, and sensitivity testing. * Automated Culture Media: BACTEC 460: Uses radioisotopes, BacT alert: A colorimetric method, BACTEC MGIT: A fluorometric detection method.  Other options: Option A: Thayer-Martin medium is used to isolate Neisseria gonorrhoeae because the antimicrobials present in it, suppress the growth of other commensal organisms which may inhibit the growth of N.gonorrhoeae. Thayer Martin Medium selectively favors the growth of Neisseria by inhibiting the growth of gram-positive organisms with Vancomycin, gram-negative organisms (except Neisseria) with Trimethoprim and Colistin, and fungi with Nystatin Thayer-Martin medium contains antimicrobials like vancomycin 3.0 mg, colistin 7.5 mg, and nystatin 12.5 units per ml of agar, in chocolate agar. Option C:  MacConkey agar is used to distinguish lactose fermenters (pink) from non-lactose fermenters (colourless or pale). It is a selective and differential media. It is selective because bile salts and dyes inhibit gram-positive organisms and gram-negative cocci. It is differential because the pH indicator turns pink-red when the lactose is fermented. Option D: Chocolate agar is used for gram‐negative intracellular diplococci within phagocytes, Chocolate agar with isovitaleX is the suitable culture medium for Haemophilus ducreyi. text: 5. A firefighter presents with fever, cough, and lung consolidation. Microbiological testing reveals a gram-negative, oxidase-positive organism. The culture shows colonies that show a property of transillumination when light is passed. What is the most likely causative agent?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Pseudomonas aeruginosa

The gram-negative, oxidase-positive organism that forms greenish-yellow colonies exhibiting transillumination is indicative of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative, catalase-positive, oxidase-positive, non-lactose fermenting bacteria that shows swarming motility. They produce a characteristic blue-green pigment called pyocyanin and a greenish-yellow pigment called fluorescein/pyoverdin. Other pigments produced by these organisms include pyorubin (Red), pyomelanin (Brown). Diseases caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa include- * Malignant otitis externa in diabetics * Pneumonia and sepsis in cystic fibrosis * Wound infection and sepsis in burns * Hot tub folliculitis/Pseudomonas aeruginosa folliculitis/ Jacuzzi syndrome is a type of folliculitis, occurring after hot tub exposure * Shanghai fever is a febrile illness that manifests as severe enteric disease, sepsis with invasive disease. * Ecthyma gangrenosum Pathogenesis - It is an obligate aerobe that exerts its pathogenicity by the production of diphtheria-like exotoxin A and a slime layer. Breach in primary body defenses as in burns predisposes to Pseudomonas infection. Clinical features - It is characterized by blue-green pus. It is notorious for being resistant to antimicrobials and antiseptics and hence is a frequent contaminant in hospital samples. Repeated isolation and associated clinical features should prompt the diagnosis of Pseudomonas. Diagnosis - It grows well on most media and pigment production makes its identification easy. Species identification is made possible by biochemical tests - arginine hydrolysis and oxidase reaction. Pseudomonas aeruginosa growth in a nutrient agar showing green coloured colonies are shown in the image below. text: 6. A baby is born with sensory neural deafness, patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and salt pepper appearance on retinoscopy. Identify the infection in the mother.
expl:
Correct answer: C. Rubella

The given clinical scenario of sensorineural deafness, patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and a salt-and-pepper appearance on retinoscopy is indicative of congenital rubella syndrome, suggesting that the mother had a rubella infection. Triad of Gregg is seen in babies with congenital rubella syndrome. The features include: * Ocular defects: congenital cataract, salt and pepper chorioretinopathy, microphthalmos, glaucoma, and anterior uveitis * Sensorineural hearing loss * Heart defects: patent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary stenosis, and ventricular septal defects. Blueberry muffin rash and microphthalmos are also seen in this condition. The image below shows a neonate with papulo-nodular erythematous-bluish lesions of a blueberry muffin baby: Rubella or German measles is a serious infection in pregnancy that causes abortions or severe fetal defects if infection occurs in the first trimester. The transplacental spread of the rubella virus is known to cause congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) in the baby.  When this infection develops in the first, second or third months, there is a 60%, 25%, or 10% chance of significant abnormalities, respectively. Transmission of the virus also occurs through nasopharyngeal secretions (droplet transmission). The mother usually has a fever and generalized body rash. The rash is maculopapular, first emerging on the face and later spreading to the trunk and limbs. The incidence and severity reduce as the pregnancy advances and are rare after 20 weeks of gestation.  There is no specific treatment for rubella virus infection in mothers. Post-exposure passive immunization can be beneficial if given within 5 days of exposure to droplets. The incidence of this disease has reduced due to the availability of MMR vaccines. MMR vaccines can be administered only to non-pregnant females as it is a live, attenuated virus. Women are advised to delay pregnancy for at least one month after being vaccinated. Other Options:  Option A: Pregnant females infected with varicella-zoster virus present with fever, dry cough, dyspnoea, tachypnoea and pleuritic chest pain. The highest risk of transmission to fetus is between 13 to 20 weeks of gestation. Option B: Congenital toxoplasmosis is due to toxoplasma gondii. The child usually presents with a classic triad of chorioretinitis, calcifications within the brain and hydrocephalus. Blueberry muffin baby appearance is also seen in this. Calcifications occur randomly throughout the brain in congenital toxoplasmosis, while periventricular calcification is characteristic of congenital CMV infection. Option D: Pregnant females affected with cytomegalovirus present with infectious mononucleosis-like symptoms, that is fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy and polyarthritis. Transmission to the fetus increases as pregnancy advances and is maximum in the third trimester. Congenital infection includes growth restriction, microcephaly, intracranial (periventricular) calcifications, chorioretinitis, mental and motor deficits, hepatosplenomegaly, hemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenic purpura. Most infected neonates are asymptomatic at birth and later present with these symptoms. In causes influenza-like respiratory infection in immunocompetent persons. In immunocompromised it disseminates to CNS causing cryptococcal meningoencephalitis and patients may complain of headaches, neck stiffness, and disorientation as in this case. Other common sites of dissemination include the skin, adrenals, bone, eye, and prostate gland. Cryptococcal meningitis is the most common cause of meningitis in an immunocompromised HIV patient. text: 9. What is the mechanism of action of botulinum toxin?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Prevents release of acetylcholine

Botulinum toxin prevents the release of acetylcholine. The botulinum toxins produced by Clostridium botulinum are neurotoxins that cleave the SNARE (soluble NSF attachment protein receptor) family of proteins involved in vesicular fusion and subsequently neurotransmitter release. Preformed toxins when ingested can cause food-borne botulism. The botulinum toxins block the release of acetylcholine in the neuromuscular junction and cause flaccid paralysis. Symptoms can include ptosis, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphonia, and dysphagia. Eight different serotypes of toxin have been identified which are produced by Clostridium botulinum. All of them are neurotoxins except C2. The various SNARE proteins cleaved are: * Synaptobrevin- cleaved by serotypes B, D, F, & G * SNAP-25 - cleaved by serotypes A & E * Syntoxin - cleaved by serotype C1 The image given below shows the site of action of botulinum toxin. Infant botulism is also called floppy baby syndrome. It is usually seen in infants less than 6 months. It is acquired by ingestion of foods like honey contaminated with C. botulinum spores. It gets established in the gut and produces toxins. Affected children usually present with paralysis, constipation, difficulty breathing, poor feeding, weakness, altered crying, and loss of head control. Diagnosis is confirmed by detecting toxins or spores in the stool. Gram staining shows gram-positive, sporing bacilli. It is managed by supportive care and assisted feeding only. The image given below shows gram staining of Clostridium botulinum. Other Options: Option B: Inhibits acetylcholine esterase: Organophosphates, carbamates, and certain nerve agents like sarin prevent acetylcholine breakdown by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase. Option C: Inhibits reuptake of acetylcholine: Hemicholinium blocks the reuptake of choline, preventing acetylcholine synthesis. Option D: Blockage of postsynaptic receptors of acetylcholine: α-bungarotoxin, curare, and α-conotoxin act as competitive antagonists at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. text: 10. A 4-year-old boy develops bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramps. The bacteria isolated from the stool specimen fermented lactose and produced colorless colonies on sorbitol MacConkey agar. The most likely etiological agent in this case is?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Shiga toxin-producing E.Coli

The given clinical scenario of a boy with bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramps with the isolated bacteria fermenting lactose and forming colorless colonies on sorbitol MacConkey agar is suggestive of infection by Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) O157: H7, also known as Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC). O157: H7 is the most common type of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC). Unlike most other E. coli serotypes, the STEC O157: H7 does not use sorbitol and produces clear colonies on the Sorbitol MacConkey agar. The non-STEC produces pink colonies. All species of E. coli are lactose fermenters and produce pink colonies. They produce two antigenic forms of the cytotoxic toxin known as Shiga-like toxin 1 and Shiga-like toxin 2. Shiga-like toxin 1 is identical to the Shiga toxin of Shigella dysenteriae type 1. E. coli O157:H7 has a small infective dose (around 100 bacilli) and spreads easily from child to child by the feco-oral route. It can cause mild non-bloody diarrhea to hemorrhagic colitis, or a severe form of diarrhea, with hemolytic uremic syndrome, a disease resulting in acute renal failure, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia. The most common cause of hemolytic uremic syndrome in the world is E.coli O157:H7. The most common cause of hemolytic uremic syndrome in India is Shigella dysenteriae type I. Other options: Option A: Campylobacter is a slender, spirally curved, gram-negative bacillus. They grow at a slower rate and thus require selective media containing antibiotics like Skirrow's media for culture. Option B: Yersinia enterocolitica causes diarrhea with symptoms resembling appendicitis (pseudoappendicitis). The patients present with abdominal pain which can be localized to the right iliac fossa, thus mimicking appendicitis. Additionally, it is a non-lactose fermenter. Option D: Shigella dysenteriae type 1 can produce the Shiga toxin and result in a clinical profile similar to EHEC. But Shigella is a non-lactose fermenting organism, unlike E. coli, and will form pale colonies on MacConkey agar. In this patient with suspected typhoid, the Widal test has shown only the H antigen being positive, the condition is most likely the reconvalescence phase of Typhoid. Widal Test: This is a test for the measurement of H and O agglutinins for typhoid and paratyphoid bacilli in the patient's sera. The titer increases steadily till the third or fourth week, after which it declines The H agglutinins persist longer than O agglutinins. text: 15. A neonate has bilateral chorioretinitis with intraparenchymal calcifications and hydrocephalus. What is the causative organism?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Toxoplasma gondi

The presence of bilateral chorioretinitis with intraparenchymal calcifications and hydrocephalus in a neonate is suggestive of Congenital toxoplasmosis. The characteristic triad of Congenital toxoplasmosis is chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications. Clinical manifestations apart from the triad include hydrops fetalis, intrauterine growth retardation, prematurity, peripheral retinal scars, persistent jaundice, and mild thrombocytopenia. Congenital toxoplasmosis occurs when a pregnant woman acquires the infection during gestation. The organism may cross to the fetus transplacentally or at the time of vaginal delivery. The severity of the disease in the neonate is greater if the woman gets infected early in her pregnancy. The causative agent is Toxoplasma gondii, an obligate intracellular protozoan. The diagnosis is made by the detection of IgM anti-toxoplasma antibodies. IgG can cross the placenta is hence, cannot confirm infection in the infant. IgM immunosorbent agglutination assay (ISAGA) and IgA ELISA are the most useful diagnostic tests. Spiramycin can be administered for cases of acute infection in early pregnancy to reduce vertical transmission. It does not cross the placenta and therefore cannot be used to treat an infected fetus. Pyrimethamine-sulfonamide (to be avoided in the first trimester) is used when a fetal infection is confirmed or in maternal infections after 18 weeks. It's prevalent in regions with poor sanitation and where pork is consumed. Head neuroimaging shows intracranial periventricular calcifications. One of the long-term sequelae is sensorineural hearing loss. Diagnosis is made by isolating the virus from the urine or blood by polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

Detection of rabies virus RNA by RT-PCR(reverse transcriptase -polymerase chain reaction) on corneal scrapings is highly sensitive and specific. This technique can detect viruses in fresh saliva samples, CSF, skin, and brain tissues. RT-PCR with genetic sequencing can distinguish among rabies variants, permitting identification of the probable source of an infection. Clinical stages of rabies:

Incubation period 20-90 Days None
Prodrome 2-10 days Fever, malaise, nausea, vomiting, paresthesia
Acute neurologic disease    
Encephalitic/Furious rabies (80%) 2-7 days Anxiety, Agitation, Hyperactivity, hallucinations, hydrophobia, autonomic dysfunction
Paralytic /dumb rabies (20%) 2-10 days Flaccid paralysis in limbs progressing to quadriparesis with facial paralysis.

 Laboratory diagnosis of rabies is performed by the following methods: * Antigen detection - Direct immunofluorescence (IF) from specimens of * Skin biopsy from the nape of the neck including hair follicles. Rabies antigen is present in cutaneous nerves at the base of hair follicles. It is the most sensitive and specific test. * Corneal smears were previously used. They are not used anymore as they are of low diagnostic yield. * Viral isolation- Intracerebral inoculation in mice can be attempted from the brain, CSF, and saliva * Antibody demonstration from serum and CSF * Viral RNA detection by RT-PCR  * Postmortem examination of brain tissue samples- demonstration of Negri bodies Pearl PF1934: Rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins schedules According to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India: WHO category II or III exposures should receive post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) immediately. One intradermal (ID) dose is 0.1 mL of vaccine and one intramuscular (IM) dose is an entire vial of vaccine, irrespective of the vial size. Should a vaccine dose be delayed for any reason, the PEP schedule should be resumed (not restarted). Rabies Immunoglobulin(RIG):  * Passive immunization * Single-dose; after initiation of PEP and not beyond 7 days after the first dose of vaccine * Max dose: hRIG - 20IU/kg , eRIG - 40IU/kg body weight * Vaccines should never be withheld regardless of the availability of RIG. * Alternatives for RIG- WHO recommends monoclonal antibodies (mAb) as a 'cocktail' containing at least two antibodies against the rabies virus. Administration of RIG: * RIG should be administered into or around the wound site or sites. * The remaining RIG, if any, should be injected IM at a site distant from the site of vaccine administration. * RIG may be diluted to a volume sufficient for all wounds to be effectively and safely infiltrated. Prioritization of RIG allocation (numbered according to priority order): * Multiple bites * Deep wounds * Bites to head, neck, and hands * Patients with severe immunodeficiency * Confirmed/probable rabies in biting animal * Bites, scratches, and exposure of mucous membranes caused by a bat Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) PrEP is considered in the following conditions: * High-risk groups- laboratory staff, wildlife wardens, veterinarians, animal handlers, and travelers to endemic regions. * Remote, rabies-endemic areas where access to PEP is difficult * Areas where dog bite incidence is >5% per year * Areas where vampire bat rabies is known to be present. Pre-exposure rabies vaccination consists of two intramuscular (IM) or two intradermal (ID) doses. These are given on days 0 and 3. * Adults - the vaccine should always be administered in the deltoid area of the arm * Young children (under 1 year of age)- Administration into the anterolateral area of the thigh is recommended. * Rabies vaccine should never be administered in the gluteal area. Administration in this manner will result in lower neutralizing antibody titers. For exposed or re-exposed patients who can document previous completion of PEP the following guidelines would be applicable: * Proper wound management should be done. * There is no need for the administration of RIG. * One site ID or IM vaccine administration on days 0 and 3. Only adequate wound washing would be required in case of re-exposure where the animal bite victim has documented proof of complete PEP within the last three months. The following cases are treated as fresh cases and given full PEP: * Those who have previously received full post-exposure treatment with neural tissue vaccines (NTV) or vaccines of unproven potency * Those who cannot document complete PEP or PrEP treatment

text: 9. A patient presents with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. He gives a history of having consumed shellfish and raw seafood a day before. The causative agent showed the Kanagawa phenomenon on Wagatsuma agar. What is the most likely organism?

text: 2. A 55-year-old man came with complaints of fever and chills since the last one week. On examination, tachycardia and low BP are present. Peripheral smear findings are given below. What is the likely causative agent?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Plasmodium falciparum

The given clinical history of fever with chills and the peripheral smear showing multiple ring forms in RBCs are suggestive of Plasmodium falciparum. Falciparum malaria shows a very high percentage of RBCs containing ring forms. This high-level parasitemia is more often seen in Plasmodium falciparum infection than in infection by other plasmodia. After the ring forms in the peripheral blood, the rest of the erythrocytic cycle occurs in the capillaries of the brain and internal organs. So, only ring forms can be seen in the peripheral blood and not the late trophozoites and schizonts. The gametocytes of P. falciparum are crescent-shaped or “banana-shaped” (as shown below), whereas those of the other plasmodia are spherical. Plasmodium falciparum causes malignant tertian malaria. This means that the fever has a periodicity of 48 hours corresponding to one cycle of erythrocytic schizogony. Malignant because it is a more severe and fatal type of malaria. Major manifestations of severe falciparum malaria include unarousable coma/ cerebral malaria (failure to localize or respond appropriately to stimuli or coma persisting for >30 min after generalized convulsion), acidosis, severe normocytic normochromic anemia, renal failure, pulmonary edema, hypoglycemia, shock, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Other manifestations include hemoglobinuria, hyperparasitemia, jaundice, and extreme weakness. The treatment of choice is artesunate given at a dose of 2.4 mg/kg stat IV, followed by 2.4 mg/kg at 12 and 24 hours, and then daily if necessary. In Plasmodium falciparum, recrudescence can be seen which is defined as the recurrence of asexual parasitemia. It usually occurs within 8 weeks of treatment and is due to incomplete treatment or drug resistance. Pearl PF0831: Difference between plasmodium species

text: 3. A 6-year-old child presents with fever, sore throat, and dyspnea. On oral examination, a pseudomembrane is seen over the tonsils. What is the mechanism of action of the toxin produced by the causative organism?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Inhibition of elongation factor-2 (EF-2)

This child with pseudomembrane over tonsil has diphtheria, in which the toxin inactivates the elongation factor EF-2. Diphtheria toxin is an exotoxin that consists of two fragments - A and B. It acts by inhibiting protein synthesis. Fragment B helps in binding the toxin to the cells while fragment A inactivates the elongation factor (EF-2) responsible for protein synthesis. Pseudomonas aeruginosa also produces toxins with a similar mechanism of action. This infection presents as fever and sore throat, which progresses to dyspnea due to obstruction by the pseudomembrane. Bull's neck appearance is seen due to cervical lymphadenitis. Complications like damage to the heart (myocarditis), kidney (tubular necrosis), liver, and adrenal glands can develop due to the toxin. Neisser's or Albert's stain will show the bacilli with metachromatic granules situated at the poles of the bacilli. Tellurite blood agar is the selective culture medium. It is treated mainly by neutralizing with antitoxin and antibiotics to arrest more toxin production. text: 4. A patient with HIV has a CD4 count of 170/ μL. The patient's chest radiograph shows symmetric interstitial infiltrates in the perihilar region. Histopathological findings are given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Pneumocystis pneumonia

In the given clinical scenario of an HIV patient with a CD4 count of 170/ μL and Gomori’s methenamine silver staining showing crescent-shaped cysts with X-ray findings of symmetric interstitial infiltrates mainly in the perihilar region are suggestive of pneumocystis pneumonia. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is an opportunistic infection in immunocompromised patients. It usually occurs when the CD4 count falls below 200 cells/μL. Patients usually present with fever and nonproductive cough with progressive shortness of breath. It can also affect other organs like lymph nodes, spleen, and liver. The classic radiographic appearance consists of diffuse bilateral symmetric interstitial infiltrates that are perihilar. CT will show diffuse ground-glass opacities. Giemsa stain, toluidine blue, methenamine silver, and calcofluor white stains demonstrate trophozoites. The cyst wall appears black with Gomori's methenamine silver stain. Shown below is an image of the Gomori’s methenamine silver staining showing crescent-shaped cysts resembling the crushed ping-pong balls of P. jirovecii. The standard treatment for PCP is trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. Prophylaxis with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole is recommended for HIV patients with CD4<200/mm3. Other options: Option A- Mycobacterium avium complex infection is generally seen when the CD4 count falls less than 50 cells/μL. CT scan of the infected lung will show peribronchial inflammation, which gives rise to a tree in a bud appearance (small round structures attached to linear structures). In severe cases, there might be bronchiectasis and cavity formation. Below image- Tree in bud appearance which is indicated by an arrowhead. Option B- Histoplasmosis occurs when the CD4 count falls below 150 cells/μL and high risk populations in endemic areas or those with occupational exposure. Chest radiograph shows the signs of pneumonitis with prominent hilar or mediastinal adenopathy. Option D- Pneumococcal pneumonia commonly appears as lobar or segmental consolidation. In some, it can involve more than one lobe. It can have pleural effusion and empyema in severe cases. text: 5. Which of the following vectors is associated with Orientia Tsutsugamushi?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Trombiculid mite

Trombiculid mite is the vector responsible for the transmission of scrub typhus caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. Scrub typhus, also known as chigger-borne typhus, is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. The vector is trombiculid mite. Humans are infected when they are bitten by the mite larvae known as chiggers. The incubation period is 1- 3 weeks. Patients develop a characteristic eschar at the site of the mite bite, along with regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash. It can be associated with fever, headache, and conjunctival injection. Meningoencephalitis, myocarditis, and pneumonia can be seen in severe cases. Serologic assays are used for diagnosis. Weil-Felix reaction is a heterophile agglutination reaction used for diagnosis, wherein the sera are tested for agglutinins to the O antigens of certain Proteus strains OX19, OX2, and OXK. OXK is agglutinated only in scrub typhus. Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for both adults and children. subject: Microbiology
text: 6. Relative bradycardia is seen in which of the following conditions?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Brucellosis

Among the given options, relative bradycardia is seen in brucellosis. Brucellosis is a zoonotic infection caused by the Brucella species, typically contracted through direct contact with infected animals or consumption of unpasteurized dairy products. The clinical presentation includes undulating fever, relative bradycardia, musculoskeletal symptoms like arthritis and myalgia, general malaise, hepatosplenomegaly, neurological symptoms in neuro brucellosis, presenting as meningitis or encephalitis. In men, epididymal-orchitis can occur, presenting as testicular pain and swelling. Laboratory diagnosis of brucellosis includes: * Polymerase chain reaction * Blood culture with the Castaneda method * Serological methods include standard agglutination test (SAT), complement fixation test, Coomb’s antiglobulin test, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). * Tests for animals and animal products: Milk ring tests and Rose Bengal card tests. Treatment includes antimicrobial therapy with IM streptomycin and oral doxycycline. The prevention of brucellosis can be achieved by pasteurizing milk and other milk products. Relative bradycardia, also known as Faget's sign, is observed when patients exhibit a lower heart rate than anticipated in relation to an increase in body temperature. Body temperature is commonly regarded as a factor that independently influences heart rate. It is estimated that for each 1°C (1.8°F) rise in temperature, the heart rate typically increases by approximately 15-20 beats per minute. While this pulse-temperature dissociation is not highly sensitive or specific for establishing a diagnosis, it can still prove beneficial in resource-limited settings due to its easy accessibility and simplicity. Infectious causes of relative bradycardia include:  * Salmonella typhi * Brucella (brucellosis) * Francisella tularensis * Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) * Leptospira interrogans * Legionella pneumophila * Rickettsia spp. * Orientia tsutsugamushi (scrub typhus) * Corynebacterium diphtheriae * Plasmodium spp. (malaria) Noninfectious causes include: * Drug fever * Beta-blocker use * Central nervous system lesions * Malignant lymphoma * Factitious fever It was found that relative bradycardia as a feature of a specific disease only occurs in diseases caused by organisms that are both gram-negative and intracellular. Other options: Shigellosis, pertussis, and dengue show tachycardia on clinical examination. ( Option A, B & C)

text: 7. Paris green dust is used to eliminate the larval form of _________________.
expl:
Correct answer: D. Anopheles

Paris green is a commonly used larvicide agent against surface feeders like Anopheles larvae. Paris green (Copper acetoarsenite) is an insecticide, which is a green powder that has 50% arsenious oxide. It is a stomach poison and to be effective, it must be ingested by the larvae.  The larvae of Anopheles are surface feeders as they lie parallel to the surface of the water due to the absence of a siphon tube. In contrast, Culicine larvae like Aedes, Culex, and Mansonia have a siphon tube that helps them to suspend in water with their head downwards and therefore not affected by pair green. The image below shows Laraval forms of different mosquitoes. Other commonly used larvicides include: * Mineral oils - diesel oil, kerosene, fractions of crude oils, mosquito larvicidal oil * Synthetic insecticides - Fenthion, Chlorpyrifos, and Abat Larvicides that are not recommended include organochlorine compounds like DDT (Dichloro-diphenyl-trichloroethane)and HCH (hexachlorocyclohexane). This is because they have a long residual effect, and contaminate water. Vector mosquitoes may also develop resistance to these compounds. Oils that are used are diesel oil, kerosene, crude oil fractions. Disadvantage is that it kills fish. * Paris green: Copper acetoarsenite is an emerald green, micro-crystalline powder and is insoluble in water. It is a stomach poison to larvae. It is not harmful to man or animals. Very effective against Anopheles as they are surface feeders. * Synthetic insecticides: Organo-phosphorous compounds like fenthion, chlorpyrifos and abate are larvicidal. Abate is least toxic. * Biological control * The fish species Gambusia affinis and Lebister reticulatus (Barbados millions) feed on mosquito larvae. * These are used in conjunction with other methods. * Anti-adult measures * Residual sprays * Adult mosquitoes can be controlled by spraying with residual insecticides like DDT, Malathion, propoxur and gamma-HCH (lindane) * Resistance to DDT has been shown by mosquitoes * Space sprays * Space sprays are those in which insecticides are sprayed into the atmosphere in the form of a mist or fog. * Pyrethrum is a contact, nerve poison and is the most common insecticide used as a space spray. text: 8. A patient presents with pain abdomen, diarrhea, and a stepladder pattern of fever for the past five days. He also complains of a headache and malaise. Which of the following is the best screening test to perform now if typhoid is suspected in this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Blood culture

The best test to screen a symptomatic patient for typhoid in the first week is blood culture. Enteric fever (typhoid fever) is caused by Salmonella species. The patient presents with stepladder pyrexia (fever), abdominal pain, diarrhoea, headache, and malaise. Diagnosis of enteric fever: * Blood culture: It is more sensitive during 1st week than in the subsequent weeks. It rapidly becomes negative on treatment with antibiotics. * Antibody testing: WIDAL test to detect rising titers of H and O agglutinins against salmonella typhi and paratyphi. Agglutinins appear by the end of the first week and rise steadily up to the 3rd or 4th week, after which they disappear. * Stool culture: It yields positive results from the 3rd week onwards. * Urine culture: Results may be positive after the 2nd week. * Bone marrow culture remains positive for 5 days even after the start of antibiotics and is the most sensitive test in the first week. The culture of duodenal aspirate may yield positive results when bone marrow culture is inconclusive. Empirical treatment of typhoid fever includes management with ceftriaxone 2g/day intravenously for 10-14 days along with azithromycin  1g/day for 5 days. Other antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin, chloramphenicol, and amoxicillin should be considered in resistant cases.

text: 9. A 30-year-old man presents with a history of diarrhea and flask-shaped ulcers in the intestine. Microscopic findings reveal quadrinucleated cysts. Which of the following can be used to treat this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Metronidazole + Paromomycin

This patient's clinical features of diarrhea and flask-shaped ulcers with quadrinucleate cysts are suggestive of amoebiasis caused by Entamoeba histolytica. The most appropriate treatment for this patient is metronidazole (or tinidazole) + a luminal amoebicide like paromomycin, diloxanide furoate, or iodoquinone. As metronidazole is so well absorbed in the gut, the levels may not be therapeutic in the colonic lumen. The drug is also less effective against cysts. Therefore, patients with amoebic colitis or amoebic liver abscess should receive a luminal agent in addition. Clinically, infection with entamoeba histolytica may present as,  * Amoebic colitis- Patients with amoebic colitis typically present with colicky abdominal pains and diarrhoea. There is associated tenesmus and heme-positive stool. In amoebiasis, the organisms attach to the colonic epithelium, invade the crypts and burrow laterally to create a flask-shaped ulcer. Tissue damage results in inflammation.  * Amoebic liver abscess- Patients usually present with fever, abdominal pain, abdominal distention, and enlargement and tenderness of the liver. A characteristic "anchovy sauce-like" pus may be seen. Flask-shaped ulcer seen in intestinal amoebiasis- Cyst form of Entamoeba histolytica- Note: Albendazole is an antihelmintic drug, used to treat hydatid cysts, roundworms, hookworms, etc. Pearl PF2048: Infective form and diagnostic forms of various protozoa

text: 10. A 28-year-old truck driver presents with painful multiple ulcers on his penis 3 days after unprotected sexual intercourse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Chancroid

Multiple painful genital ulcers 3 days after unprotected intercourse is indicative of Chancroid or Soft Chancre. Chancroid is a type of sexually transmitted infection (STI) that is caused by the bacterium Haemophilus ducreyi, a gram-negative coccobacillus. Auto-inoculation by the organism can result in new ulcers merging with the older ones. Hence, they are called "kissing ulcers." text: 11. A young man presents to the ER with complaints of sudden onset nausea, vomiting, and four episodes of rice watery diarrhea. He gives a history of having food from a nearby bakery 2 days ago. Selective culture media is shown below. Identify the likely organism.
expl:
Correct answer: A. Vibrio cholerae

The given clinical scenario of food poisoning with rice watery diarrhea and yellow-coloured colonies on thiosulfate citrate bile salts sucrose agar (TCBS) is suggestive of vibrio cholera. Vibrio cholerae is a comma-shaped, gram-negative bacillus with darting motility. It has a single polar flagellum. It causes cholera, an acute diarrheal disease. It is marked by painless, profuse, watery diarrhea with flecks of mucus (rice-water stools) associated with effortless vomiting. Infection is acquired by ingestion of contaminated food and water. The organisms produce an enterotoxin known as cholera toxin (CT). It has 1 A and 5 B subunits. The B subunit (binding units) fixes to the GM1 ganglioside receptors on jejunal epithelial cells. The A subunit dissociates into the A2 fragment, which attaches the A1 fragment to the B subunit. This results in prolonged accumulation of cAMP, which causes an outpouring of large amounts of water and electrolytes into the intestinal lumen. Ultimately, it results in profuse watery diarrhea.  Thiosulfate citrate bile salts sucrose agar (TCBS) is a selective and differential medium used for the culture of Vibrio species. Vibrio cholerae produces yellow-colored colonies against a green background on TCBS. Fluid resuscitation by rice-based ORS is recommended. Antibiotics that can be used include fluoroquinolones, tetracycline, azithromycin, ampicillin, or trimethoprim -sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX). Other options: Option B: Vibrio alginolyticus has been associated with infections of the eyes, ears, and wounds in human beings exposed to seawater. Option C:.Vibrio vulnificus may form colorless colonies on TCBS agar. Option D: Vibrio parahemolyticus forms transparent colonies with a green center on TCBS agar. The given image is of colonies formed by vibrio parahemolyticus. text: 1. A woman presents with fever after returning from a forest trip. On examination, a black eschar is seen on the abdomen/trunk. What is the drug of choice in this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Doxycycline

In the above clinical scenario, a history of a forest trip followed by the development of a characteristic eschar at the bite site along with fever suggests a diagnosis of scrub typhus, which is treated with doxycycline. Humans are infected when they are bitten by the mite larvae known as chiggers. The incubation period is 1-3 weeks. Patients develop a characteristic eschar at the site of the mite bite, along with regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash. It can be associated with fever, headache, and conjunctival injection. Meningoencephalitis, myocarditis, and pneumonia can be seen in severe cases.  Oral doxycycline is given in uncomplicated scrub typhus. In pregnancy, oral azithromycin is preferred. In scrub typhus, both the adult and nymphal stages of mites are free-living in nature; hence, they do not feed on vertebrate hosts. The larval stage (chigger) feeds on the vertebrate host and picks up the rickettsiae. Rodents are the mammalian reservoir for scrub typhus. Eschar can be seen in the image below: Serologic assays are used for diagnosis. The Weil-Felix reaction is a heterophile agglutination reaction used for diagnosis, wherein the sera are tested for agglutinins to the O antigens of certain Proteus strains, OX19, OX2, and OXK. OXK is agglutinated only in scrub typhus. Scrub typhus: * Most widespread Rickettsial disease * A mite is a vector * Vector – Trombiculid Mite * Causative agent – Rickettsia tsutsugamushi * Incubation period – 10–12 days * Typical clinical feature – Eschar * Weil-Felix reaction is strongly positive with Proteus strain OXK * Treatment – Tetracycline Renal involvement is a common systemic manifestation of scrub typhus. The severity of renal involvement can range from minor urinary abnormalities such as albuminuria and active urinary sediments such as cellular casts, pyuria, and hematuria to acute kidney injury (AKI), necessitating the immediate initiation of renal replacement therapies.

text: 2. A diabetic patient develops whitish plaques in the oral cavity. A KOH mount reveals the presence of budding yeast containing pseudohyphae. Which of the following is the most suitable culture medium for the isolation of this microorganism?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Sabouraud's dextrose agar

The most likely diagnosis for the given clinical scenario is oral candidiasis, with Sabouraud's dextrose agar (SDA) being the most suitable culture medium for Candida albicans. Candida albicans is an opportunistic pathogen that causes candidiasis. It is a yeast when part of the normal flora of mucous membranes but forms pseudohyphae and hyphae when it invades tissue. They are not dimorphic. It forms germ tubes when incubated at 37 degrees Celsius. It is gram-positive and forms colonies of yeasts on Sabouraud's dextrose agar. Oral candidiasis, or oral thrush, is a patchy, pseudomembranous lesion that can be scraped off, and it develops over the tongue, lips, gums, or palate. It is composed of epithelial cells, yeasts, and pseudohyphae. It occurs in almost all individuals with AIDS. Other risk factors include high levels of glucose, cellular immunodeficiency, and corticosteroids or antibiotics. It is treated with topical nystatin, oral ketoconazole, or fluconazole. Other options: Option A: Chocolate agar: When blood agar is heated to 80-90°C for 15-20 minutes, the V factor is released from within the erythrocytes. text: 3. A 30-year-old man vomits and has diarrhoea within three hours of eating salad and custard at a picnic. There is no fever present. Which organism is most likely to be the cause?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Staphylococcus aureus

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of acute food poisoning most likely caused by Staphylococcus aureus.  Food poisoning by Staphylococcus aureus is caused by the ingestion of preformed enterotoxin. The preformed enterotoxin is heat-stable. Eight antigenic types of enterotoxin are currently known, of which type A toxin is responsible for most cases. It contaminates food products such as meat, fish, milk products, mayonnaise, cream pastries, etc. when left at room temperature for a long time. Enterotoxin acts directly on the autonomic nervous system to cause food poisoning, rather than on the gastrointestinal mucosa. It stimulates the vagus nerve and vomiting center of the brain and also stimulates intestinal peristaltic activity. Staphylococcal food poisoning has a very short incubation period of about 1 - 8 hours. Patients usually present with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea 2-6 hrs after the consumption of contaminated food. Other options: Option A: Gas gangrene is caused by Clostridium perfringens. These gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-bearing bacilli are widely found in soil and feces.  Option B: Salmonella enterica are further divided into two clinical groups: typhoidal salmonellae and non-typhoidal salmonellae, or NTS. Infection with NTS most often results in gastroenteritis—characterized by nausea, vomiting, watery diarrhea, fever, and onset of abdominal cramps 6–48 hours after the ingestion of contaminated food (gastroenteritis is uncommon in typhoidal salmonellae). Option C: Food poisoning after consumption of fried rice or Chinese street food is suggestive of Bacillus cereus. text: 4. A 32-year-old woman is admitted to the ICU with fever and hypotension. She has rigours, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea. Her BP is 70/50 mmHg, with a pulse of 140 bpm and a temperature of 39.5°C. Skin examination reveals generalised erythroderma but no signs of skin infection. She has a history of using tampons for extended periods of time. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome

The above presentation of fever, hypotension, erythroderma, vomiting, and the finding of a retained vaginal tampon point towards a likely diagnosis of staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome. Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a toxin-mediated disease that is most commonly associated with staphylococcal and group A streptococcal infections. Staphylococcal TSS, on the other hand, is associated with the toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1), which binds directly to the MHC II complex and T-cell receptors. This results in a massive increase in the cytokines interleukin-2 (IL-2), interferon γ, and tumor necrosis factor (TNF), leading to a cytokine storm.  Staphylococcal TSS is associated with the use of a highly absorbent tampon. Nonmenstrual cases are seen in patients with surgical or postpartum wound infections, with nasal and wound packing. Clinical features include fever >102°F, hypotension, widespread macular erythroderma and subsequent desquamation after 7-14 days, and the involvement of multiple organ systems (liver, kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, and/or CNS). Patients should be managed aggressively with fluids and systemic antibiotic therapy. They can be started on drugs like intravenous vancomycin/daptomycin initially to allow for MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) coverage. Antibiotics can later be changed based on culture sensitivity reports.  The T-cell activation that produces the cytokine storm in TSS can be seen in the image below: Other options: Option A: Sepsis is a potentially fatal condition resulting from the body’s abnormal response to an infection, leading to organ dysfunction. It is diagnosed by the presence of infection with an increase of 2 or more points according to the SOFA score. Septic shock occurs in patients with sepsis who need vasopressors to keep MAP >= 65 mmHg and have a lactate level of >2 mmol/L, even after sufficient fluid therapy. Option B: PID is the inflammation of the upper genital tract, involving the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries. The most common cause of PID is sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) resulting from ascending Chlamydia & gonococcus infections. Option D: Option D: Streptococcal TSS is associated with pyrogenic exotoxin and other toxins that act as superantigens and mediate the release of proinflammatory cytokines. In contrast to patients with staphylococcal TSS, the majority with streptococcal TSS are bacteremic. The most common associated infection is a soft tissue infection—necrotizing fasciitis, myositis, or cellulitis. It can also be seen in pneumonia, peritonitis, osteomyelitis, and myometritis. The general features of the illness include fever, hypotension, renal impairment, and respiratory distress syndrome. A rash usually does not develop. In the given situation, the source of infection is the retained vaginal tampon; streptococcal TSS is not the correct answer.

text: 5. A 4-year-old child presents to the paediatric OPD with complaints of a low-grade fever, poor appetite, and a sore throat for the past two days. Upon examination, the palms, soles, and oral mucosa show numerous vesicular lesions. The child attends daycare, and several other children have similar complaints. The neurological examination is normal. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Coxsackievirus A16

The presence of vesicular lesions on the palms, soles, and oral cavity and the images showing the characteristic lesions are suggestive of hand-foot-and-mouth disease (HFMD), which is commonly caused by coxsackievirus A16. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease: It is commonly caused by Coxsackievirus A16, which is a subgroup of enteroviruses. In large outbreaks, it is also caused by enterovirus 71, coxsackie A viruses 5, 6, 7, 9, and 10, and coxsackie B viruses 2 and 5. Clinical features: * Usually, a mild illness * Vesicular lesions may be seen on the tongue, posterior pharynx, buccal mucosa, palate, lips, etc. * Maculopapular, vesicular, or pustular lesions may be present on the hands and fingers, buttocks, and groin. * Lesions are more commonly seen in the hands than in the feet. * These vesicles resolve in 1 week. * Infections with enterovirus 71 are more severe and are associated with neurological and cardiopulmonary manifestations. * Infections with coxsackievirus A16 can occasionally produce complications like encephalitis, acute flaccid paralysis, myocarditis, pericarditis, and shock. * Coxsackievirus A6 produces atypical HFMD, which is a severe form. Diagnosis: * HFMD is usually diagnosed clinically by the characteristic lesions. * Viral culture can be done to confirm the presence of an enterovirus. Blood, CSF, urine, and mucosal swabs can be cultured. * RT-PCR testing to detect the viral genome is more sensitive and specific. PCR testing of CSF in children with meningitis is frequently positive even when the cultures are negative. Treatment: * No specific antiviral agent is a proven agent for enteroviruses. Supportive care is the mainstay of treatment. * Milrinone is suggested as an effective agent for enterovirus 71 cardiopulmonary disease. * Immunoglobulins have been used to manage severe cases, but with varying outcomes. Other options: Option A: Roseola infantum, also known as sixth disease, caused by human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), is associated with a non-pruritic, pink, morbilliform rash on the trunk and back, which appears after the fever has subsided and disappears after two days. It is also typically associated with ulcers at the uvulo-palatoglossal junction called Nagayama spots. Option B: Fifth disease, or erythema infectiosum, is an exanthematous fever caused by parvovirus B19 in children, which is also self-limiting and generally requires supportive care only. Its symptoms include a classical slapped cheek rash, which can evolve into a papular purpuric glove and stocking syndrome. There is usually no prodrome or minimal symptoms before the abrupt onset of rash. The virus is known to cause transient myelosuppression and anemia. In very severe disease, IVIG has been tried in some cases. Option D: Adenovirus is a non-enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus. They are associated with infections of the respiratory tract, eye, and intestines.

text: 6. A Tzanck smear prepared from a vesicle sample revealed multinucleated giant cells. What is the most likely causative agent?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)

Tzanck cells, or multinucleated giant cells, are indicative of the herpes simplex virus. In genital herpes, clusters of vesicles are seen on an erythematous base along with painful and pruritic lymphadenopathy, and Tzanck cells or multinucleated giant cells are seen in this condition. The Tzanck smear is a rapid, sensitive, and inexpensive diagnostic method. Smears are prepared from the lesions, from the base of vesicles, and stained with a 1% aqueous solution of O-toluidine blue for 15 seconds. Multinucleated giant cells with faceted nuclei and homogeneously stained ground glass chromatin—Tzanck cells—are seen. The typical herpes lesions are thin-walled, umbilicated vesicles, the roof of which breaks down, leaving tiny superficial ulcers. They heal without scarring. The most common site of cutaneous lesions in the face is on the cheeks, chin, around the mouth, or on the forehead. Other options: Option B: Large hyperchromatic nuclei with a perinuclear halo, indicating koilocytes, are a hallmark of human papillomavirus infection. Option C: Inoculating into tissue culture: Cytopathic effect can be observed within 5–14 days for coxsackievirus. Option D: Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) doesn't show any multinucleated giant cells, but it can cause infectious mononucleosis, and peripheral smear findings show Downey cells or ballerina skirt cells. They are atypical lymphocytes with abundant basophilic cytoplasm containing clear vacuolations and prominent nucleoli. They become large as a result of antigen stimulation. text: 8. A farmer reports fever, malaise, and diarrhoea. There is a history of contact with livestock. Which of the following organisms is most likely to be the cause of the disease?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Coxiella burnetii

The most likely diagnosis is Q fever, which is caused by Coxiella burnetii. The given clinical vignette describes a farmer with fever, malaise and diarrhoea along with previous exposure to livestock. This implies that the illness may be zoonosis-associated. Q fever, or query fever, is caused by the pathogen Coxiella burnetii, which is a small, pleomorphic, gram-negative coccobacillus that was previously thought to be a Rickettsia but now has its own genus. It can be found in ticks, but it is a zoonosis transmitted to humans either through inhalation of aerosols or through contaminated milk. It is an occupational hazard among abattoir workers, shepherds, cowherds, and other individuals in close contact with animals, especially during or immediately after their parturition. Acute Q-fever presents with nonspecific signs and symptoms, such as fever, cough, vomiting, diarrhoea, photophobia, pneumonia, and less commonly, anaemia, myocarditis, etc. The disease can result in a state of chronic fatigue called "Q-fever fatigue syndrome". Chronic Q fever tends to occur months or years after the initial infection and can manifest as Q fever endocarditis, infected prostheses, infected aneurysms, and bone infections. On TEE, endothelium-covered nodules are seen as vegetations on the valves, and new-onset valve regurgitation may be seen. Diagnosis requires a high index of clinical suspicion due to non-specific features and must be considered in all cases of culture-negative endocarditis. Diagnostic methods include culture, which requires a level 3 biosafety cabinet and hence is not done in routine practice, or DNA detection using PCR. IFA (indirect fluorescent antibody test) is the most preferred test that identifies antibodies and can differentiate acute and chronic infections. The treatment of choice is with doxycycline, which may be substituted for trimethoprim-sulphamethoxazole in pregnancy. Doxycycline is given for acute Q fever as 100 mg BD for 14 days. For chronic Q fever, doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine are given. Minimum treatment for native valve endocarditis is 18 months. Due to the low minimum infective dose of Coxiella, it is a bioterrorism agent, Category B. Other Options: Option B: Rickettsia rickettsii is the causative agent for Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever (RMSF). Ticks act as a vector. Option C: Endemic typhus is caused by Rickettsia typhi and transmitted by Xenopsylla, the flea. The reservoir of the infection is rats. It is a mild, sporadic fever that is not of great public health importance. The disease presents with fever and chills. A characteristic rash appears on the fourth or fifth day, which starts on the trunk and spreads over the limbs but spares the face, palms and soles. By the second week, the patient becomes stuporous and delirious. Option D: Scrub typhus, also known as chigger-borne typhus, is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. The vector is a trombiculid mite.
