text: 11. The screening method for GDM recommended in India is done between:
expl:
Correct answer: A. 24-28 weeks of gestation

Universal screening for GDM is done for all pregnant women. The first testing should be done during the first antenatal contact as early as possible in pregnancy. The second testing should be done during 24-28 weeks of pregnancy if the first test is negative. The screening method for GDM recommended in India is a 75 gram oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) irrespective of the last meal timing. A value of ≥140 mg/dL after 2 hours is considered a positive test, indicating GDM. Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) refers to any degree of glucose intolerance having its onset or first recognition during pregnancy.  For IADPSG criteria, an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is done in the fasting state using 75 g of glucose, and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is diagnosed if any one of the following cut-offs is met i.e. * Fasting: >92 mg/dl  * 1 hour: >180 mg/dl   * 2 hour: >153 mg/dl Earlier, a two-step approach was being used to diagnose GDM. In this, the first step (screening) is a 50-gram one-hour glucose challenge test (GCT). The patients having a positive result of >140mg/dl, are candidates for the OGTT. A 100-gram, three-hour oral glucose tolerance test (GTT), is the diagnostic test for gestational diabetes mellitus. GDM is diagnosed if two or more values are positive. Diabetes in Pregnancy Societies of India(DIPSI) recommends a 1-step procedure with 75 g oral glucose without regard to the time of the last meal. A venous plasma glucose value at 2 hours >140 mg/dL is diagnosed as GDM. Some complications of GDM include: * Maternal * Hypertension, preeclampsia * Hydramnios * Increased operative interventions * Future development of diabetes mellitus * Fetal and neonatal * Fetal macrosomia * Congenital anomalies * Metabolic abnormalities such as hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and neonatal hypoglycemia. * Respiratory distress syndrome * Subsequent childhood and adolescent obesity Screening is usually done at 24-28 weeks of gestation. Early diagnosis and treatment are important to prevent complications.

The above image showing anencephaly and a contiguous bony defect of the spine, is suggestive of craniorachischisis. It occurs due to failure of complete closure of the neural tube. Rachischisis is the most severe type of neural tube defect, where the entire neural tube fails to close. Rachischisis can occur in the spinal cord or brain regions of the neural tube. The exposed neural tissues often become necrotic.  The image given below shows craniorachischisis. The splits in the vertebrae are so small that the spinal cord does not protrude. The skin at the site of the lesion may be normal, or it may have some hair growing from it. * Meningocele - The defect in the vertebra allows the meninges to protrude through the defect. * Myelomeningocele (meningomyelocele) - Defect in the vertebral column allows the spinal cord with the meningeal coverings to protrude.  The image given below shows the different types of spina bifida.

text: 14. Which of the following can not be used for emergency contraception?

options.C: Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg single dose in 72 hours

expl:
Correct answer: C. Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg single dose in 72 hours

Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg single dose in 72 hours would not be enough for emergency contraception. Levonorgestrel (LNG) 1.5 mg, i.e., 2 tablets of LNG 0.75 mg, can be used as a single-dose emergency contraceptive. This should be taken within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse. Alternatively, one tablet of LNG 0.75 mg can be followed by another tablet 12 hours later. Advantages of LNG: * It does not contain estrogen and therefore precludes the associated side effects. * It can be used in hypertensive, cardiac, and diabetic patients. * It is suitable for lactating women. * It can be given up to 120 hours after unprotected intercourse. * It can be given as a single-dose therapy.  Combined oral pills consisting of both estrogen and progesterone act on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis to inhibit the release of GnRH (and thus subsequently LH and FSH) and thus inhibit ovulation. Emergency contraception refers to backup methods for contraceptive emergencies that women can use within the first few days after unprotected intercourse to prevent an unwanted pregnancy. Administration of postcoital contraceptive agents that interfere with postovulatory events that can lead to pregnancy.  The various emergency contraceptive methods, along with their mechanism of action, have been described below: * Ethinyl estradiol 50 μg + norgestrel 0.25 mg is administered as two tablets within 72 hours of coitus, followed by the 2 tablets after 12 hours. The hormone may delay ovulation if taken soon after intercourse.  * Ulipristal is given as a 30 mg tablet and should be taken within 5 days. It is a synthetic progesterone hormone receptor modulator. The drug attaches to the progesterone receptor, delays ovulation, and suppresses the endometrium, thereby preventing implantation. * IUCD (intrauterine contraceptive device) prevents the implantation of a fertilized ovum. It does so by acting as a foreign body within the uterine cavity. This leads to increased contractility, tubal peristalsis, and leukocytic infiltration in the endometrium.  * Centchroman is administered as two tablets of 60 mg, taken twice over a duration of 24 hours and within 24 hours of intercourse. It acts by preventing the implantation of the blastocyst in the endometrium. Pearl PF1657: Hormonal contraceptives Oral pills: * Combined oral contraceptive pills (COC) * Mala D - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate * Mala N - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate (Govt. supply, free of cost) * Progesterone only pills (POP) - suitable for lactating women * Norethisterone 350 μg * Norgestrel 75 μg * Levonorgestrel (LNG) 30 μg * Once a month or long-acting pills - highly disappointing results * Quinestrol (long-acting estrogen) + short-acting progesterone * Gossypol - male pill : Cottonseed derivative and causes azoospermia and severe oligospermia * Post-coital pills or interceptive * Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg, 2 doses, 12 hours apart * Mifepristone 10-600 mg * Ulipristal 30 mg, within 5 days of intercourse * Centchroman 60 mg, 2 tablets, within 24 hrs of intercourse * GnRH agonists   * CuT IUCD, inserted within 5 days Injectable contraceptives * Progesterone only injectables * DMPA 150 mg IM every 3 months * NET-EN 200 mg IM every 2 months * Combined injectables * Cyclofem - DMPA 25 mg + Estradiol cypionate 5 mg * Mesigyna - NET-EN 50 mg  + Estradiol valerate 5 mg Subdermal implants * Norplant I - Levonorgestrel 35 mg * Norplant II or Jadelle - 2 rods with levonorgestrel 70 mg in each and released at a rate of 50 μg/day   Others * Hormonal IUCD - Mirena which contains LNG 52 mg with release rate of 20 μg/day * Orthoevra patch - Norelgestomin + Ethinyl estradiol weekly for 3 weeks, then patch free for 1 week * Vaginal ring or Nuvaring - Etonogestrel + ethinyl estradiol daily release, use for 3 weeks with withdrawal for 1 week

text: 16. A young primigravida at 32 weeks of gestation was admitted since her BP was 150/90 mmHg and urine dipstick was 2+ on antenatal checkup. On examination, she has pedal edema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Preeclampsia

The given case scenario suggests a likely diagnosis of pre-eclampsia. Pre-eclampsia occurs due to the failure of the invasion of extravillous trophoblasts into the spiral artery. It is characterized by blood pressure of >140/90 mmHg on two occasions 4 hours apart with proteinuria or signs of end-organ damage. Criteria to diagnose pre-eclampsia: * Proteinuria of ≥ 300 mg (0.3 g) in 24 hours or urine protein:creatinine ratio of ≥0.3 * Platelet count of <1 lakh/cu.mm * Serum creatinine level of >1.1 mg/dL * Serum transaminase levels twice the normal concentration * Headache, visual disturbances, or epigastric pain * Pulmonary edema Clinical types of pre-eclampsia: * Nonsevere pre-eclampsia: Blood pressure >140/90 mmHg but <160/110 mmHg without significant proteinuria * Severe pre-eclampsia: Persistent increase of systolic blood pressure above 160 mmHg or diastolic above 110 mmHg with any of the following, proteinuria, oliguria (<400 mL in 24 hours), platelet count <1 lakh/cu.mm, serum creatinine level of >1.1 mg/dL, persistent severe epigastric pain, marked elevation of liver enzyme levels, cerebral (convulsions) or visual disturbances, intrauterine growth restriction of the fetus, and pulmonary edema. Complications of pre-eclampsia: * Eclampsia * HELLP syndrome * Acute respiratory distress syndrome * Cerebral hemorrhage * Preterm labor * Postpartum hemorrhage * Shock * Sepsis

text: 17. A girl presented with complaints of irregular periods, acne, and increased facial hair growth.USG revealed multiple ovarian follicles. Which of the following would be increased in this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Serum testosterone

In the given clinical scenario history of irregular periods, acne, increased facial hair growth, and USG showing multiple ovarian follicles is suggestive of polycystic ovarian disease(PCOD). In PCOD, serum testosterone would be elevated. Insulin induces LH to cause theca-cell hyperplasia and secrete androgens, testosterone, and epiandrostenedione which are converted to estrogen in the granulosa cells. Epi-androstenedione is converted in the peripheral fat to oestrone. This leads to rise in estrogen and inhibin levels. These in turn cause high LH surge. While the oestrone level increases, the oestradiol level remains normal which raises the Oestrone: Oestradiol ratio. Endocrinological changes of PCOD: * Elevated Estrone/E1 levels. * LH level is raised over 10 IU/mL. FSH level remains normal to low, but FSH/LH ratio falls. * Testosterone and epi-androstenedione levels rise. * Testosterone elevated but < 200 ng/dL (normal range 20 - 70 ng/dL) * Testosterone > 200 ng/dL suggests androgen-secreting ovarian tumor * DHEA-S values may be normal or slightly elevated * DHEA >700 ng/mL suggests adrenal tumour * Serum SHBG is reduced. * Triglyceride level >150 mg/dL-hyperlipidaemia HDL <50 mg/dL. * Fasting blood glucose/fasting insulin <4.5 suggests insulin resistance * Prolactin is mildly raised in 15% cases * Fasting insulin is more than 10 mIU/L in PCOS in 50–70%cases * Thyroid function tests may be abnormal (hypothyroidism) * 17-a-hydroxyprogesterone in the follicular phase >300 ng/dL suggests adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. * Urinary cortisol <50 μg/24 h. Polycystic ovarian syndrome  Important clinical features of PCOS are Menstrual abnormalities (70%) - oligomenorrhea, amenorrhea, obesity, hirsutism, acne, and alopecia due to hyperandrogenism, acanthosis nigricans due to insulin resistance, and infertility. Rotterdam criterion is used to diagnose PCOS. The presence of any two of the three components of this criteria establishes the diagnosis of PCOS. * Oligo/ amenorrhoea, anovulation, infertility * Hirsutism/ acne * Ultrasound findings- Investigations * Enlarged ovaries with ovarian volume will be more than 10 mm3 * 12 or more small follicles each 2-9 mm in size placed peripherally. Hormonal studies * USG is diagnostic of PCOS - it shows enlarged ovaries with multiple follicles in the periphery. It also rules out other pathologies like ovarian tumors, endometrial hyperplasia. * Laparoscopy (therapeutic). It reveals bilateral enlarged ovarian cysts. The ultrasound image below shows an enlarged ovary with multiple follicles in the periphery. Management of PCOD is individualized. Weight reduction and lifestyle changes are the first-line therapy for PCOD. Oral contraceptive pills (OCP), preferably fourth-generation pills with 30 mcg E2 and 2-3 mg drospirenone are used to treat menstrual abnormalities. Hirsutism and acne are managed with OCP with cyproterone acetate and topical agents such as eflornithine, clindamycin lotion 1%, erythromycin gel 2%, and isotretinoin.  Patients with PCOD are more prone to developing insulin resistance which can be controlled with metformin and acarbose. Patients presenting with infertility are treated by inducing ovulation using clomiphene as a first-line drug, along with dexamethasone and letrozole. Surgical management includes laparoscopic ovarian drilling or puncture of not more than four cysts in each ovary. Note: PCOS in association with diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and cardiovascular disease presenting in reproductive age group is known as "X syndrome".

text: 18. McCall culdoplasty is done in which of the following?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Enterocele repair

McCall's culdoplasty is used in enterocele repair. An enterocele is herniation of the pouch of Douglas and small bowel loops into the rectovaginal septum. Enteroceles are most commonly associated with uterine prolapse. Patients present with the following clinical features: * Fecal incontinence * Sexual dysfunction * Constipation/diarrhea * Mass descending PV * Pelvic pain or pelvic discomfort * A bulge in the posterior vaginal wall: * Upper 1/3rd - enterocele * Lower 2/3rd - rectocele * Peristalsis may be observed in the bulge  Enterocele repair is done via the following methods: * Vaginal approach - it is usually preferred over an abdominal approach. In McCall's culdoplasty, the uterosacral ligaments are used to suspend the vaginal vault. The posterior peritoneum and uterosacral ligaments are approximated.  * Abdominal approach - it is preferred in cases where there is associated fecal incontinence. It includes: * Moschcowitz repair - the pouch of Douglas is obliterated by several purse-string sutures. * Halban's procedure - the peritoneal sac is obliterated using vertical sutures. This can also be done transvaginally.

text: 19. A female patient with post partum hemorrhage has been given ergometrine and oxytocin. The bleeding still continues. Which prostaglandin derivative can be given in this situation?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Carboprost

Carboprost, 15-methyl PGF2α can be used in a setting where both ergometrine and oxytocin have not been able to control the bleeding.  Oxytocin is used as the first-line agent in preventing postpartum hemorrhage. When oxytocin fails or is not available, ergot derivatives can be used for second-line treatment.  Carboprost, 15-methyl PGF2α is the drug of choice for PPH and can be used for uterine atony in a dose of 0.25 mg IM. This dose can be repeated if necessary at 15-90 min intervals, up to a maximum of eight doses. Misoprostol: PGE1 * In settings where injectable uterotonics are not feasible or recommended, PGE1 is a useful option. * Misoprostol-induced fever can be distressing and may result in unnecessary sepsis workups and antibiotic use. * No evidence shows that misoprostol is better than other uterotonics for treating PPH. Postpartum hemorrhage: It is defined as a loss of more than 500 ml of blood after completion of the third stage of labor (in vaginal delivery). PPH is blood loss of more than 1000 mL from the genital tract following cesarean section. Depending upon the amount of blood loss, PPH can be, minor (<1L) or major (>1L). Major is further subdivided into moderate (1L-2L) and severe (>2L). Types of PPH: Primary/early PPH: Hemorrhage occurring within 24 hours of childbirth. Causes include * Atony: Primi, grand multipara, over-distended uterus, hydramnios, precipitate labor, prolonged labor, uterine malformations, fibroid uterus * Trauma: Instrumental deliveries, episiotomy, precipitate labor, macrosomia * Retained tissues: retained placenta, blood clots * Bleeding disorders: Sepsis, Intrauterine death, HELLP syndrome. Secondary/ late PPH: Hemorrhage after 24 hours - 12 weeks postpartum. text: 21. The triad of situs inversus totalis, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis indicates the diagnosis of ___?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Primary ciliary dyskinesia

The triad of situs inversus totalis, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis indicates a diagnosis of Kartagener’s syndrome is primary ciliary dyskinesia. Primary ciliary dyskinesia (also called immotile cilia syndrome) is an autosomal recessive disorder affecting ciliary motility. It occurs due to ultrastructural defects in the dynein arm of cilia. This causes the retention of secretions due to a failed mucociliary clearance mechanism. Clinically, this manifests as chronic sinusitis and recurrent infections that ultimately lead to bronchiectasis. As ciliary function is necessary to ensure proper rotation of the developing organs in the chest and abdomen, its absence will lead to situs inversus or a partial lateralizing abnormality. Male patients with this condition tend to be infertile too, due to asthenospermia (immotile spermatozoa due to impaired sperm flagella function).  Other options: Celiac disease is an autoimmune gluten-induced enteropathy where there is an excessive inflammatory response to gluten and its breakdown product, gliadin. This leads to inflammatory infiltration of the lamina propria which subsequently impairs various nutrient absorption. Clinically, it presents as a malabsorption syndrome with diarrhea, abdominal pain, and marked weight loss. Cystic Fibrosis: is an autosomal recessive disorder with a mutation in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator (CFTR) gene on chromosome 7q. It can present as: * Sinusitis and nasal polyps * Respiratory - copious hyper-viscous and adherent pulmonary secretions with abnormal mucociliary clearance obstructing small and medium-sized airways leading to respiratory compromise. The disease can be further complicated by bronchiectasis and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). * Reproductive - males have infertility due to the congenital absence of bilateral vas deferens and defective sperm transport, resulting in obstructive azoospermia. Females have infertility due to abnormalities of the reproductive tract secretions. The diagnosis is confirmed if both of the following criteria are met: Presence of * clinical symptoms affecting at least one organ system (respiratory, gastrointestinal, or genitourinary) or * Positive newborn screening or * A sibling with cystic fibrosis Evidence of dysfunction of the CFTR gene by: * Two positive sweat chloride test results were obtained on separate days or Identification of two CFTR mutations by genetic testing or * An abnormal measurement of nasal potential difference Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a chronic respiratory disease characterized by the presence of airflow obstruction that is partially reversible. Patients with COPD present with cough, sputum production, and dyspnea on exertion.

text: 2. A young woman came to the clinic requesting a post-coital pill. Which of the following would you prescribe?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Levonorgestrel

Levonorgestrel can be prescribed to a young woman requesting a post-coital pill. Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg single dose within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse, can be used for emergency contraception. Alternatively, it can also be administered in two doses of 0.75 mg. The first dose is taken within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse, and the 2nd dose is taken 12 hours apart. The tablets can be offered up to 120 hours but the efficacy decreases with the longer coital-drug interval. Advantages of LNG tablets:  * It has no estrogen and its associated side effects. * It can be offered to hypertensive, cardiac and diabetic women. * It can be offered to a lactating woman. * It can be given as late as 120 hours after unprotected intercourse (but efficacy decreases). * Single-dose therapy is an advantage. Combined oral pills consisting of both estrogen and progesterone act on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis to inhibit the release of GnRH (and thus subsequently LH and FSH) and thus inhibit ovulation. Emergency contraception refers to backup methods for contraceptive emergencies that women can use within the first few days after unprotected intercourse to prevent an unwanted pregnancy. Administration of postcoital contraceptive agents that interfere with postovulatory events that can lead to pregnancy.  The various emergency contraceptive methods, along with their mechanism of action have been described below: * Ethinyl estradiol 50 μg + norgestrel 0.25 mg is administered as two tablets within 72 hours of coitus, followed by the 2 tablets after 12 hours. The hormone may delay ovulation if taken soon after intercourse.  * Ulipristal is given as a 30 mg tablet and should be taken within 5 days. It is a synthetic progesterone hormone receptor modulator. The drug attaches to the progesterone receptor, delays ovulation, and suppresses endometrium, thereby preventing implantation. * IUCD (intrauterine contraceptive device) prevents the implantation of a fertilized ovum. It does so by acting as a foreign body within the uterine cavity. This leads to increased contractility, tubal peristalsis, and leukocytic infiltration in the endometrium.  * Centchroman is administered as two tablets of 60 mg, taken twice over a duration of 24 hours and within 24 hours of intercourse. It acts by preventing the implantation of the blastocyst in the endometrium. text: 5. What marker is regularly monitored in the management of ectopic pregnancy?
expl:
Correct answer: B. β-hCG

The marker used in the monitoring of ectopic pregnancy is β-hCG Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is a glycoprotein. It can be detected in the maternal serum or urine as early as 8–9 days post-fertilization. Maximum levels in blood and urine are found between 60 - 70 days of pregnancy. It disappears from circulation within 2 weeks following delivery. Ectopic pregnancy has decreased levels of hCG as compared to normal pregnancy hCG, and it is used as a marker for medical management of ectopic pregnancy. Following conservative surgery or medical treatment, estimation of serum β-hCG level should be done weekly until the β-HCG values go down. Medical management is indicated when the patient is asymptomatic and hemodynamically stable. It involves the systemic or local use of chemotherapeutic drugs:  * Drugs used: Methotrexate (50 mg/m2, single dose intramuscularly) * Regular monitoring of serum β-hCG Medical management is likely to be successful when * Initial serum hCG level is <3,000 IU/L. * Ectopic mass is less than 4 cm. * Fetal cardiac activity is absent. * Intra-abdominal hemorrhage is absent. Surgical management of ectopic pregnancy includes laparoscopic salpingostomy, salpingectomy, and microsurgical laparotomy.

subject: Obstetrics and Gynecology
text: 6. Which of the following helps manage nausea and vomiting during pregnancy?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Taking small and frequent meals

Taking small and frequent meals during pregnancy can help alleviate nausea and vomiting, commonly known as morning sickness. Pregnancy can affect glucose metabolism, causing fluctuations in blood sugar levels, which may trigger nausea. Eating small, frequent meals helps maintain more stable blood sugar levels, reducing the likelihood of nausea associated with hypoglycemia. The growing uterus exerts pressure on the stomach, reducing its capacity and increasing the sensation of fullness. Large meals can cause significant gastric distension, which may exacerbate nausea and discomfort. Smaller meals are easier to digest and are less likely to cause these symptoms. During pregnancy, the hormone progesterone relaxes smooth muscle, including the gastrointestinal tract, which can slow gastric emptying and contribute to nausea. Smaller, more frequent meals may help by ensuring that food moves more consistently through the digestive system, reducing the likelihood of stomach contents lingering and causing nausea. Pregnancy hormones, such as human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and estrogen, are associated with nausea and vomiting. While the exact mechanism is not fully understood, frequent, small meals may help modulate the body's response to these hormones by preventing an empty stomach, which can sometimes worsen nausea.

text: 9. When is cord clamping ideally done?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Within 1-3 minutes

As per the AMTSL guidelines, cord clamping is practised within 1-3 minutes of the delivery of the fetus. Delayed cord clamping is done 30 to 60 seconds after birth in all the babies. This increases the amount of blood flowing from mother to baby which decreases the risk of anaemia in later life, improves hemodynamic stability, decreases the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis,intraventricular hemorrhage in preterm infants, and also decreases the need for transfusions and inotropic support. AMTSL guidelines recommended by WHO : * Immediate administration of prophylactic uterotonics (Oxytocin). Oxytocin (10 IU) is given IM or IV. * Controlled cord traction during placental delivery (in cesarean section and in vaginal birth where skilled birth attendants are present) * Delayed cord clamping * Postpartum abdominal uterine tonus assessment for early identification of uterine atony is recommended for all women. Continuous monitoring of uterine tone is done every 15 minutes for 2 hours. If uterine atony is detected, a fundal massage is performed. Recent update: Uterine massage is not recommended routinely. The goal of this is to prevent postpartum haemorrhage (PPH). Hence, uterotonics are the most important factor in decreasing PPH. Delayed cord clamping is a less important component in this direction and similarly, cord traction is not as critical. Uterine massage does not form the main component of AMTSL.

text: 15. A 26-year-old nulligravid patient came to the clinic complaining of irregular bleeding for the past month. What is the next best investigation you would perform?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Perform a urine pregnancy test

The next best investigation for a nulligravid patient presenting with irregular bleeding is a urine pregnancy test. The first investigation to be done in a case of abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) in the reproductive age group (15-49 years) is urine β-hCG estimation. This is done to rule out pregnancy. A urine pregnancy test detects pregnancy by identifying the presence of the hormone human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which is produced by the developing placenta shortly after a fertilized egg implants in the uterine wall. The test contains antibodies that specifically bind to hCG, typically providing a visible result when the hormone is detected. hCG levels rise rapidly in early pregnancy, allowing the test to indicate pregnancy as early as one to two weeks after conception. This sensitivity makes urine hCG tests a reliable early indicator of pregnancy. In the reproductive age group, anovulatory uterine bleeding is encountered less often. Therefore, pregnancy must be excluded. Pregnancy complications such as miscarriage, ectopic pregnancies, and molar pregnancies may present with AUB, hence, these need to be ruled out by urine β-hCG levels. This is done for all women in the reproductive age group.  The urine pregnancy test is non-invasive, cost-effective, and provides rapid results, making it an essential initial step in the diagnostic workup. Other investigations to be done for AUB are: * Pap smear: to rule out cervical cancer and preinvasive lesions (CIN). Cervical cancer screening should start at age 21. Women aged 21–29 should have a Pap smear every 3 years, while women aged 30-65 should have both HPV and Pap co-test every 5 years. * Transabdominal ultrasound: to visualise the pelvic organs and lesions such as endometrial hyperplasia, polyps, fibroids, etc. * Transvaginal ultrasound: to visualise the pelvic organs. It is done after evaluating β-hCG. This is more comfortable for a patient than a transabdominal ultrasound, as it doesn't require a full bladder.  is the first-line investigation in a patient with post-menopausal bleeding. All postmenopausal women with abnormal uterine bleeding should be evaluated for endometrial malignancy since age is a significant risk factor for this.

subject: Obstetrics and Gynecology
text: 16. What is the location of the Bartholin cyst?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Posterior ⅓ of the vulva

Bartholin cysts are located in the posterior 1/3 of the vulva. The Bartholin glands are known as the greater vestibular glands in females. These glands are located in the posterior part of the vestibule and open through a duct into the vaginal orifice at approximately 5 and 7 o’clock positions. They secrete mucus during sexual arousal for lubrication. They are the homologs of the male bulbourethral or Cowper glands. Bartholin cyst is caused by obstruction of the duct due to infection, trauma, mucus changes, and congenitally narrowed ducts. If the cyst gets infected, it leads to the formation of a Bartholin abscess. Escherichia coli is the most common causative agent, however, other gram-positive and gram-negative organisms can also cause the same. Clinical features: * If the size is big, it might cause abdominal and vaginal discomfort with dyspareunia.  * A vulval cleft of 'S' shape is usually noted on inspection. * It is fluctuant swelling and transillumination can be positive as the fluid collected is generally clear. Treatment: * Analgesics for pain * Antibiotic for combating infections. * Specific treatment: * Drainage under anesthesia: Generally conservative method, chances of re-infection and formation of granulation tissue can happen. * Marsupialization Complete excision of sac and cyst along with drainage of the substance. The edges are also clearly approximated. This is the ideal management.  The advantages of marsupialization over other methods include: * Simple procedure * Can be done even under local anesthesia. * Shorter hospital stay (24 hours). * The postoperative complication is almost nil. * Gland function (moisture) remains intact.  * Incision and drainage with word catheter placement: A deflated word catheter is used to tuck the vagina here and prevent it from damage that can happen during movement of the perineum and thus avert re-infection and granulation tissue formation. Alternatively, a 14 F foley catheter can also be used. * Bartholinectomy: This is a very invasive surgery and carries a greater morbidity profile. This is also associated with loss of lubricant function.  Notes: In any woman above the age of forty with recurrent Bartholin cyst, a suspicion of Bartholin gland cancer should arise and the cyst wall should be sent for biopsy.

text: 17. A woman with a non-recurring indication of a previous lower segment cesarean section now presents with an occipitoposterior fetal position. What is the best next step in management?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Attempt a normal vaginal delivery

In a woman with a non-recurring indication of lower segment cesarean sections who now presents with an occipitoposterior fetal position, the next step of management would be to try to attempt a vaginal delivery. Occipitoposterior position is an abnormal position of the vertex and can undergo normal labor in favorable circumstances. In a majority of cases, the occiput rotates through 3/8th of the circle, and the baby is born in the occipitoanterior position. Hence, when the diagnosis of occipitoposterior position is made, labor is allowed to proceed normally when there are good uterine contractions and a favorable pelvis. The occipitoposterior (OP) position of the fetus is when the occiput is situated posteriorly over the sacroiliac joint or directly over the sacrum. It is the most common fetal malposition. It is an abnormal position seen in the vertex presentation, not an abnormal presentation.  * Occipitoposterior position is commonly seen in the android pelvis/deflexed head. * The engaging diameter of this position is sub-occipitofrontal. * The most common type in the occipitoposterior position is right OP. * A persistent occipitoposterior position results from a failure of internal rotation prior to birth. Examination findings of OP position: * Inspection: The abdomen appears flattened below the umbilicus (infra-umbilical flattening). * Pelvic grips: * The head is not engaged. * The sinciput (cephalic prominence) is not prominently felt. * Auscultation: Fetal heart sounds are heard maximally over the flanks. However, in direct OP position, they are heard in the midline. Features of occipitoposterior position include infra-umbilical flattening and fetal heart sounds localized to the flank. The fetal parts are more prominently felt near the midline.  Other options  Option A: Indications of cesarean section in occipitoposterior position: * Arrest of labor * Inadequate uterine contraction * Fetal distress * Other obstetrical indications Option C: External cephalic version (ECV) is done in non-cephalic presentations like breech and transverse lie, to bring the favorable cephalic pole to the lower pole of the uterus. The ideal time to do the external cephalic version is 37 weeks. Option D: Vaccum-assisted delivery is used to help with prolonged labor, fetal distress, maternal exhaustion, or ineffective pushing and fetal malposition. text: 18. A nulligravida woman presents to the outpatient department with uterine prolapse. There is no evidence of associated cystocele or rectocele on examination. Which surgical procedure is most appropriate in this case?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Abdominal sling surgery

For a nulligravid woman with uterine prolapse and no cystocele or rectocele, we will perform an abdominal sling surgery. Abdominal sling operations are designed for women with type II or III degree prolapse and who are desirous of retaining childbearing function and menstrual function. The descent of one or more of the genital organs below their normal anatomical position is called pelvic organ prolapse (POP). It occurs when the muscles and tissues that support the pelvic organs become weakened or damaged, leading to one or more organs bulging into the vaginal canal.  Clinical types are: 1. Vaginal prolapse a) Anterior vaginal wall * * * Upper two-thirds – Cystocele * Lower one-third – Urethrocele b) Posterior vaginal wall * * * Upper one-third – Enterocele * Lower two-thirds – Rectocele 2. Uterine descent Treatment options may include pessary, pelvic floor exercises or surgery depending on the severity of prolapse. Abdominal sling surgeries: Young women desirous of retaining menstrual and reproductive functions are ideal candidates. These surgeries use tapes as slings to prevent organ descent. These include: * Abdominal wall cervicopexy (modified by Purandare and Mathre): sling attached to cervix posteriorly near uterosacral ligaments.  * Shirodkar's sling surgery: the sling fixes the cervix to the lumbosacral fascia. * Khanna's sling surgery: - sling fixed to the anterior superior iliac spine, strengthening the Mackenrodt's ligament.  Other options : Option A: Le fort's repair - is done in patients who satisfy the following criteria: * Very elderly menopausal patient with an advanced prolapse * Do not wish to retain sexual function * Medically unfit for major surgeries Option B: Fothergill surgery - Also known as Manchester's operation is suitable for women under 40 years who are desirous of retaining their menstrual and reproductive functions. It involves anterior colporrhaphy with amputation of the cervix. The mackenrodt ligaments are sutured in the front of the cervix and colpoperineorrhaphy is done. It increases the risk of cervical incompetence leading to recurrent abortions and preterm deliveries. Shirodkar's modification of Fothergill's repair avoids cervical amputation, hence subsequent pregnancy complications are avoided.   Option D: Shirodkar sling surgery - the sling fixes the cervix to the lumbosacral fascia. text: 20. A 28-year-old woman is in labour, and during delivery, the baby's head is delivered, but the shoulders get stuck. The baby's head is at the introitus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Shoulder dystocia

This clinical vignette of a 28-year-old woman in labour with the baby's head at the introitus and the shoulders being stuck is suggestive of shoulder dystocia.  Shoulder dystocia, defined as a head-to-body delivery time >60 seconds, occurs when either the anterior or the posterior (rare) fetal shoulder impacts on the maternal symphysis or the sacral promontory respectively.  A positive turtle sign may be seen which refers to a definite recoil of the head back against the perineum. Risk factors for the development of shoulder dystocia include maternal diabetes mellitus, obesity, post-dated pregnancy, excessive weight gain during pregnancy, etc.  Wood's corkscrew maneuver is used to deliver the impacted shoulder in this condition. Woods corkscrew maneuver: Pro­gressive rotation of the posterior shoulder 180 degrees in a corkscrew fashion releases the impacted anterior shoulder. Other options: Option A: Face Presentation - In a face presentation, the baby presents with the face as the presenting part instead of the vertex. The baby’s head is typically fully extended, leading to complications during delivery. However, once the head is delivered, the body usually follows without significant issues. The scenario described involves difficulty after the head is delivered, specifically with the shoulders, which is not characteristic of face presentation. Option B: Occipito-sacral arrest- This refers to the baby being in a persistent occiput posterior position (with the baby facing up towards the mother’s abdomen rather than down). Labor may progress more slowly or stop when the baby’s head fails to rotate and descend properly. However, like with CPD, occipito-sacral arrest typically results in difficulty before the head is delivered, not after. If the head has been delivered but the shoulders are stuck, it indicates a different issue. Option C: Cephalopelvic disproportion(CPD) - CPD occurs when the baby's head or body is too large to fit through the mother's pelvis. This can lead to labor not progressing or being arrested before the baby’s head is fully delivered. In CPD, labor arrest or failure to descend is seen, and the baby’s head may not pass through the pelvis at all. Since in the scenario described above, the head is already delivered and the shoulders are the issue, CPD is less likely to be the cause.

text: 21. Where is Ovoid and tandem radiotherapy used?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Cervical cancer

Ovoid and tandem radiotherapy is used for cervical cancer. Ovoid and tandem brachytherapy is a combination technique where a tandem applicator and ovoid applicators are used for radiation treatment. A tandem is a narrow tube, that is inserted through the cervix into the uterus, while the ovoids are placed in the upper part of the vagina. Once in place, a radioactive source is introduced into both the tandem and ovoids, ensuring precise radiation delivery to the cancerous tissues. Both ovoid and tandem brachytherapy are designed to deliver targeted radiation therapy, maximising the dose to the tumor while minimizing side effects to adjacent healthy structures. Brachytherapy is a form of radiation therapy in which the radiation source is placed close to the tumour. It can be either a low-dose or high-dose rate system. High-dose brachytherapy is safe and effective. Dosage is calculated with respect to the amount of radiation received at two arbitrary points A and B (Image below). text: 23. Which of the following signs suggests magnesium sulfate toxicity?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Sluggish knee jerks

Magnesium toxicity is marked by the disappearance of deep tendon reflexes, like the knee jerk. Magnesium sulfate injection is repeated only if deep tendon reflexes, like the knee jerk, are intact, urine output is more than 30 millilitres per hour, and the respiratory rate exceeds 12 breaths per minute. Monitoring of magnesium toxicity: * Loss of deep tendon reflexes * ↓ Urine output (<30 ml/h) (Option B) * ↓ respiratory rate (<12 per minute) (Option C) * Chest pain, heart block Management of magnesium toxicity: * Stop magnesium therapy * Estimation of serum magnesium and creatinine levels * Injection of calcium gluconate 10 ml (10% solution) IV Side effects of MgSO4: * Anuria * Pulmonary edema Other options: Option D: Superficial reflexes like plantar reflex are not used to assess magnesium toxicity.

subject: Obstetrics and Gynecology
text: 24. Early cord clamping is done in which of the following cases?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Non-vigorous baby

Early cord clamping will be done in the case of a non-vigorous baby.  Early cord clamping is performed within the first 60 seconds after birth, typically when the newborn requires urgent resuscitation. A non-vigorous baby, characterised by poor respiratory effort, low muscle tone, or a heart rate below 100 beats per minute, necessitates immediate intervention, making ECC necessary. Indications for early cord clamping include: * Babies needing immediate resuscitation: In emergencies, rapid neonatal stabilisation takes precedence, and delayed cord clamping (DCC) may not be possible. * Fetal hydrops * Maternal or placental complications: Situations such as placental abruption or postpartum hemorrhage may require early clamping to ensure maternal safety. Delayed cord clamping involves waiting for a minimum of 1-3 minutes after birth before clamping the umbilical cord. It is recommended for both term and preterm babies as part of standard delivery care. Benefits of DCC: * In term infants, delayed umbilical cord clamping leads to higher haemoglobin levels at birth, improved iron stores during the first few months of life, and a reduced risk of neonatal anaemia. * In preterm infants, delayed cord clamping is associated with lower rates of intraventricular haemorrhage and necrotising enterocolitis, as well as a decreased need for blood transfusions.

text: 2. What is the sign shown in the image below?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Hegar’s sign

The image depicts Hegar's sign. Hegar's sign: the examiner performs a bimanual examination. Two fingers of one hand are placed in the anterior fornix of the vagina and the fingers of the other hand are placed over the abdomen and behind the uterus. The abdominal fingers and the vaginal fingers appear to oppose each other below the body of the uterus. This can be elicited between 6 and 10 weeks. This sign is based on the fact that the lower part of the body of the uterus is empty and extremely soft, and the upper part is enlarged by the growing fetus. Other options: Option A: Osiander's sign describes the pulsations felt in the lateral fornix due to increased vascularity. It is seen around 8 weeks of gestation. Option C: Goodell's sign is the softening of the cervix by the 6th week. Option D: Palmer's sign is regular rhythmic uterine contraction during the bimanual examination, which is seen as early as 4-8 weeks. Pearl PF1633: Clinical Signs in Obstetrics * Chadwick’s Sign: Bluish hue to the vestibule and anterior vaginal wall. Seen in the first trimester of pregnancy. The cause is increased blood flow to the pelvic organs. Also known as Jacquemier’s Sign. / * Cullen Sign: Bluish discoloration of the skin around the umbilicus. Occurs due to intraperitoneal hemorrhage. Seen in ruptured ectopic pregnancy * Goodell Sign: Marked softening of the cervix in contrast to a non-pregnant state. Also due to increased blood flow * Hegar Sign: An indication of Pregnancy. The softening of the lower parts of the uterus enables the approximation of vaginal and abdominal fingers on bimanual pelvic examination. * Kustner’s Sign: Sign of placental separation. On pushing the uterus upwards does not move the cord with it due to the separation. * Ladin’s Sign: Softening in the midline of the uterus anteriorly at the junction of the uterus and cervix. It occurs at about 6 weeks gestation * Osiander’s Sign: Pulsations in the lateral fornix due to the increased vascularity. * Palmer’s Sign: Regular rhythmic contractions of uterus felt as early as 6-8 weeks. It is a sign of pregnancy * Piskacek’s Sign: Asymmetric growth occurs to the uterus in the initial stages of pregnancy due to the lateral implantation of the blastocyst. The area of implantation feels soft compared to the other parts. * Schroeder’s Sign: A sign of placental separation. Uterus rises up when the separated placenta is passed downwards * Stallworthy’s Sign: Slowing of fetal heart rate on pressing the head down into the pelvis and prompt recovery on the release of pressure is termed Stallworthy’s sign. This sign is suggestive of posterior placenta praevia. * Turtle Sign: This is when the fetal head suddenly retracts back against the mother's perineum after it has emerged from the vagina. This retraction of the fetal head is caused by the baby's anterior shoulder being caught on the back of the maternal pubic bone, preventing delivery of the remainder of the baby. * Von Braun-Fernwald's Sign: Irregular softening and enlargement of the uterine fundus during early pregnancy. It occurs at 5-8 weeks gestation.

text: 3. What is included in co-testing for cervical cancer screening?
expl:
Correct answer: C. HPV DNA + Pap smear

Co-testing in cervical cancer screening refers to performing a pap smear and HPV DNA testing together. Cervical cancer screening: * Pap smear: Screening starts at 21 years and is repeated every 3 years until 29 years. From 30 to 65 years, cytology with HPV co-testing is recommended every 5 years. After 65 years of age, screening may be discontinued if there have been three consecutive negative cytology results or two consecutive negative co-tests within the past 10 years, with the most recent test done within the last 5 years. * HPV DNA testing: If the result is positive for high-risk HPV, the next step is colposcopy followed by biopsy. If the result is negative, the smear should be repeated after 5 years. * Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA): In low-resource settings, a simple screening method is used in which, after exposing the cervix with a speculum, it is painted with 3.5% acetic acid. Any areas that turn white within one minute of application are considered suspicious and should be further evaluated with colposcopy or biopsy. * Colposcopy: Colposcopy is the direct examination of the cervix using a microscope that provides low magnification, typically between 6 and 16 times. Indications include: * * Women whose cytology shows HSIL, ASC-H, or ASCUS with a positive HPV test * Clinically abnormal cervix, even if cytology is normal * Women with persistent high-risk HPV DNA positivity * Abnormal cervical cytology accompanied by a positive HPV test   (HSIL: High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, ASCUS: Atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance, ASC-H: Atypical Squamous Cells – cannot exclude HSIL) Incorporating HPV testing with pap smear improves its predictive value and reduces the number of colposcopic evaluations. Pap smear:  The patient is put in a dorsal position and Cusco’s self-retaining speculum is introduced. The squamocolumnar junction is identified and scraped with Ayre’s spatula. Endocervix is scraped with a cytobrush. Samples are spread separately on 2 different glass slides. The slide is immediately fixed using 95% ethyl alcohol and stained with Pap stain. text: 4. During the delivery of a macrosomic baby, the shoulder became impacted, and shoulder dystocia was observed. What is the first maneuver to safely deliver the baby?
expl:
Correct answer: D. McRoberts maneuver

The first maneuver used to safely deliver a baby in shoulder dystocia is McRoberts maneuver. McRoberts maneuver: involves flexing the legs on the abdomen with concurrent suprapubic pressure. This causes straightening of the sacrum relative to the lumbar vertebrae, rotation of the symphysis pubis toward the maternal head, and a decrease in the angle of pelvic inclination. This tends to free the impacted anterior shoulder. It is shown in the image below. Shoulder dystocia is defined as a head-to-body delivery time >60 seconds. Risk factors for the development of shoulder dystocia include maternal diabetes mellitus, obesity, post-dated pregnancy, excessive weight gain during pregnancy, etc.  The correct sequence of shoulder dystocia drill is as follows: * Call for help and mobilize labour assistants, anaesthesia, and pediatric doctors. * An attempt at traction is tried followed by episiotomy to afford room posteriorly. * 1st line of management - McRoberts manoeuvre involves flexion and abduction of the thigh in conjunction with suprapubic pressure (Option B) application. * 2nd line of management - Woods corkscrew manoeuvre involves rotating the posterior shoulder to 180 degrees in a corkscrew fashion. Other manoeuvres like Rubin, Gaskin's (all four's position), can be attempted too. * 3rd line of management - Zavanelli maneuver (replacement of the fetal head into the pelvis) followed by cesarean section (Option A). * The last line of management (Not preferred nowadays) is cleidotomy(fracture of the clavicle of the baby) or symphysiotomy(dividing the pubic symphysis of the mother). Other options: Option C: Rubin maneuver: The fetal shoulders are rocked from side to side by applying force to the maternal abdomen. If this is not successful, the pelvic hand pushes the most easily accessible fetal shoulder toward the anterior surface of the chest, producing a smaller bisacromial diameter. This permits displacement of the anterior shoulder from behind the symphysis.

text: 5. A 16-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea. She has well-developed breasts but lacks axillary and pubic hair. Examination reveals normal female external genitalia. Pelvic ultrasound shows an absent uterus, and karyotyping reveals a 46,XY genotype. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Androgen insensitivity syndrome

A 16-year-old girl with primary amenorrhoea, well-developed breasts, absent axillary and pubic hair, normal female external genitalia, absent uterus, and a 46XY karyotype is most likely to have androgen insensitivity syndrome. Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) is an X-linked recessive disorder in which the androgen receptors are absent, scanty, or fail to respond to testosterone. As a result, resistance to androgens may be complete, and female external genitalia are found. The individual has a genetic makeup of 46XY but is phenotypically a female. The Wolffian duct fails to develop because of the absence of testosterone receptors. Testes produce Mullerian-inhibiting factors, so the Müllerian system fails to develop. However, the lower portion of the vagina derived from the sinovaginal bulb appears as a dimple of 1–2 cm in length. AIS can be present in two forms: * Complete variety * Incomplete variety Clinical presentation of complete AIS includes: * Primary amenorrhea and/or infertility * Well-developed breasts * ↓ growth of axillary and pubic hair * Female-looking external genitalia, short and blind vagina, absent uterus and fallopian tubes. The testes may be located in the labia, inside the abdominal cavity, or within the inguinal canal. In partial AIS, a few receptors respond to testosterone, resulting in variable clinical features. Some patients present at birth with ambiguous genitalia, and chromosome study reveals XY chromosomes, while others present at puberty, with lack of virilization in a boy or signs of virilization in a girl with primary amenorrhoea. Investigations: * Karyotype: 46, XY. * Serum testosterone: within normal limits for males. * Serum E2 level:  more than normal for males. * Serum LH level: normal or slightly raised. Other options: Option A: MRKH( Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser)-Mullerian agenesis : Present with similar findings but with 46,XX karyotype. Option B: Sweyer syndrome or pure gonadal dysgenesis occurs as a result of a mutation in the SRY gene (karyotype: 46,XY). This leads to underdeveloped, dysgenetic gonads. They have normal uterus and vagina with no breast development. Option D: Turner's syndrome is a chromosomal abnormality with partial or complete monosomy of the X chromosome (45+XO). In Turner's syndrome, gonadal dysgenesis causes primary ovarian failure that is hypogonadism. The clinical picture of amenorrhea, short stature, webbed neck, low hairline at the back of the neck, widely spaced nipples, and lack of secondary sexual characteristics is seen in Turner's syndrome. 7. A woman presents with secondary amenorrhea for 9 months and infertility. She has a history of dilatation and curettage, with both the progesterone and estrogen-progesterone challenge tests negative and normal LH and FSH levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

PCOS - Polycystic ovarian syndrome
expl:
Correct answer: D. Asherman syndrome

A history of dilatation and curettage followed by secondary amenorrhea and infertility, in the presence of normal LH and FSH levels and negative progesterone as well as estrogen-progesterone challenge tests, is highly indicative of Asherman’s syndrome. Asherman syndrome refers to the presence of uterine synechiae, due to the destruction of the endometrium. It can occur as a result of trauma to the endometrium following vigorous curettages for elective abortion, tuberculous endometritis, and uterine surgeries. Depending on the degree of scarring, patients may have amenorrhea, hypomenorrhea, or recurrent pregnancy loss because of inadequate placentation. Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is used to evaluate the uterine cavity and tubal patency, where intrauterine adhesions typically appear as irregular, angulated filling defects with a characteristic “moth-eaten” appearance. The gold standard for definitive diagnosis and treatment is hysteroscopy, with hysteroscopic adhesiolysis being the preferred surgical approach. Hormonal assays also aid in the diagnosis of Asherman syndrome. All women with amenorrhea in the reproductive age group are considered pregnant unless proven otherwise by negative urinary or serum β-HCG levels. Once negative for pregnancy, further testing is done by a progesterone challenge test. This test is done by administering medroxyprogesterone acetate as a 10-mg daily oral dose for 10 days. If the woman bleeds, then she is assumed to produce estrogen and to have a developed endometrium, and the presence of a patent outflow tract is confirmed. If she does not bleed, then she is given estrogen followed by progesterone treatment in the form of combined OCPs. If she fails to bleed after completing the 21 hormone-containing pills, then an anatomic abnormality is diagnosed such as Asherman syndrome. Below is the HSG showing moth-eaten appearance in asherman syndrome. Other options: Option A: Sheehan's syndrome/ pituitary apoplexy is hemorrhagic infarction of large pituitary adenomas or pituitary infarction due to traumatic major blood loss. If this blood loss occurs during delivery, it's called Sheehan's syndrome. Affected women may present with panhypopituitarism and may have persistent hypotension, tachycardia, hypoglycemia, and lactation failure. The most prominent symptoms are lactation failure (due to the deficiency of prolactin) and postpartum amenorrhea (due to the deficiency of gonadotropins). Option B: PCOS is a multisystem, metabolic, endocrine dysfunction that commonly occurs among women in the reproductive age group. LH level is raised over 10 IU/mL. FSH level remains normal to low, but FSH/LH ratio falls. Estrone(E1) levels are elevated but estradiol level in PCOS is low in comparison to Estrone (E1).  Option C: Premature Ovarian failure or premature menopause is the development of menopause before the age of 40 years. It is diagnosed when at least 2 serum FSH levels are elevated (>40 mIU/l) when measured at least 1 month apart in a woman <40 years. The other findings consistent with POF include low estradiol and an elevated FSH/LH ratio.

text: 8. A woman with a history of preterm birth and one miscarriage presents for cervical length assessment. Ultrasound reveals a short cervix, and a suture was placed to prevent preterm labor, as shown in the image below. What type of cerclage was most likely applied?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Modified Shirodkar cerclage

The clinical scenario of a woman with a history of preterm birth and one miscarriage, found on ultrasound to have a short cervix, is suggestive of cervical incompetence, and the procedure shown in the image is a modified Shirodkar cerclage. The given image shows the presence of a transverse incision made in the mucosa overlying the anterior cervix, passage of Mersilene tape from anterior to posterior, fully embedded under the vaginal mucosa and closure of the cervical mucosa with circular sutures (image 4), suggesting a modified Shirodkar cerclage. In cervical incompetence, the retentive power of the cervix (internal os) may be impaired functionally and/or anatomically. Repeated second-trimester painless cervical dilatation (without apparent cause) and escape of liquor amnii, followed by painless expulsion of the products of conception are highly suggestive of cervical incompetence. Diagnosis in pregnancy * Clinical examination (speculum): Painless cervical shortening and dilatation * Sonography: Short cervix with length <25 mm; funneling of the internal os with width >1 cm * Speculum examination: Detection of dilatation of internal os with herniation of the membranes Prophylactic cerclage is done around 14 weeks of pregnancy or 2 weeks earlier than the previous fetal loss. Rescue or emergency cerclage is done anytime within 24 weeks of gestation. It should only be done when there is a bulging of membranes through the dilated cervix. Removal of cerclage should be done by 37 weeks of gestation. It can be removed earlier in case of preterm labor or if signs of abortion are seen.  Contraindications of cervical cerclage include: Ruptured membranes, Intrauterine infection, Uterine contractions, Vaginal bleeding, Cervical dilatation >4 cm, Fetal death or defect Commonly used types of procedures for cervical cerclage during pregnancy: * McDonald's procedure (Option C) - The most common technique for performing a cervical cerclage is the McDonald method. A non-absorbable (Mersilene) material is inserted into the cervix as purse-string sutures at the cervicovaginal junction. The modified McDonald cerclage (Option D) is a variation of the classic McDonald technique, involving adjustments in suture placement or knot positioning, often aimed at lowering the risk of infection or optimising outcomes in selected cases. Bladder dissection is not done in this procedure. Shirodkar's procedure (Option B) - involves a non-absorbable (Mersilene) tape that is passed subcutaneously through a transverse anterior incision and tied posteriorly. The cerclage is higher in position compared to the McDonald's procedure, and the bladder is dissected. In Modified Shirodkar's procedure, bladder dissection is not done.

text: 10. A patient undergoes a vaginal delivery, after which a perineal tear is noted. The tear involves the muscle and less than 50% of the external anal sphincter, with the rectal mucosa remaining intact. What is the degree of the perineal tear?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Grade 3A

The perineal tear is more common in primigravida and results from over-stretching or sudden stretching of the perineum during childbirth. Trauma to the perineum can also result in perineal tears. Clinical features include the inability to hold the flatus and feces. Soreness over the peri-anal region can be seen due to constant irritation by stool. Palpation reveals the decreased/absence of a sphincteric grip depending on the degree of tear. All recent tears should be repaired immediately. If there is a delay of 24 hours, the repair has to be withheld and the patient has to be started on antibiotics to prevent infection. Complete perineal tears that were not repaired in the first 24 hours should be operated after 3 months. In 3 months of time, any local infection that might have been present would subside, and the general condition of the patient will also improve. However, if the perineal tear is untreated for more than 6 months, dense scar tissue forms making the surgery difficult. Pearl PF1639: Degrees of perineal laceration

text: 13. A 36-year-old P2L2 woman with severe endometriosis is found to have pelvic adhesions on laparoscopy. She has a history of prior tubal ligation and adhesiolysis. What is the most appropriate management during laparoscopy?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy

In this clinical scenario of a 36-year-old P2L2 woman with severe endometriosis and pelvic adhesions on laparoscopy, with a history of prior tubal ligation and adhesiolysis, the most appropriate laparoscopic management would be hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. The history of adhesiolysis indicates recurrence of endometriosis, while prior tubal ligation confirms that her family is complete. Therefore, in the setting of recurrent severe endometriosis with completed childbearing, the most appropriate laparoscopic management is hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Endometriosis is the presence of endometrial tissue outside the uterus. The patient usually presents with symptoms of abdominal pain, dyspareunia, dysmenorrhea, and infertility. It is an estrogen-dependent disease of the childbearing age group. The most common site of occurrence is the ovary followed by the pouch of Douglas. The gold standard for the diagnosis of endometriosis is visual inspection by laparoscopy, preferably with histological confirmation. Role of laparoscopy in endometriosis includes detection of pelvic endometriosis; location of the site of endometriosis and its staging, biopsy for histopathological confirmation and surgical treatment by ablation and / or removal. Other investigations in endometriosis include: * CA-125 levels : Raised  * Transvaginal ultrasound: Echo-free cysts or pelvic mass  * Colour doppler: Increased blood flow * Anti-endometrial antibodies  Other options: Option B: Total laparoscopic hysterectomy may not be the ideal option in this case, as the patient's childbearing is complete, symptoms are severe, and retaining the ovaries could increase the risk of developing chocolate cysts due to endometriosis. Option C: Oophorectomy alone may not be the ideal option, as the presence of endometrial tissue in the uterus can still result in the recurrence of endometriosis. Option D: GnRH antagonists may not be an ideal option for patients with severe symptoms and pelvic adhesions, as they may not provide sufficient relief or address the underlying structural issues. Pearl PF1775: Endometriosis Sites of Endometriosis: * Pelvic endometriosis: Pelvic peritoneum, the pouch of Douglas, uterosacral ligament. * Rectovaginal endometriosis. * Ovarian endometriosis. * Chocolate cyst of the ovary. * Other sites—appendix, pelvic lymph nodes. * Metastatic— lungs, umbilicus, scar endometriosis. One pathology review revealed that endometriosis has been identified on all organs except the spleen. Examination findings in endometriosis: * Abdomen: Cystic swelling, fixed and tender. * Pelvis: Cystic tender mass. * Vaginal examination: Fixed, tender, retroverted uterus. Tenderness in the lateral fornices (indicative of endometriosis even if no mass). * Speculum inspection of the Posterior fornix: Bluish/blackish puckered spots on speculum, tender to touch. The presence of puckered spots is pathognomonic of endometriosis. * Posterior Fornix Palpation: Uterosacral ligaments & pouch of Douglas feel thickened and shotty with multiple small palpable nodules. text: 14. A 26-year-old primigravida at 41+3 weeks of gestation is brought to the emergency department by her family after prolonged labor at home. She has been in labor for 18 hours with strong contractions. On examination, she is dehydrated, with a pulse of 126/min, blood pressure of 90/58 mmHg, and temperature of 100°F. The uterus is tense and contracted, and a tight ring is palpable per abdomen. Fetal parts are not felt, and the fetal heart rate is 100 bpm with late decelerations. What is this ring?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Bandl's ring

The patient has prolonged labor, dehydration, tachycardia, hypotension, a tense contracted uterus, fetal distress with late decelerations, and a palpable pathological ring, all of which are features of obstructed labor. The ring felt per abdomen is Bandl’s ring, which is typically seen in obstructed labor. Bandl's ring/ Pathological retraction ring: * In obstructed labour, the upper segment of the uterus contracts and retracts vigorously in an attempt to overcome the obstruction while the lower segment dilates. * With each contraction, there is myometrial shortening so that the actively contracting upper segment becomes progressively thicker and shorter. The passive lower segment is progressively stretched and becomes thinner. * The junction between the two segments stands out prominently as a pathological retraction ring/Bandl ring. Other options: Option A and C: Constriction ring/Schroeder's ring/ contraction ring is formed due to incoordinate uterine contraction (abnormal polarity) when there is localized spastic contraction of a ring of circular muscle fibers of the uterus. It is formed due to injudicious use of oxytocin and premature rupture of membranes (PROM). The upper segment contracts and retracts with relaxation and the lower segment remains thick and loose.  Option D: After each contraction of the upper segment, the muscles do not return to their previous length, but tension remains essentially the same. By comparison, in the lower segment, successive lengthening of the fibers with labor is accompanied by thinning, normally to only a few millimeters in the thinnest part. As a result of the lower segment thinning and concomitant upper segment thickening, a boundary between the two is marked by a ridge on the inner uterine surface - the physiological retraction ring. text: 16. A primigravida undergoing cesarean section for placenta previa begins to bleed after placental delivery. The uterus is atonic, and oxytocin along with other uterotonics have already been administered. What is the next best step in management?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Intrauterine balloon tamponade

In a primigravida with atonic PPH (Postpartum haemorrhage) unresponsive to initial measures such as oxytocin and other uterotonics, the next best step in management is intrauterine balloon tamponade as it reduces PPH by stimulating uterine contraction and exerting direct tamponade effect. For balloon tamponade, Foley catheter, Bakri balloon, Condom catheter or Sengstaken-Blakemore tube is inserted into the uterine cavity and the balloon is inflated with normal saline (200-500 mL). It reduces PPH by stimulating uterine contraction and exerting direct hemostatic pressure (tamponade effect) to the open uterine sinuses. It is kept for 4-6 hours. This can avoid hysterectomy in most cases. The given image shows Bakri balloon tamponade: The following are the steps used in controlling postpartum haemorrhage: * Feel the uterus to know the cause of the haemorrhage. If the uterus feels flabby, bleeding is likely to be due to atonicity. If it is firm and contracted, it is likely to be traumatic in origin. * In case of an atonic uterus, massage the uterus and start the patient on oxytocin drips or methergine.  * If the uterus remains atonic, manual exploration of the uterus is done for removing any retained placental fragments. Blood transfusion is started and oxytocin drips are continued. Other uterotonic agents can also be given. * Uterine massage and bimanual compression * Uterine tamponade using a hydrostatic balloon catheter (balloon tamponade) * Surgical methods to control PPH are outlined as stepwise uterine devascularization procedures: * Compression sutures: B-Lynch suture (Option D) * Ligation of uterine arteries (Option A) * Ligation of ovarian and uterine anastomosis * Ligation of internal iliac artery (Option B) * Angiographic embolization of the bleeding vessel * *  Hysterectomy

text: 19. A patient presents with antepartum hemorrhage. Previous ultrasound showed placenta previa, and Doppler demonstrates the placenta adherent to the uterus with invasion and extension into the urinary bladder. What is this pathology?

This occurs due to partial or complete absence of the decidua basalis and imperfect development of the Nitabuch layer. Risk factors include associated placenta previa and previous cesarean delivery as seen in this patient.  There are three variants of this condition based on the depth of trophoblastic growth. * Placenta accreta, the villi are attached to the myometrium. text: 20. A woman has been diagnosed with the congenital uterine malformation shown below. This condition occurs due to

options.A: Failure of fusion of Mullerian ducts
options.B: Failure of resorption of the uterine septum
options.D: Failure of development of one Mullerian duct

expl:
Correct answer: D. Failure of development of one Mullerian duct

The given image shows a single developed half of the uterus with a rudimentary horn, consistent with a unicornuate uterus (non-communicating), which results from the failure of development of one Müllerian duct. In the unicornuate uterus, the formation of the uterus and fallopian tube occurs entirely from one Müllerian duct due to the developmental arrest of the other Müllerian ducts. In this condition, a fully functional uterus, a normal cervix (option D), and a typical round ligament and fallopian tube are present on one side. On the opposite side, the Müllerian structures develop abnormally, often resulting in the absence (agenesis) or, more commonly, the presence of a rudimentary uterine horn. A unicornuate uterus lacking a rudimentary horn presents as a compact, well-defined, elliptical uterus that tilts to one side. The upper part, or fundus, exhibits a concave shape. Three-dimensional imaging reveals a characteristic "banana" configuration for the unicornuate uterus. On Hysterosalpingography, the endometrial cavity usually appears in a fusiform shape tapering at the apex and draining into a single fallopian tube. The uterus generally appears shifted off the midline. The ASRM (American Society of Reproductive Medicine) classification of Mullerian duct anomalies is as follows: * Class I—Mullerian agenesis or hypoplasia. * Class II—Unicornuate uterus, with absent or defective development of one Mullerian duct. * Class III—Uterus didelphys * Class IV—Bicornuate uterus  * Class V—Septate uterus * Class VI—Arcuate uterus * Class VII— DES related Other options: Option A: Failure of fusion of mullerian ducts leads to Uterus didelphys and Uterus bicornis. Option B: Failure of resorption of the uterine septum leads to septate uterus. Option C: In utero diethylstilbestrol exposure leads to type VII mullerian anomaly (DES related). text: 21. A 48-year-old woman presents with 9 months of amenorrhea. While her mother feels this is normal for her age, the patient is concerned as it is significantly impacting her daily activities and professional life. What would be the appropriate management for her?

options.A: Start her on Hormone Replacement Therapy
options.B: Reassure her that this is normal for her age

expl:
Correct answer: B. Reassure her that this is normal for her age

At 48 years of age with 9 months of amenorrhea, the woman is likely undergoing menopausal transition. The best management would be to reassure her that this is a normal process for her age. The menopausal transition is a progressive decline in hormone levels that takes a reproductive-aged woman from regular, cyclic menses to her final menstrual period, ovarian senescence, and beyond. Menopausal transition begins with irregularity in menstrual cycles and extends up until one year after permanent cessation of menses. The age of menopause typically ranges from 45 to 55 years, with the average being around 47 years. Symptoms associated with menopausal transition:

Menstrual pattern

Shorter cycles (typical), Longer cycles (possible), Irregular bleeding

Vasomotor

Hot flashes, Night sweats, Sleep disturbances, anxiety

Psychological/cognitive

Depression, Irritability

Mood swings, Poor concentration and memory

Sexual dysfunction

Vaginal dryness, Decreased libido, Dyspareunia

Somatic

Headache, Dizziness, Palpitations, Joint aches and back pain

Others

Urinary incontinence, Dry and itchy skin, Weight gain 
Other options: Option A: While HRT can manage severe menopausal symptoms, it's not indicated for asymptomatic amenorrhea, and carries risk of potential complications such as thromboembolism, ovarian cancer etc. Option C: Hysteroscopy with endometrial biopsy is an invasive diagnostic procedure used to investigate abnormal uterine bleeding or suspected endometrial pathology, which is not indicated in asymptomatic amenorrhea Option D: Endometrial ablation broadly describes a group of hysteroscopic procedures that destroys or resects the endometrium to reduce or eliminate menstrual flow. Not indicated in this case.

text: 22. A woman with a history of a previous cesarean section is currently in labor. She presents with mild contractions (3 in 10 minutes), intact membranes, and no signs of fetal distress. Partograph finding is given below. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.B: Perform artificial rupture of membrane (ARM) and monitor
options.C: Wait and watch for labour to progress

expl:
Correct answer: B. Perform artificial rupture of membrane (ARM) and monitor

In the clinical scenario of a woman in labor with mild contractions (3/10), no fetal distress, intact membranes, and the partograph showing rate of cervical dilatation of 0.5 cm/hour with the tracing crossing the alert line, the next best step is to augment labor with artificial rupture of membranes (ARM), followed by monitoring, as the membranes are still intact. It is evident from the partograph that in 4 hours, the cervical dilatation has only gone from 4cm to 6 cm at a rate of 0.5 cm/hour, which is slower than the expected rate of dilatation (1cm/hour), indicating a protracted active phase. Since the membranes are intact and there is no fetal distress, artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) can be done to accelerate labour. Artificial rupture of membranes is one of the surgical methods of induction of labor. It is done by pricking the membranes with an amnihook (Kocher’s forceps). Labor is induced by prostaglandins released by the separation of the membranes. There is also stretching of the cervix. Other options: Option A: If ARM fails to initiate labor within 4 hours, it should be supplemented by oxytocin. Option C: Since the partograph tracing has crossed the alert line, expectant management is no longer appropriate, and intervention is necessary. Option D: If the tracing crosses the action line, a repeat cesarean section is necessary. More frequent examination is only undertaken if indicated. * Charting starts at 4 cm of cervical dilation. * Colour of liquor mentioned as C-clear, B-blood stained, M-meconium stained. * Moulding mentioned: * bones are separated and sutures can be easily felt - (0) * bones touching (1+) * bones overlapping but can be reduced(2+) * bones severely overlapping and irreducible ( 3+). * Alert line reflects the average rate of cervical dilation of the slowest quintile of term primigravidas, if dilation slows or ceases, the partograph plot will cross the alert line. * Alert line: at 4 cm dilation and expected dilation of 1 cm/hour. * Action line is 2–4 hours after the alert line, which prompts interventions to accelerate labor or perform cesarean delivery. * Higher rates of perinatal mortality are associated with delays of 4 hours or more after the alert line. * Contractions measured for a span of 10 min (duration noted) and measured every 30 min (1 square = half hour). * Pulse: record every 30 minutes and mark with a dot (•). * Blood pressure: record every 4 hours and mark with arrows, unless the patient has a hypertensive disorder or pre-eclampsia, in which case record every 30 minutes. * Temperature: record every 4 hours. This simplified partograph is colour coded. * The area to the left of the alert line in the cervicograph is coloured green, representing normal progress. * The area to the right of the action line is coloured red, indicating dangerously slow progress in labour. * The area in between the alert and action line is coloured amber, indicating the need for greater vigilance.

text: 23. A 25-year-old woman presents with lower abdominal discomfort, and a post-operative image is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Correct answer: B. Mature teratoma

The above image shows a tumor with hair, bone, and sebaceous material which points to the diagnosis of mature teratoma.   Teratomas are germ cell tumors. They contain embryonic tissues leading to the differentiation of cells along these pathways. There are three classes of teratomas: * Mature (benign) teratomas (eg: Dermoid cyst) * Immature (essentially malignant) teratomas (eg: solid teratoma) * Monodermal tumors - eg: Struma ovarii Mature cystic teratoma, also known as dermoid cysts are unilocular in structure and have a smooth surface. Other structures like teeth, bone, cartilage, thyroid tissue, and mucous membranes can also be found.  Most patients are asymptomatic. Complications include: * rupture of the cyst and peritoneal spilling (rare) * torsion of the ovary * symptoms due to mass size of teratoma Treatment of mature teratomas involves excision in order to prevent complications. Otherwise, mature teratomas are generally innocent. Other options: Option A: Immature teratomas such as solid teratomas of the ovary are solid and trabeculated. There may be areas of necrosis or hemorrhage. Option C: Granulosa cell tumors arise from the sex cords of the gonads. They are solid and generally produce estrogen. They can cause precocious puberty in children, hyperestrogenism in adults, and post-menopausal bleeding. They vary in appearance and range from microscopic to large, solid and cystic, encapsulated masses. If hormonally active, they may be yellow due to intracellular lipids. 24. Which of the following is correct regarding endometrial hyperplasia?

options.A: Gold standard for diagnosis in hysteroscopy

Dilation and curettage(D&C) / fractional curettage is used for the diagnosis of endometrial hyperplasia. Because endometrial hyperplasia requires a histological diagnosis, sampling is best done through endometrial biopsy (EMB) or dilation and curettage (D&C). Transvaginal ultrasonography (TVS) is the first-line investigation that checks for endometrial thickness. An endometrial thickness of >4mm calls for further investigation by endometrial sampling. Endometrial sampling can be done using: * OPD procedures such as an Endometrial Aspiration Cytology (EAC) and methods like Pipelle aspirator/Vibra aspirator are used for aspiration of the uterine cavity. Hysteroscopic inspection & fractional curettage is the gold standard procedure to diagnose focal endometrial lesions. On biopsy, depending on whether endometrial hyperplasia is without or with atypia, we decide on giving continuous progesterone therapy or doing a hysterectomy for the patient, respectively. Indications of D&C: * Diagnostic: Infertility, Abnormal uterine bleeding(AUB), Postmenopausal bleeding, Amenorrhea, Endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma, Endometrila TB. * Therapeutic: AUB, Incomplete abortion, Removal of IUD, Endometrial polyp.
