text: 25. Which fetal vessel is assessed by doppler to indicate fetal anemia?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Middle cerebral artery

Fetal anemia is assessed using the peak systolic velocity (PSV) of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) on Doppler.  Fetal middle cerebral artery doppler measurements of peak systolic velocity(PSV) are the recommended test for the detection of fetal anemia. In the anemic fetus, blood is shunted preferentially to the brain to maintain adequate oxy­genation. As a result, the velocity rises because of increased cardiac out­put and decreased blood viscosity.  MCA PSV is used for the monitoring of fetuses of Rh-negative sensitized mothers, and if it exceeds 1.5 MoM and the gestational age less than 34 or 35 weeks, fetal blood sampling followed by transfu­sion is considered. Serial mea­surements of the peak systolic velocity of the fetal MCA are reliable and noninvasive. The threshold value to identify fetuses with anemia is 1.5 MoM (multiples of the median) for gestational age and is 100% sensitive. If the PSV is between 1.0 and 1.5 MoM and the slope is rising and approaching 1.5 MoM, fetal surveillance is increased to weekly doppler examination. If the MCA peak systolic velocity > 1.5 MoM and the gestational age is <34 or 35 weeks, fetal blood sampling should be considered and followed by fetal transfu­sion if needed. If the gestation age is >/=34 weeks, delivery is considered. Other options:  Option A: Umbilical artery- S/D ratio:  Abnormal flow patterns on the umbilical artery doppler: * Reduced end-diastolic flow: Uteroplacental insufficiency. * Absent end-diastolic flow: Fetal compromise. * Reverse end-diastolic flow: Impending doom of death. Option C: Uterine artery: The presence of a diastolic notch indicates incomplete trophoblastic invasion of the uterine spiral arteries and is associated with an increased risk of developing pre-eclampsia, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), and even fetal demise. Option D: Umbilical vein: Doppler assessment of the venous system (ductus venosus and umbilical vein) gives insight into cardiac forward function by evaluating cardiac compliance, contractility, and afterload.

text: 26. For a pregnant woman at 33 weeks with preterm labor, what should be administered to promote fetal lung maturity?

Steroids are administered to pregnant women in preterm labor to accelerate fetal lung maturity. In ectopic pregnancy, hCG levels should be repeated every 48 hours, as the normal doubling time of hCG in a viable intrauterine pregnancy is 48 hours. text: 28. Females often experience recurrent urinary tract infections but rarely develop vaginal infections, despite the close anatomical proximity of the vaginal opening to the anus. Which of the following best explains the natural protective mechanism of the vagina against infection?

29. A 32-year-old woman at 38 weeks of pregnancy presents with decreased fetal movements for the past 24 hours. Her medical and obstetric history are unremarkable. On NST, there is one acceleration in 20 minutes with no decelerations. What should be the next step in management?

NST - Non-Stress Test
expl:
Correct answer: B. Continue NST for 40 minutes

The next step is to continue NST for 40 minutes.  At 38 weeks, a non-stress test (NST) with only one acceleration in 20 minutes is considered non-reactive. However, before confirming any abnormality, the NST should be extended to 40 minutes.  In non-stress test (NST), a continuous electronic monitoring of the fetal heart rate along with recording of fetal movements (cardiotocography) is undertaken. There is an observed association of FHR acceleration with fetal movements, which when present, indicates a healthy fetus.  * When two or more accelerations of more than 15 beats per minute above the baseline and longer than 15 seconds in duration are present in a 20-minute observation, it is interpreted as reactive.  * A nonreactive NST is not always ominous and can be seen with a sleeping fetus. Hence, before concluding that a test is nonreactive, a 40 minute or longer tracing should be performed.  Other options: Option A: Induction of labour is not indicated at this stage because the NST has not yet been confirmed abnormal. Reactivity may still occur with extended monitoring. Option C: Emergency LSCS is indicated only if there is clear evidence of acute fetal distress, which is not present here.  Option D: Instrumental delivery applies when the woman is in the second stage of labour. This patient is not in labour, so it’s not appropriate.

text: 30. What is the earliest clinical sign of uterine rupture in a woman undergoing a trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC)?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Fetal bradycardia

Fetal bradycardia is the earliest and most consistent sign of uterine rupture during a trial of labor after cesarean. Uterine rupture is defined as a disruption in the continuity of all the uterine layers (endometrium, myometrium, and serosa) after 20 weeks of pregnancy. It is a potentially life-threatening maternal complication, often associated with an unsuccessful Trial of Labour after Caesarean (TOLAC). Clinical Features of Uterine Rupture:  Most consistent sign (seen in majority of cases): * Fetal heart rate abnormalities in CTG – bradycardia, variable decelerations, or late decelerations. Other maternal and fetal features: * Persistent lower abdominal or suprapubic pain, especially if occurring between contractions. * Sudden chest pain, shoulder tip pain, or shortness of breath (due to diaphragmatic irritation or hemoperitoneum). * Scar tenderness on palpation. * Vaginal bleeding or blood in urine. * Contractions stop after being previously adequate. * Signs of maternal compromise – tachycardia, hypotension, or shock. * Loss of station of the presenting part felt on vaginal examination.

1. A pregnant woman at 36 weeks of gestation with a prosthetic valve replacement for mitral stenosis is on warfarin therapy. Her INR is 3. What is the appropriate next step in management?

LMWH- Low molecular weight heparin

options.D: Stop warfarin, start LMWH and asprin

expl:
Correct answer: A. Stop warfarin and start LMWH

The next appropriate step in the management of a pregnant woman with a prosthetic valve on warfarin therapy at 36 weeks of gestation is to stop warfarin and start LMWH.  Warfarin is safe and effective in preventing thromboembolism in people with prosthetic valve. However, it is teratogenic and can lead to miscarriage, stillbirths, and fetal embryopathy if used in the first trimester. LMWH is safe for the fetus as it does not cross the placenta but is less effective than warfarin.

text: 2. A mother brought her 16-year-old daughter to the hospital with the complaints of primary amenorrhea. On evaluation axillary and pubic hair were present and other secondary sexual characteristics normal.LH and FSH levels are normal and USG showed absence of uterus.What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. MRKH syndrome

The child does not have any uterus but has normal sex hormones and normal secondary sexual characteristics suggesting it is a case of MRKH( Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser). Congenital absence of both the uterus and vagina is termed Mullerian agenesis or Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome. Females have a shallow vaginal pouch (1 to 2 inches deep). The uterus, cervix, and upper part of the vagina are absent. Typically, normal ovaries persist, as they originate from the genital ridge. Individual presents with primary amenorrhea, have a normal female appearance, secondary sexual characteristics, and 46 XX karyotype. Most patients with Mullerian agenesis have only small rudimentary Mullerian bulbs without endometrial activity.  With Mullerian agenesis, traditional conception is not possible, but pregnancy may be achieved using oocyte retrieval, fertilization, and gestational surrogacy. Individuals with Mullerian agenesis or hypoplasia have associated congenital renal or skeletal anomalies. Common renal anomalies include ectopic, horseshoe or pelvic kidney and collecting system anomalies. Skeletal malformations include spina bifida, sacralization, sacral bone lumbarization, and cervical vertebral anomalies. A similar presentation is seen in Androgen insensitivity but LH and FSH levels would be abnormal in that case.

text: 3. A 17-year-old female presents with primary amenorrhea but experiences abdominal pain every month. She has normal secondary sexual characteristics. On examination, an abdominal lump is noted, and a bluish bulge is observed when parting the labia. Considering the suspected diagnosis, what would be the appropriate management?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Cruciate incision on the hymen

A history of primary amenorrhea, cyclical abdominal pain, presence of a palpable abdominal lump, and visualization of a tense bluish bulging membrane on the separation of the labia suggests the diagnosis of imperforate hymen and the appropriate management would be cruciate incision on the hymen. Cryptomenorrhoea, also known as hematocolpos, is a condition where menstruation occurs but is not visible due to an obstruction of the outflow tract. The most common cause is an intact (imperforate) hymen or the presence of a vaginal septum. A vaginal septum is differentiated from the imperforate hymen by a pinkish concave covering in contrast to the bluish convex bulge in the latter. An ultrasound scan of the pelvis confirms the diagnosis. Treatment: A simple cruciate incision of the hymen allows the free drainage of the collected menstrual blood, and leads to normal reproductive function, in cases of imperforate hymen. Note: In the case of a vaginal septum (i.e. atresia), more extensive dissection and vaginoplasty are required.

text: 5. A 34-year-old G3P2L2 woman with a past history of Caesarean section and a Dilatation and curettage , presents to the ER with hypotension, tachycardia, and severe abdominal pain. On examination, fetal parts are palpable in the abdomen and Fetal heart rate is weak. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Uterine rupture

The diagnosis of the given clinical scenario is uterine rupture. Previous cesarean section and Dilatation and curettage are both potential risk factors for scar dehiscence and uterine rupture. Hypotension, tachycardia, dizziness, confusion, abdominal pain, scar site tenderness are all the signs of uterine rupture. Rarely, Hemoperitoneum can irritate the diaphragm and cause chest and shoulder tip pain.  CTG in uterine rupture will show non-reassuring variable fetal heart rate which might progress to late decelerations and bradycardia.  Differential diagnoses for uterine rupture: * Pre-eclampsia  * Eclampsia * Pulmonary embolism - amniotic fluid embolism / venous embolism * Abruptio placenta * Anaphylaxis to anesthesia * Peripartum cardiomyopathy  Management of uterine rupture: * confirm the fetal station and arrest of labor * Stabilize the patient's vitals * Immediate cesarean section should be performed, immediately/ as early as possible to avoid neurological or hypoxic sequelae in newborns. * Depending on the extent of rupture and vitals on the table decision of uterine suturing or hysterectomy or sub-total hysterectomy may be taken.

text: 10. Oligohydramnios is associated with which of the following?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Renal agenesis

Oligohydramnios is associated with renal agenesis. Oligohydramnios is a condition where the liquor amnii is deficient in an amount to the extent of less than 200mL at term. Sonographically, it is defined when the maximum vertical pocket of liquor is less than <2 cm or when amniotic fluid index (AFI) is less than 5 cm (less than 5 percentile). Fetal urine production begins between 8-11 weeks but it does not become a major component of amniotic fluid until the 2nd trimester and is the major part of amniotic fluid after 20 weeks. In a case of renal agenesis, there is decreased or no urine output leading to oligohydramnios, which does not manifest till after 18 weeks. text: 12. A young female has history of a spontaneous abortion. She has had amenorrhea since then. Her FSH now is 6 mIU/ml. Which of the following can be a cause for her amenorrhea?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Asherman Syndrome

The development of uterine synechiae is the most likely cause of amenorrhoea in the given clinical scenario, also known as Asherman Syndrome.  Normal FSH levels (4 - 25 IU/L)  are seen in this condition. FSH levels are low in Sheehan's syndrome and PCOS, and high in ovarian dysfunction. Spontaneous abortion can damage the basal layer of the endometrium. This leads to scarring, fibrous deposition, and subsequently uterine synechiae. These synechiae can produce symptoms like hypomenorrhea, amenorrhoea, infertility, or recurrent abortions. Asherman's syndrome is the presence of uterine synechiae, due to the destruction of large areas of the endometrium, most commonly as a result of trauma to the endometrium following pregnancy-related curettages. Oligomenorrhoea, amenorrhoea, dysmenorrhoea, abortion, and infertility are seen with uterine synechiae. The laboratory investigations and hormonal assays are generally normal in isolated cases of uterine synechiae. Diagnosis is generally established using hysteroscopy. Moth-eaten appearance on hysterosalpingography suggests a diagnosis of Asherman syndrome. Treatment is by hysteroscopic adhesiolysis.
Condition Lab markers 
1. Sheehan's syndrome A. Low LH, Low FSH, Low estradiol
2. Premature Ovarian failure B. High LH, High FSH, Low estradiol
3. PCOS C. High LH, Low FSH, Low estradiol
4. Asherman's syndrome D. Normal FSH, Normal LH, Normal estradiol
The image below shows a moth-eaten appearance on hysterosalpingography. Other options: Option A: Sheehan syndrome, also called post-partum pituitary necrosis, refers to the necrosis of the pituitary gland following significant post-partum bleeding, hypovolemia, and shock. Affected women may present with panhypopituitarism and may have persistent hypotension, tachycardia, hypoglycemia, and lactation failure. The most prominent symptoms are lactation failure (due to a deficiency of prolactin) and postpartum amenorrhea (due to a deficiency of gonadotropins).  Option B: Premature Ovarian failure or premature menopause is the development of menopause before the age of 40 years. It is diagnosed when at least 2 serum FSH levels are elevated (>40 mIU/l) when measured at least 1 month apart in a woman <40 years. The other findings consistent with POF include low estradiol and an elevated FSH/LH ratio. Option C: PCOS is a multisystem, metabolic, endocrine dysfunction that commonly occurs among women in the reproductive age group.

text: 13. A couple presented in the outpatient department with infertility. The husband's semen analysis was normal. The wife reported menorrhagia and a hysterosalpingogram showed a tobacco pouch appearance with distal dilatation of the tubes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Tubal salpingitis

The clinical scenario along with a hysterosalpingogram showing a tobacco pouch appearance is diagnostic of tubal salpingitis, most likely tubercular salpingitis. Hydrosalpinx occurs following acute salpingitis. The tubes are retort-shaped due to dilatation of the ampulla and filled with a clear fluid. The interstitial end of the tube is open whereas the fimbrial end is indrawn and closed. This permits the dye to enter but not exit the tube during hysterosalpingography.  Genital tuberculosis is almost always secondary to the primary focus. The fallopian tubes are the first to be involved and are bilaterally affected. It is secondary to hematogenous spread from a primary focus. The ampullary part of the tube appears dilated with the fimbrial end open and pouting. This gives the characteristic tobacco-pouch appearance as seen in the image below. HSG should not be performed in a suspected case of genital tuberculosis as it causes dissemination of the infection. This further increases the damage to the fallopian tubes. If performed, HSG findings in tubercular salpingitis include: * A rigid non-peristaltic pipe-like tube (lead pipe appearance) * Beading and variation in the filling defect * Calcification of the tube, Coiling of the tubes * Cornual block * Tobacco-pouch appearance of hydrosalpinx and pyosalpinx * Tubal diverticula and/or fluffiness of tubal outline. * Uterine cavity—irregular outline, honeycomb appearance, or presence of uterine synechia

text: 14. What is the most common cause of consumptive coagulopathy in obstetrics?

Placental abruption is the most common cause of severe consumptive coagulopathy in obstetrics. text: 16. What is the complication associated with IV bolus oxytocin?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Hypotension

An IV bolus of oxytocin can lead to hypotension. Thus, they are administered as dilute solutions at a controlled rate.  Oxytocin acts via G protein-coupled coupled receptors and the phosphoinositide-calcium second messenger system which contracts the uterine smooth muscle. It also acts via the release of prostaglandins and leukotrienes which augment the action of uterine contraction. Oxytocin at smaller doses increases both the frequency and the force of contraction while at higher doses it produces sustained contractions. Other effects include contraction of myoepithelial cells leading to the ejection of milk and weak antidiuretic and pressor activity due to activation of vasopressin receptors. Excess activation of vasopressin receptors can lead to water intoxication and hyponatremia. They also have a vasodilating property, particularly at high doses which can provoke hypotension. Contraindications to oxytocin use include fetal distress, fetal malpresentation, placental abruption, and previous extensive uterine surgery.

The label marked 2 represents the LH surge ,which is responsible for ovulation. Phases of the menstrual cycle : Follicular phase (days 0–14) * A primordial follicle develops to the Graafian stage, with atresia of neighboring follicles. * LH and FSH receptors are up-regulated in theca and granulosa cells. * Estradiol levels increase and cause proliferation of the uterus. * FSH and LH levels are suppressed by the negative feedback effect of estradiol on the anterior pituitary. * Progesterone levels are low. Ovulation (day 14) * Occurs 14 days before menses, regardless of cycle length. Thus, in a 28-day cycle, ovulation occurs on day 14; in a 35-day cycle, ovulation occurs on day 22. * A burst of estradiol synthesis at the end of the follicular phase has a positive feedback effect on the secretion of FSH and LH (LH surge). * Ovulation occurs as a result of the estrogen-induced LH surge. * Estrogen levels decrease just after ovulation (but rise again during the luteal phase). * Cervical mucus increases in quantity; it becomes less viscous and more penetrable by sperm. Luteal phase (days 14–28) * Progesterone levels are high. * The corpus luteum begins to develop, and it synthesizes estrogen and progesterone. Vascularity and secretory activity of the endometrium increase to prepare for receipt of a fertilized egg. * Basal body temperature increases because of the effect of progesterone on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center. * If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum regresses at the end of the luteal phase. As a result, estradiol and progesterone levels decrease abruptly. Menses (days 0–4) * The endometrium is sloughed because of the abrupt withdrawal of estradiol and progesterone. text: 21. A 37-week primigravida has mild labor pains for 20 hours and the cervix is persistently 1 cm dilated but non-effaced. What would be the appropriate management?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Sedation and wait

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of either prolonged latent phase. The appropriate management is to sedate the patient and wait. The first stage of labour consists of two phases : * Latent phase: It is considered to begin at the time the woman first perceives regular uterine contractions and is characterized by gradual cervical change (up to 5 cm of cervical dilatation). * Active phase: This follows the latent phase and is characterized by regular painful uterine contractions, cervical effacement, and rapid cervical dilatation from 5 cm to full dilatation. A latent phase that exceeds 20 hours in primigravidae or 14 hours in multiparae is termed as a prolonged latent phase of labour. Bed rest is the preferred treatment unless there is any indication for expediting the delivery. The presence of false labour pains for a long time may be confused with a prolonged latent phase. The differences between them include

Show Present Absent
Bag of water Formed Absent
Relief with enema No Yes
Augmentation with oxytocin is done only in those patients who even after therapeutic rest continue to be in a prolonged latent phase. There is no indication of the cesarean section unless cephalopelvic disproportion is present. Amniotomy is not useful and should be avoided in patients with prolonged latent phases due to the risk of infections. text: 23. Which of the following conditions shown below has a false positive Barr body?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Klinefelter's syndrome

A person with Klinefelter syndrome has an extra X chromosome and thus there is a false positive Barr body in this patient. Barr body is the inactivated X chromosome in the cell which is peripherally situated as a darkly stained nodule, chromatin positive, and better seen in the epithelial cell nuclei. Male cells have only one X chromosome and are called chromatin negative as they do not have a Barr body. The total number of Barr bodies is given by the formula (X-1) as the inactivated X chromosome is seen as the Barr body. Barr bodies are seen in 0-4% of genetic males (46XY) and 20-80% of genetic females (46XX and the most common sites for sampling for sex chromatin are Buccal mucosa, tooth pulp, and hair bulb. In a normal male, there are no Barr bodies as the genotype is XY. Females are XX and thus have a Barr body in them. Males with Klinefelter syndrome have XXY genotype and thus have a false positive Barr body while a female with Turner syndrome has XO and has no Barr body usually. Only in rare cases of mosaicism will Turner syndrome patients have a Barr body. The image of a Barr body in a confocal microscope is shown below and is indicated by the arrow as the inactive X (Xi).

text: 10. A patient with a history of obstructed labor and cesarean section presents with continuous dribbling of urine through vagina on day 7. What is the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Vesicovaginal fistula

The clinical scenario is suggestive of vesicovaginal fistula. Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF) is a type of genital fistula, which is an abnormal communication between the genital tract and the urinary tract. Vesicovaginal fistulae occur mostly due to obstetric injuries such as prolonged labor, and instrumental or manipulative deliveries. Patients present with true incontinence characterized by constant dribbling of urine. The presence of urine in the undergarments is uncomfortable and leads to pruritus and excoriation of the genital area In obstructed labour, ischemia necrosis occurs as a result of prolonged compression effect on the bladder base between the head and symphysis pubis leading to infection → sloughing → fistula. Thus, it takes around 3–5 days following delivery to produce a fistula. Clinical assessment by the introduction of a speculum helps to determine the size, number, and location of the fistulae. A methylene blue test helps confirm the diagnosis and determine the type of repair operation. Small fistulas due to difficult childbirth can heal spontaneously. Most established fistulas need to be repaired vaginally usually after 3 months to allow the inflammation to subside. The repair operation includes the Latzko procedure. The procedure involves denuding the vaginal epithelium around fistulous edges and approximating the raw surfaces. Another is the Chassar-Moir technique of widely separating the bladder and vagina and suturing them separately in two layers. Post-operatively, continuous bladder drainage for 14 days along with antibiotics is recommended. Vaginal or speculum examination and intercourse are not advised for 3 months. Avoiding pregnancy for a year is also recommended. A cesarean section is usually done for future pregnancies. Other options: Option A: Vesicouterine fistula occurs during cesarean section or uterine rupture or placenta accreta. Patients complain of cyclical hematuria due to the trickling of menstrual blood into the bladder through this anomalous condition. But the urinary continence of the patient remains normal. This is also known as Youssef syndrome.  Option B: In urethrovaginal fistulae, the patient is continent and dry, but may dribble urine during micturition. This usually follows surgery for a paravaginal cyst or urethral diverticulum, or after a penetrating injury from a fall or criminal abortion. The fistulous opening is visible on speculum examination. Option C: Ureterovaginal fistulae result from direct injury to the ureter during gynecologic surgery (Eg: Wertheim's procedure for Ca cervix). Urine dribbles from both vagina and urethra post-surgery. The three-swab test will not stain with methylene blue, but with urine. Pearl PF1921: Methylene blue - 3 swab test Procedure: A catheter is introduced into the bladder through the urethra. The vaginal cavity is packed with three (or four) sterile cotton swabs. 50–100 mL of dilute methylene blue dye is injected into the bladder using a catheter. Results: * Upper swabs get wet and not stained - the leak is from the ureter: Ureterovaginal fistula * Upper swabs get stained - the leak is from the bladder: Vesicovaginal fistula * Lower swabs get stained - the leak is from the urethra: Urethrovaginal fistula. text: 15. Which of the following can reduce the risk of endometrial cancer in a post-menopausal woman on hormone replacement therapy (HRT)?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Adding progesterone to oestrogen

Adding progesterone to estrogen in HRT can reduce the risk of potential endometrial cancer. For women with a uterus, it is recommended to add micronized progesterone to prevent endometrial hyperplasia which can occur after 6 months of oestrogen therapy. For women without a uterus, just estrogen therapy is sufficient.  Hormone therapy is only indicated for the treatment of vasomotor symptoms,genitourinary syndrome of menopause like vaginal and vulvar atrophy and for the prevention of osteoporosis. The daily estrogen content in most oral contraceptive pills is 35µg or less and levonorgestrel is 100-150 mg. But the HRT commonly used have a different concentration of estrogen and progesterone. text: 16. A 30-year-old woman presents with severe dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia and infertility. A diagnosis of endometriosis was made and she was posted for laparoscopy surgery. During the procedure, dense pelvic adhesions were seen with the bowel stuck to the fundus and cystic ovaries stuck to each other. What is the next step in managing this patient?

options.B: Gestrinone to decrease the LH surge

expl:
Correct answer: C. Cystectomy and adhesiolysis

The clinical scenario is suggestive of endometriosis and the next step in the management of this patient is cystectomy and adhesiolysis.  After the surgery the patient is advised to start infertility treatment too. Medical management of endometriosis: * Gestrinone is an anti-estrogenic, anti-progestational, and mildly anabolic drug that reduces sex-hormone-binding globulin to release free testosterone. It also decreases the LH surge. It causes regression of lesions and amenorrhea. It is a 19-nortestosterone derivative similar to danazol, but with fewer side effects.  * Combined oral contraceptives are used for symptom control and alleviate disease. These also cause menstrual cycle regulation and delay pregnancy.  * Oral progestogens exert an anti-estrogenic effect and cause decidualization and endometrial atrophy. This causes disease regression. It doesn't prevent ovulation, thus is suitable for women who are trying to conceive.  * Mirena IUCDs reduce dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia. It is a single-sitting treatment with minimal side effects.  * Aromatase inhibitors like letrozole are anti-estrogens given for disease regression.  * Anti-inflammatory drugs like mefenamic acid and naproxen relieve dysmenorrhea. Therapeutic procedures: * Aspiration of Peritoneal fluid from the cul-de-sac removes PGE2, relieves dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain, and improves fertility  * Destruction of endometriotic lesions <3cm with diathermy, Nd-YAG laser or CO2 vaporization can be attempted.  * Larger lesions and chocolate cysts can be excised.  * Cystectomy can be done for pelvic pain but can reduce fertility potential.  * Laparoscopic breaking of adhesions relieves dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain. It also restores tubal patency and improves ovulation. Pre-sacral neurectomy can be done simultaneously..  * Laser uterosacral nerve ablation (LUNA) is done for pelvic pain. One pathology review revealed that endometriosis has been identified on all organs except the spleen. text: 17. The most common cause of post-menopausal bleeding all over the world is
expl:
Correct answer: A. Senile endometrial atrophy

The most frequent cause of post menopausal bleeding globally is senile endometrial atrophy. Hypoestrogenism in a menopausal woman causes atrophy of the endometrium and vagina. In the uterus, the atrophic endometrial surfaces contain little or no fluid to prevent intracavitary friction. This results in microerosions of the surface epithelium and a subsequent chronic inflammatory reaction, which is prone to light bleeding or spotting. Other Options : * Cervical cancer : Cervical cancer is the most common cause of post menopausal bleeding in India, and not over the world. * Endometrial cancer : Endometrial cancer is the most common cause of postmenopausal bleeding in developed countries, and not over the world. * Hormone replacement therapy : Hormone replacement therapy is the second most common cause of post-menopausal bleeding all over the world. Note: Endometrial cancer accounts for 10% of cases of post-menopausal bleeding. Unexpected post-menopausal bleeding should be assessed for endometrial carcinoma. Remember, no cancer is as prevalent as hypoestrogenism in a postmenopausal woman, and this is why senile endometrial atrophy is the most common cause of bleeding in them, and not any cancer.

text: 22. Which of the following is the safest hysterectomy surgery to minimise the risk of ureteric injury on the OT table?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Vaginal Hysterectomy

Vaginal hysterectomy is the safest surgical approach to minimize the risk of ureteric injury on the OT table. This is because the vaginal approach allows surgeons to follow natural anatomical planes and typically requires less dissection and manipulation of the uterus. In a retrospective review of study involving 3114 hysterectomies, the following rates of ureteric injury were noted :
Procedure Incidence of Ureteric injury
Abdominal hysterectomy (5/940) 0.53%
Vaginal hysterectomy (1/304) 0.33%
Robotic hysterectomy (7/1088) 0.64%
Laparoscopic hysterectomy (4/782) 0.51%
Injuries to the urinary tract occur during major gynecologic surgeries. These injuries usually happen when dissection is carried out near the ureter or the bladder. When a hysterectomy is performed through the vaginal route, the likelihood of ureteric injury is lower. In comparison, the open and laparoscopic approaches show higher rates of such complications. Patients with ureteric injuries have a complicated post-operative period. They can present with the following features: * Fever * Flank pain * Abdominal distension * Prolonged paralytic ileus - bowel sounds are absent * High drain outputs, in case abdominal drains are placed. CT urogram and retrograde pyelography are the investigations of choice. They reveal urinary extravasation from the ureter. Ureteric injuries are prevented by careful division of tissue planes during pelvic or genitourinary surgeries. The condition is managed by prompt surgical repair by ureteroureterostomy or percutaneous ureterostomy.

The menstrual fluid gets collected in the reproductive tract. When this collection occurs in the vagina, it is known as hematocolpos. If the collection extends to the uterus, it is known as hematometra. The collection of blood in the fallopian tubes is called hematosalpinx. The most common causes of cryptomenorrhea are: * Intact/imperforate hymen - a bluish convex bulge is seen. * Transverse vaginal septum - a pinkish concave covering is seen Ultrasound pelvis confirms the diagnosis. Management: Imperforate hymen - A simple cruciate incision of the hymen allows the free drainage of the collected menstrual blood, and leads to normal reproductive function. Option A: Bartholin's cyst appears as a swelling on the inner side of the labia majora. Larger cysts can bulge across the introitus. Small cysts can remain asymptomatic. Option B - Transverse vaginal septum is a much rarer condition that occurs due to faulty fusion or canalization of the urogenital sinus and the Müllerian ducts. The majority of the cases involve the upper portion of the vagina. It can be differentiated from imperforate hymen by the presence of a short vagina and the absence of a bulging membrane. Extensive dissection and vaginoplasty are required. Option D: Endometriomas are endometriotic lesions seen on the ovary. text: 4. You are studying the optics of a patient with regular astigmatism. Identify the point at which the clearest image is formed?
expl:
Correct answer: B. D

The given figure is a Sturm's conoid. It represents a bundle of light rays formed by a regularly astigmatic surface. The image is clearest or least confusing as point D, the circle of least confusion.  When light passes through a regularly astigmatic surface(surface with toric curvature), vertical and horizontal rays converge at different points. The distance between the points of convergence (focus) of the vertical and horizontal rays is called the focal interval of strum. (distance between points B and F). The circle of least confusion/ circle of diffusion lies at the mid-point of this interval. For the given Sturm's conoid,  * At point A, a horizontal oval is formed because vertical rays converge more rapidly than horizontal rays. * At point B, vertical rays come to a focus, while horizontal rays are still converging; so, it will be a horizontal straight line. * At points C, D, and E, the vertical rays are diverging and horizontal rays are still converging. * At point D, the vertical rays have diverged as much as the horizontal rays have converged; so, we get a perfect circle called the circle of least confusion. * At point E, a vertical oval is formed. * At point F, a vertical straight line is formed * At point G and beyond, both rays are diverging, and we always get a vertical oval/prolate ellipse. Astigmatism is a type of refractive error in which the eye does not focus light evenly on the retina. This results in a distorted or blurred vision. Other symptoms include eyestrain or asthenopia with headaches. Types: * Regular astigmatism: In this refractive power changes uniformly from one meridian to another resulting in 2 principal meridians * Iregular astigmatism: It is characterized by an irregular change of refractive power in different meridians and hence it has multiple meridians. Types of regular astigmatism: With the rule astigmatism: The vertical meridian is more curved than the horizontal meridian but they are placed at right angles to one another Against-the-rule astigmatism: Here Horizontal meridians is more curved than the vertical meridian Oblique astigmatism: Here, the two principal meridians are not the horizontal and vertical meridians although they are at right angles to each other. It is a type of regular astigmatism. eg : one may be at 45 degrees and the other at 135 degrees. Bioblique astigmatism: Here, the two principal meridians are not at right angles to each other; for example, one may be at 40 degrees and the other, at 100 degrees. It is also a type of regular astigmatism. Note: Refractive types of regular astigmatism: * Simple astigmatism: rays are focused on the retina in one meridian: either in front (simple myopic as shown in the above image) of the retina or behind the retina (simple hyperopic) * Compound astigmatism: rays in both the meridia are focused in front or behind the retina * Mixed astigmatism: Light rays in one meridian are focused in front of the retina and those in the other meridian are focused behind the retina

Investigations: * Red reflex testing with a direct ophthalmoscope is a simple screening test for leukocoria. * Dilated fundus examination using indirect ophthalmoscope * MRI of the orbit + brain is the investigation of choice. Histopathology of the tumor shows small round cells with large nuclei. Microscopic features of a well-differentiated tumor include Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (highly specific of retinoblastoma), Homer-Wright rosettes, pseudorosettes, and fleurettes formation. Areas of necrosis and calcification can also be seen. Treatment typically involves chemotherapy plus focal therapy.Vincristine, Carboplatin, Etoposide are the choice of drugs for chemotherapy. Focal therapy includes cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, thermotherapy, plaque radiotherapy, and external beam radiotherapy.   Enucleation is done when the tumor involves more than half of the retina, optic nerve involvement, glaucoma, and anterior chamber involvement.

text: 10. Microanuerysms are seen in which of the following diseases?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Diabetic retinopathy

Among the following microaneurysms are seen in diabetic retinopathy. Microaneurysms are localized, saccular outpouchings of the capillary wall that are formed either by focal dilatation of the capillary wall where pericytes are absent or by fusion of two arms of a capillary loop. * Most develop in the inner capillary plexus (inner nuclear layer), frequently adjacent to areas of capillary non-perfusion. * Loss of pericytes may also lead to endothelial cell proliferation with the formation of ‘cellular’ microaneurysms. * Microaneurysms may leak plasma constituents into the retina as a result of a breakdown in the blood-retinal barrier or may thrombose. * They tend to be the earliest sign of DR. Stages and fundus picture in diabetic retinopathy: Non-proliferative/ Background Diabetic Retinopathy: * Microaneurysms  * Dot and Blot hemorrhages  * Exudates Preproliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (indicates progressive retinal ischemia): * Intra-retinal microvascular abnormalities * Venous changes (such as beading) * Cotton wool spots * Deep retinal hemorrhages Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy: * NeoVascularization of the Optic Disc (NVD) * NeoVascularization Elsewhere in the periphery of the fundus (NVE) Advanced Diabetic Eye Disease: * Tractional retinal detachment * Vitreous hemorrhage * Neovascular glaucoma Pearl PF1636: Early treatment diabetic retinopathy study (ETDRS) classification Non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR): * Mild NPDR * At least one microaneurysm must be present * Moderate NPDR * Microaneurysms/intraretinal hemorrhage in 2 or 3 quadrants * Early mild intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) * Hard exudates and cotton-wool spots may or may not be present * Severe NPDR - any one of the following (4-2-1 rule) * 4 quadrants of microaneurysms and extensive intraretinal hemorrhages * 2 quadrants of venous beading * 1 quadrant of IRMA changes * Very severe NPDR - any two of the following (4-2-1) * 4 quadrants of microaneurysms and extensive intraretinal hemorrhages * 2 quadrants of venous beading * 1 quadrant of IRMA changes Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR): * PDR without high-risk characteristics (Early PDR) * Early neovascularization at the optic disc (NVD) or neovascularization elsewhere (NVE) * PDR with high-risk characteristics as follows * NVD < 1/4 disc area with vitreous hemorrhage (VH) or preretinal hemorrhage (PRH) * NVD 1/4 to 1/3 of disc area with or without VH or PRH * NVE > 1/2 disc area with VH or PRH Clinically significant macular edema: 1 of the following 3 criteria are present on slit-lamp examination with 90D lens * Thickening of the retina at or within 500 micron of the center of the fovea. * Hard exudates at or within 500 micron of the centre of fovea associated with adjacent retinal thickening. * Development of a zone of retinal thickening one disc diameter or larger in size. At least a part of this should be within one disc diameter of the foveal center. Advanced diabetic eye disease: * Persistent vitreous hemorrhage * Tractional retinal detachment * Neovascular glaucoma

text: 16. A 45-year-old female patient with h/o chicken pox comes to the clinic with the findings shown below. What is the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Herpes Zoster Ophtalmicus

The given image along with the past history of chicken pox is suggestive of a case of herpes zoster ophtalmicus which involves the face and the eyes.  Herpes zoster Opthlamicus: It is the term used for shingles  involving the dermatome supplied by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve Pathogenesis: Varicella zoster causes both chicken pox and shingles. Usually after chicken pox, the organism travels in a retrograde fashion to the dorsal root and cranial sensory nerve ganglia and remains dormant until it is activated again. Reactivation causes necrosis and inflammation the sensory ganglia causes corneal anaesthesia and neurotrophic keratopathy. The spread is airborne and through fomites and the lesions cease to be infectious when they crust. Age and immunocompromised status are the two most important predisposing factors for this condition because of the diminishing T-cell immunity. Ocular manifestations: Hutchinson’s rule is related to herpes zoster ophthalmicus. It states that if the tip of the nose is involved, there will be a significant risk of ocular involvement. This is due to the involvement of the nasociliary nerve. text: 1. A 64-year-old woman was brought by her son, during a cataract outreach camp. She gives a history of trauma to her left eye, one year back and a complete loss of vision in that eye since then. Her left eye image is given below. What is the next line of management ?

text: 3. The patient presents with miosis,anhidrosis and mild drooping of eyelids and a small pupil that remains small even in darkness. The likely diagnosis is?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Horner syndrome

The clinical scenario with a small sized pupil which does not dilate in response to darkness is due to sympathetic palsy  seen in Horner syndrome (miosis, anhydrosis, ptosis). In a normal eye, the pupil dilates in response to dim light and constricts in response to bright light. Pupillary dilation is brought about by the contraction of dilator pupillae mediated by sympathetic innervation. Pupillary constriction is due to the contraction of sphincter pupillae mediated by parasympathetic innervation. The difference in pupillary diameter is called anisocoria. A difference of up to 0.5 mm is common even in normal individuals. Other features include: * Mild enophthalmos, * Loss of cilio-spinal reflex, * Heterochromia, i.e., the ipsilateral iris is lighter in colour, * Pupil is slow to dilate, and there occurs slight elevation of lower eyelid. Cocaine test (2% to 4%): Small pupils fail to dilate in Horner's syndrome. In congenital Horner's syndrome, the additional features seen are heterochromia iridis and unilateral straight hair. Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of the conjunctival connective tissue occurs in pinguecula (and not pterygium).  In pterygium, there is elastotic degeneration of collagen with fibrovascular proliferation. It is important to distinguish a pterygium from a pinguecula. A pterygium, while histologically similar to a pinguecula, is distinguished by fibrovascular tissue that grows onto the cornea. Pingueculae do not have vascularized tissue and do not cross the limbus. Pterygium is a subconjunctival fibrovascular tissue encroaching the cornea. It is a degenerative condition of the sub-conjunctival tissue and is never inflammatory. It occurs due to exposure to UV-B radiation and the most common site is the nasal. It is made up of three parts-a "cap" (an avascular halo-like zone at the advancing edge), a head, and a body. Pterygium Pseudo-pterygium
Degenerative process Inflammatory process
Occurs in elderly  Can occur at any age

A probe cannot be passed underneath A probe can be passed under the neck

text: 9. A 7-year-old boy presented with a white pupillary reflex for which enucleation was done. The histopathological examination of the specimen revealed Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. What could be the most probable diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Retinoblastoma

This child with a whitish pupillary reflex and Flexner-Winterstein rosettes on histopathological examination has retinoblastoma. Flexner Winterstein rosettes refer to an arrangement of columnar cells around a central lumen, which is highly characteristic of retinoblastoma. Retinoblastoma is a malignant proliferation of immature retinal neural cells and is the most common intraocular malignancy in children. It is associated with mutations in the RB1 gene at chromosome 13q14. It belongs to small round blue cell tumours because the immature retinal neural cells are seen as small round cells with large nuclei. White pupillary reflex or leukocoria is the most common presenting feature, followed by a squint which is usually convergent. Rarely, the child may present with nystagmus and defective vision. Image below showing leukocoria of left eye Histopathology of the tumor shows small round cells with large nuclei. Microscopic features of a well-differentiated tumour include Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (highly specific of retinoblastoma), Homer-Wright rosettes, pseudorosettes, and fleurettes formation. Areas of necrosis and calcification can also be seen. The histopathological image of retinoblastoma is shown below. Treatment typically involves chemotherapy plus focal therapy. The commonly used three-drug regimen is the CVE regimen consisting of Vincristine, Carboplatin, and Etoposide. Focal therapy includes cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, thermotherapy, plaque radiotherapy, and external beam radiotherapy. Enucleation is done when * The tumor involves more than half of the retina * The optic nerve is involved * Glaucoma is present and the anterior chamber is involved Other options: Option B - Medulloblastoma is a malignant embryonal tumor of childhood that occurs exclusively in the cerebellum. Patients usually present with headaches, ataxia, and signs of brainstem involvement. Histologically, the tumor is very densely cellular. Individual tumor cells have scant cytoplasm and elongated or crescent-shaped hyperchromatic nuclei. Tumor cells form Homer Wright rosettes. They express neuronal markers such as synaptophysin. Option C - Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood. The child usually presents with rapidly progressive unilateral proptosis. There are 4 subtypes - embryonal, alveolar, botyroid, and pleomorphic. Cells show light microscopic features of striated muscle differentiation. Immunohistochemistry is positive for desmin. Option D - Astrocytoma of the retina and optic nerve head is rare. It is usually asymptomatic and is most frequently seen in tuberous sclerosis. Fundus examination reveals a yellowish or white plaque, nodule, or mulberry-like lesion. These lesions are semitransparent peripherally and calcified centrally. Image showing calcified astrocytoma: Pearl PF1837: Histological Features of CNS Tumors Pilocytic Astrocytomas: * Biphasic architecture - loose microcystic component and dense fibrillary areas * Bipolar cells (tumor cells): thin, long hairlike processes that are GFAP - positive.  * Rosenthal fibers: eosinophilic corkscrew - shaped inclusions * Eosinophilic granular bodies: mulberry - like inclusions    Medulloblastoma: * Very densely cellular, with sheets of small primitive appearing small blue cells * Individual tumor cells have scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei that are frequently elongated or crescent-shaped * Tumor cells form Homer - Wright rosettes (pseudorosettes) with a central neuropil   Ependymoma: * Ependymal rosettes: gland - like round or elongated structures that resemble the embryologic ependymal canal, with long, delicate processes extending into the lumen  * Perivascular pseudorosettes: perivascular nuclear - free zone consisting of thin ependymal processes radiating toward the central blood vessel   Oligodendroglioma: * Fried - egg appearance: sheets of regular cells with spherical nuclei containing finely granular chromatin (similar to normal oligodendrocytes) surrounded by a clear halo of vacuolated cytoplasm.  * Chicken - wire capillaries: a delicate network of anastomosing capillaries   Retinoblastoma:  * Composed of collections of small, round cells with hyperchromatic nuclei * Flexner - Wintersteiner rosettes: arrangements of a single layer of tumor cells around an apparent lumen * Homer - Wright rosettes: a ring of cells with an eosinophilic fibrillary center * Fleurettes: retinoblastoma cells that have undergone greater photoreceptor differentiation and group together as a bouquet. Fleurettes lack mitosis or necrosis.

text: 10. An industrial worker was admitted to the hospital after an eye injury sustained while cutting stone with a hammer and iron chisel. A foreign body was suspected to be impacted in his eye. Which of the following is the best investigation for foreign body localization?
expl:
Correct answer: B. CT

CT scan is the best method for intraocular foreign body (IOFB) localization. The foreign bodies most likely to penetrate and be retained in the eye are minute chips of iron or steel. While chipping stone with an iron chisel, the chip of the iron chisel is more likely to enter the eye than the stone. A foreign body entering the eye may cause damage by: * mechanical effects * introduction of infection * reacting with the intraocular tissues Anteroposterior and lateral view X-rays are recommended for locating an IOFB as most foreign bodies are radio-opaque. Ultrasonographic localization can tell the position of even non-radiopaque foreign bodies. CT scan is the best method of IOFB localization. MRI is contraindicated for metallic IOFB.MRI can be detrimental for a patient with a history of an intraocular foreign body (IOFB) after cutting stone with a hammer and chisel. It can cause further damage by producing movements of the foreign body if it is magnetic. The use of MRI is contraindicated for metallic (iron) foreign bodies and is not recommended as a screening procedure. Management: A foreign body should always be removed unless: * it is inert and probably sterile * little damage has been done to vision  * the process of removal will destroy sight   Siderosis bulbi refers to the ocular degenerative changes produced by an iron foreign body. It usually occurs 2 months to 2 years after the injury. This condition is due to the electrolytic dissociation of the metal by an intrinsic resting current in the eye which disseminates the metal, combining it with cellular proteins and cause atrophy. Clinical features: * Iris: first stained greenish and later turns reddish-brown, causing heterochromia iridis. * Pupil: iron deposition in sphincter leads to mydriasis. * Lens: iron deposition in a radial fashion on the anterior capsule of the lens, leading to anterior capsular cataract. * Retina: pigmentary retinopathy; followed by atrophy of the retina and retinal pigmentary epithelium. * Secondary open-angle Glaucoma: due to damage to the trabecular meshwork.

Giant papillary conjunctivitis is a severe form of mechanically induced papillary conjunctivitis. It is most commonly associated with contact lens wear. It can also be associated with ocular prostheses, exposed sutures, and scleral buckles. The patients usually present with redness, foreign body sensation, increased mucus production, itching, blurring, and loss of contact lens tolerance. On examination, giant papillae are seen on the upper tarsal conjunctiva with hyperemia. Focal apical ulceration and whitish scarring may develop on larger papillae. Papillae are reddish, flat-topped raised areas that give a red and velvety appearance to the tarsal conjunctiva These are the hyperplasia of the normal vascular system with glomerulus-like bunches of capillaries growing into the epithelium. The image below shows papillae in the tarsal conjunctiva. Treatment includes removing the offending cause. Mast cell stabilizers such as sodium cromoglycate, and drugs like azelastine and olopatadine which have combined antihistamine and mast cell stabilizing effects are effective. Steroids can be used for resistant cases. Other options: Option A - Trachoma is caused by chlamydia trachomatis. In acute trachoma, sago grain follicles are characteristically seen as shown below. Option B - Follicular conjunctivitis has follicles which are greyish-white raised areas seen on fornices and palpebral conjunctiva. These are formed due to localized aggregations of lymphocytes in the sub-epithelial adenoid layer. It is most commonly caused by herpes and adenoviruses. The image is shown below. Option D - In spring catarrh (vernal catarrh), cobblestone appearance is a papillary reaction in the palpebral conjunctiva, ropy discharge, and Maxwell–Lyon sign are present. Horner-Tranta’s spots which are discrete whitish raised dots along the limbus can also be seen. It is more common during summer. Image showing Horner-Tranta’s spots. text: 1. The SAFE strategy given by WHO forms the mainstay of the management of trachoma. What does the S in this acronym represent?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Surgery

The S in the acronym stands for surgery. Trachoma is treated according to the WHO classification using the SAFEstrategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial hygiene, and Environmental improvement). Azithromycin is the antibiotic of choice, and surgery involves the correction of trichiasis and entropion. In case of significant corneal scarring, penetrating keratoplasty is done. Trachoma is a form of chronic infective conjunctivitis and is one of the leading causes of blindness. It is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, more specifically the TRIC (trachoma inclusion conjunctivitis) serovars A, B, Ba, C. It has an ‘active’ inflammatory stage and a ‘cicatricial’ chronic stage. The active inflammatory stage is more prevalent in children and presents with nonspecific symptoms of ocular irritation, foreign body sensation, and discharge (often mild symptoms). Examination findings at this stage show:  * Conjunctival follicles contain Leber cells (multinucleated lymphocytes) * Corneal Herbert's follicles (similar to conjunctival follicles) The cicatricial chronic stage is seen in middle age. The patient complains of pain, lacrimation, photophobia and later blurring, and finally loss of vision. Conjunctiva shows concretions (whitish deposits of inspissated mucus in depressions called glands of Henle). Corneal signs include:  * Herbert pits (pitted scars in the limbal which are remnants of healed Herbert follicles) * Corneal opacity is seen in later stages. The below image shows Herbert's pits. There can be associated trichiasis ( when at least one eyelash rubs the eyeball) and entropion. At present WHO grading with `FISTO’ is in use. text: 3. 3 months following cataract surgery, a patient comes with complaints of decreased visual acuity. On examination, posterior capsular opacification is seen. What type of laser can be used to treat this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Nd-Yag laser

The given history mentions decreased visual acuity 3 months post-cataract surgery and the presence of posterior capsular opacification is suggestive of after-cataract. A posterior capsulotomy (creating a hole in the posterior capsule) using an Nd: YAG laser is the mainstay of treatment. Posterior capsular opacification, otherwise known as after cataract/secondary cataract, is the most common late complication of uncomplicated cataract surgery. It occurs due to the proliferation of lens epithelial cells that have been left out inside the capsular bag after cataract surgery. The rate of posterior capsule opacification following extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE) and phacoemulsification varies with the age of the patient, the surgeon, the surgical technique, the type of intraocular lens used, and the duration after surgery. Symptoms of after cataract include: * Reduction of visual acuity * Slowly worsening blurring * Glare and occasionally monocular diplopia They can present in different patterns such as: * Elschnig's pearls: present as vacuolated (pearl-type) grape-like clusters of swollen cells  * Soemmering's ring: present as a white annular proliferation that is formed at the periphery of the capsular bag. * Fibrosis type: present as fibroblastic metaplasia of the epithelial cells Treatment: * Nd-YAG laser capsulotomy: The laser used in posterior capsulotomy is Nd: YAG laser (1064 nm) whose principle is photodisruption. The plasma produced at the laser target expands and disrupts the tissues creating an opening. * Surgical treatment: Posterior capsular opacification is managed by creating an opening on the posterior capsule along the visual axis, a procedure called a posterior capsulotomy. text: 4. A 68-year-old female patient has had a diabetic cataract for the past 3 months. Accumulation of which of the following substances is responsible for this?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Sorbitol + fructose

A diabetic cataract occurs due to the accumulation of sorbitol and fructose within the lens. In diabetic patients, increased levels of blood glucose lead to high levels of glucose in the aqueous humor. The excess glucose in the aqueous humor is metabolized into sorbitol through the polyol pathway by the enzyme aldose reductase. Sorbitol is then converted to fructose by sorbitol dehydrogenase but at a much slower rate. In addition, the polar nature of sorbitol prevents its intracellular removal through diffusion. Sorbitol and fructose accumulate in the lens and the osmotic stress so produced results in overhydration, hydropic lens fibers, and apoptosis of the lens epithelial cells. Thus, the secondary osmotic overhydration is responsible for cortical opacities in a distinct pattern causing snowflake cataracts as shown below. text: 5. Which of the following is the yoke muscle of the right lateral rectus?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Left medial rectus

The right lateral rectus and left medial rectus represent a pair of yoke muscles. Yoke muscles are also known as contralateral synergists. They are pair of muscles, one from each eye, which contracts simultaneously during version movements. Version movements also known as conjugate movements are synchronous (simultaneous) symmetric movements of both eyes in the same direction. Examples: * Right MR and Left LR * Right LR and Left MR * Right SO and Left IR * Right IO and Left SR * Right SR and Left IO * Right IR and Left SO (MR: Medial rectus; LR: Lateral rectus; SO: Superior oblique; IO: Inferior oblique; SR: Superior rectus; IR: Inferior rectus.) These pairs of contralateral synergists receive equal and simultaneous innervation during version movements according to Herring’s Law of Equal Innervation. text: 8. A patient who presents to the OPD has a visual field defect as shown below. What is the probable site of the lesion based on the image displayed?
expl:
Correct answer: A. 3

The visual field defect in the image is indicative of bitemporal hemianopia, so the probable site of the lesion is the optic chiasma marked as 3 in the image given.  Options marked in the image are: 1. Left optic nerve  3. Otic chiasma 4. Left optic tract  5. Left lateral geniculate nucleus Hemianopia or hemianopsia refers to loss of sight in half the visual field. Bitemporal hemianopia refers to loss of sight in the temporal halves of the visual field, seen in lesions affecting the optic chiasma. The most common cause of this is pituitary gland tumours. Other causes include suprasellar aneurysms, chronic arachnoiditis, and suprasellar tumours like craniopharyngioma and suprasellar meningioma. Damage to the middle part of the optic chiasm affects fibres crossing at the nasal retina of each eye, leaving the uncrossed fibres from the temporal retinas intact. The resulting loss of vision is confined to the temporal visual field of each eye and this is known as bitemporal hemianopia. It is also called heteronymous hemianopia to emphasize the fact that the parts of the visual field that are lost in each eye do not overlap. Individuals with this condition are able to see in both left and right central visual fields, with both eyes open. However, all information from the most peripheral parts of visual fields (which are seen only by the nasal retinas) is lost. Pearl PF1675: Lesions in the optic pathway Transection of the pathways at the locations indicated by the letters causes the visual field defects shown in the diagram above. * The fibers from the nasal half of each retina decussate in the optic chiasm, so that the fibers in the optic tracts are those from the temporal half of one retina and the nasal half of the other. * A lesion that interrupts the optic nerve causes blindness in that eye. * Lesions affecting the optic chiasma destroy fibers from both nasal hemiretinas and produce a heteronymous (opposite sides of the visual fields) hemianopia. * A lesion in one optic tract causes blindness in half of the visual field and is called homonymous (same side of both visual fields) hemianopia (half-blindness). * Occipital lesions may spare the fibers from the macula because of the separation in the brain of these fibers from the other subserving vision.

text: 9. An 3-year old child is having amblyopia in right eye. What is the preferred treatment for this child?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Occlusion therapy

The treatment of amblyopia in this child is by occlusion of the normal eye, in this case, the left eye.  Amblyopia or 'lazy eye' is a developmental defect of spatial visual processing that occurs in the central visual pathways of the eye. It is reversible if treated appropriately at the right time during the development phase(0-8 years of age) but is most commonly seen in the first 3 years of life. It is a condition with unilateral or bilateral subnormal vision without any local abnormality in the eye. It is most commonly associated with comitant squint and can be due to retinal defects, strabismus, high anisometropia with aniseikonia(a difference in the retinal image size between the two eyes). Amblyopic eyes have a characteristic vision which has: * The crowding phenomenon where single letter vision is better than when presented in a row. * A drop in visual acuity when viewed through grey neutral density filters * Decreased recognition, contrast sensitivity, spatial localization, saccadic amplitudes, and pursuit eye movements. Treatment includes occluding the normal eye for 6-12 weeks. If there is a vision problem with an underlying cause then that should be corrected initially. The brain uses the stronger eye to perceive images and hence the brain has to be trained and forced to use the amblyopic or lazy eye by occluding the normal eye. By occluding the normal eye, the amblyopic eye gets stimulated and gets corrected. Occlusion should be total and should be changed when it is dirty or loose. In children less than 8 years the occlusion has to be done in a way so that constant occlusion of the normal eye does not make it amblyopic too. It is done corresponding to the child's age (x) at a ratio of x:1. e.g if the child is 5 years old then the normal eye is occluded for 5 days and removed while only the amblyopic eye is occluded on the 6th day. It is continued in a similar fashion for 6-12 weeks.  In infants, part-time occlusion (a few hours a day) is done while in children above 8 years, constant occlusion is advised. However, the underlying cause of amblyopia should also be corrected for complete resolution.

text: 10. A 3-year-old boy has been observed by his parents to be increasingly clumsy for the past 6 months. On physical examination, there is a cauliflower-like growth in the left eye along with leukocoria and an absent red reflex. The microscopic appearance of the specimen shows Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. Which is the causative gene in the given condition?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Rb gene

The clinical history of a boy presenting with progressive clumsiness and eye findings such as leucocoria, absent red reflex, and cauliflower like growth along with the microscopic finding of Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes is highly suggestive of retinoblastoma, which occurs due to a mutation in the Rb gene located on chromosome 13q14. Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy in children. White pupillary reflex or leukocoria is the most common presenting feature, followed by a squint which is usually convergent. Rarely, the child may present with nystagmus and defective vision. Clinical features of retinoblastoma: * Present within the first two years of life * Leukocoria  * Strabismus * Painful red eye with secondary glaucoma * Orbital inflammation mimicking orbital or pre-septal cellulitis. * Orbital invasion or visible extraocular growth may occur in neglected cases. * Metastatic disease involving regional lymph nodes and the brain before the detection of ocular involvement is rare. Signs: * An intraretinal tumor is a homogeneous, dome-shaped white lesion that becomes irregular, often with white flecks of calcification. * An endophytic tumor projects into the vitreous as a white mass that may "seed" into the gel. * An exophytic tumor forms multilobular subretinal white masses and causes an overlying retinal detachment. Investigations: * Red reflex testing with a direct ophthalmoscope is a simple screening test for leukocoria. * Dilated fundus examination using indirect ophthalmoscope * MRI of the orbit + brain is the investigation of choice.  The HPE image below shows Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes, the clustering of small blue cuboidal or short columnar cells around a central lumen. Treatment typically involves chemotherapy plus focal therapy. The commonly used three-drug regimen is the CVE regimen consisting of vincristine, carboplatin, and etoposide. Focal therapy includes cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, thermotherapy, plaque radiotherapy, and external beam radiotherapy. Enucleation is done when:  * Tumor involves more than half of the retina * Optic nerve is involved * Glaucoma is present and the anterior chamber is involved In the stage of extraocular extension, the globe bursts through the sclera, usually near the limbus or the optic disc. This is followed by rapid fungation and involvement of extraocular tissues resulting in marked proptosis. Distant metastasis occurs through the lymphatic spread and the direct extension by continuity to the optic nerve and brain. Other options: Option B: COL5A1 mutation affects type 5 collagen. This mutation is seen in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Option C: Retinitis pigmentosa occurs due to inherited or acquired mutations in the rhodopsin gene.  Option D: NOTCH1 is the most commonly affected gene in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). text: 11. A 70-year-old patient who was using presbyopic glasses for the past few years is now able to comfortably read the newspaper without the glasses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Index myopia

The clinical scenario of improvement in near vision of a presbyopic patient is termed the second sight phenomenon. This is seen due to index myopia caused by the formation of nuclear cataracts. Presbyopia, also known as the eyesight of old age, is a condition of physiological insufficiency of accommodation leading to a progressive fall in near vision. The treatment of presbyopia is the prescription of appropriate convex glasses for near work. In nuclear cataracts, nuclear sclerosis occurs leading to an increase in refractive index. This leads to progressive myopia known as index myopia. When a presbyopic patient develops a nuclear cataract, this increase in the refractive index of the lens compensates for the physiological insufficiency of accommodation that the patient has. Thus, a patient with presbyopia may be able to read again, without the aid of spectacles due to this improvement in near vision, termed second sight. At the same time, this increased refractive index causes a deterioration in far vision. Option B: Index hypermetropia occurs in cortical cataracts and sclerosis that lead to a decrease in the refractive index of the lens in old age. In such patients, there will be worsening of the near vision which does not align with the history of a presbyopic being able to read with his glasses. Option C: Presbyopia occurs due to a decrease in the accommodative power of the crystalline lens with increasing age, and thus does not regress spontaneously. It can however be easily corrected with the prescription of appropriate convex glasses for near work.

text: 12. A patient presents to you with pain and redness in the right eye following an injury during welding. On examination, the image as seen below is observed. Which of the following is the appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Removal by 26G needle

A history of injury to the eye while welding along with the the given image is suggestive of a superficial foreign body in the eye. Removal of the foreign body using a 26G needle is the next step in the management of this patient. Foreign bodies, which are usually small particles of dust, iron, steel, etc., may impinge upon the conjunctiva or cornea and cause sudden discomfort and reflex blinking. The foreign body sticks to the palpebral conjunctiva and is liable to be dragged across the cornea, causing excoriation. Particles of steel and iron fly straight onto the cornea and penetrate the epithelium or substantia propria. Fluorescein or oblique illumination of the anesthetized eye with a slit lamp can be used to determine the position of a foreign body. If not removed, they expose the cornea to organisms in the conjunctival sac causing ulceration and extrusion of the foreign body in the slough. The ulcer thus formed may heal, but if virulent organisms are present, a spreading ulcer, with or without hypopyon, may develop. Foreign bodies are managed by removal as soon as possible.  * If the foreign body is found lying loose in either fornix, it can be removed with a clean swab after everting the eyelids. * Double-eversion of the upper eyelid with a Desmarres retractor can be done if required. * If embedded in the bulbar conjunctiva or cornea, it can be removed by a foreign body spud or fine forceps under topical anesthesia. * A disposable hypodermic (26 or 27 gauge) needle can be used. Following removal in all cases, an antibiotic ointment should be applied and the eye kept bandaged for a day. Foreign bodies in the eye are extremely common in industrial workers, especially in those working with grinding tools, lathe work, or hammering on a chisel, and thus eye must be protected by educative notices, lectures, and the provision of comfortable goggles. Cases of ferruginous intraocular foreign bodies (IOFB) may give rise to anterior capsular cataracts and reddish-brown staining of the iris leading to heterochromia iridis. MRI is contraindicated here and instead, CT with axial and coronal cuts is used to localize a metallic IOFB. Magnetic removal is done for the removal of ferrous foreign bodies.

text: 4. What is the most common cause of childhood blindness?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin A deficiency

The most common cause of preventable childhood blindness is vitamin A deficiency. The most common cause of blindness in adults, is however, cataract. Vitamin A deficiency is a major cause of childhood blindness, particularly in developing countries. Lack of sufficient vitamin A can lead to conditions like xerophthalmia, which includes night blindness and can progress to more severe forms, ultimately causing irreversible damage to the cornea and leading to blindness.  Other options: (a) Refractive error: Refractive errors, such as myopia (nearsightedness), hyperopia (farsightedness), and astigmatism, can cause vision problems, but they are usually correctable with glasses or contact lenses. While it can lead to vision impairment or blindness in severe cases, it is not as prevalent as vitamin A deficiency, especially on a global scale.  (d) Injuries: While injuries can certainly lead to vision impairment or blindness in children, they are not as prevalent on a population level as vitamin A deficiency.

text: 6. A patient presents to the outpatient department with complete anopia in the right eye. The lesion would be present in which specific anatomical structure?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Right optic nerve

The most likely site of the lesion causing unilateral complete anopia in the right eye is (c) Right optic nerve. This suggests that there is a problem affecting the visual information from the right eye before the optic chiasma. Unilateral complete anopia refers to complete blindness in one eye. To determine the location of the lesion, we need to understand the visual pathway: Right optic radiation: The optic radiation transmits visual information from the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) to the visual cortex in the occipital lobe. Lesions in the optic radiation typically lead to homonymous visual field defects (loss of vision on the same side in both eyes). Since the patient presents with unilateral anopia in the right eye, the optic radiation is less likely to be the site of the lesion. Optic chiasma: The optic chiasma is where the optic nerves partially cross. Lesions at the optic chiasma often result in bitemporal hemianopia, affecting the temporal visual fields of both eyes. Given that the patient's symptoms are unilateral, the optic chiasma is less likely to be the site of the lesion. Right optic nerve: The optic nerve carries visual information from the eye to the optic chiasma. A lesion in the right optic nerve would lead to unilateral blindness (anopia) in the right eye, making it a likely site of the lesion in this case. Right optic tract: The optic tract carries visual information from the optic chiasma to the visual cortex. Lesions in the optic tract could lead to homonymous visual field defects. Since the patient's anopia is unilateral, the right optic tract is less likely to be the site of the lesion. Pearl PF1675: Lesions in the optic pathway Transection of the pathways at the locations indicated by the letters causes the visual field defects shown in the diagram above. * The fibers from the nasal half of each retina decussate in the optic chiasm, so that the fibers in the optic tracts are those from the temporal half of one retina and the nasal half of the other. * A lesion that interrupts the optic nerve causes blindness in that eye. * Lesions affecting the optic chiasma destroy fibers from both nasal hemiretinas and produce a heteronymous (opposite sides of the visual fields) hemianopia. * A lesion in one optic tract causes blindness in half of the visual field and is called homonymous (same side of both visual fields) hemianopia (half-blindness). * Occipital lesions may spare the fibers from the macula because of the separation in the brain of these fibers from the other subserving vision.

text: 10. An 18-month-old child visited the ophthalmologist exhibiting a white eye reflex, and ultrasonography revealed an intraocular mass with calcifications. text: 2. A patient with a history of diabetes presents with cataract. Which of the following metabolic products is primarily responsible for cataract formation?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Sorbitol

A diabetic cataract occurs due to the accumulation of sorbitol within the lens. In diabetic patients, increased levels of blood glucose lead to high levels of glucose in the aqueous humor. Sorbitol is then converted to fructose (option B) by sorbitol dehydrogenase but at a much slower rate. In addition, the polar nature of sorbitol prevents its intracellular removal through diffusion. Sorbitol and fructose accumulate in the lens and the osmotic stress so produced results in overhydration, hydropic lens fibers, and apoptosis of the lens epithelial cells. text: 3. A patient presents with right-sided visual field defects in both eyes while central vision remains unaffected. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

Visual field defect involving the right sides of each eye with central vision preserved is called bilateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. It occurs in lesions of the occipital lobe. Homonymous hemianopia (HH) involves loss of vision on the same side of the visual field in both eyes. HH is characteristically seen in lesions involving the visual pathway posterior to the optic chiasma. Lesions involving occipital lobe usually shows macular sparing because macular representation is seperate and quite large as compared to peripheral vision. Moreover, macular area in occipital lobe is supplied both by posterior and middle cerebral artery. In case of vascular lesions (eg stroke) affecting occipital lobe, it is less likely to involve both these arteries. HH may be either complete or incomplete.  * A complete HH is characterised by loss of entire hemifield on the same side in both eyes. * An incomplete HH is characterised by partial loss of visual field on the same side in both eyes. Incomplete HH is further classified as congruous or incongruous, depending on whether the extent of partial loss of visual field in both the eyes is same or different, respectively. Option C: Damage to the middle part of the optic chiasm affects fibres crossing at the nasal retina of each eye, leaving the uncrossed fibres from the temporal retinas intact.
