text: 4. A patient came to the hospital with complaints of breathlessness and is diagnosed with a Pancoast tumor. Which of the following findings is not typically associated with this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Exophthalmus

Pancoast syndrome is associated with Horner's syndrome, resulting in ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis. It is not associated with exophthalmus. Horner syndrome occurs when the sympathetic nerves serving the head, eye, or neck are damaged at any point along their pathway. It is also referred to as oculosympathetic paresis. Clinical features include: * Ptosis - usually due to weakness of Muller’s muscle (Option D). * Miosis - due to unopposed action of sphincter pupillae leading to anisocoria (Option C).  * Anhidrosis - reduced ipsilateral sweating (Option B). * Heterochromia iridis- seen in congenital and long-standing disease. The affected eye is lighter in color.  * Anisocoria that is accentuated in dim light * Enophthalmus Pancoast syndrome  is also called a superior sulcus tumor. It develops when a tumor located at the apex of the lung extends locally. Local extension involves the C8 - T2 nerve roots. It presents with pain that radiates to the ulnar distribution of the arm, often with the destruction of the 1st and 2nd ribs. Patients with the central or endobronchial growth of the primary tumor may present with a cough, hemoptysis, wheeze, stridor, dyspnea, or post-obstructive pneumonitis. Regional spread of the tumor can cause: * Tracheal obstruction, esophageal compression with dysphagia * Recurrent laryngeal paralysis with hoarseness * Phrenic nerve palsy with the elevation of the hemidiaphragm and dyspnea * Sympathetic nerve paralysis with Horner’s syndrome (enophthalmos, ptosis, miosis, and anhydrosis). The below images show chest X-ray and management of the Pancoast tumor. Pearl PF1717: Horner's syndrome Horner's Syndrome: Horner's syndrome occurring due to occulo-sympathetic paresis is characterized by the classic triad of: * Mild ptosis (due to paralysis of Muller's muscle). * Miosis (due to paralysis of dilator pupillae). * Reduced ipsilateral sweating (anhydrosis). Other features include: * Mild enophthalmos, * Loss of cilio-spinal reflex, * Heterochromia, i.e., the ipsilateral iris is lighter in colour, * Pupil is slow to dilate, and there occurs slight elevation of lower eyelid. Cocaine test (2% to 4%): Small pupils fail to dilate in Horner's syndrome. In congenital Horner's syndrome, the additional features seen are heterochromia iridis and unilateral straight hair.

text: 7. A patient has a history of a flying foreign body injury to the eye. After 8 weeks, heterochromia iridis is noted. Which of the following substances is most likely involved in the deposition?

It usually occurs 2 months to 2 years after the injury. This condition is due to the electrolytic dissociation of the metal by an intrinsic resting current in the eye which disseminates the metal, combining it with cellular proteins and causing atrophy. It occurs due to the accumulation of dye in the macular region. CME is defined as a collection of fluid between the outer plexiform (Henle's layer) and an inner nuclear layer of the retina. This results in the formation of cyst-like cavities around the foveola. It occurs due to a break in the inner and outer blood-retinal barrier.  Common causes of CME include uveitis, previous cataract surgery (Irvine-Gass syndrome), retinal vein occlusions, diabetic retinopathy, and retinitis pigmentosa. Irvine-Gass syndrome is the late postoperative complications of cataract surgery. The characteristic flower-petal appearance is due to the accumulation of dye in the outer plexiform layer at the fovea. CME occurs due to a break in the inner and outer blood-retinal barrier. Patients may complain of blurring, distortion, and micropsia. In clinically established cases, the macula will show a 'honeycomb' appearance on ophthalmoscopy due to multiple cystoid spaces. text: 9. The cover-uncover test is performed to diagnose various eye conditions. Which of the following is not detected by this test?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Amblyopia

The cover-uncover test cannot detect Amblyopia. This test consists of two parts: * Cover test * Uncover test Cover Test: This is used to detect heterotropia (Manifest Squint) (Option B). Light is first shone and corneal reflections are observed. This is done to assess fixation in the deviating eye. The procedure for testing using an accommodative target and for distance is as follows. * The patient is asked to fixate on a target straight ahead. * The eye in which deviation is not suspected is covered first. For example, if a right eye deviation is suspected, the left eye is covered. * Any movement of the right eye to take up fixation is noted. * The following are the possible results:
Movement of the eye Suspected defect
No movements Orthotropia/ Heterotropia of the covered eye
Adduction Exotropia
Abduction Esotropia
Downward movement Hypertropia
Upward movement Hypotropia
The test is then repeated for the opposite eye. Uncover test: This is used to detect heterophoria (latent squint)(Option A). The test is performed for both near and distant as follows. * The patient fixates a distant target straight ahead. * The examiner covers an eye for 2-3 seconds and the cover is then removed. * If the covered eye had deviated, a re-fixation movement is observed on being uncovered. * The following are the possible results based on the re-fixation movements of the eye.
Movement of the eye Suspected defect
No movements Orthophoria
Adduction (Nasal recovery) Exophoria
Abduction Esophoria
Downward/Upward movement Vertical phoria
* The speed and smoothness of the recovery is noted as well as evidence of the strength of motor fusion. * The test is then repeated for the opposite eye. Other options: Option C: Amblyopia is a developmental defect of spatial visual processing that occurs in the central visual pathways of the eye.  Generally, a difference of two lines or more on an eye chart test of visual acuity between the two eyes or a best-corrected vision of 20/30 or worse would be defined as amblyopia. Treatment modalities include: * Occlusion of the normal eye (4 to 6 hours/ day) using patches. It allows an amblyopic eye to be used. * Penalization: Blurring of vision using atropine. Instilling atropine into the fixing eye, forces the squinting eye to be used for seeing near objects. Pearl PF1402: Cover tests in ophthalmology Cover–uncover test: * To detect the presence of heterophoria: Latent squint * One eye is covered with the occluder, and the other eye is made to fix an object. * In the presence of heterophoria, the eye under the cover will deviate. * When the cover is removed, the eye under the cover will return back to its normal. * This movement is observed. * The direction of movement determines the type of heterophoria. Direct Cover test: * Confirms the presence of manifest squint. * Differentiates apparent squint from a manifest squint. * The patient is asked to fixate on the point light. * The normal-looking eye is covered. * In manifest squint, the uncovered eye will move in the opposite direction to take fixation. * In apparent squint, there will be no movement of the uncovered eye. Alternate cover test: * In the below image, the patient has right exotropia with left eye fixating. * Both eyes move each time the cover alternates from one eye to the other. * It reveals if the squint is unilateral or alternate. * It differentiates between concomitant and paralytic squint.

text: 10. A 3-year-old child presents with epiphora and probing reveals a soft block at 7 mm. What is the best treatment option for this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Conjunctival Dacryocystorhinostomy

A soft stop 5–8 mm from the punctum implies a canalicular obstruction. Conjunctival Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) is the management of choice for proximal canalicular obstruction at 7mm. If present more than 8 mm from the punctum, the obstruction is probably at the common canaliculus. The canalicular obstruction is divided as proximal (<8 mm from puncta) and distal (>8 mm from puncta).It can be congenital or acquired. Acquired causes are post-traumatic, repeated syringing or chronic inflammation/infection of the system. It may follow prolonged use of idoxuridine. Conjunctival DCR (Jones procedure) creates a bypass between the conjunctival fornix and nasal cavity using a Pyrex or silicone tube. The procedure involves creating a fistula through the lacrimal bone, bypassing the blocked canalicular system entirely. The tube is placed from conjunctiva to nose, secured with sutures, and typically left in place for 3-6 months. It has a success rate of around 80% in properly selected cases. The main advantage is its ability to create an alternative drainage pathway when the proximal lacrimal system is non-functional or absent. This procedure is specifically indicated for: * Canalicular obstruction * Failed standard DCR * Cases with extensive canalicular damage * Congenital absence of canaliculi The given set of instruments is used for dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) Other Options: Option B: External DCR: An osteotomy is created between the lacrimal sac and nasal cavity through an external skin incision. While effective for nasolacrimal duct obstruction, it cannot address canalicular blocks at 7mm. Option C: Endonasal DCR: Creates similar bypass as external DCR but through nasal approach. Not suitable for proximal canalicular system problems as it only addresses distal obstruction. Option D: Dacryocystectomy: Complete removal of lacrimal sac. Too radical for this case and eliminates possibility of future reconstructive procedures. Only indicated in chronic dacryocystitis with mucocele or tumor.

The most useful projection for detecting an orbital floor fracture is Water’s view. An orbital blow-out fracture is an isolated fracture of the orbital floor when a large blunt object strikes the globe is called blow out fracture. The orbital contents herniate through the antrum. Clinical signs are periocular swelling (early stage), enophthalmos, ecchymosis and subconjunctival haemorrhage (later stages). Initial treatment consists of observation, oral antibiotics, ice packs, and nasal decongestants. Indications for surgery in a blowout fracture include diplopia not resolving significantly in the early days after trauma, a fracture with a large herniation of tissues into the antrum, incarceration of tissues in the fracture, resulting in globe retraction and increased applanation tension on attempted upward gaze and enophthalmos. If any of these conditions are present, surgical correction is required within 2 weeks. The below-given X-ray image in the Water's view shows a 'tear-drop' sign The optimal time for surgery following a blow-out fracture is 10–14 days. Indications for surgery in a "blow-out" fracture are as follows: * Diplopia not resolving significantly in the early days after trauma * A fracture with a large herniation of tissues into the antrum * Incarceration of tissues in the fracture, resulting in  globe  retraction and increased applanation tension on attempted upward gaze * Enophthalmos greater than 2 mm   Other options: Option A: Panda sign: A radiological finding in sarcoidosis showing bilateral symmetrical uptake in the lacrimal and parotid glands on gallium scan, creating an appearance resembling a panda's face. Option B: Dalrymple’s sign is the commonest and earliest sign of Grave's ophthalmopathy. It is due to overactivity of levator aponeurosis and Müller's muscle. Here the upper lid margin is at level with or above the superior limbus, causing the upper sclera to become visible (scleral show). Option C: Munson's sign is seen in keratoconus. text: 13. A patient presents with non-pulsatile proptosis that increases when bending down. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Orbital varices

This patient with non-pulsatile propotosis that increases on bending down most likely has orbital varices. Orbital varices: * They are venous malformations of the orbit caused by vascular dysgenesis. * Patients usually present with non-pulsatile, intermittent, and reducible proptosis. * On activities such as forward bending or lowering of the head, turning the head forcefully, hyperextension of the neck, and coughing, the varices fill up, causing proptosis, and then, they regress on shifting to a non-dependent position. Treatment: * Small lesions generally do not require treatment * Surgical excision is technically difficult and often incomplete because the lesions are friable and bleed easily; Specialized techniques such as embolization and carbon dioxide laser surgery may be helpful. Other options: Option A: Thyroid eye disease (TED) is the most common cause of both bilateral and unilateral proptosis in an adult in the euthyroid state. The main features of TED include lid retraction, proptosis, periorbital edema, chemosis, and restrictive myopathy. Option C:  In cavernous sinus thrombosis, proptosis is initially unilateral but soon becomes bilateral due to the spread of infection to the contralateral sinus through the intercavernous communication. Also, cavernous sinus thrombosis presents with high-grade fever with chills, rigor, and headache.  Option D: Orbital cellulitis is the most common cause of unilateral proptosis in children. It refers to the acute infection of the contents of the orbit behind the orbital septum. Features include pain, lid edema, erythema, chemosis, and axial proptosis. Increased pain with movement of eyes and ophthalmoplegia (decreased ocular motility) is a classic symptom.

text: 14. What is the accommodative amplitude of a patient with a near point at 20 cm and a far point at infinity?
expl:
Correct answer: A. 5 D

The amplitude of accommodation for the above patient would be 5 dioptres. Near point of accommodation (NPA) is the closest distance at which the near object is clearly focussed without blur. Amplitude of accommodation is the maximum power of the lens that permits clear near vision without blur. Its unit is dioptre (D). The amplitude of accommodation is the reciprocal of near point of accommodation (NPA) in meters. 20 cm is 1/5th of a metre. Therefore, the accommodative amplitude is its inverse, that is, 5D. Note: The NPA is measured clinically using a scale device such as the Prince, Berens, or Royal Air Force (RAF) ruler.

text: 1. A patient presents with right-sided visual field defects in both eyes while central vision remains unaffected. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

Visual field defect involving the right sides of each eye with central vision preserved is called bilateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. It occurs in lesions of the occipital lobe. Homonymous hemianopia (HH) involves loss of vision on the same side of the visual field in both eyes. HH is characteristically seen in lesions involving the visual pathway posterior to the optic chiasma. Lesions involving occipital lobe usually shows macular sparing because macular representation is seperate and quite large as compared to peripheral vision. Moreover, macular area in occipital lobe is supplied both by posterior and middle cerebral artery. In case of vascular lesions (eg stroke) affecting occipital lobe, it is less likely to involve both these arteries. HH may be either complete or incomplete.  * A complete HH is characterised by loss of entire hemifield on the same side in both eyes. * An incomplete HH is characterised by partial loss of visual field on the same side in both eyes. Incomplete HH is further classified as congruous or incongruous, depending on whether the extent of partial loss of visual field in both the eyes is same or different, respectively. Other Options: Option A: Optic Chiasm Lesion: Bitemporal hemianopia refers to loss of sight in the temporal halves of the visual field, seen in lesions affecting the optic chiasma.  Option B: Optic Tract Lesion : Lesions at the occipital lobe, optic tract and optic radiation would all cause homonymous hemianopia, but macular sparing will occur in the setting of optic lobe damage. Option C: Damage to the middle part of the optic chiasm affects fibres crossing at the nasal retina of each eye, leaving the uncrossed fibres from the temporal retinas intact. The resulting loss of vision is confined to the temporal visual field of each eye and this is known as bitemporal hemianopia. It is also called heteronymous hemianopia. Pearl PF1675: Lesions in the optic pathway Transection of the pathways at the locations indicated by the letters causes the visual field defects shown in the diagram above. * The fibers from the nasal half of each retina decussate in the optic chiasm, so that the fibers in the optic tracts are those from the temporal half of one retina and the nasal half of the other. * A lesion that interrupts the optic nerve causes blindness in that eye. * Lesions affecting the optic chiasma destroy fibers from both nasal hemiretinas and produce a heteronymous (opposite sides of the visual fields) hemianopia. * A lesion in one optic tract causes blindness in half of the visual field and is called homonymous (same side of both visual fields) hemianopia (half-blindness). * Occipital lesions may spare the fibers from the macula because of the separation in the brain of these fibers from the other subserving vision.

text: 4. Which of the following cataract surgery prefers suturing with nylon 10-0?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Extracapsular cataract extraction

Suturing with nylon 10-0 is preferred in extracapsular cataract extraction. In ECCE, a portion of the anterior capsule of the lens is removed, allowing extraction of the lens nucleus and cortex. This leaves the remainder of the anterior capsule, the posterior capsule, and the zonular support intact. The intact lens nucleus is then removed from the eye through a limbal incision.  An anterior capsulotomy is followed by hydro dissection using a balanced salt solution. This helps to separate the corticonuclear mass from the capsule. Removal of lens nucleus and aspiration of the cortex is done using a two-way irrigation and aspiration cannula. An intraocular lens (IOL) is then implanted and the incision is then closed. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy, which can arise in people with long-term diabetes mellitus, is a common risk factor for vitreous haemorrhage caused by the breakage of the fragile blood vessels on the retina's surface. Intravitreal blood blocks light from reaching the retina, resulting in patients experiencing sudden onset cloudy vision, sometimes with a red tint, or vision loss.  Vitreous haemorrhage has a variable presentation depending on the severity of the haemorrhage. text: 4. A 50-year-old female presents with an acute painful red-eye. An image of her eye is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Acute angle-closure glaucoma

The clinical scenario and a red eye showing corneal edema and a mid-dilated and vertically oval pupil are suggestive of acute angle-closure glaucoma. The pupil is non-reactive to both light and accommodation. Acute primary angle-closure glaucoma refers to the occlusion of the trabecular meshwork by the peripheral iris (iridotrabecular contact [ITC]), obstructing aqueous outflow. It can be primary when it occurs in an anatomically predisposed eye or secondary to another ocular or systemic factor. Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an ocular emergency that causes acute red-eye and is associated with at least two of the following symptoms: * Acute onset ocular pain with nausea or vomiting * Intermittent blurring of vision with halos * Photophobia or * Loss of vision. It is also associated with at least three of the following signs: * Ciliary congestion * Corneal edema and subsequent haziness * Fixed and mid-dilated, usually oval pupil * Shallow anterior chamber * Intraocular pressure elevated above 40 mmHg. Immediate medical management mainly aims at lowering IOP using drugs such as oral acetazolamide or intravenous mannitol. The definitive treatment is laser peripheral iridotomy. This must be followed by prophylaxis of the fellow eye, long-term glaucoma surveillance and management of intraocular pressure in both eyes.

The large, 20–50 μm trophozoite form is distinguished by spine-like pseudopodia called acanthopodia. text: 4. Identify the defect shown in the image:
expl:
Correct answer: A. Herbert pits

The image shows tiny lesions at the limbus, indicating Herbert's pits. This finding is seen in trachoma, which is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, more specifically the trachoma inclusion conjunctivitis (TRIC) serovars A, B, Ba, and C.  Trachoma is a form of chronic infective conjunctivitis and is one of the leading causes of blindness. It has an ‘active’ inflammatory stage and a ‘cicatricial’ chronic stage. The active inflammatory stage is more prevalent in children and presents with nonspecific symptoms of ocular irritation, foreign body sensation, and discharge (often mild symptoms). Examination findings at this stage show: * Conjunctival follicles contain Leber cells (multinucleated lymphocytes) * Limbal Herbert's follicles (similar to conjunctival follicles) Cicatricial chronic stage is seen in middle age. And when the chronic infection with sequelae sets in, the patient complains of pain, lacrimation, photophobia, and later blurring, and finally loss of vision. The conjunctiva shows concretions (whitish deposits of inspissated mucus in depressions called glands of Henle). Corneal signs include: * Herbert pits (pitted scars in the limbal, which are remnants of healed Herbert follicles) * Corneal opacity is seen in later stages. There can be associated trichiasis (when at least one eyelash rubs the eyeball) and entropion. At present, WHO grading with 'FISTO' is in use. Trachoma is treated according to the WHO classification using the SAFE strategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial hygiene, and Environmental improvement). Azithromycin is the antibiotic of choice, and surgery involves the correction of trichiasis and entropion. In case of significant corneal scarring, penetrating keratoplasty is done. Other options: Option B: Horner–Trantas dots (image below) are distinct white, chalky, gelatinous nodules made up of eosinophils and epithelial debris that appear at the limbus, and they are characteristic of limbal vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC). Option C: In giant papillary conjunctivitis (GPC), gelatinous papillae initially appear as small, elevated nodules on the conjunctiva. These papillae eventually grow larger, forming macropapillae and giant papillae, and may be accompanied by Trantas dots at the limbus. The image below shows giant papillae in the conjunctiva: Option D: Progressive pannus in trachoma involves the infiltration of the cornea with new blood vessels developing in the upper part, lying between the epithelium and Bowman's membrane. As the condition advances, these superficial vessels contribute to the destruction of Bowman's membrane, with corneal infiltration occurring before significant vascularization.

text: 5. Identify the refractive error in the image below.
expl:
Correct answer: B. Regular astigmatism

The given figure is a Sturm's conoid, which is characteristically seen in regular astigmatism.  When light passes through a regularly astigmatic surface (surface with toric curvature), vertical and horizontal rays converge at different points. The distance between the points of convergence (focus) of the vertical and horizontal rays is called the focal interval of Sturm (distance between points B and F). The circle of least confusion/circle of diffusion lies at the midpoint of this interval. For the given Sturm's conoid,  * At point A, a horizontal oval is formed because vertical rays converge more rapidly than horizontal rays. * At point B, vertical rays come to a focus, while horizontal rays are still converging, so it will be a horizontal straight line. * At points C, D, and E, the vertical rays are diverging and horizontal rays are still converging. * At point D, the vertical rays have diverged as much as the horizontal rays have converged, so we get a perfect circle called the circle of least confusion. * At point E, a vertical oval is formed. * At point F, a vertical straight line is formed * At point G and beyond, both rays are diverging, and we always get a vertical oval/prolate ellipse. Astigmatism is a type of refractive error in which the eye does not focus light evenly on the retina. This results in a distorted or blurred vision. Other symptoms include eyestrain or asthenopia with headaches. Types: * Regular astigmatism: In this, refractive power changes uniformly from one meridian to another, resulting in 2 principal meridians * Irregular astigmatism: It is characterized by an irregular change of refractive power in different meridians, and hence it has multiple meridians. Types of regular astigmatism: * With the rule astigmatism: The vertical meridian is more curved than the horizontal meridian but they are placed at right angles to one another * Against-the-rule astigmatism: Here the horizontal meridian is more curved than the vertical meridian * Oblique astigmatism: Here, the two principal meridians are not the horizontal and vertical meridians, although they are at right angles to each other. It is a type of regular astigmatism. e.g., one may be at 45 degrees and the other at 135 degrees. * Bioblique astigmatism: Here, the two principal meridians are not at right angles to each other; for example, one may be at 40 degrees and the other at 100 degrees. It is also a type of regular astigmatism. Note: Refractive types of regular astigmatism: * Simple astigmatism: rays are focused on the retina in one meridian: either in front (simple myopic, as shown in the above image) of the retina or behind the retina (simple hyperopic) * Compound astigmatism: rays in both the meridians are focused in front or behind the retina * Mixed astigmatism: Light rays in one meridian are focused in front of the retina and those in the other meridian are focused behind the retina

Correct answer: A. Bitemporal hemianopia

The pituitary tumour compressing the optic chiasma results in bitemporal hemianopia. This occurs when damage to the middle part of the optic chiasm affects the crossing fibres from the nasal retina of each eye while the uncrossed fibres from the temporal retinas remain intact. As a result, individuals retain central vision but lose peripheral vision on the sides. The most common cause of bitemporal hemianopia is a pituitary adenoma. text: 7. A 65-year-old elderly diabetic female presents to the emergency department with complaints of a sudden onset of severe pain in one eye, marked redness, blurred vision, and headache. On examination, there is a hazy cornea with a mid-dilated and fixed pupil with a shallow anterior chamber. What is the likely diagnosis in this case?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Acute angle closure glaucoma

This is a case of acute angle-closure glaucoma, which typically presents with sudden onset of a painful red eye, corneal haze, a mid-dilated fixed pupil, and a shallow anterior chamber. Angle-closure glaucoma involves a sudden increase in intraocular pressure due to blockage of the anterior chamber angle. It is characterized by severe eye pain, blurred vision, and a mid-dilated pupil, with diffuse redness rather than the circumcorneal congestion seen in uveitis. It has constantly raised IOP >21mmHg, optic disc cupping, and visual field defects. The primary goal in managing Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (PACG) is to prevent optic nerve damage by reducing IOP. In acute attacks, treatment involves aggressively lowering IOP using intravenous mannitol and oral acetazolamide to quickly control symptoms. Topical medications such as pilocarpine, beta-blockers, cholinergic agents, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are also used to address the acute episode. Once the immediate crisis is managed, YAG laser iridotomy (YAG PI) is performed to create an alternate drainage pathway for the aqueous humor, both in the affected eye and the fellow eye. For ongoing management, patients with PACG may require glaucoma medications to maintain target IOP. In cases where maximal medical therapy fails, surgical options such as trabeculectomy or glaucoma drainage devices may be necessary, particularly if there is progressive visual field loss or non-compliance with treatment. Cyclodestructive procedures may be considered for patients with a painful, blind eye or those with recurrent surgical failures. Signs: Corneal edema- coloured halos Conjunctiva- congestion, chemosis IOP- elevated 40–70 mm Hg AC- very shallow Pupil- vertically oval, mid-dilated Angle- completely closed, Grade 0 Other options: Option B: Retinal detachment presents with painless, sudden loss of vision, photopsia (flashes), floaters, curtain falling sensation. No corneal haze or painful red eye. Option C: Open-angle glaucoma is chronic, asymptomatic until late. Gradual painless loss of peripheral vision (tunnel vision).No redness, no acute pain. Option D: Acute uveitis presents with painful red eye but typically has constricted pupil (miosis), not mid-dilated fixed. Aqueous flare, keratic precipitates may be seen. text: 8. A 15-year-old patient presents with a history of severe itching and recurrent eye. On examination, a shield ulcer is present, which has developed as a sequela of the underlying disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?

VKC, also known as spring catarrh or warm weather conjunctivitis, is a recurrent inflammation of the conjunctiva with seasonal incidence, commonly occurring in individuals with an atopic background and seasonal allergies due to Th2 lymphocyte alteration followed by IgE response. It is a Type I hypersensitivity reaction. Classical features of conjunctiva in VKC: Palpebral VKC * Cobblestone papillae: upper tarsal conjunctiva * Associated with ropy discharge * Maxwell–Lyon sign: pseudomembrane formation of the upper lid when everted and exposed to heat  * Limbal VKC: Horner–Trantas spots are white dots consisting of eosinophils and epithelial debris in the limbal area.  Corneal signs in VKC: * Shield ulcers * Vernal plaques * Subepithelial scarring * Pseudo-Gerontoxon resembles arcus senilis; it has a cupid's bow outline The condition presents in three types, which are : * Palpebral, affecting the upper tarsal conjunctiva, characterised by hypertrophied 'cobblestone' papillae * Bulbar-limbal, characterised by dusky red triangular congestion of the conjunctiva, gelatinous limbal papillae and Horner-Tranta's spots that are formed due to eosinophils and epithelial debris at the limbus * Mixed Treatment of VKC includes allergen avoidance, antihistaminics, steroids, and immunomodulators both topical and systemic depending on the severity of the disease. The image below represents Horner-Trantas spots. The above image shows cobblestone appearance. Other options: Option B: Phlyctenular conjunctivitis presents with small whitish nodules at the limbus due to hypersensitivity (usually to TB or staphylococcus) and does not lead to shield ulcer formation. Option C: A bacterial ulcer typically presents with acute pain, redness, watering, purulent discharge, and a corneal infiltrate, often with hypopyon in severe cases and not shield ulcer. The ulcer, in this case, is oval with an associated hypopyon (shown below) Option D: Herpes simplex keratitis, a form of viral keratitis, is characterized by pain, watering, and photophobia. A distinctive feature is a dendritic ulcer on the cornea, which, upon fluorescein staining, reveals terminal bulbs.The below image shows the characteristic dendritic ulcers of herpes simplex keratitis.

text: 9. A patient presents to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. The radiological image shows the following findings. What is the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Orbital blowout fracture

The given CT image shows the characteristic "hanging drop sign" indicating a blowout fracture of the orbital wall. Hanging drop/tear-drop sign is characteristic of an orbital "blow-out" fracture, which represents the orbital contents herniating through the floor of the orbit into the maxillary antrum. Blow-out orbital fractures are caused by trauma to the orbit by a large, rounded object, e.g cricket ball, a human fist, etc. This force can cause the displacement of the eyeball backwards and an increase in intraorbital pressure. This leads to fracturing at the weakest point of the orbital wall (orbital floor and sometimes medial wall). Clinical signs are periocular swelling (early stage), enophthalmos, ecchymosis and subconjunctival haemorrhage (later stages). Definitive treatment is by surgical repair 10-14 days after injury with initial supportive management with analgesics and antibiotic Indications for surgery in a "blow-out" fracture are as follows: * Diplopia not resolving significantly in the early days after trauma * A fracture with a large herniation of tissues into the antrum * Incarceration of tissues in the fracture, resulting in globe retraction and increased applanation tension on attempted upward gaze * Enophthalmos greater than 2 mm The most useful projection for detecting an orbital floor fracture is the Water’s view. Other options: Option B: Zygomatic fracture Involves zygomatic bone (cheekbone), producing “flattened cheek” and step deformity at the infraorbital rim. Option C:  Maxillary fracture Involves alveolar process / maxillary sinus walls. Here, the fracture is confined to the orbital floor. Option D: Le-fort 1 fracture is a horizontal fracture of the maxilla, separating the upper alveolar part (upper teeth + palate) from the rest of the face. Pearl PF1981: Le-Fort's classification of Maxillary Fracture Le-Fort I is a transverse fracture of the maxilla * Fracture line passes through the lower part of nasal septum, maxillary antra and the pterygoid plates * It separates palate from the rest of the face leading to floating teeth or palate * Also called Guerin’s fracture.  Le-Fort II is a pyramidal fracture * Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, lacrimal bone, floor of the orbit, upper part of the maxillary sinus and pterygoid plates * X-ray or CT appears like hanging maxilla * It is associated with CSF rhinorrhea. Le-Fort III is craniofacial dysjunction i.e., facial skeleton completely disconnected from its cranial attachment * Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, ethmo-frontal junction, superior orbital fissure, lateral wall of the orbit, fronto-zygomatic and temporo-zygomatic sutures and the upper part of pterygoid plates * It is also associated with CSF rhinorrhea.

text: 10. Hirschberg's test is being performed in this patient with squint. Which of the following is correct about the case?
expl:
Correct answer: C. 90 Prism dioptre exotropia

From the given image of a Hirschberg test, it can be inferred that the patient has 90 prism dioptres (PD) of exotropia. In the Hirschberg test, if the light reflection is on the nasal limbus, it means 45 degrees exotropia. One degree is equal to 2 PD (prism dioptre). Therefore, 45 degrees exotropia would mean 90 PD exotropia in the right eye.The Hirschberg test is used to detect squint. The Hirschberg test gives a rough objective estimate of the angle of manifest strabismus. A pen torch is shone into the eyes from arm’s length, and the patient is asked to fixate on the light. The corneal reflection of the light will be centered in the pupil of the fixating eye but will be decentred in a squinting eye, in the direction opposite to that of the deviation. The distance of the corneal light reflection from the center of the pupil is noted; each millimeter of the deviation is approximately equal to 7°. Other options: Option A: 90 degrees exotropia is incorrect because ocular deviations are measured in prism dioptres, not in degrees. Option B: 90 Prism dioptre esotropia is incorrect as the deviation is outward (exotropia), not inward (esotropia). Option D: 90 degrees esotropia is incorrect due to wrong unit (degrees instead of prism dioptres) and wrong direction (exotropia, not esotropia). text: 11. A patient presented to OPD with complaints of ophthalmoplegia and ptosis. A diagnosis of superior orbital fissure syndrome was confirmed after examination. Which nerves are compressed in this case?
expl:
Correct answer: A. III, IV, V(1), VI

In Superior Orbital Fissure Syndrome, Cranial nerves III (oculomotor), IV (Trochlear nerve), VI (Abducens nerve), and V1 (Ophthalmic division of the Trigeminal nerve) get compressed causing ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, and sensory loss in the V1 area. The superior orbital fissure is an important anatomical opening in the skull that allows several critical structures to pass through. Among these structures, the frontal nerve and nasociliary nerve are branches of the ophthalmic nerve, the first division of the trigeminal nerve (V1), which is responsible for sensory innervation to parts of the face. The frontal nerve provides sensation to the forehead, the anterior scalp, and the dorsum of the nose, while the nasociliary nerve supplies sensation to parts of the nasal cavity. Superior orbital fissure syndrome is characterized by the following: * Pain, typically labeled as retro–orbital ache * Sensory loss/disturbances in the distribution of the ophthalmic division of the 5th cranial nerve * Ipsilateral ophthalmoplegia due to the involvement of the 3rd, 4th, and 6th cranial nerves involvement * Ptosis, due to 3rd nerve paralysis Trauma affecting the orbital region is the most common cause of superior orbital fissure syndrome. Other causes include infections such as herpes zoster ophthalmicus, inflammatory disorders, and tumors. Diagnosis is mainly clinical, supported by imaging modalities like CT or MRI to identify the underlying pathology. Management depends on the cause and may involve surgical decompression, corticosteroid therapy, or antiviral treatment. text: 12. A 50-year-old man was prescribed +12D glasses. He has deep anterior chamber with a deep jet-black pupil and no lens was seen on the slit lamp examination. What is the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Aphakia

The need for +12 D glasses, a deep anterior chamber with jet-black pupil, and absence of lens on slit lamp are classical findings that together confirm aphakia. Aphakia is the absence of the natural crystalline lens of the eye, usually caused by surgical removal, trauma, or congenital absence. Signs of surgical aphakia include the following: * Limbal scar * Anterior chamber deeper than normal * Iridodonesis (tremulousness of the iris) * Jet black color of the pupil * Only the first and second images (normally, four images are seen) seen on Purkinje’s image test * Small disc seen on fundus examination * High hypermetropia seen on retinoscopy Aphakic eyes (eyes without a lens) only produce two Purkinje images, as the absence of the lens eliminates the reflections from the anterior and posterior lens surfaces. The test helps differentiate pseudophakia from aphakia and is useful for confirming the presence of an IOL.  Intraocular lens (IOL) implantation is done to correct aphakia following cataract surgeries. Singh and Worst’s lens is fixed on the iris by enclavating the mid-peripheral iris stroma into claw-shaped haptics, without sutures. Haptics refer to the supporting structures that hold the lens in place within the eye. They are associated with a high incidence of postoperative complications. Posterior chamber lenses (PCIOLs) are placed entirely behind the iris. Anterior chamber IOLs are placed entirely in front of the iris. They are supported at the angle of the anterior chamber. Other options: Option B: Pseudophakia is wrong because in pseudophakia, the patient has an intraocular lens implant (IOL) after cataract surgery. On slit lamp examination, the IOL would be clearly visible within the pupillary area. Option C: Hypermetropia has the lens present and usually needs only low-to-moderate (+1D to +6D) correction. Option D: Myopia necessitates the use of minus (–) power lenses, not +12D. In this case, the patient requires strong positive correction due to an absent lens, thereby excluding a diagnosis of myopia.

text: 13. A patient underwent an eye examination, and when light was shone into the right eye, the pupil of the left eye also constricted. What explains the constriction in the left eye?

options.A: Contraction of the ciliary muscle due to parasympathetic stimulation
options.B: Relaxation of the ciliary muscle due to sympathetic stimulation
options.C: Stimulation of the afferent pathway from the left eye
options.D: Stimulation of the efferent pathway with crossover at the Edinger-Westphal nucleus

expl:
Correct answer: D. Stimulation of the efferent pathway with crossover at the Edinger-Westphal nucleus

The pupillary light reflex pathway involves several components, with the pretectal nucleus in the midbrain serving as the central integrative center for the reflex. When light is shone into one eye, it causes bilateral constriction of the pupils, a response known as the pupillary light reflex. This reflex has two components: Direct light reflex: constriction of the pupil in the eye being illuminated. Consensual light reflex: constriction of the pupil in the opposite eye. Pathway for light reflex * Afferent fibers travel from the retina to the optic nerve, optic chiasma, and terminate in the pretectal nucleus. * Internuncial fibers connect the pretectal nucleus with Edinger Westphal nuclei of both sides.  * Parasympathetic fibers arise from the Edinger Westphal nuclei of both sides, travel along the oculomotor nerve, and relay in the ciliary ganglion. * Postganglionic fibers travel along short ciliary nerves to innervate sphincter pupillae. Clinical correlate- Since internuncial fibers connect the pretectal nucleus with Edinger Westphal nuclei of both sides, consensual light reflex is seen. Other options: Option A: The ciliary muscle controls accommodation, not the pupillary light reflex. Option B: The sympathetic pathway mainly controls pupil dilation (by innervating the dilator pupillae muscle), not constriction. Option C: If the light is given to the right eye, the afferent pathway from the left eye is not involved at all.

text: 14. A patient presents with a painless ulcer in the eye. On examination, a long branching ulcer with desquamated epithelium is seen on the cornea. What could be the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Dendritic ulcer

A long branching corneal ulcer with desquamated epithelium is typical of a dendritic ulcer seen in herpes simplex keratitis. As shown in the image below: Herpes viral keratitis, also known as herpetic keratoconjunctivitis, is a form of keratitis caused by recurrent herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection in the cornea. The virus, which lies dormant in the trigeminal ganglion after an initial infection, periodically reactivates and replicates. These reactivations result in unilateral symptoms of epithelial or stromal keratitis.  Patients with epithelial keratitis complain of foreign-body sensation, light sensitivity, redness, and blurred vision associated with focal or diffuse reduction in corneal sensation. Stromal keratitis manifests as a disc-shaped area of corneal edema. In patients who are immunocompromised due to pre-existing disease or using corticosteroids, the ulcer may become large; in such cases, the lesion is called a geographic ulcer. Treatment: Topical antivirals are the first-line treatment. * Trifluorothymidine 1% drops four times a day for 5 days, acyclovir 3% ointment five times a day for 21 days, or 3% vidarabine ointment five times a day for 2 weeks * Systemic antivirals in cases of increased severity or recurrence * Topical antibiotics to prevent secondary bacterial infection Other options: Option A: Fungal ulcer is typically painful, with grayish-white infiltrates, feathery margins, hypopyon and satellite lesions.An immune ring, also known as a Wesseley ring, can form around the ulcer, caused by the deposition of immune complexes. Option C: Acanthamoeba keratitis usually occurs in contact lens users or after exposure to contaminated water and is very painful, often out of proportion to the clinical signs due to perineural invasion with a characteristic ring-shaped stromal infiltrate. Option D: A bacterial ulcer is typically painful, with redness, watering, and a localized corneal infiltrate that may lead to hypopyon in severe cases. It does not usually present as a long, branching, or dendritic pattern. text: 15. A 45-year-old patient presents with difficulty reacting to bright light. On examination, the pupillary reflex is absent, but the near reflex is preserved. Where is the lesion likely located?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Pretectal area of the midbrain

This is a classic case of light–near dissociation, also known as argyll robertson pupil where the lesion lies in the pretectal region of the midbrain. Argyll Robertson Pupil (ARP) is characterized by a light-near dissociation, meaning the pupils react to accommodation (near reflex) but not to light. This condition is linked to neurosyphilis, causing a dorsal midbrain lesion that affects the pupillary light pathway while sparing the more ventrally located pupillary near reflex pathway. Key features of Argyll Robertson pupil include: * Bilateral, small, and irregular pupils in dim light. * Accommodation Reflex Present: The pupil constricts when focusing on a near target. * Light Reflex Absent: The pupils do not constrict when exposed to bright light. Cocaine Eye Drops Induced Mydriasis: Pupils will dilate in response to cocaine eye drops. Other clinical features in neurosyphilis: * Fleeting and repetitive lancinating pains, primarily in the legs * acute abdominal pain with vomiting(visceral crisis) * Tabes dorsalis with Ataxia and gait disturbances due to loss of position sense * Loss of reflexes in the legs * Paresthesias, bladder disturbances Pupillary light reflex pathway: * First neurons (sensory) connect each retina with both pretectal nuclei in the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculi. * Second neurons (internuncial) connect each pretectal nucleus to both Edinger–Westphal nuclei. * Third neurons (preganglionic motor) connect the Edinger–Westphal nucleus to the ciliary ganglion. * Fourth neurons (postganglionic motor) leave the ciliary ganglion and pass in the short ciliary nerves to innervate the sphincter pupillae. Other options: Option A: If the optic nerve were damaged, both the light reflex and the near reflex would be lost, because no visual impulses would reach the brain to trigger either reflex. Option B: If the oculomotor nerve were damaged, the pupil would not constrict at all, so both the light reflex and the near reflex would be absent. Since the near reflex is still present in this patient, the lesion cannot be in the oculomotor nerve. Option C: If the Edinger-Westphal nucleus were damaged, again, both the light reflex and the near reflex would be lost because this nucleus supplies the parasympathetic fibers responsible for pupil constriction.

text: 16. A posterior staphyloma was noted on indirect ophthalmoscopy. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Pathological myopia

Posterior staphyloma is a hallmark of pathological myopia. Pathological/degenerative myopia is characterized by progressive anteroposterior elongation of the scleral envelope associated with secondary ocular changes due to the mechanical stretching of the involved tissues. The following changes are seen: * A pale tessellated (tigroid) appearance of the fundus is seen as the choroid becomes visible due to diffuse attenuation of the RPE * Temporal myopic crescent * Focal chorioretinal atrophy * Anomalous optic nerve head with tilted conformation * Acquired optic disc pit formation * Lattice degeneration * Cystoid degeneration * Lacquer cracks are fine, irregular yellow lines crisscrossing at the posterior pole due to ruptures in the Bruch membrane. * Subretinal coin hemorrhages develop from lacquer cracks. * Fuchs spot: It is a raised, circular, pigmented scar at the macula that develops after absorption of subretinal hemorrhage. * Posterior staphyloma occurs due to progressive thinning and outpouching of the posterior sclera, visible on indirect ophthalmoscopy. Staphyloma is an abnormal protrusion of the uveal tissue through a weak and thin portion of the cornea or sclera. Posterior staphyloma presents as a scleral and choroidal bulge behind the equator. Ophthalmoscopy reveals an excavated area with dipping retinal vessels. It is lined internally by uveal tissue and externally by weak cornea or sclera. Types of Staphyloma: * Anterior staphyloma: It is characterized by ectasia of the pseudo-cornea, which occurs after the total sloughing of the cornea. It is lined internally by the iris and externally by the newly formed epithelium. * Intercalary staphyloma: This is located at the limbus and is lined by the root of the iris and the anterior-most part of the ciliary body * Ciliary staphyloma: It is characterized by ectasia of weak sclera lined by the ciliary body. This affects the ciliary zone, which includes the region up to 8 mm behind the limbus. * Equatorial staphyloma: This occurs at the equatorial region up to 14 mm behind the limbus of the eye. * Posterior staphyloma: This affects the posterior pole of the eye. Note : The most common cause of anterior staphyloma is a sloughing corneal ulcer. The most common cause of posterior staphyloma is degenerative high axial myopia. Other options: Option B: Hypermetropia is a refractive error of the eye in which parallel rays of light from infinity focus behind the retina when accommodation is at rest. Fundoscopy findings in hypermetropia include shot silk appearance (retina may shine due to the greater brilliance of light reflections) and pseudopapillitis. Option C: Scleritis refers to an inflammation of the sclera proper. It usually occurs in females more than males. It is frequently associated with an underlying systemic inflammatory condition. The patient presents with moderate to severe pain, redness, lacrimation, photophobia, and diminution of vision. Option D: Corneal ulcer is an anterior segment lesion of the cornea, while posterior staphyloma is a fundus finding due to pathological myopia.

text: 3. A 45-year-old man presents to the casualty with a sudden loss of vision and painful ocular movements. Correct answer: B. Retrobulbar neuritis

The given clinical scenario of a sudden loss of vision, painful ocular movements in the absence of fundoscopic changes, RAPD and central scotoma is suggestive of optic neuritis, specifically retrobulbar neuritis.  There are 3 types of optic neuritis: papillitis, neuroretinitis, and retrobulbar neuritis. The common causes of retrobulbar neuritis include demyelinating disorders such as multiple sclerosis (MS) and neuromyelitis optica (NMO or Devic's disease). Clinically, optic neuritis is characterized by sudden, progressive visual loss.  Ocular movements are painful in retrobulbar neuritis and painless in papillitis and neuroretinitis. Glowing sensations known as phosphenes may be induced with sound or movement. Color vision may also be impaired.  On examination, Marcus Gunn pupil or relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is usually noted due to asymmetric involvement. The most common visual field defect is a central or centrocecal scotoma.

text: 5. For which of the following condition is the V-Y procedure used as a treatment modality ?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Ectropion

V-Y procedure is done for Cicatricial ectropion. Ectropion is the eversion of the lid margin and eyelashes away from the globe. Cicatricial ectropion is commonly the result of burns, trauma and chronic inflammations of the skin which shorten the anterior lamina of the eyelid which pull the eyelid away from the globe. Treatment of cicatricial ectropion requires release and relaxation of the scarred tissues, and an elongation of the skin muscle lamina by some form of surgery called as blepharoplasty. However, localized areas of scarring can be released by Z or V–Y plasty. A V incision is made just below the eyelid with the base of the triangle in line with the ectropion which is pulled up to repair the ectropion. The V incision is now in the shape of a Y which is closed and the normal structure is retained.  Types: * Involutional/senile- affects the lower lid of elderly patients. * Cicatricial- caused by the scarring or contracture of the skin and underlying tissues * Paralytic- caused by ipsilateral facial nerve palsy  * Mechanical- caused by tumors on or near the lid margin that mechanically evert the lid * Congenital Pearl PF1603: Surgical Modalities Used in Correcting Ectropion

text: 10. A child is brought to the OPD with fever, severe pain, and swelling of the left eye. He was bitten by a dog over the eye a few days back. On examination, there is mild proptosis with restriction of ocular movements. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:

In the above clinical scenario of a patient with a history of a dog bite over the eye followed by severe swelling around the eye, proptosis, with restricted eye movement, it is suggestive of orbital cellulitis. Orbital cellulitis is the acute inflammation of the soft tissues of the orbit behind the orbital septum. It can occur due to exogenous infection (penetrating injuries) or extension of an endogenous infection (dental infection). It presents with fever, severe pain, and eye swelling, which increases with movement, chemosis, axial proptosis, and restriction of ocular movements. Complications include subperiosteal abscess, orbital abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis, and general septicemia. It is the most frequent acute complication of ethmoid sinusitis. The lamina papyracea forms part of the medial wall of the orbit, is paper-thin, and perforated by numerous foramina for nerves and blood vessels. Hence, ethmoid sinusitis frequently leads to orbital cellulitis. It can vary in degree and severity and is typically graded with the Chandler classification.

text: 11. Among the following options,which is the most common treatment for recurrent Pterygium of eye?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Conjunctival autograft

The most commonly used technique for recurrent pterygium among the following is conjuctival autograft. A pterygium is a degenerative subconjunctival fibrovascular tissue encroaching the cornea. It is a connective tissue disorder and is never inflammatory. Histologically, it is made up of elastotic degenerative changes in vascularized subepithelial stromal collagen. It is most commonly seen on the nasal aspect of the eye. It is made up of three parts: * cap (an avascular halo-like zone at the advancing edge) * head * body Patients may be asymptomatic or present with irritation, grittiness, or episodes of inflammation. As they enlarge, it may obstruct vision and lead to astigmatism. Treatment:  * A pterygium is best left alone unless: * It is progressing towards the pupillary area * Causes excessive astigmatism * Restricts ocular motility * Causes disfigurement. * Excision: Simple excision of the pterygium is associated with a high recurrence rate, and should be combined with: * Mitomycin C drops- applied pre-operatively/ intra-operatively or post-operatively to prevent a recurrence. However, it may lead to complications like scleral necrosis, cataract, and iritis and should be used judiciously.  * Beta-radiation applied postoperatively to the pterygium base was popular for many years, but is associated with late scleral necrosis. * Conjunctival autografting- limbal tissue from the same or other eye is grafted and secured with fibrin glue or sutures. * Amniotic membrane graft * Peripheral lamellar keratoplasty if the lesion is deep. Currently, the most widely used techniques are conjunctival autografting, amniotic membrane transplantation, and mitomycin-C application either preoperatively or postoperatively (can be applied intraoperatively also) of which conjuctival autografting has less recurrence rates and is a simple and quick procedure which reduces the risk of granuloma formation, scleral thinning and necrosis. Note: A combination of conjuctival autografting with intraoperative mitomycin C is the most preferred as it has the least recurrence rates as per studies.

text: 16. A patient was diagnosed with stroke and his visual field testing revealed macula sparing homonymous hemianopia. Where is the likely site of lesion in optic pathway?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Occipital lobe

The likely site of the lesion is occipital lobe as the patient presents with homonymous hemianopia along with macular sparing. Homonymous hemianopia (HH) involves loss of vision on the same side of the visual field in both eyes. HH is characteristically seen in lesions involving the visual pathway posterior to the optic chiasma. Lesions involving occipital lobe usually shows macular sparing because macular representation is seperate and quite large as compared to peripheral vision. Moreover, macular area in occipital lobe is supplied both by posterior and middle cerebral artery. In case of vascular lesions (eg stroke) affecting occipital lobe, it is less likely to involve both these arteries. HH may be either complete or incomplete.  * A complete HH is characterised by loss of entire hemifield on the same side in both eyes. * An incomplete HH is characterised by partial loss of visual field on the same side in both eyes. Incomplete HH is further classified as congruous or incongruous, depending on whether the extent of partial loss of visual field in both the eyes is same or different, respectively. Pearl PF0246: Lesions in the optic pathway Transection of the pathways at the locations indicated by the letters causes the visual field defects shown in the diagram above. * The fibers from the nasal half of each retina decussate in the optic chiasm, so that the fibers in the optic tracts are those from the temporal half of one retina and the nasal half of the other. * A lesion that interrupts the optic nerve causes blindness in that eye. * Lesions affecting the optic chiasma destroy fibers from both nasal hemiretinas and produce a heteronymous (opposite sides of the visual fields) hemianopia. * A lesion in one optic tract causes blindness in half of the visual field and is called homonymous (same side of both visual fields) hemianopia (half-blindness). * Occipital lesions may spare the fibers from the macula because of the separation in the brain of these fibers from the other subserving vision.

It is reversible if treated appropriately at the right time during the development phase(0-8 years of age) but is most commonly seen in the first 3 years of life. It is a condition with unilateral or bilateral subnormal vision without any local abnormality in the eye. It is most commonly associated with comitant squint and can be due to retinal defects, strabismus, high anisometropia with aniseikonia(a difference in the retinal image size between the two eyes). Amblyopic eyes have a characteristic vision which has: * The crowding phenomenon where single letter vision is better than when presented in a row. * A drop in visual acuity when viewed through grey neutral density filters * Decreased recognition, contrast sensitivity, spatial localization, saccadic amplitudes, and pursuit eye movements. Treatment includes occluding the normal eye for 6-12 weeks. If there is a vision problem with an underlying cause then that should be corrected initially. The brain uses the stronger eye to perceive images and hence the brain has to be trained and forced to use the amblyopic or lazy eye by occluding the normal eye. By occluding the normal eye, the amblyopic eye gets stimulated and gets corrected. Occlusion should be total and should be changed when it is dirty or loose. In children less than 8 years the occlusion has to be done in a way so that constant occlusion of the normal eye does not make it amblyopic too. It is done corresponding to the child's age (x) at a ratio of x:1. e.g if the child is 5 years old then the normal eye is occluded for 5 days and removed while only the amblyopic eye is occluded on the 6th day. It is continued in a similar fashion for 6-12 weeks.  In infants, part-time occlusion (a few hours a day) is done while in children above 8 years, constant occlusion is advised. However, the underlying cause of amblyopia should also be corrected for complete resolution.

text: 6. A middle-aged woman presents with a pterygium that has been steadily progressing towards the pupillary area. What is the best means of management in this case?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Excision with conjunctival autograft

The best mode of management in the given options for progressive pterygium is excision with conjunctival autograft. A pterygium is a degenerative subconjunctival fibrovascular tissue encroaching the cornea. It is a connective tissue disorder and is never inflammatory. Histologically, it comprises elastotic degenerative changes in vascularised subepithelial stromal collagen. It is most commonly seen on the nasal aspect of the eye. It is made up of three parts: * cap (an avascular halo-like zone at the advancing edge) * head * body Patients may be asymptomatic or present with irritation, grittiness, or episodes of inflammation. As they enlarge, it may obstruct vision and lead to astigmatism. Treatment:  * A pterygium is best left alone unless: * It is progressing towards the pupillary area * Causes excessive astigmatism * Restricts ocular motility * Causes disfigurement. * Excision: A simple pterygium excision often leads to a high chance of recurrence. Measures to prevent recurrence are: * Mitomycin C drops- applied pre-operatively/ intra-operatively or post-operatively. However, it may lead to complications like scleral necrosis, cataract, and iritis and should be used judiciously.  * Beta-radiation applied postoperatively to the pterygium base was popular for many years, but is associated with late scleral necrosis. * Conjunctival autografting- limbal tissue from the same or other eye is grafted and secured with fibrin glue or sutures. * Amniotic membrane graft * Peripheral lamellar keratoplasty if the lesion is deep. Currently, the most widely used techniques are conjunctival autografting, amniotic membrane transplantation, and mitomycin-C application either preoperatively or postoperatively (can be applied intraoperatively also), of which conjunctival autografting has fewer recurrence rates and is a simple and quick procedure that reduces the risk of granuloma formation, scleral thinning, and necrosis. Note: A combination of conjunctival autografting with intraoperative mitomycin C is the most preferred as it has the least recurrence rates as per studies.

text: 13. Which of the following combination of cylindrical lenses can be used to treat with-the-rule astigmatism?
expl:
Correct answer: D. - 3.00 DC x 180, +1.00 DC x 90

- 3.00 DC x 180, + 1.00 DC x 90 can be used to correct with-the-rule astigmatism. In with-the-rule astigmatism, the vertical meridian is steeper than the horizontal meridian. Hence, to make up for this, we need a combination of cylindrical lenses with relatively greater power in the horizontal meridian than the vertical meridian. Before considering the options, also remember that a cylinder aligned along the horizontal meridian (180 axis) has action in the vertical meridian and vice versa. In option A, the cylinder acting along the horizontal meridian (- 3.00 DC x 90) has lesser power than the one acting along the vertical meridian (+ 5.00 DC x 180). This is also the case with options B and C.   Only option D has a cylinder with greater power along the horizontal meridian ( +1.00 DC x 90) compared to the vertical meridian (- 3.00 DC x 180). Hence, option D is the answer.  Alternative method: This method involves the use of the optical cross technique STEP 1: * Frame the optical cross with the given powers in their respective meridians. * While framing the optical cross, the power which is given in 180 needs to marked in 90 and vice versa. For example, option A has + 5.00 DC x 180, - 3.00 DC x 90 which means the eye gets a correction of + 5.00 in vertical meridian (i.e in 90 degree) and correction of - 3.00 in horizontal meridian (i.e in 180 degree). Keeping this in mind, if one frames the optical crosses for the given options, the end image would be as given below STEP 2: Now we need to interpret the optical crosses to find which meridian is steeper with certain hints. * If the power in one axis is ‘+’ and the power in other axis is ‘-’, then the axis with ‘-’ power is steeper. * If powers in both the axis are ‘-’, then the higher number of the two will be steeper. * If powers in both the axis are ‘+’, then the lower number of the two will be steeper. STEP 3: Applying these hints to the options will give option D as with-the-rule astigmatism.

text: 1. A young male patient sustained a right tibial shaft fracture following a road traffic accident. The patient's right leg was immobilized with a plaster cast. This patient now presents to the emergency with severe pain in the leg. On examination, the distal pulses are absent, on passive stretching the pain increases, and on opening the plaster, the right leg appears edematous and numerous blisters are seen. Considering the suspected diagnosis, what would be the most appropriate management in this case?

options.C: Opening of the plaster is sufficient

expl:
Correct answer: A. Fasciotomy

In the above given clinical scenario of a patient with tibial fracture following an RTA, now presenting with severe leg pain, absent distal pulses, increase pain on passive stretch and leg looking edematous, suggests acute compartment syndrome, and it is treated immediately with fasciotomy. Compartment syndrome is a condition characterized by elevated pressure within the osteofascial compartment resulting in impaired local circulation. The classic features of ischemia in acute compartment syndrome include the 5 Ps: * Pain: Pain is the first symptom of acute compartment syndrome. Ischemic muscle is highly sensitive to touch. On the passive stretching of the muscles, severe pain can be elicited.  * Paresthesia: Paresthesia and hypoesthesia may be noted due to compression of nerves traversing the affected compartment. They are the first signs of nerve ischemia. * Pallor: Pallor of the skin may not always be seen. The skin outside the compartment may be normally perfused, as only the intra-compartmental perfusion may be affected. * Paralysis: Paralysis of muscle groups affected in that compartment is a late sign. * Pulselessness: Usually, the peripheral pulses and capillary return are intact in the early stages, unless there is a major arterial injury. If pulses are absent, arteriography is indicated.  The diagnosis can be confirmed by measuring the intra-compartmental pressure using a split catheter introduced into the compartment. The difference between diastolic and compartment pressure is known as the differential pressure (ΔP). A differential pressure (ΔP) of less than 30 mm Hg (4.00 kilopascals) is an indication for immediate compartment decompression. Treatment: The threatened compartment must be promptly decompressed, merely splitting the plaster is utterly useless and the limb must be nursed flat. Elevating the limb causes a further decrease in end capillary pressure and aggravates muscle ischemia. In the case of compartment syndrome in the leg, Fasciotomy means opening all four compartments (anterior, lateral, deep posterior and superficial compartments). Wounds to be left open and inspected 2 days later, if tissues are healthy, the wounds can be sutured. If there is muscle necrosis, debridement is to be carried out. The image below shows a fasciotomy. Pearl PF1498: Acute compartment and Crush syndrome 1. Acute Compartment Syndrome Acute compartment syndrome is an elevation of the intracompartmental pressure (ICP) which increases the risk for tissue ischemia and necrosis. Causes: Fractures (70%) and severe soft tissue injuries (30%). Common fractures causing compartment syndrome include tibial diaphyseal (most common), distal radius, and forearm fractures.  Pathology: Increased pressure in one of the osseofascial compartments due to bleeding, oedema or inflammation. A vicious cycle of ischemia → edema→ ischemia leading to necrosis of the muscles and nerves within the compartment in 6 hours or less.  Clinical features: Five Ps: Pain, Paraesthesia, Pallor, Paralysis and Pulselessness.  Management: Fasciotomy to decompress the threatened compartment if the differential pressure (ΔP) goes < 30 mmHg.    2. Crush syndrome  Crush syndrome is the systemic manifestation of muscle necrosis. It is commonly caused due to prolonged external compression of an extremity.  Causes: Crush injuries sustained during motor vehicle accidents, earthquakes, mining and other occupational accidents. Pathology: Underperfusion of muscle causes myonecrosis. When the limb is freed, there is a release of toxic metabolites causing reperfusion injury. Reactive oxygen metabolites create further tissue injury. Free myoglobin can get precipitated in the renal glomeruli.  Clinical features: The affected limb is pulseless, red, swollen and blistered. text: 4. A 25-year-old male presented to the emergency department with pain and swelling of the right knee. Radiograph shows the following finding. What is the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Patellar fracture

The radiograph shows the displaced patellar fracture.  A patellar fracture can either occur via a direct injury to the knee or because of a violent contraction of the quadriceps. The fracture may be undisplaced either because of the pre-patellar expansion of the quadriceps tendon which holds the fragments together or because of the patellar retinaculae on the sides. Patellar fracture results in the disruption of the extensor apparatus (not the flexor apparatus). Due to the disruption of the extensor apparatus, the patient will not be able to lift his leg with the knee in full extension; it remains in a position short of full extension (extensor lag). Clinically, it can be tested using the Active Straight leg raising (SLR) test, which the patient will not be able to perform. The extensor apparatus of the knee includes the Quadriceps femoris muscle with its tendon, the patella bone and, the ligamentum patellae with its insertion into the tibial tuberosity. An un-displaced fracture of the patella is treated with a plaster cast extending from the groin to just above the malleoli, with the knee in full extension. This is called as a cylinder cast and is usually left in place for a period of at least 3 weeks. A two part fracture (Displaced transverse fracture) of the patella must be reduced, and the fragments are fixed with tension band wiring using K wires and the extensor retinaculae is repaired Other treatment options which are available for patellar fracture are: * Undisplaced patellar fractures with minimal joint incongruity and intact extensor retinaculum can be treated by cylinder cast. * Displaced patellar fractures are usually treated by tension band wiring. * Severely comminuted fractures where the reduction of the fragments is difficult are treated by patellectomy. Pearl PF1177: Tension band wiring A tension band wire is a form of internal fixation used to convert distraction forces into compression forces, promoting bone healing. It is used in: * Fracture patella * Fracture olecranon  * Fracture lateral malleolus * Fracture greater trochanter

text: 6. Which of the following is the most radiosensitive tumour?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Ewing's sarcoma

The radiosensitive tumor among the following is Ewing's sarcoma. All others are radioresistant tumors. Ewing sarcoma is a malignant bone tumor characterized by primitive round cells without obvious differentiation. It accounts for 6% to 10% of primary malignant bone tumors. Ewing sarcoma follows osteosarcoma as the second most common group of bone sarcomas in children. Approximately 80% of affected patients are younger than 20 years. Boys are affected slightly more frequently than girls. Usually, the tumor arises in the diaphysis of long tubular bones, especially the femur and the flat bones of the pelvis. Fever, elevated sedimentation rate, anemia, and leukocytosis may be seen. Plain radiographs show a destructive lytic tumor with permeative margins that extend into the surrounding soft tissues. Multiple layers of reactive bone are formed by the periosteal response, giving the bone an onion skin-like appearance. Ewing's sarcoma is managed with a combination of radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and surgery. This sarcoma is highly sensitive to radiotherapy and in certain cases, tumors affecting important bones can be treated with radiotherapy or a combination of radiotherapy and chemotherapy. text: 8. A 9-year-old boy is brought to the hospital with complaints of pain and limping. The symptoms started 6 months back and gradually worsened. The child appears to be healthy with normal height and weight. On examination, there is mild wasting on the right side, abduction ( especially in flexion ), and internal rotation is limited due to pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Perthes disease

A young male patient with normal height and weight and complaints of pain and limping gradually progressing over 6 months and examination findings of limited abduction and internal rotation is likely to have Perthes's disease. The image shows a mushroom-shaped femoral head that is laterally displaced in a dysplastic acetabular socket.  Between 4 and 7 years of age, the femoral head may depend on the lateral epiphyseal vessels for its blood supply and venous drainage almost entirely. These vessels situated in the retinacula make them susceptible to stretching and to pressure from an effusion. The disease is characterized by the disruption of blood flow to the head of the femur. Due to which the bone goes for osteonecrosis and stops growing. Over time, healing occurs by new blood vessels infiltrating the dead bone and removing the necrotic bone which leads to a loss of bone mass and a weakening of the femoral head. Clinical features include a boy of 4-8 years complaining of pain and limping. Symptoms continue for weeks on end or recur intermittently. The hip looks deceptively normal. text: 2. A person presents with complaints of clawing of the 4th and 5th fingers. Along with it, there is sensory loss at tips of these fingers. What structure is most likely to be damaged?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Ulnar nerve

The given description is of a clawing of 4th and 5th finger with loss of sensation in the tips of these fingers are classically seen in case of an ulnar nerve injury. The ulnar nerve supplies the medial two lumbricals, adductor pollicis, interossei, and hypothenar muscles in the hand. The lumbricals are primarily responsible for the extension at the interphalangeal joints. Therefore, in ulnar nerve palsy, there is clawing of the medial two fingers. In ulnar nerve palsy, only the medial two fingers develop clawing, while in a combined median and ulnar nerve palsy, all four fingers develop clawing.  The following tests are done to test the integrity of the ulnar nerve: * Egawa's test - In a positive test, due to the weakness of the dorsal interossei, side-to-side movements of the middle finger is weak. * Book test or Froment's sign - The patient is asked to hold a book between the thumb and index finger while the examiner attempt to pull it forcefully. In case of an ulnar nerve injury, the adductor pollicis is paralyzed and the patient attempts to hold the book with the flexor pollicis longus muscle supplied by the median nerve. * Card test - In the case of weak palmar interossei, the examiner can pull out the card with ease. Other options Option B - In radial nerve palsy, the patient presents with a wrist drop due to paralyzed wrist extensors. In high lesions, there is sensory loss on the dorsum of the hand over the anatomical stuff box.  Option C - In median nerve injury, paralysis of opponens pollicis muscle leads to ape thumb deformity. A pointing finger deformity can also be seen due to paralyzed flexors of the fingers. Option D - The anterior interosseous nerve supplies the flexor digitorum profundus muscle of the index finger and damage to the nerve prevents flexion of the index finger. Seddon's classification includes 3 groups

  1. Neurapraxia
  2. Axonotmesis
  3. Neurotmesis

Neurapraxia:

Reversible physiologic conduction block. Occurs due to mechanical pressure causing segmental demyelination.

E.g.,Saturday night palsy, torniquet, and crutch palsy

Axonotmesis: 

Axonal interruption. Conduction is lost but the nerve is in continuity and neural tubes are intact.

E.g.,Closed fractures and dislocations

Neurotmesis: 

Division of the nerve trunk. Endoneurial tube destruction also occurs.

E.g., Complete section of nerve in open fractures
