text: 4. A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency room following a bike accident. Examination reveals the right upper limb in abduction and external rotation. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Anterior Dislocation of the Shoulder

The upper limb in abduction and external rotation and radiograph are both suggestive of anterior dislocation of the shoulder.  The AP view radiograph shows the disturbed articulation between the humeral head and glenoid fossa. The humeral head is seen below and medial to the glenoid socket. This suggests anterior dislocation of the shoulder joint. In young adults, the common cause for anterior dislocation is athletic injuries, while in older adults, falls are a more common cause.  Anterior dislocation is the most common among shoulder dislocations. It occurs due to a fall on the hands. The head of the humerus is driven forwards and tears the capsule resulting in an avulsion in the glenoid labrum (Bankart lesion). Sometimes, the posterolateral part of the head of the humerus is crushed resulting in the Hill-Sachs lesion. The clinical features include severe pain and the patient usually supports his dislocated arm with the opposite arm. On examination, the arm is usually abducted, externally rotated and the lateral outline of the shoulder may be straightened and sometimes a prominent acromion process or a bulge below the clavicle may be appreciated. The anteroposterior radiograph shows the humeral head lying below and medial to the glenoid socket. It may also show the Bankart lesion and the Hill-Sachs lesion. Other Options: Option A: Luxatio erecta is also known as inferior dislocation of shoulder. This is caused due to severe hyperabduction. The radiograph shows that the head of the humerus is present below the glenoid and the shaft is in an abducted position. Option B:  Light bulb sign is seen on AP radiographs in the posterior dislocation shoulder. In posterior dislocation of the shoulder, the humerus rotates internally. This causes changes to the normal radiographic contour of the head of the humerus. The humerus appears similar to a lightbulb in AP views. Pearl PF2105: Tests for anterior shoulder dislocation Bryant’s test: Anterior axillary fold is at a lower level on the dislocated side.   Dugas test: The patient is made to place the hand on the opposite shoulder. The examiner then applies gentle pressure on the flexed elbow to make it touch the chest. In shoulder dislocation, the elbow cannot be made to touch the chest.    Hamilton ruler test: In a normal shoulder, a ruler (scale) placed on the lateral side of the arm will not touch the lateral condyle of the humerus and the acromion at the same time. In anterior shoulder dislocation, the ruler will simultaneously touch the lateral condyle of the humerus and the acromion.      Callway Test: The vertical circumference of the axilla is increased on the dislocated side as compared to the normal side.  Pearl PF1173: Methods of reduction of shoulder dislocation Kocher's technique - TEAM (Traction → External Rotation → Adduction → Medial Rotation)  Hippocratic method- Surgeon applies a firm and steady pull on the semi-abducted arm by keeping his foot on the axilla against the chest wall. The foot is used as the fulcrum. Stimson's gravity technique: Patient is left prone and weight is attached to the elbow or wrist on the affected side. Gravity stretches the muscle and reduction occurs in 15-20 minutes.

text: 6. Identify the type of epiphysis.
expl:
Correct answer: B. Pressure Epiphysis

The image depicts the distal end of the tibia which is an example of a pressure epiphysis. The distal tibial epiphysis, near the ankle joint, is a pressure epiphysis because it primarily bears weight and compressive forces rather than muscular forces. Pressure epiphysis is articular in nature and takes part in the transmission of weight. Examples are the head of the femur, the lower end of radius, etc. Other options: Options A: Tubercles of humerus and trochanters of femur are examples of traction epiphysis because these are the site of major muscle attachments. Option C: An avulsion epiphysis is a small, separate ossification center that develops at sites where major tendons or ligaments attach to bone, forming due to the pulling forces (traction) of these attachments - common examples include the lesser trochanter of the femur (where psoas major attaches), greater trochanter (gluteal muscles attachment), and tibial tuberosity (patellar tendon attachment). Option D: An aberrant epiphysis is an accessory ossification center that appears near a main epiphysis but remains separate and typically doesn't contribute to longitudinal growth - examples include the os trigonum behind the talus, os subfibulare near the lateral malleolus, and os tibiale externum at the navicular tuberosity; the key distinction is that avulsion epiphyses form due to mechanical forces at attachment sites.

Correct answer: D. Pott's spine

The given spine MRI shows a patient with Pott's spine. The image depicts sagittal T1W (A) and T2W (B) images in a patient with spinal tuberculosis showing a well-defined, round lesion (arrow) with T1 hypointensity and T2 iso-hypointensity. * Pott's disease, also known as tuberculous spondylitis, refers to the vertebral body and intervertebral disc involvement in tuberculosis (TB). * The spine is the most frequent location of musculoskeletal TB, and commonly related symptoms are back pain and lower limb weakness/paraplegia. * The spine is involved due to hematogenous spread via the venous plexus of Batson. * There is usually a slow collapse of one or usually more vertebral bodies, which spreads underneath the longitudinal ligaments. * This results in an acute kyphotic or "gibbus" deformity. * This angulation, coupled with epidural granulation tissue and bony fragments, can lead to cord compression. Other options:  Option A: Ankylosing spondylitis: shows Squaring and bridging of the vertebral body, leading to a bamboo spine appearance. Option B: Multiple myeloma is the malignant production of plasma cells that results in bone pain or fractures, renal failure, increased susceptibility to infections, anemia, hypercalcemia, and manifestations of hyperviscosity. Radiography shows multiple well-defined, punched-out lytic lesions of various sizes scattered throughout the skull, giving the raindrop skull appearance. Option C: Pyogenic spondylitis denotes infections impacting different components of the spine, including the vertebrae, intervertebral discs, paraspinal soft tissue, or epidural space. This umbrella term covers conditions such as vertebral osteomyelitis, spondylodiscitis, and epidural abscess.

text: 8. A person presents with complaints of numbness, tingling and paresthesias of the thumb, index finger and middle finger. There is numbness at the dorsum of the base of the thumb as well. What structure is most likely to be damaged?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Median nerve

There may be weakness of thumb opposition. In chronic cases, the thenar eminence is wasted. Carpal tunnel syndrome is a common cause and can be associated with rheumatoid arthritis, pregnancy, chronic renal failure, acromegaly, hypothyroidism and gout. The diagnosis is usually made on clinical grounds but nerve conduction studies can confirm the diagnosis. Median nerve injuries: Distal injury: Thus an injury to the distal median nerve affects the 1st and 2nd lumbricals sparing the flexor digitorum profundus. This causes hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints, involving the index and middle fingers. This attitude of the hand known as the median claw hand may be seen at rest and is more pronounced on attempting to extend the fingers (attitude is similar to proximal ulnar injury). Proximal injury: Since the opposing flexor digitorum profundus of the 2nd and 3rd digit that causes the clawing is also affected, the clawing of the hand is less pronounced in distal injuries of the ulnar nerve. The deficits present during voluntary flexion of the digits. Thus, on attempting to make a fist, the flexion of the 2nd and 3rd digits is affected while the 4th and 5th digits are normal giving the Benediction hand sign. In both cases of median nerve palsy, there is loss of sensations on lateral 3½ digits including the nail beds and distal phalanges on the dorsum of the hand. Tinel's sign is positive where percussing over the median nerve reproduces symptoms. Phalen's test is positive where the symptoms are reproduced by holding the wrists in full flexion with the dorsum of the hands pressed together. Other Options:  Option A: Injury to the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve. It results in the loss of function of both flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) and flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS). Hence, the index finger sticks out when the patient is asked to clasp their hand.  Option B: In ulnar nerve palsy, only the medial two fingers develop clawing, while in a combined median and ulnar nerve palsy, all four fingers develop clawing.  Option C:  In radial nerve palsy, the patient presents with 'wrist drop' in case of paralyzed wrist extensors, and 'finger drop' when extensor digitorum is paralyzed. text: 1. A 17-year-old boy presents to the clinic with complaints of a painless lump on the lateral aspect of his left knee. The radiograph of the patient is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Osteochondroma

The given radiograph and clinical vignette suggest the diagnosis of osteochondroma.  Osteochondromas are benign bone tumors that present commonly in the adolescent age group. They usually present as painless masses in long bones like the femur or humerus. They are seen as well-defined bony protuberances which may be pedunculated or sessile. Pedunculated osteochondromas point away from the joint, towards the diaphysis. The cortex and cancellous bone of osteochondroma blend with that of the host bone. MRI shows a classical cartilaginous cap. Osteochondromas usually grow with skeletal maturity and stop once growth stops. They rarely undergo malignant transformation. Treatment is not indicated if the lesion does not produce symptoms. Excision can be done for large lesions with local pressure effects. Other options: Option A: Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia with the proliferation of plasma cells derived from a single clone. It is associated with increased osteoclast activity with suppression of osteoblast activity, causing punched-out lytic lesions in the bone and hypercalcemia. Option B: Chondroblastoma is a benign tumor and presents as a painful mass that causes effusion or stiffness. On x-ray, they are seen as round or oval lytic lesions in the epiphysis. The bony cortex is not breached but can appear expanded. The common sites are the ends of long bones. Microscopically, chondroblastoma consists of a sheet of chondroblasts embedded in the chondroid matrix. The calcification is often present and surrounds individual cells giving the appearance of ‘chicken wire.’ Option D: Osteoid osteoma is a benign tumor formed of osteoid and woven bone. text: 2. A 6-year-old boy presents to the OPD with the following findings. On examination, there is high-riding scapula with medial rotation on the left. What is the likely diagnosis?

Correct answer: B. Sprengel deformity

The image shows an upward elevation of the left scapula relative to the thoracic cage. This is characteristically seen in Sprengel deformity. Sprengel deformity is a congenital upward elevation of the scapula. It is due to the failure of the scapula to descend completely in embryonic life. The affected scapula is smaller, shaped differently, abnormally high, and somewhat prominent. Shoulder movements are usually painless. Abduction and elevation of shoulders may be limited due to fixation of the scapula. The Cavendish classification is used to grade the severity of Sprengel deformity.  If the deformity is mild, no treatment is required. In severe deformity, surgery may be indicated. text: 6. Which test is being performed to detect fixed flexion deformity at hip?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Thomas test

Thomas test is used to detect fixed flexion deformity of the hip.  Flexion deformity is seen in the initial stages of the disease. The patient keeps the hip in flexion as this is the position of ease and maximum joint capacity. Soft tissue contractures convert this into a fixed flexion deformity, making locomotion impossible. In an effort to bring the limb on the ground and to make locomotion possible, the lumbar spine undergoes exaggerated lordosis and thus conceals the fixed flexion deformity. This is revealed by the Thomas test. The easy passage of the examiner's hand between the bed and the back of the patient is considered as a positive test as normally this is not possible. Other options:  * Trendelenburg test is used to assess the weakness or paralysis of gluteus medius muscle.  * Telescopy test: To asses the stability of the hip joint. Positive telescopy test indicates hip dislocations or fracture neck of femur. * Ober's test is used in physical examination to identify the tightness of the iliotibial band.

text: 1. A 3-year-old child presented to your OPD with genu varum and softening of skull bones. There is bony depression over the chest. What is the most likely deficiency?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin D deficiency

The clinical scenario with genu varum, craniotabes and Harrison groove of the chest with the given lab parameters suggests rickets caused by vitamin D deficiency. Rickets occurs due to a nutritional deficiency in vitamin D. Decrease in vitamin D levels leads to decreased calcium and phosphate due to reduced absorption. The decreased calcium stimulates increased parathyroid hormone(PTH) production. ALP level is increased as it is involved in bone mineralization. Clinical features of rickets include: * General features include malnourishment, abdominal distension, proximal muscle weakness, etc. * Head: Softening of the skull bones, called craniotabes, delayed closure of fontanels. * Chest: Rachitic rosary, i.e. widening of the costochondral junctions that give the feeling of rosary beads on palpation. Harrison's groove, a horizontal groove in the lower chest, may appear from the inward pull of the softened ribs by the diaphragm during respiration. * Vertebral column abnormalities like scoliosis, kyphosis, and lordosis * In the distal extremities widening of the wrists and ankles, varus/ valgus deformities, windswept deformity (valgus on the side and varus on the contralateral side), anterior tibial bowing. The laboratory findings in rickets show normal/decreased serum calcium, decreased phosphorous, elevated PTH, and increased ALP levels Metabolic bone disorders due to nutritional deficiencies include: * Vitamin D deficiency leads to Rickets- in children * Osteomalacia- in adults * Secondary hyperparathyroidism  * Vitamin C deficiency leads to scurvy Other options: Option A: Vitamin A deficiency- can lead to night blindness and recurrent childhood infections- diarrhoea, and respiratory infections. Option C: Vitamin C deficiency - can lead to scurvy which has manifestations due to poor collagen synthesis- dry skin, poor wound healing, swelling of the knee and ankle, and radiographic findings of a radiolucent band (Trümmerfeld zone) under a white line of Fränkel. Option D: Vitamin K deficiency- can be seen in neonates due to non-colonised gut, and in adults with chronic antibiotics-lead to manifestations of clotting disorders- purpura, ecchymoses. Pearl PF1660: Radiological features of rickets Radiological features of rickets: * Loss of provisional zone of calcification: earliest radiological finding of rickets.  * Delayed appearance of the epiphysis * Widening of growth plate: normal width of growth is 2-4mm. It is increased in cases of rickets due to excessive accumulation of uncalcified osteoid at the growth plate. * Cupping of metaphysis: normally metaphysis meets epiphysis as a smooth line of sclerosis. But in rickets the line is absent and the metaphyseal ends appear irregular and the cartilage accumulating in the growth plate creates a depression in the metaphysis causing cupping. * Fraying: indistinct margins of the metaphysis * Bowing of diaphysis, with thinning of cortices * In healing rickets, zone of calcification becomes denser.  The above features are prominent at the growth plates where growth is greatest: * Knee: distal femur, proximal tibia * Wrist: especially the ulna * Anterior rib ends: rachitic rosary The below image shows bowing of legs in rickets. Pearl PF0382: Important Clinical Features of Rickets Pearl PF1801: Radiological features of scurvy Radiological features of scurvy: * Generalised osteopenia * Pencil-point cortex: Cortical thinning * Periosteal reaction due to subperiosteal hemorrhage * Scorbutic rosary: Expansion of the costochondral junctions * Hemarthrosis * Wimberger ring: Circular, opaque radiological shadow surrounding epiphyseal centers of ossification, which may result from bleeding * Frenkel line: Dense zone of provisional calcification  * Trummerfeld zone: Lucent metaphyseal band underlying Frankel line * Pelken spur: Metaphyseal spurs which result in cupping of the metaphysis

Seddon's classification includes 3 groups

  2. Axonotmesis
  3. Neurotmesis

Reversible physiologic conduction block. Occurs due to mechanical pressure causing segmental demyelination.

text: 3. A 55-year-old man presents with decreased hearing. The skull radiograph shows the following appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Paget’s disease

The given clinical scenario and cotton wool skull appearance on the radiograph are suggestive of Paget's disease. Paget's disease is a disease of bone remodelling. Normally, osteoclasts remove the old bones while osteoblasts form new bones. In this disease,  osteoclasts are more active than osteoblasts. leading to more bone absorption than normal. The osteoblasts try to keep up by making new bone, but they overreact and make excess bone that is abnormally large, deformed and fits together haphazardly. Increased bone formation in Paget's disease may lead to the narrowing of the foramina of the skull. This causes compression of the cranial nerves which may lead to deafness, as seen in this patient. Deafness due to the narrowing of cranial nerve foramina is also seen in osteopetrosis. It can be differentiated from Paget's disease by the absence of lytic lesions of the bone. Other skull radiological findings in Paget's disease: * Osteoporosis circumscripta - Large well-defined lytic lesions involving the inner part of the outer table of the skull with an intact inner table * Diploic widening * Tam o' Shanter sign Option A: In thalassemia, X-ray of the skull will show crew cut appearance. text: 5. A 19-year-old man presented with progressive swelling of the lower end of the femur. X-ray of this patient shows a Codman triangle. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Osteosarcoma

The given clinical scenario of a young patient with a tumour in the distal femur with a Codmnan's triangle on X-ray suggests a probable diagnosis of osteosarcoma.  Osteosarcoma is the most common non-hematologic primary malignancy of bone. It occurs most commonly in the second decade of life. It is typically metaphyseal. The distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus are common sites. In osteosarcoma, the tumour lifts the periosteum and incites an intense periosteal reaction. The periosteal reaction is irregular and it may take the form of a Codman's triangle or it may have a sunburst (sunray) appearance on x-ray. The x-ray would show the following features. * Irregular destruction in the metaphysis is overshadowed by the formation of new bone * Lifting of the periosteum due to the formation of new bone inciting a periosteal reaction * Bone formation along the blood vessels within the tumour centrifugally gives rise to a sunburst (sunray) appearance on the radiograph. Since here safe margins are difficult to achieve limb ablation is done.  The goal of neoadjuvant and adjuvant chemotherapy is to treat micrometastasis. T-10 protocol of chemotherapy is used in the management of osteosarcoma. It involves: * High-dose methotrexate and Citrovorum factor rescue * Adriamycin * BCD (bleomycin, cyclophosphamide, dactinomycin/doxorubicin) Option A: Aneurysmal bone cysts are blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septae. X-ray shows expansile lytic lesions in the metaphyses of the upper tibia. Option B: Ewing Sarcoma- lesion with poorly marginated edges in the diaphysis of the bone. The lamellated periosteal reaction in diaphysis is suggestive of Ewing’s sarcoma which is a highly radiosensitive tumour. Option D: Osteoid osteoma is a benign tumour which occurs in the diaphyses of the femur. Classically, the pain is relieved after using NSAID. Codman's triangle is not seen. text: 1. An elderly patient presented after a fall in the bathroom. X-ray of the right hip shows the fracture depicted below. What is the most likely type of fracture?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Intertrochanteric fracture

In an elderly patient with a history of fall and X-ray clearly showing a fracture line running between the greater trochanter and the lesser trochanter of the femur points towards the Intertrochanteric fracture. Fractures in the inter-trochanteric region of the proximal femur, involving either the greater or the lesser trochanter or both, are grouped as intertrochanteric fractures. In the elderly, the fracture is normally sustained by a sideways fall or a blow over the greater trochanter. In the young, it occurs following violent trauma, as in a road traffic accident. Clinical features include a history of a fall or road accident, followed by pain in the region of the groin and an inability to move the leg. There will be swelling in the region of the hip, and the leg will be short and externally rotated. There is tenderness over the greater trochanter. According to Kyle classification, there are 4 types of Intertrochanteric fractures: * Type 1: Undisplaced, uncomminuted * Type 2: Displaced, minimal comminuted, lesser trochanter fracture * Type 3: Displaced, comminuted, greater trochanter fracture * Type 4: Severely comminuted, subtrochanter extension(Also reverse oblique) Complications include malunion and osteoarthritis. Management: The intertrochanteric fractures of the femur can be treated by intramedullary and extramedullary implants. * Intramedullary implants include proximal femoral nail and gamma nail which are used in displaced/unstable intertrochanteric fractures of the femur. Compared to dynamic hip screws, the intramedullary fixation with proximal femoral nails has smaller incisions, decreased blood loss, decreased femoral neck shortening, and decreased risk of infection. * Extramedullary implants include a dynamic hip screw which is used in undisplaced/stable inter-trochanteric fractures Other options: Option B: Subtrochanteric fracture occur between the inferior margin of the lesser trochanter and 5 cm below this point. Option C:  Femoral head fractures are always seen in association with a dislocation or subluxation of the femoral head. Acetabular, femoral shaft and femoral neck fractures are often associated with femoral head fractures. Option D: In the given X-ray, it is an oblique type of fracture.

text: 2. A 12-year-old boy presents with chronic swelling and pain over the upper tibia.There is no history of trauma. His radiographic image is shown below. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

Correct answer: C. Brodie's abscess

The given clinical scenario of a child with prolonged swelling and pain over the upper tibia, along with a radiograph showing a lytic lesion with a dense sclerotic rim and minimal periosteal reaction, suggests the diagnosis of Brodie's abscess. Brodie's abscess is a localized form of subacute osteomyelitis that occurs when organisms of low virulence infect an immunocompetent host. The abscess is walled off by the thickening of the surrounding bone trabeculae. It most commonly involves the metaphysis of the proximal tibia and distal femur. The patient is typically a child or adolescent experiencing prolonged pain near a large joint for several weeks or months. Symptoms may include a limp, slight swelling, muscle wasting, and localized tenderness. The typical radiographic finding is a circumscribed, round or oval radiolucent cavity measuring 1-2 cm in diameter, surrounded by a halo of sclerosis, with minimal or no periosteal reaction. The radioisotope scan shows markedly increased activity. MRI may be helpful in diagnosis. Open biopsy with curettage is indicated if there is any doubt in the diagnosis. Differential diagnoses include: * Cystic tuberculosis * Eosinophilic granuloma * Osteoid osteoma * Ewing's sarcoma Treatment: * Immobilization and antibiotics (flucloxacillin and fusidic acid) intravenous for 4-5 days, followed by oral administration for another 6 weeks; healing may take up to 12 months * Curettage is needed if the x-rays show no healing after conservative management. The following X-ray and MRI images show Brodie's abscess of the radius in a patient. It is common in men and most commonly occurs in the diaphysis of the femur. It is characterized by night pains relieved by medication. Nidus of osteoid osteoma is seen in the cortex and hence CT is the investigation of choice. Option D: Aneurysmal bone cysts are benign, locally destructive, multiloculated cysts filled with blood. text: 4. A young athlete presents with a meniscal tear. Imaging reveals that the tear involves the white–white zone of the meniscus. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment modality?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Meniscectomy

The white–white zone (avascular inner zone) meniscal tears heal poorly due to lack of blood supply, making meniscal repair ineffective and, leading to partial meniscectomy as the preferred treatment. The menisci are divided into three zones depending on the perfusion of blood. The menisci are supplied by perimeniscal blood vessels from superior and inferior branches of medial and lateral genicular vessels. Following birth, the menisci become increasingly avascular. By adulthood, only the peripheral 10% to 25% of the tissue is perfused. This gives rise to 3 distinct regions of the menisci: * The peripheral relatively vascularised region is called the red-red zone (Zone 1) * A zone of transition between the 2 zones, which is called the red-white zone (Zone 2) * The completely avascular inner zone, known as the white-white zone (Zone 3) There is a direct relationship between the vascularization and capacity of the tissue to heal, predisposing the white-white zone to permanent post-traumatic and degenerative lesions. Other options: Option B: Meniscal repair is suitable only in meniscal tears within the vascular zones. Option C: Conservative management can be tried for minor tears in vascular zones, but a symptomatic white–white zone injury due to avascularity results in failure.

text: 8. A young man, a road traffic accident (RTA) patient with a fracture of the shaft of the femur, develops shortness of breath, a drop in SaO₂, and altered mental status 3 days later. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Fat embolism

The clinical scenario of sudden onset breathlessness and altered mental status on 3rd day of following a femoral shaft fracture should raise suspicion of fat embolism. Fat embolism is the presence of fat globules in vital organs and peripheral circulation after fracture of the long bone or other major trauma. Fat embolism is a frequent complication after limb fractures. In most adults with closed long bone fractures, fat globules larger than 10 μm circulate in the bloodstream, and histological evidence of fat can often be detected in the lungs and other internal organs.  Clinical features of fat embolism are usually seen within 72 hours.  Pathogenesis- release of free fatty acids by the action of lipases on the neutral fats and actual obstruction of small pulmonary vessels by fat globules. Clinical features: * Early signs are fever and tachycardia. * Presenting features are of 2 types: * Cerebral type: drowsiness, restlessness, disorientation. * Pulmonary type: tachypnoea, tachycardia. * Other features: petechial rash in front of neck/anterior axillary fold/ chest/ conjunctiva. The classical clinical triad consists of  * respiratory distress * petechial haemorrhages * neurological abnormalities  Treatment of fat embolism is mainly supportive: * Respiratory support (oxygen) * Heparinization (increases lipoprotein lipase activity) * Intravenous low molecular weight dextran * Corticosteroids: To avoid pneumonitis * Prompt stabilization of long-bone fractures  Other Options: Option A: Gas gangrene wound infections are associated with severe local wound(blackish) pain and crepitus  Option B: Sepsis, usually accompanied by fever, tachycardia, hypotension, and a source of infection. Option C: Pulmonary embolism usually manifests as a sudden onset of shortness of breath, frequently accompanied by pleuritic chest pain and an increased heart rate. Pearl PF1166: Gurd's criteria for diagnosing fat embolism syndrome Major criteria * Axillary or subconjunctival petechiae * Hypoxemia with PaO2 <60 mmHg, FIO2 < 0.4 * CNS depression disproportionate to the hypoxemia * Pulmonary edema Minor criteria * Tachycardia (HR >110 beats per minute) * Pyrexia (temp >38.50C) * Emboli visible in retina * Fat globules in urine * Fat globules in sputum * Unexplanied drop in hematocrit or platelet count  * Increased ESR  At least one major criterion and four minor criteria are required to make a diagnosis of fat embolism syndrome.

text: 9. Injury at which of the following marked sites causes failure of dorsiflexion?
expl:
Correct answer: A. 3

The site marked as '3' in the x-ray given above is the neck of the fibula. Injury at this site causes failure of dorsiflexion (foot drop) due to injury to the common fibular nerve (also known as the common peroneal nerve). The common fibular nerve is derived from the dorsal branches of the 4th and 5th lumbar and 1st and 2nd sacral ventral rami. It runs obliquely along the lateral side of the popliteal fossa to the fibular head. It lies between the biceps femoris and the lateral head of the gastrocnemius. text: 2. A patient presents with hip pain and true shortening of the limb which was diagnosed as tuberculosis of the hip. Which stage of the disease is he currently in?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Stage of advanced arthritis

In a patient with tuberculosis of the hip, true shortening of the limb is seen in the advanced arthritis. Clinical features seen in the four stages of TB hip: * Stage of synovitis presents with apparent lengthening of the limb due to abduction deformity.  * Stage of early arthritis presents with apparent shortening of the limb due to adduction deformity. * Stage of advanced arthritis leads to true shortening of the limb because of the destruction of the articular cartilage of the femur and the acetabulum. * Stage of arthritis with subluxation leads to true shortening of the limb. The destruction of acetabulum leads to dislocation of the femur head. This is also known as wandering acetabulum/ mortar and pestle hip because of the widened acetabulum and diminished size of femur head. The TB of the hip finally results in fibrous ankylosis of the hip joint. Note: The apparent length of the limb is measured from the umbilicus to the medial malleolus and the true length of the limb is measured from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial malleolus. The apparent length is increased when there is abduction deformity of the limb and decreased when there is adduction deformity of the limb.

text: 4. A patient after sleeping whole night with the arm hanging over the back of the chair, wakes up with inability to extend his wrist. This is due to _____
expl:
Correct answer: D. Neuropraxia

This is a case of saturday night palsy, which is a type of neuropraxia.  Neuropraxia is a reversible physiological block in nerve conduction. Saturday night palsy occurs when radial nerve is compressed in the arm from direct pressure against a firm object. It can occur when the person sleeps on the arm, often after alcohol intoxication. Therefore, it is known as Saturday night palsy or weekend palsy. Other examples for neuropraxia include crutch palsy and tourniquet palsy. Pearl PF1196: Seddon's classification of nerve injuries

Seddon's classification includes 3 groups

  1. Neurapraxia
  2. Axonotmesis
  3. Neurotmesis

Neurapraxia:

Reversible physiologic conduction block. Occurs due to mechanical pressure causing segmental demyelination.

E.g.,Saturday night palsy, torniquet, and crutch palsy

Axonotmesis: 

Axonal interruption. Conduction is lost but the nerve is in continuity and neural tubes are intact.

E.g.,Closed fractures and dislocations

Neurotmesis: 

Division of the nerve trunk. Endoneurial tube destruction also occurs.

E.g., Complete section of nerve in open fractures

text: 1. Which of the following enzymes is responsible for the immortality of the cancer cells?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Telomerase

Telomerase is the enzyme that prevents the shortening of telomeres. With every cell division, there is some shortening of telomeres at the ends of chromosomes. Once the telomeres are shortened beyond a certain point, it may cause cell-cycle arrest or apoptosis. This is called replicative senescence. Telomerase is present in some cells, like the germ cells, and absent in most somatic cells. Reactivation of telomerase is a critical step in the development of about 85% of human cancers, which enables the cells to divide several times than normal.

text: 3. A 9-month-old boy presents with progressive pallor and abdominal distention. On investigations, hepatosplenomegaly and malar eminence is seen and his peripheral blood smear is as shown below. He has low Hb, Mentzer index is found to be less than 13. What diagnosis would this signify in this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Thalassemia

The clinical scenario, peripheral blood smear showing target cells and aniso-poikilocytes, along with the Mentzer index of less than 13 suggests Thalassemia. Thalassemia syndromes: Alpha- and beta-thalassemia are inherited disorders in which there is reduced production of alpha-globin or beta-globin chains, respectively. This leads to precipitation of the excess (unpaired) chains, interfering with red blood cell (RBC) production and survival. Disease severity is inversely correlated with the number of functioning globin chains. Clinical features in thalassemia: * Anemia * Jaundice and pigment gallstones * Skeletal deformities including facial deformities, changes in body habitus, osteopenia/osteoporosis * Iron overload * Growth impairment * Hepatosplenomegaly * Endocrine abnormalities including hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus * Heart failure and arrhythmias Laboratory studies: * Peripheral smear is likely to show microcytic hypochromic anemia with target cells, teardrop cells, and some coarse basophilic stippling in certain cases. These findings are non-specific.  * High RBC count  * Low reticulocyte count * High LDH, high indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin, and negative Coomb's test * High transferrin saturation, normal serum iron levels, elevated ferritin levels MCV/RBC count also known as Mentzer index can be used to distinguish thalassemia from iron-deficiency anemia (IDA). MCV (mean corpuscular volume) and MCH (mean corpuscular hemoglobin) are low in both IDA and thalassemia. RBC count may be normal in thalassemia, whereas it is reduced in IDA. A lower RBC count in IDA means the denominator is smaller, yielding a greater MCV/RBC ratio. Mentzer index is: * More than 13 in iron-deficiency anemia * Less than 13 in thalassemia Thalassemia syndromes and iron deficiency anemia (IDA) are the two most common etiologies of microcytic hypochromic anemia in children and adults. text: 2. During wound healing, the cells that appear first due to chemotaxis , at the site of the wound is ____________
expl:
Correct answer: A. Neutrophils

The earliest cells to appear because of chemotaxis are Neutrophils. Neutrophils appear within 24 hours but the neutrophil peak is seen on day 2 of the inflammatory phase of wound healing. Wound healing : Wound healing occurs in two distinct mechanisms -  * Wound healing by first intention / Primary union * Wound healing by secondary intention / Secondary union Primary union / Wound healing by the first intention: This is seen in cases where there is an injury that involves the epithelial layer only. An example of such healing is seen in a clean surgical incision approximated by sutures. The steps involved in primary union are as follows.  * Injury causes the activation of the coagulation cascade and subsequent clot formation. This clot attracts growth factors, cytokines, chemokines, and migrating cells. * Within the first 24 hours, the neutrophils migrate to the site of injury. Within 24-48 hours, even epithelial cells from both edges of the wound begin to migrate and form a thin layer of epidermis over the wound. * By day 3 neutrophils are mainly replaced by macrophages and granulation tissue starts forming. This process of neovascularisation reaches its peak on day 5.  * Deposition of collagen and fibroblast proliferation is seen in the second week. By the end of the first month, the scar comprises a cellular connective tissue largely devoid of inflammatory cells and covered by an essentially normal epidermis. Secondary union / Wound healing by second intention : Wounds heal by secondary intention when the wound is large involving a more significant loss of cells and tissues. It differs from primary healing in various ways such as: * Since the wound is large, the blood clot formed is large. This leads to increased inflammation and increased formation of granulation tissue. * The provisional matrix has fibrin, plasma fibronectin, and type III collagen. In two weeks it is replaced by type I collagen. By the end of 1 month, the scar tissue is mainly made of acellular connective tissue. * Myofibroblasts present in the connective tissue cause wound contraction. Note: However,the cells that appear first at the site of an injury are Platelets, as a part of initially activated coagulation pathways. Pearl PF1616: White cell peaks during wound healing

text: 5. Which amongst the following molecules helps in the adhesion of the leucocyte to the endothelium during inflammation?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Selectins

Of the above options, selectins help in the adhesion of the leucocyte to the endothelium during inflammation.  The two major families of molecules involved in leukocyte adhesion and migration are the selectins and integrins. The initial rolling interactions are mediated by a family of proteins called selectins. These are low-affinity interactions with a fast off-rate, and they are easily disrupted by the flowing blood. There are three types of selectins: * L-selectin on leukocytes - CD62L * E-selectin on endothelium - CD62E * P-selectin in platelets - CD62P The expression of selectins and their ligands is regulated by cytokines produced in response to infection and injury. The recruitment of leukocytes to the site of inflammation is a multi-step process, that is mediated by adhesion molecules and cytokines called chemokines. This process can be divided into sequential phases: * In the lumen: margination, rolling and adhesion to the endothelium occurs. * Migration of the leukocytes across the endothelium and vessel wall * Migration in the tissues towards a chemotactic stimulus. The process of leukocyte recruitment is as follows: * Margination: Because of dilation of the inflamed postcapillary venues, there is stasis of blood flow and hence more leukocytes assume a peripheral position along the endothelial surface; this process of leukocyte redistribution is called margination. * Rolling: the slowed leukocytes then sense the signals from the endothelium and start rolling on the vessel wall. * Cytokine-mediated integrin activation: the attachment of leukocytes to the endothelial cells requires adhesion molecules that are activated by cytokines. The major families of proteins involved in adhesion and migration are selectins and integrins and their ligands. * Adhesions: the weak rolling interactions slow down the leukocytes and allow them to bind more firmly to the endothelium. Chemokines that were produced at the site of injury bind to the endothelial cell proteoglycans. These chemokines then bind to the rolling leukocytes and activate them. This is turn converts the ligands for β1 and β2 integrins, VLA-4 and LFA-1 present on the leukocytes to a high-affinity state. * This combination of cytokine-induced expression of integrin ligands on the endothelium and increased integrin affinity on the leukocytes leads to firm adhesion of leukocytes to the endothelium at the site of inflammation. * Leukocyte migration: this is the movement of leukocytes through intact endothelium, called transmigration or diapedesis. This occurs in postcapillary venules. This migration occurs through the inter endothelial gap towards the chemical concentration gradient created by the chemokines at the site of injury. This occurs with the help of adhesion molecules present in the intercellular junctions such as Platelet Endothelial Cell Adhesion Molecule (PECAM-1) or CD31. Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative disorder with the peak incidence in the fifth to sixth decade of life. 8. An 18-year-old male presented to the outpatient department with gum bleeding and fever for the past 2 months. General examination showed pallor and the systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory examination revealed Hb level- 3 gm/dl, TLC- 1500/microL, platelet count- 15000/microL. Peripheral smear shows macrocytes and the reticulocyte count is 0.5. Bone marrow examination revealed fatty streaks and absent megakaryocytes but no immature cells. What is the likely diagnosis?

Hb- Hemoglobin

TLC- Total leucocyte count
expl:
Correct answer: A. Idiopathic acquired aplastic anemia

The given clinical scenario showing a young male with gum bleeding, fever, pancytopenia, and a low reticulocyte count with bone marrow showing fatty streaks and no immature cells is suggestive of idiopathic acquired aplastic anemia. Aplastic anemia is a syndrome characterized by chronic hematopoietic failure and pancytopenia. The common causes include: * Acquired  * Idiopathic (most common cause, about 65% of the cases) * Acquired stem-cell defects  * Immune-mediated * Chemical agents  * Dose-related (alkylating agents, antimetabolites, benzene, chloramphenicol, inorganic arsenals)  * Idiosyncratic (chloramphenicol, phenylbutazone, organic arsenicals, carbamazepine, penicillamine, gold salts)  * Physical agents  * Whole-body irradiation * Viral infections (hepatitis, Cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, Varicella-Zoster virus) * Inherited  * Fanconi anemia  * Telomerase defects  Pathogenesis involves an extrinsic immune-mediated suppression of bone marrow and an intrinsic abnormality of the stem cells.  Clinical features and diagnosis: There is no age or sex predisposition for aplastic anemia. It presents insidiously with features of pancytopenia such as pallor, petechiae, and ecchymosis. Recurrent infections and fever occur as a result of neutropenia. Reticulocytopenia is seen and splenomegaly is characteristically absent. Bone marrow biopsy is used for diagnosis. Histology: Bone marrow aspirate usually results in a dry tap. Examination shows a hypocellular marrow devoid of hematopoietic cells with remnant fat cells, fibrous stroma, and scattered lymphocytes. Red cells are usually slightly macrocytic and normochromic. The following image shows a hypocellular bone marrow with little hematopoiesis and several fat cells. Other options:  Option B - Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is an acquired disorder resulting from the mutation in the phosphatidylinositol glycan complementation group A gene (PIGA), an enzyme that is essential for the synthesis of membrane-associated complement regulatory proteins. Red cells deficient in these proteins are susceptible to intravascular hemolysis. Patients with PNH usually present with pancytopenia and reticulocytosis with bone marrow biopsy showing a cellular marrow with marked to massive erythroid hyperplasia. Option C - Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are a group of clonal stem cell disorders. It is a consequence of maturation defects that result in ineffective hematopoiesis with a high predisposition to conversion to AML. They are characterized by a hypercellular marrow with dysplastic cells on bone marrow aspirate. Marrow changes seen in MDS are given in the pearl below. Option D - Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and patients often present with fever, productive cough, blood-streaked sputum, night sweats, malaise, loss of appetite, and weight loss. Dysplasia of erythroid series appears as * Ring sideroblasts- Erythroblasts with stainable iron in the cytoplasm * Megaloblastoid maturation- Abnormally large erythroid cells * Nuclear budding abnormalities- Nucleus with abnormal shape   Dysplasia of myeloid series  * Neutrophils with a decreased number of secondary granules * Pseudo-Pelger-Hüet cells- neutrophils with only two nuclear lobes   Dysplasia of the megakaryocytes-  * Megakaryocyte with single nuclear lobe * Pawn ball megakaryocytes- cells with multiple separate nuclei If only one lineage is affected, then it is called single lineage dysplasia. If multiple lineages are affected, then it is called multilineage dysplasia. If the percentage of ring sideroblasts is more than 15% it is called MDS with ring sideroblasts (MDS-RS).

text: 12. What is the gene mutation seen in hemochromatosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. HFE

Mutation in the HFE gene on the short arm of the 6th chromosome is seen in hemochromatosis. Hemochromatosis is an inherited genetic disorder. Mutation of the HFE gene leads to excessive absorption of iron which gets deposited in the liver, pancreas, followed by the heart, joints, and endocrine organs. Histopathology shows golden yellow hemosiderin granules in the cytoplasm of hepatocytes which stain positive with Prussian blue stain. Serum iron is raised. Serum ferritin is significantly increased. Hepatomegaly will be present in the majority of the patients with symptoms. Skin shows bronze pigmentation due to the increased deposition of iron and melanin over the dermis. Glucose levels are deranged or diabetes mellitus is seen due to the direct damage of the pancreatic islet cells by the deposition of iron. Congestive cardiac failure is the most common cardiac manifestation of hemochromatosis. Features of cardiac failure will develop suddenly, get rapidly progressed, and if left untreated it may cause death. Hypogonadism due to failure of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis by deposition of iron. This may manifest as testicular atrophy or amenorrhea It is managed by weekly or twice weekly phlebotomy of 500 mL. Chelating agents like subcutaneous deferoxamine, and oral deferasirox are effective. The main cause of death in hemochromatosis is cardiac failure.  Other options: Option B: PTEN is a tumor suppressor gene. Mutation of this gene is associated with Cowden syndrome that leads to multiple cancers like breast cancer, prostate cancer, endometrial cancer, and colorectal cancer. Option C: ATP7B gene mutation causes Wilson's disease which is an autosomal recessive disorder. Option D: MRP2 protein is associated with Dubin-Johnson syndrome.

text: 1. A family pedigree chart is given below. Identify the mode of inheritance of this condition.
expl:
Correct answer: A. Autosomal dominant

The pedigree chart given is suggestive of an autosomal dominant inheritance. Such an inheritance has a vertical pattern in pedigree charts where individuals of each generation are affected (parents and children). Males and females are equally affected and each affected individual has a 50% chance of passing the deleterious gene to their offspring. The following flow chart helps in making out the pattern of inheritance from a given pedigree chart. According to the above flowchart: Step 1: All affected individuals have an affected parent. Since multiple generations are affected it is a dominant inheritance pattern. Step 2: Male-to-male transmission is present. The disorder thus has an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Pearl PF0346: Pedigree chart for different inheritance patterns   Autosomal Dominant Disorders: * With every autosomal dominant disorder, some patients do not have affected parents. Such patients owe their disorder to new mutations involving either the egg or the sperm from which they were derived. * Clinical features can be modified by variations in penetrance and expressivity. * In many conditions, the age at onset is delayed, and symptoms and signs may not appear until adulthood (as in Huntington disease). X-linked Recessive Conditions: * All sex-linked disorders are X-linked, and almost all are recessive. * Several genes are located in the “male-specific region of Y;” all these are related to spermatogenesis. * Males with mutations affecting the Y-linked genes are usually infertile, and hence, there is no Y-linked inheritance. * An affected male does not transmit the disorder to his sons, but all daughters are carriers. * Sons of heterozygous women have, of course, a one-in-two chance of receiving the mutant gene. * Heterozygous females express the disorder partially because of random inactivation of one X chromosome.

text: 2. Which of the following cells is responsible for the destruction of bacterial foreign bodies in liver sinusoids?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Kupffer cells

Kupffer cells, also known as stellate macrophages and Kupffer-Borowicz cells; are specialized macrophages of the liver that are responsible for the destruction of bacterial foreign bodies. These cells are present in the walls of the sinusoids and not in the perisinusoidal space (Space of Disse). They are responsible for removing cellular and microbial debris from the circulation, and also for secreting cytokines involved in defense. Macrophages can be divided into: * Blood macrophages (monocytes) are the largest of the lymphoid cells in the peripheral blood. Life span: 3 days.  * Tissue macrophages survive for months.  2 main functions of macrophages: * Phagocytosis. * Antigen presentation. All the options given are various types of cells present in an adult liver. Option A: Hepatocytes are polyhedral cells with a central spherical nucleus, arranged in a single-cell layer. Every hepatocyte has contact with adjacent hepatocytes (with gap junctions for intercellular communication), bile canaliculus, and the space of Disse/perisinusoidal space (hepatocytes project multiple microvilli into this space for active transport of substances.) Option B: Ito cells or hepatic stellate cells are present in the space of Disse and store vitamin A. They are mesenchymal in origin and take part in the development of hepatic fibrosis. Option C: Sinusoidal endothelial cells are flat cells with a central nucleus and are joined to each other by junctional complexes. Their cytoplasm contains numerous transcytotic vesicles. These are separated from hepatocytes by the space of Disse (perisinusoidal space). text: 5. A 65-year-old man dies due to myocardial infarction. Which of the following stains can be used to see the infarct in the heart while conducting an autopsy?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride

Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride stain can be used to see the infarct in the heart. Myocardial infarcts less than 12 hours old are usually not apparent on gross examination. This gross histochemical stain imparts a brick-red color to intact, noninfarcted myocardium where lactate dehydrogenase activity is preserved. text: 6. A 70-year-old male comes with complaints of hip pain. An X-ray of the hip shows lytic lesions and serum calcium levels are elevated. Bone marrow plasma cells are 42% and the cells seen are given in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Multiple myeloma

In an elderly male patient, the presence of hypercalcemia, lytic bone lesions, bone marrow plasma cells of more than 10%, and the characteristic Mott cell as seen in the image suggest multiple myeloma. Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia with the proliferation of plasma cells derived from a single clone. It is associated with increased osteoclast activity with suppression of osteoblast activity, causing punched-out lytic lesions in the bone and hypercalcemia. The incidence of multiple myeloma increases with age, and it is more commonly seen in males than in females. Signs and symptoms * Bone pain is the most common symptom * Pathologic fractures * Recurrent bacterial infections * Renal failure * Normocytic normochromic anemia elevated ESR, Hypercalcemia, normal ALP (ALP is a marker of bone growth and hence is not increased in multiple myeloma) * Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray * Electrophoresis: Monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin * Urinalysis: Free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins) * Bone marrow biopsy: 10 to 20% plasma cells (normal is < 5%) and presence of Dutcher bodies, Russel bodies, and Mott cells. * Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation (High level of M proteins in myeloma causes red cells in the peripheral blood smears to stick to one another in linear arrays, a finding referred to as rouleaux formation) Option A: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is usually asymptomatic at diagnosis but can present with easy fatigability, weight loss, and anorexia. Generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are usually seen. Peripheral smear contains a large number of monotonous, uniform-looking, mature lymphocytes, which is often described as a convent-girl appearance. Option B: Acute lymphocytic leukemia presents with a hypercellular marrow that is packed with lymphoblasts. These lymphoblasts, when compared to myeloblasts, have more condensed chromatin with less prominent nucleoli. Option C: In chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), patients typically present with a dragging sensation in the abdomen due to splenomegaly or splenic infarct, fatigue, malaise, and weight loss. The peripheral smear contains neutrophils and their precursors of various sizes and configurations like band cells, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and blasts. Hence, the histological picture is described as having a garden party or a college girl appearance. Pearl PF0569: Some Pathological Cells/Bodies in Multiple Myeloma

text: 7. A young person with recurrent seasonal conjunctivitis presents with itchiness and watering in the eyes. What is the most likely cell involved in the immediate phase of this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Mast cells

The given clinical features of allergic reactions suggest Type 1 hypersensitivity which is mediated by immunoglobulin E (IgE) binding to mast cells. Immediate (Type I) Hypersensitivity, also called allergic reactions or allergies is a rapid immunologic reaction that is triggered by the binding of an antigen to an IgE antibody on the surface of mast cells. It has two phases. Early phase: The mediators produced by the mast cells are responsible for most of the immediate hypersensitivity reactions. Histamine and leukotrienes are released rapidly from the sensitized mast cells and trigger intense immediate reactions characterized by edema, mucus secretion, and smooth muscle spasm. Other mediators involved in the early phase are,  * Enzymes: neutral proteases (chymase, tryptase) and acid hydrolases * Proteoglycans: heparin and chondroitin sulfate * Lipid mediators: Platelet-activating factor (PAF) Late-phase: The late-phase reaction is characterized by the recruitment of leukocytes, that amplify and sustain the inflammatory response without exposure to the triggering antigen. Mediators involved in the late phase of type 1 hypersensitivity reaction are: * Cytokines: TNF, IL-1, IL-4, IL-5, and chemokines (eotaxin) * Leukocytes (eosinophils) * Major Basic Protein (MBP) * Eosinophil cationic protein The sequence of events in immediate (type 1) hypersensitivity Though eosinophils and neutrophils are involved later in the pathogenesis, mast cells are central to the development of immediate hypersensitivity. In the picture given above, Reed–Sternberg (RS) cells are seen, which is a pathognomonic feature of Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL). text: 9. Which of the following is implicated in the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Autoimmunity

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic inflammatory disorder of autoimmune origin that principally attacks the joints, producing nonsuppurative, proliferative, and inflammatory synovitis. The inflammation progresses to the destruction of the articular cartilage and ankylosis of the joints. In RA, the synovium contains germinal centers with secondary follicles and abundant plasma cells, which produce antibodies, some are autoantibodies. Many of the autoantibodies produced in the lymphoid organs are specific for citrullinated peptides (CCPs). 80% of patients have serum IgM or IgA autoantibodies that bind to the Fc portions of their own IgG. These autoantibodies are called rheumatoid factor and may also be deposited in joints as immune complexes. The characteristic histologic features of RA include: * Increased vascularity due to angiogenesis * Dense inflammatory infiltrates * Synovial cell hyperplasia and proliferation * Fibrinopurulent exudate (synovial and joint surfaces) * Subcutaneous nodule: Necrotising granulomas with a central area of fibrinoid necrosis. * Osteoclastic activity (underlying bone)                        This all together leads to a mass of edematous synovium called pannus, which grows over the articular cartilage and causes its erosion.

text: 11. An 8-year-old boy presents with progressive muscle weakness and walking difficulties. On examination, pseudohypertrophy of calf muscles was noted. Which of the following is true regarding this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Absent dystrophin

History of progressive muscle weakness and walking difficulties with characteristic finding of pseudohypertrophy of calf muscles points to a diagnosis of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD).  Dystrophin protein (a sarcolemmal protein), is absent in these patients due to a mutation in the dystrophin gene. Dystrophin connects actin filaments to the transmembrane protein β-dystroglycan in the sarcolemma by the smaller proteins syntrophins in the cytoplasm. Lack of dystrophin leads to cellular instability, which leads to progressive leakage of intracellular components. Duchenne muscular dystrophy: * Most common hereditary neuromuscular disease * It is an X-linked recessive disorder, and the causative gene is located at Xp21. * Clinical features * Progressive weakness with developmental delay occurs. * Pseudohypertrophy of calves and wasting of thigh muscles are seen. * Trendelenburg gait or hip waddle is characteristic. * Gower’s sign: Indicates weakness of proximal muscles: The patient has to use hands and arms to "walk up" their own body from a squatting position. * Dilated cardiomyopathy * Diagnosis * Elevated serum creatine kinase levels * Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis for the dystrophin gene * If PCR is normal, but clinical suspicion is high, muscle biopsy with dystrophin immunocytochemistry is done. * Treatment: Treatment of cardiac decompensation, nutritional management, physiotherapy, and glucocorticoids. * Prognosis: Death occurs usually at about 18 to 20 years of age due to respiratory failure, intractable heart failure, pneumonia, or aspiration. Other options: Option A: Abnormal collagen synthesis may be seen in conditions such as Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes and osteogenesis imperfecta. Option C: Myotonic dystrophy is caused by expansions of CTG triplet repeats in the 3′-noncoding region of the myotonic dystrophy protein kinase (DMPK) gene. Myotonia, a sustained involuntary contraction of muscles, is a key feature of the disease. Option D: Marfan syndrome results from an inherited defect in an extracellular glycoprotein fibrillin-1. Pearl PF0847: Location of Important Genes on Chromosome

text: 12. Following urine microscopy and examination, a child is found to have hematuria and RBC casts in the urine. What is the probable cause for this?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN)

The clinical findings of nephritic syndrome (hematuria and red cell casts) seen in this child is most likely due to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis(PSGN) is characterized by the sudden onset of gross hematuria, edema, hypertension, and renal insufficiency. It usually occurs following a throat infection by nephritogenic strains of group A β-hemolytic streptococci. It can also occur after streptococcal skin infection or pyoderma. The typical patient develops an acute nephritic syndrome following: * 1 to 2 weeks after antecedent streptococcal pharyngitis or * 3 to 6 weeks after streptococcal pyoderma The pathogenesis involves circulating antibodies elicited by streptococcal antigens reacting with normal glomerular antigens, and complement activation by directly deposited streptococcal antigens causing the immunologic injury. In this immune complex-mediated APSGN, we see the following in most patients: * Decrease in the serum complement (C3) level (levels normalize in 6 to 8 weeks) * ASO titer is increased (the titers decrease to low levels within 4 to 6 weeks) Microscopic Findings in PSGN: * Light microscopy: Enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with diffuse mesangial proliferation and leukocyte infiltration * Immunofluorescence: Shows granular deposits of IgG and C3 along the GBM and within the mesangium. * Electron microscopy: Reveals subepithelial electron-dense deposits (“humps”) on the GBM. Below is the image showing light microscopy findings of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Other options: Option A: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) represents the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults. Hematuria is not a usual feature of nephrotic syndrome and rather presents with nephrotic range proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and edema. Option C: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) present in adolescents or young adults with nephrotic syndrome and a nephritic component manifested by hematuria. It is not frequent in children. Option D: In children, minimal change disease is the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome. Pearl PF0888: Nephrotic and nephritic syndromes

text: 13. Which of the following is a feature of hemolytic anemia?

options.A: All of the options given below

expl:
Correct answer: D. Decreased haptoglobin

Serum haptoglobin levels are decreased in hemolytic anemias. In intravascular hemolysis, free hemoglobin released from lysed red cells is promptly bound by haptoglobin, producing a complex that is rapidly cleared by mononuclear phagocytes. In cases of extravascular hemolysis, some hemoglobin inevitably escapes from phagocytes and leads to variable decreases in plasma haptoglobin. Hemolytic anemias are characterized by a shortened red cell life span of less than the normal 120 days. This leads to elevated erythropoietin levels and a compensatory increase in erythropoiesis which is seen as prominent reticulocytosis (OptionC) in the peripheral blood. In addition, there is an accumulation of hemoglobin degradation products produced due to hemolysis.    Types of hemolysis based on location: * Intravascular hemolysis - hemolysis that occurs mainly within the blood vessels * Extravascular hemolysis - hemolysis that occurs via macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system in the spleen, liver, bone marrow, and lymph nodes Features of intravascular hemolysis are: * Decreased haptoglobin * Increased lactate dehydrogenase  * Hemoglobinemia * Hemoglobinuria * Hemosiderinuria * Methemoglobinemia * Methemoglobinuria * Indirect hyperbilirubinemia Features of extravascular hemolysis are: * Anemia * Splenomegaly * Jaundice * Variable decreases in plasma haptoglobin

text: 14. Which of the following correctly represents the effect of the mutation causing sickle cell anemia?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Glutamate by valine at 6th position

Sickle cell anemia is characterized by the replacement of glutamate by valine at the 6th position. Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder occurring due to the T-to-A point mutation in the sixth codon of the β-globin gene. This results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. This leads to the formation of sickle-shaped red blood cells due to the polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbS). The clinical features of sickle cell disease are due to the tendency of HbS molecules to stack into polymers when deoxygenated. The features are: * Moderately severe hemolytic anemia with jaundice. * Painful bone crisis- hand-foot syndrome or dactylitis of the bones of hands and feet. * Acute chest syndrome typically presents with fever, cough, chest pain, and pulmonary infiltrates. * Hyposthenuria- inability to concentrate urine. * Aplastic crisis stems from the infection of red cell progenitors by parvovirus B19, which causes a transient cessation of erythropoiesis and a sudden worsening of the anemia. * Spleen * In children- splenic sequestration crises occur which results in splenomegaly due to red pulp congestion. * Adolescence or early adulthood- auto splenectomy occurs due to splenic infarction, fibrosis, and progressive shrinkage. * Increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms like pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenza septicemia, but can be reduced by vaccination and prophylactic antibiotics. * Other clinical features include priapism, leg ulcers, stroke, retinopathy, pigment gallstones, and growth retardation.  The diagnosis is suggested by the clinical findings, the presence of irreversibly sickled RBCs on peripheral smear, and hemoglobin electrophoresis showing increased HbA2, HbF, and S spike. Disease-modifying drugs such as hydroxyurea can be given to patients with sickle cell anemia since it reduces the incidence of adverse vaso-occlusive vents. Blood transfusions are used to treat and prevent complications of sickle cell disease, including preparation for surgery, symptomatic anemia, acute stroke, multi-organ failure, and acute chest syndrome Note: Standard Biochemical Nomenclature counts from the first amino acid of the mature beta-globin protein. By this method, the mutation occurs at position 6. Genomic Convention (as stated in Harrison 21E) includes the initiating methionine (AUG) from the translation start site, even though it is cleaved off in the mature protein. This shifts the numbering by +1, making Glu6 → Val become Glu7 → Val. By this method, the mutation occurs at position 7. Pearl PF0244: Structural Alterations of the β -Globin Gene

subject: Pathology
text: 15. Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein is a major component of which of the following?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Renal casts

Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein forms a major component of the organic matrix of renal casts. Tamm-Horsfall protein, also known as uromodulin, is the most common protein present in urine and is produced in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. They are membrane-bound, glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchored proteins that are released by proteolytic cleavage at the apical membrane. It is secreted as the most abundant protein in normal human urine (20 to 100 mg/day) and is not expressed by macula densa cells or the downstream distal convoluted tubule (DCT) They form the major organic matrix of all renal casts and play a role in the modulation of innate immunity in the kidney and inflammation during kidney injury. Uromodulin is coded by the UMOD gene, and mutation of this can lead to medullary cystic kidney disease (MCKD II) and familial juvenile hyperuricemic nephropathy. Casts are cylindrical structures that are formed in the DCT and collecting ducts. They assume the shape and size of the lumen in which they are formed. Several factors favor cast formation, such as urine stasis, low pH, and high concentration. All casts have an organic matrix composed primarily of Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein. text: 1. What do apoptotic bodies consist of?
expl:
Correct answer: D. All cellular content

An apoptotic body is formed during the late stages of apoptosis when a cell undergoes controlled self-destruction. Apoptotic bodies contain all the cellular components such as organelles and fragmented DNA and are typically smaller than the cell undergoing apoptosis.  Apoptosis, also known as programmed cell death, plays a vital role in the normal development and renewal of tissues. It can be initiated by external triggers like cytotoxic T cells or inflammatory molecules, as well as internal factors such as DNA damage or cellular stress. Mitochondria play a key role in processing signals that determine whether a cell will undergo apoptosis or not. If there's a predominance of signals favoring cell death, mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) occurs, releasing cytochrome C and other proteins into the cytoplasm. These proteins then activate internal pathways leading to programmed cell death.  Apoptosis has two pathways: A. Mitochondrial or intrinsic pathway: * Cell injury results in the release of cytochrome C and other pro-apoptotic proteins from mitochondria. * These then activate caspase 9 which causes nuclear fragmentation and formation of apoptotic bodies. B. Death receptor or extrinsic pathway: * In this pathway, activation of death receptors causes apoptosis by activating caspase-8. * Prototypic death receptors are the type I TNF receptor and Fas (CD95). text: 3. A 7-month-old boy presented with a two-day history of fever and abscess over the neck. The mother reveals that the child had similar recurrent infections in the past. The dihydrorhodamine test (DHR) was found to be positive. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Chronic granulomatous disease

The given clinical history of fever,abscess and recurrent infections in the past and positive dihydrorhodamine test (DHR) most likely suggests chronic granulomatous disease. Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is an X-linked recessive disorder due to the deficiency in NADPH oxidase which is important in respiratory or oxidative bursts. In CGD, there is an increased risk of catalase-positive species (Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Aspergillus spp, etc.) leading to granulomas. The condition usually manifests in the first year of life with recurrent pyogenic infections with catalase-positive organisms.   Patients have recurrent bacterial and fungal infections. The symptoms begin within the first two years of life, affecting the pulmonary, gastrointestinal, skin, and lymphatic drainage of these organs. Nitroblue tetrazolium is used as a diagnostic test. The yellow-coloured Nitroblue tetrazolium dye is converted to a purple insoluble substance (positive) in the presence of oxidative burst by the free oxygen radicals so formed. A negative test (yellow color remains) is seen in CGD. Individuals with CGD will exhibit diminished or absent fluorescence in the DHR test, indicating impaired ROS production by phagocytes. This result confirms the diagnosis of CGD and aids in distinguishing it from other conditions with similar symptoms. It can also assess the effectiveness of treatments like bone marrow transplantation or gene therapy in restoring normal phagocyte function. Other options: Option A) Chediak-Higashi syndrome is a primary immunodeficiency due to a disorder of the phagolysosome function of leukocytes, leading to delayed microbial clearance. In addition, there is a disorder of melanin (albinism), nerve defects, and bleeding disorders. Option C) Severe combined immunodeficiency is a primary immunodeficiency with a disorder of both cellular and humoral immunity. Persons with SCID are susceptible to recurrent severe infections caused by a wide variety of pathogens and usually do not survive beyond the first year of life without a stem cell transplant. Option D) Tuberculosis is a bacterial disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and is characterized by the formation of granulomas as an immune response to contain the infection. Tuberculosis presents with cavitary lesions in the upper lobes of the lungs. Histopathology reveals caseous necrosis with multinucleated giant cells. Common manifestations include fever, night sweats, anorexia, weakness, and weight loss. Blood investigations may reveal anemia with leukopenia, lymphopenia, neutrophilic leukocytosis, leukemoid reactions, and polycythemia.

subject: Pathology
text: 5. What is the most radioresistant phase of the cell cycle?
expl:
Correct answer: B. S

The most radioresistant phase of the cell cycle is the S phase. The replication of the DNA genome occurs only at a specified time period during the cell cycle. This period is referred to as the synthetic or S phase. The S phase is separated from the mitotic, or M phase, by nonsynthetic periods referred to as gap 1 (G1) and gap 2 (G2) phases, occurring before and after the S phase, respectively. The cell prepares for DNA synthesis in G1, and for mitosis in G2. The most radiosensitive phase of the cell cycle is the G2-M phase. Cells in the G2 or M phase do not have time to repair DNA damage that occurs before they start to divide. This affects mitosis, leading to catastrophe. Cells become gradually less sensitive to radiation in the G1 phase to the early S phase and are least sensitive in the late S phase. The most radiosensitive cell in the blood is the lymphocyte. The least radiosensitive cell in the blood is the platelet.

text: 9. A patient presents to the emergency department complaining of severe pain in her right index finger, back and legs along with fatigue. text: 10. During pregnancy, ABO incompatibility does not occur due to which antibody?
expl:
Correct answer: A. IgM

IgM antibodies cannot cross the placenta from the maternal to the fetal circulation. Therefore, they do not have a significant role in causing hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN) or ABO incompatibility during pregnancy. ABO incompatibility is the most common cause of hemolytic disease in newborns and affects the firstborn. It is usually mild and subclinical. This incompatibility between the mother and fetus generally results in milder disease than Rh incompatibility does.  It arises when a mother with blood group type O becomes pregnant with a fetus of a different blood type (A/B). The mother's serum contains naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B, which can cross the placenta and cause hemolysis of fetal RBCs. Although antibodies against A and B factors occur without previous immunisation (natural antibodies), they are usually IgM, which does not cross the placenta. However, IgG antibodies to A antigen may be present, which cross the placenta, resulting in A-O iso-immune hemolytic disease in the firstborn infant (A-O is more common than B-O).

text: 3. A child with a history of recurrent nosebleeds, easy bruising, and prolonged bleeding after minor injuries is diagnosed with von Willebrand disease. He inquires about the role of von Willebrand factor (vWF) in this condition. Which of the following does vWF primarily bind to facilitate platelet adhesion?
expl:
Correct answer: D. GpIb/IX

The factor that von Willebrand factor (vWF) binds to is GpIb/IX. Platelet adhesion is an interplay of interactions between glycoprotein Ib - GpIb/IX and vWF in the subendothelial matrix. Endothelial injury exposes vWF and causes the adhesion of platelets by the GpIb receptor. Adenosine diphosphate (ADP) binding to ADP receptors (Option B) induces conformational changes in platelets. This change in glycoprotein IIb/IIIa that occurs with platelet activation allows it to bind to fibrinogen, which leads to aggregation of platelets to each other and not to the endothelium. Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder that occurs due to deficiency of or defect in von Willebrand factor (vWF). vWF is stored in endothelial cells and in platelet Weibel-Palade bodies. It has two important functions: * Adhesion of the platelets to injured subendothelium * Carrier protein for factor VIII and preventing its degradation Clinical features include spontaneous bleeding from mucous membranes (epistaxis), excessive bleeding from wounds, or menorrhagia, after dental extractions and surgeries including tonsillectomies. Most individuals are asymptomatic otherwise. Type 3 VWD is the most severe form and presents with symptoms like joint bleeds, similar to those seen in mild haemophilia. Diagnosis * Normal platelet count * Prolonged BT * Normal PT * Prolonged aPTT Factor VIII is found bound to the Von-Willebrand factor(vWF) in the blood. Deficiency of vWF results in Factor VIII deficiency and prolongation of aPTT in this disease. Prolonged BT is due to abnormal platelet-mediated hemostasis. Classification: 3 types are recognized, with phenotypic variations: * Type 1 is an autosomal dominant disorder that is inherited. It manifests as a mild to moderate von Willebrand factor deficiency. It accounts for upto 70% of all cases.  * Type 2 von Willebrand disease is characterized by qualitative defects in vWF. Type 2A is the most common. It is inherited as an autosomal dominant disorder. * Type 3 disease is an autosomal recessive disorder resulting in little to no vWF synthesis. Because vWF stabilizes factor VIII in the circulation, factor VIII levels are also reduced in type 3 disease and the associated bleeding disorder is often severe. Type 1 and type 3 von Willebrand disease are associated with quantitative defects in vWF. Treatment: Desmopressin for type 1 vWD stimulates the release of vWF and Factor VIII from the endothelial stores. Von Willebrand factor (VWF) concentrates in cases of type 2 and type 3 von Willebrand disease. Other Options: Option A: Prothrombin binds to phospholipid membranes as part of its conversion to thrombin during the coagulation process. Option C: Platelet factor 3 (PF3) is exposed on activated platelet surfaces and provides a negatively charged phospholipid surface that facilitates the assembly of coagulation factor complexes.
