text: 4. cMYC gene mutation is seen in which of the following neoplasms?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Burkitt's lymphoma

Burkitt lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, characterized by the translocation of the c-Myc gene on chromosome 8. This leads to increased MYC protein levels.  It can occur in 3 forms that have distinct clinical characteristics: * African (endemic) Burkitt lymphoma presents as a mass involving the mandible. It may also involve the abdominal viscera, particularly the kidneys, ovaries, and adrenal glands. * Sporadic (non-endemic) is often seen as a mass involving the ileocecum and peritoneum. * Aggressive lymphoma or acute leukaemia is seen in immunocompromised individuals Histopathology shows tumour cells with round or oval nuclei, coarse chromatin, small nucleoli, minimal cytoplasm, and a high mitotic index. The phagocytes have abundant clear cytoplasm, creating a characteristic “starry sky” pattern. Bone marrow aspiration shows tumour cells with royal blue cytoplasm containing clear cytoplasmic vacuoles. The tumour cells express surface IgM, CD19, CD20, CD10, and BCL6, a phenotype consistent with a germinal centre B-cell origin. Other options: Option A: In Hodgkin's lymphoma, the most significant mutation is associated with the BCL6 gene on chromosome 3q27. The BCL6 gene mutation results in aberrant transcriptional regulation and contributes to the characteristic Reed-Sternberg cells seen in Hodgkin's lymphoma, which are large, abnormal lymphoid cells that are diagnostic of this type of lymphoma. Option B: Pleomorphic adenoma is associated with chromosomal rearrangements that induce overexpression of PLAG1.  It is the most common salivary gland and lacrimal gland neoplasm. Microscopically, it contains a mixture of ductal (epithelial), myoepithelial, and mesenchymal cells. Option D: Neuroblastoma is a tumour derived from primordial neural crest cells. It is the most common extracranial solid tumour in childhood. They are associated with the n-MYC gene translocation. On histopathology, small round blue cells and Homer-Wright pseudorosettes are seen.

text: 5. Alpha-fetoprotein is a tumor marker used in the diagnosis and monitoring of various conditions. In which of the following conditions is AFP typically raised?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Hepatoma

Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is raised in the setting of a hepatoma tumor.  Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is commonly produced by Hepatomas and is used as a tumor marker. AFP is typically elevated in about 50-70% of HCC cases, with levels above 200 ng/mL being particularly suggestive of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The marker is useful for both screening high-risk populations and monitoring treatment response, though it is not entirely specific and can be elevated in other liver conditions and some germ cell tumors. Other options: Option A: Dysgerminona is a type of germ cell tumor and it corresponds to the seminoma of the testis. It does not secrete either male or female sex hormones. It secretes placental alkaline phosphatase (ALP), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and β-hCG. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is usually used in monitoring individuals or disease recurrence. Option C: Choriocarcinoma is a type of mixed germ cell tumor. It is highly vascular. Histologically, the tumor shows syncytiotrophoblasts and cytotrophoblasts. It secretes large quantities of beta- human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) hormone, which is used as a tumor marker in the diagnosis and management of the tumor  Option D: Malignant epithelial cell tumors of the ovary secrete CA-125. It is a glycoprotein and surface cell antigen which is secreted by malignant epithelial tumors of the ovary. A level of more than 35 U/mL suggests a malignant and residual tumor and indicates the need for chemotherapy. CA-125 is also raised in abdominal tuberculosis and endometriosis. subject: Pathology
text: 6. An old person presented with an ulcer on the medial canthus with pearly and rolled margins. Histopathology shows nesting cells with peripheral palisading patterns. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Basal cell carcinoma

This patient, presenting with an ulcer on the medial canthus with pearly, rolled margins, and histopathology revealing nesting cells with peripheral palisading, is most likely diagnosed with basal cell carcinoma. Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is a slow-growing, locally invasive, malignant tumour of epithelial cells arising from the basal epidermis. It erodes deeply into local tissues, including cartilage and bones, causing extensive local destruction, hence the name rodent ulcer. It does not spread through blood or lymphatics.  The strongest risk factor for developing basal cell carcinoma is exposure to UV radiation. Therefore it occurs on the sun-exposed areas of the skin, most commonly on the nose and face. Most common site is the inner canthus of eye. They present as small, slowly growing pearly nodules, often with tortuous telangiectatic vessels on their surface, rolled borders, and a central crust (nodular BCC). The occasional presence of melanin in this variant of nodular BCC (pigmented BCC) may lead to confusion with melanoma. BCC can be divided into generalized and localized. Generalized can be further divided into superficial or infiltrative. The localized can be further divided into * Nodular and nodulocystic- account for the majority of BCC * Cystic * Pigmented * Naevoid. The characteristic biopsy finding of BCC is the presence of ovoid cells in nests and palisading of the peripheral cells of the nests. Treatment of BCC includes excision of the lesion or Moh's micrographic surgery. Other Options: Option A: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the malignancy of the keratinizing cells of the epidermis. It is associated with exposure to UV radiation and chronic inflammation (chronic sinus tracts, pre-existing scars, osteomyelitis, and burns). Classically, it appears as a scaly or ulcerated papule or plaque that can bleed with minimal trauma, but the pain is rare. Histologically, SCC is characterized by the proliferation of atypical squamous cells with the formation of horn pearls or keratin pearls. Option B: Marjolin's ulcer is a rare and aggressive form of squamous cell carcinoma that grows from burns, scars, or poorly healing wounds.  The image below shows a Marjolin's ulcer in a burn scar. Option D: Naevus is a common benign neoplasm caused by mutations in the RAS signalling pathway, characterized by aggregates of melanocytes at the dermis or the dermo-epidermal junction. It has various types, such as congenital naevus, blue naevus, Spitz naevus, halo naevus, and dysplastic naevus. It can get transformed into malignant melanoma and the features suggestive of malignant transformation are a change in size, shape, color, thickness, satellite lesions, and tingling/ itching/serosanguinous discharge.

text: 7. A 55-year-old female presents with complaints of persistent headaches. A CT scan of the head reveals a brain tumour. On histopathology, psammoma bodies are seen. Based on these findings, what is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Meningioma

The clinical vignette and the histopathology showing a tumour with psammoma bodies is suggestive of meningioma. Meningiomas are predominantly benign tumors in adults, typically attached to the dura and arising from the meningothelial cells of the arachnoid. They can develop along any external surface of the brain or within the ventricular system, originating from the stromal arachnoid cells of the choroid plexus. A major risk factor for meningiomas is prior radiation therapy to the head and neck. The most common cytogenetic abnormality associated with these tumors is the loss of chromosome 22, particularly the long arm (22q). Meningiomas are frequently seen in neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2), often occurring at multiple sites, especially alongside acoustic neuromas or glial tumors. The tumor mass is usually encapsulated but may also grow en plaque, where it spreads in a sheetlike manner along the dura, often leading to hyperostotic reactive changes in the adjacent bone. Histologically, meningiomas may contain numerous calcified psammoma bodies, a characteristic microscopic feature. Psammoma bodies are concentric, lamellated structures formed as a product of dystrophic calcification. They are associated with papillary histomorphology and are caused by infarction and calcification of papillae tips.  The histological section of meningioma showing psammoma bodies is given below: Histological subtypes: * WHO Grade I – Menigothelial, fibroblastic, transitional, psammomatous, secretory, microcystic * WHO Grade II- Clear cell, choroid, atypical * Grade III – Papillary, rhabdoid, anaplastic * Atypical meningiomas (WHO grade II/IV) - a higher rate of recurrence and more aggressive local growth * Anaplastic (malignant) meningioma (WHO grade III/IV) - highly aggressive tumor with the appearance of a high-grade sarcoma * Immunoreactive for epithelial membrane antigen * Keratin is restricted to lesions with the secretory pattern, and these tumors are also positive for carcinoembryonic antigen * Moderate (3: 2) female predominance, usually solitary, but when present at multiple sites, the possibility of neurofibromatosis type 2 should be considered. * Meningiomas often express progesterone receptors and may grow more rapidly during pregnancy. Other Options: Option A: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes with arrangements of a single layer of tumor cells around an apparent lumen can be seen in Retinoblastoma. Option B: Medulloblastoma is a malignant embryonal tumor of childhood that occurs exclusively in the cerebellum. Histologically, the tumor is very densely cellular. Individual tumor cells have scant cytoplasm and elongated or crescent-shaped hyperchromatic nuclei. Tumor cells form Homer Wright rosettes. They express neuronal markers such as synaptophysin. Option D: Oligodendroglioma is composed of tumor cells that resemble oligodendrocytes. The tumor contains sheets of regular cells with spherical nuclei containing finely granular chromatin, surrounded by a clear halo of vacuolated cytoplasm. This gives them a fried egg appearance. They contain a network of anastomosing capillaries, resembling chicken wire and also have calcifications. Pearl PF2095: Psammoma Bodies Psammoma bodies are visible in the following: * Meningioma * Serous cystadenocarcinoma Ovary * Papillary carcinoma thyroid. * Papillary type of renal cell carcinoma Pearl PF1837: Histological Features of CNS Tumors Pilocytic Astrocytomas: * Biphasic architecture - loose microcystic component and dense fibrillary areas * Bipolar cells (tumor cells): thin, long hairlike processes that are GFAP - positive.  * Rosenthal fibers: eosinophilic corkscrew - shaped inclusions * Eosinophilic granular bodies: mulberry - like inclusions    Medulloblastoma: * Very densely cellular, with sheets of small primitive appearing small blue cells * Individual tumor cells have scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei that are frequently elongated or crescent-shaped * Tumor cells form Homer - Wright rosettes (pseudorosettes) with a central neuropil   Ependymoma: * Ependymal rosettes: gland - like round or elongated structures that resemble the embryologic ependymal canal, with long, delicate processes extending into the lumen  * Perivascular pseudorosettes: perivascular nuclear - free zone consisting of thin ependymal processes radiating toward the central blood vessel   Oligodendroglioma: * Fried - egg appearance: sheets of regular cells with spherical nuclei containing finely granular chromatin (similar to normal oligodendrocytes) surrounded by a clear halo of vacuolated cytoplasm.  * Chicken - wire capillaries: a delicate network of anastomosing capillaries   Retinoblastoma:  * Composed of collections of small, round cells with hyperchromatic nuclei * Flexner - Wintersteiner rosettes: arrangements of a single layer of tumor cells around an apparent lumen * Homer - Wright rosettes: a ring of cells with an eosinophilic fibrillary center * Fleurettes: retinoblastoma cells that have undergone greater photoreceptor differentiation and group together as a bouquet. text: 8. Which of the following is seen in irreversible cell injury?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Large amorphous densities in mitochondria

The formation of large amorphous densities in the mitochondrial matrix is a feature of irreversible injury. The presence of vacuoles and phospholipid-containing amorphous densities within mitochondria is typically a sign of irreversible injury, indicating a permanent loss of ATP production through oxidative phosphorylation.  Severe mitochondrial damage is marked by the influx of calcium ions and the formation of large flocculent densities within the mitochondria. These densities are typically observed in irreversibly injured myocardial cells following reperfusion after injury. Once mitochondrial damage becomes irreversible, cellular recovery is no longer possible. Small amorphous densities are seen in reversible cell injury.  Reversible cell injury: * Cellular swelling * When there is adenosine triphosphate (ATP) depletion the sodium-potassium pump fails. Sodium and water accumulate within the cell. * Fatty change * Seen in cells involved in or dependent on fat metabolism, e.g., liver hepatocytes and myocardial cells. * Ultrastructure findings (seen on electron microscopy): * Mitochondrial swelling and small amorphous densities. * Plasma membrane blebs (Option B). * Swelling of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). * Detachment of ribosomes (Option D). * Nuclear changes: disaggregation of granular and fibrillar filaments and clumping of chromatin (Option C). text: 9. A 45-year-old lady with a history of long-standing goitre presented with a solitary thyroid nodule. Histopathological examination of the thyroid mass shows nests of polygonal cells and pink eosinophilic extracellular material. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Medullary carcinoma

The presence of nests of polygonal cells and pink eosinophilic extracellular material (amyloid stroma) on histopathological examination, makes medullary carcinoma of the thyroid the most likely diagnosis. Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid (MTC) arises from the parafollicular C cells. Most of the MTC are sporadic but they may also be associated with inheritable syndromes like familial MTC, MEN2A, and MEN2B.  Most patients present at 50-60 years and have a female preponderance. MTC secretes calcitonin, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), prostaglandins E2 and F2α, histaminadases, serotonin, and adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH). Features of MTC * Painful neck mass with cervical lymphadenopathy * Diarrhea due to increased intestinal motility * Cushingoid habitus due to ectopic ACTH production * Metastasis is blood-borne * Diagnosis is by careful family history, physical examination, raised calcitonin, CEA levels, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mass. Histopathology shows polygonal to spindle-shaped cells, which may form nests, trabeculae, and even follicles. Acellular amyloid deposits derived from calcitonin polypeptides are present in the stroma. These lesions secrete calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen. Total thyroidectomy with bilateral central neck node dissection is the treatment of choice in MTC patients. External beam radiotherapy can be used in patients with unresectable tumors. Other options: Option A: Papillary carcinoma thyroid shows * Papillary projections * Orphan-Annie eyed nuclei (pale empty nuclei) * Psammoma bodies (microscopic calcified deposits) Option C: Follicular carcinoma shows uniform cells forming small follicles and they are filled with colloid and normal thyroid tissue. The below image shows follicular thyroid carcinoma. Option D: Anaplastic carcinoma of the thyroid is one of the most aggressive malignancies. They are poorly differentiated thyroid carcinomas with varied morphology, including giant cells or spindle-shaped cells or both. There is minimal follicular differentiation with intratumoral necrosis.

text: 10. A 60-year-old female presents with a slow-growing, painless mass in her left breast. On physical examination, the mass is soft, well-circumscribed, and mobile. A biopsy is performed, and histopathology reveals the following. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Colloidal carcinoma

The given clinical scenario and histopathological findings are suggestive of colloid/mucinous carcinoma of the breast. Colloidal carcinoma is an invasive breast carcinoma, which shows intra and extracellular mucin deposition. In intracellular type, nuclei are pushed to the peripherally to form signet ring appearance.  Extracellular type shows tumor cells with faint nuclei arranged in clusters floating in pools/lakes of mucin on histopathological examination. Other options: Option B: Lobular carcinoma is the most common type of breast carcinoma to present as an occult primary carcinoma. Lobular carcinoma of the breast is seen bilaterally and with multicentricity. Loss of E-cadherin is the hallmark of lobular carcinoma. The histological hallmark of lobular carcinoma is the presence of discohesive infiltrating tumor cells, often arranged in a single Indian file pattern or in loose clusters or sheets. text: 11. A 30-year-old female presents with a painless, rapidly growing lump in her left breast that she noticed over the past few months. On examination, the lump is well-defined, mobile, and firm in consistency. A breast ultrasound reveals a solid mass, and a core needle biopsy is performed. Histopathological examination shows a leaf-like pattern with an overgrowth of the stromal component and ductal structures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Phyllodes tumor

The histopathology of the biopsy of the lump shows increased stromal cellularity, overgrowth, and typical leaflike architecture which is suggestive of phyllodes tumor.  Phyllodes tumor is also known as cystosarcoma phyllodes, presents as a large tumor with an unevenly bosselated surface. This tumour does not infiltrate the skin though the overlying skin becomes thin and tense due to swelling. Nipple retraction is not seen in this condition. Phyllodes tumors usually occur in women over the age of 40 years but can appear in younger women. They are mostly benign even though it is also called as cystosarcoma phyllodes or as serocystic disease of Brodie. They are usually mobile over the chest wall despite their large size.  Histologically, there is a wide variation with some of low malignant potential and others having a higher mitotic index. * They are fibroepithelial tumours that arise from the intralobular stroma. * It can be benign, borderline or malignant. * Phyllodes tumor can be differentiated from intracanalicular fibroadenoma by its subepithelial or periepithelial accentuation of stromal cellularity. * Most phyllodes tumor are of low grade. Recurrence rate is high in intermediate and high grade tumors. * Increased stromal cellularity, stromal overgrowth (absence of epithelial elements), nuclear atypia, increased mitosis(>10 per 10HPF) suggests the diagnosis of malignant phyllodes tumour. * Gain in chromosome 1q is the most frequent clonal acquired chromosomal changes seen in Phyllodes tumor. HOXB13 overexpression is associated with more aggressive clinical behaviour.  Microscopy reveals the presence of nodules of proliferating stroma covered by epithelium (leaf-like architecture). Note: "Phyllodes" means "leaf like" in Greek. Treatment of phyllodes tumor: * Benign type- Enucleation or wide local excision * Massive tumors, recurrent tumors and malignant type- Mastectomy * Axillary dissection is not done if malignant transformation occurs because the lymphatic spread is rare. Other Options: Option B: Galactocele: A galactocele is a milk-filled cavity in the breast of a woman who is usually lactating. It can be caused due to lactation problems, prolactin stimulation by drugs, or duct obstruction. It presents as a palpable, round, well-circumscribed, and freely mobile mass with no fever, pain, or inflammation. It is usually subareolar and unilateral. Option C: Paget's Disease: Presents as a chronic, eczematous eruption of the nipple which may progress to ulceration. In the majority of patients, there is also an underlying breast lump. Histology shows the presence of large, pale, vacuolated cells (Paget cells) with round or oval nuclei in the rete pegs of the epithelium. Option D: Fibroadenoma is a form of aberrations of normal development and involution of the breast (ANDI), and it is the most common cause of a breast lump in women aged 15–25 years. It arises from hyperplasia of a single lobule and presents as a well-circumscribed, smooth or lobular, firm, non-tender, freely mobile mass (mouse in the breast). text: 12. A 9-month-old child is admitted to the ICU with a history of recurrent sinusitis and otitis media caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Lab results shows low levels of Immunoglobulins (G,A,M,E) and low quantity of plasma B cells. There is a normal reaction to environmental antigens on the skin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Bruton's agammaglobulinemia

This child's presentation suggests X-linked or Bruton's agammaglobulinemia. X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton agammaglobulinemia) is an immunodeficiency disorder characterized by the failure of B-cell precursors (pro-B and pre-B cells) to develop into mature B-cells. It is caused by a mutation in a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase called Bruton tyrosine kinase (Btk) located on the long arm of the X chromosome (Xq21.22). The features of the disease are -  * B cells are absent or markedly reduced. * Decreased levels of all classes of Immunoglobulins. * Germinal centres are underdeveloped in lymph nodes, peyer's patches, and tonsils. * T-cell mediated reactions are normal. (normal reaction to environmental antigens on the skin.) * The disease usually becomes apparent after 6 months of age since it is masked by the presence of maternal antibodies until 6 months of age. The patient has recurrent pharyngitis, otitis media, sinusitis, bronchitis, and pneumonia caused by Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus, and Hemophilus influenzae. Gastrointestinal infections can occur by viruses or Giardia lamblia due to reduced IgA secretion.  The treatment is replacement therapy with immunoglobulins in the form of prophylactic intravenous IgG therapy. Other Options: Option A: Ataxia telangiectasia is caused due to mutation of the ATM gene. This gene is involved in the repair of double-strand DNA breaks. This defect in DNA repair leads to impaired Ig isotype switching and the formation of antigen receptors. As a result, the patient is immunodeficient with partial T cell deficiency, and hence live vaccines are avoided. Option C: Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD) is a rare primary immunodeficiency disorder caused by defects in the NADPH oxidase enzyme complex, which is essential for the respiratory burst in phagocytic cells (neutrophils and macrophages). This defect impairs the ability of phagocytes to produce reactive oxygen species (ROS), leading to ineffective intracellular killing of certain bacteria and fungi. Option D: DiGeorge syndrome is caused due to deletion of chromosome 22q11.2. The characteristic features are (Mnemonic CATCH-22) - Cardiac abnormality, abnormal facies, thymic aplasia, cleft palate, hypocalcemia. Pearl PF0295: Primary immunodeficiency disorders

text: 13. Which is the type of cartilage present in the histology section given below?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Hyaline cartilage

The type of cartilage shown in the above image is hyaline cartilage. On microscopy, hyaline cartilage can be identified by: * Presence of chondrocytes within lacunae. * Group of two or more chondrocytes which are known as isogenous cell aggregates or cell nests. * Basophilic territorial matrix and pale interterritorial matrix * Presence of perichondrium with outer fibrous and the inner cellular layer Hyaline cartilage is made up of chondrocytes and matrix. The chondrocytes in the deeper matrix are rounded in shape and may appear in a group of eight that originate from the mitotic divisions of a single chondroblast. These groups of cells are called isogenous cell aggregates or cell nests. The important components of the matrix are type II collagen, aggrecan (proteoglycan) and chondronectin (glycoprotein). The matrix which immediately surrounds the chondrocytes is basophilic and is known as the territorial matrix and the matrix which are more distant from the cells appears pale and is known as the interterritorial matrix. It is found in: * Larger respiratory passages (nose, larynx, trachea and bronchi) * Thyroid cartilage * Cricoid cartilage * Base of the arytenoid cartilage * Ventral end of ribs where they articulate with the sternum * The epiphyseal plate of long bones * Articular cartilage of synovial joint * Temporary skeleton in embryo Other Options: Option A: Articular cartilage despite being a type of hyaline cartilage lacks perichondrium. Option B: The elastic cartilage, like the hyaline cartilage, contains individual or small groups of chondrocytes that are surrounded by type II collagen fibrils. However, it differs from hyaline cartilage in that, much of the interterritorial matrix consists of fine yellow elastic fibres containing elastin protein and the surface of elastic cartilage is covered by perichondrium. Option D: The fibrocartilage is an intermediate between dense fibrous connective tissue (tendon and ligaments) and hyaline cartilage. It consists of bundles of collagen fibres (both type I and II) with rows of chondrocytes present between the bundles. They are not covered by perichondrium. Pearl PF0418: Types of Cartilage

text: 14. Patient underwent cholecystectomy and black pigmented gallstones were noticed. Which of the following is the least likely cause?
expl:
Correct answer: D. HbD Punjab

Pigmented gallstones are commonly found in chronic hemolytic syndromes such as sickle cell disease, HbH disease, and beta thalassemia minor, but not in HbD Punjab. Hemoglobin D-Punjab (HbD Punjab), also known as Hemoglobin D-Los Angeles, is one of the most common hemoglobin variants worldwide. It is derived from a point mutation in the beta-globin gene. It is a normal variant and rarely presents as any clinical symptoms. Moreover, this variant can exist in association with other hemoglobinopathies such as thalassemias and sickle cell disease, which can lead to hemolysis. However, just a mere presence of HbD Punjab without associated hemoglobinopathies won't cause hemolysis or pigmented gallstones. Any type of hemolytic anemia is a risk factor for the development of pigment gallstones. There are two main types of gallstones: * Cholesterol stones—which consist of crystalline cholesterol monohydrate * Pigment stones—made of bilirubin calcium salts Other Options: Option A: In sickle cell anemia, HbS is present in which valine is substituted for glutamic acid at the 6th position of the beta chain. This results in a change in the shape of the RBCs from biconcave to sickle-shaped. This can cause an increase in hemolysis and an increase in pigmented gallstones. Option B: In HbH disease, excess β-globin chains form β4 tetramers. They are seen in older children with α-thalassemia. This may lead to pigmented gallstones due to hemolysis. Option C: β-Thalassemia minor arises due to the deficient synthesis of β-chains. Normal adult RBCs have HbA, along with HbA2 and fetal hemoglobin (HbF) in small amounts. There is a deficit in the synthesis of HbA with an elevation of HbA2 and HbF levels in β-thalassemia. This can also cause an increase in hemolysis and an increase in pigmented gallstones. text: 16. Identify the histological image given below.
expl:
Correct answer: D. Lymph node

The image is that of a lymph node. Each lymph node is bean-shaped. The concave part consists of the hilum, through which the blood vessels enter and leave the node. Each lymph node is surrounded by a thin capsule. Below the capsule is the clear space, which is called the subcapsular sinus. The lymph node contains the outer cortex and an inner medulla. Cortex * The outermost region of the lymph node, located beneath the capsule. * Primary follicles: Composed primarily of small, resting B lymphocytes (naive B cells). These follicles are unactivated and appear as small, round clusters. * Secondary follicles: These form when B cells within the primary follicle are activated by antigenic stimulation. They are characterized by a germinal centre (where B cells proliferate and differentiate) and a mantle zone (where small, resting B cells surround the germinal centre). * Mantle zone: A ring of small, naive B lymphocytes surrounding the germinal centre. Paracortex (T-cell Zone) * Situated between the cortex and the medulla, this area is rich in T lymphocytes, which are involved in T-cell mediated immunity. * The paracortex also contains dendritic cells that present antigens to T cells and is crucial for T-cell dependent immune responses. * This zone lacks follicles and is more densely populated with T cells.  Medulla * The innermost part of the lymph node, containing medullary cords and medullary sinuses. * Medullary cords: These are dense clusters of plasma cells, B cells, T cells, and macrophages that are responsible for producing antibodies and providing immune surveillance. * Medullary sinuses: Spaces that allow the passage of lymph and contain macrophages that filter out foreign particles and pathogens. Option A: The thymus is a lymphoid tissue that is arranged in the form of lobules. The lobules are separated from each other by connective tissue.  Each lobule is made up of an outer darker staining cortex and an inner pale-staining medulla. The medulla contains pink rounded masses called Hassell's corpuscles. Option B: The main features that can be used to identify the spleen are: * Capsule and trabeculae extending from it. * Arterioles arising from the network of vessels that have branched from the splenic artery in the trabecular spaces. * White pulp - composed of aggregation of lymphocytes arranged around an arteriole. * Red pulp - areas between the white pulp and trabecular spaces regions where blood cells flow into. * Sinusoids -blood from spaces of the red pulp is collected by wide sinusoids that drain into veins in the trabeculae. Option C: The tonsil consists of lymphoid nodules, which are surrounded by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium on its oropharyngeal surface. The epithelium dips into the substance of the gland and forms tonsillar crypts. Pearl PF2229: Hodgkin v/s Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma

text: 17. Identify the cell marked in the histological image of the cerebellum shown below
expl:
Correct answer: B. Purkinje cell

The structure marked in the image is a flask-shaped neuron in the cerebellar cortex, which is a Purkinje cell. Purkinje cells are the flask-shaped cells present in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum. They are evenly spaced and arranged in a single layer between molecular and granular cell layers. The dendrite from each cell passes upward to enter the molecular layer and the axon of each cell passes downwards, crosses the granular cell layer, and terminates on the deep cerebellar nuclei. They are inhibitory and use GABA as their neurotransmitter. Axons of Purkinje cells are the only efferents of the cerebellar cortex. They receive excitatory input from the climbing fibers from the inferior olivary nucleus and mossy fibers.  Pathological significance of Purkinje cells: * Negri bodies in rabies are usually found as eosinophilic, cytoplasmic inclusions in the neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum. * In paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, there is the destruction of Purkinje cells due to antibodies directed against them. * Purkinje cells and neurons in pyramidal cell layers of the hippocampus and cerebral cortex are the most sensitive neurons to hypoxia and are likely to be damaged in cases of global cerebral ischemia. Pearl PF2096: Layers of the cerebellar cortex The cerebellar cortex is divided into 3 layers. They are: * Molecular layer - It is the outermost layer. It contains stellate cells and basket cells. They receive excitatory input from the parallel fibers and form inhibitory synapses on the Purkinje cells. It contains many myelinated and unmyelinated nerve fibers giving it a pale appearance in H and E staining. * Purkinje layer - It is the middle layer. It contain flask-shaped cell bodies of Purkinje cells. Their dendrites pass into the molecular layer. The axons of the Purkinje cells passes through the granular layer into the white matter and synapses with the cerebellar nuclei. * Granular layer - It is the innermost layer. It contains the cell bodies of the granule cells as well as Golgi cells. It receives excitatory input from the mossy fibers. They end on the dendrites of the granule cells and these complexes are called glomeruli. The axon from the granule cells travels to the molecular layer and bifurcates in a T-shape. These branches form the T and are called parallel fibers. These parallel fibers form excitatory synapses with the Purkinje cells. The granule cells form the only excitatory neurons in the cerebellar cortex. Golgi cells receive input from parallel fibers and mossy fibers. They send inhibitory output to the granule cells. Neurotransmitters released: * Stellate, basket, Golgi and Purkinje cells- GABA * Granule cells - Glutamate The only output from the cerebellar cortex is inhibitory from the Purkinje cells to the deep cerebellar nuclei.

text: 2. Which among the following is false regarding papillary thyroid cancer?

options.A: Most common age group is between 30- 50 years

expl:
Correct answer: D. Calcitonin is the tumour marker

The wrong statement is option d. Calcitonin is the marker for medullary carcinoma and not papillary carcinoma Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy with relatively good prognosis (option b) . It is more commonly seen in women between the ages of 30 and 50 (option a). Radiation exposure (option c) and a family history of thyroid malignancies are common etiologies. Genetic abnormalities in either the RET gene or the BRAF gene can be seen in papillary thyroid carcinoma. Clinical features include an asymptomatic thyroid swelling with cervical lymph node enlargement. In advanced disease, there may be features like hoarseness, dysphagia, cough, or dyspnea.  An ultrasound scan accurately assesses the size and number of nodules, as well as categorizes the lesions as benign, indeterminate, or malignant. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is a diagnostic test, helpful in investigating an indeterminate or malignant lesion. Histopathology shows the following features: * Branching papillae * Orphan Annie eye nuclei: optically clear nuclei with fine nuclear chromatin * Pseudo inclusions: invaginations of the nuclear membrane * Psammoma bodies: concentric calcifications in the core of the papillae. Below is the histopathological image of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid with characteristic Orphan Annie eye nuclei. Papillary thyroid carcinoma is known to spread via lymphatics, hence lymph node metastasis is commonly seen. Treatment of Papillary thyroid carcinoma is as follows: Total thyroidectomy is the treatment of choice. Routine central neck dissection is not recommended. Neck dissection is indicated in higher-risk situations, such as * Tumor size > 4 cm (T3 stage) or gross extrathyroidal extension (T4 stage) or enlarged central lymph nodes - Total thyroidectomy + Central Neck Dissection * Lateral Aberrant Thyroid - Total thyroidectomy + Modified Radical Neck Dissection + Central Neck Dissection For occult papillary cancer (<1 cm tumor size, with no lymphatic, vascular or capsular invasion) - Lobectomy can be sufficient. Radio-iodine ablation is undertaken when a whole-body iodine scan is positive after a total thyroidectomy for any differentiated thyroid cancer (papillary or follicular carcinoma).  The presence of any metastatic or residual thyroid tissue after total thyroidectomy can be detected by observing the uptake of radio-iodine in the entire body. To achieve effective uptake of radio-iodine, TSH levels need to be greatly increased, for example, by withdrawing thyroxine after the surgery for 4-6 weeks. A positive whole-body iodine scan after total thyroidectomy indicates that there is either a metastatic or residual disease present. These patients are treated with I131 for radio-iodine ablation.  A negative scan means there is no metastasis or residual thyroid tissue. They are followed up regularly with serum thyroglobulin, TSH and USG-neck.

text: 5. Which of the following inhibits ferroportin?
expl:
Correct answer: B. IL-6

IL-6 inhibits ferroportin. It is an inflammatory mediator  It stimulates the production of hepcidin from the liver and thereby inhibits ferroportin.  Dietary iron is available in two forms - heme and non-heme iron. Initially, the ferric non-heme iron is reduced to ferrous iron by duodenal cytochrome B (ferric reductase) or by vitamin C. The reduced ferrous iron is then transferred into the enterocyte by DMT 1 (divalent metal transporter).  Heme iron moves into the cytoplasm with the help of transporters. Here, it is metabolized to release ferrous iron, which then follows the same pathway as non-heme iron. Once inside the enterocyte, it can either get stored as ferritin or transferred across the basolateral membrane by ferroportin. In the plasma, iron is transported in the Fe3+ form bound to transferrin, which is a transport protein. Hephaestin is a ferroxidase that oxidizes Fe2+ to Fe3+ before it is transported. Hepcidin, an acute-phase protein secreted from the liver plays a major role in the regulation of iron absorption. When the body’s iron stores are adequate it downregulates the expression of ferroportin and thereby iron absorption too. Thus, iron is trapped in the intestinal cells which is eventually sloughed off. Hepcidin also inhibits the release of iron from macrophages by binding to ferroportin. High hepcidin levels are seen in systemic inflammation and low hepcidin levels are seen in hemochromatosis  Iron is an important component of * Hemoglobin * Myoglobin * Cytochrome P450 groups of enzymes * Components of the electron transport chain * Ribonucleotide reductase Given below is an image of iron absorption that shows ferroportin being inhibited by hepcidin at intestinal mucosal cells

text: 6. Which of the following is not a sign of irreversible injury?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Blebbing plasma membrane

Blebbing of plasma membrane is a feature of reversible injury Within limits, a cell can repair derangements and, if the injurious stimulus abates, will return to normalcy. This is called reversible cell injury. Persistent or excessive injury, however, causes cells to pass the rather nebulous “point of no return” into irreversible injury and cell death. The ultrastructural changes of reversible cell injury include: * Plasma membrane alterations, such as blebbing, blunting, and loss of microvilli * Mitochondria - swelling and the appearance of small amorphous densities * Dilation of the ER, with the detachment of polysomes * Intracytoplasmic myelin figures * Nuclear alterations- disaggregation of granular and fibrillar elements Irreversible cell injury * Increased eosinophilia, glassy homogeneous appearance * Whorled phospholipid masses called myelin figures derived from damaged cell membranes * Discontinuities in plasma and organelle membranes * Marked dilation of mitochondria with the appearance of large amorphous densities * Intracytoplsmic amorphous debris, and aggregates of fluffy material probably representing denatured protein. * Nuclear changes- karyolysis, pyknosis and karyorrhexis

text: 7. A pregnant couple presented to the OPD with concerns about thalassemia in their baby due to a positive family history. Genetic studies revealed that both she and her husband are carriers. What is the probability that the child will have thalassemia major?
expl:
Correct answer: A. 25%

There is 25% probability that their child will have thalassemia major. β-thalassemia occurs due to mutations causing an impaired synthesis of β-globin chains of hemoglobin (Hb), leading to anemia, hypoxia, and hemolysis. The mutations can be of two types: * Absent β chain synthesis (β0) * Reduced β chain synthesis (β+) Being an autosomal recessive disease, disease occurs only when both alleles are defective. When only one is defective, they are called carriers or trait. Here as both the parents are carriers, their alleles will be β/β0 or β/β+ (1 β-thalassemia allele and 1 normal allele). As the clinical disease doesn't alter much based on it being β+ or β0, its safe to use use β+ to represent a thalassemia allele.

Thalassemia major means both alleles are mutated. And from the table, that can occur in one of the four ways possible. text: 1. Which of the following is a primary lymphoid organ?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Thymus

Thymus and bone marrow are the primary lymphoid organs (also known as central lymphoid organs). It is the place where immature lymphocytes develop, differentiate, proliferate, and mature into immune competent cells.  A secondary lymphoid organ (also known as a peripheral lymphoid organ) is where the antigen is localized so that it can be effectively exposed to mature lymphocytes. These include the spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, appendix, and Peyer’s patches. Both B lymphocytes and T lymphocytes are produced in the bone marrow. B lymphocytes also mature in bone marrow, while T lymphocytes mature in Thymus. Given below is the histopathological image of the thymus. The thymus is a lymphoid tissue that is arranged in the form of lobules. The lobules are separated from each other by connective tissue.  Each lobule is made up of an outer darker staining cortex and an inner pale-staining medulla. The medulla contains pink rounded masses called Hassell's corpuscles.

text: 4. A 45-year-old patient presents to the haematologist with complaints of weakness and fatigue. Lab investigations reveal a decrease in the haemoglobin and reticulocyte count while WBC and platelet counts are normal. Bone marrow shows a selective decrease in the erythroid precursors. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Pure red cell aplasia

The given scenario along with lab investigations showing a decrease in haemoglobin and reticulocyte count, normal WBC, and platelet count with a selective decrease in the erythroid precursors are suggestive of pure red cell aplasia. Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is a primary marrow disorder that causes the suppression of erythroid progenitors only. One cause is acute parvovirus B19 infection which may lead to an aplastic crisis in patients who already had underlying hemolytic anemia. The hallmark of PRCA, in an otherwise normal marrow, is the absence of erythroblasts. Causes of pure red cell aplasia include: * Neoplasms - thymomas and large granular lymphocytic leukemia * Drug exposure - phenytoin, azathioprine, and isoniazid * Auto-immune disorders - neutralizing antibodies against erythropoietin * Parvovirus infection * Hereditary - Diamond Blackfan syndrome Patients typically present with symptoms of severe anemia such as fatigue, pallor, and dyspnea. Complete blood count (CBC) shows normocytic or macrocytic anemia with very low reticulocyte count. Bone marrow examination reveals normal cellularity but with a marked reduction or absence of erythroid precursors. Flow cytometry and immunophenotyping can be useful in diagnosing associated conditions such as thymoma or lymphoproliferative disorders. Immunosuppressive therapy is the mainstay for idiopathic PRCA, including agents like cyclosporine, corticosteroids, and antithymocyte globulin (ATG). For PRCA associated with parvovirus B19, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) is used. Other options: Option A: Megaloblastic anemia is caused by folate or vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia). Peripheral smear shows characteristic macro-ovalocytic red cells that appear hyperchromic, hypersegmented nuclei in neutrophils, and reticulocytopenia. Marrow is markedly hypercellular due to an increase in the number of hematopoietic precursors. Option B: Iron deficiency anemia is the most common nutritional disorder in the world. Peripheral smears show microcytic hypochromic red blood cells. Bone marrow shows an increase in erythroid progenitors. A significant diagnostic finding is an absence of stainable iron in macrophages which is assessed by Prussian blue stain on aspirated marrow smears. Option C: Aplastic anemia is a chronic primary hematological failure that results in pancytopenia. Clinically, the patients present with features of pancytopenia such as fatigue, recurrent infections, and petechiae and ecchymoses. Characteristically, splenomegaly will be absent. A peripheral smear will show reticulocytopenia. Bone marrow aspirates often give a 'dry tap' which means that they yield little material. Thus, a marrow biopsy would show a markedly hypocellular marrow that is devoid of hematopoietic cells (some fat cells, fibrous stroma, and scattered lymphocytes or plasma cells remain).

text: 5. A child presents with cleft lip, cleft palate and mental retardation. Which of the following chromosomal abnormalities is most consistent with these findings?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Patau syndrome

The given findings of cleft lip, cleft palate with mental retardation in a child are consistent with trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome). Trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome, is characterized by forebrain and midline facial abnormalities. Patients can develop holoprosencephaly, which is characterized by fused frontal lobes and a single ventricle. Olfactory bulbs are also absent. The midline facial abnormalities seen with trisomy 13 include cleft lip, cleft palate, mental retardation, nasal defects, and a single central eye (“cyclops”). Other defects include polydactyly, rocker-bottom feet, renal defects, and congenital heart diseases. The image below shows some facial features of Patau syndrome: Other options: Option A: Prader-Willi syndrome occurs due to the deletion of band 15q12 on the paternal chromosome and the silencing of the same set of genes derived from maternal chromosomes. It is characterized by mental retardation, obesity, hyperphagia, hypogonadism, short stature, small hands and feet. Option C: Angelman syndrome is characterized by the deletion of the ubiquitin ligase gene (UBE3A) on maternal chromosome 15q12 and the silencing of the paternal chromosomal counterpart. It is characterized by intellectual disability, microcephaly, ataxic gait, seizures, and inappropriate laughter. Due to inappropriate laughter and ataxia, they are also known as happy puppets. Option D: Trisomy 18 or Edwards syndrome is characterized by mental retardation, micrognathia, low-set ears, rocker-bottom feet, and congenital heart diseases. The most characteristic finding is a clenched fist with overlapping fingers: the index finger overlies the third and fourth fingers, while the fifth finger overlaps the fourth. It is also associated with polyhydramnios and a single umbilical artery.

The given clinical presentation of palpable purpura, colicky abdominal pain and hematuria point towards a diagnosis of IgA vasculitis also known as Henoch Schonlein purpura (HSP). text: 7. Which of the following clinical condition is a hexanucleotide repeat disorder?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Frontotemporal dementia

Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a hexanucleotide repeat disorder. The C9ORF72 gene is associated with a hexanucleotide repeat expansion mutation. It is a common cause of both FTD and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The mutation leads to the production of abnormal RNA and proteins, causing cellular toxicity. Frontotemporal dementia presents with early personality changes (frontal lobe involvement) and loss of social restraints initially, followed by memory loss. Other features include loss of insight, easy distractibility, reduced concern or empathy for others, emotional lability or withdrawal, impulsiveness, poor self-care, and perseveration. There is a second type of presentation of FTD, which is characterized by an early and progressive change in language, with problems of expression of language or severe naming difficulty, and problems with word meaning. The classic imaging findings seen in FTD are preferential atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes with occipitoparietal sparing Histopathology shows Pick cells (swollen neurons) in affected areas of the brain. These neurons appear larger than normal and are typically filled with cytoplasmic inclusions known as Pick bodies (intraneuronal argentophilic inclusions). Other options: Option B: Fragile X syndrome is the most common genetic cause of intellectual disability in males. It occurs due to CGG repeats in the untranslated regions(UTR) of the FMR1 gene.  Option C: Huntington's disease is a degenerative disease of the caudate and putamen caused by an autosomal dominant inheritance of a trinucleotide repeat (CAG) in the Huntington gene (chromosome 4), which results in motor, behavioral, oculomotor, and cognitive dysfunction.  Option D: Myotonic dystrophy is caused by expansions of CTG triplet repeats in the noncoding region of the myotonic dystrophy protein kinase (DMPK) gene.  It is associated with skeletal muscle weakness, cataracts, endocrinopathy, and cardiomyopathy Pearl PF0389: Differential diagnosis of dementia

text: 9. Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with which of the following conditions?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Celiac disease

Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with celiac disease.  Dermatitis herpetiformis, also known as Duhring’s disease is an auto-immune disease associated with HLA DQ-2 and HLA DQ-8. The antibodies target epidermal transglutaminase-3, resulting in the collection of neutrophils at the dermal papilla. This condition is closely associated with celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy).  The clinical manifestations include grouped vesicles and papules. These lesions are commonly located over the extensor aspects of knees, elbows, buttocks, back, and scalp with symmetrical distribution and are associated with intense pruritus.  The characteristic histopathology finding is subepidermal blisters with papillary tip microabscesses containing neutrophils, which is shown in the image below: The image below shows dermatitis herpetiformis on the knee. Dermatitis herpetiformis targets epidermal transglutaminase 3. Direct immunofluorescence shows focal granular deposits of IgA at papillary tips. A gluten-free diet is the mainstay of treatment, but it takes months to years to show clinical improvement. Hence, dapsone is used for short-term management in these patients. Other Options: Options A & D: Ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease are chronic inflammatory bowel diseases that are mainly idiopathic with a weak genetic component. The common cutaneous manifestations include erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, psoriasis, aphthous stomatitis, and cutaneous vasculitis.  Options B: Whipple's disease is a chronic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei, classically presents as chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, intermittent fever, weight loss, and arthralgia/arthritis with neurological and cardiological involvement. text: 10. Which of the following tests can be done for measuring long-term glucose control in patients with diabetes mellitus?
expl:
Correct answer: B. HbA1c

In patients with diabetes mellitus, HbA1c is the best method to measure long-term glucose control. Glycated haemoglobin, reported as HbA1c, has been used to monitor glycemic control in patients with diabetes for many years. HbA1c results from the attachment of glucose to the N-terminal valine of the hemoglobin β-chain. The concentration of HbA1c depends on both the glucose concentration in the blood and the lifespan of the erythrocyte. Since the half-life of an RBC is 120 days, the HbA1c test is primarily used to evaluate the average blood glucose levels over the past 3 months. Normal glucose tolerance is characterised by an HbA1c < 5.7%; any value of HbA1c equal to or exceeding 6.5 % is diagnostic of the patient being diabetic.  Other options: Fasting blood sugar, random blood sugar, and urine sugar reflect the status of blood glucose level at the instantaneous moment.

text: 12. A 12-year-old child presented with cough for 15 days. On examination, cervical lymphadenopathy was noted and the lymph node biopsy showed the following features. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Tuberculosis

The histopathological findings and clinical history are suggestive of tuberculosis. Once Mycobacterium tuberculosis enters the macrophage, it inhibits the formation of the phagolysosome. This allows it to replicate unchecked. M. tuberculosis recruits a host protein coronin to block the fusion of phagosome and lysosome. Th1 response to M. tuberculosis is mounted about three weeks following the infection. The antigen-presenting cells (APCs) present mycobacterial antigens to the T-cells in the lymph nodes and release IL-12 and IL-18 to cause the differentiation of T-cells into Th1 cells. Th1 cells produce IFN-γ. IFN-γ is the critical step in the body's defense against M. tuberculosis. It acts by activating macrophages, causing phagolysosome maturation, and inducing nitric oxide synthase enzyme to form more reactive nitrogen species. It also mobilizes anti-bacterial compounds like defensins and stimulates autophagy. Th1 response leads to the formation of a granuloma and caseous necrosis. Macrophages that are activated by the action of IFN-γ differentiate into epithelioid histiocytes. These are the cells that actually aggregate to form a granuloma. Some epithelioid cells may also fuse to form a giant cell. The microscopic picture shows the caseating granuloma. Eosinophilic necrotic debris known as caseation, bordered by collections of epithelioid cells, Langhan giant cells and lymphocytes can be seen. Epitheloid cells merge to form Langhan's giant cell where nuclei are arranged in a horseshoe shape (a characteristic feature of tuberculosis). Clinically, tuberculosis presents with chronic cough, breathing difficulty, fever, night sweats, weight loss, and swollen lymph nodes. Chest radiograph shows tree-in-bud pattern, infiltrates, and cavity formation predominantly in the upper lobes. Other options: Option B: Leprosy presents with skin lesions and nerve involvement with loss of sensation. Histopathology shows noncaseating granulomas. Option C: Sarcoidosis shows giant cells with cytoplasmic inclusions and noncaseating granuloma with fibroblastic proliferation at the periphery. Option D: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection that shows hyperplasia of the capsule accompanied by fibrosis, perivascular inflammation, and infiltration of chronic inflammatory cells with caseating granulomas. text: 16. Which of the following blood groups can be given to a patient having Bombay blood group?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Oh

Among the given options, Oh (Bombay) blood group blood can be transfused to Bombay blood group patients. The H antigen is present in all four blood groups (A, B, AB, and O). A rare blood group where there is an absence of the H antigen is known as the Bombay blood group. The absence of this H antigen results in the absence of A and B antigens. Their plasma contains anti-A, anti-B, and strong anti-H antibodies. Therefore, they do not react with anti-A, anti-B, and anti-AB antiserums, and get recognized as O blood group on cell typing. However, the O blood group has an H antigen. Thus if a patient with the Bombay blood group is transfused with the O blood group blood, the anti-H antibodies in the Bombay blood group patient react with the H antigen present in the O blood group. This can lead to fatal transfusion reactions. Therefore, patients with the Bombay blood group require the same blood group during transfusion. Other less common systems of blood grouping include MNSs, Lutheran, Kell, and Kidd systems of blood grouping.  ABO blood typing is performed by mixing the individual's red blood cells with antisera that contains the various agglutinins on a slide and observing for the presence of clumping or agglutination.

text: 4. A 65-year-old male presents with progressive anaemia and cervical lymphadenopathy. The peripheral smear is shown below. Which CD markers will be present in this case?
expl:
Correct answer: C. CD5, CD19, CD20, CD23

The likely diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the peripheral smear showing smudge cells is chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, which is positive for CD19+, CD20+, CD23+, and CD5+. Loss of tumour-suppressor genes in chromosome 13 results in overexpression of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL2. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) is a peripheral B-cell neoplasm usually affecting adults, more commonly men. Patients are often asymptomatic at diagnosis. When symptomatic, it presents non-specifically with easy fatigability, weight loss, and anorexia. Generalised lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are present in most symptomatic patients.  The chromosomal defects in CLL include * Deletion of 13q (commonest and has a good prognosis) * Deletion of 11q * Trisomy 12q * Deletion of 17p (poor prognosis) The peripheral blood smear in cases of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) contains small round lymphocytes having condensed chromatin and scant cytoplasm. Some of these cells may get disrupted while preparing the smears, producing smudge cells. An absolute lymphocyte count of >5000/mm3 is required for diagnosis. Hypogammaglobulinemia is commonly seen, making the patient susceptible to infections. A few patients may develop haemolytic anaemia or thrombocytopenia due to autoantibodies made by non-neoplastic B cells. Immunophenotyping using flow cytometry is the investigation done to arrive at the diagnosis. The classical immunophenotypic features of CLL are CD19+, CD20+, CD23+, and CD5+. On lymph node biopsy: Lymph nodes are composed of small lymphocytes admixed with larger activated lymphocytes. The large lymphocytes contain mitotically active cells and gather in loose aggregates, which are referred to as proliferation centres. These proliferation centres are pathognomonic to CLL when present. Expectant management is the treatment of choice for asymptomatic patients with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. The gold standard for therapy is a combination of fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab. Richter’s syndrome is a complication of CLL in which there is a transformation to an aggressive lymphoma, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). Other options: Option A: CD10, CD22, and CD79 are positive in Burkitt lymphoma. Option B: CD10, CD19, and CD22 are positive in follicular lymphoma. text: 8. Which of the following is most likely to cause Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)?
expl:
Correct answer: B. SOD1 gene mutation

A mutation in the SOD1 gene causes amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The anterior horn of the spinal cord and the corticospinal tracts of the spinal cord are affected by amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The pathologic hallmark of ALS is the death of the affected lower motor neurons (LMN), consisting of the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord and their homologs in the brainstem, and upper motor neurons (UMN), consisting of the corticospinal tract and corticobulbar tract originating in the motor cortex. The hereditary forms of ALS have mutations in the genes encoding for superoxide dismutase (SOD 1) present on chromosome 21. Patients with ALS present with insidious-onset, asymmetric bilateral weakness of the distal part of the lower limbs. There may be a history of cramping, particularly early in the morning. Lower motor neuron death causes muscle atrophy and fasciculations. Upper motor neuron involvement presents as exaggerated tendon reflexes and spasticity. The involvement of the corticobulbar fibres leads to exaggerated expressions of emotion, such as excessive weeping or laughing. This is called the pseudobulbar effect. Some patients also tend to develop frontotemporal dementia. However, sensory, bowel, and bladder functions and cognition are preserved, even in the late stages of the disease. Other options: Option A: FMR1 gene mutation results in Fragile X disease. Option C: CFTR gene mutation results in cystic fibrosis. Option D: HTT gene mutation results in Huntington's disease. text: 9. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction characterizes borderline tuberculoid leprosy?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Type 4

Borderline tuberculoid leprosy is characterized by Type 4 hypersensitivity reaction(Type 1 Leprosy Reaction) In tuberculoid leprosy, dermal granulomas, consisting of groups of epithelioid cells with giant cells, are seen. The granulomas are elongated and generally run parallel to the surface, following neurovascular bundles. The granulomas extend up to the epidermis, thereby obscuring the Grenz zone. It also shows high positivity of the lepromin skin (dermal) test. Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, cutaneous and peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. The commonly affected peripheral nerves are the posterior tibial nerve and the ulnar, median, and lateral popliteal nerves. The most frequently involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve. It has a long incubation period, usually 2 to 12 years. It commonly presents as an area of numbness on the skin or a visible skin lesion, which could be a hypopigmented or erythematous macule. The Grenz zone is most prominent in lepromatous leprosy, as there are scarce granulomas to fill up the space. It is also seen in the borderline spectrum. Cardinal signs for the diagnosis of leprosy: * Characteristic skin lesions—hypopigmented or erythematous lesions with definite impairment of sensation. * Peripheral nerve involvement—thickening of the nerve with sensory impairment. Nerve tenderness can also be seen. * Detection of acid-fast bacilli in slit-skin smear, skin biopsy, or positive biopsy PCR. The presence of two of the three signs can establish the diagnosis of leprosy. Other tests done for diagnosis of leprosy include nerve biopsy in pure neural leprosy and PGL-1 antibody in cases with low bacterial load. Pearl PF0982: Lepra Reactions Lepra Reactions:

text: 10. Of the following, which gene mutation is most frequently linked to medullary thyroid carcinoma?
expl:
Correct answer: A. RET

Medullary thyroid carcinoma is most commonly associated with MEN2A and MEN2B, which occur due to mutation in the RET gene. Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) is a tumour of parafollicular or C cells of the thyroid gland. They are derived from the neural crest cells of the ultimobranchial bodies. Most of the MTCs occur sporadically. However, around a quarter of the cancers are associated with familial MTC, MEN2A, and MEN2B. Patients with sporadic MTC present at an older age, whereas patients with familial MTC usually present at a younger age. Features of MTC include: * Painful neck mass with cervical lymphadenopathy * Dysphagia, dysphonia or dyspnea if locally invaded * Diarrhoea due to increased intestinal motility by serotonin * Cushingoid habitus due to ectopic ACTH production * Metastasis is blood-borne * Microscopically, they consist of sheets of neoplastic cells separated by collagen and amyloid stroma It is diagnosed by careful family history, physical examination, raised calcitonin and CEA levels, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mass. Total thyroidectomy with central neck node dissection is the treatment of choice in MTC patients. External beam radiotherapy can be used in patients with unresectable tumors. Targeted therapy can be considered using vandetanib, sorafenib, sunitinib, and cabozantinib. Prophylactic total thyroidectomy should be considered within 5 years of age in MEN2A mutation and within 1 year of age in MEN2B mutation. Surgical management of MTC is as follows:

text: 11. Which of these triggers apoptosis by activating cytochrome C?
expl:
Correct answer: C. BAX

BAX triggers apoptosis by activating cytochrome C. BAK and BAX are pro-apoptotic factors, whereas BCL2, BCL-XL, and MCL1 are anti-apoptotic proteins. Apoptosis, also known as programmed cell death, occurs due to the activation and release of certain proteases known as caspases. These enzymes are regulated by a balance between the actions of pro-apoptotic and anti-apoptotic proteins on the permeability of the mitochondrial membrane: * Pro-apoptotic proteins increase membrane permeability, thereby causing leakage of proteins that initiate apoptosis, like cytochrome c. * Anti-apoptotic proteins keep the membrane impermeable, preventing the release of cytochrome c. There are two apoptotic pathways— * The intrinsic or mitochondrial pathway * Extrinsic or death-receptor initiated pathway The intrinsic pathway is triggered by DNA damage, accumulation of misfolded proteins, and loss of survival signals. This leads to leakage of pro-apoptotic proteins like cytochrome c into the cytoplasm. Cytochrome c binds to APAF-1 (apoptosis-activating factor-1), forming an apoptosome. This complex activates caspase 9.  The extrinsic pathway is triggered by the engagement of death receptors on the plasma membrane. It activates caspases 8 and 10.  The active forms of these caspases activate executioner caspases (3 and 6), which act on various cell components to cause nuclear fragmentation, DNA degradation, etc. Cytoplasmic blebs and apoptotic bodies are then formed, which are ultimately phagocytosed.  The two pathways are shown in the image below: Pearl PF0839: Necrosis vs Apoptosis

text: 12. A 25-year-old male presents with headaches, visual disturbances, and hypertension. A cerebellar lesion is visible on MRI, and abdominal imaging reveals multiple cysts in the kidneys as well as a solid renal mass, which is suggestive of renal cell carcinoma. His father had similar findings and died of a brain tumour in his 40s. Which of the following chromosomal abnormalities is most likely to cause his condition?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Deletion on chromosome 3p

The given clinical scenario of multiple renal cysts, cerebellar lesion, visual disturbances, and hypertension with a family history is most likely to be von Hippel-Lindau disease, which is characterized by deletion on chromosome 3p. The tumor-suppressor gene VHL, which is linked to von Hippel-Lindau disease, is found on chromosome 3p. It produces a protein called VHL, which is a part of a ubiquitin ligase complex that inhibits hypoxia-induced factor 1 (HIF-1). It is an autosomal dominant syndrome characterized by the development of highly vascularized tumors in multiple organs. These include: * Hemangioblastomas of the retina and central nervous system * Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors * Pheochromocytoma * Renal cysts develop into clear renal cell cancer * Pancreatic cysts * Ovary cystadenoma * Epididymal cystadenoma Those with VHL syndrome inherit an autosomal dominant germline mutation of the VHL gene on chromosome 3p. Liquefactive necrosis refers to cell death caused by enzymatic degradation. It involves the digestion of dead cells, transforming the tissue into a viscous liquid. It occurs in focal bacterial or, on occasion, fungal infections because microbes stimulate the accumulation of leukocytes and the release of enzymes from these cells. Sodium hydroxide is a strong alkali. It is associated with liquefactive necrosis. Unlike other mineral acids, hydrofluoric acid (HF) causes liquefactive necrosis due to the formation of fluoride ions. text: 15. A newborn presents with upward-slanting palpebral fissures, a flat facial profile, and hypotonia. A 5p deletion is detected through karyotyping. Which of the following genetic syndromes result from the deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Cri-du-chat syndrome

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Cri-du-chat syndrome. Cri du Chat syndrome, also known as 5p- syndrome, is a rare genetic disorder caused by the deletion of a portion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p). The syndrome is named after the characteristic high-pitched cry of affected infants, which resembles a cat's meow due to abnormal laryngeal development. Other key clinical features include microcephaly, low birth weight, micrognathia (small jaw), low-set ears, widely spaced eyes (hypertelorism), and intellectual disabilities. Affected children often experience developmental delays, speech difficulties, and behavioral challenges. The severity varies depending on the size of the chromosomal deletion. In addition to the physical and cognitive impairments, individuals with Cri du Chat syndrome may have congenital heart defects, scoliosis, and feeding difficulties. While there is no cure, early intervention with speech therapy, physical therapy, and educational support can improve quality of life and functional abilities. The condition is typically diagnosed through genetic testing, such as karyotyping or fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), to detect the deletion on chromosome 5. With proper medical care and supportive therapies, many individuals with Cri du Chat syndrome can achieve a degree of independence and lead fulfilling lives. text: 16. Which of the following fixatives is most appropriate in Pap smear cytology for preserving cellular details immediately after smearing?
expl:
Correct answer: A. 95% ethanol

In a Pap smear, 95% ethanol is used to preserve cellular details immediately after smearing. A Pap, or Papanicolaou, test is a screening test only. A positive test requires further evaluation with colposcopy, cervical biopsy, or fractional curettage. Specific history to be elicited from patients prior to collection of sample: * The ideal time for the collection of a sample is around ovulation. Cervical squamous cells vary in appearance throughout the menstrual cycle. Thus, asking the patient for their last menstrual period and any use of contraception is a must. * A prerequisite for a Pap smear is that the patient should avoid intercourse 24 hours prior to the test. Thus, this history should be taken. * The use of lubricants and douches may prevent the detection of organisms and the cell structure. Thus, asking the patient for this history is a must to prevent missing appropriate findings. * A history of immunosuppression must be elicited, including a family history of cancer, use of steroids, sexual history for STDs, and HIV/AIDS. In women with such a history, an annual checkup should be advised instead of once every three years. * The use of intravaginal contraceptive creams should be stopped 24-48 hours before the test. The use of exogenous hormones and intrauterine devices may alter the appearance of cervical squamous cells. Hence, this history should be noted for an accurate interpretation of the test.  Screening guidelines: * Time for initiation – 21 years, regardless of the age of first sexual intercourse * Women aged 21-29 years - every 3 years * Women who are aged 30-65 years – Pap test + HPV testing every 5 years * Women can stop cervical cancer screening after the age of 65 years. If suspicious PAP, screening till 75 years * HIV+ women - annual screening  * HPV DNA testing in combination with PAP improves the sensitivity of screening. Procedure: The patient is put in a dorsal position, and Cusco’s self-retaining speculum is introduced. The squamocolumnar junction is identified and scraped with Ayre’s spatula. The endocervix is scraped with a cytobrush. Samples are spread separately on 2 different glass slides. The slide is immediately fixed using 95% ethyl alcohol and stained with Papanicolaou stain or short stain. The most common fixative used in a Pap smear is 95% ethyl alcohol. text: 17. A young boy presents with joint swelling following a fall. Laboratory tests reveal a normal PT and an elevated aPTT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Hemophilia

This patient with a history of joint swelling on minor trauma and an abnormal coagulation panel points to a probable diagnosis of haemophilia. This condition is caused by an X-linked recessive mutation leading to a deficiency of Factor VIII of the coagulation factors. This leads to a prolonged partial thromboplastin time. Haemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder. It occurs due to a deficiency of clotting factor VIII, which causes inadequate thrombin generation and thus the inability to form a tight fibrin clot to support the platelet plug. Symptoms include easy bruising, intramuscular haematomas, haemarthroses, haematuria, and bleeding from minor traumatic lacerations of the mouth can persist for hours or days. text: 18. An electrician sustains electrical burns while at work. On arrival at the ED, he was hemodynamically stable. ECG monitoring and initial fluid resuscitation are started. His urine is collected for routine lab examination and is positive for myoglobin. On histopathology of the kidneys, which of the following will be observed?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Metastatic calcification

The most likely diagnosis based on the clinical vignette given is a case of rhabdomyolysis leading to endogenous intrinsic acute kidney injury (AKI). In rhabdomyolysis with AKI, calcium-phosphate imbalance leads to metastatic calcification in normal renal tissue, especially interstitium. * Metastatic calcification can occur in normal tissues whenever there is hypercalcemia. * The major causes of hypercalcemia are  * Secretion of parathyroid hormone -related protein (PTHRP), due to malignant tumors * Paget's disease, immobilization, or tumors (increased bone catabolism associated with multiple myeloma, leukemia, or skeletal metastases) * Vitamin D intoxication and sarcoidosis * Renal failure * Metastatic calcification can occur throughout the body but mainly affects the interstitial tissues of the vasculature, kidneys, lungs, and gastric mucosa. AKI is defined as a decline in kidney function within 7 days, resulting in the accumulation of nitrogenous waste and other toxic metabolites usually excreted in the urine. It includes a variety of conditions that share some common features, such as elevated creatinine levels and reduced urine output. It is broadly divided into three categories: * Renal/intrinsic parenchymal  * Prerenal * Postrenal Other options: Option A: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in conditions like vasculitis(immune mediated), malignant hypertension. Option B: Caseous necrosis - characteristic of granulomatous infections like tuberculosis. Option C: Dystrophic calcification: * It is encountered in areas of necrosis, whether they are of coagulative, caseous, or liquefactive type, and in foci of enzymatic necrosis of fat. * Calcification is almost always present in the atheromas of advanced atherosclerosis. It also commonly develops in ageing or damaged heart valves, further hampering their function * Calcium salts appear macroscopically as fine, white granules or clumps, often felt as gritty deposits * Tuberculous lymph nodes can be affected by this * Although dystrophic calcification may simply be a telltale sign of previous cell injury, it is often a cause of organ dysfunction. * Serum calcium is normal in dystrophic calcification. text: 1. A 30-year-old female presenting with an unsteady gait, forgetfulness, labile moods, and Kayser-Fleischer rings was diagnosed with Wilson's disease. Which of the following options correctly indicate the gene mutated in this condition and its location?
expl:
Correct answer: A. ATP7B gene on chromosome 13

Wilson's disease, an autosomal-recessive disorder is caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene located on chromosome 13 The ATP7B gene, located on chromosome 13, encodes a transmembrane copper-transporting ATPase, expressed on the hepatocyte canalicular membrane. Deficiency in the ATP7B protein causes a decrease in copper excretion into the bile, impairs its incorporation into ceruloplasmin, and inhibits ceruloplasmin secretion into the blood, leading to the accumulation of toxic levels of copper in the liver, brain, and eye. Note:  Menkes disease is an X-linked metabolic disturbance of copper metabolism caused by mutations in the copper-transporting ATP7A gene.

text: 3. Asbestosis is most commonly associated with which malignancy?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Mesothelioma

Asbestosis is most commonly associated with Mesotheliomas.  Asbestos-related diseases include: * Localized fibrous plaques or diffuse pleural fibrosis * Pleural effusion * Parenchymal interstitial fibrosis (asbestosis) * Lung carcinoma * Mesotheliomas * Laryngeal, ovarian and colon carcinomas Asbestosis: * Asbestosis is a type of pneumoconiosis that occurs after 5-10 years of exposure to asbestos. However, once established, it progresses even in the further removal of the worker from its contact. Asbestosis affects the basal part of the lung causing diffuse peribronchial fibrosis. * Asbestos is of 2 types i.e Serpentine/Chrysolite variety and Amphibole type * Amphibole type has the following varieties: * Crocidolite(blue) * Amosite(brown) * Anthrophyllite(white) * Sputum shows asbestos body, which are asbestos fibres coated with fibrin. * They present with cough and exertional dyspnoea and predominantly affects the lower lobes of the lung, in contrast to other forms of pneumoconiosis, which affect the upper lobes. * Pulmonary function testing in asbestosis typically shows a restrictive pattern with a decrease in both lung volumes and diffusing capacity. * X-ray shows peripheral reticular opacities predominantly in the lower zones. HRCT findings: Honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, irregular opacities, subpleural fibrosis. Lung parenchymal involvement occurs after years of exposure (at least 10 years). * The complications that can occur are * Pulmonary fibrosis  * Carcinoma of the lung  * Malignancy of the Gastrointestinal tract * Mesothelioma of the pleura Preventive measures: * Using a safer type of Asbestos (chrysolite and amosite) * Substituting other insulants like glass fibre, mineral wool, calcium silicate, plastic foams etc * Dust control * Periodic examination of workers * Continuing research Pearl PF0935: Some common pneumoconiosis
