text: 5. A 30-year-old woman presents with a 1-month history of pain in the left knee, which is tender on palpation. X-ray shows a 5 cm mass in the distal femoral epiphysis, with "soap bubble" appearance. Microscopy is as seen below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Osteoclastoma

The most likely diagnosis is osteoclastoma/giant-cell tumor (GCT) of bone. * GCT is a relatively uncommon benign, but locally aggressive, neoplasm that usually arises in individuals in their 20s to 40s. * The neoplastic cells express high levels of RANKL, which promotes the proliferation of osteoclast precursors and their differentiation into mature osteoclasts via RANK expressed by these cells. * GCTs arise in the epiphysis but may extend into the metaphysis. * The majority arise around the knee (distal femur and proximal tibia). * Most are solitary, multicentric tumors in the distal extremities. * The tumors destroy the overlying cortex, producing a bulging soft tissue mass delineated by a thin shell of reactive tissue. * Sheets of uniform oval mononuclear cells and numerous osteoclast-type giant cells with 100 or more nuclei. Necrosis and mitotic activity may be prominent. * Typically, they are treated with curettage, but 40% to 60% recur locally. * Up to 4% of tumors metastasize to the lungs, but these sometimes spontaneously regress and they are seldom fatal. * The RANKL inhibitor, denosumab, has shown promise as adjuvant therapy in GCT.   Remember E mnemonic for GCT- * Epiphyseal * Eccentric * Egg-shell crackling * Expansile

text: 6. A 5-year-old boy presents with weight loss, fever, and a painless swelling in the area of his jaw. CBC reveals anemia and lymphocytosis. Biopsy findings from the swelling are seen in the image below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Burkitt's lymphoma

The clinical presentation and biopsy findings point to a diagnosis of Burkitt's lymphoma. The biopsy image shows tumor cells with multiple small nucleoli, minimal cytoplasm, and high mitotic index closely apposed to each other forming a dark blue background (the "sky"). These cells have a high turnover rate. The macrophages get stuffed in between along with cellular debris, they are called tingible body macrophages. Upon fixation, the cytoplasm washes away leaving behind white spaces filled with debris ( the "stars"). This produces a starry sky appearance, which is classical to Burkitt lymphoma. Burkitt lymphoma: * Most common NHL in children <15 years * Associated with translocation of MYC gene of chromosome 8 (Option A) * Translocations: t (8;14), t (2;8), t (8,22) * Three distinct clinical forms: * Endemic: affects children in Africa, affects jaw, maxilla and is EBV-associated (Option B) * Sporadic: in adults in western countries  * Immunodeficiency associated: HIV infection * It is the most rapidly proliferating human tumor, Ki-67 stains for 100% of cells (DLBCL- 40% staining with Ki-67) Bone marrow aspiration shows tumour cells with royal blue cytoplasm containing clear cytoplasmic vacuoles. The tumour cells express surface IgM, CD19, CD20, CD10, and BCL6, a phenotype consistent with a germinal centre B-cell origin Treatment: Begins within 48h of diagnosis in both children and adults with the use of an intensive combination of chemotherapy regimens with high doses of cyclophosphamide and CNS prophylaxis. text: 10. A 78 year old male presented with complaints of fatigue,breathlessness and palpitations.He has no co-morbidities and does not smoke or drink. On examination there was pedal edema and vitals were: PR-55, BP-100/70, Spo2-94%. The physician in doubt of a disease did a cardiac biopsy which showed apple-green birefringence when viewed under polarized light after staining with Congo red stain. What is the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Cardiac Amyloidosis

The clinical scenario of breathlessness, pedal edema,ECHO finding of restrictive cardiomyopathy and the apple-green birefringence when stained with Congo red stain is suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis. Cardiac amyloidosis: * Amyloidosis of the heart can develop as a consequence of systemic amyloidosis or localized amyloidosis restricted to the heart, particularly in the aged (senile cardiac amyloidosis). * It is seen in individuals 70 years and older, and it has a far better prognosis than systemic amyloidosis. * Senile cardiac amyloid deposits are largely composed of transthyretin, a normal serum protein synthesized in the liver that transports thyroxine and retinol-binding protein. * Cardiac amyloidosis most frequently produces restrictive cardiomyopathy. But, it can also be asymptomatic, manifest as dilation or arrhythmias, or mimic ischemic or valvular disease. * Another presentation of cardiac amyloidosis is congestive heart failure due to systolic dysfunction, generally a later finding. * In approximately 10% of patients with amyloidosis, orthostatic hypotension occurs and is presumed to be a result of amyloid infiltration of the autonomic nervous system. * Morphology: The chambers are usually of normal size, but can be dilated and have thickened walls. Small, semitranslucent nodules resembling drips of wax may be seen on the atrial endocardial surface, particularly on the left. * Histologically, hyaline eosinophilic deposits of amyloid may be found in the interstitium, conduction tissue, valves, endocardium, pericardium, and small intramural coronary arteries.  Image: Congo red stain viewed under polarized light, in which amyloid shows characteristic apple-green birefringence in the heart Other options: Option C- Hemosiderosis is characterized by deposition of hemosiderin, which is a hemoglobin-derived golden-yellow colored pigment. The deposition may occur in any organ or tissue. It is seen in conditions associated with iron overload. This occurs in the absence of derangements in calcium metabolism, i.e the calcium levels are normal. text: 11. A 24-year old male patient presents with anemia. His father and paternal aunt had a similar illness that was treated successfully by splenectomy. His peripheral blood smear is similar to that shown in the illustration below. Which of the following additional abnormalities is expected?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Howell-Jolly bodies

The above image showing spherocytes present on the peripheral blood smear and, along with the history, strongly suggest a diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis (HS). The presence of Howell-Jolly bodies is an additional abnormality which can be expected here. It is an autosomal dominant inheritance disorder. It is due to defective ankyrin, band 3, spectrin, or band 4.2 proteins causing a defect in the red cell membrane. This causes red cells to shed membrane vesicles and transform into spherocytes. The non-deformable spherocytes get trapped in the splenic cords and are phagocytosed by macrophages. * Most common mode of inheritance of HS: Autosomal dominant * Most common gene mutation in autosomal dominant HS: Ankyrin > Band 3 Clinical presentation: The patients usually present with anemia, gall stones, splenomegaly, and jaundice but the age of presentation varies with the severity of the disease. They might also have a family history. Aplastic crisis might occur where red cell production comes to a halt due to parvovirus infection. This lasts for 1 to 2 weeks which is usually the time required for the immune system to clear the virus. Blood transfusions may be needed during this period. Morphology : * The most common finding is spherocytosis, which presents as small, dark-staining (hyperchromic) red cells without the central zone of pallor but this is not specific to HS.  * Features seen in HS are : * Reticulocytosis- increased reticulocyte count * Howell-Jolly bodies- dense basophilic nuclear remnants in the RBCs. * Marrow erythroid hyperplasia * Hemosiderosis * Splenomegaly as a result of congested Billroth cords and increased phagocytes. Diagnosis: Based on family history, peripheral smear findings, and laboratory investigations an adequate diagnosis is made. Increased osmotic fragility is seen in majority of the cases. They also show an increased MCHC (mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration) due to cellular dehydration. Note- Heinz bodies: Undeterred oxidation of hemoglobin in the RBCs leads to the formation of denatured precipitates known as Heinz bodies. These bodies damage the RBC membrane. When these RBCs pass through the splenic cords, macrophages pluck out these precipitates, giving them the characteristic appearance of bite cells. They are seen in cases of chemical poisoning, drug toxicity, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, or the presence of unstable hemoglobin (e.g. hemoglobin Köln) Below image shows Heinz bodies and bite cells.

text: 2. The cells responsible for graft rejection are:

Multiple myeloma usually presents as destructive plasma cell tumors involving the axial skeleton. The bones most commonly affected in descending order of frequency are the vertebral column, ribs, skull, pelvis, femur, clavicle, and scapula.  Morphology: * Malignant plasma cells have a perinuclear clearing due to a prominent golgi apparatus and an eccentrically placed nucleus. * Relatively normal-appearing plasma cells, plasmablasts with vesicular nuclear chromatin and a prominent single nucleolus, or bizarre, multinucleated cells may predominate. * Other cytologic variants include flame cells, Mott cells. * Flame cells have fiery red cytoplasm, Mott cells contain multiple grapelike cytoplasmic droplets, a variety of other inclusions, including fibrils, crystalline rods, and globules. The globular inclusions are referred to as Russell bodies (if cytoplasmic) or Dutcher bodies (if nuclear). * Rouleaux formation is characteristic but not specific. High levels of M protein in the blood causes red cells to stick to one another in linear arrays in smears leading to rouleaux formation. expl:

Meconium is normally evacuated within 6 hours of birth( or earlier), but it can be delayed up to 24-48 hours and the maximum time to wait in a pre-term infant is 48 hours, however, in a term infant, it is 24 hours. text: 3. Tetralogy of Fallot is most commonly associated with which of the following:

text: 4. An 8-year-old boy presented with dark-colored urine as shown below, oliguria, hypertension, and facial puffiness for 3 days. The urine test is positive for albumin. He had a history of throat infection 2 weeks back. On microscopic examination, enlarged, pale glomeruli and epithelial humps are seen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

The clinical scenario given in the question is suggestive of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis(PSGN) is characterized by the sudden onset of gross hematuria, oedema, hypertension, and renal insufficiency. It usually occurs following a throat infection by nephritogenic strains of group A β-hemolytic streptococci. It can also occur after streptococcal skin infection or pyoderma. The typical patient develops an acute nephritic syndrome following 1 to 2 weeks after antecedent streptococcal pharyngitis or 3 to 6 weeks after streptococcal pyoderma. The pathogenesis involves circulating antibodies elicited by streptococcal antigens reacting with normal glomerular antigens, and complement activation by directly deposited streptococcal antigens causing the immunologic injury. In this immune complex-mediated APSGN, we see a decrease in the serum complement (C3) level (levels normalise in 6 to 8 weeks), and ASO titer is increased (the titers decrease to low levels within 4 to 6 weeks). Microscopic Findings in PSGN include * Light microscopy: Enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with diffuse mesangial proliferation and leukocyte infiltration. * Immunofluorescence: Granular deposits of IgG and complement C3 along the glomerular basement membrane(GBM)and in the mesangium.  * Electron microscopy: Electron-dense deposits, or humps, are observed on the epithelial side of the GBM. Below is the image showing light microscopy findings of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Other options: Option A: Post-staphylococcal glomerulonephritis is a kidney condition that occurs after a Staphylococcus infection, leading to immune complex deposition in the glomeruli. It presents with hematuria, proteinuria, oedema, and hypertension, often seen in adults with underlying health conditions. Option C: Nephrotic syndrome is a kidney disorder characterized by massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminemia, oedema, and hyperlipidemia. It results from increased glomerular permeability, leading to fluid retention and other systemic complications. Option D: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) is the most common type of glomerulonephritis worldwide. It is characterized by recurrent hematuria/ nephritic syndrome and the presence of prominent IgA deposits in the mesangium. Clinically, children and young adults present with gross or microscopic hematuria within 1-2 days of onset of an upper respiratory (synpharyngitic presentation) or gastrointestinal infection. text: 6. A newborn baby presents with irritability and cyanosis which subsides on crying. On examination, you are unable to pass a nasogastric tube and no mist formation is noted on the laryngeal mirror test. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Oro pharyngeal airway

Choanal atresia is the persistence of the bucconasal membrane, unilateral is more common and may remain undiagnosed until adult life, bilateral atresia will present as a respiratory obstruction in the newborn. The initial clinical evaluation consists of placing a large laryngeal mirror under each nostril and checking for fogging, this is known as the laryngeal mirror test. Diagnosis can be made by: * Presence of mucoid discharge in the nose * Absence of air bubbles in the nasal discharge * Failure to pass a catheter from the nose to the pharynx * Putting methylene blue dye into the nose and checking its passage to the pharynx * Putting a radio-opaque dye into the nose and taking a lateral radiograph * CT in the axial plane  Management: In bilateral atresia, emergency treatment is to provide an airway, which is done by McGovern's technique- (a feeding tube with a large hole that provides a good oral airway), this removes the need for tracheostomy. text: 7. A 10-month-old child undergoes treatment for diarrhoea with hypokalemia but the child does not respond to the treatment appropriately and on examination muscular weakness is noted, What is the most likely cause of treatment failure?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Hypomagnesemia

The given clinical scenario of a child with diarrhea, muscular weakness, and hypokalemia not responding to treatment is most likely due to hypomagnesemia. The major cause of hypomagnesemia in this scenario is severe diarrhoea/gastrointestinal loss which in turn worsens the hypokalemia. In such cases, hypokalemia can not be corrected unless the underlying hypomagnesemia is addressed.  Treatment failure in hypokalemia due to hypomagnesemia is mediated by two mechanisms: * ↓ Magnesium → inhibits Na+/ K+ - ATPase activity → ↓ influx of potassium into the cell → secondary kaliuresis. * ↓ Magnesium → decreased block of ROMK (renal outer medullary K+ channel) potassium efflux channels → increased potassium secretion by distal nephron Therefore in the presence of hypomagnesemia, hypokalemic patients are clinically refractory to potassium supplementation therapy. Hypokalemia is defined as a plasma concentration of K+ <3.5 meq/L. The following are various causes of hypokalemia: * Inadequate intake * Diet, potassium-free intravenous fluids, potassium deficient TPN * Excessive potassium excretion * Hyperaldosteronism * Medications  * Potassium losses * Direct loss of potassium from GI fluid (diarrhea) * Renal loss of potassium (to conserve sodium in response to gastric losses)  * Metabolic * Intracellular potassium shifts from metabolic alkalosis or insulin therapy Clinical features  * Weakness and paralysis * Intestinal ileus * Risk of atrial and ventricular arrhythmias * Broad flat T waves, ST depression, and QT prolongation are most marked when serum K+ <2.7 mmol/L * Sodium chloride and bicarbonate retention lead to metabolic alkalosis Management includes potassium supplementation with concurrent cardiac monitoring. Treat hypomagnesemia by supplementation. High dose propranolol if due to excess sympathetic activity Other options: Option B: The clinical features of hyponatremia are predominantly neurological as a result of the development of cerebral edema. Patients usually present with nausea, headache, vomiting, seizure, brainstem herniation, and coma. Option C: The clinical features of hypermagnesemia are dose-dependent.  * >2 mmol/L - vasodilation and neuromuscular blockade. * >4 mmol/L - refractory hypotension, progressive weakness leading to respiratory paralysis and coma. Although hypermagnesemia causes muscle weakness, the question asked is the cause of treatment failure in hypokalemia. * >10mmol/L - dilated pupils, bradycardia, PR, QRS, and QT prolongation. Option D: The clinical features of hypernatremia are neurological. The most frequent manifestation is altered mental status ranging from confusion and lethargy to deep coma.

text: 10. A child is brought to the pediatrician with short stature. On evaluation, growth hormone levels are found to be high and Insulin-like growth factor(IGF-1) levels are low. Which among the following could be the abnormality here?
expl:
Correct answer: C. GH receptor anomaly

The presence of high growth hormone levels and low Insulin-like growth factor(IGF-1) levels point towards Laron syndrome/dwarfism. It is caused by end-organ resistance to growth hormone(GH insensitivity) due to the mutation of the growth hormone receptor. Here, growth hormones are produced, but not able to act on the target tissues as growth hormone receptors in the target tissue are not responding to growth hormones. So, the resting and stimulated growth hormone levels are high and insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) levels are low. It is an autosomal-recessive disorder with clinical features that are the same as those seen in pituitary dwarfism. The primary clinical symptom associated with this condition is short stature.  Treatment is by subcutaneous injections of insulin-like growth factor 1 (a growth-promoting hormone), often called IGF-1.

text: 11. A 3-day old male neonate who has not yet passed meconium developed abdominal distension. There is no history of fever. On rectal examination, forceful expulsion of stool was observed. A barium enema is performed and the findings are shown in the image below. Which of the following is the gold standard for the diagnosis of the above condition?
expl:

The clinical scenario of a newborn presenting with failure to pass meconium, abdominal distension, forceful expulsion of stools on rectal examination, and barium enema showing dilated right colon with a transition zone in the mid-descending colon is suggestive of Hirschsprung's disease. The gold standard for the diagnosis of Hirschprung's disease is a rectal biopsy. Hirschsprung disease or congenital aganglionic colon is characterized by the absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus and submucosal (Meissner) plexus of the distal intestinal segment. This is because of the premature arrest of normal migration of neural crest cells from the cecum to the rectum. They are predominantly seen in boys and are associated with Down syndrome. Most cases present during the neonatal period with abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, and failure to pass meconium. Later they may also have poor feeding and severe constipation. Forceful expulsion of stools is observed on rectal examination as the stools accumulate in the distal colon. A barium enema is obtained on all suspected cases. This demonstrates the location of the transition zone between the dilated ganglionic colon and the distal aganglionic rectal segment.  In older children, anorectal manometry shows a high internal sphincter pressure due to the absence of normal inhibitory reflex.  Rectal biopsy is the gold standard investigation shows the following: * Absent ganglia * Hypertrophied nerve trunks * Positive immunostaining for acetylcholinesterase * Calretinin immunostain­ing (superior to acetylcholinesterase staining) The definitive surgeries are the Swenson procedure, Duhamel procedure, and Soave's procedure The most common cause of death in uncorrected Hirschprung's disease is enterocolitis.

text: 12. Which of the following is the first-line drug used to control seizures in a child presenting with febrile seizures?

Correct answer: C. Midazolam

The first-line drug to control the seizures in febrile seizures is a benzodiazepine like midazolam or lorazepam. Febrile seizures occur in children of the age of 6-60 months with a high-grade fever of 38°C (100.4 F) or higher without underlying CNS infections, metabolic abnormality, or prior afebrile seizures. Risk factors: Major: * Age less than 1 year * Duration of fever less than 24 hr * Fever range: 38-39°C (100.4-102.2°F) Minor: * Family history of epilepsy * Daycare * Male gender * Complex febrile seizure * Family history of febrile seizures * Lower serum sodium at the time of presentation Types of febrile seizures:
Simple febrile seizures Complex (atypical) febrile seizures
Occurs within 24 hours of the onset of fever Can occur at any time during a fever
Generalized seizures Focal seizures
Duration is <15 min Prolonged (>15 min)
No recurrence within 24 hrs of seizures Recurrent within 24 hours
Chances of going into epilepsy 1% Chances of going into epilepsy 6%
 Investigations: * Lumbar puncture should be performed in the first episode of seizures with fever, for all infants <6 months age (to exclude meningitis). * EEG and neuroimaging are advised for children with atypical febrile seizures. Acute treatment of febrile seizures includes lorazepam and midazolam for seizures lasting more than 5 minutes. Rectal diazepam is prescribed to use at home as rescue medication if febrile seizures last more than 5 minutes. The use of antipyretics can decrease the discomfort of the child but does not reduce the risk of having a recurrent febrile seizure. Prophylaxis: * Intermittent prophylaxis includes oral clobazam for 3 days during the fever episode, if the febrile seizures recur at the rate of ≥3 seizures in 6 months, or ≥4 in 1 year. * Continuous prophylaxis with sodium valproate and phenobarbitone can be used for failed intermittent prophylaxis and in recurrent atypical febrile seizures. Note: * Intermittent oral nitrazepam, clobazam, and clonazepam have also been used. Such therapies help reduce, but do not eliminate, the risks of recurrence of febrile seizures. * Future epilepsy does not change with or without antiepileptic therapy. * Iron deficiency is associated with an increased risk of febrile seizures, and thus screening and treating it would be appropriate.

text: 13. A 31-year-old lady with diabetes mellitus delivers a term neonate. Which of the following problems is associated with a baby born to this lady?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Hypoglycemia

The condition associated with an infant born to a mother with diabetes mellitus is hypoglycemia. In pregestational diabetes and gestational diabetes mellitus, maternal hyperglycemia causes a higher amount of blood glucose to pass through the placenta into the fetal circulation. It results in fetal hyperglycemia leading to fetal hyperinsulinism. These increased insulin levels continue to persist after delivery which leads to hypoglycemia. Extra glucose in the fetus is stored as body fat causing macrosomia. These newborns are at risk of developing various complications due to fetal hyperglycemia. They are: * Gastrointestinal: These infants may demonstrate abdominal distention caused by a transient delay in the development of the left side of the colon due to fluctuations in maternal and fetal glucose resulting in small left colon syndrome. * Metabolic: Hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia * Neural: Neural tube defects like caudal regression syndrome, encephalocele, anencephaly  * Respiratory: Respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnea of newborn, persistent pulmonary hypertension * Cardiac: Cardiomegaly, cardiac malformations like a ventricular or atrial septal defect, transposition of the great vessels(most specific), truncus arteriosus, double-outlet right ventricle, tricuspid atresia, coarctation of the aorta * Haematological: Polycythemia, renal vein thrombosis * Others: Hyperbilirubinemia, insulin resistance, diabetes, sudden intrauterine death

text: 15. Dystrophin protein is absent completely in which of the following diseases?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy

Dystrophin protein (a sarcolemmal protein), is absent in patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) due to a mutation in the dystrophin gene. Lack of dystrophin leads to cellular instability, which leads to progressive leakage of intracellular components. Dystrophin connects actin filaments to the transmembrane protein β-dystroglycan in the sarcolemma by the smaller proteins syntrophins in the cytoplasm. Duchenne muscular dystrophy: * Most common hereditary neuromuscular disease * It is an X-linked recessive disorder, and the causative gene is located at Xp21. * Clinical features * Progressive weakness with developmental delay occurs. * Pseudohypertrophy of calves and wasting of thigh muscles is seen. * Trendelenburg gait or hip waddle is characteristic. * Gower’s sign: Indicates weakness of proximal muscles: The patient has to use hands and arms to "walk-up" their own body from a squatting position. * Dilated cardiomyopathy * Diagnosis * Elevated serum creatine kinase levels * Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis for the dystrophin gene * If PCR is normal, but clinical suspicion is high, muscle biopsy with dystrophin immunocytochemistry is done. * Treatment: Treatment of cardiac decompensation, nutritional management, physiotherapy, and glucocorticoids. * Prognosis: Death occurs usually at about 18 to 20 years of age due to respiratory failure, intractable heart failure, pneumonia, or aspiration. Other options: Option A: Becker's muscular dystrophy(BMD) leads to abnormal dystrophin formation, whereas the dystrophin gene mutation in DMD leads to dystrophin deficiency. Option C: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a neuromuscular disorder that is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles, due to a decrease in the number of available acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at neuromuscular junctions as a result of antibody-mediated autoimmune attack. Option D: Lambert Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome is a neuromuscular junction disorder associated with the reduced acetylcholine (Ach) release from the presynaptic nerve terminals, despite normal ACh vesicle numbers, ACh presynaptic concentration, and postsynaptic ACh receptors.

text: 16. A 6-year-old child was brought to her pediatrician for routine well-child care. Her physical examination is normal except for a systolic murmur and a widely split-second heart sound that does not vary with respiration. She has no family history of heart disease. Which among the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Atrial septal defect

The age of the patient, normal physical findings except for a systolic murmur, and wide and fixed (does not vary with respiration) splitting of S2 are all in favor of a diagnosis of atrial septal defect. ASDs are abnormal, fixed openings in the atrial septum caused by incomplete tissue formation that allows communication of blood between the left and right atria. The ASD creates a left to right shunt that increases the blood flow to the right side of the heart. This causes the pulmonary valve to close later than the aortic valve. Since the two atria are linked, inspiration does not produce any net pressure changes between them abolishing respiration-related changes in venous return hence causing fixed S2.  Other options: Option A: TAPVC patients usually present with cyanosis and congestive cardiac failure around 4-10 weeks of age. This is when the fetal pulmonary vasculature regresses and there is increased pulmonary blood flow which results in early-onset cardiac failure. The physical findings are identical to ASD. Option B: Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is typically associated with a pan-systolic murmur best heard in the left lower sternal border. Option C: Pulmonic stenosis is an acyanotic heart disease and physical findings include an ejection systolic murmur and a thrill in the left second intercostal space and a wide and variable split S2 because of delayed closure of P2.

This malnourished child with a distended abdomen has kwashiorkor due to protein malnutrition. Kwashiorkor is a form of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) characterized by edema and apathy. Alternating bands of light and normal color hair may be seen, known as the flag sign. Children are miserable, apathetic, and often refuse to eat. There is marked muscle atrophy and growth retardation. Marasmus is another form of SAM that occurs as a result of a calorie deficiency primarily. It is characterized by severe wasting that occurs due to the consumption of fat and muscle to release energy. The child has monkey facies and baggy pants appearance due to the loss of fat pad in the face and buttocks without edema. text: 2. What is the fluid of choice for shock in a child with severe acute malnutrition?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Ringer's lactate with 5% dextrose

The fluid of choice for shock in a child with severe acute malnutrition(SAM) is Ringer's lactate with 5% dextrose. If a child with SAM is lethargic or unconscious with cold extremities plus decreased capillary refill (>3 sec) or weak fast pulse, it is said to be in shock. Intravenous fluid resuscitation in SAM is only recommended in those with shock. IV fluids that can be used in these children are * Ringer lactate with 5% dextrose * Half-normal saline with 5% dextrose  * Half-strength Darrow solution with 5% dextrose. If any of the above mixtures is not available, only then ringer lactate can be used. 10% glucose is given orally or IV in SAM to treat hypoglycemia and is not used to replenish intravascular volume.

text: 6. Which of the following is not a correct match for ABCD according to paediatrics advanced life support?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Dehydration

According to paediatrics advanced life support (PALS), the incorrectly matched one is D-dehydration. The American Heart Association, in its Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) curriculum, supports the structured format of the airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure- ABCDE for primary assessment. Airway- The primary survey's first and most important portion is the patient’s airway. A simple chin-lift or jaw thrust manoeuvre re-aligns the airway. An artificial airway that is appropriate for the patient’s situation like oropharyngeal airways (OPA), and nasopharyngeal airways (NPA) can be used. Breathing-Assessment of breathing includes respiratory rate, effort, abnormal sounds, and pulse oximetry. Central cyanosis is a sign of severe hypoxia and indicates an emergent need for oxygen supplementation and respiratory support. Circulation- Cardiovascular function is assessed by evaluation of skin colour and temperature, heart rate, heart rhythm, pulses, and capillary refill time. Disability- This refers to a child’s neurologic function in terms of the level of consciousness. An assessment of light reflex and use of either of the standard scores used in paediatrics. Any child with a depressed level of consciousness should be immediately assessed for abnormalities in cardiorespiratory status. Exposure- Exposure is the final component after the child has been stabilized. This includes exposing the child to assess for previously unidentified injuries by performing a focused physical exam, and assessing for burns, bruising, bleeding, joint laxity, and fractures.

expl:
Correct answer: B. 60

According to the neonatal resuscitation protocol, chest compressions are started when heart rate is below 60/min The response to neonatal resuscitation at various steps is assessed based on the heart rate. * If the heart rate is less than 100/min, PPV is initially provided with bag and mask on room air, and SPO2 monitoring is done. text: 11. Gonadal growth corresponds with?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Skeletal system

Gonadal growth corresponds with a growth spurt during puberty that results in somatic or skeletal growth. Gonadal growth is dormant during childhood and becomes prominent during puberty. Skeletal maturity is achieved when the epiphysis/growth plates fuse with the shaft/diaphysis, around 18 years in girls and 20-22 years in boys. The degree of skeletal maturation closely correlates with the degree of sexual maturation. A child who has advanced sexual maturity will also have earlier skeletal maturation. text: 13. A neonate was brought with a history of frothiness from the mouth and respiratory distress. An X-ray of the neonate is given below. What is the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Esophageal atresia with tracheo-esophageal fistula

The given symptoms of frothiness and respiratory distress and an X-ray showing a nasogastric (NG) tube in proximal esophagus and stomach distended with gas are suggestive of esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF). Longitudinal furrow separates the trachea from the esophagus during development. Deviation or altered growth in this septum results in the formation of an abnormal fistula communication between the esophagus and trachea called a tracheoesophageal fistula. It is associated with VACTERL (vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheal, esophageal, renal, and limb) anomalies. The newborn has excessive drooling and frothing soon after birth. On feeding, the baby develops choking and cyanosis. Regurgitation of secretion and feed through the fistulous tract into the lungs results in aspiration pneumonia. Type C consists of proximal esophageal atresia and distal TEF is the commonest. Here the air enters into stomach causing gastric distention which is seen as an air bubble. There is an inability to pass an NG tube for more than 7-10 cm, and a coiling in the proximal esophagus helps in the diagnosis. Other options Option A - Transient tachypnea of newborn is due to delayed clearance of lung fluid. They have tachypnea with minimal or no respiratory distress. Chest X-ray may show hyper-expanded lung fields, prominent vascular marking and prominent interlobar fissure. Option B: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia occurs because of the failure to close the pleuroperitoneal membrane. Intestinal loops enter the thorax and compress the developing lung causing pulmonary hypoplasia. They present with respiratory distress and a scaphoid abdomen. Chest X-ray would show multiple air-filled spaces in the thorax, a shift of mediastinum, and the absence of an outline of the left diaphragm. Option D: Respiratory distress syndrome/Hyaline membrane disease occurs primarily in premature infants due to a deficiency of surfactant in the alveoli. Clinical features include tachypnea, retractions, grunting, cyanosis, and decreased air entry. X-ray shows reticulogranular pattern, ground glass opacity, low lung volume, air bronchogram, and white-out lungs in severe disease. text: 1. A 7-year-old child presents to OPD with a painless leg deformity and widening of the wrist. Further investigations show hypocalcemia, increased parathyroid hormone and hypophosphatemia with increased alkaline phosphate. A radiograph of the child's legs is shown below. The most common cause of this deformity is ______.
expl:
Correct answer: B. Rickets

The radiograph shows the bowing of the legs of the child. The most common cause of this deformity is rickets. Rickets is a condition that affects bone development in children, leading to soft and weak bones due to a deficiency of vitamin D, calcium, or phosphate. It is commonly caused by inadequate sunlight exposure or poor dietary intake of these nutrients. Symptoms include delayed growth, bone pain, deformities like bowed legs or a pigeon chest, and dental issues. Severe cases may result in fractures or skeletal abnormalities. Treatment involves vitamin D and calcium supplementation, a balanced diet, and adequate sunlight exposure to promote healthy bone development. Early intervention is crucial to prevent long-term complications. In toddlers, bow leg or genu varum is one of the most common initial signs of rickets. In older children, genu valgum or coxa vara might be present. Other options : Option A: Scurvy is a disease caused by vitamin C deficiency, leading to symptoms like bleeding gums, joint pain, fatigue, and poor wound healing. It occurs due to impaired collagen synthesis and is treatable with vitamin C-rich foods or supplements. Option C: Hyperparathyroidism is a condition where overactive parathyroid glands produce excessive parathyroid hormone (PTH), leading to high calcium levels in the blood. It can cause symptoms like bone pain, kidney stones, fatigue, and abdominal discomfort. Option D: Hypophosphatemia is a condition characterized by low serum phosphate levels, which can lead to muscle weakness, respiratory failure, and impaired cellular function. It can result from malnutrition, refeeding syndrome, alcohol abuse, or certain medical conditions like hyperparathyroidism. It is increased in cases of rickets due to excessive accumulation of uncalcified osteoid at the growth plate. * Cupping of metaphysis: normally metaphysis meets epiphysis as a smooth line of sclerosis. But in rickets the line is absent and the metaphyseal ends appear irregular and the cartilage accumulating in the growth plate creates a depression in the metaphysis causing cupping. * Fraying: indistinct margins of the metaphysis * Bowing of diaphysis, with thinning of cortices * In healing rickets, zone of calcification becomes denser.  The above features are prominent at the growth plates where growth is greatest: * Knee: distal femur, proximal tibia * Wrist: especially the ulna * Anterior rib ends: rachitic rosary The below image shows bowing of legs in rickets. 3. A child with fused carpal bones comes to your clinic, diagnosed with hand-foot syndrome. What is the
gene associated with hand-foot syndrome?
expl:
Correct answer: A. HOXA13

In the given clinical scenario, a child with fused carpal bones is diagnosed with hand-foot syndrome, and the associated gene is HOXA13. The HOXA13 gene is part of the HOX gene family, which is crucial for the regulation of embryonic development, particularly in the formation of limbs and genital organs. Mutations in the HOXA13 gene can lead to congenital conditions such as hand-foot-genital syndrome (HFGS), which is characterized by abnormalities in the hands, feet, and reproductive organs. Hand-foot-genital syndrome (HFGS) is a rare congenital disorder caused by mutations in the HOXA13 gene, which is responsible for the development of limbs and genitalia. The condition is characterized by abnormalities in the hands and feet, such as fused or extra fingers and toes, as well as malformations in the genital organs, including underdeveloped or absent structures. Other symptoms may include urinary tract anomalies and, in some cases, growth retardation. HFGS is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, meaning that a single copy of the mutated gene is sufficient to cause the condition. Early diagnosis and management are essential to address the physical and developmental challenges associated with the syndrome. Other options: Option B: The BCL6 gene encodes a protein that acts as a transcriptional repressor, playing a key role in regulating immune system function, particularly in B cells. Mutations in BCL6 are associated with various lymphomas, including diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). Option C: FGFR (Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor) is a family of cell surface receptors involved in regulating cell growth, differentiation, and development. text: 4. A 4-week-old neonate was brought to the hospital with complaints of non-bilious vomiting. During the examination, the physician noted a firm, olive-shaped mass in the upper abdomen, which moved during feeding. What is the likely diagnosis for this child?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Idiopathic hypertrophic pyloric stenosis

The clinical scenario of projectile non-bilious vomiting with an olive-shaped mass in the upper abdomen, which moved during feeding, is suggestive of Idiopathic Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis. Idiopathic hypertrophic pyloric stenosis presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting. It is common between 2 and 8 weeks of age. Hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus results in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet. Male infants are at a higher risk. Clinically, an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium. When the infant is given a test feed, visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right(not from right to left), followed by projectile vomiting. Metabolic abnormality: * Infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis develop a characteristic metabolic abnormality i.e. Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria. * Persistent vomiting results in loss of hydrochloric acid leading to the development of metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-). * Kidneys try to compensate for alkalosis by secreting Na+ and HCO3-. However, loss of sodium stimulates the secretion of aldosterone through the RAAS pathway. * The aldosterone causes active reabsorption of sodium in exchange for K+ and H+ ions. * Loss of potassium ions leads to the development of hypokalemia. * Loss of H+ ions in urine lowers the urinary pH resulting in aciduria. It is called paradoxical aciduria since the body initially lost H+ ions due to loss of HCl, and instead of compensating for that loss, the body loses more H+ ions through urine. Ultrasound examination is the investigation of choice for this condition. The diagnostic criteria for pyloric stenosis are a muscle thickness of ≥4 mm and a pyloric length of ≥16 mm. The cervix sign and nipple sign are signs seen on USG. * Double-layered hypertrophic mucosa protrudes into the stomach, creating the so-called Nipple sign. * The sonographic appearance of the hypertrophied pylorus resembles that of the uterine cervix and is sometimes referred to as the cervix sign. Management: * The child should be rehydrated and the metabolic abnormality has to be corrected before proceeding to surgery. * The Ramstedt pyloromyotomy remains the standard surgical procedure for its treatment. Other options: Option A: Esophageal atresia is a congenital condition where the oesophagus fails to properly connect to the stomach, leading to feeding difficulties and potential aspiration. It is often associated with a fistula between the oesophagus and trachea, requiring surgical correction. Option C: Duodenal atresia is a congenital obstruction of the duodenum, often causing vomiting and inability to pass stool shortly after birth. It is commonly associated with a "double bubble" sign on abdominal X-rays due to the accumulation of air in the stomach and duodenum. Option D: Intussusception is a condition where a part of the intestine folds into an adjacent segment, causing obstruction, pain, and potential blood in the stool. It commonly affects infants and young children and can be treated with an enema or surgery if needed. This child's presentation points towards the diagnosis of uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition as he has a good appetite and the absence of oedema or any danger signs. Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in children ages 6 to 59 months is defined by WHO as any of the following: * Weight-for-length (or height) below −3 SD of the WHO Child Growth Standards. * Presence of bipedal oedema. * Mid-upper arm circumference <11.5 cm/115 mm. Assess for the following complications: * Severe edema(+++), or * Low appetite (failed appetite test), or * Medical complications, or  * One or more danger signs as per IMNCI. The presence of any one of these is characteristic of complicated SAM and requires inpatient management in a facility. Uncomplicated SAM can be managed under supervised home care. Supervised Home Management of Uncomplicated SAM. Children with uncomplicated SAM can be managed at home provided: • Family is counselled and fully engaged. • Community health worker(s) and peer counsellors are involved in supporting the family. • Supply of adequate home food and ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF), if possible. • Periodic monitoring for growth and medical conditions can be ensured. The child should be provided with 175 kcal/kg body weight/day. The general treatment involves 10 steps in 2 phases: 1. Initial stabilization phase : (mnemonic: SHIELDED- Sugar deficiency(hypoglycemia), Hypothermia, Infection, ELectrolyte imbalance, DEhydration, Deficiency of nutrients) * Focuses on restoring homeostasis and treating medical conditions. * 2-7 days of inpatient treatment 2. Rehabilitation phase:  * Focuses on rebuilding wasted tissues * Takes several weeks Steps: * Treat hypoglycemia (Blood glucose level<54 mg/dl): if symptomatic give 10% Dextrose IV 5ml/kg; Feeding should be initiated with starter F-75 (Formula with 75 kcal/100 ml of feed) * Treat hypothermia (axillary <35°C or 95°F): Skin-to-skin contact with care (“kangaroo technique”) or dress in warmer clothes, cover head, wrap in a warmed blanket, and provide indirect heat. * Treat dehydration: Hydrate with ReSoMal (45 mmol Na/L). It is a low-sodium rehydration solution for malnutrition. * Correct electrolyte imbalance: There is a deficit of potassium and magnesium and excess sodium. Give extra potassium (3 to 4 mEq/kg/day) and magnesium (4 mEq/ kg/day) for at least 2 weeks. * Treat infection: Starting on the first day, give broad-spectrum antibiotics to all children. * Correct micronutrient deficiencies: * Do not give iron in the stabilization phase, because excess iron leads to free radical injury. Give iron 3 mg/kg/day once the child starts gaining weight after the stabilization phase. * Give vitamin A on day 1. text: 6. A newborn child is having respiratory difficulty. The doctor evaluated and the child was found to have a posterolateral defect as shown in the CT image below. What is the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Bochdalek hernia

The clinical presentation of a newborn with respiratory distress and a posterolateral defect, as seen on the CT scan, suggests a diagnosis of Bochdalek hernia. A diaphragmatic hernia occurs due to intrathoracic movement of the abdominal contents through a diaphragmatic defect. The types include: * Bochdalek hernia (posterior): Most common type. Herniation occurs through the pleuroperitoneal foramen. * Morgagni hernia (anterior): Herniation occurs through the foramen of Morgagni. Clinical features : * Respiratory distress is a cardinal sign in infants with a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Early respiratory distress, within 6 hr after birth, is thought to be a poor prognostic sign. * Children with CDH may also have a scaphoid abdomen and increased chest wall diameter. * Bowel sounds may also be heard in the chest, with a bilateral decrease in breath sounds. * The point of maximal cardiac impulse may be displaced away from the side of a hernia if a mediastinal shift has occurred. * Retroperitoneal fat, left kidney, spleen or only the omentum commonly herniates through the defect. If the defect is large, most abdominal contents including the stomach may herniate. Diagnosis: * Chest radiography and passage of a nasal gastric tube confirm the diagnosis. * CDH can be diagnosed on prenatal ultrasonography (between 16 and 24 weeks of gestation) * High-speed fetal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can further define the lesion. Treatment: Variable period of time (24-72 hours) to allow for stabilization before surgical repair. Immediate respiratory support should be provided, including rapid endotracheal intubation and sedation.  Bag and Mask Ventilation is contraindicated in newborns with congenital diaphragmatic hernia because it causes distension of the stomach which in turn may limit the expansion of the already hypoplastic lung. Other options: Option B: A traumatic hernia occurs when an injury to the abdominal wall or diaphragm results in the protrusion of internal organs. It often develops after blunt or penetrating trauma and may require surgical repair depending on the severity. Option C: Morgagni hernia is the defect at the anteromedial location. It is rarer than Bochdalek hernia and accounts for only 2-5% of CDH. About 90% of the cases occur on the right side. It is less symptomatic and the diagnosis is usually delayed until childhood. The patient presents with respiratory or upper GI symptoms. Respiratory symptoms like distress, tachypnea, and recurrent pulmonary infections are common in children. Other symptoms are abdominal pain, dyspnea, flatulence, and indigestion. Radiographic findings * Radiolucent para cardiac shadow may be seen retrosternal on lateral chest x-ray if there is bowel herniation. * Rounded opacity in the right cardiophrenic angle may be seen if there is herniation of the omentum or solid organs. (Shown below) Option D: A hiatal hernia occurs when a portion of the stomach pushes through the diaphragm into the chest cavity. It can cause symptoms such as heartburn, regurgitation, and chest pain, and may require medical or surgical treatment.

text: 8. Which of the following abnormalities is a child with a single palmer transverse crease and low-set ears most likely to have?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Aneuploidy

A child with a single palmar transverse crease and low-set ears is most likely to have Down syndrome and it is a type of aneuploidy. Down Syndrome is a type of aneuploidy. It occurs due to the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21), leading to a total of 47 chromosomes instead of the normal 46. This chromosomal abnormality causes the characteristic physical features, developmental delays, and health issues associated with the condition. Mechanism: * Majority of cases -  meiotic nondisjunction (95%) of chromosome 21 in the ovum * Rarely - (4%) Robertsonian translocation (option D) of the long arm of chromosome 21 to another acrocentric chromosome (e.g., 22 or 14)  * Mosaic pattern: 1% (option A) Clinical features of Down’s syndrome include (Mnemonic: I C A PROBLEM Somewhere), intellectual disability/Incurved or short fifth finger with clinodactyly, congenital heart disease, acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia/Alzheimer's disease/Atlantoaxial instability/Atresia of the duodenum, protruding tongue, round face, occiput flat/Open wide fontanelle/Open mouth, brachycephalic/Brush field's spots, low (depressed) nasal bridge, epicanthal fold/Ears low set and dysplastic, mongoloid slant (oblique palpebral fissure), simian palmar crease and wider gap between first and second toes. The most common cause of intestinal obstruction in Down syndrome is duodenal atresia (double-bubble sign). Children with Down's syndrome have an increased risk of developing leukaemias, including acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). AML is more common during the first 3 years of life. The most common AML associated with Down Syndrome is acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia. The most common haematological manifestation of Down syndrome is transient abnormal myelopoiesis (TAM). Brushfield's spots are whitish speckling on the iris seen in light-skinned people as shown in the image below. Other options: Option A: Gonadal mosaicism is a mutation that occurs only in egg or sperm cells and the individual will be phenotypically normal. These individuals with gonadal mosaicism can transmit the disease-causing mutation to the offspring through their mutated gametes.

text: 9. What is the appropriate timing for taking a blood sample to diagnose neonatal hypothyroidism?
expl:
Correct answer: C. 72 hours after delivery

The appropriate time for taking a blood sample to diagnose neonatal hypothyroidism is 72 hours after delivery. After birth, there is a temporary elevation in TSH levels due to physiological neonatal surge, which remains elevated for the first 2-3 days of life. If sampling is done during this period, falsely elevated TSH values may be obtained. Therefore, the ideal time for sampling through a heel prick is after 72 hours of life. Screening for children for congenital hypothyroidism is very important, as early diagnosis and treatment can help in normal intellectual development. Otherwise, congenital hypothyroidism is known as the most common preventable cause of mental retardation. Children diagnosed beyond the neonatal period have a poor outcome. The most commonly used strategy is to screen for TSH first as that has have higher sensitivity compared to the T4-based approach. Although the TSH-based approach is better, it doesn't identify central hypothyroidism, which can be identified by the T4-first approach. However, the T4-based approach misses out on the cases of compensated hypothyroidism. The incidence of congenital hypothyroidism seems to be 4 times higher in India compared to Western countries. Thyroid dysgenesis has emerged as the most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism in India accounting for about 75% of all cases. Interestingly, an Increased incidence of thyroid dysgenesis is noted in Down syndrome. Clinical features of hypothyroidism:

text: 13. What is the immediate next step in the management of a 29-week gestation infant with a heart rate of less than 100/min and an oxygen saturation of 80% in the right upper limb?

options.B: Positive pressure ventilation with room air

expl:
Correct answer: A. Positive pressure ventilation with 21-30% O2

The immediate next step in managing a 29-week preterm neonate with a heart rate <100/min and SpO₂ of 80% in the right upper limb is positive pressure ventilation (PPV) with a bag and mask using 21–30% oxygen. According to the Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP) guidelines, management is based on heart rate (HR) and oxygen saturation (SpO₂) targets: * HR <100/min → Initiate PPV (Key indicator for respiratory distress or inadequate breathing). * SpO₂ at 80% in the first few minutes is slightly low but within the normal transitional range for preterm infants. However, ventilation support is needed since HR is <100/min. * Preterm infants (≤35 weeks gestation) should receive initial PPV with 21–30% oxygen (not 100%) to minimize oxidative injury. * If HR remains <60/min despite effective PPV, chest compressions and higher FiO₂ (up to 100%) should be considered. As soon as a baby is born, the tone, cry, breathing efforts, and respiratory efforts are assessed. If the tone is poor, or if the baby is not breathing, the following measures are done immediately - warming to maintain the normal temperature, proper positioning of the baby's airway, i.e. sniffing position with the head slightly extended, clearing of airway secretions, and tactile stimulation. After the initial steps of neonatal resuscitation, the heart rate of the baby must be assessed. If the heart rate is < 100 beats per minute (bpm), positive pressure ventilation is provided along with SPO2 monitoring to ensure adequate ventilation.  If the heart rate remains at < 100 bpm, ventilation corrective steps and/or endotracheal intubation have to be considered. The ventilation corrective steps are as follows and can be remembered with the mnemonic MRSOPA. * Mask has to be reapplied  * Reposition head * Suction the secretions * Open mouth slightly and ventilate * Pressure is increased slightly * Airway may be changed If the heart rate is < 60 bpm, chest compressions are initiated over the lower third of the sternum at a rate of 90 compressions/min. The ratio of compressions to ventilation is 3: 1 (90 compressions: 30 breaths).  If the heart rate still remains <60 bpm, despite effective compressions and ventilation, then epinephrine (1:10,000 solution at 0.1–0.3 mL/kg intravenously or 0.5–1 mL/kg intratracheally) should be administered. The dosage can be repeated every 3–5 minutes. Persistent bradycardia may signify inadequate ventilation or severe cardiac compromise. text: 14. A child presents with micrognathia and low-set ears. These clinical features are commonly associated with which type of genetic abnormality?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Deletion

The given clinical scenario of a child presenting with micrognathia and low-set ears is suggestive of cri-du chat syndrome, and it is associated with the deletion of chromosome 5p. Cri du Chat syndrome, also known as 5p- syndrome, is a rare genetic disorder caused by the deletion of a portion of the short arm of chromosome 5. The syndrome is named after the characteristic high-pitched cry of affected infants, which resembles a cat's meow due to abnormal laryngeal development. Other key clinical features include microcephaly, low birth weight, micrognathia (small jaw), low-set ears, widely spaced eyes (hypertelorism), and intellectual disabilities. Affected children often experience developmental delays, speech difficulties, and behavioural challenges. The severity of symptoms varies depending on the size of the chromosomal deletion. In addition to the physical and cognitive impairments, individuals with Cri du Chat syndrome may have congenital heart defects, scoliosis, and feeding difficulties. While there is no cure, early intervention with speech therapy, physical therapy, and educational support can improve quality of life and functional abilities. The condition is typically diagnosed through genetic testing, such as karyotyping or fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), to detect the deletion on chromosome 5. With proper medical care and supportive therapies, many individuals with Cri du Chat syndrome can achieve a degree of independence and lead fulfilling lives. text: 15. Dehydration occurs in both adults and children, but children become dehydrated more easily than adults. How does the ratio of extracellular fluid (ECF) to intracellular fluid (ICF) in children differ from that in adults?
expl:
Correct answer: C. ECF is higher than ICF

In infants and young children, the ECF is higher than ICF. This higher ECF-to-ICF ratio in children explains why they are more susceptible to dehydration.  At birth, ECF is approximately 1.5 times that of ICF. However, this changes rapidly to become almost equal to ICF by day 10 of life. ICF gradually increases in proportion to become twice as much as ECF by age 3 years, and this proportion (two-thirds of TBW is ICF and one-third of TBW is ECF) is maintained thereafter. Higher ECF volume in children is physiologically necessary for rapid growth and development but makes them more vulnerable to fluid losses through fever, diarrhea, or vomiting. This distinctive fluid distribution gradually shifts toward adult proportions as the child grows, with ICF increasing and ECF decreasing relatively. This is markedly different from adults where ICF predominates. In newborns, extracellular fluid makes up about 45% of body weight compared to about 15% in adults.  Other Options Option A (ICF is higher than ECF) describes the adult fluid distribution, not children's. Option B (Total body water is high) is true but doesn't address why children are more susceptible to dehydration. Option D (ECF is equal to ICF) is incorrect as the ECF clearly predominates in children.

text: 2. Which of the following channels is defective in a child with a CFTR gene defect?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Cl-

A child with a CFTR(Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator protein) mutation will have cystic fibrosis. Abnormalities in the CFTR gene lead to defective chloride (Cl-) channels. Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the lungs, digestive system, and other organs. It is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, which leads to the production of thick and sticky mucus. The CFTR gene is on chromosome 7q. The most common CFTR mutation is F508 deletion. Features of CF include: * Respiratory: Chronic cough, recurrent lung infections, bronchiectasis, and nasal polyps. * Gastrointestinal: Pancreatic insufficiency, malabsorption, meconium ileus, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies which cause bleeding diathesis. * Sweat gland: Elevated sweat chloride levels. * Reproductive: Infertility in males (due to absent vas deferens) and reduced fertility in females. * Others: CF-related diabetes (CFRD), osteoporosis, and liver disease. Diagnostic tests: 1. Immunoreactive trypsinogen for newborn screening of cystic fibrosis. 2. Sweat chloride test: Increased chloride concentration >60 mEq/L is diagnostic. 3. Genetic testing for CFTR gene mutations is the gold standard and should be done for all cases. 4. Nasal transepithelial potential difference can be estimated in equivocal cases. The diagnosis is confirmed if both of the following criteria are met: 1. Presence of * Clinical symptoms affecting at least one organ system (respiratory, gastrointestinal, or genitourinary) or * Positive newborn screening or * A sibling with cystic fibrosis. 2. Evidence of dysfunction of the CFTR gene by * Two positive sweat chloride test results were obtained on separate days or * Identification of two CFTR mutations by genetic testing or * An abnormal measurement of nasal potential difference. Cystic fibrosis requires a multidisciplinary approach to management. The correction of the defect can be done via lumacaftor, which corrects the misfolding and reverts the mutation defect, or ivacaftor, which potentiates CFTR channel opening and stimulates ion transport. End-stage pulmonary failure requires lung transplantation.

text: 7. What is the most likely diagnosis for a newborn with weak lower limb pulses and strong upper limb pulses?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Coarctation of Aorta

Coarctation of the aorta will be the diagnosis for a newborn with weak lower-limb pulses and strong upper-limb pulses. Coarctation refers to a constriction or narrowing in the aorta, which can be proximal or distal to the ductus arteriosus. CoA usually presents either in infancy or in later childhood as incidental upper limb hypertension and disparity of pulses in the upper  and lower limbs as radio-femoral delay. When the ductus arteriosus is open in an infant with severe coarctation, the left-to-right shunt established during birth across the ductus arteriosus during birth is reversed to a right-to-left shunt as there is coarctation above the ductus in the aorta. This leads to deoxygenated blood flow to the lower limbs and no change in pulse in the lower limbs. As the ductus arteriosus closes, there is a pooling of blood in the heart, leading to congestive heart failure, further leading to increased pulmonary vascular resistance as well as lack of blood flow to lower limbs (presenting as weak pulses in the lower extremities). Figure of 3 sign is pathognomonic of coarctation of the aorta. Prestenotic dilatation of the aortic arch and left subclavian artery, indentation at the coarctation site and post-stenotic dilatation of the descending aorta combine to form this sign. Treatment includes re-establishing patency of the ductus arteriosus by prostaglandin E1 infusion and heart failure medical management followed by definitive surgical management such as coarctectomy, end-to-end anastomosis, or patch aortoplasty. Restenosis of CoA areas later in childhood are common and are treated by balloon angioplasty. Other options: Option A: Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common cyanotic heart disease encountered beyond the age of 1 year. text: 8. Which of the following is associated with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Gilbert syndrome

Gilbert syndrome is associated with Inherited unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Inherited unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia: * Gilbert syndrome * Crigler Najjar type 1 * Crigler Najjar type 2 Inherited conjugated hyperbilirubinemia * Dubin Johnson syndrome (Option B) * Rotor syndrome (Option C) Gilbert syndrome is a benign, familial disorder inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern characterized by mild intermittent jaundice usually seen during stress, illnesses, or any other precipitating factors. There is no hemolysis or underlying liver disease. The condition is recognized to arise from a mutation in the promoter region of the UGT1A1 gene, which results in mildly decreased UDP - glucuronoyl transferase production. UGT1A1 activity is reduced to 10-33% of normal. It presents with mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with other liver function tests being normal. The disorder is precipitated by stress, alcohol, and reduced caloric intake. Liver histology shows increased lipofuscin pigment. It responds well to phenobarbitone. Gilbert's syndrome does not require treatment. The bilirubin levels may fluctuate over time, and patients may occasionally have jaundice, which usually resolves on its own with no ill effects. UDP-Glucoronyltransferase is required for the conjugation of bilirubin. Option B: Dubin-Johnson syndrome is a benign autosomal recessive disease that is characterized by chronic conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and conspicuous brown-black melanin-like pigment deposition in the liver. The disease is caused by mutation in multidrug resistance protein 2 (MRP-2) in hepatocytes, which is required for the transport of non-bile salt organic anions at the canalicular membranes. Liver biopsy shows characteristic deposition of black-coloured pigment. Option C: Rotor syndrome: similar to Dubin-Johnson syndrome but with a milder presentation and increased conjugated bilirubin levels. The liver biopsy does not show a black-coloured liver. Option D: Biliary atresia presents with clay-coloured stools, progressive jaundice, persistent acholic stools, and hepatomegaly. Laboratory investigations show conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT). Ultrasonography reveals a triangular cord sign (a hyperechoic area corresponding to the fibrous portion of the bile duct) and a small or absent gallbladder.

text: 10. Which of the following metabolic abnormalities is most likely to be seen in infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Hypokalemia

Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is associated with hypokalemic hypochloremic alkalosis. Infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis develop a characteristic metabolic abnormality i.e. hypokalemia  hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria. Persistent vomiting secondary to gastric outlet obstruction results in loss of hydrochloric acid leading to the development of metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-). Kidneys try to compensate for alkalosis by secreting Na+ and HCO3-. However, loss of sodium stimulates the secretion of aldosterone through the RAAS pathway. The aldosterone causes active reabsorption of sodium in exchange for K+ and H+ ions. Loss of potassium ions leads to the development of hypokalemia. Loss of H+ ions in urine lowers the urinary pH resulting in aciduria. It is called paradoxical aciduria, since the body initially lost H+ ions due to loss of HCl, and instead of compensating for that loss, the body is losing more H+ ions through urine. Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS): It most commonly presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting. It is common between 3 and 6 weeks of age. It is associated with hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus. This results in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet. First-born male infants are at the highest risk.  Infants usually present with projectile, non-bilious vomiting. Clinically, an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium. When the infant is given a test feed, visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right (not from right to left), followed by projectile vomiting. Ultrasound examination is the investigation of choice for this condition. Ultrasound examination confirms the diagnosis of congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS) in the majority of cases. The diagnostic criteria for pyloric stenosis is a muscle thickness of ≥4 mm and a pyloric length of ≥16 mm. Management includes the correction of metabolic abnormality before the correction of the pylorus. The hypertrophic pylorus is surgically corrected by Ramstedt’s pyloromyotomy. text: 1. A newborn presents with a single palmar transverse crease and low-set ears. Which of the following is the most frequently associated with this finding?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Down syndrome

A newborn with a single palmar transverse crease and low-set ears is most likely to have Down syndrome. Down syndrome is a type of aneuploidy. It occurs due to the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21), leading to a total of 47 chromosomes instead of the normal 46. There is a wide range of presentations. A few key features include characteristic facies such as a flat face, epicanthal folds, a small head, a flat nasal bridge, upward-slanting palpebral fissures, brushfield spots, a small nose, a protruding tongue, and small and low-set ears. Congenital heart defects can also be present. Mechanism: * Majority of cases – meiotic nondisjunction (95%) of chromosome 21 in the ovum * Rarely – (4%) Robertsonian translocation of the long arm of chromosome 21 to another acrocentric chromosome (e.g., 22 or 14)  * Mosaic pattern: 1% Clinical features of Down syndrome include (mnemonic: I C A PROBLEMS): Incurved or short fifth finger with clinodactyly, congenital heart disease, acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia/ alzheimer's disease/ atlantoaxial instability/ atresia of the duodenum, protruding tongue, round face, occiput flat/open wide fontanelle/open mouth, brachycephalic/Brushfield's spots, low (depressed) nasal bridge, epicanthal fold, low-set and dysplastic ears, mongoloid slant (oblique palpebral fissure), simian palmar crease and wider gap between first and second toes. A score based on eight signs in the diagnosis of Down's syndrome in the newborn (Hall's criteria) * Abundant neck skin * Mouth corners turned downwards * General hypotonia * Flat face * Dysplastic ear * Epicanthic fold * The gap between first and second toes * Protruding tongue The presence of the last 3 points is considered clinically proven Down syndrome. Combined first-trimester screening consists of serum human chorionic gonad­otropin (hCG), pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A (PAPP-A), and the measurement of the nuchal translucency (NT) on ultrasound. It is performed between 11 and 14 weeks of gestation. The most common cause of intestinal obstruction in Down syndrome is duodenal atresia (double-bubble sign). Children with Down's syndrome have an increased risk of developing leukaemias, including acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). AML is more common during the first 3 years of life. Other options: Option A: Trisomy 18 results in Edward’s syndrome as a result of meiotic nondisjunction. The clinical features include micrognathia, low-set ears, prominent occiput, and rocker-bottom feet. Patients have significant hypertonia, including clenched hands with overlapping fingers. Cardiac anomalies (ventricular septal defects and patent ductus arteriosus) and gastrointestinal anomalies (Meckel’s diverticulum and malrotations) are common.  Option C: Turner syndrome (45, XO) results from the loss or structural abnormality of one X chromosome in females, leading to gonadal dysgenesis (non-functional ovaries). It is characterised by a short fourth metacarpal, a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, and short stature.  Option D: Trisomy 13 causes Patau syndrome. It is characterised by forebrain and midline facial abnormalities, including cleft lip, cleft palate, nasal defects, and a single central eye (“cyclops”). Other defects include polydactyly, renal defects, and congenital heart disease.

text: 3. A newborn, born to a diabetic mother, presents after 24 hours of life with a blood glucose level of 35 mg/dL. The baby is asymptomatic. What is the next best step in management?

options.A: Administer IV bolus of Hartmann solution
options.B: Initiate breastfeed and recheck blood glucose
options.C: Administer IV glucose and recheck blood glucose after 20 minutes

expl:
Correct answer: B. Initiate breastfeed and recheck blood glucose

In an asymptomatic newborn with hypoglycemia (<45 mg/dL), the first-line management is to initiate breastfeeding or provide expressed breast milk, followed by reassessment of glucose levels. Infants of diabetic mothers are at a high risk of developing neonatal hypoglycemia. This is particularly applicable after the initial 2–3 hours of life. Blood sample is collected by heel prick. Babies showing plasma glucose <40 mg/dL on a reagent strip should be treated for hypoglycemia. Since reagent strips have high false-positive rates, a confirmation of hypoglycemia by a lab test is recommended. Stepwise Management of Neonatal Hypoglycemia * Initial Screening & Feeding * * All infants of diabetic mothers (IDMs) and other at-risk babies should be screened within 30 minutes of the first feed. * Feeding should begin within 1 hour after birth. * The target blood glucose is ≥40 mg/dL before feeds during the first 48 hours of life. * Treatment is indicated if glucose <47 mg/dL in asymptomatic infants. * First-Line Therapy for Asymptomatic Hypoglycemia      * Feeding is the initial treatment for asymptomatic hypoglycemia. * Options include breastfeeding, formula, or oral gavage feeds. * Dextrose gel can be used as a prophylactic alternative, but early oral feeds are equally effective. * Recurrent or Persistent Hypoglycemia * If hypoglycemia persists despite feeding, repeat feeds or IV glucose may be required. * Infants with glucose <25 mg/dL in the first 4 hours after birth or <35 mg/dL between 4–24 hours should be started on IV glucose therapy, especially if symptomatic. * IV Glucose Therapy * Give a 200 mg/kg dextrose bolus (approximately 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose). * To avoid a recurrence, administer glucose continuously via intravenous infusion (IV) at a rate of 4–8 mg/kg/min. * Hypertonic (25%) glucose bolus injections should be avoided as they can result in rebound hypoglycemia from hyperinsulinemia.

text: 5. A child presents with recurrent sinusitis and repeated lung infections. Genetic testing shows a mutation in the CFTR gene. Which test is considered the gold standard to confirm the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Sweat chloride test

The clinical scenario of a child with recurrent sinusitis and lung infections along with a mutation in the CFTR gene is highly suggestive of cystic fibrosis. Sweat chloride test is the gold standard investigation for the confirmation of the cystic fibrosis. Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the lungs, digestive system, and other organs. It is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, which leads to the production of thick and sticky mucus. The CFTR gene is on chromosome 7q. The most common CFTR mutation is F508 deletion. Features of CF include: * Respiratory: Chronic cough, recurrent lung infections, bronchiectasis, and nasal polyps (Option A). * Gastrointestinal: Pancreatic insufficiency, malabsorption, meconium ileus (Option C), and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies which cause bleeding diathesis (Option D). * Sweat gland: Elevated sweat chloride levels. * Reproductive: Infertility in males (due to absent vas deferens) and reduced fertility in females. * Others: CF-related diabetes (CFRD), osteoporosis, and liver disease. Diagnostic tests: 1. Immunoreactive trypsinogen for newborn screening of cystic fibrosis. 2. Sweat chloride test: Increased chloride concentration >60 mEq/L is diagnostic. 3. Genetic testing for CFTR gene mutations is the gold standard and should be done for all cases. 4. Nasal transepithelial potential difference can be estimated in equivocal cases. The diagnosis is confirmed if both of the following criteria are met: 1. Presence of * Clinical symptoms affecting at least one organ system (respiratory, gastrointestinal, or genitourinary) or * Positive newborn screening or * A sibling with cystic fibrosis. 2. Evidence of dysfunction of the CFTR gene by * Two positive sweat chloride test results were obtained on separate days or * Identification of two CFTR mutations by genetic testing or * An abnormal measurement of nasal potential difference. Cystic fibrosis requires a multidisciplinary approach to management. The correction of the defect can be done via lumacaftor, which corrects the misfolding and reverts the mutation defect, or ivacaftor, which potentiates CFTR channel opening and stimulates ion transport. End-stage pulmonary failure requires lung transplantation. Note: Cholestasis is seen in CF. However, this is not due to biliary atresia, which is a congenital obstruction of the biliary tree.

subject: Pediatrics
text: 6. Which action of a midwife is considered harmful to a newborn baby in the immediate postnatal period?

options.A: Cleaning the eyes with a wet sterile swab
options.B: Giving a bath immediately after birth
options.C: Helping to initiate breastfeeding within 1 hour
options.D: Placing the baby on the mother’s chest

expl:
Correct answer: B. Giving a bath immediately after birth

The harmful practice in the immediate postnatal period is giving a bath immediately after birth. Newborn infants are highly prone to heat loss because their body surface area is relatively large, subcutaneous fat is thin, and heat production mechanisms are limited. Bathing immediately after birth increases evaporative and conductive heat loss, which can cause hypothermia, metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia, and respiratory stress in the newborn. Thus, delaying the first bath is essential to avoid cold stress and to allow skin-to-skin contact and early breastfeeding, which help in maintaining warmth. Heat loss occurs by four mechanisms:  * convection of heat energy to the cooler surrounding air * conduction of heat to the colder materials touching the infant, * heat radiation from the infant to other nearby cooler objects * evaporation from skin and lungs. Other options: Option A: Cleaning the eyes with a wet sterile swab is a routine hygienic practice in newborn care. Option C: Initiating breastfeeding within 1 hour is strongly recommended, since it provides colostrum, enhances immunity, and strengthens mother-infant bonding. Option D: Skin-to-skin contact on the mother’s chest is a recommended practice for thermal regulation, bonding, and successful initiation of breastfeeding.

text: 7. An 8-year-old child presents with enuresis. The parents mention that he had a fall from the bed once during early childhood, but there is no other significant medical history. There are no signs of urinary tract infection or neurological deficits. What is the best next step in management?
