Correct answer: B. Behavioral modification

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of nocturnal enuresis. The next most appropriate management option is behavioral modification. Nocturnal enuresis refers to the occurrence of involuntary voiding at night after 5 years of age. It may be a normal phenomenon in children up to 5 years of age. If there are no daytime symptoms and physical and urine examinations are normal, then further evaluation for urinary tract pathology is not warranted. USG is done in an older child (usually >7 years) with enuresis or in those who do not respond to therapy.  Causes of Nocturnal Enuresis: * Delayed maturation of cortical mechanisms that control voluntary micturition reflex. * Defective sleep arousal, making it difficult for the child to awaken when the bladder is full. * Reduced antidiuretic hormone production at night, leading to increased nocturnal urine output (nocturnal polyuria). * Genetic predisposition, with associations noted on chromosomes 12 and 13, and a strong family history link. * Bladder factors such as reduced capacity, overactivity, or lack of inhibition. * Constipation, which can aggravate bladder dysfunction. * Organic causes like urinary tract infection, obstructive uropathy, or sickle cell anemia nephropathy. * Sleep disorders, including sleep-disordered breathing due to enlarged adenoids. Treatment:  * Behavioral therapy with positive reinforcement and bladder alarms. It helps the child to deal with enuresis psychologically and motivates the child to void at night if he wakes up with a full bladder. Bedwetting alarms make a loud tone when they sense moisture. This helps to condition the child to wake at the sensation of a full bladder. * Pharmacological therapy, including imipramine and desmopressin is reserved for cases resistant to behavioral therapy. It is intended to treat the symptoms of enuresis and thus is regarded as second-line and is not curative. In children above 5 years, Imipramine 25 mg at bedtime is effective for nocturnal enuresis. Intranasal desmopressin is also effective in the treatment of nocturnal enuresis.

text: 8. Which of the following conditions is associated with normal bone age compared to chronologic age?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Familial short stature

Here, the child with short stature has a normal US:LS ratio (1.1:1 at 12 years is within normal limits) and no other abnormalities, which makes familial short stature highly likely. Children with familial short stature have normal bone age compared to chronological age. Familial short stature refers to short stature that is inherited within families. The parents are also shorter in stature, and there is usually no underlying pathology affecting growth and development. Therefore, bone age assessments are typically consistent with chronologic age in children with familial short stature. Short stature can be defined as growth below the expected genetic potential or below -2 SD for age and sex. If a child's stature is less than -3 SD below the average for their age and gender, it is more likely to indicate pathological short stature. A child's height between -2 and -3 SD is more likely due to physiological, i.e. familial or constitutional short stature. The 2 types of normal variants of short stature are as follows: * Constitutional delay: Bone age < Chronological age * Familial short stature: Bone age = Chronological age Bone age is more than chronological age in precocious puberty. Bone age is less than chronological age in constitutional delay, undernutrition, endocrinologic short stature, and systemic illness. Other options: Option A: In constitutional delay, bone age is delayed compared to chronological age. text: 10. A child with recurrent lung infections and sinusitis is diagnosed with Cystic Fibrosis. Which channel defect is responsible for this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Chloride channel

Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is caused by mutations in the CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene, which encodes a ATP-gated chloride ion channel present in the apical membranes of the epithelial cells. It regulates the flow of ions across epithelial membranes of sweat glands, respiratory airways, pancreatic ducts, etc. The defect leads to high salt concentrations in sweat and viscous luminal secretions in the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts.  The CFTR gene is on chromosome 7q. The most common CFTR mutation is F508 deletion. Features of CF include: * Respiratory: Chronic cough, recurrent lung infections, bronchiectasis, and nasal polyps (Option A). * Gastrointestinal: Pancreatic insufficiency, malabsorption, meconium ileus (Option C), and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies which cause bleeding diathesis (Option D). * Sweat gland: Elevated sweat chloride levels. * Reproductive: Infertility in males (due to absent vas deferens) and reduced fertility in females. * Others: CF-related diabetes (CFRD), osteoporosis, and liver disease. Diagnostic tests: 1. Immunoreactive trypsinogen for newborn screening of cystic fibrosis. 2. Sweat chloride test: Increased chloride concentration >60 mEq/L is diagnostic. 3. Genetic testing for CFTR gene mutations is the gold standard and should be done for all cases. 4. Nasal transepithelial potential difference can be estimated in equivocal cases. The diagnosis is confirmed if both of the following criteria are met: 1. Presence of * Clinical symptoms affecting at least one system (respiratory, genitourinary or gastrointestinal) or * Positive screen during neonatal screening or * A sibling with cystic fibrosis. 2. Evidence of dysfunction of the CFTR gene by * Two positive sweat chloride test results obtained on different days or * Identification of two CFTR mutations by genetic testing or * Increased nasal potential difference. Cystic fibrosis requires a multidisciplinary approach to management. The correction of the defect can be done via lumacaftor, which corrects the misfolding and reverts the mutation defect, or ivacaftor, which potentiates CFTR channel opening and stimulates ion transport. End-stage pulmonary failure requires lung transplantation.

text: 12. A child diagnosed with Kawasaki disease developed multiple large coronary artery aneurysms. The child has now recovered from the acute phase. What is the most appropriate next step in long-term management?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Aspirin lifelong

Children with Kawasaki disease who develop large or giant coronary artery aneurysms (CAAs) are at high risk of thrombosis and long-term complications. Therefore, the child should continue lifelong aspirin for secondary prevention. Kawasaki's disease is also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome. It is a vasculitis condition of unknown etiology.  Clinical features include a high spiking fever that is unresponsive to antipyretics. The fever can last between 5 days to 3-4 weeks.  Diagnosis of typical Kawasaki disease is made by fever for 5 or more days along with four of the symptoms listed below: * Bilateral conjunctival congestion (not purulent conjunctivitis) * Oral changes: erythematous, cracked lips, and strawberry tongue * Non-suppurative cervical lymphadenopathy, usually unilateral * Polymorphous rash * Changes in extremities: erythema and edema, desquamation of palms and soles Laboratory findings: Important laboratory findings of Kawasaki disease are anaemia, elevated ESR and CRP.Thrombocytosis is a characteristic finding in Kawasaki disease and commonly occurs in the second week. Treatment: Acute KD: • IVIG 2 g/kg over 10-12 hr • High dose aspirin (80-100 mg/kg/day, q6h) until patient is afebrile for at least 48 hr Convalescent phase: • Aspirin 3-5 mg/kg once daily for 6-8 wk after illness onset, if  coronary findings are normal throughout the course. Major complications of Kawasaki disease are arteritis and aneurysms of coronary vessels, myocarditis, myocardial infarction and pericarditis.

text: 6. Identify the condition as shown below in the X-ray radiograph of a neonate
expl:

This rare anterior defect of the diaphragm is commonly referred to as Morgagni, retrosternal, or parasternal hernia. The above X-ray radiograph shows congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Morgagni hernia: * This rare anterior defect of the diaphragm is commonly referred to as Morgagni, retrosternal, or parasternal hernia. * It accounts for approximately 2% of all CDH cases, and is characterized by herniation through the foramina of Morgagni which are located immediately adjacent and posterior to the xiphoid process of the sternum. Diaphragm eventration: * Diaphragmatic eventration refers to an abnormal contour of the diaphragmatic dome. * Elevation of the affected portion of the diaphragm is usually seen as a smooth hump, while the remainder of the hemidiaphragm contour is normal. * This rare type of CDH occurs because in the region of eventration the diaphragm is thinner, allowing the abdominal viscera to protrude upwards. text: 9. A young boy with fatigue is found to have a haemoglobin of 9 g/dl. Peripheral smear showed sickle-shaped RBCs. What is the next best step in managing this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Blood transfusion

The given clinical scenario and image are diagnostic of sickle cell anemia. The next best step is blood transfusion.  Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to the T-to-A point mutation in the sixth codon of the β-globin gene. This results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. This causes the production of sickle-shaped red blood cells due to the polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbS). The clinical features of sickle cell disease are due to the tendency of HbS molecules to stack into polymers when deoxygenated. The features are: * Moderately severe hemolytic anemia with jaundice. * Painful bone crisis- hand-foot syndrome or dactylitis of the bones of hands and feet. * Acute chest syndrome typically presents with fever, cough, chest pain, and pulmonary infiltrates. * Hyposthenuria- inability to concentrate urine. * Aplastic crisis stems from the infection of red cell progenitors by parvovirus B19, which causes a transient cessation of erythropoiesis and a sudden worsening of the anemia. * Spleen * In children- splenic sequestration crises occur which results in splenomegaly due to red pulp congestion. * Adolescence or early adulthood- autosplenectomy occurs due to splenic infarction, fibrosis, and progressive shrinkage. * Increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms like pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenza septicemia, but can be reduced by vaccination and prophylactic antibiotics. * Other clinical features- priapism, leg ulcers, stroke, retinopathy, pigment gallstones, and growth retardation.  The diagnosis is suggested by the clinical findings, the presence of irreversibly sickled RBCs on peripheral smear, and hemoglobin electrophoresis showing increased HbA2, HbF, and S spike. Disease-modifying drugs such as hydroxyurea can be given to patients with sickle cell anemia since it reduces the incidence of adverse vaso-occlusive vents. Blood transfusions are used to treat and prevent complications of sickle cell disease, including preparation for surgery, symptomatic anemia, acute stroke, multi-organ failure and acute chest syndrome

text: 4. The graph below depicts the dose response with multiple administrations of the drug. Which of the following statements is false regarding the phenomenon shown in this graph

options.A: Drugs are given at short intervals in the same dose
options.B: Drugs are given at short intervals in gradually increasing doses
options.C: This incident is seen with drugs such as ephedrine
options.D: This action is rarely seen in clinical practice

expl:
Correct answer: B. Drugs are given at short intervals in gradually increasing doses

The graph below shows a rapidly diminishing response to repeated administration, a phenomenon known as tachyphylaxis. The false statement regarding tachyphylaxis is drugs are given at short intervals in gradually increasing doses. The term tachyphylaxis is used to describe desensitization that occurs very rapidly, sometimes with the initial dose. Continued stimulation results in a state of desensitization thus the effect of continued or repeated exposure to the same concentration of a drug is diminished.   This phenomenon is usually demonstrated in the experimental setup depicted by indirect-acting sympathomimetics such as ephedrine, amphetamine, and tyrosine. Repeated administration in the same dose usually leads to the uptake of drugs and exhaustion of neurotransmitters. Hence tachyphylaxis is a rapid development. However, tolerance encountered in the clinical setting is developed slowly. The original effect of the drug can be recovered by increasing the dose in case of tolerance. However, it is not possible in the case of tachyphylaxis due to the exhaustion of mediators or due to the fast desensitization of the target cell.

text: 7. Which of the following drugs acts by inhibiting the catechol-O-methyltransferase enzyme?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Tolcapone

Tolcapone acts by inhibiting the catechol-O-methyltransferase enzyme and is used in the management of Parkinson's disease. Parkinsons disease arises as a result of the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the striatum. Therefore the mainstay of treatment in this disease is to increase dopamine in this area. Important drugs used in the treatment of Parkinson's disease are 1. Levodopa is a prodrug. It crosses the blood-brain barrier. In the brain, levodopa is converted to dopamine by decarboxylation in dopaminergic neurons in the striatum. Levodopa therapy significantly improves the signs and symptoms of Parkinson's disease. But the major problem with levodopa is the wearing-off phenomenon. Each dose of levodopa improves the symptoms for a period of 1–2 h, but rigidity and akinesia return rapidly after the effect of the drug reduces. Increasing the dose and frequency of administration can improve this situation, but the patients often develop dyskinesias, excessive and abnormal involuntary movements. In the later stages of the disease, patients may fluctuate rapidly between being “off,” having no beneficial effects from their medications, and being “on” having some beneficial effects but along with side effects. 2. Carbidopa- is a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor. Levodopa if administered alone will undergo decarboxylation by the decarboxylases present in the intestinal mucosa and other peripheral sites. This will lead to decreased concentration of the drug reaching the brain. In order to prevent this levodopa is always given with carbidopa. 3. Catechol-O-methyl transferase (COMT) inhibitors- The addition of carbidopa to the levodopa prevents the peripheral decarboxylation of the drug. However, levodopa can now be methylated by catechol-O-methyl transferases and inactivate it. This is prevented by COMT inhibitors tolcapone and entacapone.  4. Selective monoamine oxidase B (MAO-B) inhibitors- Dopamine in the striatum is predominantly metabolized by the MAO-B enzyme. Inhibiting this enzyme will increase the dopamine concentrations in these neurons. Eg. selegiline and rasagiline. 5. Dopamine receptor agonists- They act at the dopamine receptors and help in the improvement of the symptoms. Rotigotine acts on D1 and D2 receptors, whereas ropinirole and pramipexole both act on the D2 and D3 receptors. Apomorphine acts on D4 and mildly on D2, D3, and D5 receptors. It also has adrenergic action. 6. Muscarinic receptor antagonists- these are used as adjuncts to dopamine therapy. Eg. trihexyphenidyl and benztropine. Diphenhydramine, an antihistamine is also used. 7. Amantadine is an antiviral agent used for the prophylaxis and treatment of influenza A. It has antiparkinsonian activity. It alters dopamine release in the striatum, has anticholinergic properties, and blocks-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors. It can be used in mild diseases.

text: 17. A young male patient presents with ptosis and muscle weakness which reportedly worsens in the evening and improves in the morning. This is relieved by neostigmine. What is the likely diagnosis?

From the given clinical picture, myasthenia gravis is the most likely diagnosis. This patient has symptoms of ptosis, progressive weakness, and excessive fatiguability which improves with neostigmine.  Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles. It is due to the autoantibody-mediated destruction of the acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the post-synaptic membrane. This leads to a decreased transmission at the neuromuscular junction. Failure of transmission results in muscle weakness. Females are more commonly affected than males and the disease tends to occur in middle age. text: 6. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of thiazides in DCT?

options.A: Inhibits the Na-CI pump in early distal convoluted tubule
options.B: Inhibits the Na-CI pump in late distal convoluted tubule
options.C: Inhibits the Na-K-2Cl pump in the descending limb of loop of Henle
options.D: Inhibits the Na-K-2Cl pump in the ascending limb of loop of Henle

expl:
Correct answer: A. Inhibits the Na-CI pump in early distal convoluted tubule

Thiazides act on the distal convoluted tubule (DCT). They block the Na+/Cl- co-transporter. Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide-like diuretic. It inhibits the Na Cl symporter in the early distal tubule and increases the excretion of sodium and chloride. Thiazide diuretics: They may be used for the treatment of hypertension, heart failure, nephrolithiasis due to idiopathic hypercalciuria, and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Thiazides act on the distal convoluted tubule (DCT). They block the NaCl co-transporter in the DCT. This results in the loss of sodium, chloride, and water contributing to the diuretic effect. The diuretic effect of thiazide leads to decreased osmotic pressure due to the loss of Na+, Cl-, and water leading to compensatory reabsorption of uric acid thus resulting in hyperuricemia. The intracytoplasmic Na+ concentration also decreases due to the blockade of the co-transporter. To compensate, the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger pumps sodium from the systemic circulation into the epithelial cells in exchange for calcium. The declining calcium levels inside the cell will draw more calcium from the lumen into the systemic circulation. This results in hypercalcemia. There is also increased loss of Mg2+, K+, and H+. Mechanisms of antihypertensive action: Decreases plasma and ECF volume by diuresis thereby decreasing cardiac output. Even when the compensatory mechanisms restore the Na+ levels and plasma volume, a low BP is maintained by a reduction in total peripheral resistance. This reduction in total peripheral resistance is due to the persistence of a small sodium and volume deficit even after compensation. The decreased intracellular sodium is responsible for increased compliance of the vessel wall and a reduced response to constrictor stimulus. Thiazides are the diuretic of choice for uncomplicated hypertension. Advantages of thiazide as an antihypertensive are: * It can be given as once a day dose and has a flat dose-response curve * Decreased incidence of postural hypotension and relative freedom from CNS side effects * No tolerance * No fluid retention * Decreased risk of osteoporotic fractures due to its hypocalciuric action * Low cost * Effectiveness in isolated systolic hypertension * Thiazides are ineffective both as antihypertensive and diuretic in patients with chronic renal failure.

text: 13. A given drug has a bioavailability of 30%. What does this mean?

options.A: 30% percent of the drug reaches the systemic circulation in unchanged form
options.B: The drug is 30 percent potent in producing therapeutic effec
options.C: 30 percent of the drug undergoes first pass metabolism in Liver
options.D: The drug is 30 percent pure in its chemical composition

expl:
Correct answer: A. 30% percent of the drug reaches the systemic circulation in unchanged form

If a drug has a bioavailability of 30%, it means that only 30% of the drug reaches the systemic circulation in its original, unchanged form after it is administered. The remaining 70% of the drug may undergo various processes such as metabolism, degradation, or excretion before it reaches the bloodstream. Bioavailability is defined as the fraction of a drug reaching systemic circulation in an unchanged form after administration by any route. The area under the blood concentration-time curve (AUC) is proportional to the dose and the extent of bioavailability for a drug. Bioavailability (F) = Quantity of drug reaching systemic circulation/Quantity of drug administered Bioavailability depends on two factors, absorption and 1st pass metabolism. The bioavailability of the drug injected intravenously is 100%. However it is lower after oral ingestion because of incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism in the intestinal wall or liver and lies between 5% to <100%. The bioavailability of subcutaneous and intramuscular routes lies between 75% to ≤100%. text: 2. A patient presented with paracetamol poisoning and N-acetylcysteine (NAC) was administered as an antidote. How does NAC prevent toxicity?

options.A: It inhibits the cytochrome P450 enzyme responsible for formation of toxic metabolite
options.C: It neutralizes the free radicals produced by paracetamol

expl:
Correct answer: B. It replenishes glutathione levels

N-acetylcysteine is considered a definite antidote for paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning and it works by replenishing glutathione levels. Acetaminophen toxicity is an important cause of acute liver failure. Ingestion of ≥25g can be fatal. Cytochrome P450 CYP2E1 metabolizes acetaminophen to a toxic metabolite, N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone-imine (NAPQI). NAPQI is normally neutralized through conjugation with a reduced form of glutathione(GSH), after which it is excreted in the urine. When glutathione reserves are depleted or large amounts of NAPQI are formed, it binds to hepatocyte macromolecules. This can then lead to hepatocyte necrosis. N-acetylcysteine repletes GSH stores and also conjugates with NAPQI and prevents oxidative damage to the cell. It also protects against extrahepatic injury due to its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. Early manifestations of acetaminophen toxicity(within 4-12 hours) include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. Later, renal failure and myocardial injury may be seen. Low bilirubin levels along with raised aminotransferase levels are characteristic of the condition.  Initial management includes gastric lavage and oral charcoal or cholestyramine. It should be carried out within thirty minutes of ingestion. If they are used, gastric lavage must be done afterwards before using another agent. text: 6. Which of the following is true about Cisplatin and Carboplatin?

options.A: Carboplatin is more neurotoxic than Cisplatin
options.B: Cisplatin is more nephrotoxic than Carboplatin
options.C: Cisplatin causes more myelosuppression than Carboplatin
options.D: Carboplatin causes more ototoxicity than Cisplatin

expl:
Correct answer: B. Cisplatin is more nephrotoxic than Carboplatin

Cisplatin-based chemotherapy is more nephrotoxic than Carboplatin. Cisplatin demonstrates higher nephrotoxicity compared to Carboplatin primarily due to their structural differences. Cisplatin accumulates more readily in proximal tubular cells, causing direct tubular injury, inflammation, and oxidative stress, potentially leading to acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease. In contrast, Carboplatin's more stable structure results in slower activation, less renal accumulation, and better excretion, making it a safer option for patients with reduced kidney function.  This dose-dependent nephrotoxicity can be prevented by the agent amifostine and by hydration with normal saline before drug infusion. Cisplatin is a platinum-containing chemotherapeutic agent. It is non-cell cycle specific and causes cross-linking of DNA to kill tumor cells. A copper transporter CTR1 is involved in the entry of platinum complexes into these cells. Cisplatin is very effective in the management of metastatic testicular and ovarian carcinoma. It is widely used for other solid tumors such as those of the lung, bladder, esophagus, stomach, liver, and head & neck. Cisplatin is a highly emetogenic anticancer drug. Cisplatin causes marked nausea and vomiting in almost all cases and is usually administered along with anti-emetic regimens like 5HT3 receptor antagonists, neurokinin (NK1) receptor antagonists (e.g., aprepitant), and high-dose corticosteroids. It is also an ototoxic drug that can cause tinnitus and hearing loss. It is also known to cause peripheral neuropathy and hyperuricemia.  The important side effects of carboplatin are: * Dose-limiting toxicity is myelosuppression, primarily thrombocytopenia * Nausea, neurotoxicity, ototoxicity, and nephrotoxicity (lesser than cisplatin) * Hypersensitivity reaction.

text: 7. A 15-year-old girl was brought by her mother to the emergency department 6 hours after ingesting 5 paracetamol tablets. What is most likely progression seen in this case?

options.B: Increase in liver enzymes in the first 24 hours
options.D: N-acetylcysteine should ideally be started after 8 hours of ingestion

expl:
Correct answer: B. Increase in liver enzymes in the first 24 hours

Paracetamol toxicity is likely to lead to an increase in the liver enzymes in the first 24 hours. Paracetamol is an analgesic and antipyretic with weak anti-inflammatory action. It is mainly metabolized in the liver by conjugation with glucuronic acid and sulfate and is excreted in the urine. The maximum dose of acetaminophen that can be given is 4 g/day.  The clinical course of paracetamol toxicity is divided into four stages: * During the first stage (30 min to 24 hours), the patient may be asymptomatic or may have emesis. * In the second stage (18 hours to 72 hours), there may be emesis plus right upper quadrant pain and hypotension. * In the third stage (72 hours to 96 hours), liver dysfunction is significant with renal failure, coagulopathies, metabolic acidosis, and encephalopathy. Gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms reappear, and death is most common at this stage. * The fourth stage (4 days to 3 weeks) is marked by recovery. The diagnosis of paracetamol toxicity is based on serum levels of the drug. Other laboratory studies needed include liver function tests (LFTs) and coagulation profile (PT/INR). If the ingestion is severe, LFTs can rise within 8 to 12 hours of ingestion. LFTs remain elevated in the second stage at 18 to 72 hours. At toxic doses, the glucuronide and sulfate conjugation pathway becomes saturated. The metabolites of paracetamol get converted into NAPQI. NAPQI is highly reactive and causes enzymatic dysfunction in the liver. Normally, minor amounts of NAPQI produced in our body are rapidly eliminated by conjugation with reduced glutathione(GSH) and then excreted into the urine. Therefore, paracetamol toxicity is treated with N-acetyl cysteine(NAC), which replenishes GSH. NAC thereby helps in the excretion of NAPQI from the body. N-acetyl cysteine is an anti-oxidant and functions by detoxifying NAPQI. NAC therapy should be begun within 8 hours of ingestion. Paracetamol poisoning is the most common cause of liver failure necessitating transplantation. Other Options : Option A: Liver failure within 24 hours is incorrect because, most of the time liver dysfunction occurs while in third stage, hence it would take 72 to 96 hours for it to occur. Option C: Recovery within 72 hours is also a wrong option beacuse recovery happens in fourth stage which happens to occur between 4 days to 3 weeks Option D: N-acetylcysteine should ideally be started after 8 hours is also a wrong statement because NAC therapy should be begun within 8 hours of ingestion.

text: 10. A patient with penicillin allergy presents with fever, burning micturition, ototoxicity and dizziness. Which drug is most appropriate for management?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Ciprofloxacin

In this patient with symptoms of a urinary tract infection with a penicillin allergy, ototoxicity, and dizziness, Ciprofloxacin is the most appropriate drug of choice. Ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone, inhibits bacterial DNA replication and prevents the growth of bacteria. DNA gyrase is particularly important in gram-negative bacteria, where it introduces negative supercoils into the DNA to relieve torsional strain. Ciprofloxacin binds to and inhibits this enzyme, preventing the proper replication of bacterial DNA. Additionally, topoisomerase IV is the target of gram-positive bacteria, and its inhibition by ciprofloxacin prevents chromosome segregation during cell division.  Ciprofloxacin is the most appropriate choice as it effectively treats urinary tract infections while having a relatively safe profile in penicillin-allergic patients. The symptoms (fever and burning micturition) suggest a UTI, and Ciprofloxacin achieves high urinary concentrations with good activity against common uropathogens. text: 11. A patient diagnosed with tuberculosis and HIV was started on both anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) and antiretroviral therapy (ART). After 2 months, the patient experienced a deterioration in his health. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Drug-drug interaction between TB and HIV medications
options.B: Development of drug resistance to anti-tubercular drugs
options.D: Development of drug resistance to ART

expl:
Correct answer: C. Immunological changes in the body

In a patient diagnosed with TB and HIV who was started on ATT and ART, the deterioration in health after treatment initiation point to a diagnosis of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) due to immunological changes in the body. Following the initiation of effective anti-retroviral therapy, a paradoxical worsening of preexisting or untreated opportunistic infections may be seen in people living with HIV (PLHIV). This is known as immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). IRIS is seen in up to 30% of the patients who are started on ART, and is particularly common in patients with untreated mycobacterial or fungal infections, or with CD4+ T-cell counts <50 cells/μL. Other risk factors for the development of IRIS include: * Rapid initial fall in HIV viral load due to ART * Severity of TB disease * Male sex and younger age The underlying pathogenesis appears to be similar to a type IV hypersensitivity reaction and reflects the immediate improvements in immune function as there is a drop in the levels of HIV RNA. IRIS related to a known pre-existing infection is called paradoxical IRIS; IRIS associated with a previously undiagnosed condition is referred to as unmasking IRIS. Signs and symptoms can appear within two weeks to two years of starting ART and can include lymphadenitis, prolonged fever, pulmonary infiltrates, hepatitis and increased intracranial pressure. IRIS is generally self-limiting and interruption of ART is rarely indicated. In most cases, recognition and management of ongoing infection with antimicrobial therapy is sufficient. Short-term therapy with corticosteroids or NSAIDs can be given to reduce the inflammation. Temporary cessation of ART is to be considered for potentially life-threatening forms of IRIS. For the prevention of IRIS in a patient with HIV and TB co-infection, anti-tubercular treatment is started first and then ART is added two weeks later. Pearl PF2098: Opportunistic Infections/HIV related conditions and ART initiation
Clinical scenario Action 
Any undiagnosed active infection with fever Diagnose and treat first; start Anti-Retroviral Therapy (ART) when stable
Tuberculosis (TB) Start TB treatment first; start ART as soon as possible after 2 weeks and before 2 months. For those with CD4 less than 50/cmm, start ART within 2 weeks Caution is needed for PLHIV with TB meningitis, since immediate ART is associated with more severe adverse events than initiating ART 2 months after the start of TB treatment

Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP)

 Treat PCP first; start ART when PCP treatment is completed
Invasive fungal diseases: Oesophageal candidiasis, penicilliosis, histoplasmosis Start treatment for oesophageal candidiasis first; start ART as soon as the patient can swallow comfortably. Treat penicilliosis, and histoplasmosis first; start ART when the patient is stabilized or opportunistic infection treatment is completed.
Cryptococcal meningitis Treat cryptococcal meningitis. ART initiation should be deferred until there is evidence of sustained clinical response to anti-fungal therapy and after 4 weeks of induction and consolidation treatment with amphotericin B containing regimen.
Bacterial pneumonia Treat pneumonia first; start ART when treatment is completed
Malaria Treat malaria first; start ART when treatment is completed
Acute diarrhoea which may reduce absorption of ART Diagnose the cause and treat diarrhoea first; start ART when diarrhoea is stabilized or controlled
Non-severe anaemia (Hb< 9 g/dl) Start ART if no other causes for anaemia are found (HIV is often the cause of anaemia) 
Skin conditions such as PPE and seborrhoeic dermatitis, psoriasis, HIV-related exfoliative dermatitis Start ART (ART may resolve these problems) 
Suspected Mycobacterium Avium Complex (MAC), Cryptosporidiosis and Microsporidiosis Start ART (ART may resolve these problems)
Cytomegalovirus retinitis Start treatment for CMV urgently and start ART after 2 weeks of CMV treatment 
Toxoplasmosis Treat toxoplasmosis; start ART after 6 weeks of treatment and when the patient is stabilized

text: 12. A male develops tightness in the chest, associated with breathlessness and altered sensorium during his trek towards a mountain peak. The drug prescribed for symptomatic relief acts of which part of the nephron?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Proximal convoluted tubule

The symptoms are suggestive of acute mountain sickness and acetazolamide can be given for symptomatic relief. It acts on the proximal convoluted tubule. Acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, acts on the enzyme in epithelial cells of the proximal convoluted tubule. By inhibiting carbonic anhydrase, HCO3- reabsorption is blocked and diuresis occurs. Acetazolamide (125–250 mg twice a day), administered for 1 day before ascent and continued for 2 or 3 days is very effective. It can also be used for prophylaxis. Paresthesia and a tingling sensation are common side effects of acetazolamide. Bone marrow depression is rare but a serious side effect. It is contraindicated in liver disease. Acute mountain sickness: When individuals arrive first at a high, altitude, many develop transient 'mountain sickness'. This syndrome develops 8-24 hours after arrival at altitude and lasts 4-8 days. Characterized by: * Headache * Irritation * Insomnia * Breathlessness * Nausea and vomiting Cause: Appears to be associated with cerebral edema The low PO2 at high altitudes causes arteriolar dilation, and if cerebral autoregulation does not compensate, there is an increase in capillary pressure that favours increased transudation of fluid into brain tissue leading to cerebral edema. In high-altitude cerebral edema, the capillary leakage in mountain sickness progresses to frank brain swelling, with ataxia, disorientation, and in some cases coma and death due to herniation of the brain through the tentorium. Treatment: * Descent to a lower altitude * Diuretics like acetazolamide: inhibits carbonic acid anhydrase, and results in stimulated respiration, increased PaCO2, and reduced formation of CSF * Glucocorticoids are administered as well. Their mechanism of action is not clear.

In this case, a diabetic patient with cardiac and renal failure is started on a suitable medication. The drug is likely an sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor. It is responsible for the reabsorption of 80-90% of filtered glucose. It inhibits glucose reabsorption resulting in glycosuria and a change in the renal threshold. Paresthesia and a tingling sensation are common side effects of acetazolamide. Bone marrow depression is rare but a serious side effect. It is contraindicated in liver disease. Acute mountain sickness: When individuals arrive first at a high, altitude, many develop transient 'mountain sickness'. This syndrome develops 8-24 hours after arrival at altitude and lasts 4-8 days. Characterized by: * Headache * Irritation * Insomnia * Breathlessness * Nausea and vomiting Cause: Appears to be associated with cerebral edema The low PO2 at high altitudes causes arteriolar dilation, and if cerebral autoregulation does not compensate, there is an increase in capillary pressure that favours increased transudation of fluid into brain tissue leading to cerebral edema. In high-altitude cerebral edema, the capillary leakage in mountain sickness progresses to frank brain swelling, with ataxia, disorientation, and in some cases coma and death due to herniation of the brain through the tentorium. Treatment: * Descent to a lower altitude * Diuretics like acetazolamide: inhibits carbonic acid anhydrase, and results in stimulated respiration, increased PaCO2, and reduced formation of CSF * Glucocorticoids are administered as well. Their mechanism of action is not clear.

text: 2. Which of the following drugs is used in GERD?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Metoclopramide

Metoclopramide has both antiemetic and prokinetic action and is used in the treatment of GERD. In GERD, the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) weakens or relaxes, allowing stomach acid to flow back into the esophagus, causing irritation and symptoms like heartburn and regurgitation. Metoclopramide is useful in this condition because it increases LES tone, preventing acid reflux, and enhances gastric emptying by promoting gastrointestinal motility. Additionally, it reduces nausea and vomiting by blocking dopamine D2 receptors in the central nervous system. These combined effects help alleviate the symptoms and discomfort associated with GERD. Metoclopramide works in GERD by enhancing gastrointestinal motility through its antagonism of dopamine D2 receptors. In GIT, acetylcholine increases gastrointestinal motility and increases the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) tone. Therefore, D2 receptor inhibition augments ACh release and enhances GI motility and LES tone. Additionally, it exerts antiemetic effects by blocking D2 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone of the central nervous system. The combined actions help alleviate symptoms associated with GERD. Metoclopramide is a prokinetic and antiemetic. It has the following pharmacological actions: * Dopamine receptor antagonist  * Serotonin (5HT4) receptor agonist  * Serotonin (5HT3) antagonist * Sensitization of muscarinic receptors on smooth muscle. This results in increased lower esophageal sphincter tone and stimulates gastric antral contractions. Adverse effects of metoclopramide are mainly extrapyramidal effects, and these include acute dystonia, Parkinson-like symptoms (tremors, bradykinesia, rigidity), tardive dyskinesia, galactorrhea due to hyperprolactinemia, and methemoglobinemia in neonates. Extrapyramidal symptoms can be treated by discontinuing metoclopramide and administering anticholinergics or antihistaminics. Other options : Option A: Ondansetron is a 5 HT3 receptor antagonist. It blocks impulses at the peripheral origin in GIT and does not suppress vomiting caused by motion sickness. It is most commonly indicated for the treatment of postoperative and chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Option C: Loperamide has μ opioid receptor activity and is an orally active antidiarrheal agent. The drug is more potent than morphine as an antidiarrheal agent and penetrates the CNS poorly. It is effective in patients with 5-fluorouracil-induced diarrhea and can be regarded as the treatment of choice. Loperamide is effective against traveler’s diarrhea and can be used alone or in combination. If clinical improvement in acute diarrhea does not occur within 48 hours, loperamide should be discontinued. Option D - Diphenoxylate is an opioid agonist that is structurally similar to meperidine. It is used in the treatment of acute, chronic, and traveller's diarrhea. Upon administration, it undergoes de-esterification to difenoxin, which is its active metabolite. Its side effects include constipation, toxic megacolon, paralytic ileus and can give rise to CNS depression in children.

text: 4. A 50-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a unilateral throbbing headache associated with nausea and vomiting. She has had similar episodes in the past where the headache usually lasts for 1-2 days, and she prefers sitting in a dark room during the attacks. She also gives a history of a myocardial infarction 2 years ago. Which of the following drugs cannot be prescribed to this patient to treat this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Sumatriptan

The clinical vignette is suggestive of an acute attack of migraine. Sumatriptan is contraindicated in a patient with a history of myocardial infarction. Triptans are selective 5HT 1B/1D agonists. They are indicated in the management of acute attacks of migraine. They act by arresting the nociceptive nerve signalling in the trigeminovascular system. They also act by vasoconstricting, not only the intracranial vessels but other vessels too. Hence it is contraindicated in patients with a history of ischemic or vasospastic coronary artery disease (history of stroke or transient ischemic attacks), cerebrovascular or peripheral vascular disease, hemiplegic or basilar migraines, or ischemic bowel diseases. Triptans are also contraindicated in patients with uncontrolled hypertension. Migraine is the second most common cause of headaches and is seen more commonly in women. It presents as an episodic headache associated with nausea, vomiting, photosensitivity, and sensitivity to sound (phonophobia). Common triggers include bright lights, sounds, and hunger. The release of vasoactive peptides such as calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) by the trigeminal nucleus cells is the theory used to explain the pathogenesis of the condition. The neurotransmitters serotonin and dopamine also play a part. A migraine attack has four phases: premonitory (prodrome), aura, headache, and postdrome; each has distinct and sometimes disabling symptoms, which may overlap. Migraine can broadly be classified into: * Migraine without aura (70-80%): Common migraine. * Migraine with aura (20-30%): Classic migraine. The migraine disability assessment score (MIDAS) can be used to assess the severity of the condition. Avoidance of recognized triggers is helpful to avoid symptoms. The various drugs used to treat an acute attack of migraine are: * Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen (Option C) * Triptans * CGRP Receptor Antagonists (rimegepant) * 5-HT1/F receptor agonists (lasmiditan- Option D) * Dopamine receptor antagonists (domperidone) The various FDA-approved drugs used in prophylaxis include propranolol (Option A), valproate, topiramate, and flunarizine. text: 1. In a patient with pheochromocytoma, what is the recommended preoperative medication for controlling blood pressure?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Phenoxybenzamine

The drug of choice to control blood pressure prior to surgery is oral phenoxybenzamine at 0.5–4 mg/kg of body weight. Beta-blockers such as propranolol are given only after adequate alpha blockade is achieved. Pheochromocytoma: Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor derived from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla. It can be sporadic or hereditary. Hereditary pheochromocytoma occurs in association with syndromes such as MEN 2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2), familial paraganglioma syndrome, Von Hippel Lindau (VHL) syndrome, and neurofibromatosis (NF) type 1. Clinical features: It most commonly presents as a classic triad of intermittent headache, palpitation, and profuse sweating along with hypertension. The patient can also present with anxiety, panic attacks, nausea, abdominal pain, weight loss, and weakness. Symptoms may be precipitated by surgery, pregnancy, position changes, exercise, and medications such as metoclopramide and tricyclic antidepressants. text: 2. A 28-year-old male presents with complaints of excessive thirst and frequent urination throughout the day, as well as having to wake up several times at night to urinate. When questioned further, he admits to having sustained a head injury one month prior. His fasting blood glucose is within normal limits. What is the most appropriate treatment?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Desmopressin

The clinical vignette suggests the probable diagnosis of central diabetes insipidus, which is treated with desmopressin. Diabetes insipidus of central or nephrogenic origin is characterised by low urine osmolality and high plasma osmolality. Diabetes insipidus (DI) is a syndrome characterised by the excretion of abnormally large volumes of dilute urine. The 24-hour urine volume exceeds 40 mL/kg body weight, and the 24-hour urine osmolarity is <280 mOsm/L. There will be a slight increase in plasma osmolarity/sodium that stimulates thirst (polydipsia). Hence, clinical symptoms and signs of dehydration are uncommon unless thirst and/or water intake are also impaired. Desmopressin is the drug of choice for neurogenic diabetes insipidus. Desmopressin is a selective vasopressin V2 receptor agonist. V2 receptors are present throughout the collecting ducts. The V2 receptor is a G-protein-coupled receptor, which, when activated, results in a signaling cascade of adenyl cyclase, prompting an increase in cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) in the renal tubule cells, ultimately resulting in increased water permeability. This activity leads to a decrease in urine volume and an increase in urine osmolality. Extrarenal V2-like receptors are involved in the release of coagulation factor VIII and von Willebrand factor, which increases platelet aggregation. Desmopressin is used for the management of nocturnal polyuria, hemophilia A, central diabetes insipidus, and von Willebrand disease. Desmopressin can be administered orally at high doses and is contraindicated in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Its major adverse effect is water intoxication. It can also give rise to flushing and transient headaches. In post-traumatic DI, patients lose their ability to concentrate urine due to the failure of anti-diuretic hormone secretion in acceleration-deceleration injury, leading to ischaemia and discontinuity of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. This leads to hypotonic polyuria with low osmolality. When this is associated with altered mentation and damage to the central osmoreceptors in the anterior hypothalamus, thirst regulation is also impaired, preventing adequate fluid intake to compensate for the losses, leading to severe hypernatremia. DI can be central or nephrogenic. * Central DI occurs due to damage to the neurohypophysis in the posterior pituitary. It is characterised by decreased ADH. It can be treated with desmopressin, an ADH analogue.  * In nephrogenic DI, ADH levels may be normal or increased because the kidney has become resistant to its effects. Nephrogenic DI requires treatment with a thiazide diuretic, amiloride, a low-sodium diet, and indomethacin.

text: 5. Which of the following is a correct triple drug regimen for the treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Omeprazole + Clarithromycin + Metronidazole

The correct triple-drug regimen treatment for Helicobacter pylori infection is omeprazole, clarithromycin and metronidazole. H. pylori is a gram-negative motile rod with flagella. It has a unique feature of urease production, which is helpful in diagnosis. The sole source of H. pylori is human gastric mucosa. In some patients, H. pylori causes mild acute gastritis lasting for about two weeks. In others, it can cause peptic ulcer disease, which may lead to chronic atrophic gastritis in later stages. This is a risk factor for gastric malignancies like adenocarcinoma and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphomas.  Several eradication therapies are present for the eradication of H. pylori: * The standard triple therapy regimen consists of 7-10 days of omeprazole, clarithromycin and metronidazole. Clarithromycin resistance causes failure of eradication for standard triple therapy. * The standard sequential therapy regimen consists of a 5-day dual therapy with omeprazole and amoxicillin followed by 5 days of triple therapy with omeprazole, clarithromycin, and metronidazole or tinidazole. * Concomitant therapy is a four-drug regimen that includes omeprazole, clarithromycin, amoxicillin, and metronidazole. This therapy is superior to triple therapy and less complex than sequential therapy. The urea breath test, stool antigen test, and biopsy-based tests are all appropriate tools to evaluate eradication. Among these, the urea breath test and stool antigen test are non-invasive and are commonly used in follow-up. It is recommended to perform follow-up testing at least 4 weeks after completion of treatment, as testing earlier can result in false negatives due to suppressed bacterial load. Additionally, testing should be delayed by at least 2 weeks after stopping PPIs or 4 weeks after antibiotics or bismuth-containing compounds, as these can also affect accuracy. text: 6. Following the administration of a specific antibiotic, a patient experienced Achilles tendonitis and leg swelling. Fluoroquinolones are frequently associated with this side effect. What is the most likely mechanism of action for the drug involved?

options.A: Inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis at 50S ribosomal subunit
options.B: Inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis
options.C: Inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
options.D: Inhibition of bacterial folic acid synthesis

expl:
Correct answer: C. Inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV

The most likely mechanism of action for this drug is inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA replication and prevent the growth of bacteria. DNA gyrase is particularly important in gram-negative bacteria, where it introduces negative supercoils into the DNA to relieve torsional strain. Fluoroquinolones bind to and inhibit this enzyme, preventing the proper replication of bacterial DNA. Additionally, topoisomerase IV is the target of gram-positive bacteria, and its inhibition by fluoroquinolones prevents chromosome segregation during cell division.  Other options: Option A: Oxazolidinone binds to the P site of the 50S ribosomal subunit and inhibits bacterial protein synthesis.  Option B: Glycopeptides inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding with D-alanyl-D-alanine, and the class originator drug is vancomycin. Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase that converts para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) to dihydrofolate. Trimethoprim is a selective inhibitor of microbial dihydrofolate reductase. Both these enzymes are essential for the synthesis of folic acid in a bacterial cell. Inhibition of folic acid synthesis will cause disruption of basic metabolic functions in the microbe, leading to its death.

text: 8. A patient with hypertension, tachycardia, and early renal involvement is prescribed Telmisartan. What is the most likely mechanism by which this medication improves heart rate and blood pressure?

options.C: Increases sodium excretion via loop diuresis

expl:
Correct answer: A. Decreases peripheral vascular resistance

The most likely mechanism of action of telmisartan in this case is the decrease in peripheral vascular resistance. Telmisartan, an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB), has shown evidence of having PPARγ agonist action. It is very useful in hypertensive patients with diabetes. PPARγ agonists are the thiazolidinedione group of drugs that act by inducing several insulin-sensitising genes, thereby reducing overall insulin resistance. Common side effects of telmisartan are hypotension, hyperkalaemia, teratogenicity, headache, gastrointestinal upset, and dizziness.  By acting as an agonist on the PPARγ receptor, telmisartan regulates the downstream glucose and lipid metabolism. It increases basal and insulin-stimulated uptake of glucose into the adipocytes via GLUT-4. It also decreases the amount of reactive oxygen species and increases serum adiponectin. By these mechanisms, it improves oxidative stress and insulin resistance in patients with type II diabetes mellitus. Furthermore, it has been shown to reduce cardiac fibrosis and hypertrophy. Telmisartan can be given safely to a patient with chronic renal failure (CRF) because it is mainly cleared from the circulation by biliary excretion. The drugs that reduce mortality in patients with HFrEF are * Beta-blockers block β1 receptors and prevent ventricular remodelling promoted by the stimulated RAAS and sympathetic system. Metoprolol and bisoprolol are selective for the β1 receptor, whereas carvedilol also blocks the β2 and α1 receptors, resulting in vasodilation. Adverse effects include fluid retention, worsening HFrEF, fatigue, bradycardia or heart block, and hypotension.  * ACE inhibitors—enalapril and lisinopril—reduce mortality. ACE inhibitors decrease peripheral resistance and reduce the load on the failing myocardium by inhibiting the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Hereby, it prevents vasoconstriction and causes relaxation of the vasculature.  * Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) – They inhibit the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) by blocking the binding of angiotensin II to its receptor, which in turn leads to vasodilation and prevents the release of aldosterone. They are found to reduce mortality and morbidity in HFrEF cases. * Angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) sacubitril/valsartan is a novel therapy that was approved in July 2015 to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death and hospitalisation for patients with HFrEF. Sacubitril/valsartan consists of the neprilysin inhibitor sacubitril and the ARB valsartan. * Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like spironolactone and eplerenone are also known to decrease the mortality risk. Diuretics like furosemide and torsemide are not found to reduce mortality or hospital readmission. They are the only agents that can adequately control the fluid retention associated with HFrEF.  Prazosin, an alpha-1 adrenergic blocker, does not decrease mortality risk in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), unlike other neurohormonal antagonists such as beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors. text: 11. A hypertensive patient is taking three antihypertensive medications, including diuretics, but his blood pressure is uncontrolled. In addition, he has hypokalaemia. Which of the following drugs should be prescribed to treat this patient?

Correct answer: D. Eplerenone

The given clinical case with resistant hypertension and labs showing hypokalaemia suggests a diagnosis of primary hyperaldosteronism, which is treated with aldosterone receptor antagonists like spironolactone and eplerenone. For the diagnosis of resistant hypertension, the patient should have uncontrolled hypertension despite taking three antihypertensive drugs, including at least one diuretic. Most patients with CKD/diabetes develop resistant hypertension.  While a calcium channel blocker, beta blocker, or alpha blocker can be part of the antihypertensive regimen, the inclusion of a diuretic is necessary for the diagnosis of resistant hypertension. The diuretic helps in addressing fluid retention, which is often a significant contributor to hypertension. Resistant hypertension is more common in patients aged >60 years than in younger patients. It may be related to nonadherence to therapy, obesity, and excessive alcohol intake. In the absence of a specific identifiable cause, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like spironolactone have been found to be the most effective add-on drugs for the treatment of resistant hypertension. Management of resistant hypertension according to NICE guidelines: * Aldosterone antagonist (spironolactone) is to be used only when serum potassium is <4.5 mmol/L. * A higher dose of thiazide is to be used only when serum potassium is >4.5 mmol/L. * β-blocker or α1-blocker is to be considered only if an aldosterone antagonist or higher-dose thiazide is ineffective or not tolerated or contraindicated. Primary hyperaldosteronism, also known as Conn’s syndrome, is characterized by excessive production of aldosterone by the adrenal glands, leading to sodium retention, potassium excretion, and subsequent hypertension. Drug-resistant hypertension is a hallmark of this condition. The initial test for this condition is the concurrent measurement of plasma renin and aldosterone, followed by the calculation of the aldosterone-renin ratio (ARR). The aldosterone-renin ratio is the most appropriate screening test for primary hyperaldosteronism; this can be followed by a saline infusion test, which is used to confirm the diagnosis of Conn’s syndrome.  Spironolactone has some significant adverse effects, especially in men (erectile dysfunction, gynecomastia, and benign prostatic hyperplasia). It is given at a daily dose of 100 mg for 48-52 weeks. Lamivudine can cause nausea, headache, fatigue, anemia, neutropenia, and lactic acidosis. Tenofovir and lamivudine are both safe and effective treatments for chronic hepatitis B in pregnant women. Lamivudine is a safe and effective treatment for chronic hepatitis B in pregnant women, and it has been shown to reduce the risk of vertical transmission of hepatitis B. However, lamivudine is less effective than tenofovir in suppressing viral replication, and there is a higher risk of developing drug resistance with lamivudine.  Other options: Option B: Ombitasvir inhibits HCV NS5A RNA-dependent polymerase protein and is used for the treatment of HCV infection. Hepatitis B: HBsAg (Hepatitis B surface antigen) is the first marker to appear in the serum, and it indicates the presence of infection. If it is persistent for more than 6 months, it is suggestive of chronic infection.  Anti-HBs are the antibodies to HBs and are seen after clearance of HBsAg or post-vaccination. Thus, it is suggestive of recovery, non-infectivity and immunity. Anti-HBc (antibodies to hepatitis B core antigen) has IgM and IgG. IgM anti-HBc is diagnostic of acute hepatitis, and it appears soon after HBsAg. It persists for 3-6 months and can reappear in flare-ups. IgG anti-HBc appears during acute infection and persists indefinitely, irrespective of recovery or progression to chronic disease. HBV DNA is a sensitive indicator for viral replication and infectivity. HBeAg also indicates viral replication and infectivity. It appears shortly after HBsAg, and if it is persisting beyond 3 months, it is suggestive of chronic hepatitis.  Hepatitis B virus is mainly transmitted by the percutaneous route, followed by perinatal and sexual transmission. Chronic hepatitis B is a progression of acute hepatitis. Chronic hepatitis B infection has five phases: the immune tolerant phase, the immune active phase, the inactive HBsAg carrier state, the reactivated chronic hepatitis B phase, and the HBsAg negative phase. Treatment options include interferon, lamivudine, adefovir, entecavir, telbivudine, and tenofovir. Prophylaxis is by hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) and recombinant vaccine.

NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes, which form the rate-limiting step of prostaglandin synthesis in the GI tract. Prostaglandins promote gastric and duodenal mucosal protection via mucin and bicarbonate secretion and increased mucosal blood flow. NSAIDs impair these protective mechanisms, increasing the risk of peptic ulcers. COX-1 is present in the GIT and converts arachidonic acid to prostaglandins in the stomach. Prostaglandins maintain the gastric mucosa and prevent its corrosion. No dose of NSAID is completely safe. Most patients with NSAID-induced gastric ulcers present with complications such as ulcer perforation and bleeding without preceding dyspepsia symptoms. Concomitant use of glucocorticoids, anticoagulants, cigarette smoking, alcohol consumption, or concomitant H. pylori infection increases the risk of complications in NSAID-induced gastric ulcers. According to the Modified Johnson anatomic classification, NSAID-induced gastric ulcers are classified as Type V and may occur in any part/anywhere in the stomach. H. pylori and NSAID use are the most important factors in the development of peptic ulcer disease. text: 17. Which of the following is used as an abortive treatment for cluster headache?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Sumatriptan

For aborting an acute attack of cluster headache, subcutaneous sumatriptan (6 mg), a selective 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor agonist, is most effective. High-flow oxygen is also effective in the management of an acute attack. 100% oxygen at 10–12 L/min for 15–20 min is required as treatment. If injectable sumatriptan is unavailable, then high-flow oxygen is the next best treatment option. Verapamil is the best prophylactic treatment for cluster headaches to reduce the frequency and severity of cluster headaches. Verapamil, which is a calcium channel blocker, is the drug of choice for the long-term prophylaxis of cluster headaches. Cluster headache is characterised by severe, one-sided headaches that occur in clusters, often associated with autonomic symptoms, such as tearing, redness of the eye, runny nose and unilateral headache that typically lasts between 15 to 180 minutes. The important feature of this headache is periodicity. At least one of the daily attacks of pain recurs at the same hour each day. It is also associated with autonomic features, such as unilateral lacrimation and rhinorrhoea. Occasionally, features of Horner's syndrome may be seen.  The typical cluster headache patient has daily bouts of one to two attacks of relatively short-duration unilateral pain for 8–10 weeks a year; this is usually followed by a pain-free interval that averages a little less than 1 year. The acute (abortive) management relies on therapies that terminate the attack quickly, whereas prophylactic treatment prevents recurrence during cluster periods. The treatment includes: Abortive treatment: * Sumatriptan (subcutaneous or intranasal) is the first-line abortive therapy, highly effective in rapidly terminating attacks. * High-flow oxygen inhalation (100% O₂, 7–10 L/min for 15 min) is safe, fast-acting, and commonly used. * Non-invasive vagal nerve stimulation (nVNS) has also been shown to abort attacks in some patients and is FDA-approved. Prophylactic treatment: Depends on the length of bouts and whether the patient suffers from chronic cluster headaches (period of remission less than 3 months while not medicated)

Mechanism of action: Increased accumulation of intracellular sodium is caused by inhibition of Na+/K+ ATPase pump in the myocardium. Increased intracellular sodium prevents the efflux of calcium ions. This results in increased intracellular calcium which increases the contractility of the muscle. It can also cause bradycardia via its vagotonic and sympatholytic activity. Gastrointestinal manifestations- Nausea, vomiting, anorexia, diarrhea, abdominal pain. Cardiac manifestations - Palpitations, dyspnea, syncope, hypotension. The most serious side effect of digoxin is arrhythmia. They can present as extreme bradycardia, atrial fibrillation, ventricular extrasystoles, bigeminy, ventricular tachycardia, and fibrillation. text: 5. A farmer presents to the emergency department with diarrhea, sweating, excessive lacrimation, and salivation. Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the treatment of the condition?

options.B: Atropine is used as an antidote for OP poisoning
options.C: Pralidoxime has a role in reversing the enzyme in carbamate poisoning
options.D: Succinylcholine use is avoided in rapid sequence intubation

expl:
Correct answer: C. Pralidoxime has a role in reversing the enzyme in carbamate poisoning

The clinical scenario is suggestive of organophosphate poisoning.  Oximes like pralidoxime are used to restore neuromuscular transmission in organophosphate anti­ChE poisoning. It attaches to the anionic site of the cholinesterase enzyme, which remains unoccupied in the presence of organophosphates. It binds and forms oxime-phosphonate which diffuses away, leaving the reactivated cholinesterase. Pralidoxime is not an effective anti­dote to carbamates like carbaryl. This is because the anionic site of the cholinesterase enzyme is not free for attachment to pralidoxime. Hence, it does not reactivate the carbamylated enzyme. Carbamates spontaneously disassociate from AChE and recover in 24-48 hours. Pralidoxime may potentiate the toxicity of carbaryl. Therefore, pralidoxime should be avoided in known single-agent carbaryl poisonings. However, pralidoxime is considered for use in mixed poisonings with an organophosphorus compound and a carbamate.  Atropine is useful in organophosphate poisoning because it is a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine. An acetylcholinesterase enzyme has an active and anionic site. The organophosphates bind to the active site of AChEs (acetylcholine esterases) and deactivate it. This results in excessive Ach causing muscarinic activity. It has relatively insignificant action on nicotinic receptors.  Organophosphates and carbamates are powerful acetylcholinesterase inhibitors. Organophosphates are irreversible inhibitors of acetylcholinesterase (AChE). They form covalent bonds with the enzyme, leading to long-lasting inhibition, which is why they are used as pesticides and nerve agents. Carbamates, on the other hand, are reversible inhibitors of acetylcholinesterase. They bind to AChE, but the enzyme is regenerated after a short period, usually within minutes to hours. This makes them less toxic and more controllable than organophosphates. The predominant initial signs are of muscarinic excess, including: (DUMBBELSS) * Diarrhea * Urination * Miosis * Bronchospasm * Bradycardia * Emesis * Lacrimation * Salivation * Sweating Nicotinic manifestations include twitching of eyelids, tongue, and facial muscles which then leads to paralysis. CNS stimulation results in headache, tremors, ataxia, coma, and death.  Patients who present with organophosphate and carbamate poisoning require early endotracheal intubation to avoid respiratory depression, which is a common complication. Succinylcholine is avoided as it can exacerbate the neuromuscular blockade. Pearl PF1113: Drugs used in Organophosphorus Poisoning

options.A: A-Right LMN facial nerve palsy B-Left UMN facial nerve palsy
options.B: A-Right UMN facial nerve palsy B-Right LMN facial nerve palsy
options.C: A-Left UMN facial nerve palsy B-Right LMN facial nerve palsy

expl:
Correct answer: C. A-Left UMN facial nerve palsy B-Right LMN facial nerve palsy

Patient 1 has left UMN facial nerve palsy, and patient 2 has right LMN facial nerve palsy. In an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion, wrinkling of the forehead and eyelid closure remain intact because the upper facial muscles receive bilateral cortical innervation. In this case, the right side of the face is affected, as evidenced by deviation of the angle of the mouth towards the left (normal) side - a key indicator of facial palsy, since the mouth always deviates towards the normal side due to loss of muscle tone on the affected side. The first-order neurons originate from the left cerebral hemisphere, cross over to the right facial nerve nucleus in the pons, and synapse there. From this nucleus, second-order neurons of the right facial nerve descend to supply the right side of the face. Hence, a left UMN lesion causes paralysis of the lower half of the face on the right side, while forehead movement is preserved. In contrast, a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion affects both the upper and lower facial muscles on the same (ipsilateral) side, leading to loss of forehead wrinkling, incomplete eye closure, and drooping of the mouth. In this patient, since the mouth deviates towards the left, it indicates a right LMN facial nerve palsy. Features of facial nerve palsy:

text: 2. In the following LV pressure-volume loop diagram, point C denotes ______
expl:
Correct answer: B. Aortic valve opens

The aortic valve will open at point C. The volume-pressure curve represents the changes in volume and pressure in the left ventricle during a single cardiac cycle. The relationship between ventricular pressure (Y-axis) and volume (X-axis) throughout the cardiac cycle is represented by this loop. * A - Mitral valve opens * B - Mitral valve closes * C - Aortic valve opens * D - Aortic valve closes Phase I: Period of filling It begins at a ventricular volume of about 50 ml (end-systolic volume) and a diastolic pressure of 2 to 3 mm Hg. As venous blood flows into the ventricle from the left atrium, the ventricular volume normally increases to about 120 ml, called the end-diastolic volume and the diastolic pressure rising to about 5 to 7 mm Hg. Phase II: Period of isovolumic contraction During isovolumic contraction, the volume of the ventricle does not change because all valves are closed. However, the pressure inside the ventricle increases to equal the pressure in the aorta (80 mm Hg) as depicted by point C. Phase III: Period of ejection During ejection, the systolic pressure rises even higher because of still more contraction of the ventricle. At the same time, the volume of the ventricle decreases because the aortic valve has now opened and blood flows out of the ventricle into the aorta. Phase IV: Period of isovolumic relaxation At the end of the period of ejection (point D), the aortic valve closes and the ventricular pressure falls back to the diastolic pressure level. The line labeled “IV” traces this decrease in intraventricular pressure without any change in volume. Thus, the ventricle returns to its starting point, with about 50 ml of blood left in the ventricle and at an atrial pressure of 2 to 3 mm Hg. The area subtended by this functional volume-pressure diagram (the shaded area, labeled “EW”) represents the net external work output of the ventricle during its contraction cycle.

text: 4. A 65-year-old female patient presents to the OPD with complaints of shortness of breath and tiredness. There is no history of reactive airway disease or heart diseases previously. expl:
Correct answer: A. Constrictive pericarditis

The clinical features and the JVP findings of rapid X and Y descent  are suggestive of constrictive pericarditis. Constrictive pericarditis: * It is the condition where a thickened, fibrotic, and often calcified pericardium restricts the diastolic filling of the heart. * In developing countries, infectious etiologies like tuberculosis or viral infections are the most common cause of this condition. * Cardiac surgery and radiation therapy are also common causes. * Other causes include connective tissue disease, uremia, neoplasm, or idiopathic. * Clinically the patients present with dyspnea, orthopnea, and fatigue. * JVP findings - There is a rapid 'x' and 'y' descent. The rapid 'y' descent is more prominent and reflects rapid early ventricular diastolic filling. This occurs due to the constricting pericardium, increasing the atrial pressures. Diagnosis: * Diagnosis is difficult and is confirmed by multiple investigations * Hallmark findings of pericardial constriction are pericardial thickening, calcification, and abnormal ventricular diastolic function. * The X-ray can be normal or there may be non-specific cardiac enlargement, calcification, and roughened cardiac outline. * Echo can assess the hemodynamic function but it is accurate in identifying pericardial thickening. * CT and MRI are more sensitive investigations. * CT has an edge over MRI as it can detect calcification associated with this condition. * Pericardial thickness of > 4mm along with clinical features of constriction is highly suggestive of this diagnosis. * Cardiac MR may show diastolic septal bounce. * Hepatomegaly and ascites can be seen associated with this condition. Constrictive pericarditis will have prominent y descent, prominent x descent, and Kussmaul's sign. Normally, the venous pressure should fall by at least 3 mmHg with inspiration. Kussmaul’s sign is defined by either a rise or a lack of fall of the JVP with inspiration. subject: Physiology
text: 8. Lysosomal enzymes are present in___?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Cytosol

Lysosomal enzymes (hydrolytic enzymes) are present in the lysosome, which is located in the cytoplasm of the cell. In the given options, cytosol is the best choice. The interior of lysosomes is more acidic than the rest of the cytoplasm, and external material such as endocytosed bacteria, as well as worn-out cell components, is digested in them. The interior is kept acidic by the action of a proton pump, or H+ ATPase, which uses the energy of ATP to move protons from the cytosol up their electrochemical gradient and keep the lysosome relatively acidic, near pH 5.0. Lysosomes contain over 40 types of hydrolytic enzymes, which are all acid hydrolases, and they function best at the acidic pH of the lysosomal compartment. This can be a safety feature; if the lysosomes were to break open and release their contents, the enzymes would not be efficient at the near-neutral cytosolic pH of 7.2 and thus would not be able to digest cytosolic targets they may encounter.  When a lysosomal enzyme is congenitally absent, the lysosomes become engorged with the material the enzyme normally degrades and lead to lysosomal storage diseases. e.g., Fabry disease caused by a deficiency in α-galactosidase, Gaucher disease caused by a deficiency in glucocerebrosidase, and Tay-Sachs disease caused by the loss of hexosaminidase A. subject: Physiology
text: 9. In the cardiac muscle, the inhibition of Na+K+ATPase results in __?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Depolarisation

The inhibition of Na+K+-ATPase results in depolarisation. An energy (ATP)-dependent pump system (Na+/K+-ATPase), is located on the sarcolemma, which pumps Na+ out and K+ into the cell.The Na+/K+-ATPase pump is electrogenic because it extrudes three Na+ for every two K+ entering the cell. By pumping more positive charges out of the cell than into it, the pump creates a negative potential within the cell. This electrogenic potential may be up to −10 mV. If this pump stops working (such as when ATP is lost under hypoxic conditions), or if the activity of the pump is inhibited by cardiac glycosides such as digoxin, Na+ accumulates within the cell and intracellular K+ falls,resulting in a less negative (more depolarized) resting membrane potential. Inhibition of this pump, therefore, causes depolarization resulting from changes in Na+ and K+ concentration gradients and from the loss of an electrogenic component of the membrane potential. Action potential of myocardium: * Phase 0: Depolarisation: Influx of Na+ into myocyte. * Phase 1: Early repolarization: Efflux of K+ from myocyte. * Phase 2: Plateau: Ca2+ enters myocardial cells via voltage regulated L-type Ca2+ channels. * Phase 3: Repolarisation: Efflux of K+. * Phase 4: Restoration of RMP: Restoration of Na+ and K+ by Na-K ATPase.

text: 1. The first heart sound coincides with which phase of the cardiac cycle?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Isovolumetric contraction

The first heart sound coincides with the isovolumetric contraction phase of the cardiac cycle. The time between the closure of the mitral valve and the opening of the aortic valve is the isovolumic contraction period. It begins with the closure of mitral and tricuspid valve which is responsible for the first heart sound. During this period, the ventricles contract as a closed chamber till the aortic and pulmonary valves open.  Events of the Cardiac Cycle Systole  * Isovolumetric Contraction The ventricular muscle continues to contract, even though the ventricular volume does not change, with all valves closed.  It correlates with the ‘c’ wave of JVP. * Ventricular Ejection When the ventricular pressures rise above aortic and pulmonary pressures the valves open, and ventricular ejection begins. Peak pressures in the left and right ventricles are about 120 and 25 mmHg, respectively.  Diastole  * Protodiastole Before the semilunar valve closes, even though ventricular muscle is relaxed, blood flow into great vessels is due to momentum of blood. * Iso-volumetric Relaxation The ventricular muscle continues to relax, even though the ventricular volume does not change, with all valves closed. * Ventricular Filling Isovolumetric relaxation ends when the ventricular pressure falls below the atrial pressure and the AV valves open, permitting the ventricles to fill. * Atrial Systole During the last third of diastole, the atria contract and give additional thrust to the inflow of blood into the ventricles. text: 4. A new resident to a high-altitude area develops hypoxia. What is the causative factor?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Low partial pressure of 02

Hypoxia in high altitude is due to the low partial pressure of O2. Adaptation at High Altitudes: * The work capacity is reduced at high altitudes and is directly proportional to the decrease in O2 uptake. * Immediate exposure to low PO2 at higher altitudes stimulates the arterial chemoreceptors, and this stimulation increases alveolar ventilation. * This immediate increase in pulmonary ventilation upon rising to a high altitude blows off large quantities of CO2, reducing the PCO2 and increasing the pH of the body fluids causing respiratory alkalosis. This raised pH inhibits the brain stem respiratory center and opposes the increased ventilation. So, respiratory alkalosis will hinder maximal exercise effort. * To compensate for this respiratory alkalosis, kidneys reduce hydrogen ion secretion and increase bicarbonate excretion. This reduces plasma and cerebrospinal fluid bicarbonate concentration, bringing the pH to normal. It removes the inhibitory effect of alkalosis on respiration. Hence fall in blood bicarbonate facilitates the exercise effort. * Lactic acid levels increase which causes extreme fatigue. When there is insufficient oxygen (at high altitudes), most of the pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid, which diffuses out of the muscle cells into the interstitial fluid and blood. text: 8. Hemoglobin with iron in ferric form is _______
