text: 1. A 25 year old male has thoughts of cutting his fingers, he plans and imagines doing it but never actually does it. He says that his sister is influencing his thoughts. His mother reports that he has no sister, and he talks to someone who is not present in the room. Which of the following is the cause?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Thought insertion

In the above scenario, the patient is suffering from thought insertion. Thought insertion is seen in schizophrenia. The delusion of thoughts being placed into patient’s mind by someone else. The first rank symptoms of schizophrenia described by Kurt Schneider include : 1. Hallucination: Audible thoughts - auditory hallucinations of a person’s voice being spoken aloud. Voices arguing or discussing - auditory hallucinations of two or more voices arguing or discussing, usually about the person experiencing the hallucination. Voices commenting on the patient’s actions - auditory hallucinations commenting on a person’s behavior or actions. 2. Thought Phenomenon :  * Thought withdrawal -  thoughts being actively removed from a person’s mind. * Thought insertion - thoughts inserted into a person’s mind by some external agent. * Thought broadcasting - the sense that a person’s thoughts are experienced by others - the thoughts are made audible or may be experienced by others through telepathy. 3. Made Phenomenon: * Made affect - feelings are imposed on that person by an external agent. * Made impulses or drives - an impulse for action is imposed on a person by some external agent. * Made volitional acts - a person’s actions are controlled by an external agent; the person is a passive participant in the action. 4. Delusional perception - the person attaches an abnormal significance/meaning to a normal perception, which leads to delusional interpretation. 5. Somatic passivity - tactile or visceral hallucinations that are thought to be imposed on a person's body by some external agent. These symptoms are not specific for schizophrenia and may also be present in other psychiatric disorders. Other options: Option A: Forced thinking is usually seen in patients with frontal lobe epilepsy.The thoughts are formed are not in the control of the patient and are distressing thoughts. Option C: Crowding of thoughts is also seen in schizophrenia. The patient has thoughts that are too fast and excessive and unexplainable. The patient can even locate these thoughts crowding at the back of the head. Option D: The obsessive-compulsive symptoms are not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (e.g., a drug of abuse, a medi­cation) or another medical condition.The patient feels the need to carry out certain behaviours to get rid of these thoughts. text: 3. The finding of the immunohistochemistry studies of a patient with a neurodegenerative disease is given below. Identify the structure marked in the image.
expl:
Correct answer: C. Lewy body

The given image is the histological sample of the substantia nigra showing neurons with a Lewy body, extracellular neuromelanin, and pigment-laden macrophages in Parkinson's disease. Lewy bodies are single or multiple intracytoplasmic, round to elongated, eosinophilic inclusions that often have a dense core surrounded by a pale halo. Accumulations of these are seen in subcortical regions (basal ganglia, striatum, locus coeruleus, substantia nigra, thalamus) as well as the cerebral cortex. Lewy bodies are aggregates of insoluble fibrillar proteins called alpha-synuclein (specific) and ubiquitin in the neural cells. They are typically seen in Parkinson's disease, Lewy body dementia, and a few variants of Alzheimer's disease. They mainly disrupt the excitatory dopaminergic pathways. Other options: Option A: Pick bodies are cytoplasmic, round to oval, weakly basophilic filamentous inclusions that stain strongly with silver methods. It contains 3R tau and is seen in frontotemporal lobar degeneration. Option B: Negri bodies are cytoplasmic, round to oval, eosinophilic inclusions found in pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum. They are pathognomonic microscopic findings seen in rabies. Option D: Lafora bodies are seen in the cytoplasm of neurons in myoclonic epilepsy. Lafora bodies are aggregates of polyglucosans, poorly constructed glycogen molecules with inordinately long strands that render them insoluble.

text: 5. A 20-year-old survivor of a terrorist attack that happened 2 weeks ago comes to the psychiatry OPD with complaints of persistent flashbacks about the incident. She has been unable to sleep properly and is avoiding going to crowded places. She is no longer interested in doing activities with her friends. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Acute stress disorder

The likely diagnosis in this patient is acute stress disorder, because the symptoms have been present for less than one month. Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and acute stress disorder both present with the same set of symptoms: * Intrusive symptoms such as recurrent nightmares and flashbacks of the event, psychological distress due to stimuli that are reminders of prior trauma * Avoidance of external reminders of trauma * Negative mood or cognition related to the trauma, such as diminished interest in activities and withdrawal * Altered level of arousal, such as sleep disturbances and hypervigilance A diagnosis of PTSD is made if these symptoms present ≥1 month following the traumatic event. If these symptoms are present prior to 1 month, then a diagnosis of acute stress disorder is made. The treatment modalities for PTSD and acute stress disorder include trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing therapy (EMDR), and SSRIs.  Adjustment disorder (option B) is diagnosed when the patient has emotional or behavioral changes following a stressor in his life. However, the distress is out of proportion to the stressor itself — that is, the feeling of distress is subjective. Major depressive disorder (option C) presents with low mood, loss of interest in pleasurable activities, and decreased energy. Although this patient has a loss of interest in activities, the presence of hypervigilance symptoms and flashbacks following a traumatic event points towards a diagnosis of a stress-trauma related disorder.

text: 6. A 7 year old child is noted to be extremely naughty, unable to sit in a place for a long time, excessively talking, and unable to concentrate on a thing for a long time. Which of the following drug is used in the management of this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Methylphenidate

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder(ADHD). The drug of choice for ADHD is Methylphenidate. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neuro­ psychiatric condition characterized by a pattern of diminished attention span and increased impulsivity or hyperactivity. The prefrontal cortex of the brain has been implicated in its etiology and dopamine is the main neurotransmitter.  ADHD can begin during infancy but is usually rec­ognized between 1-3 years of age. ADHD was known as minimal brain dysfunction earlier. The characteristics of children with ADHD, in order of frequency, are * Hyperactivity * Attention deficit (short attention span, distractibility) * Impulsivity (action before thought, abrupt shifts in activity, lack of organization) * Memory and thinking deficits * Specific learning disabilities * Speech and hearing deficits. Under DSM-5 criteria, for diagnosis of ADHD, it is necessary for symptoms to be present prior to age 12, persist for at least 6 months, have a negative impact on social, academic, or occupational activities, and be present in two or more settings. The course of ADHD is variable. The majority of the cases persist into adult life. The hyperactivity may sometimes disappear, but the decreased attention span and impulse-control problems usually persist. Patients with ADHD are vulnerable to antisocial behavior, conduct disorder, substance use disorders, and mood disorders. Pharmacotherapy is the first line of treatment for ADHD. CNS stimulants are the first-choice agents as they have shown the greatest efficacy with mild tolerable side effects. The CNS stimulants used are dopamine agonists like methylphenidate, amphetamine salts, and dextroamphetamine. Non-stimulant medications used in the treatment of ADHD include atomoxetine (norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor), clonidine, and guanfacine (Alpha agonists). Psychosocial interventions such as academic organization skills remediation, parent training, behavior modification in the classroom and at home, cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), and social skills training are also used as an adjunct to pharmacotherapy. Note: Modafinil is used in the management of narcolepsy (Option B). Other Options: Option A: Atenolol is a beta-blocker used for cardiovascular conditions like hypertension and angina that would be ineffective for attention difficulties and might even worsen symptoms through sedation.  Option D: Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant used for depression and certain pain conditions that would be particularly inappropriate due to its anticholinergic properties and sedating effects, which would likely exacerbate attention problems rather than improve them.

text: 7. A patient stopped alcohol consumption for 3 days and presented with irritability, disorientation, paranoid delusions, agitation, visual hallucinations, and altered sensorium. What is the likely diagnosis in this case?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Delirium tremens

The given clinical scenario of a patient who has not consumed alcohol for the past 3 days with disorientation, paranoid delusions, visual hallucinations, and altered sensorium is suggestive of delirium tremens. Delirium tremens is a medical emergency that occurs during alcohol withdrawal. It is an acute condition and usually develops within 72 hours after the last drink. It has symptoms of both delirium and alcohol withdrawal. The clinical features of delirium tremens are: * Altered sensorium with disorientation * Perceptual distortions, most frequently tactile or visual hallucinations * Autonomic hyperactivity with tachycardia, fever, anxiety, insomnia, hypertension. And sweating * Fluctuating levels of psychomotor activity, ranging from agitation to lethargy * Altered sleep-wake cycle Other options: Option B - Wernicke’s encephalopathy (alcoholic encephalopathy) is associated with thiamine deficiency. Alcohol abuse may lead to thiamine deficiency because of poor nutritional habits, or malabsorption. It is an acute neurological disorder characterized by: * Global confusion * Ocular abnormalities like horizontal nystagmus, gaze palsy, anisocoria, and sluggish pupillary reflex * Ataxia - mainly affecting the gait * Vestibular dysfunction It may resolve with thiamine therapy or progress to Korsakoff's syndrome. Option C - Korsakoff’s psychosis can follow Wernicke’s encephalopathy due to thiamine deficiency. It is a chronic amnestic syndrome that is characterized by the following clinical symptoms in an intact and responsive patient: * Impaired mental syndrome, especially recent memory * Anterograde amnesia * Confabulation Option D - Alcohol-induced psychosis is characterized by the development of auditory hallucinations or paranoid delusions in the context of a heavy drinking or alcohol withdrawal. These patients have a clear sensorium, unlike the patients having delirium tremens. Note: Tremulousness is the first alcohol withdrawal symptom.

text: 2. A doctor asks a patient about her age, and the patient responds, "You know doctor, I'm from a village, I was married at a very young age of 12 years and my husband was just 5 years older than me. Then I had two kids when I was around 18 or something. Now I am 38, but I look like their older sister". What is most likely thought disorder displayed by patient?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Circumstantiality

Circumstantiality best describes this patient’s thought disorder, as she provides irrelevant and unnecessary details when asked her age before eventually giving the actual answer. Circumstantiality refers to a formal thought disorder in which a patient gives irrelevant and unnecessary details. This is before finally getting to the point or the correct answer. It may be seen in schizophrenia, obsessional distur­bances, and certain cases of dementia. An example is given below. Doctor: "How did you get that bruise?" Patient: "I woke up and had a cup of coffee, read the newspaper, and went for a walk. It was a wonderful day in the park. I returned home and watched the TV. I took a nap in the afternoon after lunch. I slipped and fell in the bathroom. The fall gave me this bruise." A formal thought disorder is a disturbance in the formulation of thoughts and their expression. It is characterized by loosened associations, illogical constructs, and neologisms. Derailment, neologism, perseveration, and thought blocking are some examples. Other options: Option A: Clang association is a formal thought disorder where the thoughts are associated with the sound of words through rhyming, rather than the meaning of the words. It is usually seen in schizophrenia or mania. An example is "I am Sam...I like jam...I travel in a tram" Option B: Flight of ideas refers to a rapid succession of multiple associations, where the thoughts appear to abruptly shift from one idea to another. It is usually seen in mania. An example is "I like mangoes, the weather is nice, India is great" Option D: Tagentiality is a formal thought disorder where the patient says something that is related to the general topic. Although, the actual answer is not given. An example is as below. Doctor: "How has your appetite been lately?" Patient: "I usually have dinner with my wife, but now I eat alone" Pearl PF1257: Disorders of thought and perception DISORDERS OF THOUGHT  

DISORDER OF STREAM OF THOUGHT

(A) Disorder of tempo

(i) Flight of Ideas

Continuous flow of rapid speech that jumps from topic to topic

  • "I like mangoes, the weather is nice, India is great"

(ii) Retardation of thinking

Slow speed of speech and a prolonged latent period before a response

  • "I went to the market (pause)......... the shop was closed"

(iii) Circumstantialities

Inclusion of irrelevant details and going on in a roundabout manner, but their thought ultimately reaches the answer

  • Doctor: "How did you get that bruise?"

  • Patient: "I woke up and had a cup of coffee, read the newspaper and went for a walk. It was a wonderful day in the park. I returned home and watched the TV. I took a nap in the afternoon after lunch. I slipped and fell in the bathroom. The fall gave me this bruise."

(iv) Clang associations

Jumping from one word to another irrelevant rhyming word

  • I am Sam...I like jam...I travel in a tram"

(B) Disorder of continuity

(i) Perseveration

Repetition of out of context words, phrases, or ideas beyond the point of relevance.

  • Q1. What's your name?: "Rahul"

  • Q2. Where are you from?: "Rahul"

  • Q3. How old are you?: "Rahul"

(ii) Thought blocking

A sudden disruption of thought or a break in the flow of ideas

  • "I went to the market (extreme silence)...................."
 

DISORDER OF FORM OF THOUGHT

(i) Tangentiality

In response to a question, the patient gives a reply that is appropriate to the general topic but does not answer the question exactly. The speech moves away from the actual answer.

  • Doctor: "Have you had any trouble sleeping lately?"
  • Patient: "I usually sleep in my bed, but now I'm sleeping on the sofa"

(ii) Derailment

A breakdown in both the logical connection between ideas and the overall sense of goal-directedness. The words make sentences, but the sentences do not make sense.

  • "Some people just don't understand why I had breakfast in America during the first world war"

(iii) Neologisms

Bringing in new words that do not exist.

  • The world is not 'gooder' for people like me"

(iv) Desultory thoughts

Speech is grammatically correct, however, sudden unrelated ideas force their way in from time to time.

  • My actual problem is that the people never understand me and my stomach feels like an empty bucket"

(v) Word salad

Using a mixture of unintelligible meaningless words and sentences

  • Tree bus rain food home car tiger"
   

DISORDER OF POSSESSION OF THOUGHT

(A) Obsession and compulsion

(i) Obsessions

Recurrent and persistent thoughts, impulses. or images that cause distress to oneself.

  • Fear of dirt or contamination
  • Fear of becoming ill
  • Constant thoughts of a certain number
  • Need for symmetry or exactness
  • Worry about whether something has been done "right"
  • Forbidden sexual or religious thoughts

(ii) Compulsions

Repetitive behaviors or actions that the person feels driven to perform in response to an obsession

  • Washing hands
  • Blinking eyes
  • Counting items, such as currency
  • Checking to see if doors are locked
  • Arranging items in a certain way
  • Requiring constant approval from people around them
(B) Thought alienation

(i) Thought insertion

Thoughts are being inserted into the patient's mind and they recognize them as being foreign and coming from without any stimulus

  • "I have repeated thoughts of killing my neighbors and I believe aliens are putting these ideas into my head at night"

(ii) Thought withdrawal

Delusion that someone or something is removing from one's mind and the patient has no power over this.

  • "Lately, I am losing all my memories and I believe that the 'government agents' are stealing them when I go to sleep"

(iii) Thought broadcasting

Belief that one's thoughts are quietly escaping from one's mind and that other people might be able to access them and hear or see them.

  • "I believe my exact thoughts appear on the TV and the internet and I think I can broadcast them globally" 

(iv) Thought echo

Patient hears the 'echo' of his own thoughts in the form of a voice after he has made the thought.

  • "I thought of making a sandwich in the morning and surprisingly a voice, from nowhere, told me to make a sandwich out loud"
 

DISORDER OF CONTENT OF THOUGHT

(i) Phobias

Persistent fear of an object or situation, typically disproportional to the actual danger posed, in which the sufferer goes to great lengths in avoiding it

  • Arachnophobia - fear of spider
  • Barophobia - fear of gravity
  • Cynophobia - fear of dogs
  • Hemophobia - fear of blood
  • Nosocomephobia - fear of hospitals

(ii) Religious preoccupations

Thoughts involving religious themes or subject matter.

  • "I get instructions from God on how to make my country great"

(iii) Ideas of hopelessness

Thoughts of complete despair where the patient strongly believes that the circumstances will never get better for him.

  • "I am never going to pass my final exams, no matter how hard I study"

(iv) Antisocial urges

Thoughts of indulging in some behaviors or actions that harm or lack consideration for the well being of others.

  • "I have these urges to go rob a bank or blackmail my neighbors for their money"

(v) Derealization

Alteration in the perception or experience of the external world so that it seems unreal

  • "The world and everything around is nothing but just a dream"

(vi) Depersonalization

Feeling as if one is disconnected from reality, feeling detached from one's own thoughts and one's own physical body

  • "I sometimes drift into a dream-like state where I lose contact with my own self"

(vii) Delusions

False beliefs that are strongly held and unchangeable in the face of refuting evidence and that are not consistent with the person's educational, social and cultural background.

The three main criteria for a belief to be considered a delusion are:

  • Certainty (held with complete confidence)
  • Incorrigibility (not changeable by proof to the contrary)
  • Impossibility or falsity of content (implausible, bizarre or patently untrue)
  DISORDERS OF PERCEPTIONS

  • Illusion: Misinterpretation of real external stimuli.

  • Hallucination: False sensory perception, externally.

  • Pseudohallucination: False sensory perception from within and having an insight.

text: 4. A lady came to the hospital after fighting with her husband. She reports that she is unable to speak. However, all neurological and physical examinations are normal, and she does not seem concerned about her condition. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: D. La-belle indifference

La-belle indifference is seen in conversion disorder. It is the absence of concern towards one’s problem despite the apparent severe disability. Conversion disorder is also called functional neurological symptom disorder, and there is no bodily cause involved in this condition. A conversion reaction is an acute and temporary loss or alteration in motor or sensory function triggered by psychosocial stress. Most of the patients have a history of a traumatic event in childhood. The symptoms or deficits of conversion disorder are not intentionally produced. It is more commonly seen in females. Primary gain refers to keeping internal conflicts outside of awareness and the relief from stress. Secondary gain refers to the attention gained by the patient (from bystanders) as a result of being sick. If the secondary gain is intentional, then it would lead to the diagnosis of malingering. A related phenomenon is la belle indifference, in which the patient is not concerned about the serious symptoms. Symptoms of conversion disorder: * One or two neurologic symptoms affecting the voluntary or sensory function * Must have psychologic factors associated with the onset or exacerbation of the symptoms. * Mutism, blindness, and paralysis are the most common symptoms. * Sensory system: Anesthesia and paresthesia * Motor system: Abnormal movements, gait disturbance (astasia abasia), weakness, paralysis, tics, jerks, etc. * Central nervous system: Pseudo-seizures Other Options: Option A: Adjustment reaction is a psychological response to an identifiable stressor that results in the development of clinically significant emotional or behavioral symptoms. The condition develops within 3 months of exposure to the stressor and lasts no longer than 6 months after the stressor or its consequences have ended. Notably, the emotional or behavioral symptoms must be out of proportion to the stressor when considering cultural and contextual factors. Option B: Somatic symptom disorder is the presence of one or more somatic symptoms for more than 6 months in the absence of an organic cause is suggestive of somatic symptom disorder. It is characterized by the fear of having a serious illness based on the person's misinterpretation of bodily symptoms. Option C:Malingering is the intentional falsification of physical or psychological symptoms to achieve some practical gain such as financial compensation, avoidance of criminal responsibility or military service, or leave from work. Pearl PF1521: Conversion Disorder Conversion disorder: Also called functional neurological symptom disorder. Common presenting symptoms: * Weakness and/or paralysis * Non-epileptic seizures * Movement disorders * Speech or visual impairment * Swallowing difficulty * Sensory disturbances * Cognitive symptoms Diagnostic criteria: * Symptoms of altered neurological function-voluntary motor or sensory * Often precipitated by a psychological stressor (the temporal relationship between stressor and symptoms is present) * Not feigned or intentionally produced (as in factitious disorder or malingering) * Findings incompatible with a recognized neurological condition * Symptoms cause significant social or occupational impairment Other important features: * Presence of primary and secondary gain * La-belle indifference: refers to an absence of concern towards one’s problem despite severe disability Management options: * First-line: Education and self-help technique * Second-line: Cognitive-behavioral therapy * Physical therapy for motor symptoms

text: 1. Which among the following is not a feature of pseudohallucination?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Perceived in objective space

Pseudohallucination is a disorder of perception like hallucinations. They are sensory deceptions without any actual stimulus. These perceptions are often vivid and not under voluntary control. They are triggered by various events * Intense emotional triggers * Suggestions from immediate surroundings * Psychiatric disorders like schizrophrenia  * Diseases of sense organs * Sensory deprivation * Diseases of central nervous system The prime difference of pseudohallucinations lies in the fact that they occur in the inner subjective space, i.e., they are experienced in the mind of the subject. Hallucinations on the other hand are perceived in the objective space, ie the surroundings of the subject and can be heard or seen form the surroundings by the subject. Pseudohallucinations don't point towards a psychological pathology as it can occur in psychologically sound individuals as well.

The symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupa­tional, or other important areas of functioning. C. The episode is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or to another medical condition. D. The occurrence of the major depressive episode is not better explained by schizoaf­fective disorder, schizophrenia, schizophreniform disorder, delusional disorder, or other specified and unspecified schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders. E. There has never been a manic episode or a hypomanic episode. text: 1. A chronic alcoholic consuming alcohol for the last 20 years had his last drink 3 days back. He presents with altered sensorium, disorientation, tremors, and a feeling of insects crawling over his body. What is the diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Delirium tremens

The given clinical scenario of a chronic alcoholic patient who has not consumed alcohol for the past 3 days with disorientation, visual hallucinations, and altered sensorium is suggestive of delirium tremens. Delirium tremens is a medical emergency that occurs during alcohol withdrawal. It is an acute condition and usually develops within 72 hours after the last drink. It has symptoms of both delirium and alcohol withdrawal. The clinical features of delirium tremens are: * Altered sensorium with disorientation * Perceptual distortions, most frequently tactile or visual hallucinations * Autonomic hyperactivity with tachycardia, fever, anxiety, insomnia, and hypertension and sweating * Fluctuating levels of psychomotor activity, ranging from agitation to lethargy Altered sleep-wake cycle  Other options: Option B: Wernicke’s encephalopathy (alcoholic encephalopathy) is associated with thiamine deficiency. Alcohol abuse may lead to thiamine deficiency because of poor nutritional habits or malabsorption. It is an acute neurological disorder characterized by: * Global confusion * Ocular abnormalities like horizontal nystagmus, gaze palsy, anisocoria, and sluggish pupillary reflex * Ataxia - mainly affecting the gait * Vestibular dysfunction Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam (intravenously) or chlordiazepoxide (orally every 4 hours) are given. It is also recommended to administer thiamine in patients with alcohol-related disorders to prevent Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Option C: Korsakoff’s psychosis can follow Wernicke’s encephalopathy due to thiamine deficiency. It is a chronic amnestic syndrome that is characterized by the following clinical symptoms in an intact and responsive patient: * Impaired mental syndrome, especially recent memory * Anterograde amnesia * Confabulation Option D: Alcohol-induced psychosis is characterized by the development of auditory hallucinations or paranoid delusions in the context of heavy drinking or alcohol withdrawal. text: 3. A 16-year-old girl has intense food cravings. After eating her food in one go, she induces forceful vomiting. Her BMI is 27 kg/m2. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Bulimia nervosa

The given scenario of a 16-year-old girl with intense food cravings followed by self-induced vomiting and a BMI of 27 kg/m2, points towards the diagnosis of bulimia nervosa. Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder, often seen in young women. It is characterized by binge-eating episodes, followed by inappropriate, compensatory measures to stop weight gain, like self-induced vomiting, laxative abuse, diuretics, enema, and emetic abuse. These binge-eating episodes occur at least once a week and are present for at least 3 months. The patient fears gaining weight and has a relentless drive to be thin.  The weight is normal in most patients with bulimia nervosa. However, few patients may either be overweight or underweight. There is a risk of dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.  Treatment modalities are cognitive behavioral therapy, psychotherapy, and antidepressants such as fluoxetine. Other options: Option A: Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder that is often seen between the ages of 10 and 30. Typical features are self-induced starvation, voluntary and unhealthy reduction in weight, intense drive for thinness, and fear of becoming obese. Associated features can include depression, anxiety, amenorrhea in females, hypothermia, and bradycardia.  Option C: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a condition where scrupulous individuals are overly concerned that something they thought or did might be a sin or a violation of religious or moral doctrine. The treatment of choice for OCD is cognitive behavioral therapy. Option D: Binge-eating disorder is the most common eating disorder. It is characterized by rapid intake of abnormally large quantities of food over a short period of time, even when not hungry. There are feelings of guilt about the eating episodes, but these patients do not compensate in any way following the episodes of binge. Pearl PF1282: Eating Disorders

text: 5. A 41-year-old woman presents with low mood, lack of interest in activities, poor appetite, and disturbed sleep. She had a similar episode five years ago, from which she made a full recovery. There is no history of elevated mood, rapid thoughts, or reduced need for sleep. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Recurrent depressive disorder

The given clinical scenario of low mood, lack of interest in activities, poor appetite, and disturbed sleep, along with a similar episode 5 years ago, followed by complete recovery, is indicative of recurrent depressive disorder. ICD-11 code 6A71 refers to Recurrent Depressive Disorder, which is defined by the presence of at least two depressive episodes, each separated by a period of several months without significant mood symptoms. However, according to the DSM-5, Major Depressive Disorder is classified as recurrent when there is a gap of at least 2 consecutive months between episodes, during which the individual does not meet the criteria for a major depressive episode. A depressive episode is characterised by a period of depressed mood or diminished interest in activities occurring most of the day, nearly every day during a period lasting at least two weeks accompanied by other symptoms such as difficulty concentrating, feelings of worthlessness or excessive or inappropriate guilt, hopelessness, recurrent thoughts of death or suicide, changes in appetite or sleep, psychomotor agitation or retardation, and reduced energy or fatigue. There have never been any prior manic, hypomanic, or mixed episodes, which would indicate the presence of bipolar disorder. People with recurrent depressive disorder have more severe symptoms and have an episodic disorder, which sets them apart from people with dysthymia.  Other options: Option B: Cyclothymia is a chronic disorder characterized by at least 2 years of fluctuating, mild hypomanic & depressive symptoms (that do not meet the full criteria for hypomanic episodes or major depressive episodes). It is a symptomatically milder form of bipolar II disorder. Option C: Dysthymia (persistent depressive disorder) is characterized by at least 2 years of depressed mood that does not satisfy the criteria for a major depressive episode and with no episodes of mania or hypomania. In children, a diagnosis of dysthymia is made if depressive symptoms are present for more than 1 year. Option D: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a psychiatric disorder characterized by low mood, anhedonia (lack of interest in usual activities), loss of appetite, insomnia or hypersomnia, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness, and/or suicidal thoughts. While this episode does qualify in terms of symptoms, she has a history of a previous episode, which now qualifies her for recurrent rather than single-episode MDD. text: 6. A patient is diagnosed with a phobic disorder. Which of the following defense mechanisms is likely to be present in this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Displacement

Displacement is the defense mechanism in phobias. It is the shifting of emotions about one object/individual onto another object/individual. Pearl PF0613: Defense mechanisms that operate in various diseases * OCD - reaction formation, undoing * Phobia - displacement * Neurosis - repression * Grief - denial * Borderline personality - Splitting * Schizophrenia - projection * Enuresis - Regression Pearl PF0612: Defense mechanisms
Narcissistic-psychotic defenses

Denial: Used to avoid becoming aware of some painful aspects of reality.

  • Eg: I know I do not have cancer.

Distortion: Grossly reshaping the experience of external reality to suit inner needs.

  • Eg: I possess special powers and abilities and am superior to others.

Projection (psychotic): Attributing your own wishes, thoughts, or feelings onto someone else.

  • Eg: I’m sure my wife is cheating on me.

Splitting: External objects are divided into all good or all bad.

  • Eg: The morning staff is perfect, the evening staff is terrible.
Immature defenses

Acting out: Behavioral or emotional outburst.

  • Eg: My 10-year-old started getting into trouble right after his mother and I got divorced.

Blocking: Temporary block in thinking.

  • Eg: I have known him for years but can never seem to remember his name.

Hypochondriasis: A defense style in which people say that no one understands their pain.

  • Eg: No one understands the depth of my pain.

Introjection: Features of the external world are taken and made part of the self.

  • Eg: The resident physician dresses like the attending whom he admires.

Passive-aggressive behavior: Aggressive intent is cloaked by a passive method.

  • Eg: Procrastinating at work for not getting the promotion.

Projection (non-psychotic): Unwanted feelings are displaced onto another person.

  • Eg: A man who has been unfaithful to his wife but accuses his wife of cheating on him.

Regression: Return to an earlier stage of development, most immature.

  • Eg: Ever since my divorce, my 5-year-old has begun to wet the bed.

Schizoid fantasy: Tendency to retreat into fantasy in order to resolve inner and outer conflicts.

  • Eg: Adolescents day dreaming on pornographic materials.

Somatization: Psychic derivatives are converted into bodily symptoms.

  • Eg: Just thinking of the exam I get butterflies in my stomach.
Neurotic defenses

Externalization: Perceiving one’s personality, impulses, moods and attitudes in the external world.

  • Eg: An argumentative person perceives the doctor as argumentative whilst believing himself to be blameless.

Displacement: Shifting emotions about one object/ individual onto another object/ individual.

  • Eg: Getting angry at your parents because you had a bad day at work.

Inhibition: conscious or unconscious constraint of a process or behavior.

  • Eg: A desire to eat dessert versus the desire to lose weight.

Intellectualization: Excessive use of intellectual processes to avoid affective expression or experience.

  • Eg: It is interesting to note the specific skin lesions which seem to arise as a consequence of my end-stage disease.

Isolation: Separation of an idea from the affect that accompanies it.

  • Eg: As she arrived at the station to identify the body, she appeared to show no emotion.

Rationalization: Rational explanations are used to justify unacceptable attitudes, beliefs, or behaviors.

  • Eg: I did not pass the test because it was harder this year than ever before.

Reaction formation: An unacceptable impulse is transformed into its opposite; results in the formation of character traits.

  • Eg: Listen to him tell his family he was not afraid when I saw him crying.

Repression: An idea or feeling is withheld from consciousness; unconscious forgetting.

  • Eg: I do not remember having had a dog.

Sexualization: Endowing an object or function with sexual significance.

Undoing: Acting out the reverse of unacceptable behavior; consists of an act.

  • Eg: I need to wash my hands whenever I have these thoughts.

Retroflexion: Self-destruction due to rage.

  • Eg: A person cutting his wrist because he is angry with himself.

Mature defenses

Altruism: Getting pleasure from giving to others what the individual would have liked to receive.

  • Eg:  A former alcoholic funding a rehabilitation center.

Anticipation: Realistically planning or anticipating future inner discomfort.

  • Eg: Moderate amount of anxiety before surgery.

Asceticism: Gratification derived from renunciation.

Humor: Permits the expression of feelings and thoughts without personal discomfort.

  • Eg: Before execution, firing squad leader offers the man a cigarette. He replies "no thanks I'm trying to quit".

Sublimation: Impulse gratification has been achieved, but the aim or object has been changed from unacceptable to acceptable; allows instincts to be channeled. Most mature of the defenses.

  • Eg: Jack the Ripper becomes a surgeon.

Suppression: Conscious forgetting. The only conscious defense mechanism.

  • Eg: I would rather talk about my operation after the party is over.

text: 2. A person has the false belief that he owns a lot of property and is wealthy, and that someone he knows wants to kill him to take it away. He appears depressed and physically unwell. What is seen here?

Correct answer: A. Delusion of grandeur and persecution

This scenario where he has lots of property and somebody wants to kill him points towards diagnosis of delusion of grandeur and persecution. A person has the false belief that he possesses vast property and is very rich, which represents a delusion of grandeur, characterized by an exaggerated sense of self-importance, wealth, exceptional abilities, or fame. He also believes that someone wants to kill him and take away his property, which corresponds to a delusion of persecution, the most common type of delusion. Thus, both delusions of grandeur and persecution are present in this case. A delusion is a false, firm, fixed belief that is not in keeping with the patient’s socio-cultural and educational background. Delusions are of two types based on their origin: Primary: Delusions that do not occur in response to another psychopathological form such as mood disorder. They are understandable when a detailed psychiatric history and examination are available. Other options: * Delusion of reference means delusion in which events, objects, or other persons in one’s immediate environment have a particular and unusual significance in reference to the person experiencing the delusion. text: 3. A 28 year old software engineer visits a psychiatry clinic as he is suffering from sleep disturbances, low mood, stress in his current job from the past 3 months. He cannot work properly and has difficulty balancing family and work. He has no prior psychiatry history. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Adjustment disorder

The given scenario where a software engineer is stressed in his job from the last 3 months suggests it is an adjustment disorder. Adjustment disorder is a common psychiatric condition, especially seen in adolescents and women, where an individual develops a maladaptive response to a stressful life event. According to ICD-10, it begins within 1 month of a significant stressor and is typically seen in those with poor coping skills or vulnerable personality traits. The disorder usually lasts less than 6 months, except in cases of prolonged depressive reaction. Subtypes include brief or prolonged depressive reaction, mixed anxiety and depression, or predominant disturbance of emotions or conduct. Supportive psychotherapy is the treatment of choice, and most patients recover within about 3 months. Diagnosing criteria for adjustment disorder include: * Development of emotional or behavioural response within 3 months of the onset of the stressor. * The symptoms or behaviour are clinically significant, where, any one of the following are met: * The response is out of proportion to the severity or intensity of stressor. * Significant impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning. * Stress-related disturbance does not meet criteria for another mental disorder or exacerbation of pre-existing mental disorder. * The symptoms do not represent normal bereavement. * Once the stressor is terminated, the symptoms do not persist for more than an additional 6 months. Other options: Option B: It is not Generalized anxiety disorder as it requires ≥6 months of symptoms. Here the duration is only 3 months. Generalized anxiety disorder is defined as excessive worry and anxiety about several activities and events for most days during a 6 month period which interferes with various aspects of life. Option C: Acute stress disorder is characterised by intrusive symptoms like distressing memories, dreams and flashbacks of the event occurring after death, serious injury, or sexual violation lasting less than one month. Option D: PTSD requires a traumatic event + symptoms persisting >1 month (re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal). The treatment modalities for PTSD and acute stress disorder include trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing therapy (EMDR), and SSRIs.  Here, there is no trauma and only job stress, so it's not PTSD. text: 2. A known alcoholic patient is brought to the emergency in a disoriented state. He complains of seeing snakes and insects crawling on his skin. Which of the following should be given to this patient?

text: 3. Which of the following is not a likely symptom of a panic attack?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Suicide attempt

A suicide attempt is not a likely symptom of a panic attack. A panic attack is characterized by a sudden onset of overwhelming fear or severe discomfort, which can persist for several minutes to hours.Recurrent panic attacks are termed panic disorders. Panic attacks can occur in other disorders, particu­larly in specific phobias, social phobias, and post-traumatic stress disorder.  Unexpected panic attacks occur at any time and are not associated with any identifiable situational trigger. Attacks in patients with social and specific pho­bias are usually expected in response to a specific stimulus. Some panic attacks do not fit into unexpected or expected attacks, and these attacks are referred to as situationally predisposed panic attacks. They may or may not occur on exposure to a specific trigger, or may occur immediately after exposure or after a considerable period of time. text: 4. What is the earliest symptom of alcohol withdrawal?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Tremors

Coarse tremors are the earliest symptom of alcohol withdrawal which develops around 6-8 hours post-cessation of drinking. After 8-12 hours have passed, psychotic symptoms are seen like hallucinations which are predominantly auditory in nature. Seizures are seen after 12-24 hours and can progress to delirium tremens at around 72 hours. text: 2. A 39-year-old man reported that he washes his hands 15-20 times a day, to the point of it taking a toll on his workplace performance. He says this is due to repetitive thoughts that his hands are contaminated with dirt. What is the most probable diagnosis in this case?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Obsessive compulsive disorder

The man is suffering from obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), as evidenced by the obsession (doubt that his hands are contaminated), followed by a compulsion (washing his hands way too many times). An obsession with contamination is a common symptom of adult OCD. Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) comprises symptoms that include intrusive thoughts, ritu­als, preoccupations, and compulsions. These recurrent obses­sions or compulsions cause severe distress to the patient. The patient might have an obsession, a compulsion, or both. The recurrent and intrusive thoughts, feelings, ideas, and sensations are referred to as obsessions. A compulsion is a conscious, standardized, recurrent behavior, eg: counting, and checking, and is done in order to reduce the anxiety associated with the obsession. Treatment of OCD includes: * Pharmacotherapy: SSRIs or clomipramine * Behavioral therapy: Approaches include: * exposure and response prevention * desensitization * thought stopping * flooding * implosion therapy * aversive conditioning A combination of behavioural and pharmacotherapy is most effective. Other Options: Option A: Bipolar disorder is characterized by alternating episodes of mania and depression, with periods of normal mood in between. The patient's presentation shows no evidence of mood cycling, elevated mood, grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, or other manic symptoms.  Option C: Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder characterized by delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, and negative symptoms like flat affect and avolition. The patient's concern about hand contamination might superficially resemble a delusion, but it differs significantly. In OCD, patients typically recognize their thoughts are excessive or irrational (though they still feel compelled to act on them), whereas in schizophrenia, delusions are firmly held false beliefs that the person fully believes.  Option D: Mania is characterized by abnormally elevated mood, increased energy, decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, pressured speech, grandiosity, increased goal-directed activity, and often poor judgment. The patient's repetitive hand washing isn't driven by elevated mood or energy but rather by anxiety and intrusive thoughts about contamination.

text: 4. A 51-year-old man complains of abdominal pain and blood stained stools. The barium enema study of his intestines shows the following finding. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Correct answer: A. Intussusception

The given clinical scenario and the radiological image of the claw sign/pincer sign in barium enema is suggestive of intussusception. Intussusception occurs when a portion of the alimentary tract is telescoped into an adjacent segment. It is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction between 5 months and 3 years of age. The most common location of intussusception is ileocolic.  The combination of paroxysmal abdominal pain, vomiting, and a palpable abdominal mass is a highly characteristic clinical presentation; the presence of associated rectal bleeding invariably confirms the diagnosis. Palpation of the abdomen usually reveals a slightly tender, "sausage-shaped" mass, sometimes ill-defined, which might increase in size during an episode of pain and is most often in the right upper abdomen, with its longitudinal axis cephalocaudal. However, approximately 30% of patients do not have a palpable mass. Barium contrast enemas demonstrate a filling defect or cupping in the head of the contrast media where its advance is obstructed by the intussusceptum. This is known as the claw sign (shown below). A central linear column of contrast media may be visible in the compressed lumen of the intussusceptum, and a thin rim of contrast may be seen trapped around the invaginating intestine in the folds of mucosa within the intussuscipiens (coiled-spring sign). The intussusception appears as a sausage-shaped mass in a longitudinal plane or a target mass in the transverse plane on CT and USG.  Ultrasound signs include: * Target sign -also known as the doughnut sign * Pseudokidney sign: this is seen in the longitudinal section of the bowel: * The edematous bowel resembles renal parenchyma and * the mesentery, which is dragged into the intussusception, resembles the renal hilum. * Crescent in a doughnut sign. Option C: Barium enema radiograph in colonic diverticulitis shows multiple barium-coated outpouchings from the colonic wall and gives the appearance of a saw-tooth. text: 12. A patient with head and neck cancer was told by his oncologist that needs radiotherapy at a total dose of 70 Gy over a 7 week period for his tumor. He was scheduled to receive a dose of 1.8-2Gy per fraction, once daily over 5 days a week, for 7 weeks. What is this type of radiotherapy called as?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Regular Fractionated radiotherapy

Since the patient needs 70Gy in total for his tumour and his dose per fraction is at 1.8-2.0 Gy, 5 days a week, for 7 weeks, it is called Regular/Conventional Fractionated Radiotherapy. Radiotherapy: The total dose of radiation needed for a tumour is usually given as fractions over the entire treatment period as it maximises the effects of the radiation on the malignant cells and minimises the damage on the healthy cells. The reasons for this are due to : 1. Re-distribution: Cells are more resistant to damage in the late S2 phase while sensitive in the M and G2 phase. Only some tumour cells will be in the sensitive phase of the cell cycle when the radiation is given. Hence, giving another dose at a later time helps in killing the other cells who were in the resistant part of the cell cycle, thus increasing the success rate of the therapy. 2. Re-oxygenation: Hypoxic cells are less sensitive to the indirect effects of radiation. The tumour cells which are closer to oxygen sources are killed first and in the intervening time, the other relatively hypoxic cells can improve their oxygenation so that the next fraction of radiation is effective on them.  3. Repair: The ability to repair DNA is more for healthy cells than malignant cells and thus when a radiation dose has been received, the healthy cells repair their DNA faster than the malignant cells. The malignant cells whose DNA is not fully repaired are highly susceptible to the next dose of radiation. Types of fractionation: * In the case of Head and neck cancer, the conventional schedule of radiotherapy involves the delivery of 70 Gy in 1.8-2 Gy fractions(total around 35-36 fractions) over 7 weeks, treating 5 days per week. * However, this dose can be delivered at 1.10-1.25 Gy/fraction for 56 fractions over the same time period of 7 weeks which is called hyperfractionation(Option B). This delivers a lower dose with more fractions and the efficacy improves as the healthy cells have more ability to repair themselves in the intervening time.  * Accelerated fractionation(Option C) is when the same 70 Gy, is given at around 1.6-1.8 Gy/fraction but it is delivered more than once daily, decreasing the total treatment time to around 6 weeks. These aim to decrease tumor proliferation which can lead to failure of the therapy.  Note: * Shorter schedules remain useful for small-volume treatments: 50 Gy in 16 fractions over 3 weeks or 55 Gy in 20 fractions over 4 weeks. * Accelerated schedules although is easier to implement than hyperfractionation result in a lesser survival gain. Option D: Brachytherapy is a method of treatment in which sealed radioactive sources are used to deliver radiation at a short distance by interstitial, intracavitary, or surface application.  The following isotopes are used in brachytherapy: * I-125 and Iridium-192 - are used in low-dose rate (LDR) brachytherapy. * Cobalt-60 - is used for high-dose rate (HDR) brachytherapy. Afterloading is the process of placing the radioactive material into the target region. This is either done manually by the oncologist, or by using remote afterloading devices. Remote afterloading devices enable us to eliminate direct contact with radioactive sources while administration. It provides protection from radiation exposure to healthcare professionals by securing the radiation source in a shielded safe manner.

Therefore, CT limbs is the exception and is not typically included in the whole-body CT scan protocol for trauma patients.

text: 2. Which of the following radioisotopes is used in a PET-CT scan?
expl:
Correct answer: B. 18F-FDG

18F-FDG is the radioisotope used in a PET-CT scan. Positron emission tomography - CT (PET-CT): * PET imaging is based on the detection of an injected positron-emitting radioactive tracer. * It relies on the coincidence detection of the annihilation photons (γ), which are released when a positron combines with an electron. * A glucose analogue called FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose) is used in PET imaging. FDG is taken up by metabolically active cells, where it undergoes phosphorylation to form FDG-6-phosphate. Unlike glucose, FDG-6-phosphate cannot undergo further metabolism and becomes trapped within the cell. (So, the patient must be fasted for 4-6 hrs prior to imaging). * The trapped FDG-6-phosphate is detected by the PET scanner.  * Before injecting FDG, the blood glucose level should be measured. It should be < 150 mg/dL. Good blood glucose control is essential as FDG uptake is competitively inhibited by glucose. * Imaging is started 60 minutes following FDG injection. Indications of PET-CT: * PET-CT is used in oncology imaging to detect malignant cells as they demonstrate increased glucose metabolism relative to normal tissues. * It is indicated for the differentiation of a malignant from a benign lesion. * It is indicated in tumour staging and evaluation of tumour recurrence. Areas of normal physiological uptake in PET CT: * Brain tissue * Skeletal muscle, especially after strenuous activity, and laryngeal muscles following speech * Myocardium * Gastrointestinal tract, e.g. intestinal wall * Genitourinary tract (FDG is excreted via the renal system and passes into the collecting systems) * Brown fat (FDG accumulates here as glucose and ATP are required for heat production) * Thymus * Bone marrow Other options: Option A: 16F-FDG (Fluorodeoxyglucose) is a radiolabeled glucose analogue used in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) to assess metabolic activity in tissues. It is particularly useful for detecting cancer, and infections, and monitoring neurological disorders due to its ability to highlight areas with high glucose consumption. Option C: Carbon-11 (C-11) is used for certain types of PET imaging, particularly in neurology and oncology. Option D: Gallium-68 (Ga-68) is used for imaging certain types of neuroendocrine tumours and somatostatin receptor imaging.

text: 2. A non-smoker patient with a history of cardiac disease suddenly develops chest pain and breathlessness. An X-ray is performed and given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Cardiogenic pulmonary edema

The given chest X-ray shows increased interstitial markings, vascular redistribution, and alveolar oedema in a butterfly pattern points to a diagnosis of pulmonary oedema.  Acute severe hypertension, acute myocardial infarction, or exacerbation of chronic heart failure are some of the common causes of cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. It can be precipitated by the discontinuation of medications (non-compliant patient), excessive salt intake, or tachyarrhythmias.  It presents with severe dyspnea, pink frothy sputum production, diaphoresis, and cyanosis. Auscultation reveals rales and rhonchi in all lung fields. Cardiomegaly might be seen in cases of chronic heart failure. Management of pulmonary oedema includes the use of diuretics, nitrates, and morphine to decrease the preload. Nitroglycerin and isosorbide dinitrate have a rapid onset of action and can be given sublingually. If there is a persistence of pulmonary oedema and no hypotension, it can be administered intravenously. Oxygen therapy to maintain a saturation of >92% is recommended. If saturation is not maintained even with supplemental oxygen, positive-pressure ventilation through a face mask or endotracheal intubation is required. A sitting position with legs hanging by the side of the bed can be used to reduce venous return in patients without hypotension. Non-cardiac causes of pulmonary oedema are high altitude, sepsis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation.  Heart failure is a manifestation of most chronic cardiac conditions such as hypertension, valvular heart disease, and coronary artery disease. Symptoms such as shortness of breath, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea point to left heart failure due to pulmonary congestion. In contrast, symptoms such as pedal oedema, weight gain, early satiety, and hepatic congestion are characteristic of right heart failure. text: 4. A patient with a history of breast cancer underwent tele cobalt-60 radiotherapy. She now presents with respiratory distress, and imaging shows bilateral perihilar ground glass opacities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Radiation pneumonitis

A patient with a history of breast cancer who previously received Tele cobalt-60 radiotherapy now presents with respiratory distress. Imaging shows bilateral perihilar ground glass opacities, suggesting a likely diagnosis of radiation pneumonitis. Radiation pneumonitis is an inflammatory reaction in the lungs that occurs as a result of radiation therapy, commonly seen in patients treated for breast cancer, lung cancer, or lymphomas. It typically develops within weeks to months after radiation exposure and presents with symptoms such as cough, fever, chest pain, and progressive shortness of breath. The condition arises due to damage to the alveolar and capillary structures, leading to increased vascular permeability, inflammatory infiltration, and pulmonary oedema. Imaging findings, particularly on CT scans, may show areas of ground-glass opacities, consolidation, or haziness, often in the radiation field. If left untreated, radiation pneumonitis can progress to pulmonary fibrosis, causing long-term respiratory complications. Management involves corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and supportive care, including oxygen therapy if needed. Prevention strategies include limiting the radiation dose, using advanced radiotherapy techniques to minimize lung exposure, and closely monitoring high-risk patients. Early recognition and intervention are crucial to improving outcomes and preventing long-term lung damage in affected individuals.

text: 5. A 20-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after a RTA. On presentation, his pulse is 110/minute, RR is 18/minute and BP is 80/60 mmhg. What is the next step in management?
expl:
Correct answer: A. eFAST

Cardiogenic shock, hemorrhagic shock, or pneumothorax are the most likely causes of hypotension in a trauma patient. Ultrasound evaluation using eFAST to look for pericardium, pleural cavities, and abdomen in combination with plain radiographs of the chest and pelvis will usually identify the source of the bleed.  In patients with hypotension due to blunt trauma, the pelvis should be wrapped in a sheet for stabilization until radiography can be done.  eFAST stands for extended FAST and incorporates left and right thoracic views to assess for pneumothorax and haemothorax. The best diagnostic technique to assess renal perfusion is the MAG-3 (Mercaptoacetyltriglycine) or DTPA (Diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid) scan. The above radiograph depicts the miliary pattern seen in tuberculosis. Miliary tuberculosis is a form of disseminated pulmonary tuberculosis that occurs when organisms draining through the lymphatics enter the venous blood and circulate back to the lung. text: 3. A patient underwent the following investigation for suspected malignancy. Which of the following compounds is used in this investigation?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Fluorodeoxyglucose

The image shows a positron-emission tomography (PET) scan. PET involves the use of a radiolabeled bio-compound such as 2-fluoro-2-deoxy-D-glucose (FDG), which is injected intravenously. It is based on the principle that tumor cells have a high metabolic rate and can metabolize FDG. However, tumor cells can metabolize FDG only to FDG-6-phosphate, and no further. Hence, it accumulates in tumor cells and can be detected and quantified. Applications of PET: * Oncologic: * Detection, staging, drug response * Differentiation between radiation necrosis and recurrence * Neurologic: * Early diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease * Localization of seizure focus in the interictal phase * Localizing eloquent areas (e.g. speech, motor function) * Cardiac: * Identification of hibernating myocardium The combination of PET imaging with CT (PET-CT) combines the metabolic information (PET) with the cross-sectional anatomic information (CT). PET-CT is used in oncology imaging to detect malignant cells as they demonstrate increased glucose metabolism relative to normal tissues.

subject: Radiology
text: 4. Positron emission tomography is based on which of the following mechanisms?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Glucose metabolism

Positron emission tomography (PET) utilizes the mechanism of glucose metabolism. PET imaging is based on the detection of an injected positron-emitting radioactive tracer. It relies on the coincidence detection of the annihilation photons (γ), which are released when a positron combines with an electron. A glucose analog called fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) is used. FDG is taken up by metabolically active cells, where it undergoes phosphorylation to form FDG-6-phosphate. Unlike glucose, FDG-6-phosphate cannot undergo further metabolism and thus accumulates within the cell. The trapped FDG-6-phosphate is detected by the PET scanner. Before injecting FDG, the blood glucose level should be measured. It should be < 150 mg/dL. Good blood glucose control is essential as FDG uptake is competitively inhibited by glucose.

text: 8. Which of the following statements is correct regarding the device shown below?

options.A: It is used to measure infrared rays emitted by red blood cells
options.B: It is used for the localisation of calcified plaque
options.C: It is used to measure systolic blood pressure
options.D: It is used to measure blood flow and detect blood flow abnormalities in the blood vessel

expl:
Correct answer: D. It is used to measure blood flow and detect blood flow abnormalities in the blood vessel

The given image is of a handheld doppler device. It is used to measure blood flow and detect blood flow abnormalities in the blood vessel. The Doppler ultrasound device utilizes the doppler effect to assess the movement of red blood cells within blood vessels. The doppler effect is the change in frequency or wavelength of a wave in relation to an observer moving relative to the wave source. The device emits ultrasound waves that reflect off moving red blood cells. The frequency shift between the transmitted and received sound waves is used to calculate the velocity and direction of blood flow. By analyzing these frequency shifts, the device can provide information about the speed and pattern of blood flow. This is particularly useful in detecting abnormalities such as blockages or stenosis. Other options: Option A: Doppler ultrasound does not measure infrared rays. Infrared measurements are typically related to thermal imaging or other specific applications unrelated to blood flow measurement. Option B: Doppler ultrasound can help identify areas of reduced blood flow due to plaques, it is not specifically used for the localization of calcified plaque. Techniques like computed tomography (CT) or MRI are better suited for visualizing calcified plaques. Option C: While Doppler can assist in certain vascular assessments, it is not a primary tool for measuring systolic or diastolic blood pressure.

text: 5. What are the rays used in linear accelerator (LINAC) therapy for curing cancer?
expl:
Correct answer: C. X-ray

X-rays are the most common form of radiation used in radiotherapy. They are produced from a LINAC (linear accelerator). It is used in radiation therapy to deliver high-energy X-rays or electrons to target specific areas of the body, typically to treat cancerous tissues. It uses microwave technology to accelerate charged particles (such as electrons) at a high speed and then directs them into a target (usually a heavy metal) to produce X-rays. These X-rays are then carefully directed at the patient's body to deliver therapeutic radiation doses to the tumor while minimising damage to surrounding healthy tissues. For precise therapy, this LINAC is referred to as a CyberKnife when it is mounted on an electronic robotic arm. It is used in inoperable cranial lesions as stereotactic radiotherapy.  Other options: Option A: Proton beams offer a therapeutic advantage of having a steep dose falloff at the end of their path. Advantages are mostly physical, not biological; however, new data suggest different genes may be induced after proton versus X-ray treatment Option B: Neutron beams are used in visualizing soft tissue and can even provide better contrast than X-rays in some cases, but are rarely used clinically due to complex setup and limited availability. Option D: Cobalt 60 undergoes beta-decay and emits 1.25 MeV (average) gamma rays, which penetrate deeper tissues while sparing skin, used in the Gamma Knife. The gamma knife is mainly used to treat inoperable intracranial lesions.

text: 7. What is the definition of Electron Volt (EV)?

options.A: The speed of an electron in a magnetic field
options.B: The force acting on an electron in an electric field
options.C: The energy gained by an electron when accelerated through a potential difference of one volt.
options.D: The kinetic energy of an electron at rest in a vacuum

expl:
Correct answer: C. The energy gained by an electron when accelerated through a potential difference of one volt.

An electronvolt (eV) is defined as the energy required to accelerate a single electron at rest through an electron potential difference of one volt in a vacuum. This is different from the electrical potential difference applied to the X-ray tube in terms of kilovolts (kV). However, the kV applied to an X-ray tube is approximately equal to the maximum photon energy achievable by a photon (keVmax).

text: 4. Which of the following radioisotopes is used in a PET-CT scan?
expl:
Correct answer: B. 18F-FDG

18F-FDG is the radioisotope used in a PET-CT scan. Positron emission tomography - CT (PET-CT): * PET imaging is based on the detection of an injected positron-emitting radioactive tracer. * It relies on the coincidence detection of the annihilation photons (γ), which are released when a positron combines with an electron. * A glucose analogue called FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose) is used in PET imaging. Once taken up by active cells, FDG is phosphorylated into FDG-6-phosphate, which cannot undergo further metabolism, resulting in intracellular trapping. Because of this, patients are required to fast before the procedure. A fasting period of about 4–6 hours is recommended prior to imaging * The trapped FDG-6-phosphate is detected by the PET scanner.  * Before injecting FDG, the blood glucose level should be measured. It should be < 150 mg/dL. Good blood glucose control is essential as FDG uptake is competitively inhibited by glucose. * Imaging is performed about 1 hour after the administration of FDG. Indications of PET-CT: * In oncology, PET-CT helps detect cancerous cells due to their increased uptake and metabolism of glucose relative to healthy tissue. * PET-CT is used in oncology imaging to detect malignant cells as they demonstrate relative to normal tissues. * It is indicated for the differentiation of a malignant from a benign lesion. * It is indicated in tumor staging and evaluation of tumor recurrence. The clinical vignette along with the ultrasound image showing multiple septations and rosette or honeycomb appearance is diagnostic of active hydatid cyst. Hydatid cyst: Echinococcus granulosus is the most common causative agent in hydatid cysts, while Echinococcus multilocularis and Echinococcus ligartus account for a small number of cases. The hydatid cyst usually develops three weeks after the infection. The cyst is surrounded by a fibrous capsule called the pericyst that is derived from the host tissue. The cyst wall is composed of two layers, ectocyst (outer gelatinous membrane), and endocyst (inner germinal membrane). Ectocyst is a laminated membrane, which is acellular. It helps in the passage of nutrients. The endocyst helps in producing the laminated membrane and scoleces. The brood capsules are cellular masses in the hydatid fluid which consists of scoleces. In a definitive host, these scoleces develop into adult tapeworm while in the intermediate hosts these develop into new hydatid cysts. The brood capsules are attached to the endocyst by a pedicle or stalk. The brood capsules may mature and detach from the mother cyst and become the daughter cysts, which are an exact replica of the mother cysts. The freed brood capsules and scoleces present in the hydatid fluid are called hydatid sand. The image attached below shows the C.S of hydatid cyst. Investigations:  Computed tomography (CT) scan is the best imaging modality for hydatid cyst. It shows the presence of a space-occupying lesion with a smooth outline with septa. CT scan has an accuracy of 98% in the detection of hydatid cysts and higher sensitivity to demonstrate the daughter cysts and extra-hepatic cysts.  The indirect hemagglutination test and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) have a sensitivity of 80% overall and are the initial screening tests of choice. text: 17. A 25-year-old morbidly obese male patient presented with complaints of severe abdominal pain and urinary disturbances. His urine microscopy shows the following type of crystals and an ultrasound of the kidney revealed a renal stone of size 2.5 cm. What is the treatment of choice?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL)

Urine microscopy shows hexagonal crystals, typical of cystine stones that are radio-opaque (due to high sulfur content). The treatment of choice for renal calculi of size 2.5 cm is percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL). Indications of PCNL: * Staghorn calculi * Stones >2 cm in size * Stone composition - struvite, calcium oxalate monohydrate and cystine stones * Multiple stones * Obese patients in whom ESWL is contraindicated * Stones not responding for ESWL Endoscopic instruments are passed into the kidney using a percutaneous technique and stones are removed. Complications of percutaneous nephrolithotomy include: * Haemorrhage from the punctured renal parenchyma * Perforation of the collecting system with extravasation of saline irrigant * Perforation of the colon or pleural cavity during placement of the percutaneous track Extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy:  ESWL is a non-invasive method that generates shockwaves outside the body, which are focused on the stones. It is the commonest method of treating urinary tract stones nowadays. Stones up to approximately 2 cm in size are suitable for this form of treatment.Cystine stones are very hard stones as a result of disulphide bonds and do not fragment with ESWL. Other stones that are difficult to disintegrate by ESWL include cystine, brushite, and calcium oxalate monohydrate stones. ESWL is only 45-60% effective in the treatment of large stones. It causes frequent complications including pain, hydronephrosis, fever, and occasional urosepsis, due to difficulties in the passage of stone particles, especially in cases of insufficient disintegration. Complications: Infection, haematuria, parenchymal haemorrhage, and perirenal hematoma.  Contraindications: Obese patients, pregnant patients, and patients taking oral anticoagulants. Stone fragments collecting in the distal ureter following ESWL are called steinstrasse  (a german word, which means 'street of stones'). The most common site of the column of stone fragments obstruction is the distal ureter, followed by the proximal ureter and mid ureter. The postoperative image is attached below. Ureteroscopic removal: Ureteric calculi are directly visualized through semi-rigid ureteroscopes. Stones are then fragmented and extracted using a dormia basket. These are generally preferred for stones <6mm and specifically those present in the distal ureter. The most significant complications relate to injury to the ureteric mucosa or wall and include ureteric perforation and extravasation, avulsion of the ureter and ureteric stricture. Open surgery: A longstanding obstructing calculus can result in chronic inflammatory change in the kidney. Open surgeries are generally indicated for xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XGP). text: 20. An 11-month-old boy with had a recent urinary tract infection that resolved with antibiotics. Vital signs are within normal limits. expl:
Correct answer: C. Orchidopexy

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of cryptorchidism and the next best step is to perform an orchidopexy. Orchidopexy is the treatment of choice for incompletely palpable unilateral undescended testis. Orchidopexy is usually performed before the boy reaches 12 months of age. About 4% of boys are born with one or both testes incompletely descended. About two-thirds of these reach the scrotum during the first 3 months of life, but full descent after that is uncommon. Cryptorchidism is the failure of the descent of the intra-abdominal testes into the scrotal sac.  It is the most common congenital abnormality of the genitourinary tract. The testes can arrest anywhere during descent, and the most common site is the inguinal region. Phases of testicular descent: * Transabdominal phase: Testes come to lie in the lower abdomen or pelvis, and this descent is regulated by Mullerian-inhibiting substances. * Inguinoscrotal phase: Testes descend along the inguinal canal and reach the scrotal sac, and this phase of the descent is regulated by androgen-induced calcitonin gene-related peptide from the genitofemoral nerve. The exact pathogenesis remains unknown; however, deficiency in gonadotropins and Mullerian-inhibiting substance (MIS) and increased expression of estradiol in the placenta are thought to play a role.  Cryptorchidism is histopathologically characterized by the following:  * Testicular atrophy: thickening of the basement membrane, arrested germ cell development, marked hyalinization * Tubules showing Sertoli cells but no spermatogenesis * Increase in the interstitial Leydig cells  It is associated with testicular atrophy and dysfunction, which result in sterility. Cryptorchid testes carry a 3–5-fold higher risk for testicular cancer (usually seminoma). Thus, observation is never the policy. (Option -A)   When the testis is impalpable, ultrasound may be helpful in identifying the intracanalicular testis, while laparoscopy may be needed to differentiate between the abdominal testis and a truly absent testis. He has progressive difficulty in urination and had an episode of urinary retention 2 days back which was relieved by catheterization.PSA was done which was 5.2 ng/ml and an X-Ray LS spine shows osteoblastic changes. Carcinoma of the prostate is the most common malignant tumour in men over the age of 65 years. The growth and survival of prostate cancer cells depend on androgens.  Approximately 70% of carcinomas of the prostate arise in the peripheral zone of the gland, classically in a posterior location. Most cancers are clinically silent and are detected on routine rectal examination or PSA measurements. Grossly, malignant tissue is gritty and firm in consistency (in contrast to the spongy appearance of benign tissue) and thus more readily palpable on digital rectal examination. Local extension most commonly involves the periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicles, and the base of the urinary bladder. Metastasis spreads via the lymphatics to the obturator nodes and the para-aortic nodes. Hematogenous spread occurs chiefly through the bones to the axial skeleton and rarely to the viscera. The bony metastasis is blastic in origin and involves the lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and ribs in decreasing order of frequency.  Grading of prostate cancer by the modified Gleason system correlates with pathologic stage and prognosis. Measurement of serum PSA levels is widely used to assist in the diagnosis, prognosis, and management of prostate cancer. text: 18. Which of the following fluids should not be given in a hypotensive patient with a head injury?
expl:
Correct answer: B. 5 % Dextrose

5 % Dextrose(hypotonic solutions) should be avoided in patients with a head injury as they cause increased intravascular hydrostatic pressure and cause fluid accumulation in the brain. Dextrose is essentially water since the sugar is metabolized very quickly which provides free water that disperses throughout the intracellular and extracellular compartments with little use as a resuscitative fluid. However, isotonic or iso-osmolar solutions, such as 0.9% (normal saline), Ringer’s solution, or plasmalyte, do not change plasma osmolality and do not increase the brain water content. They also contain sodium at physiological plasma concentrations and distribute freely within the ECF compartment causing little change in sodium concentration and osmolality. As a result, this limits the movement of water out of the extracellular fluid (ECF) into the intracellular fluid (ICF) compartment and vice versa. Hypertonic solutions like mannitol and hypertonic saline are used in the treatment of patients with post-traumatic cerebral edema and raised ICP resulting from traumatic brain injury. They improve cardiac output and cerebral oxygenation whilst reducing cerebral edema.

text: 8. What is the preferred management of the condition given in the image below?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Surgical excision

The image shows a dermoid cyst and the preferred management of this condition is surgical excision. A dermoid cyst is a benign developmental anomaly that arises from the entrapment of ectodermal elements along the lines of embryonic closure. They are lined by stratified squamous epithelium with mature skin appendages found on their wall and their lumens filled with keratin and hair. They are considered to be congenital and usually present within the first year of life and grow slowly. They occur most commonly on the head and neck in the frontal, occipital, and supraorbital areas, with the outer third of the eyebrow being the most frequently affected region. They present as a flesh-coloured, dome-shaped, firm, deep-seated, subcutaneous nodule. They are usually asymptomatic, non-pulsatile, and non-compressible.  On ultrasound, they show a well-defined, homogenous and hypoechoic cystic lesion. They have the potential to grow over time and extend intracranially or intraspinally. MRI is the preferred means of revealing evidence of intracranial or intraspinal extension.  Since dermoid cysts typically enlarge over time, the preferred treatment is careful surgical removal of the entire cyst, ensuring that the cyst wall is not ruptured.
