text: 19. Whitaker test is indicated for which of the following conditions?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Hydronephrosis

Whitaker test is indicated for Hydronephrosis to compare the hydrostatic pressure between the renal pelvis and bladder. Hydronephrosis is the aseptic dilatation of the kidney caused by obstruction. WHITAKER TEST The Whitaker test accurately detects the functional effect of upper urinary tract dilatation by measuring hydrostatic pressures in the renal pelvis and bladder while infusing a saline and contrast solution into the renal pelvis through a catheter. The patient is positioned in the prone position on the fluoroscopic table with a bladder catheter in place, and a cannula is introduced percutaneously into the renal pelvis and attached to a pressure transducer. At a rate of 10 mL/min, a mixture of saline and contrast material is administered through the renal cannula, and pressures are monitored. The urinary tract is deemed nonobstructed if the renal pelvic pressure is less than 15 cm H2O, equivocal between 15 and 22 cm H2O, and obstructed if the pressure is greater than 22 cm H2O. With the introduction of noninvasive imaging technology, the test should be used exclusively in the following situations to examine probable upper urinary tract obstruction: * equivocal results from less invasive testing, * suspected blockage with poor kidney function, * loin discomfort with negative diuresis renogram findings, * suspected intermittent obstruction, * extensive dilatation with positive diuresis renogram findings are all possibilities. text: 20. A 40-year-old male presents with diffuse abdominal pain. He has a known history of Crohn's disease . Physical examination reveals rigidity and guarding. On imaging Ileal Perforation is diagnosed. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?

The next best step in the management of this patient is urgent surgical exploration with an ileostomy. Perforation of a viscus is a life-threatening condition that occurs following the rupture of the alimentary tract. Common causes include iatrogenic (surgery, scopes) blunt or penetrating injury, bowel obstruction, peptic ulcer disease, corrosive agents, or particular medications. This leads to the leakage of the enteric contents, thereby leading to acute bacterial peritonitis. Peritonitis is the generalized or localized inflammation of the peritoneum either due to the free spillage of fluids into the peritoneal cavity or secondary bacterial infection. Clinical features of hollow viscous perforation occur due to the developed peritonitis and the features include abdominal pain and distension, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, tenderness, rebound tenderness, decreased or absent bowel sounds, and guarding on palpation. Fever may be present. Sometimes, features of septic shock can be seen at later stages. Investigations include estimating the white blood cell count, urea, serum electrolytes, and an erect abdominal radiograph showing free gas under the diaphragm. A supine radiograph may show dilated gas-filled loops of the bowel, suggestive of paralytic ileus. The below image shows a hollow viscus perforation. Management - Initial management includes intravenous (IV) fluid therapy, cessation of oral intake, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Indications for immediate bowel exploration are * Sepsis/diffuse peritonitis(as in this patient) * Bowel ischemia * Complete or closed-loop bowel obstruction Resection or repair of the perforated site with or without drainage and diversion is usually undertaken. Duodenal perforations, on the other hand, are generally treated with omental patch repair without resection.

text: 25. What is the minimum external pressure that leads to the formation of pressure sores?
expl:
Correct answer: A. 30

The minimum external pressure that leads to the formation of pressure sores is 30 mm of Hg. Pressure sores also known as bedsores, pressure ulcers, or decubitus ulcers are defined as tissue necrosis with ulceration due to prolonged pressure. When the external pressure exceeds the capillary occlusive pressure, blood flow ceases leading to tissue anoxia, necrosis, and ulceration. Thus an external pressure of >30mmHg leads to the formation of pressure sores. The common sites of pressure sores in decreasing frequency are: * Ischium * Greater Trochanter * Sacrum * Heel * Malleolus (lateral followed by medial) * Occiput A staging system for the description of pressure sores is:  Stage 1 - Non-blanchable erythema without a breach in the epidermis Stage 2 - Partial-thickness skin loss involving the epidermis and dermis Stage 3 - Full-thickness skin loss extending into the subcutaneous tissue but not through underlying fascia Stage 4 - Full-thickness skin loss through fascia with extensive tissue destruction, maybe involving muscle, bone, tendon, or joint Prevention is the best treatment for pressure sores. It can be done through good skincare, the use of air-fluidised beds, special pressure dispersion cushions, or foams. The position of the bedridden patients should be changed once every 2 hours, and wheelchair-bound patients should be taught to get out of their chairs for 10 seconds every 10 minutes. Surgical treatment of pressure sores mainly involves wound management. The pressure sores should be adequately debrided and vacuum-assisted closure (VAC).VAC is done by applying intermittent negative pressure of approximately -125mmHg to hasten debridement and promote granulation tissue formation in chronic wounds and ulcers. Negative pressure decreases edema, removes interstitial fluid, and increases blood flow. This decreases bacterial growth and increases cell proliferation. Large skin flaps that have muscle with sensory innervation are best for reconstruction(example-extensor fascia lata flap with the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh). Faecal or urinary diversion can be considered in special cases depending on the site of the ulcer, being prone to urine or faecal contamination. text: 1. Which of the following is seen in all kinds of shock?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Reduced tissue perfusion

Shock is defined as a systemic state of low tissue perfusion that is inadequate for normal cellular respiration. The classification of shock and its features are as follows:
  Cardiac output Venous pressure Vascular resistance Mixed venous saturation Base deficit
Hypovolemic Low Low High Low High
Obstructive Low High High Low High
Cardiogenic Low High High Low High
Distributive High Low Low High High
Hypovolemic shock: It is due to reduced circulating volume. Causes include hemorrhage, dehydration, vomiting, and third spacing. Obstructive Shock: This leads to a reduction in preload due to mechanical obstruction of cardiac filling. Causes include cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, massive pulmonary embolus, or air embolus. Cardiogenic shock: Due to the failure of the heart to pump blood to tissues. Causes include myocardial infarction, cardiac dysrhythmias, valvular heart disease, blunt myocardial injury, and cardiomyopathy. Distributive shock: Distributive shock is the condition of reduced oxygen delivery where the primary physiologic disturbance is a reduction in systemic vascular resistance leading to vasodilation. It is unique among the types of shock in that there is a compensatory increase in cardiac output. Causes include spinal shock, anaphylaxis, and septic shock.

text: 2. A man came with complaints of recurrent discharge and pain due to lesions around the anus for 3 years. A diagnosis of fistula-in-ano is made. What is the gold standard investigation for this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: D. MRI

In cases of fistula-in-ano, MRI is the gold standard investigation. A fistula-in-ano is an abnormal connection between the anal canal and the perianal skin, lined with granulation tissue. It may follow the drainage of a perianal abscess or may be seen in association with diseases like tuberculosis or Crohn's disease. Clinical features are perianal pain, swelling, and intermittent purulent discharge, which might be blood-stained. On examination, one or more external openings may be visible. Goodsall’s rule can be used as a guide in determining the location of the internal opening of the fistula. Fistulas with an external opening anteriorly connect to the internal opening by a short, radial tract. Fistulas with an external opening posteriorly track in a curvilinear fashion to the posterior midline. However, exceptions to this rule often occur. Fistulas with an anterior external opening greater than 3 cm from the anal margin usually track to the posterior midline. The investigations done for fistula-in-ano can include a fistulogram, endoanal ultrasound with hydrogen peroxide, MRI, and computed tomography (CT) scan. An MRI is the gold standard investigation for fistula imaging. It helps us to identify the secondary extensions of the track, which when missed may cause persistence of the fistula.  Surgical management includes fistulotomy, fistulectomy, ligation of the intersphincteric fistula tract (LIFT), setons, or advancement flaps.

text: 5. A soldier presents to a referral hospital one day after sustaining a high-velocity shrapnel injury to his right thigh. He complains of severe pain at the wound site. On examination, crepitus is present. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of his condition?

Early systemic complications like circulatory collapse and organ failure can occur without adequate treatment. It is most commonly associated with prolonged antimicrobial use which interferes with the commensal colonic microflora. The most commonly implicated antibiotics are cephalosporins, ampicillin, and clindamycin.

text: 7. A 50-year-old male patient underwent an emergency laparotomy for grossly contaminated peritonitis due to a perforated hollow viscus. On postoperative day 7, the patient developed signs of wound infection, including erythema, tenderness, and serosanguinous discharge. Subsequently, the wound showed evidence of dehiscence with exposure of underlying tissues. The patient's vital signs are stable, with no evidence of ongoing intra-abdominal sepsis. Considering the current wound status, what should be the most appropriate management strategy for the laparotomy wound?

options.A: Vaccum assisted negative pressure wound therapy
options.B: Antibiotic irrigation of the wound followed by delayed primary closure
options.C: Initiating primary wound closure to reduce risk of further contamination

expl:
Correct answer: A. Vaccum assisted negative pressure wound therapy

The clinical scenario is suggestive of burst abdomen and the most appropriate management would be Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) therapy. Burst abdomen/Acute wound dehiscence is the mechanical wound failure causing separation of the closed abdominal wound associated with abdominal content evisceration. It usually occurs between the 5th and 8th postoperative days. A sudden giving way feeling from the wound precipitated by bouts of cough, and pinkish serosanguinous discharge can be seen. Omentum or coils of the intestine are forced out of the wound. Management includes delayed closure with initial mesh wrap or Bogota bag, placing a subcutaneous drain, suitable antibiotic therapy, and prevention of abdominal compartment syndrome as described above and VAC. Vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) is a method of wound management, which uses negative pressure for spontaneous healing or by lesser reconstructive options. Negative pressure therapy stabilizes the wound environment by reducing wound edema and bacterial load,as well as improves tissue perfusion by angiogenesis and thereby stimulating granulation tissue formation. All this improves the possibility of primary closure of wounds and reduces the need for plastic procedures.The ideal pressure applied is 125 mm Hg.  Indications of VAC therapy includes diabetic foot ulcers, bed sores,burn injuries,crush injuries, sternal/abdominal wound dehiscence, fasciotomy wounds and animal bites/frostbite wounds. VAC therapy is contraindicated in patients with malignant wounds such as Marjolin’s ulcer,untreated osteomyelitis, presence of fistulae or necrotic tissue underneath the dressing. Below is an image showing VAC. Other Options: Option B: Antibiotic irrigation followed by delayed primary closure is insufficient because it doesn't address the immediate need for ongoing drainage and decompression, and local antibiotics aren't effective for managing severe contamination. Option C: Primary closure of the abdomen immediately after laparotomy would be dangerous in this scenario as it risks abdominal compartment syndrome due to ongoing edema and doesn't allow for adequate drainage of contamination; forced closure could lead to tissue necrosis and organ dysfunction. Options D: Normal saline-soaked gauze dressing is inadequate because it doesn't provide active negative pressure, fails to effectively remove edema and inflammatory exudates, and requires frequent dressing changes that increase infection risk and nursing workload; additionally, it can lead to tissue maceration and doesn't promote wound edge approximation.

text: 13. All of the following are true about nephroblastoma except:

options.A: Treatment is chemotherapy followed by surgery
options.D: Most common intraabdominal malignancy in children

expl:
Correct answer: D. Most common intraabdominal malignancy in children

Neuroblastoma, not nephroblastoma, is the most common intra-abdominal malignancy in children. Wilms tumor/nephroblastoma is an embryonal renal neoplasm caused by faulty renal development that results in the metanephric blastema multiplying excessively. It is usually diagnosed before the age of five.  Children may present with a mass abdomen, fever, and hematuria, which is indicative of the extension of the tumor into the renal pelvis. Hypertension is also observed in a considerable percentage of patients. Prognostic factors for Wilms tumor: * Histology * Stage * Age * Tumor weight * Response to therapy * Loss of heterozygosity at 1p and 16q  The two most important factors are the histology and the stage of the tumor. Most of the tumors have favorable histology and are characterized as the “classic” type that consists of three components—blastemal, stromal, and epithelial (tubules) tissues.  Unfavorable tumors are those with focal or diffuse anaplasia. Two principal staging systems are used: * The COG system is based on findings prior to the initiation of treatment. There exists a local stage and a disease stage. The local stage defines the extent of abdominal disease while the disease stage considers both local disease and metastasis. Metastasis commonly occurs in the lungs. * The SIOP classification is based on the histologic appearance of the tumors at resection and the outcomes. They are classified as completely necrotic (low risk), blastemal (high risk) and other histological types. Imaging with USG abdomen and pelvis, CT scan, MRI, etc., shows a solid space-occupying lesion in the kidney. Management is mainly by chemotherapy and nephrectomy.

text: 14. A patient presents with urinary symptoms due to benign prostatic hyperplasia. Which of the following is used to manage the urinary symptoms in the initial stage of this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Tamsulosin

Tamsulosin is used for the management of urinary symptoms in the initial stages of Benign prostatic hyperplasia(BPH). It improves the urinary flow by inhibiting the smooth muscle contraction of the prostate thereby reducing the resistance at the bladder neck. BPH is characterized by symptoms of urinary frequency, urgency, nocturia, incontinence, slow urinary stream, straining to void, urinary intermittency (stream starting and stopping during micturition), or hesitancy, splitting of the voiding stream, and terminal dribbling. Physical examination reveals a smooth enlarged and non-tender prostate. Lab investigations reveal a normal PSA (prostate-specific antigen). Diagnosis is made based on clinical presentation and a lack of lab findings suggestive of malignancy (elevated PSA). A biopsy is rarely indicated. Conservative treatment is recommended for men with mild symptoms, flow rate >10ml/s, and good bladder emptying with residual urine <100ml.  Medical management includes alpha-adrenergic blocking agents that inhibit the contraction of smooth muscle that is found in the prostate. Tamsulosin is an adrenoreceptor antagonist with receptor selectivity at α1A. It is used in the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia. The other class of drugs is the 5α-reductase inhibitors, which inhibit the conversion of testosterone to DHT, the most active form of androgen. Finasteride is a 5α-reductase enzyme inhibitor. It is effective in the treatment of palpable enlarged prostate. These drugs result in a 25% shrinkage of the prostate gland. Indications for surgical management: * Lower urinary tract symptoms that are refractory to medical therapy * Refractory urinary retention * Recurrent urinary tract infection (UTI) * Hematuria * Stone formation * Hydronephrosis, hydroureter with renal functional impairment Surgical management involves the use of the transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP). Laser ablative techniques using holmium YAG can also be done. text: 15. A 17-year-old woman with no comorbidities presents with numbness and paraesthesia of the fingers along with the characteristic finding as shown in the image below. She has no history of smoking or history of other illnesses. She mentions the episodes occur when she is under excess stress or during cold temperatures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Raynaud's phenomenon

The image along with the history of no previous illness in a young female is most likely of Raynaud's phenomenon. Raynaud's phenomenon: * Episodic digital ischemia due to the vasospasm of digital arteries. * Cold exposure or emotional stress can trigger it. * The blanching/ischemic phase of the phenomenon with pallor/cyanosis is often accompanied by numbness and paraesthesia. * Capillaries and venules dilate and cyanosis results from the deoxygenated blood that is present in these vessels. * Color changes are usually well-demarcated and are confined to the fingers or toes. * In the rewarming phase, digital vasospasm resolves and blood flows into the dilated arterioles and capillaries increase dramatically causing reactive hyperemia which imparts bright red color to the digits. * Some may experience only pallor cyanosis while others experience both pallor and cyanosis. Types of Raynaud's:      1.Primary/idiopathic       2. Secondary associated with other diseases like:  * Collagen vascular diseases: scleroderma, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, dermatomyositis, polymyositis * Arterial occlusive diseases: atherosclerosis of the extremities, thromboangiitis obliterans, acute arterial occlusion * Neurologic disorders: intervertebral disk disease, syringomyelia * Blood dyscrasias: cold agglutinins, cryoglobulinemia, cryofibrinogenemia, * Trauma: vibration injury, electric shock, cold injury, typing, piano playing * Drugs and toxins: ergot derivatives, methysergide, β-adrenergic receptor blockers Management: * Reassurance, warm clothing, and avoiding cold exposures. exposure. * Reduce or abstain from smoking and reduce stress levels. * Drug treatments such as CCB's(nifedipine, amlodipine), alpha 1 blockers ( prazosin) are used only for advanced cases. * In secondary Raynauds's Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors like sildenafil, tadalafil may improve symptoms. Other options: Buerger's disease or thromboangiitis obliterans involves occlusive disease of small- and medium-sized arteries, thrombophlebitis of the superficial or deep veins, and Raynaud’s syndrome. It occurs in male smokers, usually under the age of 30 years. It is an arterial occlusive disorder, so compression stockings will have no therapeutic effect. Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) presents as intermittent claudication, which is pain that increases with walking and may sometimes present with rest pain. It is generally caused by atherosclerosis but may also be due to trauma. The initial investigation done is an ABPI. Physical exam findings include atrophied skin, pallor on raising leg (Buerger's test), nail changes, and decreased peripheral pulses.

text: 17. Which is the least commonly used graft for coronary artery bypass graft (CABG)?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Intercostal artery

The intercostal artery is the least likely to be used as a graft in CABG. The left internal mammary artery (LIMA) provides long-lasting results in a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG). The conduit with the highest patency rate is the left internal mammary artery or internal thoracic artery. Long patency rates of >98 percent have been reported. Venous grafts: * The long saphenous vein is the most common vein used as a conduit as it is straightforward to harvest, provides good length, and is easy to handle. * The ten-year patency rate for long saphenous vein grafts is reported to be 50–60 percent. Arterial grafts: * The Left internal mammary artery (LIMA) or internal thoracic artery has become the conduit of choice for the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery. The radial artery can be used as a second or alternative arterial bypass graft. Other arterial bypass grafts include the gastroepiploic artery and the inferior epigastric artery. text: 21. A patient was brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. Skin grafting was done wherein the graft was taken from the same person. Which type of graft is it?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Autograft

The given image shows a split skin graft obtained from the same person. This type of graft is autograft. Skin grafting is the transfer of skin from the donor area to the recipient area. The most preferable donor site is the buttocks in cosmetically sensitive individuals and children. The most commonly used donor site is the thigh.  Autograft is the transfer of tissue from one location to another location on the same patient. Skin grafts can be broadly divided into two categories: Split-thickness skin graft (Thiersch graft): Partial-thickness skin grafts consisting of the epidermis and a portion of the dermis are called split-thickness skin grafts. Less dermis in the split-thickness skin graft translates into less primary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks in surface area after harvesting and before grafting) and more secondary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks during healing). Full-thickness skin grafts (Wolfe graft) include the epidermis and entire dermis, with portions of the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles. More dermis in the full-thickness skin graft translates into more primary contraction and less secondary contraction. Other options: Option B:Xenograft is tissue transfer from a donor of one species to a recipient of another species. It is also known as heterograft. Option C: Allograft is the tissue transfer between two genetically different members, e.g. kidney transplantation (human to human). It is also known as homograft. Option D: Isograft is the tissue transfer between two genetically identical individuals, i.e. between two identical twins. Pearl PF1917: Skin graft : phases of uptake of the graft The take of skin graft occurs in three phases: * Imbibition (Plasmatic circulation): during the first 48 hours, the graft is nourished with plasma exudate from host bed capillaries. * Inosculation, in which cut vessels from the host bed line up with the cut ends of the vessels of the graft to form anastomoses * Neovascularization, in which blood vessels grow from the recipient bed into the graft Sensibility returns to the graft over time, with reinnervation beginning at approximately 4 to 5 weeks and being completed by 12 to 24 months. Pain returns first, with light touch and temperature returning later. Note: some books give that the 3 phases are imbibition,revascularisation (inosculation+neovascularisation) and organisation (fibrin layer holds the graft in place and this is replaced by postgraft day 7 with fibroblasts)

text: 22. A male patient presented with a sudden onset tearing type of chest pain radiating to the back, shortness of breath, and nausea. CT chest image is given.What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Labetolol and urgent surgery

The above clinical scenario of a male patient with tearing chest pain is suggestive of aortic dissection. Beta-blockers such as Labetalol should be given to all patients with aortic dissection and surgical repair is done after stabilizing the patient. So, option A is the correct answer. Aortic dissection occurs when a tear or flap occurs in the intima or inner media of the aorta resulting in progressive separation of the layers of the aorta. Risk factors for aortic dissection are: * Smoking * Hypertension * Atherosclerosis  * Hypercholesterolemia * Aortopathy, aortitis, bicuspid aortic valve, or preexisting medial degenerative disease. * Aortic injury during cardiac catheterization, surgery, endovascular aortic repair (Iatrogenic)  * Cocaine or amphetamine abuse  The most typical presentation of aortic dissection is tearing chest pain. Other clinical features include dyspnea, nausea, vomiting, murmurs due to aortic valvular insufficiency, and shock. A discrepancy between the extremities in pulse, blood pressure, or both is the classic physical finding in patients with aortic dissection. The dissection can extend distally down the aorta to involve the: * Renal arteries (renal pain and renal failure) * Mesenteric arteries (abdominal pain and bowel ischemia) * Spinal arteries (paraplegia, incontinence) * Iliofemoral arteries (leg pain, pallor, loss or reduced pulses, and limb ischemia). The dissection may track proximally to involve the: * Head and neck vessels (syncope and focal neurological deficits) * Coronary vessels (cardiac ischemia, cardiac tamponade) * Aortic root (aortic regurgitation) Investigations in aortic dissection: * Transesophageal echocardiography can be done at the bedside in patients who are hemodynamically unstable; it can give information about flow in the true and false lumen and shows very high sensitivity for confirmation of the aortic dissection. * Currently, a CT scan is the initial best investigation for the diagnosis of aortic dissection in the hemodynamically stable patent. Additionally, it tells about the segments involved and the acuity, and complications of the dissection. The classic feature seen in the CT scan is a double-lumen aorta. Treatment: The initial management of patients diagnosed with aortic dissection is beta-blocker medication to control hypertension, along with pain management. The preferred beta-blocker drug is esmolol, a cardio-selective beta blocker. These reduce cardiac contractility and blood pressure. It can be used in patients with bronchospastic disorders. Labetalol, a non-selective beta blocker decreases systemic vascular resistance without impairing the cardiac output. Enalapril and other angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors can be used if there is decreased renal perfusion.  Calcium channel blockers like diltiazem may be used IV if beta-blockers cannot be employed. Once hypertension is controlled, definitive surgical repair of aortic dissection is done. Nitroprusside, a direct vasodilator is given after adequate beta-blockade is achieved. Definitive management is by surgical repair. Types:  * Stanford type A (DeBakey types I and II) requires surgical intervention once the patient's blood pressure is stabilized. * Stanford type B (DeBakey type III) is best managed by antihypertensive drugs. Surgical intervention is indicated in complicated cases if the pain increases (signaling impending rupture) or when there is evidence of malperfusion of organs or neurological symptoms.

text: 24. A 30-year-old female patient involved in a road traffic accident had nausea and vomiting. She was brought unconscious to the emergency room. NCCT brain reveals the following findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Correct answer: A. Extradural hemorrhage

The given history and CT image showing a typical biconvex hyperdense lesion are characteristic of an extradural hemorrhage (EDH), and it is most commonly due to bleeding from the middle meningeal artery. EDH refers to the accumulation of blood in the potential space between the inner table of the skull and the dura mater. The hematoma arises from arterial disruption, especially of the middle meningeal artery. The middle meningeal vein and diploic veins may also be implicated. Patients present with head injury with lucid interval, ipsilateral mydriasis, and ipsilateral hemiparesis. There is a transient loss of consciousness after injury; 6-12 hours later the condition of the patient deteriorates. The time period between which the patient appears normal is known as the lucid interval. The patient presents with features of raised intracranial pressure such as high blood pressure, vomiting, bradycardia, and convulsions. Double-layered hypertrophic mucosa protrudes into the stomach, creating the so-called Nipple sign. The sonographic appearance of the hypertrophied pylorus resembles that of the uterine cervix and is sometimes referred to as the cervix sign. text: 32. A 73 old male smoker with a past history of coronary artery disease presents with blackening of the toes. An image of the foot is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Atherosclerosis

The given clinical scenario of an elderly smoker with past history of coronary artery disease and gangrene of the first three toes is likely to have atherosclerosis.  Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease in which there is a build-up of plaques inside arteries.  It is common after 50 years.These plaques are principally composed of lipids that induce an inflammatory reaction causing turbulent flow leading to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease(ASCVD). This results in atheroma formation in arteries throughout the body hampering the blood flow and leading to ischemia.  Risk factors include smoking, hypertension, diabetes, and elevated cholesterol. The infrarenal part of the abdominal aorta, coronary arteries, iliofemoral vessels, carotid bifurcation, and popliteal arteries are the common arteries involved. The presence of atherosclerotic disease in one part of the body suggests there could be blockade in other parts as well.  Patients with chronic limb ischemia present with rest pain and tissue loss such as gangrene and ulceration. An ischemic ulcer is painful, pale, and cyanotic in appearance with absent pulsations. It may be associated with transient ischemic attacks, chest pain, eye problems, mesenteric ischemia, and altered renal function. Doppler or angiogram can be done to identify the block. It is important to evaluate these patients for intercurrent cardiac disorders. Management involves cessation of smoking and modification of other risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, and hypercholesterolemia. High-intensity statins should be given irrespective of cholesterol levels in ASCVD. Other drugs that can be used include pentoxifylline, aspirin, clopidogrel, and cilostazol. Surgical options include thrombectomy, endarterectomy, bypass grafting, and amputations if the limb is gangrenous.  Complications of atherosclerosis include * Narrowing of the arteries: Coronary, cerebral, renal, mesenteric, iliofemoral. > 70% narrowing (severe) causes reduced blood flow. * lschaemia, ulcerations, gangrene  * Embolism: From atheromatous plaques * Aneurysm formation: Mainly abdominal aorta and also in peripheral arteries Option A: Buerger’s disease is a progressive nonatherosclerotic segmental inflammatory disease that most often affects small- and medium-sized arteries, veins, and nerves of the upper and lower extremities. * Typically presents in young male smokers, with symptoms beginning prior to age 40. * Patients initially present with the foot, leg, arm, or hand. * Claudication may progress to rest pain to calf claudication and eventually ischemic rest pain and ulcerations on the toes, feet, or fingers and even gangrene. If the patient continues to smoke, the disease progresses into the collaterals, blocking them eventually, leading to severe ischemia which is called decompensatory peripheral vascular disease/ critical limb ischemia which presents as rest pain, ulceration, and gangrene. Option C: Raynaud's disease usually occurs in females and affects bilateral upper limbs. Patients present with pallor/blanching (syncope), dusky cyanosis (asphyxia), and rubor/painful red de-engorgement (recovery). Peripheral pulses are normal. Option D: Giant cell arteritis is characterized by giant cell infiltration of the arterial wall (giant cell arteritis) involving superficial temporal, facial, retinal, upper limb, coronary and vertebral arteries. Patients present with severe headaches, visual abnormalities, jaw claudication, and a tender superficial temporal artery. Pearl PF1741: Ankle–brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) The ankle-brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) is the ratio of systolic pressure at the ankle to that in the arm. The numerator is the highest pressure in the dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, or peroneal artery and the denominator is the highest brachial systolic pressure.
ABPI Reading Interpretation
>0.91 < 1.3 Normal
<0.9 Diagnostic of occlusive arterial disease in patients with symptoms of claudication or other signs of ischemia

text: 33. A 50-year-old woman after thyroidectomy comes to you for 2nd opinion for further treatment of papillary thyroid cancer. What would you recommend for this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Radioiodine scan

A radioiodine scan will be recommended to this patient following the thyroidectomy, to look for residual or metastatic disease. Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy. It is more commonly seen in women between the ages of 30 and 50. Radiation exposure and a family history of thyroid malignancies are the common etiologies. Genetic abnormalities in either the RET gene or the BRAF gene can be seen in papillary thyroid carcinoma. Clinical features include an asymptomatic thyroid swelling with cervical lymph node enlargement. In advanced disease, there may be features like hoarseness, dysphagia, cough, or dyspnea.  An ultrasound scan accurately assesses the size and number of nodules, as well as categorizes the lesions as benign, indeterminate, or malignant. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is a diagnostic test, helpful in investigating an indeterminate or malignant lesion. Histopathology shows the following features: * Branching papillae * Orphan Annie eye nuclei: optically clear nuclei with fine nuclear chromatin * Pseudo inclusions: invaginations of the nuclear membrane * Psammoma bodies: concentric calcifications in the core of the papillae. Below is the histopathological image of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid with characteristic Orphan Annie eye nuclei. Papillary thyroid carcinoma is known to spread via lymphatics, hence lymph node metastasis is commonly seen. Treatment of Papillary thyroid carcinoma is as follows: Total thyroidectomy is the treatment of choice. Routine central neck dissection is not recommended. Neck dissection is indicated in higher-risk situations, such as * Tumor size > 4 cm (T3 stage) or gross extrathyroidal extension (T4 stage) or enlarged central lymph nodes - Total thyroidectomy + Central Neck Dissection * Lateral Aberrant Thyroid - Total thyroidectomy + Modified Radical Neck Dissection + Central Neck Dissection For occult papillary cancer (<1 cm tumor size, with no lymphatic, vascular or capsular invasion) - Lobectomy can be sufficient. Radio-iodine ablation is undertaken when a whole-body iodine scan is positive after a total thyroidectomy for any differentiated thyroid cancer (papillary or follicular carcinoma).  The presence of any metastatic or residual thyroid tissue after total thyroidectomy can be detected by observing the uptake of radio-iodine in the entire body. To achieve effective uptake of radio-iodine, TSH levels need to be greatly increased, for example, by withdrawing thyroxine after the surgery for 4-6 weeks. A positive whole-body iodine scan after total thyroidectomy indicates that there is either a metastatic or residual disease present. These patients are treated with I131 for radio-iodine ablation.  A negative scan means there is no metastasis or residual thyroid tissue. They are followed up regularly with serum thyroglobulin, TSH and USG-neck.

text: 34. A patient who was diagnosed with prostate cancer is being investigated. The bone scan is reported as a super scan with increased uptake in the bones and reduced activity in the spleen. What is the reason for this super scan appearance?

options.A: Increased uptake due to diffuse metastasis
options.D: Decreased uptake by adrenal glands and kidney

The super scan appearance is due to increased uptake due to diffuse metastasis.  Diffuse osteoblastic metastatic diseases such as carcinoma breast and prostate carcinoma lead to a generalized increase in the skeletal uptake relative to soft tissue and absent or faint renal activity on a bone scan. This is known as a super scan. It may also be seen in generalized bone diseases such as hyperparathyroidism. Carcinoma of the prostate is the most common malignant tumor in men over the age of 65 years. Most cancers are clinically silent and are detected on routine rectal examination or PSA measurements. Grossly, malignant tissue is gritty and firm in consistency (in contrast to the spongy appearance of benign tissue) and thus more readily palpable on digital rectal examination. They usually arise in the peripheral zone of the gland. Local extension most commonly involves the periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicles, and the base of the urinary bladder. Metastasis spreads via the lymphatics to the obturator nodes and the para-aortic nodes. Hematogenous spread occurs chiefly through the bones to the axial skeleton and rarely to the viscera. The bony metastasis is blastic in origin and involves the lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and ribs in decreasing order of frequency.  Prognosis and staging: The Gleason grading system correlates with the pathological stage, spread, and prognosis. The CT image showing renal lesions that has hypo-attenuating components consistent with macroscopic fat is highly suggestive of renal angiomyolipoma. MRI: It is an excellent tool to demonstrate intramural fat components. Two sequences are used: * Fat-saturated techniques  * Phase-in and phase-out imaging that shows India ink artifacts at the junction between fat and non-fat components. It usually occurs in the age group 50-70 years and macroscopic hematuria is seen in about 60% of the cases. It is a differential for angiomyolipoma but it is important to note that macroscopic fat is almost always associated with ossification or calcification. Renal oncocytoma: They are relatively benign in nature and usually present in the 6th to 7th decade. An important point regarding this tumor is its similarity with RCC and hence it is very difficult to differentiate between them preoperatively. A sharp central stellate scar may be seen in one-third of the cases. But RCC may also show this stellate scar appearance in some cases. text: 38. A 51-year-old lady presents with complaints of a mass in the right breast. On examination, the mass was larger than 2cm and ipsilateral mobile axillary lymph nodes were present. What is the staging, considering the mass is malignant?
expl:
Correct answer: A. cT4N1M0

The clinical scenario of a 51-year-old lady with a breast mass >2cm, lymph node involvement (N1), and the image showing an ulcerative mass near the nipple of the right breast (T4), is clinically suggestive of inflammatory breast carcinoma. Its likely staging is cT4N1M0 Inflammatory breast carcinoma (stage T4) is an aggressive form of locally advanced breast cancer (LABC) and is associated with the worst prognosis among all subtypes of breast cancer. It accounts for <3% of breast cancers. It is characterized by skin changes of brawny induration, erythema, and edema (peau d’orange). The term peau d’orange describes the orange-peel appearance of the skin resulting from edema and dimpling at sites of hair follicles. In order to determine the best course of treatment for a patient with IBC, it is important to stage cancer. Staging is the process of determining the extent to which cancer has spread within the breast and to other parts of the body. Some prefixes and suffixes are used with the cTNM (clinical) and pTNM (pathologic) staging systems to designate special cases. These do not affect the stage group but indicate that they must be analyzed separately. The “y” prefix, denotes patients who have received systemic therapy before surgery. In this patient, since the staging is being done clinically, "c" is added as a prefix.  The diagnostic criteria for inflammatory breast cancer are -  * Rapid onset of breast erythema, edema and/or peau d’orange, and/or warm breast (with or without an underlying palpable mass) * Duration of history no more than six months * Erythema occupies at least one-third of the breast * Pathologic confirmation of invasive carcinoma The pathologic hallmark is the presence of tumor cells within dermal lymphatics in skin biopsy specimens, but it is not a prerequisite for diagnosis. Mammography may be normal or show skin thickening. A PET-CT scan should be considered at the time of diagnosis to rule out concurrent metastatic disease. Axillary nodal metastases are common, and there is a significant risk for distant metastases. Combined-modality treatment is used, which includes * Neoadjuvant chemo­therapy * Modified radical mastectomy * Radiation therapy * Hormonal therapy (for ER-positive tumors) * Trastuzumab (for HER-2-positive tumors) Pearl PF0193: TNM Staging of carcinoma breast

text: 1. A 35-year-old man sustained a spinal cord injury as a result of a road traffic accident. On examination, his blood pressure is found to be 90/60 mmHg. The patient most likely suffered from which of the following conditions?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Neurogenic shock

The clinical scenario of the presence of hypotension associated with the spinal cord injury is suggestive of neurogenic shock. Neurogenic shock refers to reduced tissue perfusion due to loss of vasomotor tone to peripheral arterial beds. Neurogenic shock is usually secondary to spinal cord injuries due to vertebral body fractures of the cervical or high thoracic region that disrupts the sympathetic regulation of peripheral vascular tone. Loss of vasoconstrictor impulses results in increased vascular capacitance, decreased venous return and decreased cardiac output. Primary injury in neurogenic shock occurs due to damage to axons and the membrane of neurons. Secondary injury occurs doe to vascular damage hours to days after the primary insult. The clinical features are bradycardia, temperature dysregulation, hypotension and autonomic dysreflexia. The skin often appears warm and flushed and there is also presence of radiological evidence of vertebral fracture. Treatment involves securing of airways, adequate ventilation and perfusion with fluids and blood products followed by administration of vasoconstrictors to improve vascular tone.  Other options: Option A: Cardiogenic shock is caused due to the failure of the myocardial pump. Option B: Septic shock is not likely in this clinical scenario, as there is no evidence of any infection. Option D: Hypovolemic shock is caused due to a significant decrease in blood or plasma volume, caused by the loss of fluid from the vascular compartment. Haemorrhage, fluid loss from severe burns, diarrhea, excessive urine formation, perspiration, and trauma are some of the major mechanisms of fluid loss that can lead to hypovolemic shock.

text: 9. What is the correct order of the normal phases of wound healing?

options.A: Proliferative phase &gt; Hemostatic phase &gt; Inflammatory phase &gt; Remodeling phase
options.B: Hemostatic phase &gt; Inflammatory phase &gt; Proliferative phase &gt; Remodeling phase
options.C: Inflammatory phase &gt; Hemostatic phase &gt; Proliferative phase &gt; Remodeling phase
options.D: Remodeling phase &gt; Proliferative phase &gt; Destructive phase &gt; Inflammatory phase

expl:
Correct answer: B. Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase

The correct order of the normal phases of wound healing is as follows: Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase. Inflammatory phase: begins immediately after wounding and lasts 2-3 days. Bleeding is followed by vasoconstriction and thrombus formation to limit blood loss. Occasionally, the early part of inflammatory phase is called hemostatic phase. Proliferative phase lasts from 3rd day to 3rd week consisting mainly of fibroblast activity with production of collagen and ground substance, growth of new blood vessels and re-epithelialization of the wound surface. Remodeling phase is characterized by maturation of collagen- type 1 replacing type 3 until a ratio of 4:1 is achieved. The mature collagen leads to increased tensile strength and represents approximately 80% of the uninjured skin strength.

It is a type of ventral hernia. Incisional hernias are usually asymptomatic, but can occasionally present with pain. Strangulation and bowel obstruction is rare due to the large neck of the defect. text: 26. A newborn presents with jaundice. Biliary atresia is suspected when jaundice is persistent and exceeds:

Correct answer: B. 2 weeks

Newborns with persistent jaundice for more than 2 weeks suggests a diagnosis of biliary atresia.  Biliary atresia may also be termed as noncystic obliterative cholangiopathy. It is a disease of the intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts of unknown etiology.  Clinical features include persistent jaundice, clay-colored stools, and hepatomegaly. Untreated newborns will show signs of liver cirrhosis and failure (ascites, portal hypertension, and failure to thrive).  Laboratory evaluation will show elevated levels of direct and indirect bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase. Ultrasound will show a hypoplastic or absent gall bladder and triangular cord sign.  Hepatobiliary scintigraphy can also be performed.  Classification of biliary atresia and its treatment are:
Management of extrahepatic biliary atresia
Type I

Atresia restricted to the common bile duct

Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy
Type II

Atresia of the common hepatic duct

 Kasai procedure (Roux-en-Y hepatoportoenterostomy)
Type III

Atresia of the right and left hepatic duct
In the Kasai procedure, the extrahepatic biliary tree is dissected proximally till the liver capsule, the porta hepatis is transected and a jejunal loop is anastomosed in order to provide a drainage pathway for bile.  Infants with biliary atresia, who do not achieve successful drainage after Kasai's procedure, require liver transplantation within the first year of life. This is the most common reason for liver transplantation in children.

text: 4. A patient with grade 4 haemorrhoids underwent surgery. Identify the instruments used during the procedure from the image below.
expl:
Correct answer: A. Haemorrhoids banding kit

The instruments depicted above are the components of a hemorrhoid banding kit. Hemorrhoids are cushions of submucosal tissue containing venules, arterioles, and smooth muscle fibers that are located in the anal canal. They can be classified according to their location into 2 types: * Internal hemorrhoids  * External hemorrhoids External hemorrhoids are distal to the dentate line and are covered with anoderm; these may engorge causing pain. Thrombosis of these external hemorrhoids causes severe pain. Internal hemorrhoids are characterized by bright red, painless bleeding, or prolapse. Internal hemorrhoids are stratified into four grades as follows:

GRADE

SYMPTOMS AND SIGNS

First degree

Bleeding; no prolapse

Second degree

Prolapse with spontaneous reduction

Third degree

Prolapse requiring manual reduction

Fourth degree

Prolapsed, cannot be reduced
Management of external hemorrhoids:  External hemorrhoids do not require treatment unless they become thrombosed. Acutely thrombosed external hemorrhoids cause intense pain and perianal mass during the first 24 to 72 hours. Patients who present within 72 hours of thrombosis are treated with elliptical excision performed under local anesthesia. If the patient presents to the hospital after 72 hours, then it is treated conservatively with analgesics and a sitz bath. Once the symptoms come down, definitive surgery is performed.  Management of internal hemorrhoids: Bleeding from grade 1 and grade 2 hemorrhoids often improves with the addition of dietary fiber, stool softeners, increased fluid intake, and avoidance of straining. Grade 1, grade 2, and some grade 3 hemorrhoids with only an internal component can be treated with simple procedures like rubber band ligation, sclerotherapy, infrared and laser coagulation, and cryotherapy. Rubber band ligation involves pulling mucosa located 1 to 2 cm proximal to the dentate line into a rubber band applier. The rubber band strangulates the underlying tissue, causing scarring and sloughing off of the mass in a few days. Sclerotherapy involves injecting 1 to 3 mL of a sclerosing solution (phenol in olive oil, sodium morrhuate, or quinine urea) into the submucosa of internal hemorrhoids. Surgery is indicated in:  * Internal grade 3 or grade 4 hemorrhoids * Hemorrhoids with a significant external component * Early-grade hemorrhoids not responding to simple procedures Surgical procedures used in the removal of internal hemorrhoids are: 1) Doppler-guided hemorrhoidal artery ligation 2) Open hemorrhoidectomy- the artery forceps are applied to the skin-covered external components of the hemorrhoid and traction is given to reveal the internal components. Dissection of the lateral pedicle is performed and finally, the pedicles are transfixed. Mucocutaneous bridges are left intact in this technique. The image below shows the procedure. 3) Closed (Ferguson) hemorrhoidectomy- the hemorrhoid is excised with the overlying mucosa. The hemorrhoid is dissected from the underlying sphincter and the mucus defect is then closed. The image below describes the procedure. 4) Stapled hemorrhoidopexy (Longo operation)- the hemorrhoids are pulled up and a purse-string suture is placed a few centimeters above the dentate line. Then, a circumferential rectal mucosectomy is performed using a circular stapler. This technique is associated with higher chances of recurrence, however, it is quick to perform, less painful, and less traumatic. The image below shows stapled hemorrhoidopexy.

text: 9. During a laproscopic surgery while inserting a lateral trocar for surgery which of the following is most prone to injury ?

options.C: Both superior and inferior epigastric artery

expl:
Correct answer: C. Both superior and inferior epigastric artery

The most common source of bleeding during laparoscopic surgery is through both superior and inferior epigastric arteries.  These vessels run vertically in the posterior rectus sheath along the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle, creating a high-risk zone for trocar placement. The superior epigastric artery descends from the internal thoracic (mammary) artery, while the inferior epigastric artery ascends from the external iliac artery, and they anastomose within the rectus muscle. Their consistent anatomical location and the fact that they run in a relatively superficial plane within the anterior abdominal wall makes them particularly vulnerable during trocar insertion. To avoid injury, surgeons must carefully identify the lateral border of the rectus muscle and place trocars either medial or significantly lateral to this zone, and transillumination of the abdominal wall can help identify these vessels. Injury to these arteries can result in significant bleeding, making it the most common source of haemorrhage in this type of surgery. Proper identification and careful dissection are essential to avoid this complication.

It usually occurs between the 5th and 8th postoperative days. A sudden giving way feeling from the wound precipitated by bouts of cough, and pinkish serosanguinous discharge can be seen. Omentum or coils of the intestine are forced out of the wound. text: 16. A patient is diagnosed with prostate cancer. What is the mode of spread of prostate cancer to the lumbar vertebra?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Venous

In prostate cancer, metastasis to the lumbar vertebra is through the Batson's venous plexus. Batson venous plexus is a valveless vertebral venous plexus communicating with the prostatic venous plexus. Carcinoma of the prostate metastasizes to the bone usually by the bloodstream through this Batson plexus. The bones most frequently involved are the pelvic bones and the lower lumbar vertebrae. The femoral head, ribcage and skull are other common sites. Other routes of spread of prostate carcinoma are local spread to the seminal vesicles, bladder neck, trigone, and lymphatic spread. Carcinoma of the prostate is the most common malignancy in men above 65 years. The clinical features of prostate cancer are bladder outlet obstruction, pelvic pain, hematuria, arthritis, anaemia, and renal failure. Per rectal examination reveals a hard, nodular, irregularly indurated gland.  Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is useful in assessing the follow-up. PSA >10 ng/mL is suggestive of cancer and levels >35 ng/mL are diagnostic of advanced prostate cancer. The prostatic biopsy is indicated when there is a raised PSA level or suspicion of prostate cancer. Localized cancer is treated by radical prostatectomy and radiation therapy, while in advanced cancer palliative and hormone ablation should be carried out.    Options B, C and D: Arterial spread is exemplified by lung cancer's common metastasis to the brain, breast cancer's spread to brain and liver, and choriocarcinoma's predilection for lung metastases. Lymphatic spread is demonstrated by breast cancer's typical progression to axillary nodes, head and neck cancers spreading to cervical nodes, and melanoma's spread to regional lymph node basins. Direct spread occurs when cancers invade adjacent structures, such as pancreatic cancer extending into the duodenum and stomach, lung cancer invading the chest wall, or colorectal cancer penetrating through the bowel wall into nearby tissues. text: 19. A 25-year-old man is brought to ER after a car accident. He had multiple injuries and a femoral shaft fracture. He was treated and stabilized. But 48 hours later, he suddenly develops breathing difficulty, increased heart rate and petechial rashes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Pathogenesis- release of free fatty acids by the action of lipases on the neutral fats and actual obstruction of small pulmonary vessels by fat globules. Clinical features: * Early signs are fever and tachycardia * Presenting features are of 2 types- Cerebral type: drowsiness, restlessness, disorientation or Pulmonary type: tachypnoea, tachycardia * Other features: petechial rash in front of neck/anterior axillary fold/ chest/ conjunctiva The classical clinical triad consists of respiratory distress, neurological abnormalities, and petechial haemorrhages Treatment of fat embolism is mainly supportive: * Respiratory support (oxygen) * Heparinization (increases lipoprotein lipase activity) * Intravenous low molecular weight dextran * Corticosteroids: To avoid pneumonitis * Prompt stabilization of long-bone fractures  Other Options: Option A: Beck's triad (hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds) is seen in cardiac tamponade.  Option B: Pneumothorax can cause sudden, sharp chest pain and difficulty breathing, but it often presents with hyper-resonant percussion (tapping on the chest) and decreased breath sounds on the affected side. This leads to the leakage of the enteric contents, thereby leading to acute bacterial peritonitis. Peritonitis is the generalized or localized inflammation of the peritoneum either due to the free spillage of fluids into the peritoneal cavity or secondary bacterial infection. Fever may be present. Sometimes, features of septic shock can be seen at later stages. Investigations include estimating the white blood cell count, urea, serum electrolytes, and an erect abdominal radiograph showing free gas under the diaphragm. A supine radiograph may show dilated gas-filled loops of the bowel, suggestive of paralytic ileus. The below image shows a hollow viscus perforation. Management of a hollow viscous perforation is mainly resuscitation, analgesics, intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, and emergency laparotomy. Peritonitis is managed by nutritional support, pain relief, correction of fluid loss and circulating volume, urinary catheterization with or without gastrointestinal compression, antibiotics, analgesics, and specific surgical treatment of the cause. Other Options:  Option A: Clinical presentation of acute pancreatitis is characterized by epigastric pain radiating to the back which is relieved by bending forward, nausea, and vomiting.  Option C: Duodenal ulcer pain occurs 1.5 to 3 hours after a meal and is frequently relieved by antacids or food. Gastric Ulcer pain/discomfort may be precipitated by food. text: 25. A 30-year-old male presents with persistent swelling and discomfort over the dorsal aspect of the index finger. He gave a history of penetrative trauma to the area a few days ago. On examination, there is a firm, tender mass with limited mobility of the distal interphalangeal joint. The image is shown below. If left untreated, what is the most likely complication?

options.A: Gangrene of the fingertip due to compromised vascular supply
options.B: Secondary infection requiring removal of the nail bed
options.C: Frog-like deformity of the finger caused by chronic inflammation and tendon dysfunction
options.D: Injury to blood vessels during wound cleaning leading to ischemia

expl:
Correct answer: C. Frog-like deformity of the finger caused by chronic inflammation and tendon dysfunction

In the given clinical scenario of penetrating trauma followed by swelling over the dorsal aspect of the index finger that could progress to a "frog-like" deformity, making this the correct answer. A "frog-like" finger refers to a Boutonnière deformity - a condition where the middle joint of a finger is bent inward while the tip joint is bent excessively outward, creating a distinctive appearance similar to a frog's leg bent at the knee; essentially, the finger looks like it's making a "buttonhole" shape.  The progressive tendon dysfunction leading to the frog-like deformity represents the natural history of untreated cases due to the anatomical relationship between the central slip of the extensor tendon and the dorsal aspect of the middle phalanx where the infection is located. This deformity occurs when chronic inflammation and infection of the extensor tendon mechanism leads to destruction of the central slip at the dorsal aspect of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint. This results in the characteristic deformity where the PIP joint becomes flexed while the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint becomes hyperextended. text: 30. An abdominal X-ray of a baby presenting with abdominal distension and hematochezia reveals air in the bowel wall. What is the greatest risk factor for the development of this condition?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Prematurity

The above clinical scenario of a baby presenting with abdominal distension and hematochezia, with X-ray findings of pneumatosis intestinalis (air in the bowel wall) is suggestive of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). Prematurity is the greatest risk factor for developing NEC. NEC is the most common life-threatening gastrointestinal disorder in newborns. It is characterized by mucosal or transmural inflammation resulting in necrosis of the intestinal tract. It most commonly affects the distal ileum and proximal colon. Three major risk factors implicated are prematurity (the greatest risk factor), formula feeding, and bacterial colonization of the intestine. Babies usually present within the 2nd or 3rd week of life with abdominal distension and tenderness, feed intolerance, and occult/gross blood in the stool. Systemic features include hypotension, bradycardia, lethargy, and temperature instability. Diagnosis can be made with a plain abdominal X-ray. The important signs are pneumatosis intestinalis (air in the bowel wall), portal vein gas, and pneumoperitoneum (indicates perforation). The given X-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis (black arrows). Management of NEC includes supportive measures like keeping the baby nil per oral (NPO), nasogastric decompression, intravenous fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and inotropic support if indicated. Perforation is an absolute indication for surgery. The most effective preventive strategy is the use of human milk.

text: 31. For infants and children under the age of 2, which of the following samples are the best to diagnose UTI?

Correct answer: B. Suprapubic aspiration and urethral catheterization

For infants and children under age 2, suprapubic aspiration and urethral catheterization are the preferred methods due to their high reliability and minimal contamination risk. Clinical features in UTI neonates include fever, vomiting, diarrhea, poor weight gain, and lethargy. If the child cries during voiding or has a weak urine stream with a palpable bladder, it implies urinary obstruction. High fever (>39ºC), persistent vomiting, dehydration, renal angle tenderness, or raised creatinine is considered a complicated UTI.  The chief cause of UTI in children is Escherichia coli, others include Klebsiella, Enterobacter, and Staphylococcus saprophyticus. Risk factors for recurrent UTI are age <6 months, obstructive uropathy, female sex, vesicoureteric reflux (VUR), bladder dysfunction, constipation, and repeated catheterization. Bowel and bladder dysfunction increases the risk of recurrence, and micturating cystourethrogram (MCU) is done in children with recurrence of UTI. A colony count of >105/mL of a clean catch sample is considered significant bacteriuria. Any colonies on suprapubic aspiration and >50,000/mL on urethral catheterization are considered significant. Patients with recurrent UTIs need to be evaluated with ultrasonography, DMSA scan (dimercaptosuccinic acid), and MCU.  Evaluation following the first episode of UTI is given below: 
Age Evaluation
<1 year USG, MCU, DMSA renal scan
1 to 5 years USG, DMSA scan. MCU is done if USG is abnormal
>5 years USG. If USG is abnormal,  MCU and DMSA are done.
Third-generation cephalosporins or aminoglycosides are preferred empirical antibiotics for urinary tract infections (UTIs). Treatment duration is 7-10 days for simple UTIs and 10-14 days for complicated UTIs. Asymptomatic bacteriuria doesn't require treatment. Infants <3 months and those with complicated UTIs should receive parenteral antibiotics.  Cotrimoxazole, nitrofurantoin, cephalexin, and cefadroxil are given as prophylaxis to prevent recurrent UTIs. Cotrimoxazole and nitrofurantoin can be given in infants >3 months of age.  Other Options: (Options A and C): For toilet-trained children (typically over age 2-3), a clean-catch midstream urine specimen is the recommended method. text: 33. A 53-year-old male patient was admitted following a road traffic accident. Paradoxical respiration was seen. His chest X-ray is shown below. He was given analgesics and oxygen was administered via face mask but he developed respiratory failure. What is the best line of management in this case?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Mechanical ventilation

The given clinical scenario and the X-ray showing contiguous rib fractures on the right side suggest flail's chest. It is characterized by contiguous rib fractures and paradoxical respiration following blunt trauma to the chest wall. Mechanical ventilation (like Intermittent Positive Pressure Ventilation) is the management of flail chest with respiratory failure. Flail Chest : * A flail chest occurs when a segment of the chest wall does not have bony continuity with the rest of the thoracic cage. * This condition results from blunt trauma associated with multiple rib fractures, i.e. 2 adjacent ribs or 3 or more ribs fractured in two or more places. * The blunt force required to disrupt the integrity of the thoracic cage typically produces an underlying pulmonary contusion as well. Clinical Features: On inspiration, the loose segment of the chest wall is displaced inwards and less air, therefore, moves into the lungs. On expiration, the segment moves outwards(paradoxical respiration). Diagnosis - Made clinically, not by radiography. To confirm the diagnosis the chest wall can be observed for the paradoxical motion of a chest wall segment for several respiratory cycles and during coughing. Voluntary splinting as a result of pain, mechanically impaired chest wall movement, and the associated lung contusion are all causes of hypoxia and respiratory failure. The patient is also at high risk of developing a pneumothorax or hemothorax. text: 3. A 70-year-old male patient presents with halitosis, dysphagia, and regurgitation of food. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Pulsion pseudodiverticulum

The clinical history of halitosis and regurgitation in an elderly man suggests a diagnosis of Zenker's diverticulum or pulsion pseudodiverticulum.  Zenker diverticulum, or cricopharyngeal achalasia/pharyngeal pouch, is a pulsion pseudodiverticulum (false diverticula occurring due to a motor disorder causing increased intraluminal pressure). It results from the herniation of mucosa and submucosa through Killian's triangle (dehiscence of Killian). Killian's triangle is an area of weakness between: Thyropharyngeus - oblique fibers Cricopharyngeus - transverse fibers It is usually seen in the seventh decade of life and is thought to occur due to loss of muscle tone and elasticity causing incomplete relaxation. The impaired relaxation and spasms of the cricopharyngeus muscle after swallowing results in increased pressure within the distal pharynx and the development of Zenker's diverticulum. Patients complain of dysphagia, halitosis, recurrent regurgitation, and respiratory infections. The most serious complications are aspiration pneumonia and lung abscess. Diagnosis is by barium swallow studies and video laryngoscopy. The gold standard of treatment is either endoscopic or open surgery. The transoral endoscopic approach is known as the Dohlman procedure in which the common wall between the diverticulum and the cervical esophagus is ablated using laser, electrocautery, or stapler devices. It can be used for diverticula between 2 and 5 cm in size. Lesions less than 2 cm are managed with myotomy. A sac more than 5 cm is usually excised. Other options: Option A: Cancer esophagus also presents with dysphagia and regurgitation of food, but halitosis is more classically seen with Zenker's diverticulum. The patient would also have weight loss, anorexia and other cancer related symptoms. Option B: Achalasia is a type of esophageal motility disorder and a premalignant condition that occurs due to hypertension of the lower esophageal sphincter and thereby failure to relax. The classic triad of presentation is dysphagia, regurgitation, and weight loss. Esophagogram shows the classic bird beak appearance (dilated esophagus with distal narrowing).  Option D: GERD also presents with dysphagia and regurgitation of food, but halitosis is not seen in GERD, it is more classic of Zenker's diverticulum.

It occurs due to the rapid emptying of the stomach contents into the small intestine, leading to symptoms like diarrhea, nausea, sweating, and palpitations, typically occurring shortly after meals. Increasing the protein content of meals can also help stabilize blood sugar levels and reduce the severity of symptoms. text: 8. What nutrient deficiency is commonly associated with delayed wound healing following minor surgery?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin C

Delayed wound healing after minor surgery can be attributed to a deficiency in vitamin C. Vitamin C, also known as ascorbic acid, plays a crucial role in collagen synthesis, a protein that is essential for wound healing and tissue repair. Collagen provides structural support to the skin, blood vessels, and other connective tissues. A deficiency in vitamin C can lead to impaired collagen formation, weakening of blood vessels, and delayed wound healing. Factors influencing healing: * Infection: one of the most important causes of delay in healing; prolongs inflammation; increases the local tissue injury * Diabetes: most important systemic cause of abnormal wound healing * Nutritional status: protein deficiency and vitamin C deficiency inhibit collagen synthesis and retard healing. * Glucocorticoids (steroids): anti-inflammatory effects; results in weakness of the scar due to inhibition of TGF-β production and diminished fibrosis * Mechanical factors: such as increased local pressure or torsion; may cause wounds to pull apart or dehisce * Poor perfusion: due to arteriosclerosis, diabetes, or obstructed venous drainage; also impairs healing * Foreign bodies: such as fragments of steel, glass, or even bone; impede healing * Type and extent of tissue injury: affect subsequent repair; * Location of the injury and the character of the injured tissue: also important Even though zinc also causes poor wound healing, Vitamin C is more commonly implicated.

Cushing reflex causes a triad of symptoms: * Reflex bradycardia (via arterial baroreceptors) * Hypertension (with widened pulse pressure) * Irregular respiration (bradypnea). When intracranial pressure is increased, the blood supply to rostral ventrolateral neurons is compromised. This leads to local hypoxia and hypercapnia which in turn increase the discharge of the central chemoreceptors located on the ventrolateral medullary surface. This activation causes a rise in blood pressure which then restores the blood flow to the medulla. However, the arterial baroreceptors sense this increase in the systemic blood pressure and cause a reflex decrease in the heart rate.  Other Options: Option A: CT head is not the immediate priority in a patient with compromised consciousness and potentially raised ICP. text: 15. A 6-year-old child presented with a midline neck swelling that moves with deglutition and tongue protrusion. CT confirms the diagnosis of a thyroglossal cyst. Which of the following procedures is used in the management of this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Sistrunk operation

The treatment of choice for a thyroglossal cyst is the Sistrunk operation. Thyroglossal duct cyst (TDGC) The thyroid gland descends early in fetal life from the base of the tongue towards its position in the lower neck. Once the gland reaches its position, where the isthmus is at the level of the second and third tracheal rings, the tract of the thyroglossal duct disappears. A thyroglossal cyst represents the persistence of this track and can be found adjacent to the midline. Classically, swellings associated with the thyroid move with deglutition. Thyroglossal cyst moves upwards on swallowing and on tongue protrusion, and it indicates attachment to the hyoid bone. Although they often occur in children, they may also present in adults, even as late as the 6th or 7th decade. Diagnosis:  CT scan commonly confirms the diagnosis by showing well-circumscribed lesions with homogenous fluid attenuation surrounded by a thin, enhancing rim. text: 3. A 35-year-old male presented to a surgical emergency with complaints of severe epigastric pain for 1 day. On examination, HR was 120/min and BP was 100/60 mm Hg. On palpation, there is tenderness, guarding and rigidity. What is the probable cause of the condition shown in the X-ray below?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Hollow viscus perforation

The clinical scenario of hypotension and tachycardia with abdominal tenderness, guarding and rigidity with free air under the diaphragm in X-ray is indicative of hollow viscus perforation.  Acute abdomen is a common surgical emergency. Common causes include appendicitis, hollow viscus perforation, cholecystitis, and pancreatitis. An erect abdominal X-ray is commonly done as the first investigation. Free air under the diaphragm can result from hollow viscus perforation including Gastric, duodenal, small bowel and large bowel perforations. Causes of hollow viscus perforation are blunt or penetrating injury, bowel obstruction, peptic ulcer disease, infections(TB, typhoid, Crohn's), corrosive agents etc. Clinical features include abdominal pain and distension, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, tenderness, rebound tenderness, decreased or absent bowel sounds, and guarding on palpation. Fever may be present. Features of septic shock can be seen at later stages. Investigations include estimation of the white blood cell count, urea, serum electrolytes, and an erect abdominal radiograph showing free gas under the diaphragm. A supine radiograph may show dilated gas-filled loops of the bowel suggestive of paralytic ileus. However, CECT is the most sensitive investigation to detect minimal/ suspected pneumoperitoneum. Management of a hollow viscous perforation mainly includes resuscitation, analgesics, intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, and emergency exploratory laparotomy. Other options: None of the other options have free air under the diaphragm. Option A: Acute cholecystitis presents with pain in the right upper quadrant with fever and nausea. They may have tenderness and guarding. Rigidity is uncommon. Additionally, free air under the diaphragm may be seen in cases of gall bladder perforation only.  Option B: Sigmoid volvulus shows a large, dilated loop of the colon, often with a few air-fluid levels. Specific signs include the coffee bean sign and the absence of rectal gas. On the x-ray abdomen, the apex of the sigmoid volvulus extends towards the right upper quadrant and the haustrations are usually lost. Option D: In small bowel obstruction, the obstructed bowel loops are centrally located and lie transversely. In cases of jejunal obstruction, valvulae conniventes, which are mucosal folds that span the entire diameter of the bowel, create a ladder effect. Additionally, a distended cecum may exhibit a gas shadow in the right iliac fossa.

text: 4. A male patient following an accident presented with complex injuries including degloving injuries of the foot and leg. What type of flap/graft was used during surgery?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Thiersch graft

The image given shows a Thiersch graft which is also known as a split-thickness skin graft.  Skin grafts can be broadly divided into two categories: Split-thickness skin graft (Thiersch graft): Partial-thickness skin grafts consisting of the epidermis and a portion of the dermis are called split-thickness skin grafts. Less dermis in the split-thickness skin graft translates into less primary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks in surface area after harvesting and before grafting) and more secondary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks during healing). Full-thickness skin grafts (Wolfe graft- Option A) include the epidermis and entire dermis, with portions of the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles. More dermis in the full-thickness skin graft translates into more primary contraction and less secondary contraction. Advantages of split skin graft over full-thickness skin graft: * Large grafts can be harvested. * In the case of thinner split-thickness grafts, the donor site heals more rapidly and can be reused in severe cases such as burns. * Uptake is good. Meshing can be done i.e. small splits are made in graft and any exudates collected can come out through this and this improves graft takeup.  * Meshing also allows the graft to expand. Advantages of full-thickness skin graft over split skin graft: * It has a lesser degree of post-graft contraction. * Best cosmetic appearance as they include the highest number of skin appendage elements.Other options:  Grafts derive their blood supply from the target bed while flaps carry their own blood supply. Option B: Free flaps - A flap where its blood vessel is disconnected and the vessel is reconnected using microsurgery at the new site. Option C: Pedicled/islanded flaps - They are the repositioned flaps which maintain their original blood supply even after the transfer. Pearl PF1917: Skin graft : phases of uptake of the graft The take of skin graft occurs in three phases: * Imbibition (Plasmatic circulation): during the first 48 hours, the graft is nourished with plasma exudate from host bed capillaries. * Inosculation, in which cut vessels from the host bed line up with the cut ends of the vessels of the graft to form anastomoses * Neovascularization, in which blood vessels grow from the recipient bed into the graft Sensibility returns to the graft over time, with reinnervation beginning at approximately 4 to 5 weeks and being completed by 12 to 24 months. Pain returns first, with light touch and temperature returning later. Note: some books give that the 3 phases are imbibition,revascularisation (inosculation+neovascularisation) and organisation (fibrin layer holds the graft in place and this is replaced by postgraft day 7 with fibroblasts)
