text: 5. A 15-year-old male patient presented to emergency with pain in the right lower quadrant. He was diagnosed with acute appendicitis. Which of the following is the most commonly used incision for appendectomy?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Gridiron incision

The most commonly used incision for an appendectomy is McBurney's Gridiron incision. The incision is made at McBurney’s point (two-thirds from the umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine). They involve passing through all of the abdominal muscles, transversalis fascia, and then the peritoneum, before entering the abdominal cavity. Other options:  Option A: Mildline laparotomy incision is commonly used when the diagnosis is uncertain and in cases where an appendicular perforation is suspected. It is for better abdominal exposure. Option B: Pfannential incision is used for the lower segment caesarean section.  Option D: Kocher's subcostal incision is used for open cholecystectomy.  The major anterior abdominal incisions have been illustrated below: * 1 is Kocher incision - A subcostal incision used to gain access for gall bladder and/or biliary tree pathology. * 2 is midline incision - The most common incision for laparotomy, a vertical incision which follows the linea alba which is particularly favored in diagnostic laparotomy, as they allow wide access to most of the abdominal cavity. * 3 is McBurney's incision (also called gridiron incision) is an oblique incision (superolateral to inferomedial) passing along McBurney's point. It is popularly used for open appendicectomy. * 4 is battle incision a lower right paramedian incision but placed more laterally than the standard paramedian incision. It is suitable for dealing with acute appendicitis and pathologies in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. * 5 is Lanz incision, a transverse or skin crease incision for appendicitis, 2 cm below the umbilicus, centered on the midclavicular–mid-inguinal line. Due to its continuation with Langer’s lines, the Lanz incision produces much more aesthetically pleasing results with reduced scarring. * 6 is paramedian incision - this incision runs 2-5 cm away from the midline used to access much of the lateral viscera, such as the kidneys, spleen, and the adrenal glands. * 7 is transverse incision - A supraumbilical transverse incision offers excellent exposure of the upper abdomen. A transverse incision may be superior to a midline incision in terms of recovery and complications postoperatively. * 8 is Rutherford Morrison incision, an oblique muscle cutting incision used for access to sigmoid colon and pelvis in patients where the midline is scarred due to previous surgery. * 9 is Pfannenstiel incision - An infraumbilical transverse incision in the lower abdomen, often used for gynecological and obstetric procedures.

text: 14. During a laproscopic surgery while inserting a lateral trocar for surgery which of the following is most prone to injury ?

options.C: Both superior and inferior epigastric artery

expl:
Correct answer: C. Both superior and inferior epigastric artery

The most common source of bleeding during laparoscopic surgery is through both superior and inferior epigastric arteries.  These vessels run vertically in the posterior rectus sheath along the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle, creating a high-risk zone for trocar placement. The superior epigastric artery descends from the internal thoracic (mammary) artery, while the inferior epigastric artery ascends from the external iliac artery, and they anastomose within the rectus muscle. Their consistent anatomical location and the fact that they run in a relatively superficial plane within the anterior abdominal wall makes them particularly vulnerable during trocar insertion. To avoid injury, surgeons must carefully identify the lateral border of the rectus muscle and place trocars either medial or significantly lateral to this zone, and transillumination of the abdominal wall can help identify these vessels. Injury to these arteries can result in significant bleeding, making it the most common source of haemorrhage in this type of surgery. Proper identification and careful dissection are essential to avoid this complication.

It can occur secondary to trauma, endoscopic instrumentation, corrosive ingestion, or severe repetitive vomiting against a closed GE junction. It presents with retrosternal chest pain and other symptoms depending on the size of the perforation and contamination of the mediastinum. Patients may have dysphagia, regurgitation, and possibly halitosis. However, it does not typically present with acute severe chest pain or crepitus. Option D: Acute pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium, often presenting with sharp chest pain that may worsen with deep breaths or when lying down. Acute pericarditis is unlikely given the history of vomiting, hematemesis, and crepitus.

text: 25. A 55-year-old man presents with pain abdomen. Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen was done. What is the likely source of pain in this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Kidney

The history of an elderly male presenting with pain abdomen and an axial CECT image showing renal lesions with irregular enhancement is suggestive of renal origin of pain likely renal cell carcinoma (RCC). It is the most common malignant tumour of the kidney. It usually occurs in the age group 50–70 years and macroscopic hematuria is seen in about 60% of the cases. It usually presents with painless gross hematuria, flank pain, or painless flank mass. Contrast-enhanced CT is the investigation of choice for RCC. On CT, small lesions enhance homogeneously, whereas larger lesions have irregular enhancement due to areas of necrosis. The clear cell subtype may show much stronger enhancement is a differential for angiomyolipoma. Still, it is essential to note that macroscopic fat is almost always associated with ossification or calcification. Surgeries done for RCC:  Partial nephrectomy, the goal is the complete removal of the primary tumor while preserving healthy renal parenchyma. It is used for renal tumors <7cm in size.  Classic radical nephrectomy involves the removal of the kidney, perirenal fat, adrenal gland, and regional lymph nodes.  Targeted therapies for RCC include tyrosine kinase inhibitors (sorafenib, sunitinib), anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) monoclonal antibodies (bevacizumab), and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitors (everolimus and temsirolimus). Primary hyperparathyroidism is one of the most common endocrine disorders, and it is an important cause of hypercalcemia. Tumours of the parathyroid glands usually come to attention because of excessive secretion of PTH rather than mass effects. It can also be associated with MEN1 and MEN 2A syndromes.  The clinical manifestations of hyperparathyroidism can be summarized as “painful bones, renal stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans.” Skeletal manifestations of hyperparathyroidism include bone resorption, osteitis fibrosa cystica, and brown tumours. Ectopic locations are difficult to locate.  Option D: Multiphase CT imaging has become widely utilized to localize the disease. text: 33. A 40-year-old male presented with diffuse abdominal pain. Physical examination revealed rigidity and guarding. Abdominal X-ray demonstrated free air under the diaphragm. The patient was taken up for surgery and intraoperatively, ileal perforation was noted with gross contamination of the abdomen with enteric and purulent content. The clinical vignette with Ileal perforation and physical examination findings of rigidity and guarding suggest peritonitis due to perforation. The next best step in the management of this patient is urgent surgical exploration with an ileostomy. Perforation of a viscus is a life-threatening condition that occurs following the rupture of the alimentary tract. Common causes include iatrogenic (surgery, scopes) blunt or penetrating injury, bowel obstruction, infections( TB, typhoid) peptic ulcer disease, corrosive agents, or particular medications This leads to the leakage of the enteric contents, thereby leading to acute bacterial peritonitis. Peritonitis is the generalized or localized inflammation of the peritoneum due to the free spillage of fluids into the peritoneal cavity or secondary bacterial infection. Clinical features of hollow viscous perforation occur due to the developed peritonitis and the features include abdominal pain and distension, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, tenderness, rebound tenderness, decreased or absent bowel sounds, and guarding on palpation. Fever may be present. Sometimes, features of septic shock can be seen at later stages. Investigations include estimating the white blood cell count, urea, serum electrolytes, and an erect abdominal radiograph showing free gas under the diaphragm. A supine radiograph may show dilated gas-filled loops of the bowel, suggestive of paralytic ileus. The below image shows a hollow viscus perforation. Management - Initial management includes intravenous (IV) fluid therapy, cessation of oral intake, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Indications for immediate bowel exploration are * Sepsis/diffuse peritonitis(as in this patient) * Bowel ischemia * Complete or closed-loop bowel obstruction Other options: Option A: Resection is considered in a patient with multiple perforation, suspected gangrene or malignancy. Anastomosis is avoided in patients in shock, peritonitis with gross contamination Option B: Primary repair is usually taken for small perforation with minimal contamination and no sign of peritonitis. It is commonly done for traumatic enteric perforation Option D: Duodenal perforations, on the other hand, are generally treated with omental patch repair without resection.

2. What is the correct sequence of Damage control surgery?

* Patient selection

* ICU care

* Secondary exploration

Correct answer: C. 1,2,3,4,5

The correct answer is option C: 1,2,3,4,5 The correct sequence  of five stages of damage control surgery are: * Patient selection * Control of haemorrhage and control of contamination(primary exploration) * Resuscitation continued in the intensive care unit * Deﬁnitive surgery(secondary exploration) * Abdominal closure Damage control surgery is minimal intervention done to stabilize the patient and do the definite surgery later. It centers on coordinating staged operative interventions with periods of aggressive resuscitation to salvage trauma patients sustaining major injuries. The aim of the DCS is to restore physiology over anatomy. It is applied to trauma patients with combined vascular and visceral injuries. The phases are: * Phase 1 involves recognition of the severity of the injury. Here,rapid-sequence induction of anesthesia and intubation is done. This is followed by early rewarming and prompt movement of the patient to the operating theatre. * Phase 2 involves performing immediate laparotomy. Here, the focus is to control bleeding and contamination. Abdominal packing and temporary wound closure are done. * Phase 3 involves movement to the intensive care unit (ICU). The aim is to normalize the biochemical and physiological parameters. * Phase 4 involves re-exploration in the operating theatre. Here, definitive repair of all injuries is done. Multiple procedures on multiple occasions may be required. Pearl PF2177: Damage Control Surgery Five stages of damage control surgery: 1. Patient selection 2. text: 3. A patient presents with breast skin dimpling as shown in the image. This occurs due to the infiltration of which of the following?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Cooper's ligament

Skin dimpling of the breast occurs due to traction on Cooper’s ligaments by a carcinoma. The fibrous bands shorten as they are infiltrated and pulled by tumor or associated fibrosis, producing the characteristic puckering or dimpling on the breast surface. The condition is most often seen in carcinoma of the breast, where the tumor induces fibrosis and collagen deposition (desmoplastic reaction). As the tumor increases in size and invades adjacent breast parenchyma, it contracts the fibrous tissue (Cooper’s ligaments), leading to tethering of the overlying skin. text: 5. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for esophageal varices ?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Endoscopic variceal ligation

The first-line treatment for active variceal bleeding is endoscopic therapy, with endoscopic variceal ligation (banding) preferred. Esophageal variceal bleeding is a complication of portal hypertension, most commonly due to cirrhosis. . After initial resuscitation and stabilization, endoscopic intervention is the mainstay of treatment for bleeding esophageal varices. The two most commonly used techniques are endoscopic band ligation (EVL), where rubber bands are applied to the base of the varix, and endoscopic sclerotherapy, which involves injecting a sclerosant into or around the varix. Endoscopy is usually performed in a head-down position with good suction and visualization using a double-channel endoscope and power washers. Once the bleeding site is identified, treatment is focused only on the active varices. Both EVL and sclerotherapy effectively control bleeding, but EVL is preferred as it significantly reduces the risk of rebleeding, and a single session is often sufficient.  Initial management of variceal bleeding involves the following:  * Admission to the intensive care unit * Placement of two large-bore peripheral cannulae * Blood transfusion * Correction of coagulopathy with fresh frozen plasma, vitamin K, and tranexamic acid * Terlipressin, a splanchnic vasoconstrictor * Prophylactic antibiotic * Endotracheal intubation for airway protection if bleeding is uncontrolled * Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy TIPSS or Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Stent Shunt placement involves the placement of a shunt to redirect blood flow and reduce portal pressure. It is very effective but requires analgesia, sedation, and fluoroscopic guidance. It is done if medical and endoscopic measures fail to control bleeding.

text: 10. A 30-year-old female presented with pain in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen 4 days after undergoing a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. On ultrasonography, a significant collection was detected in the right upper quadrant. What is the next appropriate step?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the collection

The clinical scenario of a patient presenting with pain in the right upper quadrant and a significant collection after laparoscopic cholecystectomy (4 days) points towards a bile duct injury with a possible leak. So, The next step of management is ultrasound-guided aspiration, followed by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) and stenting. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the most common cause of bile duct injury. Major biliary leakage is usually seen 2 to 10 days after cholecystectomy. Affected patients typically present with: * Pyrexia * Abdominal pain * Bilious ascites * Mild jaundice * Leukocytosis * Elevations in the serum levels of ALP and GGT. Iatrogenic bile duct injury should be considered in any patient who develops new or worsening symptoms following laparoscopic cholecystectomy. In the absence of an external drainage site, bile leakage may present as a localized biloma, either sterile or infected, or as biliary ascites. Additional warning signs include persistent or increasing postprandial or shoulder pain, generalized malaise, and fever, all of which should prompt strong suspicion of a bile duct injury. Management of bile duct injury: * If detected on table with * Duct injury less than 3 mm or those draining less than single segment of the liver: Ligation * Lateral injury—Ducts larger than 4 mm or those that drain multiple hepatic segments: Repair using T-tube. * Transection with minimal loss of duct length: Repair using T-tube is used; in case of extensive loss of duct length, billiary enteric anastomosis is performed. * Cystic duct leaks can be treated by the percutaneous drainage of intra-abdominal collection and endoscopic biliary drainage.  * Radiological workup: Abdominal ultrasonography to determine the extent of the leak. * For definitive leaks, ultrasound-guided aspiration is performed; alternatively, the collection is drained and a transhepatic biliary drain is placed. After 6–8 weeks, the definitive repair is ascertained.  * Ultrasonography confirmation and aspiration of the leak is followed by ERCP and stenting.

text: 11. A 2-month-old male infant presents with a scrotal swelling that has been present since birth and is exacerbated by crying. The swelling has suddenly become painful, red, and irreducible. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Correct answer: C. Strangulated inguinal hernia

The clinical scenario of a 2-month-old male infant with a reducible scrotal swelling that is exacerbated by crying present since birth (congenital) and has become suddenly painful, red, and irreducible is most suggestive of a strangulated inguinal hernia. Infants are at high risk for incarceration of an inguinal hernia because of the narrow inguinal ring. An inguinal hernia represents a protrusion of abdominal contents through a patent processus vaginalis into the inguinal canal and sometimes into the scrotum. It is a common indication for surgical repair in children. When a hernia becomes incarcerated and is not reducible, it can lead to strangulation of its contents.  Management of a strangulated inguinal hernia requires emergency surgical repair. It is usually performed by open inguinal repair, and a contralateral side evaluation may be considered. Laparoscopic approaches can also be used in certain cases. The repair of a patent processus vaginalis is emphasized to prevent recurrence. Other options: Option A: Epididymitis occurring before 6 months of age is usually due to infected urine ascending through the vas deferens. In contrast, epididymo-orchitis typically develops after puberty in sexually active boys and presents with acute testicular pain, fever, dysuria, increased frequency of urination, and urethral discharge. Option D: A hydrocele refers to the accumulation of fluid between the parietal and visceral layers of the tunica vaginalis, usually limited to the scrotum. They are generally asymptomatic, non-tender, and may fluctuate in size, often decreasing overnight; they can also occur bilaterally. text: 12. A 13-year-old male presents to the OPD with severe pain in the right testis after being hit by a cricket ball 2 hours ago. On examination, there is severe testicular pain and an absent cremasteric reflex. What is the next step?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Surgical exploration

The given clinical vignette of severe pain in the right testis along with a negative cremasteric reflex is highly suggestive of testicular torsion.  It is a surgical emergency, and if left untreated, the testes may become gangrenous. Early surgery undertaken to untwist the testis gives a better outcome. Testicular torsion is the twisting of the spermatic cord and its contents such that the testicular blood supply becomes compromised. Etiology and risk factors-  * High investment of the tunica vaginalis(like a clapper in a bell). Most common cause. * Inversion of the testis. * Separation of the epididymis from the body of the testis. Clinical features of testicular torsion are - scrotal pain and swelling, erythema, negative cremasteric reflex, nausea, and vomiting, the testis seems high in the scrotum and the twisted cord can sometimes be palpated. * Prehn’s Sign is used to differentiate the torsion of testis from acute epididymo orchitis. In the case of acute epididymo orchitis, the pain gets relieved on the elevation of the testis but not in torsion of testes. * Deming’s sign: Spasm of the cremaster muscle and the cord twisting cause the affected testis to be positioned higher in torsion testes. Even though Doppler ultrasound scanning can confrm the absence of the blood supply to the affected testis, false-positive results are commonly seen, hence it is not routinely recommended. Urgent scrotal exploration in case of doubtful diagnosis.  A transverse scrotal incision is taken. If the testis is viable, twisting is prevented by fixation with three non-absorbable sutures between the tunica albuginea of the testis and the scrotal raphe. If the testis is infarcted after the cord is untwisted, an orchidectomy must be undertaken and the opposite testis must be fixed to the scrotum to preserve fertility and prevent torsion. If the affected testis is viable after the cord is untwisted, both the affected and the contralateral testes are fixed to the scrotum (bilateral orchiopexy) using non-absorbable sutures. Other options: Option A and D: The optimal timeframe for surgical intervention and testicular salvage is within 6 hours from the onset of pain. Hence, seeking early urological consultation at presentation is essential, even if confirmatory tests are not yet available. Option B: Ultrasound guided arterial doppler has to be taken, not venous. Also even for USG arterial doppler false positives are commonly seen.

text: 13. A neonate presents with thickened, edematous intestines protruding from the abdomen without any external covering. What will be the next best line of management?

options.C: Cover the contents with a silo bag and wait

expl:
Correct answer: C. Cover the contents with a silo bag and wait

The clinical scenario of a neonate presenting with thickened and edematous protruding intestines without any covering points towards a diagnosis of gastroschisis. The next best line of management would be to cover the contents with a silo bag and wait. A neonate with gastroschisis would need an immediate primary closure. However, in the given scenario, in neonates with thickened and edematous intestines, it may not be possible to return the bowel to the peritoneal cavity immediately after birth. In such cases, a plastic spring-loaded silo bag can be placed over the bowel, facilitating the gradual reduction of the bowel wall edema. This is followed by definitive surgical closure in about 1–2 weeks. Gastroschisis is an abdominal wall defect located on one side of the umbilicus (right side commonly), allowing protrusion of the intestines, stomach, bladder, and sometimes ovaries or undescended testes. The loops of the bowel are not covered by amnion as they herniate through the abdominal wall directly into the amniotic cavity. The affected bowel loops can be damaged by exposure to amniotic fluid. The intestines are matted and covered by a thick peel. Longer exposure in utero to amniotic fluid can cause trauma to the intestines. The intestines are also not fully rotated, and these factors increase the risk of intestinal volvulus, postnatal intestinal dysfunction with delayed mobility, and prolonged need for hospitalization and enteral feeding. Risk factors include teenage pregnancy, recreational drug use, smoking, and genitourinary infection during pregnancy. After birth, careful management is required to prevent twisting or kinking of the blood supply to the intestines.  Management: Immediate surgical intervention is required after birth to prevent complications such as infection, dehydration, and damage to the exposed abdominal organs. In the immediate postoperative period, if abdominal wall closure is tight, aggressive fluid resuscitation may be required to ensure adequate tissue perfusion and prevent metabolic acidosis. Patients are supported with TPN until bowel function returns. Surgical repair typically involves gently placing the protruding abdominal contents back(primary reduction) into the abdominal cavity and closing the abdominal wall defect surgically. Primary reduction is successful in 50% to 80%, with eviscerated contents placed into the abdominal cavity without excessive tension. Parenteral nutrition is often needed for several weeks to support intestinal recovery.  Note: Covering the bowel with saline-soaked gauze is a temporary measure to prevent fluid loss and infection, but it’s not the next best line of management. The definitive step is silo placement. Pearl PF0342: Difference between gastroschisis and omphalocele

text: 14. An elderly man, a follow-up patient of GERD with recurrent reflux symptoms, is found to have a nodule in the second part of the duodenum on endoscopy. Which hormone is most likely to be raised?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Gastrin

The given clinical scenario of a nodule in the second part of the duodenum in a patient with recurrent reflux (GERD) and symptoms suggestive of persistent acid-related disease is suggestive of a gastrinoma, a neuroendocrine tumor that secretes gastrin. Gastrinoma if associated with marked gastric acid production and recurrent peptic ulcer, is called Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES)/Gastrinoma is a neuroendocrinal tumour characterized by hypersecretion of gastrin resulting in gastrointestinal tract ulcers. It occurs more commonly in a sporadic pattern but can be associated with MEN-1 (multiple endocrine neoplasia-1) syndromes in the familial pattern. Gastrinoma is most commonly located in the gastrinoma triangle (Passaro's triangle) bounded by the lines connecting the: * Cystic duct * Junction between the second and third parts of the duodenum * Junction between the neck and body of the pancreas The most common presentations of gastrinoma are epigastric pain, diarrhoea, and peptic ulcers. The ulcers occur at typical locations (proximal duodenum) and atypical locations (distal duodenum, jejunum). Duodenal ulcers are the most common. Treatment of ZES : High-dose Proton Pump Inhibitor followed by surgery. Surgeries that can be done are: * Distal Pancreatectomy– if lesion in body or tail of the pancreas * Enucleation– if the lesion is in the head of the pancreas * Full-thickness excision– if the lesion is in duodenum * MEN associated– surgery done only if size>2.5cm Other options: Option A: VIPoma is characterized by watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome). It is caused by the release of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) from the tumor. Option C: Glucagonomas, α-cell tumors are associated with increased serum levels of glucagon. The patient presents with mild diabetes mellitus, a characteristic skin rash (necrolytic migratory erythema), and anemia. They occur most frequently in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women and are characterized by extremely high plasma glucagon levels. Option D: Insulinomas, β-cell tumors are the most common pancreatic endocrine neoplasms. These are usually benign and often cause symptomatic hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemic symptoms appear when blood glucose levels fall below 50 mg/dL. The symptoms usually develop after fasting or exertion and improve after glucose intake. Pearl PF2047: Clinical features of gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome) Most common symptom: Abdominal pain. Gastrin hypersecretion stimulates gastric acid secretion, leading to peptic ulcers that occur at atypical sites like the duodenum and jejunum and are refractory and multiple. Diarrhea is due to * Acid-induced injury to the small intestine mucosa * Inability of the intestinal tract to absorb large volumes of fluids secreted by the stomach * Inactivation of pancreatic lipase by low pH * Precipitation of bile salts. The unique characteristic of acid-induced diarrhea is that it is controlled by nasogastric aspiration of gastric secretions. An increase in serum gastrin >200pg/ml following an IV bolus of secretin (2U/kg) is diagnostic. Other tests: * BAO >15mEq/h (or >5mEq/h if they have had a procedure for peptic ulcer) * BAO: MAO ratio is increased (>0.6) (BAO=Basal acid output; MAO=Maximal acid output) For localization * Initial investigation - CT or MRI * Best investigation - Endoscopic ultrasound * If the tumor is not localized - Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy.

text: 15. A patient with a 40% burn injury on the arm underwent split-thickness skin grafting on post-burn day 3. On post-operative day 5, during physiotherapy, the patient develops stiffness and a limited range of motion in the arm. The graft appears healthy and well-adhered. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.C: Forceful passive extension of the joint under direct visualization of the graft

expl:
Correct answer: B. Continue physiotherapy without intervention

Supervised movements by physiotherapists, usually under direct vision of any affected joints, should begin after about 5 days in case of burn wounds. In this case, the patient is on post-operative day 5 with a healthy graft and stiffness during physiotherapy, which aligns with the recommendation to continue supervised physiotherapy at this stage.  Physiotherapy and splints are essential in maintaining the range of movement and reducing joint contracture after skin grafting. Elevation of the affected limb is important. After grafting, the hand should be splinted in the functional position, but the graft itself must be placed in the position of maximal stretch. Grafts are tissues that are transferred without their blood supply and therefore need to be revascularised through the recipient wound bed. For the graft to take successfully, the wound bed must be healthy and well-vascularized to support angiogenesis into the graft tissue. There are two types of skin grafts: * Split thickness skin graft (Thiersch graft ): Partial-thickness skin grafts consisting of the epidermis and a portion of the dermis. * Full-thickness skin grafts (Wolfe graft): include the epidermis and entire dermis, with portions of the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles.  Advantages of split skin graft over full-thickness skin graft: * Large grafts can be harvested. * In the case of thinner split-thickness grafts, the donor site heals more rapidly and can be reused in severe cases such as burns. * Uptake is good. Meshing can be done i.e. small splits are made in graft and any exudates collected can come out through this and this improves graft take up.  * Meshing also allows the graft to expand. Advantages of full-thickness skin graft over split skin graft: * It has a lesser degree of post graft contraction * Best cosmetic appearance as they include the highest number of skin appendage elements. The most preferable donor site is buttock in cosmetically sensitive individuals and children. The most commonly used donor site is the thigh. * The graft is taken from the donor site with a handheld Humby knife or electric dermatome. * Grafts are perforated to allow exudates to escape and improve ‘take’. It can further be meshed to allow expansion. * Grafts will take up only on the beds which are vascularized, hence preparation of wound bed is an essential step. * Skin grafts are completely dependent on nutrition on the tissue over which they are placed and can heal well over muscle, perichondrium, and periosteum. They do not take well over bone or cartilage or on tissue that has been irradiated or infected or is hypovascular. * A clean healthy wound bed with a meshed graft tied in place to stop movement will encourage take. * The presence of group A beta-hemolytic streptococci is a contraindication in grafting as it can destroy split grafts completely and also convert donors to full-thickness defects. * The donor area is dressed appropriately and the dressing is opened after 10 days and not earlier.  The given image shows Humby's knife. The average thickness of the graft obtained from a Humbys knife is 0.3 mm. Other options: Option A: Stricture release(surgical intervention) is indicated when a well-formed contracture or significant scar tissue is restricting joint motion. In this patient’s scenario, the graft appears healthy and well-adhered, and stiffness is expected during early physiotherapy. Option C: Forceful passive stretching or forceful manipulation is not recommended soon after grafting, as it can damage the delicate graft, impair graft take, and disrupt the healing process. Supervised physiotherapy is recommended. Option D: Tendon repair not indicated, as there are no signs of tendon rupture in this case. Pearl PF1917: Skin graft : phases of uptake of the graft The take of skin graft occurs in three phases: * Imbibition (Plasmatic circulation): during the first 48 hours, the graft is nourished with plasma exudate from host bed capillaries. * Inosculation, in which cut vessels from the host bed line up with the cut ends of the vessels of the graft to form anastomoses * Neovascularization, in which blood vessels grow from the recipient bed into the graft Sensibility returns to the graft over time, with reinnervation beginning at approximately 4 to 5 weeks and being completed by 12 to 24 months. Pain returns first, with light touch and temperature returning later. Note: some books give that the 3 phases are imbibition,revascularisation (inosculation+neovascularisation) and organisation (fibrin layer holds the graft in place and this is replaced by postgraft day 7 with fibroblasts)

Correct answer: A. Great Saphenous Vein

The image shows prominent, tortuous, dilated veins(varicosities) on the medial aspect of the leg and thigh, which is the characteristic course of the Great Saphenous Vein (GSV). The dorsum of the foot, at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch, medial aspect of the leg and thigh forms the surface marking of the great saphenous vein. The surface marking for it is marked by joining the following points from foot to thigh: * On the dorsum of the foot, at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch. * On the anterior surface of the medial malleolus. * On the medial border of the tibia at the junction of the upper 2/3rd and lower 1/3rd of the leg. * At the adductor tubercle * Just below the centre of the saphenous opening. Varicose veins are subcutaneous dilated, tortuous veins 3mm or more in diameter. They commonly present with a sensation of dragging pain, heaviness, itching or burning over the affected area or the whole limb, and swelling of the feet. These symptoms increase throughout the day or with prolonged standing and are relieved by elevation or compression hosiery. Risk factors: * Female gender * Increasing age * Increasing body mass and height * Pregnancy * Family history * Smoking * Occupations involving prolonged standing Management of varicose veins
Incompetence Management

  • Endothermal ablation (gold standard treatment for varicose veins). It includes:

  • Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)
  • Trendelenburg procedure (Flush Ligation of Saphenofemoral Junction (SFJ) after ligation of 6 tributaries) ± stripping (retrogradely up to the knee, to prevent saphenous nerve injury.)

  • Flush ligation of SPJ (Stripping is not done to prevent sural nerve injury)

  • Endothermal ablation:

  • Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)
New treatment modalities: * Foam sclerotherapy - The Tessari method is a widely used method to prepare foam for sclerotherapy. Sclerosant: air ratio taken is 1:3 or 1:4. * Endovenous glue therapy - endoluminal application of cyanoacrylate adhesive  * TriVex - Transilluminated powered phlebectomy Other options: Option B: The small saphenous vein courses from the lateral of the dorsal venous arch to the center of popliteal fossa. Option C: The femoral vein runs upward in the thigh, accompanying the femoral artery within the femoral sheath and it is a deep vein. Option D: Perforators: Connect superficial veins to deep veins. They may become incompetent, causing varicose veins, but the main visible dilated vein here is the GSV.

text: 17. Which of the following veins is involved in esophageal varices?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Left gastric vein

Varices of the lower end of the esophagus receive their portal venous supply mainly from the left gastric vein, which communicates with the veins of the lower esophagus. Therefore, the vein involved in esophageal varices is the left gastric vein. It is a tributary of the portal vein. In portal hypertension,when the pressure in the portal vein increases, the submucosal veins of the proximal stomach and distal esophagus which receive portal flow from the short gastric veins and the left gastric vein can become dilated, forming varices with a high risk of hemorrhage. Esophageal variceal bleeding is a complication of portal hypertension, most commonly due to cirrhosis. Endoscopic intervention is the mainstay of treatment for bleeding esophageal varices. The two most commonly used techniques are endoscopic band ligation (EVL), where rubber bands are applied to the base of the varix, and endoscopic sclerotherapy, which involves injecting a sclerosant into or around the varix. Endoscopy is usually performed in a head-down position with good suction and visualization using a double-channel endoscope and power washers. Once the bleeding site is identified, treatment is focused only on the active varices. Both EVL and sclerotherapy effectively control bleeding, but EVL is preferred as it significantly reduces the risk of rebleeding, and a single session is often sufficient. The protocol for the management of variceal bleeding involves the following: TIPSS or Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Stent Shunt placement involves the placement of a shunt to redirect blood flow and reduce portal pressure. It is very effective but requires analgesia, sedation, and fluoroscopic guidance. It is done if medical and endoscopic measures fail to control bleeding. Pearl PF2179: Causes of Portal Hypertension

text: 18. A person presented with a history of road traffic accident (RTA) and a crush wound in the thigh. He came to the doctor the next day. On examination, the wound appeared black with crepitus. What is the most likely organism involved?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Clostridium perfringens

The given clinical scenario of a present with blackish colored wound with crepitus following a extensive wound injury (crush injury) is highly suggestive of gas gangrene/ clostridial myonecrosis, which is caused by Clostridium perfringens. Military wounds and trauma which cause extensive tissue damage provide an ideal environment for gas gangrene. C.perfringens is gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-bearing bacilli present in nature, especially in soil and faeces. Patients who are immunocompromised, diabetic, or have malignant disease are also at greater risk. The usual incubation period is <24 hours of injury. Gas gangrene wound infections are associated with severe local wound pain and crepitus (gas in the tissues). The wound produces a thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate, in which Gram staining will reveal bacteria. Edema and spreading gangrene occur due to the release of collagenase, hyaluronidase, other proteases, and alpha-toxin. Early systemic complications like circulatory collapse and organ failure can occur without adequate treatment. Management includes high doses of intravenous penicillin and aggressive debridement of affected tissues. Amputations should be performed under antibiotic prophylaxis. Other options: Option A: C. tetani is an anaerobic, terminal spore-bearing, Gram-positive bacterium. It causes tetanus following implantation into tissues or a wound, and it usually presents with spasms. Option B: C. difficile, a gram-positive anaerobic bacillus, causes Clostridioides (formerly Clostridium) difficile infection (CDI) after ingestion of spores of the organism. The more severe form of the condition is known as pseudomembranous colitis (PMC). It is most commonly associated with prolonged antimicrobial use which interferes with the commensal colonic microflora. The most commonly implicated antibiotics are cephalosporins, ampicillin, and clindamycin. Option C: C. botulinum causes botulism, a paralytic disease that usually presents as a form of food poisoning.

text: 19. A 7-year-old male child weighing 40 kg presents with thermal burns involving 22% of the total body surface area. What is the approximate amount of fluid that should be administered in the first 8 hours of resuscitation?
expl:
Correct answer: D. 1,320 mL

The amount of fluid that needs to be administered in the first 8 hours in this case is 1,320 mL Hartmann’s solution or Ringer’s lactate is the crystalloid most commonly used for burn resuscitation, as it closely matches the osmolality of plasma. It is cheaper compared to colloid solutions and is effective in maintaining intravascular volume. The modified Parkland formula is the standard method for fluid calculation, expressed as:  * TBSA% burn × weight (kg) × 3 = Volume in mL. * substituiting the given values, 22 ✖️ 3 ✖️ 40 = 2,640 mL. To complete 24-hour resuscitation, half (1,320 mL) of this is given in the first 8 hours and the other half over the remaining 16 hours. Urine output serves as a reliable endpoint to guide resuscitation and should be maintained at 0.5–1.0 mL/kg/hour in children. Urine output greater than 2 mL/kg/hour indicates the need to reduce the infusion rate.  Resuscitation fluids in burn patients must always be commenced from the time of burn injury, and if there is any delay, the deficit should be compensated. Intravenous fluid therapy is indicated for adults with burns exceeding 15% of total body surface area (TBSA) and for children with burns exceeding 10% TBSA. In children, maintenance fluids are required in addition to resuscitation fluids, usually in the form of dextrose–saline. The regimen is weight-based: * 100 mL/kg for 24 hours for the first 10 kg * 50 mL/kg for the next 10 kg * 20 mL/kg for each kilogram above 20 kg body weight Pearl PF2125: Burns – Formulae for Fluid Calculation(Updated according to ATLS 10th edition 2018 guidelines) Parkland’s formula gives the total fluid requirement for 24hours. Half of this volume is infused in the first 8 hours, and the remaining half is infused in the next 16 hours. This formula is recommended for those who have sustained large deep partial-thickness or full-thickness burns that cover more than 20% of the TBSA in adults and more than 10% in children.  Formulas provide a starting target rate; Subsequently, the amount of fluid provided should be adjusted based on urine output.
Category of burn Age Amount of Ringer’s Lactate given for 24 hours (ml) Target urine output (ml/kg/hour)
2nd/3rd-degree burns Adults  2 x weight in kgs x % TBSA 0.5
<14 years 3 x weight in kgs x % TBSA 1
< 1 year or <30kgs 3 x weight in kgs x % TBSA + 5% dextrose on a maintenance rate 1
4th-degree burns / Electrical burns All ages 4 x weight in kgs x % TBSA 1-1.5 (until urine clears)
Dextrose maintenance: * 100 ml/ kg in 24 hours for 10 kg * 50 ml/kg for next 10 kg * 20 ml/kg for every kg after 20 kg Evan’s formula is used for normal saline. For the first 24 hours: * Amount of NS administered = weight in kgs x % TBSA * Amount of colloid administered = weight in kgs x % TBSA * 5% Dextrose administered= 2000 ml After 24 hours, the amount of NS and colloid administered is half. 2000 ml of dextrose is maintained. Muir and Barclay’s formula for colloids: * 1 portion of colloid = (weight in kgs x % TBSA)/2 * 6 portions of colloid are administered over 36 hours

text: 20. A 16-year-old female presents with multiple episodes of abdominal pain and a history of passing blood in stools. On examination, she has dark pigmented spots on her lips and oral mucosa. Endoscopy reveals multiple hamartomatous polyps in the small intestine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: B. Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome

The clinical scenario of passage of blood in stools with mucocutaneous pigmentation (dark pigmented spots on lips and oral mucosa) and the presence of hamartomatous polyps in the small intestines in endoscopy is highly suggestive of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by multiple gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps and mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation. Due to germline heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the gene STK11. The hyperpigmentation typically appears as dark blue to brown macules on the lips, nostrils, buccal mucosa, palmar surfaces of the hands, genitalia, and perianal region.  Complications: * Intussusception * Risk for gastric and small intestinal cancers, and subsequently for colon, pancreatic, breast, lung, ovarian, and uterine cancers. Treatment of Peutz–Jeghers syndrome mainly involves resection of polyps when there is heavy, persistent, or recurrent bleeding, or if intussusception develops. Polyps may be removed surgically by enterotomy or laparotomy, or endoscopically using a colonoscope introduced via an enterotomy. In severe cases where large segments of the small intestine are involved, resection of the affected portion may be required. Other options: Option A: Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP) is an inherited disorder presenting with numerous colorectal adenomatous polyps. It is an autosomal dominant disease caused by mutations in the APC gene, which is a regulator in the Wnt signaling pathway. At least 100 polyps are required to make a diagnosis of FAP.  Option C: Juvenile polyposis (JPS) is an autosomal dominant inherited condition that presents with hamartomatous polyps due to mutations in the BMPR1A, SMAD4 or ENG genes. Pigmentation is not present. Option D: Cowden disease is characterised by polyps of stomach or colon with mucocutaneous lesions, thyroid adenomas and goitre, fibroadenomas and fibrocystic disease of the breast, Uterine leiomyomas, macrocephaly. Pearl PF0932: Peutz–Jeghers Syndrome * Autosomal-dominant disease * Germline defects in the tumor suppressor serine-threonine kinase 11 (STK11) gene on chromosome 19. Features: * Hyperpigmentation of the buccal mucosa, lips, and digits * Hamartomatous polyps of the intestinal tract * Increased (2% to 10%) risk for cancer of the intestinal tract, with cancers reported throughout the intestinal tract, from the stomach to the rectum. * Increased risk for extraintestinal malig­nant neoplasms, including cancer of the breast, ovary, cervix, fallopian tubes, thyroid, lung, gallbladder, bile ducts, pancreas, and testicles. Screening: Baseline colonoscopy and upper endoscopy at age 20 years, followed by annual flexible sigmoidoscopy thereafter. Pearl PF0293: Features of Familial Adenomatous Polyposis Gastrointestinal manifestations: * Colon and rectum: Multiple adenomatous polyp usually >100 * Gastric and duodenal polyps are present in 50% cases. * Gastric polyp: fundal gland polyp, gastric adenoma. * Duodenal polyp usually in the ampullary region: Adenomatous and premalignant Extraintestinal manifestations * Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) seen in 75% of cases; it is detected by indirect ophthalmoscopy. * Epidermoid cysts * Desmoid tumors in the abdomen * Osteoma: In the skull, mandible, and tibia * Brain tumors * Tumors of the thyroid, adrenal, liver, pancreas, gallbladder, and bile duct

text: 21. A patient presents with a rapidly progressing, edged-out ulcer on the lateral aspect of the nasal fold, below the eye. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Squamous Cell Carcinoma

The clinical description of a rapidly progressing, edged-out ulcer on a sun-exposed site like the lateral nasal fold is characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma(SCC). SCC is a malignant tumour of keratinising cells of the epidermis or its appendages. It arises from the stratum basalis of the epidermis and is the second most common skin cancer. The primary risk factor and driving force for the development of this common cancer is UV exposure. Variants of SCC include, Bowen's disease and Erythroplasia of Queyrat. It initially presents as smooth nodular, verrucous, papillomatous lesions. All these lesions later ulcerate and have a characteristic everted edge and are surrounded by inflamed, indurated skin. When a SCC appears in a scar it is known as a Marjolin’s ulcer. Surgical excision is the treatment of choice SCC. It provides both histological confirmation and complete clearance. The excision margins depend on tumor size: * lesions <2 cm require a 4-mm margin, * while those >2 cm need a 1-cm margin. Other options: Option B: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is a slow-growing, locally invasive malignant tumor that originates from pluripotential epithelial cells of the basal epidermis and hair follicles, typically involving pilosebaceous skin. Option C: Malignant Melanoma is a malignancy of melanocytes and may develop in the skin, mucous membranes, retina, or leptomeninges. There are four common macroscopic variants of malignant melanoma. It doesn’t present as an edged-out ulcer. Option D: Keratoacanthoma presents with a reddish papule with a horny crust in the centre. It is a rapidly evolving tumour of the skin considered as a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.

text: 22. A 30-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a history of penetrating chest trauma. On examination, breath sounds are absent on the right side of the chest, and there is severe tracheal deviation. What is the immediate step in management?

options.A: Wide-bore needle insertion in the 2nd intercostal space

expl:
Correct answer: B. Needle decompression at 5th intercostal space

The given clinical presentsation of tracheal deviation and absent breath sounds on right side on auscultation following a penetrating chest trauma is highly suggestive of tension pneumothorax. Immediate management is done with needle decompression or needle thoracostomy i.e. insertion of a wide-bore needle in the 5th ICS anterior to the midaxillary line. Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening emergency when air leaks from the lungs into the pleural cavity and cannot escape. This leads to compression of the lung field with mediastinal shift and collapse of lung parenchyma. This can be diagnosed clinically with high index of suspicion and immediate decompression with wide bore needle in the 5th intercostal space should be done.  The most common causes of a tension pneumothorax are: * Penetrating chest trauma. * Blunt chest trauma leading to a parenchymal lung injury and a persistent air leak. * Iatrogenic lung injury, such as that caused by central venipuncture. * Mechanical positive-pressure ventilation. The clinical presentation is dramatic, with the patient appearing increasingly restless, dyspneic, and tachypneic. Physical examination reveals distended neck veins, hyper-resonance, and decreased or absent breath sounds on the affected side.  Current medical practice for the treatment of tension pneumothorax involves immediate decompression. Historically, this was taught as the rapid insertion of a large-bore cannula into the second intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line on the affected side. This was then followed by the insertion of a chest tube through the fifth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line. However, the current recommendation is to perform the initial decompression within the "safe triangle." Definitive management - tube thoracostomy or chest tube insertion in the 5th ICS in the triangle of safety. Triangle of safety: The boundaries are  * Anteriorly - lateral border of the pectoralis major * Posteriorly- latissimus dorsi * Inferiorly- a line perpendicular to the nipple going to the back For pediatric patients, needle decompression is done at the midclavicular line in the 2nd intercostal space. text: 23. A child is rescued from a major train accident. During triage, the child is found to be stable and can walk, but he has a large laceration on the leg with severe inflammation around the wound. What is the most appropriate triage category for this child?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Yellow

A child with a large laceration on the thigh which is inflamed but is stable, will be classified under the yellow category. The yellow (medium priority) category includes patients who need resuscitation or surgery within 24 hours and have a good chance of survival with prompt treatment. Spinal injuries, along with moderate head injuries, compound fractures, and pelvic fractures, typically fall under this category due to the potential for delayed complications. Triage includes rapid classification of the injured based on their injuries and the chances of survival with prompt medical intervention into four categories- red (high priority), yellow (medium priority), green (low priority) and black (least priority). It provides maximum benefit to the greatest number of injured in a disaster situation. It lessens the burden on medical facilities. text: 24. A patient with untreated hyperthyroidism is scheduled for a total thyroidectomy. Pre-anesthetic check-up (PAC) was not done adequately. Which of the following complications is most likely to occur during surgery?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Arrhythmia

A patient with untreated hyperthyroidism undergoing surgery(thyroidectomy) is at significant risk for a thyroid storm (also known as a thyrotoxic crisis), which usually presents with hypotension, cardiac arrhythmias, hyperpyrexia and other symptoms. Thyroid storm is a rare but severe life-threatening complication of hyperthyroidism induced by the release of excessive thyroid hormones. Causes: * Abrupt cessation of antithyroid medications * Infection * When a thyrotoxic patient has been inadequately prepared for thyroidectomy. * Thyroid or non-thyroid surgery * Trauma in patients with untreated thyrotoxicosis * Amiodarone administration * Exposure to iodinated contrast agents * Following RAI (radioactive iodine) therapy Features: * They present 12–24 hours after surgery with hyperpyrexia and severe dehydration * Cardiovascular: Circulatory collapse, hypotension, palpitations, tachycardia, cardiac arrhythmias, cardiac failure * GI symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice. * Neurological symptoms: restlessness, irritability, delirium, tremor, convulsions, and coma  Treatment: * Supportive measures – rehydration by proper fluid therapy, tepid sponging, cooling blankets * Thionamides like Propylthiouracil (PTU), methimazole or carbimazole are used as they inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis. Propylthiouracil blocks the peripheral conversion of thyroxine (T4) into the more active triiodothyronine (T3) and serves as the preferred drug in thyroid storm. However, the risk for severe liver injury and acute liver failure associated with PTU therapy makes either carbimazole or methimazole the first choice thionamides in patients with deranged liver function tests. * Lugol’s iodide is given one hour after intake of thionamides. They inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis by Wolff- Chaikoff effect. Large doses of iodide inhibit the organic binding of the iodide and hence decrease thyroid hormone synthesis. * Propranolol is used to reduce tachycardia and other adrenergic manifestations. It also reduces the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3. * Glucocorticoids – reduce the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 and controls the shock.  * Digoxin, cardiac monitoring is crucial. Pearl PF1414: Thyroid storm / Thyrotoxic crisis: It is an emergency caused by an acute exacerbation of hyperthyroidism.  Precipitating factors: * Abrupt cessation of antithyroid medications * Infection * When a thyrotoxic patient has been inadequately prepared for thyroidectomy. * Thyroid or non-thyroid surgery * Trauma in patients with untreated thyrotoxicosis * Amiodarone administration or exposure to iodinated contrast agents * Following RAI therapy. Clinical features: * Fever * Central nervous system agitation or depression * Cardiovascular and GI dysfunction, including hepatic failure Treatment of thyroid storm:

text: 25. A patient with abdominal injury following a road traffic accident (RTA) has lost approximately 200 mL of blood. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, but the heart rate is elevated. What should be the next step in management?
expl:
Correct answer: C. eFAST

In a trauma patient with abdominal injury, tachycardia along with loss of 200mL blood, early shock should be suspected. Therefore, the immediate step is to evaluate for ongoing intra-abdominal bleeding by eFAST (extended-focused assessment with sonography for trauma) A quick diagnostic modality called eFAST is used to evaluate patients who may have thoracoabdominal injuries. It is used to determine whether free fluid is present in the abdominal cavity, thoracic cavity, and pericardium. It takes two to four minutes.  More than 100 mL of free fluid can be detected by eFAST. The standard order of evaluation is: * Pericardial cavity - subxiphoid * Flank of right side - perihepatic view or Morison's pouch * Flank of left side - perisplenic view * Pelvic cavity - retrovesical views * Right anterior thoracic * Left anterior thoracic Disadvantages: * It is not reliable in detecting less than 100 mL of free blood. * Hollow viscus injuries cannot be accurately identified. * Unreliable in penetrating trauma. * Subjective findings. * Unreliable for retroperitoneal injuries If there is a doubt, eFAST may be repeated or supplemented with other investigations. Other options: Option A: Wait and watch cannot be done, as ongoing internal bleeding may be missed and may lead to shock. Option B: Chest X-ray, not the first-line when abdominal trauma with shock is suspected. Useful for chest injuries, pneumothorax. Option D: USG abdomen is time-consuming, as it is not done as a bedside assessment.

text: 26. A patient presents with a severe headache and neck stiffness. There is no history of fever. The CT brain taken is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Subarachnoid haemorrhage

The given clinical scenario of an afebrile patient with a severe headache, neck stiffness with CT head showing hyperdense areas in the basal cisterns and sulci, is highly suggestive of Subarachnoid haemorrhage. Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is the bleeding into the subarachnoid space, which is the area between the arachnoid membrane and the pia mater surrounding the brain. It usually occurs due to bleeding from a ruptured aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation. Most of the ruptured aneurysms are located at the circle of Willis. Patients present with a sudden and severe headache referred to as thunderclap headache, which may be associated with vomiting, decreased consciousness, and seizures. Neck stiffness and photophobia may develop after a few hours. Non-contrast CT scan is the imaging modality of choice if done within 12 hours. It shows an increased density of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) spaces. A lumbar puncture should be done if there is a strong suspicion of SAH but negative CT findings. It is ideally done 12 hours later. This allows for red blood cell lysis to occur and bilirubin to be detected in the CSF. Other options: Option A: Bacterial meningitis is characterised by high fever, neck stiffness, and positive Brudzinski's sign.  Option B: Subdural haemorrhage is often due to the rupture of bridging veins that crosses the subdural space. In subdural hemorrhage, the CT shows crescentic opacity.  Option D: Extradural haemorrhage is mostly due to the rupture of the middle meningeal artery. Since the dura matter tends to adhere to the skull, the hemorrhage is seen in CT as a biconvex dense area. They usually do not cross cranial sutures. Pearl PF2181: Types of Intracranial Hemorrhage 1. Extradural hemorrhage/epidural hematoma (EDH) * Source: Arterial - middle meningeal artery (m/c) * Cause: Trauma - fracture of the squamous part of the temporal bone * Lens or lentiform shaped opacity * Presence of a characteristic lucid interval * Treatment: Surgical evacuation of large/rapidly evolving EDH   2. Acute subdural hemorrhage (SDH) * Source: Venous - bridging veins * Cause: Trauma * Common in old age, alcoholics, patients on anticoagulants, shaken baby syndrome (a form of child abuse seen in infants and toddlers) * Clinical features: Acute SDH may be associated with a lucid interval; chronic SDH is associated with drowsiness, headache * CT findings: Crescent opacity * Treatment: May resolve spontaneously or require surgical drainage   3. Acute on chronic SDH * Source: Venous - bridging veins * Cause: Usually, trivial trauma in old age or patients on anticoagulants * Crescent clots * Presence of a history of headache, confusion, and being prone to falls   4. Subarachnoid hemorrhage * Source: Arterial * Causes: Trauma (most common), berry aneurysm (2nd most common) * M/c sites: Terminal ICA, MCA bifurcation, top of basilar artery * Clinical features: Characteristic thunderclap headache * CSF: Xanthochromia * Hyperdensity in the subarachnoid space * Treatment: Early repair by clipping/coiling of berry aneurysm. Nimodipine and IV fluids with monitoring to prevent vasospasm.   5. Intra-parenchymal hemorrhage * Most common type of intracranial hemorrhage * Cause: Hypertension (most common cause) * Hyperdensity within the brain parenchyma * Site: Putamen of the basal ganglia (most common) * Treatment: Correction of any identified coagulopathy by infusing prothrombin complex concentrates, FFP, or fresh platelets as required; surgical evacuation for cerebellar hematoma >3 cm in size

text: 27. A patient presents with a history of severe head injury following a road traffic accident (RTA) and a poor Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score. CT scan of the brain appears normal, but the patient dies within a few hours. Brain biopsy shows multiple punctate hemorrhages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: A. Diffuse axonal injury

The clinical vignette of an initially poor GCS score and later death following a high-energy accident(RTA) with a normal CT scan and brain biopsy showing multiple haemorrhages is suggestive of diffuse axonal injury. Diffuse axonal injury is a type of primary brain injury commonly associated with high-energy accidents. It is caused by damage to axons throughout the brain due to rotational acceleration followed by deceleration. There is disruption and shearing of axons leading to microhemorrhages. Most commonly, it occurs in automobile accidents. Patients are usually unconscious from the moment of impact and remain the same until death. The immunohistochemistry marker with beta-amyloid precursor protein is considered to be the most reliable indicator of axon damage. Seen earliest at 2-3 hours.   The histological features :  Initially, there will be dilation of the axons, followed by the formation of club-shaped structures known as retraction balls. These retraction balls later decrease in number over 2-3 weeks, followed by microglial cell proliferation. Later in the course, astrocytosis and demyelination will be observed. Diffuse axonal injury is characterized by multiple focal lesions with a characteristic distribution: * CT may be normal. * MRI is the modality of choice for assessing suspected diffuse axonal injury even in patients with entirely normal CT of the brain. It detects the micro-bleeds within the brain. Other options: Option B: Cerebral contusion occurs due to traumatic brain injury, at the sites that come in direct contact with the skull. Imaging may show microhemorrhages and edema. Usually, no treatment is required. Option C: Subdural hemorrhage is caused by rupture of cerebral bridging veins. In subdural hemorrhage, the CT shows crescentic opacity.  The image below shows a CT of a subdural hemorrhage. Option D: Extradural hemorrhage is mostly due to the rupture of the middle meningeal artery. Since the dura mater tends to adhere to the skull, the hemorrhage is seen in CT as a biconvex dense area. They are confined by cranial sutures. The image below shows a CT of an extradural hemorrhage. Pearl PF1100: Diffuse Axonal Injury
Features of diffuse axonal injury
Mechanism Primarily a non-impact rotational acceleration-decceleration injury (this leads to deformation of the axons by stretching them)
Pathology

Changes in permeability of the axolemma

Axonal swelling

Intracellular calcium accumulation

Proteolysis

However, in between the contractions, peristalsis remains normal. Pathologically, there is marked hypertrophy of the circular muscles. text: 6. An old person presented with an ulcer on the medial canthus with pearly and rolled margins. Histopathology shows nesting cells with peripheral palisading patterns. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Basal cell carcinoma

This patient, presenting with an ulcer on the medial canthus with pearly, rolled margins, and histopathology revealing nesting cells with peripheral palisading, is most likely diagnosed with basal cell carcinoma. Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is a slow-growing, locally invasive, malignant tumour of epithelial cells arising from the basal epidermis. It erodes deeply into local tissues, including cartilage and bones, causing extensive local destruction, hence the name rodent ulcer. It does not spread through blood or lymphatics.  The strongest risk factor for developing basal cell carcinoma is exposure to UV radiation. Therefore it occurs on the sun-exposed areas of the skin, most commonly on the nose and face. Most common site is the inner canthus of eye. They present as small, slowly growing pearly nodules, often with tortuous telangiectatic vessels on their surface, rolled borders, and a central crust (nodular BCC). The occasional presence of melanin in this variant of nodular BCC (pigmented BCC) may lead to confusion with melanoma. BCC can be divided into generalized and localized. Generalized can be further divided into superficial or infiltrative. The localized can be further divided into * Nodular and nodulocystic- account for the majority of BCC * Cystic * Pigmented * Naevoid. The characteristic biopsy finding of BCC is the presence of ovoid cells in nests and palisading of the peripheral cells of the nests. Treatment of BCC includes excision of the lesion or Moh's micrographic surgery. Other Options: Option A: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the malignancy of the keratinizing cells of the epidermis. It is associated with exposure to UV radiation and chronic inflammation (chronic sinus tracts, pre-existing scars, osteomyelitis, and burns). Classically, it appears as a scaly or ulcerated papule or plaque that can bleed with minimal trauma, but the pain is rare. Histologically, SCC is characterized by the proliferation of atypical squamous cells with the formation of horn pearls or keratin pearls. Option B: Marjolin's ulcer is a rare and aggressive form of squamous cell carcinoma that grows from burns, scars, or poorly healing wounds.  The image below shows a Marjolin's ulcer in a burn scar. Option D: Naevus is a common benign neoplasm caused by mutations in the RAS signalling pathway, characterized by aggregates of melanocytes at the dermis or the dermo-epidermal junction. It has various types, such as congenital naevus, blue naevus, Spitz naevus, halo naevus, and dysplastic naevus. It can get transformed into malignant melanoma and the features suggestive of malignant transformation are a change in size, shape, color, thickness, satellite lesions, and tingling/ itching/serosanguinous discharge.

options.A: It is seen in sites of chronic wounds or scars.
options.C: It can progress to squamous cell carcinoma.

Correct answer: B. Whipple's procedure

The image shows the Whipple procedure which is a complex surgery done for carcinomas involving the head of the pancreas. It is done only in cases when: * The entire duodenum has to be removed e.g. in familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) * Tumor encroaches in the first part of the duodenum, or stomach * A clear resection margin is not achieved by PPPD The following structures are removed during Whipple’s procedure: * Distal stomach * Duodenum * Proximal jejunum * Head of the pancreas * Gallbladder * Common bile duct (CBD) * Regional lymphatics The reconstruction following Whipple’s procedure or pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy involves anastomosis in the following order: Pancreati­cojejunostomy               ↓ Choledochojejunostomy               ↓ Gastrojejunostomy This is controversial since there is a difference in the reconstruction procedures mentioned in standard textbooks: Bailey and Love, 27th edition (Pg no: 1236) - Pancreaticojejunostomy + choledochojejunostomy + duodenojejunostomy  Schwatrz, 11th edition (Pg no: 1493) - Pancreaticojejunostomy + choledochojejunostomy + gastrojejunostomy/duodenojejunostomy Sabiston, 20th edition (Pg no: 1546) - Pancreaticojejunostomy + hepaticojejunostomy + duodenojejunostomy Pearl PF0333: Resection and Hybrid Surgical Procedures for Chronic Pancreatitis Beger’s procedure: Duodenum-preserving pancreatic head resection (DPPHR) * The completed resection after transection of the pancreatic neck and subtotal removal of the pancreatic head, with preservation of the distal common bile duct and duodenum (Marked A). * Completion of the reconstruction of the anastomosis to the distal pancreas and to the proximal pancreatic rim by the same Roux limb of the jejunum. Frey’s procedure: * The local resection of the pancreatic head with longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy (LR-LPJ) provides complete decompression of the entire pancreatic ductal system. Reconstruction is performed with a side-to-side Roux-en-Y pancreaticojejunostomy. Warren’s modification of Beger’s procedure: Berne modification (Beger + Frey) involves excavation of the central portion of the head without formal division of the neck. text: 11. A 30-year-old lactating mother presents with pain in her left breast and fever. On examination of the affected side, there is localized erythema, warmth, point tenderness,fluctuation test is positive. There is mild axillary lymphadenopathy on the affected side and contralateral breast is normal.What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Breast abscess

The given case scenario points towards a diagnosis of breast abscess. The latest guidelines for the management of breast abscess specify that multiple aspirations under antibiotic cover should be attempted before an incision and drainage is done. This often allows resolution without the need for an incision scar and also allows the patient to continue breastfeeding. Mastitis occurs due to the growth of staphylococcus or streptococcus due to breast milk stasis. This occurs secondary to blockage of lactiferous duct or due to incomplete emptying of breast milk or due to retracted nipple. Overgrowth of these bacteria results in the development of breast abscess. It is commoner in new mothers at the beginning of lactation who are inexperienced with breastfeeding or during weaning when nipple trauma occurs due to the infant's growing teeth.  Signs and symptoms of this condition involve: * Fever and malaise * Localized pain and tenderness  * Redness and swelling of the affected breast * Fluctuation test positive due to pus in the abscess. It is a late sign. The initial treatment should involve providing pain relief with analgesics. The abscess should then be localized preferably under USG guidance and percutaneous aspiration carried out. The pus should be sent for microbiological examination to find the organism and antibiotic sensitivity. Repeated aspirations may be carried out under antibiotics cover if needed. In some conditions mentioned below, the breast abscess may be unresponsive to repeated aspirations and antibiotic cover. In such cases, incision and drainage is performed. The conditions include: * Presence of thick pus * Bacteria resistant to antibiotics * If just superficial part has been aspirated in the presence of a multiloculated abscess * A non-healing breast abscess due to tuberculosis of breast or Inflammatory carcinoma of the breast, or an immunocompromised host. text: 13. A 36-year-old man presents with dull aching epigastric pain. He gives a history of acute abdominal pain following a binge of alcohol 5 weeks back which was managed conservatively. Correct answer: A. Pancreatic pseudocyst

The given clinical scenario with a history of acute pancreatitis, epigastric mass, and the CT image showing a cyst is suggestive of pancreatic pseudocyst. The capsule of the cyst is composed of collagen and granulation tissue, and it is not lined by epithelium. Hence, it is called a pseudocyst. Pseudocysts are post-inflammatory cysts that arise following an attack of mild acute pancreatitis. Formation of a pseudocyst requires 4 weeks or more from the onset of acute pancreatitis. They are also the most common complication of chronic pancreatitis. Pseudocysts are usually solitary and most commonly seen in the lesser omental sac. The most common artery involved is the splenic artery.  Complications of pancreatic pseudocyst include: * Abscess * Systemic sepsis * GI bleeding * Fistula formation * Peritonitis * Obstructive jaundice * Bowel obstruction * Hemorrhage into the cyst * Hemoperitoneum Pancreatic pseudo­cysts can be distinguished from cystic neoplasms by having high amylase levels and absence of mucin and low serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels.

Correct answer: C. Right side undescended testis and left sided ectopic testis

Since the right testis is found in the inguinal canal which is along the normal path of descent it is called an undescended testis, while the left testis lies in the perineum which is an ectopic site of descent and is called an ectopic testis. Cryptorchidism is the failure of the descent of the intra-abdominal testes into the scrotal sac.  It is the most common congenital abnormality of the genitourinary tract. The testes can arrest anywhere during descent, and the most common site is the inguinal region. Phases of testicular descent: * Transabdominal phase: Testes come to lie in the lower abdomen or pelvis, and this descent is regulated by Mullerian-inhibiting substances. * Inguinoscrotal phase: Testes descend along the inguinal canal and reach the scrotal sac, and this phase of the descent is regulated by androgen-induced calcitonin gene-related peptide from the genitofemoral nerve. Ectopic testis is can be present anywhere along the normal path of descent from the abdomen to the scrotum. Other ectopic sites outside the normal path includes:  * Femoral triangle * The root of the penis * Perineum. An ectopic testis is usually treated with orchidopexy. The image below shows the possible ectopic sites of the testes: A retractile testis is a normally developed and descended testis that retracts back into the inguinal canal due to hyper reflexive cremasteric muscle contraction. Therefore any stimulation of the skin of the scrotum or thigh causes the testis to ascend and temporarily disappear into the inguinal canal. When the cremaster relaxes, the testis reappears in the scrotum. The scrotum of a boy with such a retractile testis is normal (normal rugosity is seen). Retractile testes require no treatment  Note: Chair test helps to differentiate retractile testis from ectopic testis because both of them describe a condition, wherein the testis lies in an abnormal position.  Chair Test:  Here, The young patient is asked to sit on a chair hugging his knees to his chest. This maneuver helps the retractile testis to get pushed down back to the bottom of the scrotum. By this test retractile testis can be differentiated from the ectopic testis.

text: 20. A 45-year-old alcoholic with a history of binge drinking presents with an episode of vomiting bright red blood. His vitals are stable. What is the probable diagnosis?
expl:
Correct answer: C. Mallory Weiss Tear

The most probable diagnosis for the above-mentioned clinical presentation is Mallory Weiss tear . Mallory Weiss Syndrome is due to a longitudinal tear in mucosa or submucosa of the gastroesophageal junction. It is a common cause of upper gastrointestinal bleeding due to the presence of longitudinal superficial mucosal lacerations (Mallory-Weiss tears). The left gastric artery is the most common vessel to bleed. It mainly occurs in patients with repetitive forceful retching and vomiting and is associated with heavy alcohol intake. The presence of portal hypertension with oesophagal varices and hiatal hernia may aggravate the condition. The investigation of choice is endoscopy. Management of Mallory Weiss tear is conservative, as it usually is self-limiting. Endoscopic electrocoagulation or sclerosant therapy is done in some cases. Angiographic embolization or high gastrotomy is necessary only in rare cases that don't respond to conservative management. Boerhaave syndrome is characterized by a tear in the lower third of the oesophagus which occurs when a person vomits against a closed glottis, causing a leak into the mediastinum, pleural cavity and peritoneum. Here all layers are involved. The patients initially present with severe chest pain, tachypnea, and shock. Clinical features include Mackler's triad * Retching * Chest pain * Subcutaneous emphysema This catastrophic event produces severe mediastinitis(deranged vitals tachypnea, tachycardia, fever, and hypotension) and generally requires surgical intervention.

text: 33. A 77-year-old man presented with worsening hip and back pain. He also reports weight loss and loss of appetite. The X-ray revealed the given lesions. His PSA levels are elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis here?
expl:
Correct answer: D. Prostate cancer

Blastic lesions on X-Ray along with elevated PSA levels, loss of weight, and loss of appetite are suggestive of prostatic carcinoma with metastasis to bones. Carcinoma of the prostate: It is the most common malignant tumor in men over the age of 65 years  They may range from indolent lesions that cause no harm to aggressive metastatic tumors. Most cancers are clinically silent and are detected on routine rectal examination or PSA measurements. Grossly, malignant tissue is gritty and firm in consistency (in contrast to the spongy appearance of benign tissue) and thus more readily palpable on digital rectal examination. They usually arise in the peripheral zone of the gland. Prostate carcinoma is a type of adenocarcinoma. Therefore, histopathology shows the malignant cells arranged in the form of glands. In contrast to benign glands, malignant glands have tightly packed cells and characteristically lack branching and papillary infoldings. The outer basal cell layer typical of benign glands is absent. The cells may show increased nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, nuclear atypia, etc. α-methyl acyl-coenzyme A-racemase (AMACR) is positive and is upregulated in prostate cancer. Local extension most commonly involves the periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicles, and the base of the urinary bladder. Advanced disease may produce ureteral obstruction. Metastasis spreads via the lymphatics to the obturator nodes and the para-aortic nodes. Hematogenous spread occurs chiefly through the bones to the axial skeleton and rarely to the viscera. The bony metastasis is blastic in origin and involves the lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and ribs in the decreasing order of frequency.

text: 7. A patient sustained a crush injury on their right arm as depicted in the given image. He was brought to the hospital and on examination, his arm is pulseless, swollen and dark red. What would be the best way to manage this case?
